title: מבנה הסוגיות – Eruvin
note: חלוקה לסוגיות ולשלבי הדיון שנוצרה בבינה מלאכותית באתר talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).
note_de: KI-erzeugte Einteilung in Sugjot und Argumentationsschritte von talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum); englisch, hebräisch wo dort vorhanden.
note_en: AI-generated sugya sections and argument steps from talmud.dev (Shaun Regenbaum).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a mavoy taller than twenty cubits must be reduced, and Rabbi Yehuda says it does not need reduction. It also rules that a mavoy wider than ten cubits must be reduced, unless it has a tzurat hapetach (doorway shape).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a mavoy taller than twenty cubits must be reduced, and Rabbi Yehuda disputes this.
The Mishnah adds that a mavoy wider than ten cubits must be reduced, unless it has a צורת הפתח (doorway shape).

items.text: Gemara's question on the difference between sukkah and mavoy
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the difference between sukkah and mavoy
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah for sukkah (which is also invalid above twenty cubits) uses the term 'invalid' (pesulah), while for mavoy it prescribes a remedy (takkanta). Two answers are given: first, sukkah is a Torah law so it is invalid, while mavoy is rabbinic so a remedy suffices; second, even for Torah law a remedy could be stated, but sukkah's many details lead to a definitive 'invalid', whereas mavoy's fewer details allow a remedy.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah for sukkah uses 'invalid' (pesulah) while for mavoy it prescribes a remedy (takkanta).
First answer: sukkah is a Torah law so it is invalid, while mavoy is rabbinic so a remedy suffices.
Second answer: even for Torah law a remedy could be stated, but sukkah's many details lead to a definitive 'invalid', whereas mavoy's fewer details allow a remedy.

items.text: Source of the twenty-cubit height limit: the Heikhal and the Ulam
items.text_en: Source of the twenty-cubit height limit: the Heikhal and the Ulam
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that the Sages derived the height limit from the Heikhal's entrance (twenty cubits), while Rabbi Yehuda derived it from the Ulam's entrance (forty cubits). Both interpret the verse 'at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting' differently: the Sages hold that the Heikhal and Ulam have separate sanctity, so the verse refers only to the Heikhal; Rabbi Yehuda holds they share one sanctity, so the verse applies to both.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that the Sages derived the height limit from the Heikhal's entrance, while Rabbi Yehuda derived it from the Ulam's entrance.
A baraita is cited giving the dimensions of the Heikhal's entrance (20 cubits high, 10 wide) and the Ulam's entrance (40 cubits high, 20 wide).

The Gemara explains that both sides interpret the same verse 'at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting'; the Sages hold that the Heikhal and Ulam have separate sanctity, so the verse refers only to the Heikhal.
Rabbi Yehuda holds that the Heikhal and Ulam share one sanctity, so the verse applies to both, allowing a larger entrance.

items.text: Alternative explanation for Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.text_en: Alternative explanation for Rabbi Yehuda's position
items.desc_en: An alternative explanation is offered: even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that the Heikhal and Ulam have separate sanctity, but he derives his leniency from a different verse: 'to the entrance of the Ulam of the House'. The Sages counter that the verse means 'the house that opens to the Ulam' (i.e., the Heikhal), not the Ulam itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that the Heikhal and Ulam have separate sanctity, but he derives his leniency from the verse 'to the entrance of the Ulam of the House'.

The Sages counter that if the verse had said 'to the entrance of the Ulam', it would support Rabbi Yehuda, but since it says 'to the entrance of the Ulam of the House', it means 'the house that opens to the Ulam' (i.e., the Heikhal), not the Ulam itself.

items.text: Objection and resolution: applying Tabernacle verses to the Temple
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: applying Tabernacle verses to the Temple
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'to the entrance of the Ulam of the House' is written about the Tabernacle (Mishkan), not the Temple. It resolves by establishing that the Tabernacle is called 'Mikdash' and the Temple is called 'Mishkan', citing examples: the verse 'I will place My Mishkan among you' refers to the Temple, and the verse about the Kehatites carrying 'the Mikdash' refers to the Tabernacle.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse 'to the entrance of the Ulam of the House' is written about the Tabernacle (Mishkan), not the Temple.

The Gemara resolves that the Tabernacle is called 'Mikdash' and the Temple is called 'Mishkan', citing the verse 'I will place My Mishkan among you' for the Temple and the verse about the Kehatites carrying 'the Mikdash' for the Tabernacle.

The Gemara elaborates that the Temple is called 'Mishkan' from the verse 'I will place My Mishkan among you', and seeks a source for the Tabernacle being called 'Mikdash', citing the verse about the Kehatites.

items.text: Attempt to derive from the gate of the courtyard
items.text_en: Attempt to derive from the gate of the courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that both the Rabbis and Rabbi Yehuda could learn the required height (five amot) and width (twenty amot) from the gate of the courtyard of the Tabernacle, citing verses about the courtyard's dimensions and the curtains.

items.text: Rejection: 'gate of the courtyard' is specific
items.text_en: Rejection: 'gate of the courtyard' is specific
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the derivation because the verse specifies 'gate of the courtyard,' not a general 'gate,' so it cannot serve as a source for a standard gate.

items.text: Alternative explanation: curtains refer to height
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: curtains refer to height
items.desc_en: An alternative answer suggests that the verses about the curtains refer to their height, not width. The Gemara objects that the verse explicitly states 'height five amot,' and resolves that this height was measured from the lip of the altar upward.

items.text: Challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's position in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that if Rabbi Yehuda derives from the Ulam, he should have disputed the Mishnah's rule about width, but he did not. Abaye answers that Rabbi Yehuda does dispute in a baraita.

items.text: Why not dispute in the Mishnah?
items.text_en: Why not dispute in the Mishnah?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yehuda did not dispute in the Mishnah itself, and answers that he disputed regarding height, and the same applies to width.

items.text: Further challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's height leniency
items.text_en: Further challenge: Rabbi Yehuda's height leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that Rabbi Yehuda permits a mavoi up to forty or fifty amot high, but the Ulam was only forty amot. It questions the source for fifty amot, and notes that bar Kappara's hundred amot is hyperbolic.

items.text: Rav Chisda's explanation: a mistaken baraita
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's explanation: a mistaken baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda explains that a baraita misled Rav: it said 'more than the entrance of the Heichal,' and Rav thought the Rabbis learn from the Heichal while Rabbi Yehuda learns from the Ulam, but actually Rabbi Yehuda learns from the 'gate of kings.'

items.text: Objections and resolution regarding doors and form of entrance
items.text_en: Objections and resolution regarding doors and form of entrance
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the Rabbis learn from the Heichal, they would require doors, but the Mishnah allows a lechi or korah. It answers that the Heichal's doors were for privacy. Further, the Heichal had a form of entrance, yet the Mishnah allows it for wide mavoi. The Gemara then recounts that Rav Yehuda taught a baraita before Rav saying 'does not need to reduce,' and Rav corrected him to 'needs to reduce.'

items.text: Incomplete continuation
items.text_en: Incomplete continuation
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new line of reasoning with 'ela me'atah' but the text is cut off, indicating an incomplete argument.

items.text: Initial challenge and response about the height of the Heichal's ledge
items.text_en: Initial challenge and response about the height of the Heichal's ledge
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that a ledge (אֲמַלְתְּרָא) can make a korah valid even above twenty cubits, citing a mishnah about five ledges on the Heichal. It then deflects the challenge by suggesting the mishnah refers to the Ulam, and further deflects by noting the Heichal's structure might be like the Ulam.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that a ledge (אֲמַלְתְּרָא) can validate a korah above twenty cubits, citing a mishnah about five ledges on the Heichal.
The Gemara deflects the challenge by suggesting the mishnah about ledges might refer to the Ulam, not the Heichal.
The Gemara further objects that the Heichal's structure might be like the Ulam, so the challenge remains.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a ledge's effect
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a ledge's effect
items.desc_en: Rav, via Rabbi Ila'a, rules that a korah four handbreadths wide is valid even if not thick, and if it has a ledge, it is valid even above twenty cubits without needing to reduce the height.

sub.desc_en: Rav, via Rabbi Ila'a, rules that a korah four handbreadths wide is valid even if not thick, and if it has a ledge (אמלתרא), it is valid even above twenty cubits without needing to reduce the height.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita and Rav's response
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita and Rav's response
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef notes a baraita that contradicts Rav's ruling, and Abaye points out that the baraita was taught by Rav's own son. Rav responds that contradictions between baraitot are common, and this is just a dispute among Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rav's ruling by noting that the baraita about the lintel (אמלתרא) is a Mishnah, and asks who taught it.
Abaye objects that the baraita was taught by Rav's own son, Chama bar Rabba bar Avuha, so it should be a difficulty for Rav.
Rav responds that contradictions between baraitot are common, and this is just a dispute among Tannaim, so his ruling stands.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution and the need for two disputes
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution and the need for two disputes
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita's mention of the Heichal's height is merely a sign, not a limit. He then explains why both the dispute about sukkah and mavoy are necessary, as each case has unique reasoning.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by asserting that the baraita's mention of the Heichal's height is merely a sign (סִימָנָא בְּעָלְמָא), not a halachic limit, and that the Rabbis' requirement for a korah is for recognition (הֶיכֵּרָא).

The Gemara questions: if Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak does not accept Rabbah's reasoning about sukkah (that above 20 amot the eye does not dominate), then his resolution stands; but if he does accept it, then both sukkah and mavoy disputes are about recognition, so why are two disputes needed?
The Gemara asks: since even regarding sukkah the dispute is about recognition, why do we need two separate disputes (sukkah and mavoy)?

Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that both disputes are necessary (צְרִיכָא): each case has unique reasoning that would prevent deriving one from the other, so both are needed to fully establish the positions of Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

items.text: Definitions of אֲמַלְתְּרָא
items.text_en: Definitions of אֲמַלְתְּרָא
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines אֲמַלְתְּרָא: Rav Chama bar Rabbah bar Avuha says it means 'nests' (קִינֵּי), while in the West they say 'planks of cedar' (פִּסְקֵי דְאַרְזָא). The Gemara explains the reasoning behind each definition and concludes that since it is significant, it makes a sound.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what אֲמַלְתְּרָא means, and cites two definitions: Rav Chama bar Rabbah bar Avuha says 'nests' (קִינֵּי), and in the West they say 'planks of cedar' (פִּסְקֵי דְאַרְזָא).
The Gemara notes that the one who says 'planks of cedar' certainly includes 'nests', but the one who says 'nests' excludes 'planks of cedar'.

The Gemara objects: why does the one who says 'planks of cedar' exclude 'nests'? If the reason is that it has a large surface area (נפיש משכיה), then a sukkah also has a large surface area, yet the Rabbis rule it invalid above twenty cubits.
The Gemara resolves: rather, the reason is that since the plank is significant (חֲשִׁיב), it makes a sound (אִית לֵיהּ קָלָא), distinguishing it from ordinary sukkah roofing.

items.text: Partial korah or s'chach above twenty cubits: Rabbah's ruling
items.text_en: Partial korah or s'chach above twenty cubits: Rabbah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbah rules that if part of the korah or s'chach is within twenty cubits and part above, the mavoy is valid but the sukkah is invalid. The Gemara challenges this, and the discussion involves the concepts of קְלוֹשׁ (thinning) and the need for the korah not to be easily removed by wind, while for sukkah the shade must exceed sunlight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the status of a korah or s'chach that is partially within twenty cubits and partially above.
Rabbah rules that for a mavoy the korah is valid, but for a sukkah the s'chach is invalid.
The Gemara asks why the mavoy is valid, suggesting that the principle of קְלוֹשׁ (thinning) should apply to the sukkah as well.
The Gemara explains that if the s'chach thins, the sunlight would exceed the shade, invalidating the sukkah.
The Gemara objects that for the mavoy, thinning would make the korah easily removed by wind, which should also invalidate it.
The Gemara resolves that the korah is treated as if it were metal skewers (strong), and the s'chach's shade exceeds sunlight by necessity, so both are valid.

items.text: Rava mi'Parzakya and Ravina's explanations for the difference
items.text_en: Rava mi'Parzakya and Ravina's explanations for the difference
items.desc_en: Rava mi'Parzakya explains that a sukkah is for an individual who might forget, while a mavoy is for many who remind each other. Ravina explains that sukkah is biblical and the Sages were stringent, while mavoy is rabbinic and they were not stringent.

sub.desc_en: Rava mi'Parzakya explains that a sukkah is for an individual who might forget the height limit, while a mavoy is for many who remind each other.
Ravina explains that the sukkah is biblical and the Sages were stringent, while the mavoy is rabbinic and they were not stringent.

items.text: Alternative version of Rabbah's ruling and further explanations
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbah's ruling and further explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Matna teaches Rabbah's statement in reverse: the mavoy is invalid and the sukkah is valid. The Gemara again challenges the distinction, and Rava mi'Parzakya and Ravina offer alternative explanations based on individual vs. communal responsibility and the need for reinforcement.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Matna's alternative version
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Matna's alternative version
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Matna teaches Rabbah's statement in reverse: the mavoy is invalid and the sukkah is valid.
The Gemara asks why the sukkah is valid by invoking the principle of 'קלוש' (weakened status), and why the same reasoning does not apply to the mavoy.

The Gemara objects that if the beam is weakened it becomes a beam that can be carried by the wind, and similarly for the sukkah the shade would be greater than the sun, but both are resolved by assuming the materials become like metal spits.

Rava mi'Parzakya explains that a sukkah is for an individual who reminds himself, while a mavoy is for many who rely on each other and forget, as the proverb says: a pot of partners is neither hot nor cold.
Ravina explains that the sukkah, being a Torah law, does not require reinforcement, while the mavoy, being a rabbinic law, requires reinforcement.

items.text: Final rulings on the partial korah/s'chach case
items.text_en: Final rulings on the partial korah/s'chach case
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Ulla rules that both are invalid, while Rava rules that both are valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the final ruling is regarding the partial korah/s'chach case.
Rabbah bar Rav Ulla rules that both the partial korah and the partial s'chach are invalid.
Rava rules that both the partial korah and the partial s'chach are valid.

items.text: Gemara's initial objection and resolution regarding the height of a mavoy
items.text_en: Gemara's initial objection and resolution regarding the height of a mavoy
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a baraisa supporting Rava's view that a mavoy's height limit is based on the Heichal's space of twenty amos. Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects, citing a mishnah that one places the beam from twenty amos and below. The Gemara resolves that 'below' means 'above,' teaching that just as the Heichal's space is twenty amos above, so too the mavoy's space is ten amos below.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by noting that the Mishnah teaches the space of a sukkah and the space of a mavoy.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's citation of a baraisa
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's citation of a baraisa
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a baraisa supporting Rava's view: a mavoy taller than twenty amos must be reduced, because the Heichal's space itself is twenty amos.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi objects by citing a mishnah that one places the beam from the edge of twenty amos and below, implying the limit is twenty amos, not ten.
The Gemara suggests that the mishnah actually means 'above,' but the objector retorts that it explicitly says 'below.'
The Gemara resolves that the mishnah teaches a parallel: just as the Heichal's space is twenty amos above, so too the mavoy's space is ten amos below.

items.text: Abaye's tradition on amah measures for sukkah and mavoy
items.text_en: Abaye's tradition on amah measures for sukkah and mavoy
items.desc_en: Abaye cites Rav Nachman that the amah for sukkah and mavoy is a five-handbreadth measure, while for kilayim it is six. The Gemara questions the practical application for mavoy (height and breach) and sukkah (height and curved wall), and addresses the issue of the four-amah length of a mavoy and the four-amah minimum of a sukkah, offering alternative answers based on Rabbi's opinion or the Rabbis' leniency.

sub.desc_en: Abaye reports in the name of Rav Nachman that the amah for sukkah and mavoy is a five-handbreadth measure, while for kilayim it is six handbreadths.
The Gemara asks to which halakhot of mavoy the five-handbreadth cubit applies, and answers that it applies to the height and the breach of the mavoy.
The Gemara objects that the length of a mavoy is also measured in cubits, and using a small cubit there would be a leniency.
The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman follows the opinion that the length of a mavoy need only be four handbreadths, so the small cubit is not used there.
Alternatively, the Gemara says that the length of a mavoy is indeed four cubits, but Rav Nachman's statement about a five-handbreadth cubit applies only to most cubits, not to the length.
The Gemara asks to which halakhot of sukkah the five-handbreadth cubit applies, and answers that it applies to the height and the curved wall.

The Gemara objects that the minimal length of a sukkah is four cubits, and using a small cubit there would be a leniency, citing Rabbi's statement that a sukkah without four cubits by four cubits is invalid.
The Gemara answers that Rav Nachman follows the Rabbis, who hold that a sukkah is valid even if it only holds one's head, most of his body, and his table, so the four-cubit minimum does not apply.
Alternatively, the Gemara says that Rav Nachman's statement can align even with Rabbi's opinion, because the five-handbreadth cubit applies only to most cubits, not to the length of the sukkah.

items.text: Application of the six-handbreadth amah for kilayim
items.text_en: Application of the six-handbreadth amah for kilayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the six-handbreadth amah for kilayim applies to the laws of a bald spot in a vineyard (karachat hakerem) and the border of a vineyard (mechol hakerem), citing the Mishnah with Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's measurements. It then addresses the issue of vines planted less than four amos apart (retzufim), resolving that the leniency follows the Rabbis' view, or alternatively, Rabbi Shimon's view with 'most amos.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for which halakhot the six-handbreadth amah for kilayim applies, and answers that it applies to the bald spot in a vineyard and the border of a vineyard.
The Gemara cites the Mishnah that records the measurements for a bald spot in a vineyard and the border of a vineyard according to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
The Mishnah defines a bald spot in a vineyard and explains the rule for sowing there based on the measurement.
The Mishnah defines the border of a vineyard and explains the rule for sowing there based on the measurement.
The Gemara objects that the law of vines planted less than four amos apart (retzufim) would be a leniency with large cubits, citing the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Naḥman follows the Rabbis' view that a densely planted vineyard is a vineyard, or alternatively, that he follows Rabbi Shimon but 'most amos' are six handbreadths.

items.text: Rava's alternative tradition on amah measures
items.text_en: Rava's alternative tradition on amah measures
items.desc_en: Rava cites Rav Nachman that all amos are six handbreadths, but some are 'playful' (loose) and others 'sad' (tight). The Gemara raises an objection from a baraisa stating that all amos mentioned by the Sages are six handbreadths, except for some, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: Rava cites Rav Nachman: all amos are in a six-handbreadth amah, except: these are laughing, and these are sad.
Rava reports in Rav Nachman's name that all amos are six handbreadths, but some are 'playful' (loose) and others 'sad' (tight).
The Gemara cites a baraita: all amos that the Sages spoke of are in a six-handbreadth amah, provided that…
The Gemara raises an objection from a baraisa stating that all amos mentioned by the Sages are six handbreadths, except for some, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Abaye's difficulty with Rava's explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's difficulty with Rava's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that according to Rava, the Mishnah's statement that the cubits for kilayim should not be precise makes sense, but for Abaye it is problematic.

sub.desc_en: Abaye questions Rava's explanation of the Mishnah's statement about imprecise cubits for kilayim.

items.text: Abaye's answer and support from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Abaye's answer and support from Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Abaye responds that the cubit for kilayim is a six-handbreadth cubit. He argues that the Tanna Kamma's statement about all cubits is contradicted by the Mishnah's mention of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who agrees with Abaye that only the kilayim cubit is six handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that the cubit for kilayim is a six-handbreadth cubit.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah's continuation implies the Tanna Kamma spoke of all cubits, contradicting Abaye's limitation.
Abaye resolves the objection by noting that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel supports his position, so he aligns with that Tanna.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the dispute is between Tanna'im for Rava as well. Rava responds that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel merely teaches that the kilayim cubit should not be exact, not that it is a different standard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether, according to Rava, the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel is necessarily a dispute between Tanna'im.
Rava responds that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel merely teaches that the cubit for kilayim should not be exact, not that it is a different standard.

items.text: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the cubit's exclusion
items.text_en: Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the cubit's exclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel only meant not to be exact, why mention a six-handbreadth cubit? It must exclude the cubit of sukkah and mavoy. The Gemara answers that it excludes the cubit of the altar's foundation and surrounding ledge, as derived from Ezekiel's vision.

items.text: Introduction of shi'urin as halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai
items.text_en: Introduction of shi'urin as halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav that measurements (shi'urin), interpositions (chatzitzin), and partitions (mechitzin) are halakha from Sinai. The Gemara questions this, noting that shi'urin are derived from the verse about the Land of Israel. It then provides examples: wheat for the measure of eating a peras, barley for the size of a bone, and grape for the measure of wine for a nazirite.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav that measurements (שיעורין), interpositions (חציצין), and partitions (מחיצין) are a law from Sinai.
The Gemara objects that measurements (שיעורין) are derived from the Torah, not from Sinai.
The Gemara cites the verse 'a land of wheat and barley' and Rav Chanan's statement that the entire verse is for measurements.
The Gemara explains that 'wheat' refers to the measure of eating a peras (פרס) of wheat bread for entering a leprous house.
The Gemara explains that 'barley' refers to the size of a barley-corn bone that conveys impurity through contact and carrying.
The Gemara explains that 'grape' refers to the measure of a quarter-log of wine for a nazirite.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Measurements for fig, pomegranate, olive, honey
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Measurements for fig, pomegranate, olive, honey
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a fig-sized object is used for Sabbath carrying, a pomegranate-sized object for vessel measurements, and an olive-sized object for land measurements; honey is like a thick writing tablet for Yom Kippur.

items.text: Gemara's question: Are these measurements Torah law or rabbinic?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Are these measurements Torah law or rabbinic?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether these measurements are Torah law or rabbinic enactments, and concludes they are halachic traditions supported by scriptural allusions.

items.text: Chatzitzah laws: Torah requirement for full body immersion
items.text_en: Chatzitzah laws: Torah requirement for full body immersion
items.desc_en: The Torah requires that nothing interpose between the body and the mikveh water; the Sages set the minimum water volume at 40 se'ah (3x3x3 amot).

items.text: Hair as chatzitzah: Rabba bar Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Hair as chatzitzah: Rabba bar Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that a single tied hair is a chatzitzah, three untied hairs are not, and two are uncertain.

items.text: Hair is Torah-level chatzitzah: Scriptural basis
items.text_en: Hair is Torah-level chatzitzah: Scriptural basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara confirms that hair is a Torah-level chatzitzah because the verse 'wash all his flesh' includes hair as part of the body.

items.text: Rabbi Yitzchak's distinction: Majority and intent matter
items.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak's distinction: Majority and intent matter
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak rules that a Torah-level chatzitzah requires both majority coverage and intent; non-intentional majority is rabbinically prohibited; minority with intent is also rabbinic.

items.text: Gemara's objection: Should we also decree on non-intentional minority?
items.text_en: Gemara's objection: Should we also decree on non-intentional minority?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the rabbis did not also decree on non-intentional minority due to intentional minority, or due to non-intentional majority; and answers that a decree on a decree is not made.

items.text: Partitions (mechitzot) are Torah-level
items.text_en: Partitions (mechitzot) are Torah-level
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that partitions (mechitzot) are Torah-level requirements, citing Mar's statement about the Ark and the cover being ten handbreadths.

items.text: Dispute on amah measurements: Rabbi Yehuda vs Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Dispute on amah measurements: Rabbi Yehuda vs Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda holds the building amah is 6 handbreadths and vessel amah is 5; Rabbi Meir says all amot are intermediate (6 handbreadths).

items.text: Rabbi Meir's ruling on curved walls, Gud, Lavud, and Doffen
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's ruling on curved walls, Gud, Lavud, and Doffen
items.desc_en: Rabbi Meir applies the principles of Gud (imaginary extension), Lavud (attachment within 3 handbreadths), and curved walls (Doffen) to halachic measurements.

items.text: Reducing a high sukkah: How much to lower?
items.text_en: Reducing a high sukkah: How much to lower?
items.desc_en: If a sukkah is over 20 amot high, the Gemara asks how much to reduce it; the answer depends on width — Rav Yosef says a handbreadth, Abaye says four handbreadths.

items.text: Dispute on using space under the sukkah roof
items.text_en: Dispute on using space under the sukkah roof
items.desc_en: The dispute is whether one may use the space under the sukkah roof: Rav Yosef (handbreadth) permits it, Abaye (four) prohibits it.

items.text: First resolution: dispute over using space under the korah
items.text_en: First resolution: dispute over using space under the korah
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rav Yosef (who requires four handbreadths) and Abaye (who requires four cubits) stems from a disagreement about whether it is prohibited to use the space under the korah.

items.text: Second resolution: dispute over the function of the korah
items.text_en: Second resolution: dispute over the function of the korah
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the first answer and proposes that all agree it is permitted to use under the korah; rather, they dispute whether the korah serves as a recognition (heker) or as a partition (mechitzah).

items.text: Third resolution: dispute over upper vs. lower recognition
items.text_en: Third resolution: dispute over upper vs. lower recognition
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another answer: all agree the korah is for recognition, but they dispute whether a lower recognition is considered like an upper recognition.

items.text: Fourth resolution: dispute over a decree lest one reduce
items.text_en: Fourth resolution: dispute over a decree lest one reduce
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests a final answer: all agree that lower recognition is like upper recognition, but they dispute whether to decree that one might reduce the korah's height.

items.text: The dispute between Rav Yosef and Abaye on the alleyway's width
items.text_en: The dispute between Rav Yosef and Abaye on the alleyway's width
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses an alleyway less than ten handbreadths high that was dug to complete ten; the Gemara asks how much must be dug, then clarifies that the question is about the thickness of the korah. Rav Yosef says four handbreadths, Abaye says four cubits.

items.text: Connecting the dispute to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
items.text_en: Connecting the dispute to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Yosef and Abaye's dispute parallels that of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi regarding an alleyway breached on its side toward its head, where a four-handbreadth post permits a breach up to ten cubits.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: end of alleyway vs. beginning
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: end of alleyway vs. beginning
items.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes the cases: there it is the end of the alleyway, here it is the beginning; only four cubits suffice at the beginning.

items.text: Abaye's proof from a baraita and Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from a baraita and Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita that an alleyway is only permitted with a lechi and korah if houses and courtyards open into it, and argues that with only four handbreadths this is impossible. Rav Yosef counters that it could open via a corner, citing Rav Nachman's definition of an alleyway.

items.text: Abaye's second proof from Rami bar Chama and Rav Yosef's response
items.text_en: Abaye's second proof from Rami bar Chama and Rav Yosef's response
items.desc_en: Abaye cites Rami bar Chama citing Rav Huna that a lechi protruding from the alleyway wall is judged as a lechi if less than four cubits, but as an alleyway if four cubits. Rav Yosef responds that this only excludes it from the category of lechi until four cubits, but it is still an alleyway even with four handbreadths.

items.text: Repetition of the statement of Rami bar Chama
items.text_en: Repetition of the statement of Rami bar Chama
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the statement of Rami bar Chama citing Rav Huna about a lechi protruding from the alleyway wall.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Breach width determines need for lechi
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Breach width determines need for lechi
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: a breach less than 4 amot is treated as a lechi (side-post) and needs no additional lechi; a breach of exactly 4 amot is treated as a mavoi (alley) and requires another lechi.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a breach less than 4 amot is treated as a lechi and needs no additional lechi; a breach of exactly 4 amot is treated as a mavoi and requires another lechi.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Where to place the lechi?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Where to place the lechi?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if the breach is exactly 4 amot, where should the additional lechi be placed? If placed alongside the existing lechi, it merely adds length; if placed on the other side, it creates a new side-post.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: where should that additional lechi be placed? If placed alongside the existing lechi, it merely adds length.

items.text: Rav Papa's answer: Place on the other side
items.text_en: Rav Papa's answer: Place on the other side
items.desc_en: Rav Papa answers: place the additional lechi on the other side (the opposite side of the alley) to effectively create a new side-post, not merely extend the existing one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa answers: place it on the other side (the opposite side of the breach), creating a new side-post.

items.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's alternative: Place alongside or reduce breach
items.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's alternative: Place alongside or reduce breach
items.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua suggests either placing the lechi alongside the existing one (which adds length but may still suffice) or reducing the breach width to less than 4 amot, thereby eliminating the need for an additional lechi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua limits his earlier statement to an eight-cubit alleyway, but for a seven-cubit alleyway, the standing walls exceed the breach and permit it without a lechi.

sub.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's kal vachomer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's kal vachomer
sub.desc_en: He argues a kal vachomer (a fortiori) from a courtyard: if a courtyard, which is not permitted by a lechi or beam, is permitted by standing walls exceeding the breach, then an alleyway, which is permitted by a lechi or beam, should certainly be permitted by standing walls exceeding the breach.
The gemara objects: the kal vachomer is flawed because a courtyard's breach is up to ten cubits, whereas an alleyway's breach is only four cubits, making the cases incomparable.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's position
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua holds that an alleyway's breach is also ten cubits, but then questions how he can disagree with Rav Huna, who holds the breach is four cubits.
The gemara resolves that Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua is stating his own independent opinion, not responding to Rav Huna.

Rav Ashi argues that even in an eight-cubit alleyway, no lechi is needed: if the standing walls are greater, it is permitted by the majority standing; if the breach is greater, it is treated as a lechi itself.

sub.text: Gemara's conclusion on Rav Ashi's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's conclusion on Rav Ashi's view
sub.desc_en: The gemara concludes that if the standing and breach are equal, it is a doubt regarding rabbinic laws, and such doubts are resolved leniently, so no lechi is needed.

items.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's clarification: Only for 8-amot alley
items.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua's clarification: Only for 8-amot alley
items.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua clarifies that his leniency applies only to an alley of 8 amot width; for a 7-amot alley, a standing wall exceeding the breach suffices without an extra lechi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Kal vachomer argument from courtyard to alley
items.text_en: Kal vachomer argument from courtyard to alley
items.desc_en: The Gemara draws a kal vachomer (a fortiori) argument: if a courtyard (which requires no lechi or korah) is permitted by a standing wall exceeding its breach, then an alley (which requires lechi and korah) should certainly be permitted by such a wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Objection: Courtyard breach is 10 amot, alley breach is 4
items.text_en: Objection: Courtyard breach is 10 amot, alley breach is 4
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: the courtyard's breach is 10 amot (large), while the alley's breach is only 4 amot (small), so the kal vachomer may not hold because the courtyard's leniency stems from its larger breach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua counters: Alley breach also 10 amot
items.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua counters: Alley breach also 10 amot
items.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua argues that an alley's breach can also be 10 amot (like a courtyard), and the question is directed to Rav Huna who holds alley breach is 4 amot — but Rav Huna himself might accept the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua states his own reasoning
items.text_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua states his own reasoning
items.desc_en: Rav Huna brei d'Rav Yehoshua declares that he is stating his own reasoning (not Rav Huna's), and that he holds an alley's breach can be 10 amot, thus supporting the kal vachomer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Rav Ashi's extreme leniency: Even 8-amot alley needs no lechi
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's extreme leniency: Even 8-amot alley needs no lechi
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that even an 8-amot alley may not need a lechi: if the standing wall exceeds the breach, it suffices; if the breach is larger, the alley is treated as a lechi itself (since the breach defines it as a side-post).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Gemara's uncertainty: Are both cases equivalent?
items.text_en: Gemara's uncertainty: Are both cases equivalent?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the two scenarios (standing wall exceeds breach vs. breach defines as lechi) are truly equivalent, leading to a doubt that should be resolved leniently.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Rav Chanin bar Rava's ruling: Breached mavoi requires lechi
items.text_en: Rav Chanin bar Rava's ruling: Breached mavoi requires lechi
items.desc_en: Rav Chanin bar Rava citing Rav rules: a breached mavoi (alley) requires a lechi (side-post) — implying that leniency does not apply universally.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the two (standing post and breach) are equal, it is a doubt (safek) between them, and doubts are resolved leniently.

items.text: Opening statement: breach measurements
items.text_en: Opening statement: breach measurements
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a breach from the side of an alleyway is permitted up to ten cubits, while from the front it is only permitted up to four cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a breach from the side of an alleyway is permitted up to ten cubits, while from the front it is only permitted up to four cubits.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rav Huna's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Huna's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a breach from the side is treated differently from the front, suggesting both should be considered an opening. Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that the case is when the breach is at a corner, as people do not make openings at corners.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a breach from the side is treated as an opening at ten handbreadths, but from the front should not also be considered an opening.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that the case is when the breach is at a corner, as people do not make openings at corners.

items.text: Rav Huna's alternative opinion and incident
items.text_en: Rav Huna's alternative opinion and incident
items.desc_en: Rav Huna argues that both side and front breaches are limited to four cubits. He cites an incident where Rav acted in accordance with his view, but Rav Chanan bar Rava dismisses this as Rav finding a 'field' and building a fence.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna says: Both this and that are four cubits.

items.text: Support for Rav Huna from a dispute about a crooked alleyway
items.text_en: Support for Rav Huna from a dispute about a crooked alleyway
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak supports Rav Huna by citing a dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a crooked alleyway (מבוי עקום). The Gemara infers that Rav's position implies a side breach is limited to four cubits.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak introduces a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about a crooked alleyway (מבוי עקום) to support Rav Huna's position.
The Gemara questions the context of the dispute, rejecting the possibility that it deals with a breach wider than ten cubits, as Shmuel would not then call it 'closed'.

The Gemara concludes that the dispute concerns a breach of exactly ten cubits, and Rav's ruling that it is 'like an open alleyway' implies that a side breach of an alleyway is limited to four cubits, supporting Rav Huna.

items.text: Distinction between the cases
items.text_en: Distinction between the cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara distinguishes Rav Chanan bar Rava's case from Rav Huna's: in the former, the public traverses the breach, while in the latter it does not. It further distinguishes based on the presence of partitions (גידודי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that Rav Chanan bar Rava's case is different because the public traverses the breach.
The Gemara questions: from this inference, Rav Huna holds that even without public traversal, what distinguishes his case from that of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi?
The Gemara answers that there, in the case of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, there are partitions (גידודי), while here there are none.

items.text: Baraita on eruv through a public domain
items.text_en: Baraita on eruv through a public domain
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses how to establish an eruv across a public domain: one makes a צורת הפתח on one side and a lechi and korah on the other. Chananya cites Beit Shammai requiring doors on both sides, while Beit Hillel require a door on one side and lechi and korah on the other. The Gemara questions whether a public domain can be incorporated at all, citing a contradiction from another baraita.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating the method for establishing an eruv through a public domain: one makes a צורת הפתח (doorway frame) on one side and a lechi and korah on the other.

sub.text: Chananya citing Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Chananya citing Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: Chananya reports that Beit Shammai require a door on both sides, while Beit Hillel require a door on one side and a lechi and korah on the other.
The Gemara questions whether a public domain can be incorporated into an eruv at all, citing a contradiction from another baraita.
The Gemara introduces a supporting baraita where Rabbi Yehuda adds a stricter requirement, implying that a public domain cannot be incorporated.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who has two houses on opposite sides of a public domain may make a side post on each side or a beam on each side, and carry in between. The Sages said that the public domain is not permitted in this manner.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the Tanna Kamma's ruling that one with two houses on opposite sides of a public domain may use side posts or beams to permit carrying between them, and the Sages' objection that the public domain cannot be enclosed in this manner.

items.text: Gemara's objection from Jerusalem and Mahoza
items.text_en: Gemara's objection from Jerusalem and Mahoza
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah implies that doors would permit the public domain, then why did Rabbi Yochanan say that Jerusalem would be liable as a public domain if its doors were not locked at night? Similarly, Ulla said about the gates of Mahoza that they would be liable as a public domain if not locked.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the Mishnah implies that doors would permit the public domain, then why did Rabbi Yochanan say that Jerusalem would be liable as a public domain if its doors were not locked at night?
Ulla similarly states that the gates of Mahoza would be liable as a public domain if not locked at night.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's reinterpretation
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's reinterpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah actually means: how does one permit alleyways that open into the public domain? By making a צורת הפתח on one side and a side post and beam on the other.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reinterprets the Mishnah: the case is about alleyways that open into the public domain, and the solution is a צורת הפתח (doorway frame) on one side and a side post and beam on the other.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: It was stated: Rav said the halakha is like the first Tanna, and Shmuel said the halakha is like Chananya.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states that Rav rules the halakha follows the first Tanna, while Shmuel rules it follows Chananya.

items.text: Inquiry about Chananya's position
items.text_en: Inquiry about Chananya's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: according to Chananya, following Beit Hillel, is it necessary to lock the doors or not? It brings evidence from Rav Yehuda and Rav Mattana citing Shmuel that it is not necessary to lock.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara inquires whether according to Chananya, following Beit Hillel, one must lock the doors of an alley or not.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda and Rav Mattana citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda and Rav Mattana citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings evidence from Rav Yehuda and Rav Mattana, both citing Shmuel, that locking is not required.

items.text: Rav Anan's testimony and Rav Kahana's clarification
items.text_en: Rav Anan's testimony and Rav Kahana's clarification
items.desc_en: They asked Rav Anan whether locking is required. He pointed to the gates of Neharde'a that were half-buried in dirt, and Shmuel entered and exited without saying anything. Rav Kahana said those were doors that could be closed (מגופות).

sub.desc_en: They asked Rav Anan whether locking is required for a מבוי (alleyway) that has a צורת הפתח (doorway structure).
Rav Anan pointed to the gates of Neharde'a that were half-buried in dirt, and Shmuel entered and exited without saying anything, implying locking is not required.
Rav Kahana objected that those gates were actually doors that could be closed (מגופות), so they do not prove that locking is unnecessary.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and explanation
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and explanation
items.desc_en: When Rav Nachman came, he said to clear away their dirt. The Gemara asks if this means he holds that locking is required, and answers: no, since they are fit to be locked, even if not actually locked.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs to clear the dirt from the gates, implying they should be made functional.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Nachman's action indicates he holds that locking is required.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Nachman's intent was to make the gates fit for locking, but actual locking is not required.

items.text: Case of the crooked alleyway and the principle of not combining stringencies
items.text_en: Case of the crooked alleyway and the principle of not combining stringencies
items.desc_en: A crooked alleyway in Neharde'a was treated with the stringencies of both Rav and Shmuel, requiring doors. The Gemara questions this, citing a baraita that one may not combine the stringencies of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel. It resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the Bat Kol, or by saying both statements are after the Bat Kol.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara describes a crooked alleyway in Neharde'a where they imposed both the stringency of Rav and the stringency of Shmuel, requiring doors.

The Gemara questions how Rav's stringency (treating the alleyway as a מפולש (open thoroughfare)) can be applied, given that Rav himself ruled like the first Tanna (תנא קמא) who permits a simpler solution.
The Gemara objects that one may not combine two stringencies, citing a baraita (תוספתא) that forbids picking the stringencies of both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, calling such a person a fool.
The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in the baraita itself: it first says the הלכה (binding law) always follows Beit Hillel, then says one may choose to follow Beit Shammai.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after the Bat Kol (Heavenly voice) that decided in favor of Beit Hillel.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: both statements in the baraita refer to the period after the Bat Kol, and the apparent contradiction is resolved differently.

items.text: Identifying the first opinion as Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Identifying the first opinion as Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the earlier statement follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who disregards a bat kol.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the earlier anonymous statement follows Rabbi Yehoshua, who disregards a bat kol (heavenly voice).

items.text: Alternative explanation and difficulty
items.text_en: Alternative explanation and difficulty
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative: whenever there are two Tannaim and two Amoraim disputing like Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, one should not follow both leniencies or both stringencies, but either follow one authority entirely. Nevertheless, a difficulty remains.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the entire law was enacted like Rav, who said the halacha is so but we do not instruct accordingly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers: the entire ruling was established like Rav, who said the halacha is so but one does not instruct others to act accordingly.

items.text: Challenge from Rav Adda bar Ahavah and Rav Sheizvi's answer
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Adda bar Ahavah and Rav Sheizvi's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what to say according to Rav Adda bar Ahavah who says Rav taught that the halacha is so and we instruct accordingly. Rav Sheizvi answers that we do not follow the stringencies of two authorities only when they contradict each other.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges: according to Rav Adda bar Ahavah, who says Rav taught that the halacha is so and we instruct accordingly, what can be said to resolve the contradiction?
Rav Sheizvi answers that we do not follow the stringencies of two authorities only when they contradict each other.

items.text: Example of contradicting opinions: spine and skull
items.text_en: Example of contradicting opinions: spine and skull
items.desc_en: The Gemara gives an example from a mishna about the spine and skull where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree, and Rav Yehuda said Shmuel ruled similarly for tereifah. The Gemara concludes that where they do not contradict, we follow both stringencies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the example of spine and skull from a mishna where Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disagree on the minimum missing amount for each.
Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel applied the same dispute to the laws of טריפה (a ritually unfit animal).
The Gemara concludes that where the opinions do not contradict each other, we follow both stringencies.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Akiva's practice and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Akiva's practice and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenges from a story where Rabbi Akiva followed both Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the etrog. The Gemara answers that Rabbi Akiva was uncertain about the dates and acted stringently in both cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenges from a story where Rabbi Akiva picked an etrog on the first of Shevat and treated it with two tithes, one according to Beit Shammai and one according to Beit Hillel, contradicting the rule against following both leniencies.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Akiva was uncertain whether Beit Hillel's date was the first or fifteenth of Shevat, so he acted stringently in both cases, not following both leniencies.

items.text: Laws of mavoi with different adjacent areas
items.text_en: Laws of mavoi with different adjacent areas
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports in the name of Rav Yehuda that the dispute about a mavoi applies when there are streets on both sides, but if one side is a street and the other a field, one makes a tzurat hapetach on one side and a lechi and korah on the other. Abaye notes that this is actually from Shmuel.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports in the name of Rav Yehuda that the dispute about a mavoi applies when there are streets on both sides.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef adds that if one side is a street and the other a field, one makes a tzurat hapetach on one side and a lechi and korah on the other.
The gemara questions why the case of a field on both sides is not explicitly mentioned, given that the case of a street and a field is already stated.
The gemara resolves that the statement means a street on one side and a field on the other is treated like a field on both sides.
Rav Yehuda adds that if a mavoi opens into a wide area, no correction is needed.
Abaye notes to Rav Yosef that this ruling of Rav Yehuda is actually from Shmuel.

items.text: Contradiction in Rav's rulings
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rav's rulings
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between Rav's statement here and another ruling of Rav: if an alleyway is entirely breached into a courtyard and the courtyard is breached opposite it, the courtyard is permitted but the alleyway is forbidden. The Gemara questions why the alleyway is not treated like an alleyway that ends in an open area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rav's ruling here and another ruling of Rav: if an alleyway is entirely breached into a courtyard and the courtyard is breached opposite it, the courtyard is permitted but the alleyway is forbidden, yet the alleyway should be treated like an alleyway that ends in an open area.

Rav Sheshet responds that he does not know the resolution, but reports a practical case where Rav Yehuda did not require anything for an alleyway that ends in an open area, and suggests attributing the problematic ruling to Shmuel instead of Rav.

Rav Sheshet now provides a definitive resolution: the case where the alleyway is forbidden is when the residents did not establish an עירוב (eruv), while the case where it is permitted is when they did establish an עירוב.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction between Rav's two rulings by distinguishing: the case where the alleyway is forbidden is when the courtyard residents did not establish an עירוב with the alleyway residents, while the case where it is permitted is when they did establish an עירוב.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's initial response
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's initial response
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet admits he does not know the answer, but recounts a case in the generation of Rav Yehuda where an alleyway ending in an open area was brought before Rav Yehuda and he required nothing. He suggests that if the contradiction is difficult, attribute the second ruling to Shmuel instead of Rav.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet admits he does not know the answer, but recounts a case in the generation of Rav Yehuda where an alleyway ending in an open area was brought before Rav Yehuda and he required nothing.
Rav Sheshet suggests that if the contradiction is difficult, attribute the second ruling to Shmuel instead of Rav.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet now explains the distinction: in one case the residents had joined an eruv, in the other they had not. This resolves the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet now explains the distinction: in one case the residents had joined an eruv, in the other they had not. This resolves the contradiction.

items.text: Application to Rav's contradiction
items.text_en: Application to Rav's contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara applies the same distinction to resolve the contradiction in Rav's rulings: one case is where the residents of the courtyard and alleyway joined an eruv, the other where they did not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rav's contradiction by distinguishing between cases where the residents of the courtyard and alleyway joined an עירוב (eruv) and where they did not.

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the original assumption that the dispute applies both when they did and did not establish an eruv, asking what they disagree about in each case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the original assumption that the dispute applies both when they did and did not establish an eruv, asking what they disagree about in each case.

items.text: Answer for when they did not establish an eruv
items.text_en: Answer for when they did not establish an eruv
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when they did not establish an eruv, the dispute is about a case where the breach is visible from outside but equal from inside.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that when they did not establish an eruv, the dispute concerns a case where the breach is visible from outside but equal from inside.

items.text: Answer for when they did establish an eruv and Rav Yosef's distinction
items.text_en: Answer for when they did establish an eruv and Rav Yosef's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when they did establish an eruv, the dispute is based on Rav Yosef's ruling, which distinguishes between an alleyway that ends in the middle of a plaza (permitted) and one that ends at the side of a plaza (forbidden). Rabba and Rav Mesharshiyya further qualify this ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that when they did establish an eruv, the dispute is based on Rav Yosef's ruling, which distinguishes between an alleyway that ends in the middle of a plaza (permitted) and one that ends at the side of a plaza (forbidden).

Rabba qualifies Rav Yosef's ruling, stating that the permission for an alleyway ending in the middle of a plaza applies only when the alleyways are not opposite each other, but if they are opposite, it is forbidden.

Rav Mesharshiyya further qualifies Rabba's ruling, stating that the permission for alleyways not opposite each other applies only to a public plaza, but for a private plaza, one might build houses there, making it like an alleyway ending at the side of a plaza and thus forbidden.

items.text: Proof for the distinction between public and private plaza
items.text_en: Proof for the distinction between public and private plaza
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a story involving Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi about an alleyway that ended at the sea and a garbage dump, where he did not rule either way due to concern that the dump might be removed or the sea might deposit silt. The Gemara then supports this concern with a mishna about a garbage dump in the public domain, establishing a distinction between a public and private dump, and by extension, between a public and private plaza.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for a source proving the distinction between a public plaza (רחבה דרבים) and a private plaza (רחבה דיחיד).

sub.text: Ravin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda citing Rabbi Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: Ravin bar Rav Adda in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak recounts a story of an alleyway ending at the sea and a garbage dump, where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refrained from ruling either way.

The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's reasoning: he did not forbid because the partitions were standing, but did not permit due to concern that the dump might be removed or the sea might deposit silt.

The Gemara objects: do we really fear the dump might be removed? It cites a mishna that a garbage dump in the public domain ten handbreadths high is treated as a valid partition for throwing on Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between a public dump (אשפה דרבים) and a private dump (אשפה דיחיד), and analogously between a public plaza and a private plaza.

items.text: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Sages hold, and Rav Yosef bar Avdimi teaches a baraita with two versions: one where the Sages forbid and Rav Nachman rules accordingly, and another where the Sages permit and Rav Nachman rules against them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Sages hold in this dispute.
Rav Yosef bar Avdimi teaches a baraita that the Sages forbid, and Rav Nachman rules accordingly.
Rav Nachman rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows the Sages who forbid.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef bar Avdimi's baraita
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef bar Avdimi's baraita
sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that the Sages permit.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's ruling in the alternative version
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling in the alternative version
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that the הלכה (binding law) does not follow the Sages who permit.

items.text: Marimar's ruling in Sura
items.text_en: Marimar's ruling in Sura
items.desc_en: Marimar ruled in Sura regarding an alleyway that ended at the sea, forbidding it due to concern that the sea might deposit silt.

sub.desc_en: Marimar rules in Sura that an alleyway ending at the sea is forbidden, because we fear the sea may deposit silt and create a new partition.

items.text: Case of a crooked alleyway in Sura
items.text_en: Case of a crooked alleyway in Sura
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a crooked alleyway in Sura where they placed a reed mat at its curve. Rav Chisda criticizes this, saying it does not satisfy either Rav or Shmuel's requirements, unless the mat is affixed with a peg.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of a crooked alleyway in Sura where a reed mat was placed at its curve.
Rav Chisda objects that the reed mat does not satisfy either Rav's requirement of a צורת הפתח (doorway form) or Shmuel's requirement of a proper side-post, because the wind will blow it away.
The Gemara resolves that if the mat is affixed with a peg, it is valid.

items.text: Rav's ruling on an alleyway breached into a courtyard
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on an alleyway breached into a courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quotes Rav: if an alleyway is entirely breached into a courtyard, and the courtyard is breached opposite it, the courtyard is permitted but the alleyway is forbidden. Rabba bar Ulla questions this from a mishna about a small courtyard breached into a large one, and Rav Bibi bar Abaye distinguishes the cases based on whether the public treads there, citing a baraita about a courtyard where the public enters and exits.

sub.text: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quotes Rav's ruling: if an alleyway is entirely breached into a courtyard, and the courtyard is breached opposite it, the courtyard is permitted but the alleyway is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabba bar Ulla's question to Rav Bibi bar Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Ulla's question to Rav Bibi bar Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Ulla objects by citing a mishna: a small courtyard breached into a large one — the large is permitted, the small forbidden — which seems identical to Rav's case.
Rav Bibi bar Abaye distinguishes: the mishna applies where the public does not tread, but here the public treads, so one might think even the courtyard is forbidden.

A baraita is cited: a courtyard where the public enters and exits is considered רשות הרבים (public domain) for טומאה (ritual impurity) but רשות היחיד (private domain) for שבת (Sabbath), showing the public's presence matters.
Rav Bibi bar Abaye concludes: from that baraita one might think the ruling applies only when the breaches are not opposite each other, but here they are opposite, so Rav's ruling stands.

items.text: Resolution of Rav's statement about parallel openings
items.text_en: Resolution of Rav's statement about parallel openings
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between Rav's statement and Rabbah's position. It explains that Rav's ruling applies to a case where the openings are not parallel, and the additional teaching is needed to clarify that the leniency extends to carrying as well as throwing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav's statement about parallel openings would permit carrying, suggesting it might not.
The Gemara objects that according to Rabbah, who forbids parallel openings, Rav's statement would be redundant if it only addresses non-parallel openings.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's additional statement teaches that the leniency applies to carrying as well as throwing.

items.text: Dispute about a mavoy shaped like a sandal
items.text_en: Dispute about a mavoy shaped like a sandal
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava dispute how to permit a mavoy with multiple openings like a sandal. Abaye says to make a doorway for the large opening and permit the rest with a side post and beam. Rava objects, citing Shmuel's view and a precedent from Nehardea, and instead says to make a doorway for all on one side and permit the other side with a side post and beam.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute about a mavoy (alleyway) shaped like a sandal (with multiple openings), and presents Abaye's position: one makes a doorway (צורת הפתח) for the large opening, and all the others are permitted with a side post and beam (לחי וקורה).
Rava objects to Abaye's position, questioning whose opinion it follows (Shmuel's), and citing a precedent from Nehardea of a curved mavoy that was treated stringently according to Rav.
Rava presents his own solution: one makes a doorway (צורת הפתח) for all the openings on one side, and the other side is permitted with a side post and beam (לחי וקורה).

items.text: Mavoy with one long side and one short side
items.text_en: Mavoy with one long side and one short side
items.desc_en: A tradition from Rav Kahana's chain discusses a mavoy with one long and one short side. If the difference is less than four cubits, the beam may be placed diagonally; if four cubits, it must be placed opposite the short side. Rava disagrees and says it must always be opposite the short side. The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rava holds the beam is for recognition, so a diagonal placement doesn't provide recognition, while the other opinion holds it is for a partition, which works diagonally. Rav Kahana adds a qualification about the diagonal not exceeding ten cubits.

sub.desc_en: A tradition transmitted through a chain of Kahana sages introduces the case of a mavoy with one long side and one short side.
The tradition rules: if the difference is less than four cubits, the beam may be placed diagonally; if four cubits, it must be placed opposite the short side.
Rava disagrees and holds that in both cases the beam must be placed opposite the short side.
The Gemara explains Rava's reasoning: the beam is for recognition (היכר), and a diagonal placement does not provide recognition.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of the other opinion's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the other opinion's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains the opposing view: the beam is for a partition (מחיצה), which works even diagonally.
Rav Kahana adds a qualification: the diagonal placement is only valid if the diagonal does not exceed ten cubits; otherwise, all agree the beam must be opposite the short side.

items.text: Dispute about using the space under the korah
items.text_en: Dispute about using the space under the korah
items.desc_en: A dispute is recorded: Rav, Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Yochanan permit using the space under the korah, while Shmuel, Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish forbid it. The Gemara suggests three possible explanations for the dispute: whether the korah is for recognition or as a partition; whether recognition is from inside or outside; or whether the inner edge or outer edge descends and seals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether one may use the space under the korah, and records the dispute: Rav, Rabbi Chiyya, and Rabbi Yochanan permit it, while Shmuel, Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi, and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish forbid it.
The Gemara suggests the dispute is about whether the korah functions as recognition (היכר) or as a partition (מחיצה).
The Gemara rejects that explanation and offers a second: all agree the korah is for recognition, but they dispute whether the recognition is from inside or outside.
The Gemara offers a third explanation: all agree the korah is a partition, but they dispute whether the inner edge or outer edge descends and seals.

items.text: Case of a korah placed on pegs outside the mavoy
items.text_en: Case of a korah placed on pegs outside the mavoy
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree using the space between the cheeks (the area between the side posts) is forbidden. Rami bar Chama asks about a case where pegs are driven into the walls outside and a korah is placed on them. Rav Chisda says it is forbidden according to the one who permits under the korah, and permitted according to the one who forbids. Rava disagrees, saying even the one who forbids would forbid because the korah is not above the mavoy. The Gemara begins to cite a supporting baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that all agree using the space between the cheeks (the area between the side posts) is forbidden.
Rami bar Chama asks Rav Chisda about a case where pegs are driven into the walls outside the mavoy and a korah is placed on them.
Rav Chisda answers that according to the one who permits using the space under the korah, this case is forbidden, and according to the one who forbids, it is permitted.
Rava objects, arguing that even according to the one who forbids using the space under the korah, this case is forbidden because the korah is not positioned above the mavoy.
Rav Adda bar Matna begins to cite a baraita to challenge Rava's position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the korah is drawn back or suspended, less than three handbreadths from the wall does not require another korah, but three does. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says less than four does not require another, but four does.

items.text: Gemara's initial interpretation and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial interpretation and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes 'drawn back' means outside and 'suspended' means inside, but rejects this, explaining both are inside: drawn back from one side, suspended from two sides. It then clarifies that the Mishnah teaches that the principle of לבוד applies even from two sides.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah refers to a case where the korah is both drawn back and suspended, such as when two curved pegs are inserted into the walls, each less than three handbreadths in height and curvature. The Mishnah teaches that we combine לבוד and חבט.

items.text: Rabbi Zakkai's statement and Rabbi Yochanan's rejection
items.text_en: Rabbi Zakkai's statement and Rabbi Yochanan's rejection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zakkai taught before Rabbi Yochanan that the area between the לחיים and under the korah is considered a כרמלית. Rabbi Yochanan told him to go teach outside.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's dispute on the area between the לחיים
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's dispute on the area between the לחיים
items.desc_en: Abaye infers that Rabbi Yochanan permits under the korah but forbids between the לחיים. Rava argues that even between the לחיים is permitted.

items.text: Rava's proof from Rav Dimi
items.text_en: Rava's proof from Rav Dimi
items.desc_en: Rava supports his view with a statement from Rav Dimi in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a place less than four by four handbreadths is permitted for both public and private domain residents to rest burdens, provided they do not exchange. Abaye counters that case involves a height of three handbreadths.

items.text: Abaye's proof from Rav and Rava's distinction
items.text_en: Abaye's proof from Rav and Rava's distinction
items.desc_en: Abaye cites Rav that the inside of a doorway requires another side-post to permit it. Rava distinguishes that case as one where the doorway opens to a כרמלית, not a public domain.

items.text: Rava's rhetorical question and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's rhetorical question and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava asks rhetorically if for a public domain it would be permitted, and answers with a metaphor: it is like a peg fixed in the ground and a convert in heaven, meaning it is impossible. The Gemara concludes that the two domains find each other and are stirred.

items.text: Rav Huna's challenge and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Huna's challenge and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua challenges Rava with a statement from Rabbi Yochanan that a מבוי paved with side-posts less than four handbreadths apart is subject to the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis, but all agree the area between the posts is forbidden. Rava again distinguishes that the case involves a מבוי opening to a כרמלית.

items.text: Repeated rhetorical question and conclusion
items.text_en: Repeated rhetorical question and conclusion
items.desc_en: Rava again asks rhetorically if for a public domain it would be permitted, and the Gemara repeats the metaphor and conclusion that the two domains find each other and are stirred.

items.text: Rav Ashi's explanation of the case
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation of the case
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the case involves a wall built with less than four handbreadths of space between each pair of beams over a span of four cubits. According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who applies the principle of לבוד, this constitutes a valid alleyway requiring another lechi; according to the Rabbis, who reject לבוד, no additional lechi is needed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi describes the case: a wall built with beams spaced less than four handbreadths apart over a span of four cubits.

Rav Ashi explains the dispute: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel applies לבוד (the principle of joining gaps) so the wall is valid and requires another lechi, while the Rabbis reject לבוד and require no additional lechi.

items.text: Question about נראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים
items.text_en: Question about נראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: According to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, should this case be considered as 'visible from the outside and flush from the inside'? It then notes that Rabbi Yochanan rules that such a configuration is not considered a lechi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether, according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, the case should be considered as 'visible from the outside and flush from the inside' (נראה מבחוץ ושוה מבפנים).
The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan rules that such a configuration is not considered a lechi (לֶחִי).

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: regarding a wall visible from the inside and flush from the outside, it is considered a lechi. Regarding visible from the outside and flush from the inside, Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi disagree. A baraita supports that Rabbi Chiyya rules it is considered a lechi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens a dispute: regarding a wall visible from inside and flush outside, it is considered a lechi; regarding visible from outside and flush inside, Rabbi Chiyya and Rabbi Shimon bar Rabbi disagree.
