A baraita supports that Rabbi Chiyya rules it is considered a lechi, citing his teaching that a wall recessed on one side is always considered a lechi.

items.text: Challenge: Did Rabbi Yochanan know the baraita?
items.text_en: Challenge: Did Rabbi Yochanan know the baraita?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Did Rabbi Yochanan not hear this baraita? It answers that he heard it but did not accept it. But then it questions: If Rabbi Chiyya did not accept his own baraita, why did he teach it?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yochanan had not heard the baraita of Rabbi Chiyya, and answers that he heard it but did not accept it.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Chiyya did not accept his own baraita, why did he teach it?

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling and challenge
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna's ruling and challenge
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that a wall visible from the outside and flush from the inside is considered a lechi. Rabbah challenges this from a mishna about a small courtyard breached into a large one, where the small one is forbidden; if the rule applied, the small one should be permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna rules that a wall visible from the outside and flush from the inside is considered a lechi.
Rabbah challenges the ruling from a mishna about a small courtyard breached into a large one, arguing that if the rule applied, the small courtyard should be permitted.

items.text: Resolutions: Rabbi Zeira, Ravina, and the לבוד argument
items.text_en: Resolutions: Rabbi Zeira, Ravina, and the לבוד argument
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the case involves the walls of the small courtyard extending into the large one. The Gemara suggests applying לבוד, but notes the gap is too large. Ravina specifies the gaps are two and four handbreadths respectively. The Gemara then asks why not apply לבוד from one side.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira answers that the case involves the walls of the small courtyard extending into the large one, so the breach is not a simple opening.
The Gemara asks why not apply the principle of לבוד (the legal fiction of a closed gap) to permit the small courtyard.
The Gemara objects that the gap might be too large, but cites Rav Ada bar Avimi's baraita that the small courtyard is ten cubits and the large one eleven, so the gap is only one cubit.
Ravina specifies that the walls protrude two handbreadths from one side and four from the other, creating gaps too large for לבוד.
The Gemara asks why not apply לבוד from one side alone to permit the small courtyard.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a small and large courtyard
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah's ruling on a small and large courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's ruling that a small courtyard is permitted with a ten-cubit opening and a large one with eleven cubits. It considers whether this supports the view that a side-post visible from the outside but flush on the inside is not considered a valid lechi, or whether it supports the opposite view. The Gemara concludes that it supports the former.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as following Rabbi's view that a courtyard requires two side-posts (פסין).
The Gemara proposes that if a side-post visible outside but flush inside is not considered a valid lechi, then Rabbi's ruling aligns with Rabbi Yosei, explaining the Mishnah's measurements.
The Gemara objects that if such a side-post is considered a valid lechi, then the Mishnah's requirement of eleven cubits for the large courtyard becomes superfluous.
The Gemara refutes the alternative hypothesis by showing that neither purpose (permitting the large nor forbidding the small) justifies the eleven-cubit measurement.
The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah supports the view that a side-post visible outside but flush inside is not considered a valid lechi.

items.text: Rav Yosef's forgotten tradition and Abaye's reminder
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's forgotten tradition and Abaye's reminder
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says he does not know this tradition. Abaye reminds him that he himself taught them a baraita of Rami bar Abba quoting Rav Huna about a lechi that extends along the wall of a mavoy, and that from this baraita three rulings were derived, including that a side-post visible from the outside but flush on the inside is considered a lechi.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that he does not know this tradition.

Abaye reminds Rav Yosef that he himself taught them a baraita of Rami bar Abba quoting Rav Huna about a lechi that extends along the wall of a mavoy, with rulings for less than four amot and exactly four amot.
Abaye adds that Rav Yosef himself derived three rulings from that baraita, including that a side-post visible from the outside but flush on the inside is considered a lechi.

items.text: The halakha and its support from Rabbi Chiyya
items.text_en: The halakha and its support from Rabbi Chiyya
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha: a side-post visible from the outside but flush on the inside is considered a lechi. It questions how this can be both a refutation and the halakha, and answers that it is because Rabbi Chiyya taught a baraita in support of this view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha (הלכה) that a side-post (לחי) visible from outside but flush inside is considered a valid lechi.
The Gemara questions how this ruling can simultaneously be a refutation (תיובתא) and the halakha (הלכה).
The Gemara answers that it is because Rabbi Chiyya taught a baraita (ברייתא) in support of this view, so the ruling stands despite the refutation.

items.text: The width of a mavoy and the kal vachomer from passei bira'ot
items.text_en: The width of a mavoy and the kal vachomer from passei bira'ot
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a mavoy is wider than ten cubits, one must narrow it. Abaye cites a Tanna who says this, and Rabbi Yehuda says one need not narrow it. Rav Achai attempts to derive a limit of thirteen and a third cubits via a kal vachomer from passei bira'ot (the posts of wells), but the Gemara refutes this with a counter-argument.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a mavoy wider than ten cubits must be narrowed, and Abaye cites a Tanna who says this, while Rabbi Yehuda says it is not necessary; the Gemara then asks 'up to how much?'
Rav Achai proposes before Rav Yosef that the limit is thirteen and a third cubits, derived via a kal vachomer (a fortiori argument) from the passei bira'ot (posts of wells).

Rav Achai argues that if passei bira'ot, which allow a majority of breach over standing, are limited to thirteen and a third cubits, then a mavoy, which does not allow such a breach, should certainly not exceed that limit.

The Gemara refutes the kal vachomer by reversing it: since passei bira'ot allow a majority breach, they are lenient in that respect, so one might argue that a mavoy, which does not allow such a breach, should be more lenient and permit a greater width.

Alternatively, the Gemara argues that passei bira'ot, which are lenient in one respect (allowing a majority breach), might be lenient in another (allowing a greater width), but a mavoy, which has no such leniency, should not be compared at all.

items.text: Levi's ruling on a mavoy twenty cubits wide
items.text_en: Levi's ruling on a mavoy twenty cubits wide
items.desc_en: Levi taught a baraita that if a mavoy is twenty cubits wide, one may place a pole in its center and it suffices. However, he also said that the halakha is not like that Mishnah. Some say Shmuel said this in Levi's name. The Gemara then asks what one should do instead, and Shmuel answers in Levi's name.

sub.desc_en: לוי (Levi) teaches a ברייתא (baraita) that if a מבוי (alleyway) is twenty אמות (cubits) wide, one may stick a קנה (reed) in its center and that suffices.
לוי (Levi) himself taught this ברייתא (baraita) and also said that the הלכה (binding law) is not like that משנה (Mishnah).
Some say that שמואל (Shmuel) said in the name of לוי (Levi) that the הלכה (binding law) is not like that משנה (Mishnah).
The גמרא (Gemara) asks: Rather, how should one act to permit carrying in such a מבוי (alleyway)?
שמואל (Shmuel) begins to answer in the name of לוי (Levi), but the text is cut off here.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's rule: one makes a side-post ten handbreadths high spanning four cubits and places it along the length of the alleyway.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: one makes a side-post ten handbreadths high spanning four cubits and places it along the length of the alleyway.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Yehuda's statement about a fifteen-cubit wide alleyway: why not make two posts of one and a half cubits each with a two-cubit gap? This implies that standing space from two sides does not count as standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Yehuda's ruling: why not make two posts of one and a half cubits each with a two-cubit gap, concluding that standing space from two sides does not count as standing.

items.text: First answer: air from both sides nullifies
items.text_en: First answer: air from both sides nullifies
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that even if standing from two sides is valid, here the air from both sides combines to nullify the standing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that even if standing from two sides is valid, here the air from both sides combines to nullify the standing.

items.text: Second question and answer: standing equal to breach
items.text_en: Second question and answer: standing equal to breach
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not make a one-cubit post, a one-cubit gap, another one-cubit post, etc., implying that standing equal to breach is forbidden. The answer is again that air from both sides nullifies.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why not make a one-cubit post, a one-cubit gap, another one-cubit post, etc., implying that standing equal to breach is forbidden.
The Gemara answers that even standing equal to breach is permitted, but here the air from both sides nullifies the partition.

items.text: Third proposal and resolution
items.text_en: Third proposal and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests making a one-cubit gap and a one-and-a-half cubit post on each side, but concludes that the Sages did not impose such a burden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes making a one-cubit gap and a one-and-a-half cubit post on each side of the alleyway.
The Gemara concludes that indeed this would work, but the Sages did not impose such a burden on the residents.

items.text: Concern about leaving a large entrance
items.text_en: Concern about leaving a large entrance
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that one might leave the large entrance and enter through the small one. Rav Ada bar Masna answers with a presumption that a person does not leave a large entrance for a small one. The Gemara distinguishes this from the case of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, where the concern was about reducing walking distance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern that one might leave the large entrance and enter through the small one.
Rav Ada bar Masna answers with a presumption (חזקה) that a person does not leave a large entrance for a small one.
The Gemara objects: what is the difference between this case and the case of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, where a similar concern was raised?
The Gemara distinguishes: there, the concern was about reducing walking distance (ממעט בהילוכא), but here, there is no reduction in walking distance.

items.text: Dispute about the dimensions of the toilet seat cover
items.text_en: Dispute about the dimensions of the toilet seat cover
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about the cover of a toilet seat (or ha'asla) and its hollow combining to a handbreadth. Rav Dimi and Ravin give different dimensions. Abaye questions if they disagree. Rav Dimi says they do not, but Abaye argues they do, specifically on the principle of standing from two sides. The Gemara concludes that if they disagree, it is on the principle of breach equal to standing.

items.text: Conclusion: shape of an entrance suffices for width
items.text_en: Conclusion: shape of an entrance suffices for width
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that if an alleyway has a shape of an entrance (tzurat hapetach), even if it is wider than ten cubits, it does not need to be reduced. It finds that a shape of an entrance is effective for width, and a cross-beam (amaltera) is effective for height.

items.text: Question about the inverse case
items.text_en: Question about the inverse case
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what if the situation is reversed (i.e., the alleyway is too wide rather than too high)?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the law is in the inverse case, where the alleyway is too wide rather than too high.

items.text: Bringing a baraita about a high alleyway and a wide alleyway
items.text_en: Bringing a baraita about a high alleyway and a wide alleyway
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that an alleyway over twenty cubits high requires reduction, but if it has a tzurat hapetach it does not. It then asks about an amaltra in a wide alleyway, and another baraita clarifies that both height and width require reduction unless there is a tzurat hapetach or an amaltra. The Gemara debates whether the amaltra exemption applies to the first clause (height) or the second clause (width).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that an alleyway over twenty cubits high requires reduction, but if it has a צורת הפתח (doorway frame) it does not.
The Gemara asks what the rule is regarding an אמלתא (projecting beam) in a wide alleyway.
The Gemara cites another baraita that explicitly states both height and width require reduction unless there is a צורת הפתח or an אמלתא.
The Gemara asks whether the אמלתא exemption refers to the second clause (width) of the baraita.
The Gemara rejects that and says the exemption applies to the first clause (height).

items.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching and Rav's correction
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching and Rav's correction
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda taught the baraita to Chiyya bar Rav before Rav, saying 'does not require reduction,' but Rav corrected him: 'teach that it requires reduction.'

sub.text: Rav Yehuda's teaching and Rav's correction
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda's teaching and Rav's correction
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda taught the baraita to Chiyya bar Rav before Rav, saying 'does not require reduction,' but Rav corrected him: 'teach that it requires reduction.'

items.text: Rav Yosef's deduction about a courtyard with many openings
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's deduction about a courtyard with many openings
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef deduces from Rav's ruling that a courtyard whose majority consists of doors and windows is not permitted by a tzurat hapetach. He draws an analogy: just as an alleyway wider than ten cubits is not permitted by a tzurat hapetach, so too a courtyard where the breached area exceeds the standing walls is not permitted by a tzurat hapetach.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef deduces from Rav's ruling that a courtyard whose majority consists of doors and windows is not permitted by a צורת הפתח (gateway frame).

Rav Yosef explains the reasoning: just as an alleyway wider than ten cubits is not permitted by a צורת הפתח, so too a courtyard where the breached area exceeds the standing walls is not permitted by a צורת הפתח.

items.text: Refutation of the analogy
items.text_en: Refutation of the analogy
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Yosef's analogy: the case of an alleyway wider than ten cubits is different because even by the pasin bira'ot (the walls of enclosures for wells) according to Rabbi Meir, you did not permit it; but in the case of a courtyard with a majority of breaches, you did permit it by pasin bira'ot according to all opinions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is the reason? Because more than ten prohibits in an alleyway, and a breach majority over the standing prohibits in a courtyard. Just as more than ten in an alleyway is not permitted by doorway form, so a breach majority over the standing in a courtyard is not permitted by doorway form.

items.text: Supporting baraita about corners with many openings
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about corners with many openings
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that seems to support Rav Yosef: corners that have many doors and windows are permitted, provided the standing area exceeds the breached area. The Gemara corrects the text: it should say 'that have many doors and windows' (not 'most of them').

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that a baraita supports Rav Yosef: corners with many doors and windows are permitted only if the standing area exceeds the breached area.

The Gemara rejects the original wording and corrects the baraita: it should say 'that added many doors and windows' (not 'most of them'), still requiring the standing area to exceed the breached area.

items.text: Rav Kahana's explanation about 'openings of the sky'
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's explanation about 'openings of the sky'
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana says that baraita refers to 'pitchei shima'ei' (openings of the sky). Rav Rechumi and Rav Yosef dispute what that means: one says they have no lintels, the other says they have no roof.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana explains that the baraita about a courtyard with many openings refers only to 'פיתְחֵי שִׁימָאֵי (openings of the sky)', i.e., incomplete doorways.
The Gemara asks what 'פיתְחֵי שִׁימָאֵי' means.

sub.text: Rav Rechumi and Rav Yosef's dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Rechumi and Rav Yosef's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rav Rechumi and Rav Yosef dispute the meaning: one says they lack doorposts (שִׁקְפֵי), the other says they lack a lintel (תִּיקְרָה).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish dispute about a field structure
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish dispute about a field structure
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rav's principle. A story is told about a man who planted four poles and stretched a vine over them, and the Sages permitted it for kilayim. Resh Lakish says they also permitted it for Shabbat, but Rabbi Yochanan says they permitted it only for kilayim, not for Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that Rabbi Yochanan agrees with Rav's principle, citing a story about a man who planted four poles and stretched a vine over them, which the Sages permitted for kilayim.
Resh Lakish states that just as the Sages permitted the structure for kilayim, they also permitted it for Shabbat.
Rabbi Yochanan disagrees, asserting that the Sages permitted the structure only for kilayim, not for Shabbat.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute and resolution
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the case: if the poles were placed on the side, Rav Chisda says a tzurat hapetach from the side is invalid. If on top, and if the height was ten cubits, would Rabbi Yochanan really say it's not permitted for Shabbat? So it must be more than ten cubits. Alternatively, it could be ten cubits and from the side, and they dispute Rav Chisda's ruling. The Gemara then notes contradictions within Rabbi Yochanan's and Resh Lakish's own statements, citing Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what case is being discussed, noting that if the poles were on the side, Rav Chisda rules that a tzurat hapetach (doorway form) made from the side is invalid.
The Gemara suggests the poles were on top, but then questions whether Rabbi Yochanan would really say it's not permitted for Shabbat if the height was ten cubits.
The Gemara resolves that the case must involve a height greater than ten cubits.
The Gemara objects that it could still be ten cubits and from the side, and they dispute Rav Chisda's ruling.
The Gemara shifts to note contradictions within Rabbi Yochanan's and Resh Lakish's own statements, citing Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yehuda bar Chanina.

items.text: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on partitions
items.text_en: Dispute between Reish Lakish and Rabbi Yochanan on partitions
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish permits a 'pe'ah' (projection) for kilayim but not for Shabbat, while Rabbi Yochanan rules it is invalid for both. The Gemara notes the contradiction between Reish Lakish's statements and between Rabbi Yochanan's statements.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: Reish Lakish permits a projection (פֵּיאָה) for kilayim but not for Shabbat, while Rabbi Yochanan rules it is invalid for both.
The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's statements are not contradictory (one is his own, one his teacher's), but Rabbi Yochanan's statements are contradictory.
The Gemara proposes that the contradiction could be resolved if one case is on top (עַל גַּבָּן) and the other from the side (מִן הַצַּד), but if both are from the side, the contradiction remains.
The Gemara answers that both are from the side, but one case involves a gap of ten handbreadths and the other more than ten.

sub.text: Supporting baraita (story of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri)
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita (story of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri)
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a story where Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri told Rabbi Yehoshua that a projection from the side is permitted within ten handbreadths but prohibited beyond ten, supporting the distinction.
The Gemara objects: if the story is about a projection on top, a baraita says that even beyond ten handbreadths it is permitted, contradicting the story's ruling.
The Gemara concludes that the story must be about a projection from the side, confirming the distinction between ten and more than ten handbreadths.

items.text: Resolution of the contradictions
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradictions
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradictions by distinguishing between a partition on top (על גבן) and one on the side (מן הצד), and between a height of ten handbreadths and more than ten. A story about Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri supports this distinction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Reish Lakish's self-contradiction is resolved by attributing one view to himself and one to his teacher, but Rabbi Yochanan's self-contradiction remains problematic.

The Gemara proposes a first resolution: the contradiction is resolved if one case involves a partition on top (על גבן) and the other on the side (מן הצד), but if both are on the side, the problem remains.
The Gemara offers a second resolution: both cases are on the side, but one involves a height of ten handbreadths and the other more than ten.

Rabbi Yochanan cites a story where Rabbi Yehoshua asked Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri about planting under a vine stretched between trees, and the answer distinguished between ten handbreadths (permitted) and more than ten (forbidden).
The Gemara objects: if the story is about a partition on top, more than ten should be forbidden, but a baraita permits even more than ten for a top partition.
The Gemara concludes that the story must be about a side partition, confirming the distinction between ten and more than ten handbreadths.

items.text: Laws of צורת הפתח
items.text_en: Laws of צורת הפתח
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a צורת הפתח (doorway form) made on the side is invalid, and that it must be sturdy enough to hold a door, even a straw one. Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai requires a היכר ציר (sign of a hinge), identified as אבקתא (dust/socket). Rav Acha bar Rav Avya finds that the students of Rav Ashi said nothing about this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that a צורת הפתח (doorway form) made on the side is invalid.
Rav Chisda adds that a valid צורת הפתח must be sturdy enough to hold a door, even a straw one.

sub.text: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish in the name of Rabbi Yannai
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish citing Rabbi Yannai requires a היכר ציר (sign of a hinge), identified as אבקתא (dust/socket).
Rav Acha bar Rav Avya finds that the students of Rav Ashi said nothing about this matter.

items.text: Dispute on whether the reeds must touch
items.text_en: Dispute on whether the reeds must touch
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a צורת הפתח consists of a reed on each side and one on top. Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet dispute whether the reeds must touch. Rav Nachman acts according to his view, and Rav Sheshet has his attendant remove the reeds, leading to a confrontation. Rav Sheshet then cites a mishna about a כיפה (arch) to support his position, with Abaye explaining the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages regarding completing the width by hollowing out.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines a צורת הפתח (doorway form) as a reed on each side and one on top.
The gemara asks whether the reeds must touch each other.
Rav Nachman rules that the reeds need not touch.
Rav Sheshet rules that the reeds must touch.
Rav Nachman acts according to his view in the house of the Exilarch.
Rav Sheshet instructs his attendant Rav Gadda to remove the reeds.

sub.text: Narrative: Rav Gadda's imprisonment and release
sub.text_en: Narrative: Rav Gadda's imprisonment and release
sub.desc_en: Rav Gadda is caught and imprisoned, but Rav Sheshet miraculously frees him by calling him out.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet's inquiry to Rabbah bar Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet's inquiry to Rabbah bar Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet asks Rabbah bar Shmuel if he knows a tannaitic source about a צורת הפתח.
Rabbah bar Shmuel cites a mishna about a כיפה (arch) where Rabbi Meir obligates a mezuzah and the Sages exempt, but both agree if its legs are ten handbreadths high it is obligated.
Abaye clarifies that all agree that if the arch is ten high without three handbreadth legs, or has three handbreadth legs but is not ten high, it is invalid.
Abaye explains that the dispute is when the arch has three handbreadth legs and is ten high but is not four handbreadths wide, and there is space to hollow out to complete it to four.
Abaye states that Rabbi Meir holds we hollow out to complete the width, while the Sages hold we do not.
Rav Sheshet tells Rabbah bar Shmuel not to reveal the mishna about the arch to the house of the Exilarch.

items.text: Mishnah: Validation of a מבוי
items.text_en: Mishnah: Validation of a מבוי
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on how to validate a מבוי (alleyway). Beit Shammai requires both a side-post (לחי) and a cross-beam (קורה), while Beit Hillel requires either. Rabbi Eliezer requires two side-posts. A student before Rabbi Akiva reports a dispute about the width of the alleyway.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on validating a מבוי (alleyway): Beit Shammai requires both a side-post (לחי) and a cross-beam (קורה), while Beit Hillel requires either.

The Mishnah continues with Rabbi Eliezer requiring two side-posts, a student before Rabbi Akiva reporting a dispute about the width of the alleyway, and Rabbi Akiva stating that the dispute applies to both narrow and wide alleyways.

items.text: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara: Analysis of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the anonymous Mishnah's attribution, then explains the positions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding the number of walls required by Torah law. It then raises a question about Rabbi Eliezer's opinion: whether he requires two side-posts and a cross-beam or just two side-posts. A story is brought to resolve this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the anonymous Mishnah follows, noting it aligns with neither Chananya nor the first Tanna.
Rav Yehuda explains that the Mishnah is discussing a closed alleyway (מבוי סתום), and Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute its permissibility.
The Gemara infers that Beit Shammai require four walls by Torah law (דאורייתא) since they demand both a side-post and a cross-beam.
The Gemara rejects the inference, distinguishing between liability for throwing (requires three walls) and permission to carry (requires four walls).
The Gemara infers that Beit Hillel require only three walls by Torah law since they permit either a side-post or a cross-beam.
The Gemara rejects the inference, distinguishing between liability for throwing (requires two walls) and permission to carry (requires three walls).
The Gemara raises a doubt about Rabbi Eliezer's opinion: whether he requires two side-posts and a cross-beam, or just two side-posts without a cross-beam.
The Gemara brings a story about Rabbi Eliezer visiting his student Rabbi Yosei ben Perida to resolve the doubt.

items.text: Opening story about a student and Rabban Gamliel
items.text_en: Opening story about a student and Rabban Gamliel
items.desc_en: A student finds Rabban Gamliel sitting in an alleyway with only one lechi. Rabban Gamliel tells him to make another lechi, and the student questions whether he needs to block it entirely. Rabban Gamliel responds that blocking is fine.

items.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on alleyway width
items.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling on alleyway width
items.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel states that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel agree that an alleyway less than four cubits wide needs nothing, and they only dispute over a width between four and ten cubits: Beit Shammai requires both a lechi and a korah, while Beit Hillel requires either.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the student's question
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the student's question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the student's statement 'Do I need to block it?' If the requirement were two lechis and a korah, the question makes sense. But if only two lechis without a korah, what does 'block it' mean? The Gemara explains that the student meant 'Do I need to block it with lechis?'

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says an alleyway less than four cubits needs nothing, but a baraita says it is permitted with either a lechi or a korah. Rav Ashi resolves that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel means it does not need both a lechi and a korah like Beit Shammai, nor two lechis like Rabbi Eliezer, but rather either a lechi or a korah like Beit Hillel.

items.text: Measurement for lechi width
items.text_en: Measurement for lechi width
items.desc_en: Rav Achlai or Rav Yechiel states that the lechi must be up to four handbreadths wide.

items.text: Dispute about courtyard partitions (pasei chatzer)
items.text_en: Dispute about courtyard partitions (pasei chatzer)
items.desc_en: Rav Sheishet quotes Rav Yirmeya bar Abba quoting Rav that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding courtyard partitions. Rav Nachman says the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak clarifies that 'the Sages' refers to Rabbi, and the one who disagrees is the Rabbis, as taught in a baraita: a courtyard is permitted with one pas, but Rabbi says two.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling and resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi quotes Rabbi Yochanan that a courtyard requires two pasin. Rabbi Zeira questions this, citing that Rabbi Yochanan said pasin need to be four handbreadths. If two pasin, that would be four on each side, but a baraita says a small courtyard needs ten and a large one eleven. Rabbi Zeira resolves that for one side, four handbreadths suffice; for two sides, any amount on each side. The baraita of Adda bar Avimi follows Rabbi, who holds like Rabbi Yosei.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling and resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling and resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef quotes Shmuel that a courtyard is permitted with one pas. Abaye objects, citing Shmuel's instruction to Rav Chananya bar Sheila to act only with a majority of the wall or two pasin. Rav Yosef explains that the case was a tongue of the sea entering a courtyard, and Rav Yehuda required only one pas. Abaye notes that water is lenient. The Gemara cites a related question about a hanging partition in a ruin, and resolves the contradiction by explaining that for one side, four handbreadths suffice; for two sides, any amount.

items.text: Rav Pappa's difficulty and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's difficulty and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa questions Shmuel's instruction: why require a majority of the wall when a pas of four handbreadths suffices? And if the wall is seven handbreadths, why need four? Three and a bit would suffice, as Rav Achlai said up to four. The Gemara offers two resolutions: one applies to a courtyard, the other to an alleyway; or Rav Achlai's statement itself is disputed among Tannaim.

items.text: Baraita on a tongue of the sea entering a courtyard
items.text_en: Baraita on a tongue of the sea entering a courtyard
items.desc_en: The baraita rules that one may not draw water from a tongue of the sea entering a courtyard on Shabbat unless it has a partition ten handbreadths high. This applies when the breach is more than ten cubits, but if exactly ten, no partition is needed. The Gemara questions why carrying is permitted if the courtyard is breached entirely to a forbidden area.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's initial ruling on an alleyway without partnership
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's initial ruling on an alleyway without partnership
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case involves an alleyway with projections (gidudei). Rav Yehuda rules that if an alleyway has not been joined by a partnership (shituf), a side-post (lechi) makes it a private domain for Shabbat, so throwing into it incurs liability, while a beam (korah) does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case involves an alleyway with projections (gidudei).

Rav Yehuda rules that if an alleyway has not been joined by a partnership (shituf), a side-post (lechi) makes it a private domain for Shabbat, so throwing into it incurs liability, while a beam (korah) does not.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's objection and supporting baraita
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's objection and supporting baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Rav Yehuda's ruling, arguing that if partnership were made, even a beam would render throwing liable, which is absurd. He cites a baraita stating that for courtyards of many and non-through alleyways, whether or not they joined, throwing is always liable.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet objects to Rav Yehuda's ruling, arguing that if partnership were made, even a beam would render one liable, which is absurd, and questions whether a loaf makes it a private or public domain.
A baraita is cited stating that for courtyards of many and non-through alleyways, whether or not they joined, throwing into them is always liable.

items.text: Revised version of Rav Yehuda's statement and the dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.text_en: Revised version of Rav Yehuda's statement and the dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a corrected version of Rav Yehuda's ruling: an alleyway unfit for partnership. It then explains that Rav Yehuda, Rabbah, and Rava debate the rationale: lechi is a partition (mechitzah) and korah is a recognition (heker), while Rava holds both are merely recognition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the corrected version of Rav Yehuda's statement: an alleyway unfit for partnership, if fitted with a lechi, throwing into it is liable; if fitted with a korah, throwing into it is exempt.
The Gemara explains that Rav Yehuda and Rabbah hold that a lechi is a partition (מחיצה) and a korah is a recognition (היכר), while Rava holds both are merely recognition.

items.text: Rav Yaakov bar Abba's objection to Rava and Rava's response
items.text_en: Rav Yaakov bar Abba's objection to Rava and Rava's response
items.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Abba cites a baraita that throwing into an alleyway with a lechi is liable, without a lechi is exempt. Rava explains that the baraita means only a lechi is needed; if there is a lechi and something else (like a korah), throwing is exempt.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yaakov bar Abba objects to Rava by citing a baraita that states throwing into an alleyway that has a lechi is liable, and without a lechi is exempt.
Rava explains that the baraita means only a lechi is needed; if there is a lechi and something else (like a korah), throwing is exempt.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on two houses across a public domain and the Sages' objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on two houses across a public domain and the Sages' objection
items.desc_en: A baraita states that Rabbi Yehuda permits a person with two houses on opposite sides of a public domain to use a lechi or korah on each side to carry between them. The Sages object that a public domain cannot be joined in this way. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that two partitions are biblically valid.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that a person with two houses on opposite sides of a public domain may place a lechi or korah on each side and carry between them.
The Sages object that a public domain cannot be joined in this manner.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds that two partitions are biblically valid, resolving the objection.

items.text: Rav's ruling on a square alleyway and Rabbi Zeira's explanation
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a square alleyway and Rabbi Zeira's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Rav rules that an alleyway whose length equals its width cannot be permitted with a minimal lechi. Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quoting Rav adds that it also cannot be permitted with a one-handbreadth beam. Rabbi Zeira explains that such an alleyway is considered a courtyard, which requires a four-handbreadth board.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's question and resolution regarding the lechi as a minimal board
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question and resolution regarding the lechi as a minimal board
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira questions why the lechi cannot serve as a minimal board (pas mashehu) to permit the courtyard. He resolves that he forgot the statement of Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan that courtyard boards require a width of four handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira questions why the lechi (side-post) cannot serve as a minimal board (pas mashehu) to permit the courtyard.
The gemara resolves that Rabbi Zeira forgot the statement of Rabbi Asi quoting Rabbi Yochanan that courtyard boards require a width of four handbreadths.

items.text: Rav Nachman's summary and the dispute between Shmuel and Rav
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's summary and the dispute between Shmuel and Rav
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states a rule: an alleyway whose length exceeds its width and has houses and courtyards opening into it is permitted with a lechi or korah; a square courtyard requires a four-handbreadth board. Shmuel thought the length must be double the width, but Rav said even a minimal excess suffices, citing a teaching from Rabbi Yishmael's student.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states a general rule: an alleyway whose length exceeds its width and has houses and courtyards opening into it is permitted with a lechi or korah, while a square courtyard requires a four-handbreadth board.
The gemara questions whether the rule implies that only a square courtyard requires a board, but a round one does not.
The gemara clarifies that Rav Nachman meant: if the length exceeds the width, it is an alleyway and suffices with a lechi or korah; otherwise, it is a courtyard.
The gemara asks how much the length must exceed the width.
Shmuel thought the length must be double the width.
Rav said that even a minimal excess suffices, citing a teaching from Rabbi Yishmael's student.
The gemara cites a teaching from a student of Rabbi Yishmael as support for Rav's position.

items.text: Identifying the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the first Tanna
items.text_en: Identifying the dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the first Tanna
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Akiva's statement differs from the first Tanna's view, and notes a dispute between Rav Ahlai and Rav Yechiel that remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Akiva's statement that the dispute applies to both cases.
The Gemara asks how Rabbi Akiva's view differs from the first Tanna's view.
The Gemara notes a dispute between Rav Ahlai and Rav Yechiel that remains unresolved, indicating the difference between the two views.

items.text: Rabbi Akiva attributes the statement to a student
items.text_en: Rabbi Akiva attributes the statement to a student
items.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Akiva saying that Rabbi Yishmael did not say this, but rather a certain student did, and the halakha follows that student.

sub.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Akiva denying that Rabbi Yishmael said this statement and attributing it instead to a certain student, with the halakha following that student.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes an internal contradiction: Rabbi Akiva first says Rabbi Yishmael did not say it (implying the halakha is not like him), then says the halakha follows that student. Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that Rabbi Akiva only said this to sharpen the students, while Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says the version is 'it seems' (nir'in).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out an internal contradiction in Rabbi Akiva's statement: he first says Rabbi Yishmael did not say it, implying the halakha is not like him, but then says the halakha follows that student.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel explains that Rabbi Akiva only said this to sharpen the students, not as a definitive ruling.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak offers an alternative resolution: the version of the baraita says 'it seems' (נִרְאִין), not a definitive statement.

items.text: Identifying the anonymous student as Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Identifying the anonymous student as Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that wherever it says 'a student said before Rabbi Akiva in the name of Rabbi Yishmael', it refers to Rabbi Meir, who served both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva. A baraita supports this with Rabbi Meir's testimony about his practice with inkwell (kankantum).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi identifies the anonymous student who said before Rabbi Akiva in the name of Rabbi Yishmael as Rabbi Meir, who served both Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Akiva.
A baraita cites Rabbi Meir's testimony that Rabbi Yishmael permitted him to put inkwell (kankantum) into the ink, while Rabbi Akiva forbade it.

items.text: Contradiction in traditions about Rabbi Meir's practice
items.text_en: Contradiction in traditions about Rabbi Meir's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a contradictory tradition: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel citing Rabbi Meir says that when studying with Rabbi Akiva he used kankantum without objection, but Rabbi Yishmael forbade it based on the verse 'write and erase'. Rabbi Meir then explains his concern for scribal errors, and Rabbi Yishmael's response about the requirement for erasable writing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a contradictory tradition: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel quoting Rabbi Meir says that when studying with Rabbi Akiva he used קַנְקַנְתּוֹם (iron sulfate) without objection, but Rabbi Yishmael warned him about scribal errors.

sub.text: Rabbi Meir's response to Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabbi Meir's response to Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir tells Rabbi Yishmael about his use of קַנְקַנְתּוֹם (iron sulfate), and Rabbi Yishmael objects based on the verse 'וְכָתַב וּמָחָה' (write and erase), requiring erasable writing.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yishmael meant and what Rabbi Meir answered.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir was saying he is not concerned about defective or plene spellings, nor about a fly blotting out a letter, because he uses קַנְקַנְתּוֹם (iron sulfate) to make the ink indelible.

items.text: Resolving the contradictions in service and prohibition
items.text_en: Resolving the contradictions in service and prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes two contradictions: one about which rabbi Rabbi Meir served first, and one about who forbade kankantum. The service contradiction is resolved by saying he first studied with Rabbi Akiva, then with Rabbi Yishmael for tradition, then returned to Rabbi Akiva for reasoning. The prohibition contradiction remains unresolved.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises two contradictions: one regarding which rabbi Rabbi Meir served first, and one regarding who prohibited the use of קַנְקַנְתּוֹם (iron sulfate).

The Gemara resolves the contradiction about service: Rabbi Meir first studied with רבי עקיבא (Rabbi Akiva), then with רבי ישמעאל (Rabbi Yishmael) for tradition, then returned to רבי עקיבא for reasoning.
The Gemara notes that the contradiction regarding who prohibited the use of קַנְקַנְתּוֹם (iron sulfate) remains unresolved.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about kankantum for Sotah passage
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about kankantum for Sotah passage
items.desc_en: A baraita records Rabbi Yehuda citing Rabbi Meir that kankantum may be used for all Torah writing except the Sotah passage, while Rabbi Yaakov in his name says except the Sotah passage in the Temple. Rav Yirmeya explains the difference is whether one may erase it from the Torah scroll.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records two versions of Rabbi Meir's ruling: Rabbi Yehuda reports that Rabbi Meir permitted kankantum (vitriol) for all Torah writing except the Sotah passage, while Rabbi Yaakov reports in his name that the exception is only the Sotah passage in the Temple.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two versions of Rabbi Meir's ruling.
Rav Yirmeya explains that the difference lies in whether one may erase the Sotah passage from the Torah scroll for reuse in the Temple ritual.

items.text: Comparing disputes about Sotah scroll and Torah erasure
items.text_en: Comparing disputes about Sotah scroll and Torah erasure
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares this dispute to another about whether a Sotah scroll can be used for another woman. Rav Pappa and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak each suggest that the earlier dispute may not apply to Torah erasure, as the Torah is written for study purposes, unlike a Sotah scroll designated for a specific woman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a baraita that parallels the earlier dispute: one Tanna says a Sotah scroll is not valid for another woman, while Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya permits it.

Rav Pappa argues that the first Tanna's ruling is limited to a scroll designated for a specific woman, but regarding a Torah scroll written for general study, erasing the Sotah passage would be permitted.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak counters that Rabbi Achai bar Yoshiya's leniency applies only to a scroll written for a Sotah, but a Torah written for study purposes may not be erased.
The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's position by citing a Mishnah about a get written for one wife and used for another, implying a parallel that might contradict his distinction.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling about a get found by a fellow townsman, arguing that the requirement for a get is writing for her sake, while for a sukka the requirement is making for her sake, which is erasure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling by contrasting the requirement of writing for her sake (כתיבה לשמה) in a get with the requirement of making for her sake (עשייה לשמה) in a sukka, arguing that the making here is erasure (מחיקה).

items.text: Praise for Rabbi Meir and his name
items.text_en: Praise for Rabbi Meir and his name
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Chanina explains why the halakha was not established like Rabbi Meir despite his greatness, and a baraisa discusses his name and that of Rabbi Nehorai.

sub.desc_en: רבי אחא בר חנינא (Rabbi Acha bar Chanina) states that it is known before God that no one in Rabbi Meir's generation equaled him, yet the halakha was not established like him because his colleagues could not fathom the depth of his reasoning, as he could argue for any position.
A ברייתא (baraita) teaches that Rabbi Meir's real name was Rabbi Nehorai, and he was called Meir because he illuminates the eyes of the sages in halakha.
The ברייתא (baraita) continues: Rabbi Nehorai's real name was Rabbi Nechemya (or Rabbi Elazar ben Arakh), and he was called Nehorai because he enlightens the eyes of the sages in halakha.

רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) says that his own incisiveness comes from having seen Rabbi Meir from behind; had he seen him from the front, he would be even sharper, citing the verse 'ועיניך רואות את מוריך' (and your eyes shall see your teacher).

items.text: The student Sumchus and a case of purity
items.text_en: The student Sumchus and a case of purity
items.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan about Rabbi Meir's student Sumchus who could give 48 reasons for impurity and purity. A baraisa tells of a veteran student who could purify a sheretz with 150 reasons, and Ravina attempts to do so but is dismissed.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Avahu quotes Rabbi Yochanan that Rabbi Meir had a student named Sumchus who could give 48 reasons for impurity and 48 for purity.
A baraita tells of a veteran student in Yavne who could purify the sheretz with 150 reasons.
Ravina attempts to purify the sheretz with a kal vachomer argument from the snake.
The Gemara rejects Ravina's argument, saying the snake is like a mere thorn that causes death but is not impure.

items.text: The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: The dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba quotes Shmuel about a three-year dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, resolved by a bat kol saying both are divine words but halakha follows Beit Hillel due to their humility. A story illustrates this, and a lesson about humility is derived.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba reports in the name of Shmuel that Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel disputed for three years, each claiming the halakha follows them, until a bat kol declared both views are divine words but the halakha follows Beit Hillel.
The Gemara asks: Since both opinions are words of the living God, why did Beit Hillel merit that the halakha be established according to them?
The Gemara answers: Because Beit Hillel were gentle and humble, they taught both their own words and those of Beit Shammai, and even gave precedence to Beit Shammai's words.

A baraita illustrates Beit Hillel's humility: in a dispute about a sukkah, Beit Hillel cited a precedent involving Rabbi Yochanan ben Hachoranit, but Beit Shammai rebutted that the precedent actually proves their own position.
The Gemara derives a moral lesson: one who humbles himself is elevated by God, and one who pursues greatness finds it fleeing from him, while one who flees from greatness is pursued by it.

items.text: Debate on whether it is better to be created or not
items.text_en: Debate on whether it is better to be created or not
items.desc_en: The rabbis taught a two-and-a-half-year dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel about whether it is better for a person not to have been created, concluding it is better not to have been created, but now that one is created, one should examine one's deeds.

sub.desc_en: A baraita records a dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel over whether it would have been better for man not to have been created, concluding that it would have been better, but since he was created, he should examine his deeds.
The baraita concludes that they voted and agreed it is better not to have been created, but now that one is created, one should examine one's deeds.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of the sukka beam
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of the sukka beam
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the requirements for the beam (korah) of a sukka: it must be wide enough to receive a brick (ari'ach), which is half a brick of three handbreadths, and strong enough. Rabbi Yehuda allows width without strength. Various cases of materials and shapes are addressed.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by defining the required width of the sukka beam (korah) as sufficient to receive a brick (ari'ach), which is half a brick of three handbreadths, so the beam must be at least one handbreadth wide.
The Mishnah states the Tanna Kamma's requirement that the beam be both wide and strong enough to hold a brick, while Rabbi Yehuda permits width without strength.

The Mishnah concludes with rules for beams made of straw, reeds, curved or round materials, treating them as if they were metal, straight, or square, and states that any beam with a circumference of three handbreadths has a width of one handbreadth.

items.text: Gemara's question on beam width
items.text_en: Gemara's question on beam width
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a beam needs to be one handbreadth wide, given that it must also support a half-brick. It answers that the beam is one handbreadth wide to receive the brick, and the extra half-handbreadth is filled with clay on both sides to stabilize it.

items.text: Dispute on strength of beam and supports
items.text_en: Dispute on strength of beam and supports
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna and Rav Chisda disagree about whether the supports of the beam need to be as strong as the beam itself. Rabbah bar Rav Huna says only the beam needs to be strong enough to hold a brick, while Rav Chisda says both beam and supports must be strong enough.

items.text: Case of beam covered by a mat
items.text_en: Case of beam covered by a mat
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet presents a case where a beam is placed over an alleyway and covered with a mat that is raised three handbreadths from the ground. He rules that it is neither a valid beam (since it is covered) nor a valid partition (since kids can break through it).

items.text: Baraita on beams that do not reach the opposite wall
items.text_en: Baraita on beams that do not reach the opposite wall
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses cases where a beam does not reach the opposite wall, or two beams do not meet. If the gap is less than three handbreadths, no additional beam is needed; if three or more, one is needed. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel argues the threshold is four handbreadths. Additional cases include beams that together can hold a brick, and beams one above the other, with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's ruling on viewing them as if they were aligned.

items.text: Abaye's analysis of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's opinion
items.text_en: Abaye's analysis of Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's opinion
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda agrees with his father Rabbi Yehuda in one respect (the principle of 'we view') but disagrees in another: Rabbi Yehuda allows a beam above twenty cubits, while Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda only allows it within twenty cubits.

items.text: Dispute on beam width and strength
items.text_en: Dispute on beam width and strength
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says a beam is valid if it is wide even if not strong. Rav Yehuda taught this before Rav, who corrected him to say 'wide and strong'. Rabbi Ila'a citing Rav says a beam four handbreadths wide is valid even if not strong, distinguishing it from a narrower beam.

items.text: Mishnah cases: beam of straw, bent beam, curved beam
items.text_en: Mishnah cases: beam of straw, bent beam, curved beam
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needs to specify that a beam of straw is valid (to teach that we view it as if it were of a different material), that a bent beam is valid (to teach Rabbi Zeira's rule about the bend being outside the alleyway or above twenty cubits), and that a curved beam is valid (to teach that we view it as if it were straight, and to address concern about being drawn after the curve).

items.text: Rule of circular beam and proof from Solomon's Sea
items.text_en: Rule of circular beam and proof from Solomon's Sea
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a circular beam is viewed as if it were square, and any circle with a circumference of three handbreadths has a diameter of one handbreadth. Rabbi Yochanan derives this from the verse about Solomon's Sea. The Gemara addresses objections about the lip of the Sea and the slight thickness, concluding that the measurement was from the inside.

items.text: Baraita on the capacity of Solomon's Sea
items.text_en: Baraita on the capacity of Solomon's Sea
items.desc_en: A baraita taught by Rabbi Chiya states that Solomon's Sea held 150 ritual baths (mikva'ot), and a mikveh is 40 se'ah. The Gemara begins to discuss this but is cut off.

items.text: Calculating the volume of Solomon's sea
items.text_en: Calculating the volume of Solomon's sea
items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the volume of a mikveh (40 se'ah) and compares it to the dimensions of Solomon's sea, which was round. It notes that a square has a quarter more area than a circle, leading to a discrepancy in the volume calculation.

items.text: Rami bar Yechezkel's tradition on the sea's shape
items.text_en: Rami bar Yechezkel's tradition on the sea's shape
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel teaches that Solomon's sea had its lower three amot square and upper two amot round, resolving the volume discrepancy.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the sea's capacity
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the sea's capacity
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the verse says 'its lip was round,' implying the entire sea was round, but then resolves that the capacity of 2000 bat (6000 se'ah) matches the dimensions, with the extra 3000 bat attributed to the 'gudsah' (the bulge).

items.text: Abaye's deduction and a supporting Mishnah
items.text_en: Abaye's deduction and a supporting Mishnah
items.desc_en: Abaye deduces that the gudsah is one-third of the total capacity, and cites a Mishnah about vessels that hold 40 se'ah wet but 2 kor dry, showing that the bulge accounts for the difference.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara on the lechi
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara on the lechi
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states the lechi must be ten handbreadths high, with any width and thickness; Rabbi Yosei requires three handbreadths width. The Gemara clarifies that the dispute refers to the lechi debated by Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, and Rabbi Chiyya teaches that even a thread suffices for width.

items.text: Rava's ruling on a lechi placed improperly
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on a lechi placed improperly
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case where a lechi is made for half a mavoy, and Rava rules that if the lechi is raised three handbreadths from the ground or separated three from the wall, it is invalid, even according to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's principle of lavud, since goats can break through below.

items.text: Dispute over the halakha like Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Dispute over the halakha like Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef quotes Shmuel that the halakha does not follow Rabbi Yosei regarding helmei (a type of partition) or lechi. Rav Huna bar Chinana questions this, and Rav Yosef explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Yosei on lechi. Rava later retracts, citing that Rabbi Yosei's reasoning is sound. Finally, Rava bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye for the halakha, who says to follow popular custom.

items.text: Alternative version of the custom ruling
items.text_en: Alternative version of the custom ruling
items.desc_en: Some teach the same principle (follow popular custom) regarding the blessing for drinking water, where Rabbi Tarfon has a different formulation. Rav Chanan asks Abaye for the halakha, and Abaye again says to follow popular custom.

items.text: Dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding a side-post that came on its own
items.text_en: Dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding a side-post that came on its own
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava disagree about a side-post that grew on its own. Abaye holds it is valid if they relied on it from yesterday, while Rava holds it is never valid because it was not originally intended as a side-post.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding a side-post that came on its own: Abaye says it is valid, Rava says it is not.

items.text: Gemara's assumption that the dispute extends to partitions
items.text_en: Gemara's assumption that the dispute extends to partitions
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that the same dispute applies to a partition that came on its own, not just a side-post.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that the dispute between Abaye and Rava regarding a side-post (לחי) that came on its own also applies to a partition (מחיצה) that came on its own.

items.text: First attempt to prove from a sukkah between trees
items.text_en: First attempt to prove from a sukkah between trees
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a sukkah made between trees that are pruned for it, which is valid. It explains that the case is where the trees were planted for that purpose, and the teaching is to prevent using the tree itself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a sukkah made between trees that are pruned for it, which is valid, as a potential proof regarding a partition that came about on its own.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the trees were planted for that purpose from the outset, so it does not prove the general rule.
The Gemara explains that the baraita's novelty is to prevent a concern that one might use the tree itself, teaching that it is permitted לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

items.text: Second attempt: a tree that shades the ground
items.text_en: Second attempt: a tree that shades the ground
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case of a tree whose branches are within three handbreadths of the ground, allowing carrying underneath. It explains that the tree was planted for that purpose, but limits the area to beit se'atayim because it is a dwelling for airspace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a tree whose branches shade the ground within three handbreadths, permitting carrying underneath.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the tree was planted from the outset for that purpose.
The Gemara objects that if so, one should be allowed to carry in the entire area under the tree.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua answers that only a beit se'atayim (an area of two se'ah) is permitted for carrying.
The Gemara explains that the tree is considered a dwelling for airspace (דירה שתשמישה לאוויר), which limits carrying to beit se'atayim.

items.text: Third attempt: a mound or ravine, and resolution of the dispute
items.text_en: Third attempt: a mound or ravine, and resolution of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a case of a mound or ravine that is ten handbreadths high/deep and up to beit se'atayim, where one may walk the entire area. It rejects the forced explanation that it was made for that purpose, and concludes that the dispute is only about a side-post, not a partition. Abaye holds a side-post is valid because it is like a partition, and a partition that came on its own is valid; Rava holds a side-post requires recognition, which only exists if made by hand.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a mound or ravine ten handbreadths high/deep and up to beit se'atayim, where one may walk the entire area and beyond.
The Gemara objects that the baraita's case of a mound or ravine cannot be explained as made intentionally for a partition, unlike the previous cases of a tree or grain field.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute between Abaye and Rava is only about a side-post (לחי), not a partition; Abaye holds a side-post is valid because it is like a partition, and a partition that came on its own is valid, while Rava holds a side-post requires recognition, which only exists if made by hand.

items.text: Fourth attempt: stones protruding from a fence
items.text_en: Fourth attempt: stones protruding from a fence
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about stones protruding from a fence that are less than three handbreadths apart, which do not require another side-post. It explains that the stones were built for that purpose, and the teaching is that they are not merely a building addition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about stones protruding from a fence that are less than three handbreadths apart, which do not require another side-post.
The Gemara explains that the stones were built for that purpose from the start, and the teaching is that they are not merely a building addition.

items.text: Fifth attempt: a wall with one side recessed
items.text_en: Fifth attempt: a wall with one side recessed
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita from Rabbi Chiyya about a wall where one side is recessed, which is considered a side-post. It explains that the wall was made for that purpose, and the teaching is that it is valid whether the recess is visible from outside or inside.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chiyya's baraita
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rabbi Chiyya's baraita
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from Rabbi Chiyya about a wall with one side recessed, which is considered a side-post (לחי).
The Gemara explains that the wall was made for that purpose from the start, and the teaching is that it is valid whether the recess is visible from outside or inside.

items.text: Proof from Rav's action and final resolution
items.text_en: Proof from Rav's action and final resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where Rav used a fallen palm branch as a side-post, and Rav Huna questioned him because they had not relied on it from yesterday. The Gemara infers that if they had relied on it, it would be valid. It then notes that Abaye and Rava's dispute is about a case where they did not rely on it from yesterday, but the story of Bar Havu shows they also disputed where they did rely on it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a story where Rav used a fallen palm branch as a side-post, and Rav Huna questioned him because they had not relied on it from yesterday.
The Gemara infers that if they had relied on it from yesterday, the branch would be a valid side-post.
The Gemara suggests that Abaye and Rava's dispute is only about a case where they did not rely on it from yesterday.
The Gemara rejects this, noting that the story of Bar Havu shows Abaye and Rava disputed even where they did rely on it from yesterday.

items.text: Mishnah: materials for side-posts and impurity of a grave cover
items.text_en: Mishnah: materials for side-posts and impurity of a grave cover
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that any material may be used for side-posts, even something living, though Rabbi Meir forbids it. It also states that such a side-post can become impure as a grave cover (golel).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that any material may be used for side-posts, even something living (though Rabbi Meir forbids it), and such a side-post can become impure as a grave cover (golel).

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir permits writing a get on a living animal, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili disqualifies it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir permits writing a get on a living animal, while Rabbi Yosei HaGelili disqualifies it.

items.text: Gemara cites a baraita expanding the dispute
items.text_en: Gemara cites a baraita expanding the dispute
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited where Rabbi Meir prohibits using any living creature as a wall for a sukkah, a side-post for a alleyway, planks for wells, or a tombstone. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili adds that one may not write a get on it.

sub.desc_en: A baraita elaborates that Rabbi Meir prohibits using a living animal for various halachic structures, and in the name of Rabbi Yosei HaGelili, also prohibits writing a get on it.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning from a verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning from a verse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's source: from the verse "sefer" (book) and "ve-khatav lah" (and he shall write for her), he derives that the get must be written on something without a living spirit and not food.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's reasoning, citing a baraita that derives from 'ספר' (a book) and 'וכתב לה' (and he writes for her) that the get must be on something without life and not food.
The baraita expounds the verse: from 'sefer' alone only a book is included, but 've-khatav lah' expands to any material, then 'sefer' restricts to something without a living spirit and not food.

items.text: Rabbis' response and alternative derivation
items.text_en: Rabbis' response and alternative derivation
items.desc_en: The Rabbis argue that "sefer" means merely a written document, not excluding living animals. They use "ve-khatav lah" to teach that divorce is by writing, not by money, countering a possible analogy from betrothal.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the Rabbis interpret the word 'ספר' (sefer), and answers that it means merely a count of things, not excluding living animals.
The Gemara explains that the Rabbis derive from 'וְכָתַב לָהּ' (and he wrote for her) that divorce is by writing, not by money, countering a possible analogy from betrothal.

items.text: Further derivation and dispute on 'sefer keritut'
items.text_en: Further derivation and dispute on 'sefer keritut'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives from "sefer keritut" that only a document severs the marriage. The Rabbis use that phrase to require a complete severance, not conditional divorce. Rabbi Yosei HaGelili learns from the double language of "karet" and "keritut", while the Rabbis do not derive from that.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derive the reasoning that only a document (ספר) severs marriage, excluding other materials?
The Gemara answers: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives it from the phrase 'ספר כריתות' (a book of severance), meaning only a document severs her, not any other thing.

The Gemara objects: The Rabbis require the phrase 'ספר כריתות' for a different derivation — that the divorce must be a complete severance between husband and wife, as taught in a baraita about conditional divorce.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives the severance requirement from the double language of 'כרת' and 'כריתות', while the Rabbis do not derive from that double language.

items.text: Mishnah on a caravan encamped in a valley
items.text_en: Mishnah on a caravan encamped in a valley
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a caravan encamps in a valley and surrounds itself with animal equipment, they may carry within, provided the fence is ten handbreadths high and breaches are not more than the standing wall. A breach up to ten cubits is permitted as a doorway; more is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a caravan that encamped in a valley and surrounded itself with animal equipment, permitting carrying within if the fence is ten handbreadths high and breaches are not more than the standing part, with a breach up to ten cubits considered a doorway.
The Mishnah concludes that a breach up to ten cubits is permitted as a doorway, but more than that is forbidden.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Huna on 'parutz ke-omed'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Huna on 'parutz ke-omed'
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua dispute whether a breach equal to the standing wall is permitted. Rav Pappa says permitted, citing a tradition that the Torah did not require a majority to be standing. Rav Huna says forbidden, citing a tradition that the majority must be standing.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a dispute between Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua regarding whether a breach equal to the standing wall (פָּרוּץ כְּעוֹמֵד) is permitted or forbidden.
Rav Pappa rules that it is permitted, citing a tradition that the Torah taught Moses not to breach the majority (לָא תִּפְרוֹץ רוּבָּה).
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua rules that it is forbidden, citing a tradition that the Torah taught Moses to fence in the majority (גְּדוֹר רוּבָּה).

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa from the Mishnah's phrase "breaches not more than the standing wall," implying that if equal, it is permitted. The Gemara reinterprets: it means if the standing wall exceeds the breaches, it is permitted; if equal, it is forbidden. This leaves a difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Pappa from the Mishnah: the phrase 'breaches not more than the standing wall' implies that if they are equal, it is permitted, contradicting Rav Pappa's ruling.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah: it means that if the standing wall exceeds the breaches, it is permitted, not that equality is permitted.
The Gemara objects: if equality is forbidden, the Mishnah should have said 'breaches not equal to the standing wall,' leaving the difficulty unresolved.

items.text: Attempted proofs from sukkah and caravan cases
items.text_en: Attempted proofs from sukkah and caravan cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a proof from a sukkah roofed with spits or bed poles: if the gaps equal the beams, it is valid. The Gemara deflects by saying the case is where the beams are inserted and removed. Rabbi Ami says it is when they overlap slightly. Rava says if they were placed as warp, one places them as woof. The Gemara then cites a baraita about a caravan surrounded by camels and saddles.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove the principle of 'פָּרוּץ כְּעוֹמֵד' (breach equals standing) from a baraita about a sukkah roofed with spits or bed poles, where if the gaps equal the beams it is valid.
The Gemara deflects the proof by explaining the baraita deals with a case where the beams are inserted and removed (נִכְנָס וְיוֹצֵא), not a fixed structure.
The Gemara objects that it is impossible to precisely adjust the beams to exactly match the gaps.
Rabbi Ami answers that the case is where the beams overlap slightly (מַעֲדִיף), so the gaps are not exactly equal to the beams.
Rava answers that if the beams were placed as warp (עֵרֶב), one places them as woof (שְׁתִי), and vice versa, changing the configuration.
The Gemara brings another attempted proof from a baraita about a caravan surrounded by camels and saddles (אוּכָּפוֹת).

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists materials (עביטין, שליפין, קנים, קולחות) used for partitions, permitting carrying within them provided the gaps between camels, saddles, or troughs are not as wide as the object itself.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah lists materials (עביטין, שליפין, קנים, קולחות) used for partitions, permitting carrying within them provided the gaps between camels, saddles, or troughs are not as wide as the object itself.

items.text: Gemara's initial resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's initial resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's allowance applies when the objects are inserted and removed (נכנס ויוצא), implying a gap smaller than the object's full measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the Mishnah's allowance by explaining that the objects are inserted and removed (נכנס ויוצא), meaning the gap is less than the object's full measure.

items.text: Baraita on three measures of partitions
items.text_en: Baraita on three measures of partitions
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited detailing three categories of partition height: less than 3 handbreadths (requires gap less than 3), 3 to 4 handbreadths (gap less than its measure), and 4 to 10 cubits (gap less than its measure, with rules for breach vs. standing). It concludes with a case of reeds and a top beam allowing larger gaps.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating there are three measures for partitions, and defines the first: a partition less than 3 handbreadths high requires gaps less than 3 handbreadths to prevent a goat from sticking its head through.

The baraita defines the second measure: a partition of 3 to 4 handbreadths requires gaps less than its own measure to avoid a breach exceeding the standing part, and if the breach exceeds the standing part, even opposite the standing part is forbidden.

The baraita defines the third measure: a partition of 4 to 10 cubits requires gaps less than its own measure, with rules for when breach equals standing (opposite standing permitted, opposite breach forbidden) and when standing exceeds breach (even opposite breach permitted).
The baraita concludes: if the breach exceeds 10 cubits it is forbidden, but if there are reeds with a top beam, even a breach greater than 10 cubits is permitted.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Pappa
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Pappa
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's first clause (3 to 4 handbreadths) requires the gap not to be its full measure (מלואו), which contradicts Rav Pappa's position that the Mishnah's allowance requires a gap of exactly its full measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the baraita's first clause explicitly requires the gap not to be its full measure (מלואו), which contradicts Rav Pappa's position that the Mishnah's allowance requires a gap of exactly its full measure.

items.text: Rav Pappa's defense and support
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's defense and support
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that 'מלואו' in the baraita means 'inserted and removed' (נכנס ויוצא), not the exact full measure. The Gemara finds support from the baraita's continuation that when breach exceeds standing, only opposite standing is forbidden, implying opposite breach is permitted—consistent with Rav Pappa's interpretation.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that 'מלואו' in the baraita means 'inserted and removed' (נכנס ויוצא), not the exact full measure.

The Gemara finds support from the baraita's continuation that when breach exceeds standing, only opposite standing is forbidden, implying opposite breach is permitted—consistent with Rav Pappa's interpretation.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge to Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua from the baraita's end clause (standing exceeds breach permits opposite breach), implying opposite standing is forbidden. Both challenges are resolved: Rav Pappa's difficulty with the end is due to stylistic pairing, and Rav Huna's difficulty with the beginning is similarly explained.
