sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a challenge to Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua from the baraita's end clause, which implies that when standing exceeds breach, the area opposite the breach is permitted, but when they are equal, it is forbidden.
The Gemara notes that the end clause poses a difficulty for Rav Pappa, while the first clause poses a difficulty for Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua.

The Gemara resolves that the end clause poses no difficulty for Rav Pappa, because the tanna paired the expression 'breach exceeds standing' in the first clause with 'standing exceeds breach' in the end clause for stylistic symmetry.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution for Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution for Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the first clause poses no difficulty for Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua, because the tanna, intending to teach 'standing exceeds breach' in the end clause, taught the parallel 'breach exceeds standing' in the first clause for stylistic symmetry.

items.text: Analysis of why Rav Pappa and Rav Huna differ on combining clauses
items.text_en: Analysis of why Rav Pappa and Rav Huna differ on combining clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav Pappa does not combine the first two clauses because their disqualifications differ (one for goat's head, one for breach). Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua would have combined them, but the Gemara notes the disqualifications are not comparable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that according to Rav Pappa, it is understandable why the tanna did not combine the first two clauses.
The Gemara objects that according to Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua, the tanna should have combined the first two clauses into one.

The Gemara resolves that the clauses were not combined because the disqualification in the first clause (preventing a goat from leaping headlong) is not similar to the disqualification in the latter clause (preventing the breached segment from equaling the standing segment).

items.text: Attribution of the first clause to the Rabbis
items.text_en: Attribution of the first clause to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the first clause (less than 3 handbreadths) as following the Rabbis, who apply the principle of לבוד (joining) only for gaps less than 3 handbreadths. It then begins citing the second clause (3 to 4 handbreadths).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the first clause (less than 3 handbreadths) as following the Rabbis, who apply the principle of לבוד (joining) only for gaps less than 3 handbreadths.
The Gemara begins citing the second clause (3 to 4 handbreadths) to test the positions of Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua.

items.text: Analysis of the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis regarding lavud
items.text_en: Analysis of the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis regarding lavud
items.desc_en: The Gemara examines the positions of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis concerning the principle of lavud (joining) for gaps less than four handbreadths. Abaye argues that the Rabbis agree that a gap of less than three handbreadths is considered joined, while Rava maintains that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling applies only above, not below, where the partition is ineffective because kids can break through.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and the Rabbis regarding the principle of לָבוּד (joining) for gaps less than four handbreadths, noting that the Rabbis treat three and four handbreadths as equivalent.

Abaye argues that both the first and second clauses of the Mishnah reflect the Rabbis' view, and the Rabbis concede that a gap of less than three handbreadths is considered joined, while a gap of three to four is significant only if it creates a space of four handbreadths.

Rava counters that both clauses follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who applies לָבוּד only above (where kids cannot break through), but below the partition is ineffective because kids can break through, so לָבוּד is not invoked.

items.text: Refutation of Rav Pappa and the ruling in accordance with him
items.text_en: Refutation of Rav Pappa and the ruling in accordance with him
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about courtyards with many doors and windows, which implies that if the standing part is greater than the breached part, it is permitted, but if the breached part is greater, it is prohibited. This serves as a refutation of Rav Pappa's position, yet the halakha is ruled in accordance with Rav Pappa because the Mishnah supports him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about courtyards with many doors and windows, which states that it is permitted only if the standing part exceeds the breached part, to challenge Rav Pappa's position.
The Gemara objects to the wording 'most of them' and corrects it to 'many of them', while maintaining the condition that standing must exceed breached.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita refutes Rav Pappa, yet the halakha is ruled in accordance with Rav Pappa.
The Gemara explains the apparent contradiction: the halakha follows Rav Pappa because the Mishnah supports him, as it implies that if the building part equals the breached part, it is permitted.

items.text: Mishnah: Enclosing with ropes and reeds
items.text_en: Mishnah: Enclosing with ropes and reeds
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one may enclose an area with three ropes placed one above the other, provided there is no gap of three handbreadths between them, and the total height is ten handbreadths. It also discusses enclosures with reeds and the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding whether the rules were stated for a caravan or for the general case, and between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and the Sages regarding the requirement of both warp and woof for a valid partition.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one may enclose an area with three ropes placed one above the other, provided there is no gap of three handbreadths between them.
The Mishnah adds that the ropes' thickness must exceed a handbreadth so that the total height reaches ten handbreadths.
The Mishnah states that one may also enclose with reeds, provided there is no gap of three handbreadths between them.
Rabbi Yehuda says the Mishnah's rules were stated only for a caravan (שיירה), not for an individual.
The Sages disagree, saying the rules were stated for the general case (ההוה), not specifically for a caravan.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda rules that any partition lacking both warp (שתי) and woof (ערב) is not a valid partition.
The Sages counter that a partition with either warp or woof alone suffices.

items.text: Gemara: Rav Hamnuna's inquiry about standing partition in the woof
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav Hamnuna's inquiry about standing partition in the woof
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna asks whether the principle of 'standing greater than breached' applies to the woof as well as the warp. Abaye attempts to prove it from the Mishnah's requirement that the ropes be more than a handbreadth thick, but the Gemara refutes this by showing that a different arrangement would not work. Rav Hamnuna's actual question is about a mat with a hollow, and Rav Ashi explains that the inquiry is about a suspended partition in a ruin.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna, citing Rav, notes that the principle of 'standing greater than breached' applies to the warp (שתי) and asks whether it also applies to the woof (ערב).
Abaye attempts to prove from the Mishnah's requirement that the ropes' thickness exceed a handbreadth that the woof is considered standing, since otherwise a thinner arrangement would suffice.

The Gemara refutes Abaye by showing that a different arrangement of gaps and ropes would not work due to the problem of a partition that kids breach or air from both sides nullifying it, and incidentally proves that standing greater than breached from two sides is valid.

The Gemara clarifies that Rav Hamnuna's actual question concerns a mat with a hollow of three handbreadths, leaving a standing portion of four-plus handbreadths, placed within less than three handbreadths of the ground.

Rav Ashi explains that Rav Hamnuna's inquiry was about a suspended partition (מחיצה תלויה) in a ruin, citing Rabbi Tavla's question to Rav and Rav's answer that a suspended partition only permits carrying in water, as it is a leniency the Sages granted regarding water.

items.text: Gemara: The dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and the Sages regarding an individual vs. a caravan
items.text_en: Gemara: The dispute between Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda and the Sages regarding an individual vs. a caravan
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's allowance for a caravan applies only to a group, not an individual, and brings a baraita where Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda distinguishes between an individual (two se'ah) and a caravan (six se'ah), while the Sages allow all their needs. Rav Nachman initially rules like Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda but retracts after being challenged, ultimately ruling that three people are considered a caravan and receive all their needs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's allowance of encircling with reeds applies only to a caravan and not to an individual.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda states that for an individual, Shabbat partitions are only permitted up to two se'ah of space.

sub.text: Rav Nachman / Rav Bivi bar Abaye's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman / Rav Bivi bar Abaye's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman (or Rav Bivi bar Abaye) explains that the Mishnah's distinction is not about the size of the enclosed area but about providing the caravan with all their needs.
The Gemara digresses to clarify the original context of Rav Nachman's statement, linking it to the dispute about partitions of warp and woof.
The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda actually holds that view, citing a baraita that equates an individual and a caravan regarding ropes.
The baraita details Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda's position: an individual gets two se'ah, two people get two se'ah, and three become a caravan receiving six se'ah.
The baraita continues with the Sages' position: both an individual and a caravan receive all their needs, provided that two se'ah are not left empty.

sub.text: Rav Nachman / Rav Bivi bar Abaye's answer
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman / Rav Bivi bar Abaye's answer
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman (or Rav Bivi bar Abaye) reiterates that the dispute is about providing all their needs, not about the size of the enclosed area.
Rav Nachman initially rules in accordance with Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda, citing Shmuel: an individual gets two se'ah, two get two se'ah, and three become a caravan receiving six se'ah.
The Gemara challenges Rav Nachman for abandoning the Sages' position and ruling like Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's retraction and final ruling
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's retraction and final ruling
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman retracts his earlier ruling and declares that three people are considered a caravan and receive all their needs, aligning with the Sages.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction in the mishnah
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction in the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the beginning of the mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and the end follows the Rabbis, and answers that this is indeed the case because his father (Rabbi Yehuda) follows his own consistent approach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the beginning of the mishnah follows Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Yehuda and the end follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara answers that this is indeed the case because his father (Rabbi Yehuda) follows his own consistent approach.

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement about three in five and seven
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement about three in five and seven
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel reports in the name of Rav that three sukkot in an area of five se'ah are forbidden, but in seven se'ah they are permitted. When questioned, he insists Rav indeed said this. Rav Ashi explains that Rav meant that if they needed six se'ah and enclosed seven, even seven is permitted; if they needed only five and enclosed seven, even five is forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Giddel in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel reports in the name of Rav that three sukkot in an area of five se'ah are forbidden, but in seven se'ah they are permitted.
The Gemara questions Rav Giddel, asking whether Rav actually said this.
Rav Giddel swears by the Torah, Prophets, and Writings that Rav indeed said this.

Rav Ashi resolves the apparent contradiction by explaining that Rav meant: if they needed six se'ah and enclosed seven, even seven is permitted; if they needed only five and enclosed seven, even five is forbidden.

items.text: Clarifying the mishnah's phrase 'empty beit se'atayim'
items.text_en: Clarifying the mishnah's phrase 'empty beit se'atayim'
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnah's condition that there not be an empty beit se'atayim means empty of people or empty of vessels, and concludes it means empty of vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the mishnah's phrase 'empty beit se'atayim' means empty of people.
The Gemara answers that it means empty of vessels, not people.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yitzchak: Shabbat or residents determine
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rabbi Yitzchak: Shabbat or residents determine
items.desc_en: A dispute is recorded: if three people established an eruv and one died, or two and others joined, Rav Huna says Shabbat determines the matter (once permitted, it remains permitted), while Rabbi Yitzchak says the residents determine it. The Gemara concludes that Rav Huna holds that Shabbat determines, based on Rabba's inquiry about a blocked entrance and Rav Huna's response that once Shabbat is permitted, it remains permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: if three people established an eruv and one died, or two and others joined, one authority says Shabbat determines the matter, and another says the residents determine it.

The Gemara concludes that Rav Huna is the one who says Shabbat determines, citing Rabba's inquiry to Rav Huna about a blocked entrance and Rav Huna's response that once Shabbat is permitted, it remains permitted.

items.text: Linking the dispute to Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda's debate
items.text_en: Linking the dispute to Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Yehuda's debate
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rav Huna and Rabbi Yitzchak's dispute corresponds to the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding a breached courtyard. Rav Huna explains that even Rabbi Yosei would agree here because the partitions still exist, while Rabbi Yitzchak explains that even Rabbi Yehuda would agree here because there are no residents. The Gemara then notes a difference between the Tanna Kamma and the Sages regarding a single resident in a settled area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Huna and Rabbi Yitzchak's dispute corresponds to the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding a breached courtyard, citing the Mishnah.
The Gemara proposes that Rav Huna follows Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yitzchak follows Rabbi Yosei.
Rav Huna explains that even Rabbi Yosei would agree here because the partitions still exist, unlike in the Mishnah's case.
Rabbi Yitzchak explains that even Rabbi Yehuda would agree here because there are no residents, unlike in the Mishnah's case.
The Gemara asks whether the Sages' statement that one of two things is required is identical to the Tanna Kamma's position.
The Gemara answers that the difference between the Tanna Kamma and the Sages is the case of a single resident in a settled area.

items.text: Mishnah: Four leniencies in a military camp and Gemara's discussion
items.text_en: Mishnah: Four leniencies in a military camp and Gemara's discussion
items.desc_en: The mishnah lists four things permitted in a military camp: gathering wood from anywhere, exemption from hand-washing, from doubtfully tithed produce, and from eruv. The Gemara cites a baraita that permits gathering dry wood, and questions whether this is not already Joshua's condition. It distinguishes between thorns and other wood, attached and detached, moist and dry. It also discusses Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima's ruling about burying the dead on site, noting that a met mitzvah acquires its place.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by listing four leniencies permitted in a military camp: gathering wood from anywhere, exemption from hand-washing, from doubtfully tithed produce, and from eruv.
A baraita is cited that permits gathering dry wood in a discretionary war camp, and Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima adds that they may camp anywhere and bury the dead on site.
The Gemara questions whether this permission is not already part of Joshua's ten conditions, which allowed gathering wood from fields.
The Gemara distinguishes: Joshua's condition applied only to thorns and brambles, while the baraita permits other types of wood.
Alternatively, the Gemara distinguishes: Joshua's condition applied to attached wood, while the baraita permits detached wood.
A third distinction: Joshua's condition applied to moist wood, while the baraita permits dry wood.
The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda ben Teima's ruling about burying the dead on site, noting that a met mitzvah (abandoned corpse) acquires its place by default.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary even though the principle of met mitzvah applies, implying a further nuance (the text is cut off).

items.text: Definition of מת מצוה and its acquisition of place
items.text_en: Definition of מת מצוה and its acquisition of place
items.desc_en: The Gemara defines a מת מצוה as one with no buriers, and questions whether such a corpse acquires its place. Rav Bivi resolves that the case involves a corpse lying on the boundary, allowing it to be moved to any side.

sub.desc_en: The Tanna defines a מת מצוה (neglected corpse) as one who has no buriers; if someone calls and others respond, it is not a מת מצוה.
The Gemara questions whether a מת מצוה acquires its place, citing a baraita that one may move a corpse found on a road to either side.
The baraita elaborates that a corpse found on a boundary between fields may be moved to the less cultivated side, and if both are equal, to any side.
Rav Bivi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the case involves a corpse lying on the boundary (מֵיצַר), so permission to move it from the boundary allows moving it to any side.

items.text: Exemption from hand-washing and the obligation of אחרונים
items.text_en: Exemption from hand-washing and the obligation of אחרונים
items.desc_en: Abaye clarifies that the exemption applies only to first waters, but last waters are obligatory due to Sodomite salt that can blind. Rav Acha bar Rava asks about measuring salt, and Rav Ashi says it is unnecessary.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that those eating in the sukkah are exempt from hand-washing.
Abaye clarifies that the exemption applies only to first waters (מים ראשונים), but last waters (מים אחרונים) are obligatory.
Rav Chiya bar Ashi explains that last waters are obligatory because of Sodomite salt (מלח סדומית) that can blind the eyes.
Abaye notes that such salt is found only in small quantities, like a kurta in a kor measure.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi whether one must measure the salt to determine if it is the dangerous Sodomite type.
Rav Ashi responds that such measurement is unnecessary.

items.text: Exemption from feeding demai to the poor
items.text_en: Exemption from feeding demai to the poor
items.desc_en: The Mishnah exempts from demai; Rav Huna teaches that Beit Shammai prohibit feeding demai to the poor and guests, while Beit Hillel permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the poor are exempt from the tithe of demai (doubtfully tithed produce).
A baraita is cited: one may feed demai to the poor and to guests.
Rav Huna teaches that Beit Shammai prohibit feeding demai to the poor and guests, while Beit Hillel permit it.

items.text: Exemption from eruv and the debate on lashes for תחומין
items.text_en: Exemption from eruv and the debate on lashes for תחומין
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses exemption from eruv; the school of Rabbi Yannai distinguishes between עירובי חצירות and עירובי תחומין. Rabbi Yonatan challenges whether one is lashed for a negative commandment with 'אל', and Rav Ashi notes the verse says 'אל יצא' not 'אל יוציא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the exemption from eruv; the school of Rabbi Yannai distinguishes between עירובי חצירות (courtyard eruvin) and עירובי תחומין (Sabbath boundary eruvin), stating that only the former is exempt.
Rabbi Chiya's baraita is cited, stating that one is lashed for violating עירובי תחומין (Sabbath boundary eruvin) by Torah law.
Rabbi Yonatan objects: does one receive lashes for a negative commandment introduced with 'אל' (do not)? Rav Acha bar Yaakov counters with a verse 'אל תפנו' (do not turn) where lashes are given.

Rabbi Yonatan clarifies his objection: the negative commandment regarding תחומין (boundaries) is a warning for a capital offense (מיתת בית דין), and for such a לאו (negative commandment) one is not lashed.

Rav Ashi resolves the issue by noting that the verse says 'אל יצא' (he shall not go out), not 'אל יוציא' (he shall not bring out), so the prohibition is not a warning for a capital offense and lashes apply.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the phrase 'הדרן עלך מבוי'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'הדרן עלך מבוי' (we return to you, alleyway).

items.text: New Mishnah: Making partitions for wells
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Making partitions for wells
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses making partitions for wells, with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Meir debating the number of boards. Details include height, width, thickness, and spacing, and the condition that a cow's head and most of its body must be inside while drinking.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that partitions (פסין) are made for wells.
Rabbi Yehuda says four upright boards appear as eight.
Rabbi Meir says eight boards appear as twelve — four upright and four flat.
Rabbi Meir specifies the height, width, thickness, and spacing of the boards.
Rabbi Yehuda says the boards are of four handbreadths, tied but not loose, with one entering and one exiting.
The Mishnah concludes that it is permitted to bring the cow close to the well, provided its head and most of its body are inside while drinking.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about pasin for wells
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about pasin for wells
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages regarding the maximum area for which pasin (partitions) can be made for a well. Rabbi Yehuda limits it to beit se'atayim, while the Sages allow any size for certain enclosures like a pen or courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule allowing pasin for wells, then records Rabbi Yehuda's position limiting the area to beit se'atayim.
The Sages respond to Rabbi Yehuda, stating that the beit se'atayim limit applies only to a garden or karpaf, but for a pen, courtyard, or similar enclosure, any size is permitted.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Is the Mishnah against Chananya?
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Is the Mishnah against Chananya?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah aligns with Chananya's view, who distinguishes between a bor (pit) and a be'er (well) regarding pasin and chavalin (ropes). Two resolutions are offered: either the Mishnah follows Chananya by distinguishing between bor and be'er, or Chananya is responding to the first Tanna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah contradicts Chananya, who distinguishes between a bor (pit) and a be'er (well) regarding pasin (boards) and chavalin (ropes).
The Gemara offers a first resolution: the Mishnah can align with Chananya by distinguishing between a bor (pit) and a be'er (well).
An alternative version argues that since Chananya's statement does not distinguish between bor and be'er, the Mishnah still seems to contradict him.
The Gemara offers a second resolution: Chananya is merely responding to the first Tanna, not stating his own independent position.

items.text: Second question: Is the Mishnah against Rabbi Akiva?
items.text_en: Second question: Is the Mishnah against Rabbi Akiva?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks if the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Akiva, who distinguishes between a public well and a private pit. The Mishnah only mentions be'erot (wells), not borot (pits). The answer is that Rabbi Akiva's distinction is based on flowing vs. stagnant water, and the Mishnah only discusses flowing wells.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Akiva, since the Mishnah only mentions be'erot (wells) and not borot (pits), while Rabbi Akiva distinguishes between a public well and a private pit.

The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Akiva, the Mishnah only discusses be'erot (flowing wells) because they are flowing water (מים חיים), while borot (pits of stagnant water) are not mentioned because they are not flowing.

items.text: Third question: Is the Mishnah against Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava?
items.text_en: Third question: Is the Mishnah against Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, who limits pasin to public wells only. The Mishnah says 'leveira'ot' (for wells) without specifying public or private. The answer is that 'beira'ot' here refers to wells in general, including private ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah contradicts Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, who permits pasin only for a public well, whereas the Mishnah says 'leveira'ot' (for wells) without distinction.
The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, the Mishnah's 'beira'ot' refers to wells in general, including private ones, so there is no contradiction.

items.text: Excursus: Meaning of 'dyomdin' and 'dyofra'
items.text_en: Excursus: Meaning of 'dyomdin' and 'dyofra'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the term 'dyomdin' as 'dyo amudin' (two pillars) and 'dyofra' as a tree that produces fruit twice a year, citing Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar and Ulla.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the term 'dyomdin' means.
Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar explains that 'dyomdin' means 'dyo amudin' (two pillars).
The Gemara cites a baraita about 'dyofra' and Ulla explains it as a tree that produces fruit twice a year, providing a parallel for the 'dyo' prefix.

items.text: Debate: Was Eve created from a face or a tail?
items.text_en: Debate: Was Eve created from a face or a tail?
items.desc_en: A major debate between Rav and Shmuel: one says Adam was created with two faces (a 'partzuf'), the other says he had a tail. The Gemara brings scriptural proofs for each view, including verses about 'achor vakedem', 'vayitzer', 'zachar uneikevah', and 'vayisgor basar'. Various Amoraim offer interpretations to reconcile the opposing views.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar states that Adam was created with two faces (a 'partzuf'), citing the verse 'Achor vakedem tzartani' (You formed me from behind and before).
The Gemara introduces the debate between Rav and Shmuel: one says Adam was created with a 'partzuf' (two faces), the other says he had a tail (zanav).
The Gemara asks: for the one who says 'partzuf', the verse 'achor vakedem' fits; but for the one who says 'zanav', what does the verse mean?
Rabbi Ami explains: 'achor' refers to the last day of creation (Adam was created late), and 'kedem' refers to the punishment (the Flood).
The Gemara accepts the explanation for 'achor' but questions: what is the 'kedem' punishment? It cannot be the curses, since the snake was cursed first, then Eve, then Adam.
The Gemara answers: 'kedem' refers to the Flood, which destroyed all living beings from man to beast.
The Gemara asks: for the one who says 'partzuf', the double yod in 'vayitzer' (וַיִּיצֶר) fits; but for the one who says 'zanav', what does the double yod teach?
Rabbi Shimon ben Pazzi explains: the double yod alludes to two inclinations (yetzer) — 'woe to me from my evil inclination, woe to me from my Creator.'
The Gemara asks: for the one who says 'partzuf', the verse 'zachar uneikevah bera'am' (male and female He created them) fits; but for the one who says 'zanav', what does this verse mean?
Rabbi Avahu resolves the contradiction: initially God intended to create two (male and female), but ultimately only one was created (with the female later separated).
The Gemara asks: for the one who says 'partzuf', the verse 'vayisgor basar tachtenah' (He closed the flesh beneath it) fits; but for the one who says 'zanav', what does this verse mean?
Rav Zevid (or others) explains: the verse refers to the place of the cut (where the tail was removed), where flesh was closed over.
The Gemara asks: for the one who says 'zanav', the verse 'vayiven' (He built) fits; but for the one who says 'partzuf', what does 'vayiven' mean?
Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya explains: 'vayiven' means God braided Eve's hair (like a builder), as in coastal cities they call a braider a 'banayta'.
Rav Chisda (or a baraita) adds an alternative interpretation: 'vayiven' teaches that God built Eve like a building (with structure and beauty).

items.text: Analogy of woman to a storehouse
items.text_en: Analogy of woman to a storehouse
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the verse 'He built the rib' by comparing a woman to a storehouse (אוֹצָר) that is wide below and narrow above to receive fruit, so too a woman is wide below and narrow above to receive the fetus.

items.text: God as best man for Adam
items.text_en: God as best man for Adam
items.desc_en: The verse 'And He brought her to the man' teaches that God served as a best man (שׁוֹשְׁבִינוּת) for Adam, establishing that a great person should serve as best man for a lesser one without resentment.

items.text: Which face walked first?
items.text_en: Which face walked first?
items.desc_en: For the view that Adam was created with two faces, Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak determines that the male face walked first, citing a baraita that a man should not walk behind a woman, even his wife, and one who does so has no share in the World to Come.

items.text: Handing money to a woman for gazing
items.text_en: Handing money to a woman for gazing
items.desc_en: The Sages taught that one who hands money to a woman from his hand to hers or from hers to his in order to gaze at her will not be cleansed from the judgment of Gehinnom, even if he is like Moses, as the verse says 'Hand to hand, he will not be cleansed from evil.'

items.text: Manoach as an ignoramus
items.text_en: Manoach as an ignoramus
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that Manoach was an ignoramus (עַם הָאָרֶץ) because the verse says 'Manoach arose and went after his wife.' Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects, citing similar phrases about Elkana and Elisha. The Gemara resolves that 'after' means after her words and advice, not literally behind her.

items.text: Rav Ashi's support for Manoach's ignorance
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's support for Manoach's ignorance
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that even according to Rav Nachman's view that Manoach was an ignoramus, he did not even read the verse about Rivka, who rode after the man, not before him, showing that walking after a woman is proper.

items.text: Hierarchy of what to walk after
items.text_en: Hierarchy of what to walk after
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan teaches: It is better to walk after a lion than after a woman; after a woman than after idolatry; after idolatry than after a synagogue when people are praying.

items.text: Adam's offspring during his separation
items.text_en: Adam's offspring during his separation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar says that during the 130 years Adam was under a ban (נִידּוּי), he fathered spirits, demons, and liliths, as the verse implies he only begot in his likeness after that. An objection from Rabbi Meir states Adam was a great pietist who fasted and separated from his wife for 130 years. The Gemara resolves that the spirits came from involuntary emissions.

items.text: Praising a person partially in their presence
items.text_en: Praising a person partially in their presence
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar teaches that part of a person's praise may be said in their presence, but all of it only in their absence, citing verses about Noah.

items.text: The dove's preference for bitter sustenance from God
items.text_en: The dove's preference for bitter sustenance from God
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar interprets the olive leaf in the dove's mouth: the dove said to God, 'Let my sustenance be bitter as an olive but in Your hand, rather than sweet as honey but dependent on flesh and blood,' as derived from a verbal analogy on 'taraf.'

items.text: A house where Torah is heard at night
items.text_en: A house where Torah is heard at night
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar says that any house where words of Torah are heard at night will never be destroyed, as the verse says 'He gives songs in the night.'

items.text: The world suffices with two letters since the Temple's destruction
items.text_en: The world suffices with two letters since the Temple's destruction
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar says that since the Temple was destroyed, the world suffices with two letters (יָהּ) of God's name, as the verse says 'Every soul praises Yah, Halleluyah.'

items.text: Babylon cursed, Samaria blessed
items.text_en: Babylon cursed, Samaria blessed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar says that when Babylon was cursed, its neighbors were cursed; when Samaria was cursed, its neighbors were blessed, as shown by verses.

items.text: Opening: The difference between human and divine justice
items.text_en: Opening: The difference between human and divine justice
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar contrasts human and divine justice: a human condemned to death is gagged to prevent cursing the king, but one condemned by God remains silent, praises God, and is considered as if offering a sacrifice. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets a verse about those who pass through the valley of weeping, explaining that sinners in Gehinnom accept their judgment as just.

items.text: Contradiction: Do sinners repent at the gates of Gehinnom?
items.text_en: Contradiction: Do sinners repent at the gates of Gehinnom?
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said that even at the gates of Gehinnom, wicked people do not repent, citing a verse that describes them as 'rebelling' perpetually. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between Jewish sinners and gentile sinners.

items.text: Support: Jewish sinners are spared from Gehinnom's fire
items.text_en: Support: Jewish sinners are spared from Gehinnom's fire
items.desc_en: The Gemara supports the distinction by citing Reish Lakish's own statement that the fire of Gehinnom does not affect Jewish sinners, using a kal vachomer from the golden altar. It then explains that the verse about the valley of weeping refers to those who are temporarily punished in Gehinnom but are rescued by Abraham, except for a Jew who cohabits with a gentile woman.

items.text: Objection: Grammatical challenge to the interpretation
items.text_en: Objection: Grammatical challenge to the interpretation
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana objects to the interpretation of the verse, arguing that the participle form 'ha'posh'im' implies continuous action, not a past state. The Gemara defends the interpretation by comparing it to other participles that refer to past actions.

items.text: The three gates of Gehinnom
items.text_en: The three gates of Gehinnom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya ben Elazar states that Gehinnom has three gates: one in the desert, one in the sea, and one in Jerusalem, each supported by a biblical verse. The Gemara questions whether there are more, citing a tradition about two palm trees in Gei Ben Hinnom that emit smoke, which is identified as the entrance to Gehinnom, but concludes that this is the same as the gate in Jerusalem.

items.text: The seven names of Gehinnom
items.text_en: The seven names of Gehinnom
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi lists seven names for Gehinnom: Sheol, Avadon, Be'er Shachat, Bor Shaon, Tit Hayaven, Tzalmavet, and Eretz Hatachtit, each supported by a verse. The Gemara adds that 'Gehinnom' itself is not counted because it refers to a deep valley where people descend due to 'hinam' (gratuitous sin), and 'Tofteh' is also excluded as it refers to those enticed by their evil inclination.

items.text: The location of Gan Eden and the dimensions of the cow
items.text_en: The location of Gan Eden and the dimensions of the cow
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish discusses the location of Gan Eden, suggesting possible entrances in Beit She'an, Beit Gerem, Dumasknin, or Babylon, with Abaye and Rava praising local fruits. The Gemara then clarifies a Mishnah about two cows tied together entering and exiting a public domain, explaining that they were indeed tied and not merely appearing so, and provides the dimensions of a cow's head and body.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's measurements
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda's measurements
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the phrasing of the Mishnah: Rabbi Meir says the breach can be 'like ten' cubits, but ten is exactly ten; Rabbi Yehuda says 'like thirteen or fourteen cubits', but thirteen is less than thirteen. Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah means 'more than thirteen but not reaching fourteen'.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Meir's and Rabbi Yehuda's measurements for the breach in a partition.
The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing 'like ten' when ten is exactly ten, and explains it is because the latter part says 'like thirteen'.
The Gemara questions 'like thirteen' when it is more, and 'like fourteen' when it is not fourteen.
Rav Pappa explains that the Mishnah means more than thirteen but not reaching fourteen.

items.text: Rav Pappa's ruling on the need for extra side-posts
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's ruling on the need for extra side-posts
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that for a well of eight cubits, all agree no extra side-posts are needed; for a well of twelve cubits, all agree extra side-posts are needed. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is only for a well between eight and twelve cubits. The Gemara questions why Rav Pappa teaches this, and explains that he was unaware of a baraita that already states this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa opens by stating that for a well of eight cubits, all agree no extra side-posts are needed.
Rav Pappa continues that for a well of twelve cubits, all agree extra side-posts are needed.
Rav Pappa concludes that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is only for a well between eight and twelve cubits.
The Gemara questions why Rav Pappa teaches this, since it is already taught in a Mishnah.
The Gemara answers that Rav Pappa was unaware of the baraita that already states this, so he teaches it as if it were a baraita.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry: extending the diagonal as extra side-posts
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry: extending the diagonal as extra side-posts
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether, according to Rabbi Meir, extending the diagonal (דיומדין) to the length of extra side-posts (פשוטין) is valid. Rabbah cites a baraita: 'provided he increases the side-posts'. One version interprets this as extending the diagonal; another as adding extra side-posts. The Gemara concludes that the baraita's wording supports the interpretation of extending the diagonal.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether, according to Rabbi Meir, extending the diagonal (דיומדין) to the length of extra side-posts (פשוטין) is valid.
Rabbah cites a baraita: 'provided he increases the side-posts', and interprets it as extending the diagonal.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might instead mean adding extra side-posts (פשוטין).
The Gemara argues that if it meant adding side-posts, the baraita should have said 'עד שירבה פסין' (until he increases side-posts), not 'ובלבד שירבה בפסין'.
An alternative version: Rabbah cites the baraita and interprets it as extending the diagonal, rejecting the interpretation of adding side-posts.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita's wording supports the interpretation of extending the diagonal.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry: more than thirteen and a third cubits for Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry: more than thirteen and a third cubits for Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah what to do if the breach is larger than thirteen and a third cubits according to Rabbi Yehuda: should one add extra side-posts or extend the diagonal? Rabbah cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits a courtyard of two se'ah but forbids more, and the Sages object that a pen or courtyard of five or ten kor is permitted. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: that is a partition, these are side-posts. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda means the partition has a different law (breach up to ten cubits), while side-posts have a different law (breach up to thirteen and a third).

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah what to do if the breach exceeds thirteen and a third cubits according to Rabbi Yehuda: should one add extra side-posts or extend the diagonal?
Rabbah cites a baraita about the minimum and maximum distance between partitions for a pen or courtyard.
The baraita states Rabbi Yehuda's rule: a courtyard of two se'ah is permitted, more is forbidden, and the Sages object that a pen or courtyard of five or ten kor is permitted.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: that case involves a partition, these involve side-posts.
The Gemara objects: if the distinction were simply partition vs. side-posts, Rabbi Yehuda should have said 'this is a partition and that is a partition'.
The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yehuda means that the partition has a different law (breach up to ten cubits), while side-posts have a different law (breach up to thirteen and a third cubits).

items.text: Abaye's inquiry: a mound of ten handbreadths within four cubits
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry: a mound of ten handbreadths within four cubits
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether a mound that accumulates to ten handbreadths within four cubits is considered a valid diagonal (דיומד). Rabbah cites a baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says if there is a square stone that, if divided, has a cubit on each side, it is considered a diagonal; otherwise not. Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says even a round stone, if it could be hollowed and divided to have a cubit on each side, is considered a diagonal. The dispute is whether we apply one 'we see' (רואין) or two.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether a mound that accumulates to ten handbreadths within four cubits is considered a valid diagonal (דיומד).
Rabbah cites a baraita: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says a square stone that, if divided, has a cubit on each side is considered a diagonal; otherwise not.

sub.text: Rabbi Yishmael's position in the baraita
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yishmael's position in the baraita
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yishmael the son of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says even a round stone, if it could be hollowed and divided to have a cubit on each side, is considered a diagonal.
The gemara explains the dispute: one sage applies one 'we see' (רואין) principle, the other applies even two 'we see' principles.

items.text: Abaye's inquiry: a fence of reeds with less than three handbreadths between them
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry: a fence of reeds with less than three handbreadths between them
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether a fence of reeds where each reed is less than three handbreadths apart is considered a valid diagonal. Rabbah cites a baraita: if there is a tree, a fence, or a fence of reeds, it is considered a diagonal. The Gemara debates whether this refers to reeds with gaps less than three handbreadths or to a thicket of reeds. Two versions of the discussion are presented, each concluding that the baraita must refer to two types of trees or two types of fences.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether a fence of reeds where each reed is less than three handbreadths apart is considered a valid diagonal.
Rabbah cites a baraita: if there is a tree, a fence, or a fence of reeds, it is considered a diagonal, and suggests it refers to reeds with gaps less than three handbreadths.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might refer to a thicket of reeds, but then notes that would be equivalent to a tree.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita must refer to two types of fences or two types of trees, so no proof can be brought.
An alternative version: Abaye's dilemma was about a thicket of reeds, and Rabbah cites the same baraita, suggesting it refers to a thicket.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might refer to reeds with gaps less than three handbreadths, but that would be equivalent to a fence.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita must refer to two types of trees or two types of fences, leaving the dilemma unresolved.

items.text: Opening analogy: two types of tree, two types of fence
items.text_en: Opening analogy: two types of tree, two types of fence
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the concept that just as there are two types of tree (one permitted, one forbidden for use on Shabbat), so too there are two types of fence (one that permits carrying, one that does not).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an analogy: just as there are two types of tree (one permitted, one forbidden for use on Shabbat), so too there are two types of fence (one that permits carrying, one that does not).

items.text: Abaye's inquiry about a courtyard entering between the posts
items.text_en: Abaye's inquiry about a courtyard entering between the posts
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one may carry from a courtyard whose head enters between the posts into the area between the posts and vice versa. Rabbah permits for one courtyard but forbids for two.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one may carry from a courtyard whose head enters between the posts into the area between the posts and vice versa.
Rabbah permits carrying for one courtyard.
Abaye asks about the case of two courtyards.
Rabbah forbids carrying for two courtyards.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rava dispute two courtyards with an eruv
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rava dispute two courtyards with an eruv
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that two courtyards are forbidden even if they made an eruv, due to a decree lest people say the eruv is effective for the area between the posts. Rava permits if they made an eruv.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that two courtyards are forbidden even if they made an eruv, due to a decree lest people say the eruv is effective for the area between the posts.
Rava permits two courtyards if they made an eruv.

items.text: Support for Rava from a baraita and Rav Huna's resolution
items.text_en: Support for Rava from a baraita and Rav Huna's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita supporting Rava: two courtyards are forbidden only if they did not make an eruv, but if they made an eruv they are permitted. Rav Huna deflects the challenge by explaining the baraita refers to a case where the courtyards later made an eruv (after the water dried).

sub.desc_en: Abaye cites a baraita that supports Rava's position: two courtyards that made an eruv are permitted to carry between them and the area between the posts.
The gemara raises an objection: does this baraita not refute Rav Huna's position that two courtyards are forbidden even if they made an eruv?
Rav Huna deflects the challenge by explaining that the baraita refers to a case where the courtyards later made an eruv (after the water dried), not before.

items.text: Abaye asks about water drying up on Shabbat
items.text_en: Abaye asks about water drying up on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah: if the water in the well dries up on Shabbat, what is the status of the partition? Rabbah rules that since the partition was only for the water, once the water is gone, the partition is nullified.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether the partition remains valid if the water in the well dries up on Shabbat, and Rabbah answers that since the partition was only for the water, once the water is gone the partition is nullified.

items.text: Ravin's inquiry about water drying and returning on Shabbat
items.text_en: Ravin's inquiry about water drying and returning on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Ravin asks about a case where water dried on Shabbat and then returned. Abaye responds that the case of drying is already resolved as forbidden, and the case of returning is a partition made on Shabbat, which is valid according to a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Ravin asks whether a partition formed by water that dried on Shabbat and then returned is valid.
Abaye tells Ravin that the case of drying is already resolved as forbidden, based on his earlier inquiry with Rabbah.
Abaye adds that the case of returning water is also resolved: it is a partition made on Shabbat, and a baraita rules that any partition made on Shabbat is valid.

items.text: Rav Nachman's distinction: throwing vs. carrying
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's distinction: throwing vs. carrying
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman qualifies the baraita: the rule that a partition made on Shabbat is valid applies only for throwing (i.e., liability for throwing into it), but not for carrying within it. This distinction was stated specifically regarding an intentional act.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Nachman's statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Nachman's statement
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman qualifies the baraita: the rule that a partition made on Shabbat is valid applies only for throwing (i.e., liability for throwing into it), but not for carrying within it.
The gemara clarifies that Rav Nachman's distinction was stated specifically regarding an intentional act (מזיד), not an unintentional one.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on throwing between the posts and the strength of partitions
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on throwing between the posts and the strength of partitions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who throws into the area between the posts of wells is liable. The Gemara explains this is necessary even when the posts are in the public domain and the public breaches them, teaching that the public does not nullify the partition. This is consistent with a prior teaching of Rabbi Elazar, but here it is stated to show he holds that view.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who throws an object into the area between the well posts is liable, and the Gemara questions why this is not obvious since the posts serve as partitions permitting drawing water.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary when one made posts resembling well posts in the public domain and threw into them, teaching liability.
The Gemara objects that this too is obvious, since without the posts being valid partitions, drawing water from the well would be prohibited.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling is necessary even when the public breaches the partition, teaching that the public does not nullify it.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar already taught this principle elsewhere, so why repeat it here?
The Gemara cites a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda and the Sages dispute about a public path, and Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both explain that the Mishnah demonstrates the strength of partitions.
The Gemara explains that from the Mishnah one might think Rabbi Elazar does not accept the principle, so here he explicitly affirms it.
The Gemara resolves that the two teachings were stated together as one unit, so both were necessary.

items.text: Mishnah citation: drinking in the public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah citation: drinking in the public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah from elsewhere: one may not stand in the public domain and drink in the private domain, or vice versa, unless one inserts one's head and most of one's body into the place where one drinks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a mishnah from elsewhere that prohibits drinking in a different domain unless one inserts one's head and most of one's body into the drinking place.

items.text: Opening Mishnah reference
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah reference
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the same rule applies to a winepress vat (גת) as to a well, implying a discussion about the laws of carrying on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the same rule applies to a winepress vat (גת) as to a well.

items.text: Gemara's first question about the cow
items.text_en: Gemara's first question about the cow
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a cow requires its head and most of its body to be inside the domain when drinking, similar to a person. It distinguishes between cases where the person holds the bucket and the cow, and where he holds only the bucket. A baraita is cited to resolve the issue, but the interpretation is debated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether a cow requires its head and most of its body to be inside the domain when drinking, just as a person does.
The Gemara distinguishes between cases: when the person holds the bucket but not the cow, the cow's head and body must be inside; when he holds both, the question remains.
A baraita is cited stating that the cow's head and most of its body must be inside, and the Gemara debates whether this refers to holding the bucket and the cow or only the bucket.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding filling water
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding filling water
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the person holds only the bucket, it should be forbidden to fill water for the animal on Shabbat, as a baraita prohibits this. Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a trough in the public domain, where there is a concern that one might come to repair it and carry the bucket from a private to a public domain. The Gemara further discusses the liability for such an action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the person holds only the bucket and not the animal, it should be forbidden to fill water for the animal on Shabbat, citing a baraita that prohibits this.

Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to a trough in the public domain, where there is a concern that one might come to repair it and carry the bucket from a private to a public domain.

The Gemara objects that in such a scenario one would not be liable for carrying, citing Rav Safra in the name of Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yochanan that one who moves objects and later decides to take them out is exempt.
The Gemara resolves that the concern is not about carrying out but about times when one repairs the trough and then brings the bucket back in, carrying from the public domain into the private domain.

items.text: Alternative version of the question
items.text_en: Alternative version of the question
items.desc_en: An alternative version of the discussion is presented, where the question is whether a cow suffices with its head and most of its body inside, and the debate is about the case where the person holds the bucket but not the cow. The same baraita and objection are raised, and Abaye's resolution is repeated.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version: regarding a person we said his head and most body suffice; regarding a cow, does its head and most body suffice or not?
The Gemara refines: when he holds both vessel and animal, it is obvious that head and most body suffice; the question is when he holds the vessel but not the animal.

A rabbi cites a baraita: provided the cow's head and most body are inside and it drinks; the Gemara infers this refers to holding the vessel but not the animal, but the rabbi rejects that and says it refers to holding both.

The Gemara objects: it stands to reason that if he holds the vessel but not the animal, is it permitted? A baraita forbids filling water and placing it before the animal, but allows filling and pouring while the animal drinks on its own.

Abaye resolves: the baraita refers to a feeding trough in the public domain, ten handbreadths high and four wide, with its head entering between the posts, and the concern is lest he fix it and carry the bucket out.
The Gemara objects: in such a case is one liable? Rabbi Yochanan ruled that one who moves objects and then decides to take them out is exempt because the initial lifting was not for that purpose.
The Gemara resolves: sometimes he fixes the trough and then brings it back in, thereby carrying from the public domain into the private domain.

items.text: Proof from a camel and a general animal
items.text_en: Proof from a camel and a general animal
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a camel that requires its head and most of its body inside, even though the trough is like holding the bucket and the animal. Rav Acha bar Rav Huna distinguishes a camel due to its long neck. Another baraita about a general animal is interpreted as referring to a camel, and Rabbi Elazar prohibits a camel for the same reason.

items.text: Restriction on the use of well partitions
items.text_en: Restriction on the use of well partitions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Adda states that the partitions around wells (פסי ביראות) were only permitted for pilgrims, and a baraita specifies they were only for animals of pilgrims, not for people.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Adda states: the posts of wells (פסי ביראות) were permitted only for pilgrims (עולי רגלים), but a person...
A baraita is cited that the well partitions were only permitted for animals, not for people.
The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by interpreting 'animal' in the baraita as referring specifically to the animals of pilgrims.

items.text: Opening statement on climbing for humans
items.text_en: Opening statement on climbing for humans
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that a person may climb up and down using the passei bira'ot (well enclosures). This sets the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that a person may climb up and down using the passei bira'ot (well enclosures).

items.text: Challenge from Rav Yitzchak's statement
items.text_en: Challenge from Rav Yitzchak's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the opening statement by citing Rav Yitzchak quoting Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel, who said that passei bira'ot were only permitted for a well of living water. If for animals, why distinguish between living and collected water? The Gemara explains that it must be fit for humans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the opening statement by citing Rav Yitzchak quoting Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel, who said that passei bira'ot were only permitted for a well of living water, and argues that if for animals, there should be no distinction between living and collected water, concluding that it must be fit for humans.

items.text: Resolution: passei bira'ot for animals only
items.text_en: Resolution: passei bira'ot for animals only
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by stating that passei bira'ot were only permitted for animals, but a person must climb up and down. If the enclosure is wide, it is also permitted for humans. One may not draw water for his animal, but may pour water and let the animal drink on its own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by stating that passei bira'ot were only permitted for animals, but a person must climb up and down; if the enclosure is wide, it is also permitted for humans, and one may not draw water for his animal but may pour water and let the animal drink on its own.

items.text: Rav Anan's objection and Abaye's answer
items.text_en: Rav Anan's objection and Abaye's answer
items.desc_en: Rav Anan objects: if so, what benefit do passei bira'ot provide? The Gemara clarifies that the benefit is for filling water. Then Abaye explains that the case involves a trough in the public domain that is ten handbreadths high and four wide, with its head entering between the posts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Anan objects: if so, what benefit do passei bira'ot provide? The Gemara clarifies that the benefit is for filling water.
Abaye explains that the case involves a trough in the public domain that is ten handbreadths high and four wide, with its head entering between the posts.

items.text: Abaye's detailed explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's detailed explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye specifies that the discussion involves a trough in the public domain that is ten handbreadths high and four wide, with its head entering between the posts. This clarifies the scenario for the previous objection.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the objection by specifying that the case involves a trough in the public domain, ten handbreadths high and four wide, with its head entering between the posts.

items.text: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba's ruling on burgnin and passei bira'ot
items.text_en: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba's ruling on burgnin and passei bira'ot
items.desc_en: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba quoting Rav states that there are no burgnin (watchmen's huts) in Babylonia and no passei bira'ot outside the Land of Israel. The Gemara explains the reasons: in Babylonia, burgnin are not needed due to frequent inspections; outside the Land, passei bira'ot are not needed because yeshivot are not common. An alternative version adds that burgnin are not found outside the Land due to thieves, and passei bira'ot are not found in Babylonia due to abundant water.

sub.text: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba states in the name of Rav that there are no burgnin (watchmen's huts) in Babylonia and no passei bira'ot (upright boards for wells) outside the Land of Israel.

The Gemara explains the reasons: burgnin are absent in Babylonia due to frequent floods, and passei bira'ot are absent outside the Land because yeshivot are not common; however, the opposite practice is followed.

An alternative version states that Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba said in the name of Rav that both burgnin and passei bira'ot are absent in Babylonia and outside the Land, explaining that burgnin are absent outside the Land due to thieves.
The alternative version adds that passei bira'ot are absent in Babylonia due to abundant water, and outside the Land because yeshivot are not common.

items.text: Rav Chisda's challenge and resolution regarding burgnin
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's challenge and resolution regarding burgnin
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Mari, son of Rav Huna, son of Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba, how they relied on burgnin to travel from Barnish to the synagogue of Daniel, three parasangs on Shabbat, given that his grandfather said there are no burgnin in Babylonia. Mari showed him certain villages that were swallowed up within seventy cubits and a remainder, indicating that the distance was within the techum.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda challenges Mari, son of Rav Huna, son of Rav Yirmiyah bar Abba, asking how they relied on בורגנין (watchmen's huts) to travel three parasangs from Barnish to Daniel's synagogue on Shabbat, given that his grandfather said there are no בורגנין in Babylonia.

Mari went out and showed Rav Chisda certain ruined towns that were subsumed within seventy cubits and a remainder of each other, indicating that the distance was within the techum and they relied on the ruins rather than on the huts.

items.text: Aggadic interpretation of verses by David, Job, Ezekiel, and Zechariah
items.text_en: Aggadic interpretation of verses by David, Job, Ezekiel, and Zechariah
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda, citing Mari bar Mar, explains a verse from Psalms that David, Job, and Ezekiel each said but did not explain, until Zechariah ben Iddo came and explained it. The verse refers to the vastness of Torah, which is measured as one part in 3,200 of the entire world. The explanation involves the dimensions of a scroll and the measurement of the world.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Mari bar Mar
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Mari bar Mar
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda, citing Mari bar Mar, introduces a verse from Psalms that David, Job, and Ezekiel each said but did not explain, until Zechariah ben Iddo came and explained it.
The Gemara cites the verse from Psalms that David said, and the verse from Job that Job said, both alluding to the vastness of Torah.

The Gemara cites Ezekiel's vision of a scroll written on both sides, and interprets the words 'קִינִים', 'וָהֶגֶה', and 'וָהִי' as referring to the punishment of the righteous in this world, the reward of the righteous in the future, and the punishment of the wicked in the future.

Zechariah ben Iddo explains the verse by describing a scroll of twenty by ten cubits, which when unrolled becomes forty by twenty, and through a גזירה שווה (verbal analogy) with a verse about measuring the world, concludes that the entire world is only one part in 3,200 of the Torah.

items.text: Beginning of another aggadic teaching on figs
items.text_en: Beginning of another aggadic teaching on figs
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda, citing Mari bar Mar, begins a new teaching about a verse concerning two baskets of figs placed before the Temple, one very good and one very bad. The segment ends mid-verse.

sub.text: Rav Chisda citing Mari bar Mar
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda citing Mari bar Mar
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda, citing Mari bar Mar, introduces a new aggadic teaching about the verse describing two baskets of figs placed before the Temple, one very good and one very bad.

items.text: Allegorical interpretation of good and bad figs
items.text_en: Allegorical interpretation of good and bad figs
items.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse about good and bad figs as referring to completely righteous and completely wicked individuals, concluding that both will ultimately give off a fragrance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the good figs as completely righteous and the bad figs as completely wicked, concluding that both will ultimately give off a fragrance.

items.text: Rava's allegorical exposition of Song of Songs
items.text_en: Rava's allegorical exposition of Song of Songs
items.desc_en: Rava expounds verses from Song of Songs, interpreting 'the fig tree putteth forth her green figs' as Israelite youths who never tasted sin, and 'at our doors are all manner of precious fruits' as Israelite maidens who open their doors to their husbands. The congregation of Israel declares that she kept more decrees than God commanded.

sub.desc_en: Rava interprets 'the mandrakes give forth fragrance' as the Israelite youths who never tasted sin.
Rava interprets 'at our doors are all manner of precious fruits' as the Israelite maidens who open their doors to their husbands.
The congregation of Israel declares that she kept more decrees than God commanded.

items.text: Rav Chisda's question about 'new and old'
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's question about 'new and old'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks a rabbinic storyteller about the meaning of 'new and old', initially receiving an answer about light and heavy commandments. Rav Chisda objects that the Torah was not given piecemeal, and instead explains that 'new' refers to rabbinic decrees and 'old' to Torah laws.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks a rabbinic storyteller about the meaning of the verse 'חֲדָשִׁים גַּם יְשָׁנִים' (new and old).
The storyteller answers that 'new' refers to light commandments and 'old' to heavy commandments.
Rav Chisda objects that the Torah was not given piecemeal, so the distinction between light and heavy commandments cannot be described as 'new and old'.
Rav Chisda resolves that 'new' refers to rabbinic decrees (דברי סופרים) and 'old' to Torah laws (דברי תורה).

items.text: Rava's exposition on the severity of rabbinic words
items.text_en: Rava's exposition on the severity of rabbinic words
items.desc_en: Rava expounds a verse to teach that one must be more careful with rabbinic words than Torah words, as violating rabbinic decrees carries a death penalty. He addresses the objection that if they have substance they would have been written, and interprets another verse to mean that one who studies them tastes the flavor of meat.

sub.desc_en: Rava expounds a verse to teach that one must be more careful with rabbinic words (דברי סופרים) than Torah words, because violating rabbinic decrees carries a death penalty.
The gemara raises an objection: if rabbinic words have substance, why were they not written in the Torah?
Rava answers by citing the verse 'making many books there is no end' to explain why rabbinic words were not written.

sub.text: Rav Pappa bar Rav Acha bar Ada citing Rav Acha bar Ulla
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa bar Rav Acha bar Ada citing Rav Acha bar Ulla
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa bar Rav Acha bar Ada cites Rav Acha bar Ulla that one who mocks rabbinic words is punished with boiling excrement.
Rava rejects the interpretation, noting that the verse says 'לַהַג' (study) not 'לַעַג' (mockery).
Rava resolves that the verse means one who studies rabbinic words tastes the flavor of meat.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Akiva's dedication to hand-washing in prison
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Akiva's dedication to hand-washing in prison
items.desc_en: The Sages relate a story about Rabbi Akiva in prison, where his attendant Rabbi Yehoshua the Garsi brought water. When the guard spilled half the water, Rabbi Akiva insisted on using the remaining water for hand-washing rather than drinking, saying he would rather die than violate the rabbinic decree on hand-washing. The Sages praised his piety.

sub.desc_en: The Sages relate a story about Rabbi Akiva in prison, where his attendant Rabbi Yehoshua the Garsi brought water daily, but one day the guard spilled half the water.
Rabbi Akiva asks Rabbi Yehoshua why he brought less water, noting that his life depends on the attendant's actions.

sub.text: Rabbi Yehoshua's report and Rabbi Akiva's response
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua's report and Rabbi Akiva's response
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua recounts the incident, and Rabbi Akiva insists on using the remaining water for hand-washing rather than drinking, saying he would rather die than violate the rabbinic decree.
The Sages praise Rabbi Akiva's piety, concluding that if he was so scrupulous in his old age and in prison, how much more so in his youth and outside prison.

items.text: Solomon's institution of eruvin and hand-washing
items.text_en: Solomon's institution of eruvin and hand-washing
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that when Solomon instituted eruvin and hand-washing, a heavenly voice declared approval, citing verses from Proverbs.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that when Solomon instituted eruvin and hand-washing, a heavenly voice declared approval, citing verses from Proverbs.

items.text: Rava's allegorical exposition of 'Let us go out into the field'
items.text_en: Rava's allegorical exposition of 'Let us go out into the field'
items.desc_en: Rava expounds a verse from Song of Songs, interpreting 'let us go out into the field' as the congregation of Israel asking God to judge them among Torah scholars, 'let us lodge in the villages' as those who denied God despite His goodness, 'let us get up early to the vineyards' as synagogues and study halls, and the blossoming vine, bud, and pomegranates as masters of Scripture, Mishnah, and Gemara.

sub.desc_en: Rava introduces the verse from Song of Songs, setting up the allegorical exposition.
Rava interprets 'let us go out into the field' as the congregation of Israel asking God to judge them among Torah scholars who study under hardship.
Rava interprets 'let us lodge in the villages' as those who denied God despite His goodness.
Rava interprets the vineyards, vine, bud, and pomegranates as synagogues, study halls, and masters of Scripture, Mishnah, and Gemara, concluding with God showing His glory.

items.text: Solomon's wisdom and the structure of Torah and rabbinic law
items.text_en: Solomon's wisdom and the structure of Torah and rabbinic law
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that Solomon spoke 3000 parables on Torah and 1005 reasons on rabbinic law. Rava expounds that Solomon taught the people with signs and analogies. Ulla in the name of Rabbi Eliezer says that initially the Torah was like a basket without handles until Solomon made handles. Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva says that every jot of the Torah yields mounds of laws.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna states that Solomon spoke 3000 parables on Torah and 1005 reasons on rabbinic law.
Rava expounds that Solomon taught the people with signs and analogies.

sub.text: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: Ulla in the name of Rabbi Eliezer says that initially the Torah was like a basket without handles until Solomon made handles.

sub.text: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva
sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva says that every jot of the Torah yields mounds of laws.

sub.text: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva (continued)
sub.text_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Mar Ukva (continued)
sub.desc_en: The verse 'black as a raven' is interpreted: in whom do you find them? — in those who are cruel to their children like a raven, i.e., those who study Torah with self-denial.

items.text: Interpretations of 'cruel as a raven'
items.text_en: Interpretations of 'cruel as a raven'
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rava offer different interpretations of the phrase 'cruel as a raven' from the previous Mishnah. Rabbah says it refers to one who darkens his face for Torah study, while Rava says it refers to one who acts cruelly towards his family for Torah, citing the story of Rav Adda bar Matna.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the phrase 'cruel as a raven' from the Mishnah, setting up the interpretations.
Rabbah interprets 'cruel as a raven' as referring to one who darkens his face (i.e., endures hardship) for Torah study.

Rava interprets 'cruel as a raven' as referring to one who acts cruelly toward his family for Torah, citing the story of Rav Adda bar Matna who asked his wife if reeds in the swamp were finished (i.e., if there was food for his children).

items.text: Exegesis on divine retribution and reward
items.text_en: Exegesis on divine retribution and reward
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Ila expound on verses about God's punishment and reward. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets 'He repays His enemies to their face' as God carrying a burden He wishes to cast off. Rabbi Ila says God delays punishment for enemies but not for the completely righteous. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi then explains that 'today to do them' means today for action, tomorrow for reward.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi interprets the verse 'He repays His enemies to their face' as God carrying a burden He wishes to cast off.
Rabbi Ila explains that God delays punishment for enemies but not for the completely righteous.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi explains that 'today to do them' means today for action, tomorrow for reward.

items.text: Interpretation of 'long of nostrils'
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'long of nostrils'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chaggai (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) questions why the verse says 'long of nostrils' (plural) instead of 'long of nose' (singular). He explains that it means God is patient with both the righteous and the wicked.

sub.text: Rabbi Chaggai / Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chaggai / Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chaggai (or Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani) questions why the verse uses the plural 'ארך אפים' (long of nostrils) instead of the singular 'ארך אף' (long of nose).

sub.text: Rabbi Chaggai / Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's answer
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chaggai / Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani's answer
sub.desc_en: He answers that the plural indicates God is patient (ארך אפים) with both the righteous and the wicked.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question about Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the Mishnah that a corral for a well is limited to two se'ah. It asks whether Rabbi Yehuda means the well is permitted with the partitions (pasin) or without them, and explores the reasoning behind each possibility regarding the owner's focus and the concern for error.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Yehuda mean the well is permitted with the upright boards (pasin) or without them?
One possibility: the owner focuses on his cistern, so we do not decree that he might carry in a larger karpef.
The other possibility: the owner focuses on his partition, so we decree that he might confuse this with a larger karpef.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that states Rabbi Yehuda permits a corral up to two se'ah for a well, but more is forbidden. The Sages challenge him with cases of a pen, shed, courtyard, and enclosure, which are permitted even if larger. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes by saying those have proper partitions, while this has only pasin. Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds that a well of two se'ah by two se'ah is permitted, and the required distance is only for the cow's head and body.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: the Sages permit a corral for a well up to any size, but Rabbi Yehuda limits it to two se'ah.
The Sages challenge Rabbi Yehuda: a pen, shed, courtyard, and enclosure are permitted even if larger than two se'ah.
Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes: those have proper partitions, while this has only pasin.
Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar adds: a well of two se'ah by two se'ah is permitted, and the required distance is only for the cow's head and body.

items.text: Resolution of the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.text_en: Resolution of the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement that he holds 'well without pasin', implying Rabbi Yehuda holds 'well with pasin'. But it rejects this, stating Rabbi Yehuda also holds 'well without pasin'. The difference between them is only regarding a long or short corral.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement that he holds 'well without pasin', implying that Rabbi Yehuda holds 'well with pasin'.
The Gemara rejects this inference, stating that Rabbi Yehuda also holds 'well without pasin'.
The Gemara asks: If so, that is exactly what Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said — what is the difference between them?
The Gemara resolves: The difference between them is regarding a long or short corral — Rabbi Yehuda permits it while Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar requires a square area.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's general principle
