items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's general principle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states a general rule: any airspace used for dwelling, like a pen or courtyard, is permitted even up to five or ten kor; but any dwelling used for airspace, like field huts, is limited to two se'ah, and more is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's general principle
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's general principle
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states a general rule: any airspace used for dwelling is permitted even up to five or ten kor, but any dwelling used for airspace is limited to two se'ah.

items.text: Dispute about a public domain dividing two courtyards
items.text_en: Dispute about a public domain dividing two courtyards
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a public domain separates two courtyards, Rabbi Yehuda says one must divert it to the side, while the Sages say it is unnecessary. The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar say this teaches the power of partitions. A contradiction is raised from Rabbi Yochanan's statement about Jerusalem, and resolved by distinguishing between cases with two proper partitions and those without. Similarly, contradictions in Rabbi Yehuda's and the Sages' positions are resolved by considering the presence of proper partitions or the status of four partitions.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says one must divert a public domain that separates two courtyards to the side, while the Sages say it is unnecessary.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar both state that this Mishnah teaches the power of partitions (מחיצות).

The Gemara objects: Does Rabbi Yochanan really hold this view? For Rabbah bar bar Chanah said in his name that Jerusalem would be liable as a public domain if its gates were not locked at night, implying that partitions are ineffective without gates.
The Gemara raises contradictions: Compare Rabbi Yehuda's position here with another statement of his, and similarly compare the Sages' position here with another statement of theirs.

A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says one who has two houses on opposite sides of a public domain may place a side-post (לחי) or beam (קורה) on each side and carry in between, but the Sages say one does not thereby merge a public domain.
The Gemara states the contradictions explicitly: Rabbi Yehuda's position here conflicts with his position in the baraita, and the Sages' position here conflicts with theirs in the baraita.
The contradiction regarding Rabbi Yehuda is resolved: In the baraita there are two proper partitions (שתי מחיצות מעלייתא), while in the Mishnah there are not.
The contradiction regarding the Sages is resolved: In the Mishnah there is the status of four partitions (שם ארבע מחיצות), while in the baraita there is not.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan on the Land of Israel and public domain
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan on the Land of Israel and public domain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef quotes Rabbi Yochanan saying that the Land of Israel is not liable for the laws of public domain. Rav Dimi teaches this, and Abaye asks him for the reason.

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yosef reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that the Land of Israel is not liable for the laws of public domain.
Rav Dimi was sitting and teaching this tradition, and Abaye asked him for the reason.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on slopes and inclines
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling on slopes and inclines
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the exemption of Eretz Yisrael from reshut harabim might be due to natural barriers, but rejects this by noting that Babylon and the whole world also have such barriers. It then clarifies that Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is specifically about slopes and inclines (מעלות ומורדות) that are not like the camp in the wilderness.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Eretz Yisrael might be exempt from reshut harabim because it is surrounded by natural barriers, but rejects this by noting that Babylon and the whole world also have such barriers.
The Gemara asks if Rabbi Yochanan's ruling is specifically about slopes and inclines (מעלות ומורדות).
Rav Yosef confirms that Rabbi Yochanan's statement indeed refers to slopes and inclines.

sub.text: Supporting tradition from Ravin or Rabbi Avahu
sub.text_en: Supporting tradition from Ravin or Rabbi Avahu
sub.desc_en: A supporting tradition is cited in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: slopes and inclines in Eretz Yisrael are not liable as reshut harabim because they are unlike the camp in the wilderness.

items.text: Rachbah's question about a mound of ten within four
items.text_en: Rachbah's question about a mound of ten within four
items.desc_en: Rachbah asks Rava whether a mound that is ten handbreadths high within four cubits, which many people traverse, is considered reshut harabim. He clarifies that the question is only according to Rabbi Yehuda, since according to the Rabbis, even a comfortable path does not become reshut harabim, so certainly this mound does not. Rava answers that it is indeed reshut harabim.

sub.desc_en: Rachbah asks Rava whether a mound that is ten handbreadths high within four cubits, which many people traverse, is considered reshut harabim (public domain) for Shabbat violations.

The Gemara clarifies that Rachbah's question is only according to Rabbi Yehuda, since according to the Rabbis, even a comfortable path does not become reshut harabim, so certainly this mound does not.
Rachbah refines his question according to Rabbi Yehuda: does the mound's uncomfortable use prevent it from being reshut harabim, or is it no different from a comfortable path?
Rava answers that one is liable for carrying on the mound, meaning it is considered reshut harabim.

items.text: Clarification: even with a rope or steep incline
items.text_en: Clarification: even with a rope or steep incline
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the ruling applies even if one needs a rope to climb, and even if it is as steep as the ascent of Beit Maron. Rava confirms both.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks Rava whether the ruling applies even if one needs a rope to climb the mound.
Rava confirms that the ruling applies even with a rope.
The Gemara asks Rava whether the ruling applies even if the mound is as steep as the ascent of Beit Maron.
Rava confirms that the ruling applies even with a steep incline.

items.text: First attempted proof: a courtyard with two entrances
items.text_en: First attempted proof: a courtyard with two entrances
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that a mound is reshut harabim from a mishna about a courtyard that the public enters and exits through different sides, which is reshut harabim for impurity but reshut hayachid for Shabbat. The Gemara analyzes whether this follows Rabbi Yehuda or the Rabbis, concluding that it can be explained according to the Rabbis as well.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a courtyard that the public enters and exits through different sides, which is reshut harabim for impurity but reshut hayachid for Shabbat, as a potential proof regarding the mound.

The Gemara questions whether the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda or the Rabbis, first suggesting it cannot be the Rabbis since they hold that public use does not nullify partitions even in a comfortable courtyard.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must follow Rabbi Yehuda, who holds that public use can nullify partitions in a comfortable courtyard.
The Gemara rejects the conclusion and explains that the baraita can be according to the Rabbis, who only needed to teach the impurity status of reshut harabim, not the Shabbat status.

items.text: Second attempted proof: alleyways leading to wells
items.text_en: Second attempted proof: alleyways leading to wells
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita about alleyways that lead to wells, which are reshut hayachid for Shabbat and reshut harabim for impurity. Again, the Gemara tries to identify the author as Rabbi Yehuda, but concludes it can be explained according to the Rabbis.

items.text: Third attempted proof: paths of Beit Gilgul
items.text_en: Third attempted proof: paths of Beit Gilgul
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about the paths of Beit Gilgul, which are reshut hayachid for Shabbat and reshut harabim for impurity. The Gemara attempts to prove that this follows Rabbi Yehuda, but Rava explains that Joshua, who loved Israel, established these paths, giving comfortable ones to the public and uncomfortable ones to individuals.

items.text: Mishnah: partitions for wells and cisterns
items.text_en: Mishnah: partitions for wells and cisterns
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that for a public cistern, public well, or private well, one may make a partition of boards (פסין), but for a private cistern one must make a partition ten handbreadths high, according to Rabbi Akiva. Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava limits the leniency of פסין to a public well only, requiring a belt-like partition for others.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that for a public cistern, public well, or private well, one may make a partition of boards (פסין).
Rabbi Akiva rules that for a private cistern, one must make a partition ten handbreadths high.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava limits the leniency of פסין to a public well only, requiring a belt-like partition ten handbreadths high for all others.

items.text: Rav Yosef's citation of Shmuel's rulings and their necessity
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's citation of Shmuel's rulings and their necessity
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports two rulings from Shmuel: that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, and that passei bira'ot were only permitted for a spring-fed well. The Gemara explains that both statements are necessary: without the second, one might think the first applies even to gathered rainwater; without the first, one might think the second applies to both public and private wells.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef reports two rulings from Shmuel: the law follows Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, and passei bira'ot were only permitted for a spring-fed well.
The Gemara explains that the first statement alone would have led one to think that the leniency applies even to gathered rainwater, so the second statement is needed to restrict it to spring water.
The Gemara explains that the second statement alone would have led one to think it applies to both public and private wells, so the first statement is needed to restrict it to public wells.

items.text: Mishnah: Dispute about carrying in a garden or courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: Dispute about carrying in a garden or courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's ruling that a garden or courtyard of 70 cubits and a fraction by 70 cubits and a fraction, surrounded by a wall ten handbreadths high, permits carrying inside, provided it has a guardhouse or dwelling, or is adjacent to a city. Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Eliezer, and Rabbi Yosei offer varying opinions on the requirements. Rabbi Il'ai reports hearing from Rabbi Elazar that even if it is as large as a beit kor, it is permitted, and also reports other halakhot about an eruv and about using arkevalin on Pesach.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's ruling that a garden or courtyard of 70 cubits and a fraction by 70 cubits and a fraction, surrounded by a wall ten handbreadths high, permits carrying inside, provided it has a guardhouse or dwelling, or is adjacent to a city.
Rabbi Yehuda states that even if the enclosure contains only a water cistern, ditch, or cave, one may carry inside.
Rabbi Akiva rules that even without any of these features, one may carry inside, provided the area does not exceed 70 cubits and a fraction by 70 cubits and a fraction.
Rabbi Eliezer says that if the length exceeds the breadth by even one cubit, one may not carry inside.
Rabbi Yosei permits carrying even if the length is double the breadth.
Rabbi Il'ai reports that he heard from Rabbi Elazar that carrying is permitted even if the garden is as large as a beit kor.

Rabbi Il'ai reports another halakha from Rabbi Elazar: if one resident of a courtyard forgot to join in the עירוב (eiruv), his house is forbidden for him to carry in and out, but permitted for the others.

Rabbi Il'ai reports a third halakha from Rabbi Elazar: one may fulfill the obligation of bitter herbs on פסח (Pesach) with ערקבאלין (arkablin), and adds that he sought a colleague who had heard these traditions but found none.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the term 've'od' in the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the term 've'od' in the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah uses the term 've'od' (and furthermore) for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava's statement. It considers whether it is because he taught one lenient ruling and then another, but notes that Rabbi Yehuda also taught two lenient rulings without using 've'od'. The Gemara resolves that in Rabbi Yehuda's case, the Sages interrupted his statements with other material, whereas here they did not. It then challenges this with Rabbi Eliezer in Sukkah, where the Sages interrupted but 've'od' is used, and distinguishes that there the interruption was within his own statement, while here it was with a different matter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah uses the term 'וְעוֹד' (and furthermore) for Rabbi Yehuda ben Bava, and objects that Rabbi Yehuda also taught two lenient rulings without using 'וְעוֹד'.
The Gemara answers that in Rabbi Yehuda's case the Sages interrupted his statements with other material, whereas here they did not.
The Gemara objects that in the case of Rabbi Eliezer in Sukkah, the Sages interrupted his statements yet 'וְעוֹד' is used.
The Gemara resolves that there the interruption was within his own statement, while here it was with a different matter.

items.text: Repetition of Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.text_en: Repetition of Rabbi Akiva's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rabbi Akiva's statement from the Mishnah: 'Rabbi Akiva says: Even if it has none of these, one may carry inside it.' This likely serves as a citation for further discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rabbi Akiva's statement from the Mishnah that even without any dwelling or water source, one may carry within a garden or courtyard of seventy cubits and a remainder.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Akiva's opinion in the Mishnah is not identical to the Tanna Kamma, implying a redundancy.

items.text: The difference between them: the 'small matter' and the source for beit se'atayim
items.text_en: The difference between them: the 'small matter' and the source for beit se'atayim
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the difference is a 'small matter' (davar mu'at) regarding the extra space beyond 70 amot. It then cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda defines this, and proceeds to derive the measure of beit se'atayim from the dimensions of the courtyard of the Tabernacle, with Abaye explaining the verse.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and the dispute with Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's opinion and the dispute with Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer states that if the length of the karpaf exceeds twice its width by even one cubit, one may not carry inside. Rav Bibi bar Abaye notes that the Mishnah also teaches this condition, leading to the question: is this the same as Rabbi Yosei? The Gemara answers that the difference between them is the 'square that the Sages squared' (ribbu'a de'ribbuha rabbanan).

items.text: The halakhic ruling: both lenient opinions
items.text_en: The halakhic ruling: both lenient opinions
items.desc_en: The Gemara records two versions of a ruling by Shmuel: one says the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei, the other says it follows Rabbi Akiva. The Gemara explains that both rulings are needed for leniency, each addressing a different potential stringency.

items.text: The case of a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim enclosed for dwelling
items.text_en: The case of a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim enclosed for dwelling
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim that was enclosed for dwelling: if most of it was sown, it is considered a garden and prohibited; if most was planted, it is considered a courtyard and permitted. Rav Huna brei deRav Yehoshua limits this to a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim, but one of exactly beit se'atayim is permitted even if sown, aligning with Rabbi Shimon's view that all such areas are a single domain for vessels that rested within them.

items.text: Initial statement about nullification of majority
items.text_en: Initial statement about nullification of majority
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a statement that if the majority (of the karpaf) is nullified to the minority, the karpaf becomes larger than beit se'atayim and is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that if the majority of the karpaf is nullified to the minority, the karpaf becomes larger than beit se'atayim and is forbidden.

items.text: Rav Huna's two versions of the ruling
items.text_en: Rav Huna's two versions of the ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua clarifies that the leniency of the minority applies only when the karpaf is less than beit se'atayim, but if it is exactly beit se'atayim it is forbidden, aligning with the Rabbis. Rav Yirmiyah from Difti teaches a more lenient version: the minority permits only up to beit se'atayim, but more than that is forbidden, aligning with Rabbi Shimon.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the earlier version and states the correct version: the minority permits.
Rav Huna bar Rav Yehoshua limits the leniency to a karpaf smaller than beit se'atayim; exactly beit se'atayim is forbidden.
The Gemara identifies that this ruling aligns with the Rabbis (who forbid a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim).
Rav Yirmiyah from Difti teaches a more lenient version: the minority permits only up to beit se'atayim, but more than that is forbidden.
The Gemara identifies that this lenient version aligns with Rabbi Shimon (who permits a karpaf up to beit se'atayim).

items.text: Dispute about planted trees and istablot
items.text_en: Dispute about planted trees and istablot
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Avimi rules that a karpaf planted mostly with trees is like a courtyard and permitted only if the trees are arranged in rows (istablot). Rav Nachman permits even without rows. Mar Yehuda encounters a case without rows and permits it, following Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The stam states a general rule: if one planted most of a karpaf with trees, it is considered like a courtyard and carrying is permitted.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Avimi qualifies the rule: the trees must be arranged in rows (איצטבלאות, istablot).
Rav Nachman disputes Avimi's qualification and permits carrying even without rows.
Mar Yehuda visits Rav Huna bar Yehuda and sees people carrying in a karpaf without rows.
Mar Yehuda asks Rav Huna bar Yehuda whether he does not hold by Avimi's restrictive view requiring rows.
Rav Huna bar Yehuda answers that he follows Rav Nachman's lenient position, permitting carrying without rows.

items.text: Rav Nachman's solution for a karpaf not enclosed for dwelling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's solution for a karpaf not enclosed for dwelling
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel teaches that for a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim not enclosed for dwelling, one may breach a gap larger than ten cubits and then rebuild it to exactly ten cubits, permitting carrying.

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel presents a remedy for a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim not enclosed for dwelling: breach a gap wider than ten cubits, then rebuild it to exactly ten cubits, making it permitted.

items.text: Inquiry about sequential breaches and the analogy to a sandal
items.text_en: Inquiry about sequential breaches and the analogy to a sandal
items.desc_en: An inquiry is raised: if one breaches a cubit and rebuilds it, repeating until the total breach exceeds ten cubits, what is the law? The Gemara compares this to a Mishnah about a sandal whose ear is repaired, and Rabbi Yochanan's principle of 'new faces have come here' applies, permitting the action.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an inquiry: if one breaches a cubit and rebuilds it, repeating until the total breach exceeds ten cubits, what is the law?
The Gemara objects: is this not analogous to the Mishnah that states all household vessels have their measure as pomegranates?
Chizkiyah asks: if a vessel was punctured to the size of an olive and sealed, then punctured again and sealed, until the total hole reaches the size of a pomegranate, what is the law?
Rabbi Yochanan answers: Rabbi, you taught us the Mishnah about a sandal whose one ear broke and was repaired — it remains טמא מדרס (impure with midras impurity).
The Mishnah continues: if the second ear broke and was repaired, the sandal is pure from midras impurity but still impure with מגע מדרס (contact with midras).
The Gemara asks: what is the difference between the first repair (where the second ear remains) and the second repair (where the first ear remains)?
Rabbi Yochanan resolves: new faces have come here — the second repair creates a new entity, so the impurity does not revert.
The Gemara applies the same principle here: each breach and repair creates new faces, permitting the action.

items.text: Reaction to Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Reaction to Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: Some praised Rabbi Yochanan's statement, calling him a worthy person, while others disparaged him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that some called Rabbi Yochanan 'not a man' (for his sharpness), while others called him 'such a man' (for his brilliance).
Others praised Rabbi Yochanan, calling him a worthy person like this one.

items.text: Law of a rehava behind houses and the effect of a door
items.text_en: Law of a rehava behind houses and the effect of a door
items.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that a rehava (alley) behind houses is limited to four cubits. Rav Nachman adds that if one opens a door to it, the entire area becomes permitted, but only if the door was opened before the enclosure was made, not after. The Gemara clarifies that this applies even if there are upper stories, as one might think the door was made for them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Kahana rules that a rehava (alley) behind houses is limited to four cubits for carrying.
Rav Nachman adds that if one opened a door to the rehava before the enclosure was made, the entire area becomes permitted, but not if the enclosure preceded the door.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling applies even if there are upper stories, lest one think the door was made for them.

items.text: Water in a karpaf enclosed for dwelling
items.text_en: Water in a karpaf enclosed for dwelling
items.desc_en: The Rabbis thought water in a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim enclosed for dwelling is like seeds and forbidden, but Rav Abba citing Rava rules that water is like trees and permitted.

sub.text: Stam (anonymous statement of the Rabbis' initial position)
sub.text_en: Stam (anonymous statement of the Rabbis' initial position)
sub.desc_en: The Rabbis initially thought that water in a karpaf (enclosed area) larger than beit se'atayim that was enclosed for dwelling is like seeds and therefore forbidden to carry within.
Rav Abba, citing Rava, rules that water is like trees (which are permitted in such a karpaf), and therefore carrying within is permitted.

items.text: Amemar and Rav Ashi's ruling on a courtyard suitable for use
items.text_en: Amemar and Rav Ashi's ruling on a courtyard suitable for use
items.desc_en: Amemar rules that a courtyard (רחבה) is permitted only if it is fit for use (חזיין לתשמישתא). Rav Ashi adds that even if fit, it is permitted only if its depth does not exceed two se'ah; otherwise, it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Amemar rules that a courtyard (רחבה) is permitted only if it is fit for use (חזיין לתשמישתא).
Rav Ashi adds that even if fit, the courtyard is permitted only if its depth does not exceed two se'ah; otherwise, it is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's dismissal of Rav Ashi's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's dismissal of Rav Ashi's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara dismisses Rav Ashi's statement as insignificant, comparing it to a trivial matter (אכריא דפירי).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara dismisses Rav Ashi's statement as insignificant, comparing it to a trivial matter (אכריא דפירי).

items.text: Description of a specific courtyard case
items.text_en: Description of a specific courtyard case
items.desc_en: A specific case is presented: a courtyard (רחבה) at the mouth of a river, open on one side to the city and on the other to a vineyard path that ascends to the riverbank.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a specific case of a courtyard (רחבה) at the mouth of a river, open to the city on one side and to a vineyard path ascending to the riverbank on the other.

items.text: Abaye's first rejected proposal: partition on the riverbank
items.text_en: Abaye's first rejected proposal: partition on the riverbank
items.desc_en: Abaye proposes making a partition on the riverbank, but the Gemara objects that one cannot make a partition on top of another partition.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes making a partition on the riverbank, but the Gemara objects that one cannot make a partition on top of another partition.

items.text: Abaye's second rejected proposal: a doorway form at the vineyard path
items.text_en: Abaye's second rejected proposal: a doorway form at the vineyard path
items.desc_en: Abaye then suggests making a צורת הפתח (doorway form) at the entrance of the vineyard path, but the Gemara notes that camels would knock it down.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes making a צורת הפתח (doorway form) at the entrance of the vineyard path to permit carrying.
The Gemara objects that camels would knock down the doorway form, rendering it ineffective.

items.text: Abaye's third proposal and Rava's objection: a side post for the vineyard path
items.text_en: Abaye's third proposal and Rava's objection: a side post for the vineyard path
items.desc_en: Abaye proposes placing a side post (לחי) at the entrance of the vineyard path, arguing that since it benefits the path, it also benefits the courtyard. Rava objects that people will say the side post is effective for any vineyard path, implying a general leniency.

sub.desc_en: Abaye proposes placing a side post (לחי) at the entrance of the vineyard path, arguing that since it benefits the path, it also benefits the courtyard.
Rava objects that people will say the side post is effective for any vineyard path, implying a general leniency.

items.text: Rava's solution: a side post at the city entrance
items.text_en: Rava's solution: a side post at the city entrance
items.desc_en: Rava proposes placing a side post at the city entrance, arguing that since it benefits the city, it also benefits the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes placing a side post at the city entrance, arguing that since it benefits the city, it also benefits the courtyard.

items.text: Conclusion and dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina
items.text_en: Conclusion and dispute between Rav Acha and Ravina
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that carrying within the city and within the courtyard is permitted, but carrying between them is disputed: one Sage forbids and one permits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that carrying within the city itself is permitted.
The Gemara concludes that carrying within the plaza itself is permitted.
The Gemara notes that carrying between the city and the plaza is disputed by Rav Acha and Ravina.
The Gemara reports that one Sage forbids carrying between the city and the plaza, and one permits it.

items.text: Dispute about a karpaf with no residents
items.text_en: Dispute about a karpaf with no residents
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: one permits carrying in a karpaf because there are no residents, while another prohibits it because sometimes residents are present and one might come to carry.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents two opposing opinions regarding a karpaf (enclosure) with no residents: one permits carrying because there are no residents, and the other prohibits it because sometimes residents are present and one might come to carry.

items.text: Reducing a karpaf with a pillar: dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.text_en: Reducing a karpaf with a pillar: dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses reducing a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim that was not enclosed for dwelling. Planting trees does not reduce it. Building a pillar ten handbreadths high and four wide reduces it; less than three does not. Between three and four, Rabbah says it reduces, Rava says it does not. Their reasons are given: Rabbah invokes the principle of lavud, Rava says it is insignificant because it is not a place of four.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the general rule: a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim that was not enclosed for dwelling cannot be reduced by planting trees.
The Gemara specifies that a pillar ten handbreadths high and four wide reduces the karpaf, but less than three handbreadths does not.
The Gemara introduces the dispute: for a pillar between three and four handbreadths, Rabbah says it reduces, Rava says it does not.
Rabbah argues that the pillar reduces because it exits the category of lavud (the principle of joining gaps less than three handbreadths).
Rava argues that the pillar does not reduce because it is not a place of four handbreadths and therefore is insignificant.

items.text: Partition distanced from the wall: dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.text_en: Partition distanced from the wall: dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.desc_en: If one distances a partition four handbreadths from the wall, it is effective. Less than three, it is not. Between three and four, Rabbah says it is effective, Rava says it is not. Their reasons mirror the previous dispute: Rabbah uses lavud, Rava says it lacks significance.

sub.desc_en: The gemara states the basic case: a partition distanced four handbreadths from the wall is effective, but less than three is not.
The gemara presents the dispute between Rabbah and Rava regarding a gap of three to four handbreadths.
Rabbah explains his ruling: the gap is considered closed by the principle of לָבוּד (the gap is treated as filled).
Rava explains his ruling: since the gap is less than four handbreadths, it lacks significance and is not considered a valid partition.

items.text: Plastering a pillar with mud: dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.text_en: Plastering a pillar with mud: dispute between Rabbah and Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Shimi teaches leniently: if one plasters a pillar with mud and it can stand on its own, it is a valid reduction. If not, Rabbah says it is a reduction because it stands now, Rava says it is nothing because it cannot stand on its own.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shimi teaches leniently: if one plasters a pillar with mud and it can stand on its own, it is a valid reduction; if not, the dispute between Rabbah and Rava applies.
Rabbah rules that even if the mud cannot stand on its own, the pillar is a valid reduction because it currently stands.
Rava rules that if the mud cannot stand on its own, the pillar is nothing and not a valid reduction.

items.text: Partition on a mound: dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna, and related cases
items.text_en: Partition on a mound: dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna, and related cases
items.desc_en: If one distances a partition four handbreadths from a mound, it is effective. Less than three or on the edge of the mound, Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna dispute. The Gemara concludes that Rav Chisda said it is effective, citing a case of a partition on top of a partition: Rav Chisda says it is effective on Shabbat but not for acquiring a ger's property; Rav Sheishes says it is not effective even on Shabbat. Rav Chisda concedes that if one made a partition on the mound itself, it is effective because one dwells in the airspace of the upper partitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the basic case: if one distances a partition four handbreadths from a mound, it is effective; if less than three handbreadths or on the edge of the mound, a dispute arises.
The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Hamnuna regarding the effectiveness of a partition placed less than three handbreadths from the mound or on its edge.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Chisda is the one who said it is effective, citing a related case of a partition on top of a partition.
Rav Chisda rules that a partition on top of a partition is effective for Shabbat but not for acquiring a ger's property.
Rav Sheishes objects, stating that even for Shabbat the partition is not effective.
Rav Chisda concedes that if one made a partition on the mound itself, it is effective because one dwells in the airspace of the upper partitions.

items.text: Question about swallowed lower partitions and a story about a woman's partition
items.text_en: Question about swallowed lower partitions and a story about a woman's partition
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah asks: if lower partitions are swallowed but upper ones remain, what is the law? The Gemara distinguishes between acquisition of a ger's property (citing Yirmeyah Bira'ah's ruling about flax seeds) and Shabbat (where a partition made on Shabbat is valid, but Rav Nachman limits it to throwing, not carrying, and only for an unintentional act). A story follows: a woman made a partition on a ger's property, a man added a little, and Rav Nachman awarded it to the man, telling the woman she did not establish a chazakah like others.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah asks: if lower partitions are swallowed but upper ones remain, what is the law?
The Gemara asks: to what context does this question apply? If it's about acquisition of a ger's property, that is already covered by Yirmeyah Bira'ah's ruling.

sub.text: Yirmeyah Bira'ah's ruling via Rav Yehudah
sub.text_en: Yirmeyah Bira'ah's ruling via Rav Yehudah
sub.desc_en: Yirmeyah Bira'ah citing Rav Yehudah rules: one who throws flax seeds on a ger's threshing floor and another adds a little — the latter acquires, because the first did not cause growth and the growth came on its own.
The Gemara answers: the question applies to Shabbat, where a partition made on Shabbat is valid.
A baraita supports: any partition made on Shabbat, whether unintentionally or intentionally, is called a valid partition.
Rav Nachman objects: the baraita's leniency applies only to throwing, but carrying is forbidden.
The Gemara resolves: Rav Nachman's statement was said specifically regarding an intentional act (מזיד), not an unintentional one.
A story: a woman made a partition on a ger's property, a man added a little, and Rav Nachman awarded it to the man, telling the woman she did not establish a chazakah (חזקה) like others.

items.text: Dispute about a karpaf with a roofed area: Rava and Rabbi Zeira, linked to Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Dispute about a karpaf with a roofed area: Rava and Rabbi Zeira, linked to Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: A karpaf of three se'ah with a roofed area of one se'ah: Rava says the airspace of the roofed area enlarges the karpaf (making it prohibited), Rabbi Zeira says it does not. The Gemara suggests this corresponds to a dispute between Rav and Shmuel about an ach-sadrah (portico) in a field: Rav permits carrying throughout because the roof's edge descends and seals, Shmuel restricts to four amot because we do not say the roof's edge descends and seals.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rava says the airspace of a roofed area within a karpaf (enclosure) enlarges it, making it prohibited to carry; Rabbi Zeira says it does not enlarge it.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rava and Rabbi Zeira corresponds to the earlier dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding an ach-sadrah (portico) in a field.

sub.text: Citation of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
sub.text_en: Citation of the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute: Rav permits carrying throughout the ach-sadrah because the roof's edge descends and seals, while Shmuel restricts carrying to four amot because we do not say the roof's edge descends and seals.

The Gemara explains the reasoning: Rav holds that the roof's edge descends and seals, making the ach-sadrah a closed domain, while Shmuel rejects this principle, leaving the ach-sadrah open and restricted.

items.text: Clarification of the case: built like an אורזילא
items.text_en: Clarification of the case: built like an אורזילא
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling applies when the structure is built like an אכסדרה (portico), but here the case is when it is built like an אורזילא (a type of small structure).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier ruling applied when the structure was built like an אכסדרה (portico), but here the case is when it is built like an אורזילא (a small structure).

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's ruling: a karpaf breached into a courtyard is prohibited
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's ruling: a karpaf breached into a courtyard is prohibited
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that he concedes in the case of a karpaf that is breached entirely into a courtyard that it is prohibited, because the airspace of the courtyard renders it superfluous.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira states that he concedes in the case of a karpaf breached entirely into a courtyard that it is prohibited, because the airspace of the courtyard renders it superfluous.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection: does permitted airspace prohibit?
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection: does permitted airspace prohibit?
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabbi Zeira's reasoning, questioning whether airspace that is permitted to the courtyard can prohibit the karpaf.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef challenges Rabbi Zeira's reasoning, questioning whether airspace that is permitted to the courtyard can prohibit the karpaf.

items.text: Abaye's response and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's response and Rav Chisda's resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye asks if Rav Yosef's objection is according to Rabbi Shimon, but notes that even for Rabbi Shimon, the airspace of the partition's place is an issue. Rav Chisda then rules that the courtyard is permitted and the karpaf is prohibited, and the Gemara explains the distinction: the courtyard has its partitions' airspace rendering it superfluous, while the karpaf does not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks whether Rav Yosef's objection follows Rabbi Shimon's view, and notes that even for Rabbi Shimon, the airspace of the partition's place remains an issue.
Rav Chisda rules that when a karpaf (enclosure) is breached entirely into a courtyard, the courtyard is permitted and the karpaf is prohibited.
The Gemara objects that the courtyard's leniency cannot be due to its having side-posts (גיפופי), since sometimes the opposite configuration is found.

The Gemara resolves that the courtyard is permitted because its partitions' airspace renders it superfluous, while the karpaf is prohibited because its partitions' airspace does not render it superfluous.

items.text: Case of a garden adjacent to a palace wall
items.text_en: Case of a garden adjacent to a palace wall
items.desc_en: A garden was adjacent to a palace wall, and the outer wall of the palace fell. Rav Bibi thought to rely on the inner wall, but Rav Papi objected, saying that the partitions were made for the inside, not the outside.

sub.desc_en: The gemara presents a case: a garden (בוסתנא) was adjacent to the wall of a palace, and the outer wall of the palace collapsed.
Rav Bibi thought to rely on the inner wall of the palace as a valid partition for the garden.
Rav Papi objected, stating that those partitions were made for the inside of the palace, not for the outside, and therefore cannot serve as a partition for the garden.

items.text: The Exilarch's garden and Rav Huna bar Chinana's solution
items.text_en: The Exilarch's garden and Rav Huna bar Chinana's solution
items.desc_en: The Exilarch had a garden and asked Rav Huna bar Chinana to make a remedy so they could eat there the next day. He went and made a row of reeds less than three handbreadths apart, and Rava...

sub.desc_en: The narrator introduces that the Exilarch had a garden and asked Rav Huna bar Chinana to make a remedy so they could eat bread there the next day.
Rav Huna bar Chinana went and made a row of reeds less than three handbreadths apart, and Rava then intervened.

items.text: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua take the partitions
items.text_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua take the partitions
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua take the partitions from behind Rav Pappa's house, setting up the context for the following discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua take the partitions from behind Rav Pappa's house, setting the context for the discussion.

items.text: Ravina's objection: the new city is measured from its settlement
items.text_en: Ravina's objection: the new city is measured from its settlement
items.desc_en: Ravina cites a baraita that a new city is measured from its settlement, while an old city is measured from its wall. He argues that the case at hand is like a new city, so the partition should not be valid.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rava by citing a baraita that a new city is measured from its settlement, arguing that the case at hand is analogous to a new city, so the partition should not be valid.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection: a partition for privacy is not a partition
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection: a partition for privacy is not a partition
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects based on Rav Asi's ruling that a partition made for privacy (like a curtain) is not considered a valid partition. Since the partition here is for privacy, it should be invalid.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Rava by citing Rav Asi's ruling that partitions made for privacy (אדרכלין) are not valid partitions, and argues that since the partition here is for privacy, it should be invalid.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection: a partition for cattle is not a partition
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection: a partition for cattle is not a partition
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects based on Rav Huna's ruling that a partition made for cattle (to prevent them from entering) is not a valid partition. He cites the case of Rabbah bar Avuha who made eruvin for all of Mahoza in separate sections because of the cattle enclosure, which is like a partition for cattle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects to Rava by citing Rav Huna's principle that a partition made for cattle (to prevent them from entering) is not a valid partition, and supports this with the case of Rabbah bar Avuha who made eruvin for all of Mahoza in separate sections because of the cattle enclosure.

items.text: The Exilarch's rebuke
items.text_en: The Exilarch's rebuke
items.desc_en: The Exilarch quotes the verse "They are wise to do evil, but to do good they do not know" about the rabbis who objected, implying they are overly strict.

sub.desc_en: The Exilarch rebukes the rabbis by quoting the verse 'They are wise to do evil, but to do good they do not know', implying their strictness is misguided.

items.text: Dispute about the size of the royal colonnade
items.text_en: Dispute about the size of the royal colonnade
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ilai reports that Rabbi Eliezer said the colonnade is even a beit kor in size. The Gemara notes that this disagrees with Chananya, who says it is forty se'ah. Rabbi Yochanan explains that both derive from the same verse about the middle court, but disagree on the size of the intermediate cities.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Ilai reports that Rabbi Eliezer said the royal colonnade can be as large as a beit kor (a large area).
The Gemara notes that this opinion disagrees with Chananya, who limits the colonnade to forty se'ah.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that both opinions derive from the same verse about the middle court, which teaches that the colonnade was like intermediate cities.
The Gemara clarifies the dispute: one sage holds intermediate cities were a beit kor, the other holds they were forty se'ah.

items.text: Why was Isaiah there? A lesson about visiting a sick Torah scholar
items.text_en: Why was Isaiah there? A lesson about visiting a sick Torah scholar
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah says that Hezekiah fell ill, and Isaiah went and established a yeshiva at his entrance. From here we learn that when a Torah scholar is ill, a yeshiva is established at his entrance. But the Gemara rejects this, lest the Satan come to incite him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Isaiah was present at Hezekiah's palace, prompting the following narrative.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that Hezekiah fell ill, and Isaiah went and established a yeshiva at his entrance.
The Gemara derives a practical lesson: when a Torah scholar falls ill, a yeshiva is established at his entrance.
The Gemara rejects this practice, lest the Satan come to incite the sick scholar.

items.text: A contradiction about the one who forgot to join the eruv
items.text_en: A contradiction about the one who forgot to join the eruv
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a teaching that if one person in a courtyard forgot to join the eruv, his house is forbidden. But a mishnah says his house is forbidden to take out and bring in for him and for them. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: one who heard from a sage that if one person in a courtyard forgot to join the eruv, his house is forbidden.
The Gemara objects: but a mishnah says his house is forbidden to take out and bring in for him and for them, implying a different ruling.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua in the name of Rav Sheshet resolves the contradiction, stating that there is no difficulty.

items.text: Opening dispute: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbis on nullification
items.text_en: Opening dispute: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Rabbis on nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the core dispute: according to Rabbi Eliezer, one who nullifies his courtyard domain also nullifies his house domain; according to the Rabbis, he does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the dispute: Rabbi Eliezer holds that nullifying one's courtyard domain also nullifies one's house domain, while the Rabbis hold it does not.

items.text: Gemara's question and Rakhava's explanation
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Rakhava's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why this is obvious, and Rakhava explains the case: five residents in one courtyard, one forgot to join. According to Rabbi Eliezer, the forgetful one need not nullify to each individually; according to the Rabbis, he must.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rav Sheshet's explanation is obvious.
Rakhava explains that Rav Sheshet's statement was necessary for the case of five residents in one courtyard, one of whom forgot to join in an eiruv.
According to Rabbi Eliezer, the forgetful resident need not renounce authority to each individual.
According to the Rabbis, the forgetful resident must explicitly renounce authority to each individual.

items.text: Identifying the anonymous baraita with Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Identifying the anonymous baraita with Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that one who nullifies need not nullify to each individually, and identifies it as following Rabbi Eliezer. Two versions of the tradition are given, one by Rav Kahana and one by Rav Tavyomei citing Rav Sheishet.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which tanna the baraita follows, and answers that it follows Rabbi Eliezer.
Rav Kahana teaches the tradition that the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer.

sub.text: Rav Tavyomei's version citing Rav Sheishet
sub.text_en: Rav Tavyomei's version citing Rav Sheishet
sub.desc_en: Rav Tavyomei teaches an alternative version, citing Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheishet, that the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer.

items.text: Rav Pappa's query and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's query and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: what if one explicitly states he does not nullify (for Rabbi Eliezer) or does nullify (for the Rabbis)? Abaye resolves that since he revealed his intent, it is effective, regardless of the underlying rationale.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Abaye: according to Rabbi Eliezer, if one says he does not nullify, and according to the Rabbis, if one says he does nullify, what is the halakha?

sub.text: Gemara's first hypothetical rationale for Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Gemara's first hypothetical rationale for Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests one possible reason for Rabbi Eliezer: he holds that nullifying the courtyard automatically nullifies the house, so if one says he does not nullify, perhaps his statement is effective.

sub.text: Gemara's second hypothetical rationale for Rabbi Eliezer
sub.text_en: Gemara's second hypothetical rationale for Rabbi Eliezer
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative reason for Rabbi Eliezer: people do not live in a house without a courtyard, so nullifying the courtyard necessarily nullifies the house regardless of his statement.

sub.text: Gemara's first hypothetical rationale for the Rabbis
sub.text_en: Gemara's first hypothetical rationale for the Rabbis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests one possible reason for the Rabbis: they hold that nullifying the courtyard does not automatically nullify the house, so if one says he does nullify, perhaps his statement is effective.

sub.text: Gemara's second hypothetical rationale for the Rabbis
sub.text_en: Gemara's second hypothetical rationale for the Rabbis
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests an alternative reason for the Rabbis: one does not completely remove himself from house and courtyard, so even if he says he nullifies, his statement is disregarded.
Abaye resolves: both according to the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer, once he has revealed his intent, it is effective.

items.text: Transition: a related teaching about arqabalin
items.text_en: Transition: a related teaching about arqabalin
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly notes a teaching about going out with arqabalin on Passover, which Resh Lakish explains as 'woven straps'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Papa adds that he heard from him that they go out with עַרְקַבָּלִין (a type of basket) on Passover. Resh Lakish explains: אַצְווֹתָא חָרוּזְיָאתָא (woven palm branches).
The Gemara asks what arqabalin means.
Resh Lakish explains that arqabalin are woven straps.

items.text: New Mishnah: materials for eruv and partnership
items.text_en: New Mishnah: materials for eruv and partnership
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists what may be used for eruv and partnership (everything except water and salt), and discusses related laws of maaser sheni, vows, and eruv for a nazir, Israelite, priest, and in a beit hapras.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah introduces a new chapter with the standard closing formula for the previous chapter.
The Mishnah states that all items may be used for eruv and partnership except water and salt.
The Mishnah rules that all items may be purchased with maaser sheni money except water and salt, and a vow from food permits salt and water.
The Mishnah states that one may establish an eruv for a nazir with wine and for an Israelite with terumah, while Somkhos says only with חולין (non-sacred food).
The Mishnah rules that an eruv may be placed for a priest in a beit hapras (a field with scattered bones), and Rabbi Yehuda permits even between graves.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not use water or salt for an eiruv, because they can be pressed and eaten.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that water and salt cannot be used for an eiruv because they can be pressed and eaten.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and its proof
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and its proof
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one cannot derive absolute conclusions from general rules, even when the rule includes the word 'except'. The Gemara questions where this principle applies, and demonstrates it with the general rule about time-bound positive commandments, which has exceptions like matzah, simchah, and hakhel for women, and non-time-bound commandments like Torah study, procreation, and pidyon haben for women.

sub.desc_en: רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) states that one cannot derive absolute conclusions from general rules, even when the rule includes the word 'except'.
The Gemara infers from the phrase 'even where it says except' that רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) was not referring to the mishna here, and asks which mishna he was referring to.
The Gemara answers that he was referring to the general rule about time-bound positive commandments, where men are obligated and women exempt.

An objection is raised: is it a general principle that women are exempt from all time-bound positive commandments? The examples of מצה (matzah), שמחה (rejoicing), and הקהל (assembly) show that women are obligated in some time-bound commandments.

A further objection is raised: are women obligated in all non-time-bound positive commandments? The examples of תלמוד תורה (Torah study), פרייה ורבייה (procreation), and פדיון הבן (redemption of the firstborn) show that women are exempt from some non-time-bound commandments.
רבי יוחנן (Rabbi Yochanan) resolves the issue by reiterating his principle: one cannot derive absolute conclusions from general rules, even when the rule includes the word 'except'.

items.text: Support from the laws of zav
items.text_en: Support from the laws of zav
items.desc_en: Abaye or Rabbi Yirmeyah brings a Mishnah about zav that states a general rule with an exception, but the Gemara finds an additional exception (the saddle's back), proving that general rules are not absolute.

sub.desc_en: Abaye or Rabbi Yirmeyah cites a Mishnah about a zav that states a general rule: anything carried upon a zav is impure, anything the zav is carried on is pure, except for items used for lying/sitting and a human.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah omitted the category of a riding accessory (מרכב), which should also be an exception.
The Gemara initially suggests that a riding accessory is just a type of seat, so it is already included in the exception.

The Gemara refines the objection: the back of a saddle (גבא דאוכפא) is a riding accessory that is not a seat, as shown by a Tosefta distinguishing between the saddle (impure as a seat) and the pommel (impure as a riding accessory).
The Gemara concludes that this proves the principle: one may not learn from general statements, even when the word 'except' is used.

items.text: Support from the laws of eiruv
items.text_en: Support from the laws of eiruv
items.desc_en: Ravina or Rav Nachman brings another Mishnah about eiruv that lists an exception, but the Gemara finds additional exceptions (truffles and mushrooms), further proving the principle.

sub.desc_en: Ravina (or Rav Nachman) cites the Mishnah itself — that everything can be used for an eiruv except water and salt — as another example of a general statement with exceptions.
The Gemara asks: are there no other exceptions? What about truffles and mushrooms?
The Gemara concludes again: learn from this that one cannot derive general rules from general statements, even where it says 'except'.

items.text: Dispute about the Mishnah's application
items.text_en: Dispute about the Mishnah's application
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina disagree whether the Mishnah's rule about water and salt applies to eiruv or ma'aser. The Gemara explains that one who applies it to ma'aser certainly applies it to eiruv, but not vice versa. A baraita with Rabbi Yehudah ben Gadish's testimony supports the ma'aser application, but only for fish brine, not plain water and salt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina over whether the Mishnah's rule applies to eiruv or ma'aser.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina (first position)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina (first position)
sub.desc_en: One sage applies the Mishnah to eiruv, ruling that water and salt separately are invalid for eiruv, but combined they are valid.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina (second position)
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer or Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina (second position)
sub.desc_en: The other sage applies the Mishnah to ma'aser, ruling that water and salt separately are not purchasable with ma'aser money, but combined they are.

The Gemara explains that the one who applies the rule to ma'aser certainly applies it to eiruv, but not vice versa, because ma'aser requires a פֵּירָא (produce) and water and salt alone are not produce.
Rabbi Yitzchak teaches the Mishnah as applying to ma'aser, and a baraita with Rabbi Yehudah ben Gadish's testimony supports this for fish brine (צִיר) but not for plain water and salt.

items.text: Rav Yosef's statement
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef begins to speak, but the text cuts off, likely introducing a further discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef begins a statement (the continuation is on the next daf).

items.text: Abaye's question about oil
items.text_en: Abaye's question about oil
items.desc_en: Abaye questions why the Gemara needed to explain that the case involves oil added to water and salt, since oil itself is prohibited. The Gemara answers that the oil's value was absorbed in the price of the water and salt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the case involves oil added to the water and salt.
Abaye asks why the oil itself is not prohibited, making the explanation unnecessary.
The Gemara answers that the oil's value was absorbed in the price of the water and salt, so it is not considered a separate prohibited item.

items.text: Ben Bag Bag's baraita on buying with byproducts
items.text_en: Ben Bag Bag's baraita on buying with byproducts
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Ben Bag Bag derives from the Torah's phrase 'with cattle' that one may buy cattle along with its hide, and similarly for sheep with its wool, wine with its container, and fermented wine with its lees.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether buying with byproducts (הבלעה) is permitted.

The Gemara answers affirmatively, citing a baraita where Ben Bag Bag derives from the Torah's phrase 'with cattle' that one may buy cattle along with its hide, and similarly for sheep with its wool, wine with its container, and fermented wine with its lees.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge and the necessity of each term
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's challenge and the necessity of each term
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that whoever can explain the term 'with cattle' according to Ben Bag Bag will be honored. The Gemara explains that all the terms are necessary except 'with cattle', as each teaches a unique case that could not be derived from the others, and ultimately shows that 'with cattle' is superfluous.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan declares that whoever can explain the term 'בבקר' (with cattle) according to Ben Bag Bag will be honored.
The Gemara asks why 'בבקר' is the only superfluous term among the four listed by Ben Bag Bag.
The Gemara explains that each of the other three terms is necessary to teach a unique case that could not be derived from the others, as shown by a series of hypothetical derivations.
The Gemara shows that 'בשכר' (with strong drink) and 'בצאן' (with flock) are also necessary to teach their respective cases, which would otherwise be excluded.
The Gemara asks what purpose 'בבקר' serves, and considers the possibility that it teaches the permissibility of buying cattle with its hide, while 'צאן' teaches buying sheep with its wool.
The Gemara rejects the previous explanation, arguing that if 'בקר' were not written, one would not have inferred that sheep can be bought with its wool, so 'צאן' alone suffices for both cases.
The Gemara concludes that since 'צאן' already permits buying sheep with its wool, 'בבקר' is entirely superfluous, confirming Rabbi Yochanan's challenge.

items.text: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: The dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer interpret the verses using the method of ריבויי ומיעוטי (amplifications and restrictions), deriving that all items are permitted except for brine (according to Rabbi Eliezer) or water and salt (according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the fundamental methodological dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer and the later Tannaim.

The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer interpret the verses using the method of ריבויי ומיעוטי (amplifications and restrictions), deriving that all items are permitted except for brine (according to Rabbi Eliezer) or water and salt (according to Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish).

items.text: The other Tannaim using כלל ופרט
items.text_en: The other Tannaim using כלל ופרט
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the alternative exegetical method of כלל ופרט (general and particular), used by other Tannaim, which limits purchases to items similar to the particulars: fruit from fruit and produce of the ground, or offspring of the earth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces that the other Tannaim (those not Rabbi Yehuda ben Gadish and Rabbi Eliezer) use the method of כלל ופרט (general and particular), and cites a baraita.

The first baraita applies the rule of כלל ופרט וכלל (general, particular, general) to the verse, concluding that only items similar to the particulars — fruit from fruit and produce of the ground — are permitted.
The second baraita offers an alternative formulation of the rule, limiting purchases to offspring of the earth (ולד ולדות הארץ).

items.text: Abaye's distinction and a question on fish
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction and a question on fish
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the difference between the two baraitot is fish: according to the first, fish are included as produce of the ground, but according to the second, they are not, since they come from water. The Gemara then questions Abaye's own statement about fish.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the practical difference between the two baraitot that interpret the verse using different hermeneutical principles.
Abaye answers that the difference is fish: according to the first baraita, fish are included as produce of the ground, but according to the second, they are excluded because they come from water.
The Gemara objects that Abaye himself elsewhere stated that fish are not considered produce of the ground, contradicting his own position here.

items.text: Question on the Mishnah's list of prohibited creatures
items.text_en: Question on the Mishnah's list of prohibited creatures
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why eating a putita (a type of insect) incurs only four lashes, suggesting it should also be liable under the general prohibition of 'the swarming thing that swarms on the earth'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why eating a putita incurs only four lashes, suggesting it should also be liable under the general prohibition of 'the swarming thing that swarms on the earth'.

items.text: Ravina's answer and the dispute about birds
items.text_en: Ravina's answer and the dispute about birds
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that the difference lies in birds, which are created from mud and thus not considered 'fruit of the ground'. The Gemara then explores the reasoning behind the two opinions regarding whether birds are included in the general category.

sub.desc_en: Ravina explains that the dispute between the two opinions about the general category of 'fruit of the ground' is resolved by the case of birds, which are created from mud and thus not considered 'fruit of the ground' by one opinion.
The Gemara asks what the reasoning is behind each opinion regarding whether birds are included in the general category.

The opinion that includes birds holds that the later general term is decisive, applying the rule of 'a general and a specific' to include everything, while the earlier general term only excludes items dissimilar in two aspects.

The opinion that excludes birds holds that the earlier general term is decisive, applying the rule of 'a specific and a general' to include only what is in the specific, while the later general term only includes items similar in three aspects.

items.text: Rav's statement on eruv with certain vegetables
items.text_en: Rav's statement on eruv with certain vegetables
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that one may establish an eruv with certain types of vegetables (pa'pu'in, chalaglogot, gudgedaniyot) but not with others (chaziz, kafniyot).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav Shmuel bar Shilat in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda transmits Rav's ruling that one may establish an eruv with certain vegetables (pa'pu'in, chalaglogot, gudgedaniyot) but not with others (chaziz, kafniyot).

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding gudgedaniyot
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding gudgedaniyot
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's statement by citing a baraita that gudgedaniyot are only eaten by those with many children, implying they are not fit for all. The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement applies when they have not been hardened for seed, and for those with many children, or alternatively, that they are fit for some even if not for others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav's ruling that gudgedaniyot are fit for an eruv by citing a baraita that restricts them to those with many children, implying they are not universally fit.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement applies specifically when the gudgedaniyot have not been hardened for seed and are intended for those with many children.

The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: even if gudgedaniyot are unfit for those with few children, they are fit for those with many children, just as wine is fit for a nazirite and terumah for an Israelite.

items.text: Alternative explanation: gudgedaniyot of Media
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: gudgedaniyot of Media
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another resolution: Rav's statement refers to a specific type of gudgedaniyot from Media, which are always fit for consumption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: Rav's statement refers specifically to gudgedaniyot of Media (הנדקוקי מדי), which are always fit for consumption.

items.text: Contradiction regarding chaziz and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction regarding chaziz and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rav said one may not use chaziz for eruv, but elsewhere he said one may. The resolution is that the first statement was before Rav came to Babylon, and the second after, when he saw that chaziz was not commonly eaten there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav's statement that chaziz is not used for eruv, citing a contradictory statement from Rav Yehuda in Rav's name that chaziz is used for eruv and a blessing is recited over it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first statement was before Rav came to Babylon, and the second after, when he saw that chaziz was not commonly eaten there.

items.text: Challenge from the baraita on vegetables and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from the baraita on vegetables and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the idea that Babylon's practice is decisive, citing a baraita about vegetables that are tithed differently based on intent. The Gemara concludes that Rav's statement about chaziz was specific to his context.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Babylon's practice is decisive, citing a baraita about vegetables whose tithing status depends on intent, showing that local custom does not override general halachic principles.
The Gemara resolves that Rav's statement about chaziz was specific to his context in Babylon, not a universal ruling.

items.text: Keshut and Chaziz: Berakha and Eruv
items.text_en: Keshut and Chaziz: Berakha and Eruv
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses keshut (a type of mushroom) and chaziz (a type of fungus), questioning their berakha. Rabbi Yochanan explains that early generations used keshut as a substitute for pepper. A story with Rabbi Zeira and a child from the house of Rav concludes that the halakha follows the child: keshut requires 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' and chaziz requires 'Shehakol', because keshut grows from the ground and is a complete fruit, while chaziz grows from the air and is not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces keshut (a mushroom) and chaziz (a fungus), questioning their berakha, and Rabbi Yochanan explains that early generations used keshut as a pepper substitute.
Rabbi Zeira, when weak from study, would sit at the entrance of Rav Yehuda bar Ami's house to gain reward by standing before the rabbis.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's question to the child
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question to the child
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks a child from the house of Rav what his rabbi taught him, and the child answers: keshut requires 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' and chaziz requires 'Shehakol'.
Rabbi Zeira objects that the opposite seems logical: keshut grows from the ground and chaziz grows from the air.

The Gemara rules like the child: keshut requires 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' because it is a complete fruit, and chaziz requires 'Shehakol' because it is not, and the objection about growth source is rejected since keshut also grows from the ground, as seen when killing its root kills it.

items.text: Caphniyot: Eruv and Tum'at Ochalin
items.text_en: Caphniyot: Eruv and Tum'at Ochalin
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether caphniyot (a type of mushroom) can be used for an eruv, citing a baraita that distinguishes between kor (a type of fungus) and caphniyot regarding ma'aser and tum'at ochalin. Rabbi Yehuda states that kor is like wood except for ma'aser, and caphniyot are like fruit except for ma'aser. The Gemara initially answers that the baraita refers to nischani (a different species), but this is rejected.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether caphniyot (a type of mushroom) cannot be used for an eruv, citing a baraita that distinguishes between kor and caphniyot regarding ma'aser and tum'at ochalin.
The Gemara cites a baraita stating that kor can be bought with ma'aser money but does not contract tum'at ochalin, while caphniyot can be bought with ma'aser money and do contract tum'at ochalin.
Rabbi Yehuda states that kor is like wood for all purposes except ma'aser, and caphniyot are like fruit for all purposes except ma'aser.
The Gemara initially answers that the baraita refers to nischani (a different species), not to caphniyot.

items.text: Caphniyot and Tum'at Ochalin: Rabbi Yochanan's Principle
items.text_en: Caphniyot and Tum'at Ochalin: Rabbi Yochanan's Principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the answer of nischani, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda mentions paggei beitoni and ahinei de-tovina as obligated in ma'aser. Instead, it explains that caphniyot are susceptible to tum'at ochalin because they can be sweetened by fire, as Rabbi Yochanan said regarding bitter almonds. The Gemara then cites the source for Rabbi Yochanan's statement about almonds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: If the baraita refers to dates that never ripen, would Rabbi Yehuda really say they are exempt from ma'aser? It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda states that unripe figs of Beityoni and unripe dates of Tuvina are obligated in ma'aser.

The Gemara resolves: Actually, the baraita is not about dates that never ripen; rather, regarding טומאת אוכלין (ritual impurity of foods) the rule is different, as Rabbi Yochanan said: since they can be sweetened by fire, they are considered food for that purpose.

The Gemara asks: Where was Rabbi Yochanan's statement originally said? It cites a baraita about bitter and sweet almonds and their obligation in ma'aser, and notes that Rabbi Chanina ruled in Tzippori like the one who says both are exempt.
The Gemara answers: For the one who says both are obligated, for what are large bitter almonds fit? Rabbi Yochanan said: since they can be sweetened by fire, they are considered food.

items.text: Kor: Distinction between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Kor: Distinction between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the difference between Rabbi Yehuda and the Tanna Kamma regarding kor. Abaye suggests the difference is whether kor is cooked or fried. Rava objects, citing a baraita that cooked skin is susceptible to tum'at ochalin. Rava instead says the difference lies in the berakha: Rav Yehuda says 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' because it is food, while Shmuel says 'Shehakol' because it hardens. Shmuel concedes to Rav Yehuda regarding tznon (radish), but the halakha follows Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yehuda's statement that kor is like wood in all respects except for being purchasable with second-tithe money is identical to the first tanna's position — what is the difference between them?

Abaye answers: The difference between them lies in a case where one boiled or fried the kor — according to Rabbi Yehuda it still does not contract food impurity, while the first tanna holds that it does.

Rava objects: Is there anyone who says that even after boiling or frying it does not contract food impurity? He cites a baraita that boiled hide and intended placenta do contract food impurity, implying that cooking renders anything edible susceptible.

Rava resolves: The difference between them is the blessing recited over kor — Rav Yehuda says 'בורא פרי האדמה' (Who creates the fruit of the ground) while Shmuel says 'שהכל נהיה בדברו' (By Whose word all things came to be).
The Gemara explains: Rav Yehuda holds that kor is food and therefore merits the blessing 'בורא פרי האדמה'; Shmuel holds that since it will eventually harden, we do not recite that blessing over it.
Shmuel tells Rav Yehuda: Your opinion seems correct, because a radish (צנון) eventually hardens yet we recite 'בורא פרי האדמה' over it.
The Gemara rejects the analogy: people plant radish for the radish itself, but they do not plant palm trees for the kor; therefore the halakha follows Shmuel.

items.text: Measurements for Eruv with Various Vegetables
items.text_en: Measurements for Eruv with Various Vegetables
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides specific measurements for eruv with keshut, chaziz, kilya (a type of vegetable), and fresh beans. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says keshut and chaziz require the berakha 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah' and their measure is a handful. For chaziz, the measure is the size of a farmer's ear. Rav Chilkiya bar Toviya says one can use kilya, but the Gemara clarifies it is the vegetable of kilya, with a handful measure. Rabbi Yannai says one can use fresh beans, also a handful. Rav Hamnuna says one can use raw teradin (beets), but Rav Chisda warns that raw beets can kill a healthy person.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav states that keshut and chaziz may be used for an eruv and require the blessing 'Borei Pri Ha'adamah'.
Rav Yechiel provides the measure for keshut as a handful, and the Gemara applies the same measure here.

sub.text: Rabbah bar Toviyah bar Yitzchak citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar Toviyah bar Yitzchak citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Toviyah bar Yitzchak in the name of Rav gives the measure for chaziz as the size of a farmer's ear.
Rav Chilkiya bar Toviya says one can use kilya for an eruv, but the Gemara objects that kilya is a type of bean, not a vegetable.
The Gemara clarifies that the reference is to the vegetable of kilya, and Rav Yechiel gives its measure as a handful.
Rabbi Yirmeya is asked whether one can use fresh beans for an eruv, but he does not have an answer.
Rabbi Yannai rules that fresh beans may be used for an eruv, and Rav Yechiel gives the measure as a handful.
Rav Hamnuna says one can use raw teradin (beets) for an eruv.
The Gemara objects by citing Rav Chisda's warning that raw beets can kill a healthy person.

items.text: Dispute about beets for eruv
items.text_en: Dispute about beets for eruv
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna says one cannot use raw beets for an eruv, citing Rav Chisda that raw beets are dangerous. The Gemara questions why people eat them without dying, and answers that they are partially cooked.

items.text: Benefits of cooked beets
items.text_en: Benefits of cooked beets
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda praises cooked beets for health, and Abaye adds that they should be cooked thoroughly.

items.text: Question about apples for eruv
items.text_en: Question about apples for eruv
items.desc_en: Rava compares himself to Ben Azzai, and when asked about the price of apples, he questions whether apples can be used for an eruv.

items.text: Challenge from Mishnah about all foods
items.text_en: Challenge from Mishnah about all foods
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rava's doubt by citing a Mishnah that includes all foods for eruv. It rejects the proof because general statements are not definitive, and then argues that apples are indeed fit for food impurity.

items.text: Quantity of apples for eruv
items.text_en: Quantity of apples for eruv
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that apples require a kav for an eruv. A baraita lists other fruits with specific quantities, and the Gemara explains that apples are less significant than those fruits.

items.text: Rav Yosef's correction about the source
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's correction about the source
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef criticizes Rav Menashya for citing a baraita instead of a Mishnah. He cites a Mishnah about poor people's portions and Rav's ruling that the same applies to eruv. The Gemara concludes that Rav's statement refers to that Mishnah.

items.text: Definition of two meals for eruv
items.text_en: Definition of two meals for eruv
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef thought that two meals must be from two different foods, but Rabbah says even half, third, or quarter of a food suffices.

items.text: Quantity of wine for eruv
items.text_en: Quantity of wine for eruv
items.desc_en: Rav says two quarter-logs of wine are needed for an eruv. A baraita challenges this, but the Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to cooked wine.

items.text: Vinegar and onions for eruv
items.text_en: Vinegar and onions for eruv
