items.desc_en: Rav Giddel explains the amount of vinegar needed. A story about Rabbi Meir allowing an eruv with onions is reconciled: the baraita refers to onion leaves, not bulbs, as bulbs are dangerous.

items.text: Beer for eruv: condition of date-beer
items.text_en: Beer for eruv: condition of date-beer
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that date-beer that has not fully fermented is valid for eruv, but if it has fermented it is not. Rav Pappa adds that this applies only if one did not drink beer, but if one did drink beer, even unfermented date-beer is invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that date-beer which has not fully fermented is valid for an עירוב (eiruv), but if it has fermented it is invalid.
Rav Pappa adds a condition: the ruling applies only if one did not drink beer afterward, but if one did drink beer, even unfermented date-beer is invalid.

items.text: Baraita: danger of onions and a miracle
items.text_en: Baraita: danger of onions and a miracle
items.desc_en: A baraita warns against eating an onion due to a snake within it, and recounts that Rabbi Chanina ate half an onion with half a snake, became deathly ill, and was only saved by his friends' prayers because the hour needed him.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with a general warning: a person should not eat an onion because of the snake (toxin) inside it.
The baraita recounts a story about Rabbi Chanina who ate half an onion and half a snake, and fell deathly ill.
The baraita concludes that his friends prayed for him and he survived, only because the generation needed him.

items.text: Beer's dual status: eruv and mikveh
items.text_en: Beer's dual status: eruv and mikveh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira quotes Shmuel that beer can be used for eruv and also invalidates a mikveh in three log. Rav Kahana objects that this is obvious, comparing it to dye-water which also invalidates a mikveh. The answer distinguishes: dye-water is called water, while beer is called beer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports in the name of Shmuel that beer can be used for eruv and also invalidates a mikveh in three log.
Rav Kahana objects that this is obvious, comparing beer to dye-water which also invalidates a mikveh in three log according to Rabbi Yossi.
The Gemara answers that dye-water is still called water, whereas beer is called beer, so the ruling is not obvious.

items.text: Measure for beer eruv: one quarter-log
items.text_en: Measure for beer eruv: one quarter-log
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Yosef suggests that the measure for beer eruv is two quarter-log, based on the mishna's measure for wine (a quarter-log after dilution). Rav Nachman quotes Rabba bar Avuh that a cup of blessing requires a quarter-log of undiluted wine, and Rava states that wine is diluted with three parts water. The baraita's seifa states that all other liquids require a quarter-log, so beer also requires a quarter-log.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what measure of beer is required for an eruv, and Rav Acha bar Yosef proposes an answer.

Rav Acha bar Yosef suggests that the measure for beer eruv is two quarter-log, based on the mishna's measure for wine (a quarter-log after dilution), citing the cup of blessing requiring a quarter-log of undiluted wine.
Rava states that wine is diluted with three parts water, supporting the calculation that the original quarter-log of wine becomes a full quarter-log after dilution.
The baraita's seifa states that all other liquids require a quarter-log, so beer also requires a quarter-log, not two quarter-log.

items.text: Rejection: beer measure is not a quarter-log
items.text_en: Rejection: beer measure is not a quarter-log
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the comparison: for wine, less than a quarter-log is insignificant, but for beer, people drink a cup in the morning and evening and rely on it, so a smaller amount suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the analogy, explaining that there a smaller amount is insignificant, but here people drink a cup in the morning and a cup in the evening and rely on them, so a smaller measure suffices.

items.text: Dates for eruv: a kab, and proof from a baraita
items.text_en: Dates for eruv: a kab, and proof from a baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that dates require a kab for eruv, citing a baraita that one who eats dried figs and repays with dates is blessed. Abaye challenges that the baraita might refer to monetary value, but Rav Yosef argues it refers to volume, showing dates are superior. Abaye counters that it refers to value but the blessing is for getting a readily sold item.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what quantity of dates is required for an eruv.
Rav Yosef states that dates require a kab for eruv.
Rav Yosef cites a baraita that one who eats dried figs and repays with dates is blessed, to prove dates are superior.
The Gemara questions the baraita: if it refers to monetary value, why is there a blessing for repaying the same value?
The Gemara concludes the baraita refers to volume: one repays a larger value in dates, showing dates are superior.
Abaye argues the baraita still refers to monetary value, but the blessing is for repaying with a readily sold item.

items.text: Other foods: shetita, kisa'ei, and folk remedies
items.text_en: Other foods: shetita, kisa'ei, and folk remedies
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Pinchas says shetita requires two shargushei. Abaye says kisa'ei require two bunei of Pumbedita. Abaye then quotes his mother about the benefits of kisa'ei for the heart and a remedy for heart weakness involving meat, willow branches, and wine.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Pinchas states that the measure for shetita (a drink) is two shargushei (a unit of volume).
Abaye states that the measure for kisa'ei (a type of food) is two bunei of Pumbedita (a local unit).
Abaye reports his mother's teaching that kisa'ei are beneficial for the heart and eliminate harmful thoughts.
Abaye further quotes his mother prescribing a folk remedy for heart weakness: meat from the right thigh of a ram, willow branches, and diluted wine.

items.text: Meat: raw vs. roasted, and a Persian custom
items.text_en: Meat: raw vs. roasted, and a Persian custom
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: for a relish, the measure is enough to eat with it; for a non-relish, enough to eat from it. Raw meat is enough to eat from it. For roasted meat, Rabba says enough to eat with it, Rav Yosef says enough to eat from it. Rav Yosef supports his view by noting Persians eat roasted meat without bread, but Abaye objects that Persians are not the majority.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel's general rule: for a relish (ליפתן), the measure is enough to eat with it; for a non-relish, enough to eat from it.
The stam applies the rule to raw meat: its measure is enough to eat from it (i.e., a piece that can be eaten alone).
Rabba rules that for roasted meat, the measure is enough to eat with it (i.e., as a relish with bread).
Rav Yosef disagrees and rules that for roasted meat, the measure is enough to eat from it (i.e., a piece that can be eaten alone).
Rav Yosef supports his view by noting that Persians eat roasted meat without bread, showing it is eaten alone.
Abaye objects that Persians are not the majority of the world, citing the principle that garments of the poor are measured for the poor, garments of the rich for the rich.

items.text: Opening statement: clothing of rich for poor not allowed
items.text_en: Opening statement: clothing of rich for poor not allowed
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that clothing of rich people cannot be used for an eiruv for poor people, implying a general principle that items not suitable for the person's status are invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that clothing of rich people cannot be used for an eiruv for poor people, implying a general principle that items not suitable for the person's status are invalid.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says we eiruv for a sick or old person according to their needs, and for a glutton according to an average meal, which seems to conflict with the previous statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if both cases are stringent, why does a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar allow eiruv for a sick or elderly person with their food, and for a glutton with an average meal, which seems inconsistent.

items.text: Discussion about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement on Og
items.text_en: Discussion about Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement on Og
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar really said that, citing another baraita about Og's bed being nine cubits. Abaye objects, and then a query is raised whether the Rabbis disagree with him. Rav Yosef bar Chanina's statement resolves the issue by explaining that there were many small openings.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar really said that, citing a baraita where he says Og's opening was full-sized.
Abaye objects that there was no alternative but to bring Og out through the full-sized opening.
A query is raised whether the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Chanina citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Chanina citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Chanina cites Rabbi Yochanan that Og's opening was only four cubits, implying the Rabbis disagree.
The Gemara resolves that there were many small openings and one four-cubit opening, and the expansion was through that one.

items.text: Eiruv with raw meat and eggs
items.text_en: Eiruv with raw meat and eggs
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Ashi in the name of Rav says one can eiruv with raw meat. Rav Shimi bar Chiya says with raw eggs. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak specifies one egg, while Sinai says two.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Rav Ashi citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Ashi citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Rav Ashi cites Rav that one may establish an eiruv with raw meat.
Rav Shimi bar Chiya adds that one may establish an eiruv with raw eggs.
The Gemara asks how many eggs are needed for an eiruv.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that one egg suffices.
Sinai answers that two eggs are required.

items.text: Challenge to Rav and Shmuel from the Mishnah on 'noder min ha-mazon'
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav and Shmuel from the Mishnah on 'noder min ha-mazon'
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says one who vows from 'mazon' is permitted water and salt, implying other things are called 'mazon'. This challenges Rav and Shmuel who say 'Borei minei mezonot' is only for the five grains. Rav Huna resolves by saying the Mishnah refers to one who says 'all that nourishes me'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah that one who vows from 'mazon' is permitted water and salt, implying all other items are called 'mazon'.
The Gemara challenges Rav and Shmuel, who say the blessing 'Borei minei mezonot' is only recited over the five grains.
The Gemara objects that this challenge was already raised once, and now it is raised again from this Mishnah.
Rav Huna resolves the challenge by explaining that the Mishnah refers to one who vows 'all that nourishes me', so water and salt do not nourish, but all other things do.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Yochanan eating Ginosar fruit
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Yochanan eating Ginosar fruit
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chanah relates that when following Rabbi Yochanan to eat Ginosar fruit, they would distribute portions based on group size, and Rabbi Yochanan would eat them all, swearing by 'zeyuna' (weapons), but the Gemara corrects to 'meizona' (food).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects from Rabbah bar bar Chanah's story about Rabbi Yochanan eating many fruits and saying 'shevuata d'la t'ima li ziyuna', suggesting the term should be 'mezon' not 'zon'.
The Gemara corrects the word from 'zeyuna' (weapons) to 'meizona' (food), explaining that Rabbi Yochanan swore by his sustenance.

items.text: Dispute about eiruv with a loaf subject to a vow
items.text_en: Dispute about eiruv with a loaf subject to a vow
items.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav distinguishes between 'shevuah shelo ochal kikar zo' (eiruv is valid) and 'kikar zo alai' (invalid). The Gemara challenges this from a Mishnah, and after analysis, concludes that there are two Tannaitic versions of Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna in the name of Rav distinguishes between a vow formula 'שבועה שלא אוכל ככר זו' (eiruv is valid) and 'ככר זו עלי' (invalid).
The Gemara challenges Rav Huna from a Mishnah that says 'one who vows from a loaf — we make an eiruv for him with it', and suggests it applies even when he said 'עלי', but answers it refers to 'זו'.
The Gemara supports the answer by noting the Mishnah's continuation explicitly says 'when he said: shevuah shelo ete'amenna'.
The Gemara objects: if 'עלי' invalidates the eiruv, why did the Mishnah not teach this distinction explicitly in the case of 'ככר זו הקדש'?
Rav Huna responds: if you think 'עלי' always permits eiruv, then the beginning of the Mishnah is difficult; the Mishnah is defective and must be explained as missing a clause.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is defective and should read: 'one who vows from a loaf — we make an eiruv for him, even if he said עלי, it is as if he said shevuah shelo ete'amenna'.

The Gemara objects that the Mishnah still contradicts Rav Huna, and answers that Rav Huna follows Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between 'שבועה שלא אוכל' (valid) and 'עלי' (invalid).
The Gemara objects that another baraita shows Rabbi Eliezer actually says 'ככר זו עלי' permits eiruv, contradicting the first baraita.
The Gemara resolves that there are two Tannaitic versions of Rabbi Eliezer's opinion.

items.text: Mishnah on eiruv for a nazir with wine and dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Mishnah on eiruv for a nazir with wine and dispute of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one can eiruv for a nazir with wine, etc. The Gemara notes this is not like Beit Shammai, who argue in a baraita that one cannot eiruv for a nazir with wine or for an Israelite with terumah, while Beit Hillel permit it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah: one may establish an eiruv for a nazirite with wine.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Beit Shammai.

sub.text: Baraita citing Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Baraita citing Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Beit Shammai who forbid eiruv for a nazirite with wine and for an Israelite with terumah, while Beit Hillel permit it, and Beit Hillel argue with Beit Shammai.

items.text: Beit Shammai's objection to eiruv for nazir and Israelite
items.text_en: Beit Shammai's objection to eiruv for nazir and Israelite
items.desc_en: Beit Hillel argues that just as one may establish an eiruv for an adult on Yom Kippur (who cannot eat), so too one may establish an eiruv for a nazir with wine and an Israelite with terumah. Beit Shammai counters that in the case of Yom Kippur there is a meal fit for consumption from before the day, but here there is no such meal.

sub.desc_en: Beit Hillel objects that just as one may establish an eiruv for an adult on Yom Kippur (who cannot eat), so too one may establish an eiruv for a nazir with wine and an Israelite with terumah.
Beit Shammai counters that in the case of Yom Kippur there is a meal fit for consumption from before the day, but here there is no such meal.

items.text: Attribution of Beit Shammai's view to Chananyah
items.text_en: Attribution of Beit Shammai's view to Chananyah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In accordance with whom is this dispute? It is not in accordance with Chananyah, who taught that Beit Shammai would not agree to an eiruv unless one moved his bed and all his utensils there.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In accordance with whom is this dispute? It is not in accordance with Chananyah.
A baraita is cited: Chananyah says that Beit Shammai would not agree to an eiruv unless one moved his bed and all his utensils there.

items.text: Chananyah's view on eiruv with black or white garments
items.text_en: Chananyah's view on eiruv with black or white garments
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita: If one established an eiruv with black garments, he may not go out in white. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says this is Chananyah's view in accordance with Beit Shammai. The Gemara then clarifies that Chananyah means that even if one established an eiruv with white and needed black, he may not go out in white either.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks in accordance with whose opinion is the baraita that says one who established an eiruv with black garments may not go out in white, and vice versa.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers that this baraita follows the opinion of חנניה (Chananyah) in accordance with בית שמאי (Beit Shammai).

The Gemara objects: According to חנניה (Chananyah), does the baraita mean that with black he may not go out, but with white he may? But חנניה (Chananyah) requires moving his bed and utensils to the location for the eiruv to be effective.
The Gemara resolves: The baraita means that if one established an eiruv with white and needed black, he may not go out even in white.
The Gemara again asks in accordance with whose opinion is this baraita.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers again that this is the opinion of חנניה (Chananyah) in accordance with בית שמאי (Beit Shammai).

items.text: Somkhos's opinion and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Somkhos's opinion and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: Somkhos says the eiruv is established with non-sacred food, but does not dispute regarding a nazir with wine because the nazir might later be released from his vow. The Gemara questions why terumah is different, and explains that if released, it returns to its untithed state, and one cannot separate terumah from elsewhere due to the rule of min hamukaf. Ultimately, Somkhos holds like the Rabbis who say that any shvut is prohibited during bein hashemashot.

sub.desc_en: Somkhos rules that an eiruv is established with non-sacred food, but does not dispute regarding a nazir with wine.
The Gemara explains that a nazir can have his vow annulled, making the wine permissible.
The Gemara questions why terumah cannot similarly be annulled.
If terumah is annulled, it reverts to tevel (untithed produce) and remains forbidden.
The Gemara suggests separating terumah from another source.
Chaverim are not suspected of separating terumah from non-adjacent produce.
The Gemara suggests separating terumah from the eiruv produce itself.
The produce lacks the minimum quantity for an eiruv after terumah is removed.
The Gemara concludes that Somkhos holds like the Rabbis that any shevut (rabbinic prohibition) applies during bein hashemashot (twilight).

items.text: Attribution of a mishnah to Somkhos
items.text_en: Attribution of a mishnah to Somkhos
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In accordance with whom is the mishnah that says 'everything is according to the person' regarding measures for eiruv? Rabbi Zeira says it is Somkhos, who holds that we require what is fit for him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: In accordance with whom is the mishnah that says 'everything is according to the person' regarding measures for eiruv?
Rabbi Zeira answers that it is Somkhos, who holds that we require what is fit for him.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view on eiruv for a glutton
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's view on eiruv for a glutton
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Somkhos might disagree with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who says we establish an eiruv for a sick or elderly person according to his needs, but for a glutton according to an average person's meal. The Gemara explains that this applies only to a sick or elderly person, but a glutton's opinion is nullified relative to others.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Somkhos disagrees with Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, who rules that an eiruv for a sick or elderly person is set according to his needs, but for a glutton it is set according to an average person's meal.

The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's statement applies only to a sick or elderly person, but a glutton's opinion is nullified relative to others, so Somkhos does not necessarily disagree.

items.text: Eiruv for a kohen in a beit hapras and the dispute over ohel zaruk
items.text_en: Eiruv for a kohen in a beit hapras and the dispute over ohel zaruk
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses eiruv for a kohen in a beit hapras, citing Rav Yehuda and Shmuel about sifting, and Rabbi Yehuda bar Ammi about a trampled beit hapras. Rabbi Yehuda permits even a cemetery because one can go in a chest, box, or cabinet, holding that a movable tent is considered a tent. This is linked to a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda regarding entering the land of the nations in such containers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the topic of an eiruv for a kohen in a beit hapras, citing Rav Yehuda and Shmuel about sifting, and Rabbi Yehuda bar Ammi about a trampled beit hapras being pure.
Rabbi Yehuda permits even a cemetery for a kohen's eiruv because one can go in a chest, box, or cabinet, holding that a movable tent (אוהל זרוק) is considered a tent.

The Gemara links Rabbi Yehuda's position to the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda regarding entering the land of the nations in such containers, concluding that they disagree about whether a movable tent is considered a tent.

items.text: Introduction of another baraita of Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Introduction of another baraita of Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite another baraita of Rabbi Yehuda, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite another baraita of Rabbi Yehuda, but the text is cut off.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah: how can a pure priest use pure terumah for an eruv in a grave?
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah: how can a pure priest use pure terumah for an eruv in a grave?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how a priest can use pure terumah for an eruv when he must go to a grave. It answers that he transports it via a chest or cabinet, that the terumah was not susceptible to impurity, and that he brings it behind his back to avoid overshadowing the grave.

items.text: Reason of the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Reason of the Sages and Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Sages prohibit using terumah for an eruv because they hold it is forbidden to benefit from forbidden items, while Rabbi Yehuda permits it because he holds that mitzvot are not given for benefit.

items.text: Rava's statement aligned with the Tannaic dispute
items.text_en: Rava's statement aligned with the Tannaic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rava's statement that mitzvot are not given for benefit aligns with the Tannaic dispute. It answers that Rava would say all agree on that principle, but they dispute whether eruv is only for a mitzvah or even for a discretionary matter.

items.text: Rav Yosef's statement and the alternative dispute
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's statement and the alternative dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Yosef's statement that eruv is only for a mitzvah aligns with the Tannaic dispute. It answers that all agree eruv is only for a mitzvah and mitzvot are not for benefit, but they dispute whether the owner is pleased that the eruv is guarded or prefers to eat it if needed.

items.text: Mishnah: acceptable and unacceptable foods for eruv
items.text_en: Mishnah: acceptable and unacceptable foods for eruv
items.desc_en: The Mishnah lists foods that may be used for an eruv: demai, first tithe from which terumah was taken, second tithe and consecrated property that were redeemed, and challah for priests. It excludes tevel, first tithe without terumah removed, and unredeemed second tithe and consecrated property.

items.text: Gemara: why is demai valid for eruv?
items.text_en: Gemara: why is demai valid for eruv?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how demai, which is doubtfully tithed, can be used for an eruv since it may not be fit for the owner. It answers that since the owner could declare his property ownerless and become poor, making demai permissible for him, it is considered fit even now, as per the Mishnah that we feed demai to the poor.

items.text: Question about the Mishnah's list
items.text_en: Question about the Mishnah's list
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of demai is referred to in the Mishnah's list of invalid eiruvin.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what type of demai (doubtfully tithed produce) is referred to in the Mishnah's list of invalid eiruvin.

items.text: Rav Huna's answer about demai
items.text_en: Rav Huna's answer about demai
items.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a baraita: Beit Shammai say one may not feed demai to the poor, while Beit Hillel permit it, explaining the Mishnah's reference.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna cites a baraita where Beit Shammai forbid and Beit Hillel permit feeding demai to the poor, explaining the Mishnah's reference.

items.text: Clarification of first tithe case
items.text_en: Clarification of first tithe case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to specify first tithe from which terumat ma'aser was taken but not terumah gedolah, citing Resh Lakish's principle that first tithe taken while still in sheaves is exempt from terumah gedolah. Rav Pappa's objection and Abaye's answer are given.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's case of first tithe from which terumat ma'aser was taken is obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case is necessary when the first tithe was taken while still in sheaves, and terumat ma'aser was taken from it but not terumah gedolah.
Resh Lakish's principle is cited: first tithe taken while in sheaves is exempt from terumah gedolah, based on the verse 'מעשר מן המעשר' (a tithe from the tithe).
Rav Pappa objects that if the exemption applies to sheaves, it should also apply when the tithe was taken while still in a pile (כרי).
Abaye answers that the verse 'מכל מעשרותיכם תרימו את כל תרומת ה׳' applies only to grain that has been fully processed (אידגן), not to sheaves.

items.text: Clarification of second tithe and consecrated property case
items.text_en: Clarification of second tithe and consecrated property case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the necessity of the Mishnah's case of second tithe and consecrated property that were redeemed: one paid the principal but not the surcharge, teaching that the surcharge does not invalidate the redemption.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's case of second tithe and consecrated property that were redeemed is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case is necessary when one paid the principal but not the added fifth, teaching that the fifth does not impede the redemption.

items.text: Clarification of tevel case
items.text_en: Clarification of tevel case
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's prohibition of tevel refers to tevel that is only rabbinically prohibited, such as produce grown in an unperforated pot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's exclusion of tevel (untithed produce) is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case refers to tevel that is only rabbinically prohibited, such as produce grown in a pot without a hole.

items.text: Clarification of first tithe without its terumah
items.text_en: Clarification of first tithe without its terumah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the necessity of the Mishnah's case of first tithe from which terumah was not taken, referring to the earlier discussion of Rav Pappa and Abaye, and concludes that the Mishnah follows Abaye's answer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's exclusion of first tithe from which its terumah was not taken is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case is necessary when the tithe was taken early in a heap, so terumah gedolah was not yet separated.
The Gemara notes that one might have thought to apply Rav Pappa's objection, but the Mishnah teaches the resolution as Abaye answered.

items.text: Clarification of second tithe and consecrated property not properly redeemed
items.text_en: Clarification of second tithe and consecrated property not properly redeemed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the necessity of the Mishnah's case of second tithe and consecrated property that were not properly redeemed: second tithe redeemed with uncoined metal and consecrated property redeemed with land, which are invalid redemptions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's exclusion of second tithe and consecrated property that were not redeemed is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the case is necessary when they were redeemed improperly: second tithe with uncoined metal, which the Torah requires to be silver with a form.
The Gemara explains that consecrated property was redeemed with land instead of money, which the Torah requires for redemption.

items.text: Mishnah: Sending an eiruv via an unreliable agent
items.text_en: Mishnah: Sending an eiruv via an unreliable agent
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one sends his eiruv via a deaf-mute, imbecile, minor, or someone who does not acknowledge eiruv, it is invalid. But if he tells another to receive it from that agent, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that sending an eiruv via a deaf-mute, an imbecile, a minor, or one who does not believe in eiruv is invalid, but if one tells another to receive it from them, it is valid.

items.text: Gemara's question about a minor
items.text_en: Gemara's question about a minor
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's inclusion of a minor, citing Rav Huna that a minor can collect an eiruv. The resolution distinguishes between eiruvei techumin and eiruvei chatzeirot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that a minor cannot be used, citing Rav Huna that a minor may collect an eiruv.
The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah refers to eiruvei techumin (Sabbath boundaries), while Rav Huna's statement refers to eiruvei chatzeirot (courtyard eiruvin).

items.text: Identity of 'one who does not acknowledge eiruv'
items.text_en: Identity of 'one who does not acknowledge eiruv'
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda identifies the person who does not acknowledge eiruv as a Samaritan (Kuti).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is meant by 'one who does not believe in eiruv'.
Rav Chisda answers that it refers to Samaritans (Kutim), who do not believe in the concept of eiruv.

items.text: Discussion of the Mishnah's second clause
items.text_en: Discussion of the Mishnah's second clause
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises concerns about the Mishnah's ruling that if one tells another to receive the eiruv from the agent, it is valid. It addresses the possibility that the agent might not deliver it or the recipient might not accept it, citing Rav Chisda's principle of standing and watching and Rav Yechiel's principle that a messenger is presumed to carry out his mission. The source of these principles is a baraita about an elephant and a monkey.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a concern: perhaps the agent (deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor) will not bring the eiruv to the designated recipient.
Rav Chisda answers that the case is where the sender stands and watches the agent deliver the eiruv.
The Gemara raises another concern: perhaps the recipient will not take the eiruv from the agent.
Rav Yechiel answers that there is a legal presumption (חזקה) that an agent fulfills his agency, so the recipient is presumed to accept the eiruv.
The Gemara asks where the statements of Rav Chisda and Rav Yechiel were originally stated.

The Gemara cites a baraita about an elephant and a monkey, where Rav Chisda and Rav Yechiel's principles were applied: the sender must stand and watch, and the recipient is presumed to accept the eiruv.

items.text: Rav Nachman's limitation of the principle
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's limitation of the principle
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that in Torah law, there is no presumption that a messenger carries out his mission.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that in Torah law, there is no presumption that a messenger carries out his mission.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rav Sheshet and Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet holds that the principle applies even to rabbinic matters, while Rav Nachman limits it to biblical matters. The Gemara begins with Rav Sheshet's position.

sub.desc_en: The Stam opens by stating that in rabbinic matters, the principle of 'a messenger fulfills his mission' (חזקה שליח עושה שליחותו) applies.
Rav Sheshet asserts that the principle applies equally to both biblical and rabbinic matters.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's first proof from the Omer
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's first proof from the Omer
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a mishnah about the new grain (חדש) becoming permitted after the Omer offering, noting that distant people are allowed to eat from midday, implying trust that the court performed the offering.

items.text: Rav Nachman's rejection of the first proof
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's rejection of the first proof
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the mishnah's reason is not trust in an agent but the known fact that the court does not delay the Omer offering.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman objects: There the mishnah gives a different reason — because they know the court is not idle with it.

items.text: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's objection and Rav Sheshet's response
items.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Nachman's objection and Rav Sheshet's response
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Rav Nachman explicitly argues that the mishnah's reason shows the court is not negligent, but an agent might be. Rav Sheshet counters that the court acts only until midday, while an agent acts all day.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version presents Rav Nachman's argument: the mishnah's explicit reason (that the court is not negligent) implies that an agent might be negligent.
Rav Sheshet counters that the court acts only until midday, while an agent acts all day, so the mishnah's reason does not apply to an agent.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's second proof from the woman with childbirth or zavah
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's second proof from the woman with childbirth or zavah
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about a woman who brings money for her offering and then eats sacred food in the evening, implying trust that the priest deposited the money. Rav Nachman explains it is due to the priests' diligence, not general agency.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's third proof from the fig gatherer and the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's third proof from the fig gatherer and the dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about one who sends another to pick figs, where the agent may eat untithed figs and must tithe them as demai. The Gemara notes that both Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agree on the principle of agency, differing only on whether associates are suspected of improper tithing. Rav Nachman explains the case is due to the associate's reliability.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet cites a baraita about one who sends another to pick figs, where the agent may eat untithed figs and must tithe them as demai.

The baraita specifies that the leniency applies only to an am ha'aretz (ignoramus) agent; for a chaver (associate), Rabbi exempts from tithing while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel requires tithing due to suspicion of improper tithing.
The Gemara concludes that Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel agree on the principle of agency (חזקה שליח עושה שליחותו), differing only on whether associates are suspected of improper tithing.
Rav Nachman rejects the proof, explaining that the case relies on Rav Chanina Chozah's principle that an associate is presumed not to release untithed produce from his possession.

items.text: Clarification of the baraita's cases by Ravina
items.text_en: Clarification of the baraita's cases by Ravina
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita's wording, questioning who is speaking to whom. Ravina resolves it: the first clause refers to an ignoramus speaking to an associate, the latter clause to an associate speaking to an ignoramus with another associate listening.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's first clause, where Mar states that the ruling about an ignoramus applies to an ignoramus, but a haver (associate) may eat without tithing, according to Rabbi.

The Gemara questions who the ignoramus is speaking to in the baraita, analyzing both the first clause and the end clause where Rabbi mentions 'ammei ha'aretz' (ignoramuses) in a context that seems inconsistent.
Ravina resolves the difficulty: the first clause refers to an ignoramus speaking to a haver, while the end clause refers to a haver speaking to an ignoramus with another haver listening.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the reasoning behind the dispute: Rabbi holds that a fellow prefers to commit a minor prohibition himself rather than let an am ha'aretz commit a major one, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that the fellow prefers the am ha'aretz commit a major prohibition rather than commit even a minor one himself.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi holds the fellow may eat without tithing because the first fellow certainly tithed, and Rabbi prefers that fellows be suspected of tithing improperly rather than feed amei ha'aretz untithed produce.
The Gemara asks what is the fundamental point of dispute between Rabbi and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

The Gemara answers that Rabbi holds the fellow prefers to commit a minor prohibition himself rather than let an am ha'aretz commit a major one, while Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the fellow prefers the am ha'aretz commit a major prohibition rather than commit even a minor one himself.

items.text: Mishnah: Eruv in a tree or pit
items.text_en: Mishnah: Eruv in a tree or pit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one places an eruv in a tree above ten handbreadths, it is invalid; below ten handbreadths, it is valid. If placed in a pit, even one hundred cubits deep, it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one placed an eiruv in a tree above ten handbreadths it is invalid, below ten it is valid; if placed in a pit even one hundred cubits deep it is valid.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and difficulty
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and difficulty
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman and the other rabbis ask: in what domain is the tree standing? If in a private domain, the height is irrelevant. If in a public domain, if one intends to rest above, the eruv and person are in the same place; if below, he is using the tree, which is prohibited.

sub.text: Rav Nachman and the other rabbis' question
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman and the other rabbis' question
sub.desc_en: The rabbis ask: in what domain is the tree standing? If in a private domain, the height is irrelevant because a private domain extends to the sky.

sub.text: Rav Nachman and the other rabbis' alternative question
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman and the other rabbis' alternative question
sub.desc_en: If the tree is in a public domain, the rabbis ask: where did one intend to rest? If above, the eruv and person are in the same place; if below, he is using the tree, which is prohibited.

items.text: Resolution: Tree in public domain, intention below, and Rabbi's principle
items.text_en: Resolution: Tree in public domain, intention below, and Rabbi's principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the tree is in a public domain, the person intends to rest below, and the case follows Rabbi's view that shvut restrictions do not apply during twilight. Rav Nachman confirms this as Shmuel's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the tree stands in the public domain, the person intends to rest below, and the case follows Rabbi's view that שְׁבוּת (rabbinic prohibitions) do not apply during twilight.

Rav Nachman confirms the resolution, stating that Shmuel also rules this way, and after a brief exchange about whether this is established in the Gemara, he reiterates the full explanation: a tree in the public domain, ten handbreadths high and four wide, intention to rest below, and Rabbi's principle.

items.text: Rava's distinction: tree within or outside the city's boundary
items.text_en: Rava's distinction: tree within or outside the city's boundary
items.desc_en: Rava states that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to a tree outside the city's boundary; if the tree is within the boundary, even above ten handbreadths, the eruv is valid, as the city is considered filled.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes that the Mishnah's ruling applies only to a tree outside the city's boundary; if the tree is within the boundary, even above ten handbreadths, the eruv is valid, as the city is considered filled.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the tree outside the boundary
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the tree outside the boundary
items.desc_en: An objection is raised: if the tree is outside the boundary, the person has four cubits of private domain, which extends to the sky. Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya resolves that the tree extends beyond those four cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the tree is outside the city's boundary, the person's four cubits of private domain should extend to the sky, making the eruv valid even above ten handbreadths.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's resolution
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya's resolution
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Mesharshiya resolves that the case involves a tree that extends beyond the four cubits of the person's private domain, so the domain does not reach the tree's location.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's terms
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's terms
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's terms 'above' and 'below' refer to the eruv being placed above or below ten handbreadths, and that the intention was to rest in the tree's base, but the branch later bent upward.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's terms 'above' and 'below' refer to the eruv being placed above or below ten handbreadths, and that the intention was to rest in the tree's base, but the branch later bent upward.

items.text: Objection and resolution via Ulla
items.text_en: Objection and resolution via Ulla
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one could bring the eruv via the tree's top, and resolves that the case is where many people are shouldering the tree, as per Ulla's ruling about a pillar in the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that one could bring the eruv via the tree's top, undermining the earlier distinction.
The Gemara resolves that the case is where many people are shouldering the tree, citing Ulla's ruling about a pillar in the public domain.

items.text: Introducing the Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Introducing the Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who Rabbi and the Rabbis are, and cites a baraita where Rabbi rules that placing the eruv in a basket hung on a tree is valid even above ten handbreadths, while the Rabbis say it is invalid wherever it is forbidden to take it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who is meant by 'Rabbi' and 'the Rabbis' in the previous discussion.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi rules that placing the eruv in a basket hung on a tree is valid even above ten handbreadths, while the Rabbis say it is invalid wherever it is forbidden to take it.

items.text: Determining which part of the baraita the Rabbis address
items.text_en: Determining which part of the baraita the Rabbis address
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Rabbis' statement refers to the latter clause (basket case) or the first clause (direct placement), concluding it must refer to the first clause, as otherwise they would be permitting use of the tree's sides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which clause of the baraita the Rabbis' statement refers to.
The Gemara objects that if the Rabbis referred to the latter clause (basket case), they would be holding that the sides of the tree (צדדין) are forbidden for use, which is unlikely.
The Gemara concludes that the Rabbis' statement must refer to the first clause (direct placement in the tree), not the basket case.

items.text: Analyzing the tree's dimensions
items.text_en: Analyzing the tree's dimensions
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the tree's width: if less than four handbreadths it is a exempt domain, if four or more then the basket case is irrelevant. Ravina resolves that the first clause deals with a tree of four handbreadths, the latter with less than four where the basket completes it to four.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the tree's dimensions: if it lacks four handbreadths it is a exempt domain, but if it has four, what relevance does the basket case have?
Ravina resolves that the first clause deals with a tree of four handbreadths, the latter with less than four where the basket completes it to four.

items.text: Rabbi's dual alignment with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah
items.text_en: Rabbi's dual alignment with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Judah
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi holds like Rabbi Meir regarding the principle of carving out to complete, and like Rabbi Judah regarding the requirement that the eruv be placed on a four-handbreadth area, which is lacking here.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Judah's baraita
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Judah's baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Judah says that if one placed an eruv on a pole in the public domain, it is valid only if the pole is ten handbreadths high and four wide. It then corrects the baraita's wording: if the pole is ten high, its top must be four wide; if not, it need not be four wide.

items.text: Comparison with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Judah's view
items.text_en: Comparison with Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Judah's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose view this is, noting it is not like Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Judah, who says that if one placed a basket on a reed and threw an object onto it, he is liable. The Gemara answers that even according to Rabbi Yosei bar Rabbi Judah, there the partitions are restored, but here they are not.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's distinction regarding a basket
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's distinction regarding a basket
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya says that a basket is different because one can tilt it and bring it within ten handbreadths, thus it is considered a valid partition.

items.text: Rav Pappa's teaching and Rav bar Shabba's objection
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's teaching and Rav bar Shabba's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa was teaching this halakha, and Rav bar Shabba raised an objection based on a baraita describing how one carries an eruv on the first day and then on the second day, implying a different procedure.

items.text: Gemara's initial question
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah invalidates an eruv placed above ten handbreadths in a public domain, arguing that since one could potentially bring it down, it should be considered as if already brought down.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah invalidates an eruv placed above ten handbreadths in a public domain, arguing that since one could potentially bring it down, it should be considered as if already brought down.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's answer
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's answer
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the invalidation is a decree due to a Festival that falls after Shabbat, to prevent one from carrying the eruv on the Festival.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira answers: It is a decree due to a Festival that falls after Shabbat, to prevent carrying the eruv on the Festival.

items.text: Objection from a baraita and Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita and Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that distinguishes between an eruv in a wall and on a dovecote or cabinet, ruling that above ten handbreadths is valid for the latter. The Gemara objects that the same logic should apply, and Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the case involves a cabinet that is 'summar' (narrow and fixed), preventing easy retrieval.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that distinguishes between an eruv placed in a wall (valid below ten handbreadths, invalid above) and one placed on a dovecote or cabinet (valid above ten handbreadths, invalid below).
The Gemara asks why the same logic of 'since he could tilt and bring it within ten handbreadths' does not apply to the cabinet case.
Rabbi Yirmeya answers that the case involves a cabinet that is 'מסומר' (narrow and fixed), preventing easy retrieval of the eruv.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different answer: even if the cabinet is not narrow, it is tall, and moving it slightly would cause it to extend beyond four cubits, making retrieval impossible without violating Shabbat. The Gemara then clarifies that this applies when there are no windows or beams to facilitate moving it.

sub.desc_en: Rava offers an alternative explanation: even if the cabinet is not narrow, it is tall, so moving it slightly would cause it to extend beyond four cubits, making retrieval impossible without violating Shabbat.
The Gemara asks: if there are windows or beams, why not bring it through them?
The Gemara resolves: the case is where there are no windows or beams to facilitate moving it.

items.text: Transition to the case of a pit
items.text_en: Transition to the case of a pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins analyzing the Mishnah's ruling about an eruv placed in a pit, even one hundred cubits deep, and asks where the pit is located, first suggesting it is in a private domain.

sub.desc_en: Gemara asks: How does this case compare? If there is a window and a ladder, bring it through window and ladder. If not, what then?

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's case of a pit
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's case of a pit
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of an eruv placed in a pit, initially assuming it is obvious. It then reframes the case as involving a person standing in a karmelit who intends to rest above, invoking Rabbi's view that rabbinic decrees do not apply during twilight.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah's case of a pit is not obvious, since a private domain (רשות היחיד) extends upward to the sky and downward as well.

The Gemara reframes the case: if the person intends to rest above or below, the eruv is either in a different place or obviously valid, so the Mishnah's case must involve a person standing in a public domain (רשות הרבים).

The Gemara answers that the case involves a person standing in a karmelit (כרמלית) who intends to rest above, and follows Rabbi's view that rabbinic decrees (שבות) do not apply during twilight (בין השמשות).

items.text: Mishnah: Eruv on a detached and inserted reed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Eruv on a detached and inserted reed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one placed the eruv on top of a reed or pole that is detached and inserted into the ground, even if it is one hundred cubits high, it is a valid eruv.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one placed the eruv on top of a reed or pole that is detached and inserted, even if it is 100 cubits high, it is a valid eruv.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction between the Mishnah and the Rabbis
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction between the Mishnah and the Rabbis
items.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana raises a contradiction: the Mishnah requires the reed to be detached and inserted, implying it is invalid otherwise, which aligns with the Rabbis who apply decrees during twilight. But the earlier Mishnah (about the pit) followed Rabbi. The Gemara resolves that the first clause is Rabbi and the latter clause is the Rabbis, or alternatively, the entire Mishnah is Rabbi and the latter clause is a decree lest one cut a branch.

sub.text: Rav Adda bar Mattana's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Adda bar Mattana raises a contradiction: the Mishnah requires the reed to be detached and inserted (תלוש ונעוץ), implying it is invalid otherwise, which aligns with the Rabbis who apply decrees during twilight, but the earlier pit Mishnah followed Rabbi; he asks whether the first clause is Rabbi and the latter clause the Rabbis.

sub.text: Rava's answer citing Rami bar Chama
sub.text_en: Rava's answer citing Rami bar Chama
sub.desc_en: Rava answers that Rami bar Chama already raised this to Rav Chisda, who resolved it: the first clause follows Rabbi and the latter clause follows the Rabbis.
Ravina offers an alternative: the entire Mishnah follows Rabbi, and the latter clause is a decree lest one cut a branch.

items.text: Story of the polemos in Neharde'a and the distinction between reeds with and without branches
items.text_en: Story of the polemos in Neharde'a and the distinction between reeds with and without branches
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman instructs to make reed beds in the marsh for an eruv. Rami bar Chama objects based on the Mishnah requiring detached and inserted reeds. Rav Nachman distinguishes between reeds with branches (עוזרדין) and those without, citing a beraita about kilayim. The Gemara then questions whether קידה is a vegetable, and Rav Papa distinguishes between קידה and קידה לבנה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts that a polemos (military conflict) came to Neharde'a, and Rav Nachman instructed the people to make reed beds in the marsh for an eruv.

sub.text: Rami bar Chama (or Rav Ukva bar Abba) to Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rami bar Chama (or Rav Ukva bar Abba) to Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama objects by citing the Mishnah: only detached and inserted reeds (תלוש ונעוץ) are valid for an eruv, not attached reeds.

Rav Nachman distinguishes between reeds with branches (עוזרדין) and those without, citing a beraita about kilayim that classifies certain reeds as trees and others as vegetables, creating an apparent contradiction.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by concluding that one beraita refers to reeds with branches (עוזרדין) and the other to those without, confirming Rav Nachman's distinction.
The Gemara questions whether קידה (a plant mentioned in the beraita) is a vegetable, citing a Mishnah that forbids grafting פיגם onto קידה לבנה because it is a vegetable grafted onto a tree.
Rav Papa distinguishes between קידה (a vegetable) and קידה לבנה (a tree), resolving the apparent contradiction.

items.text: Mishnah: Eruv in a cabinet with a lost key
items.text_en: Mishnah: Eruv in a cabinet with a lost key
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one placed the eruv in a cabinet and the key was lost, it is a valid eruv. Rabbi Eliezer disagrees, requiring knowledge of the key's location.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states: if one placed the eruv in a cabinet and the key was lost, it is a valid eruv; Rabbi Eliezer says if one does not know where the key is, it is not a valid eruv.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the cabinet case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the cabinet case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the eruv is valid, as the person and eruv are in different places. Rav and Shmuel explain it deals with a brick cabinet and follows Rabbi Meir, who permits breaking into it. Rav Nachman bar Adda specifies it is in the airspace of bricks. Rabbi Zeira limits this to Yom Tov, not Shabbat. The Gemara then questions a related Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between city and field, which would not apply on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the eruv is valid, as the person and the eruv are in different places.
Rav and Shmuel explain that the case deals with a brick cabinet and follows Rabbi Meir, who permits breaking into it לכתחילה (the ideal standard).

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Adda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Adda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Adda specifies that the eruv is in the airspace of bricks, and the Gemara applies this here as well.
Rabbi Zeira objects that this ruling applies only on Yom Tov (יום טוב), not on Shabbat (שבת).
The Gemara resolves that here too the case is on Yom Tov (יום טוב).
The Gemara questions a related Mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between city and field, which would not apply on Yom Tov (יום טוב).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of lost key and found key
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of lost key and found key
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case where an eruv was placed in a cabinet and the key was lost; on Yom Tov it is valid, on Shabbat not. If the key is later found, whether in the city or field, the eruv is invalid, except Rabbi Eliezer who says if found in the city it is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara emends the Mishnah to present the case of a lost key in a cabinet, distinguishing Yom Tov from Shabbat, and then records the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a found key.

items.text: Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara explains Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling in the city follows Rabbi Shimon's view that roofs, courtyards, and enclosures are a single domain for vessels that rested there, while in the field he follows the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rabbi Eliezer's position: in the city he follows Rabbi Shimon's view that roofs, courtyards, and enclosures are a single domain for vessels that rested there, while in the field he follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef: dispute about wooden cabinet
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef: dispute about wooden cabinet
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both say the case involves a wooden cabinet; one view holds it is a vessel (no building or demolition in vessels), the other holds it is a tent.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both state that the case involves a wooden cabinet, disagreeing whether it is a vessel (no building or demolition in vessels) or a tent.

items.text: Support from Tannaitic dispute about chests
items.text_en: Support from Tannaitic dispute about chests
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute: one who knocks on a chest, box, or cabinet is impure; Rabbi Nehemiah and Rabbi Shimon declare pure. The Gemara suggests the dispute is whether it is a vessel or a tent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Tannaitic dispute about knocking on chests, box, or cabinet, where the first Tanna declares impurity and Rabbi Nehemiah and Rabbi Shimon declare purity.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute is whether the chest is a vessel (כלי) or a tent (אוהל).

items.text: Abaye's rejection and alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's rejection and alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye rejects the previous explanation, citing a baraita about tent and vessel impurity. He explains that all agree on the impurity rules, but the dispute is about whether a tremor caused by one's force is considered 'moved' or not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the explanation by citing a baraita about impurity: a vessel moved by force is impure, by tremor is pure. He asks whether the tremor here is due to force (making it impure) or not.

items.text: Abaye and Rava: the Mishnah involves a lock tied with a cord
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava: the Mishnah involves a lock tied with a cord
items.desc_en: Abaye and Rava explain that the Mishnah deals with a lock tied with a cord that requires a knife to cut. The first Tanna follows Rabbi Yosi that all vessels may be moved on Shabbat except a large saw and plowshare; Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi Nehemiah that vessels are only moved for their use.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how to interpret the Mishnah's case of the lock.
Abaye and Rava explain that the Mishnah deals with a lock tied with a cord that requires a knife to cut.
The first Tanna follows Rabbi Yosi that all vessels may be moved on Shabbat except a large saw and plowshare.
Rabbi Eliezer follows Rabbi Nehemiah that vessels are only moved for their use.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Eruv rolled out of boundary, covered, burned, or impure
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Eruv rolled out of boundary, covered, burned, or impure
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the eruv rolled outside the boundary, was covered by a pile, burned, or became impure before nightfall, it is invalid; after nightfall, valid. If uncertain, Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda say it is like a חמר גמל; Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon say uncertain eruv is valid, citing Avtulmos' testimony.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that if the eruv rolled outside the boundary, was covered by a pile, burned, or became impure before nightfall, it is invalid; after nightfall, it is valid.
Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda rule that in a case of uncertainty, the eruv is like a חמר גמל (a donkey-driver and a camel-driver, i.e., neither here nor there).
Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon rule that an uncertain eruv is valid.
Rabbi Yosi supports his position by citing Avtulmos' testimony from five elders that an uncertain eruv is valid.

items.text: Gemara on the second Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara on the second Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rava limits the case of rolling outside the boundary to beyond four cubits. The Gemara considers whether the Mishnah about a pile follows Rabbi's view that a שבות is not prohibited during twilight, but concludes it requires a pick and axe. The Gemara explains why both cases of rolling and pile are needed, and questions why burning and impurity are mentioned separately.

sub.desc_en: Rava limits the Mishnah's case of rolling outside the boundary to beyond four cubits, because within four cubits the one who placed the eiruv still has four cubits of movement.
The Gemara initially assumes that the case of a pile falling on the eiruv is one where the person could retrieve it if they wanted.
The Gemara challenges that the Mishnah might not follow Rabbi's view that a שבות (rabbinic prohibition) is not prohibited during twilight.
The Gemara resolves that even according to Rabbi, the case requires a pick and axe, which is a more severe prohibition, so the Mishnah is valid.
The Gemara explains why both cases of rolling and pile are necessary: each teaches a unique scenario where one might think the eiruv is valid, but it is not.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah separately mentions burning and impurity, since both are cases of destruction.
The Gemara begins to cite a baraita that explains the distinction between burning and impurity, but the section ends here.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishna's cases
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishna's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishna includes cases of teruma that became impure to demonstrate the leniency of Rabbi Yosei, and cases of teruma that became impure to demonstrate the stringency of Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishna includes cases of teruma that became impure to demonstrate the leniency of Rabbi Yosei, and cases of teruma that became impure to demonstrate the stringency of Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's stringency from a Mishna about doubtful impurity
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's stringency from a Mishna about doubtful impurity
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Meir's stringency by citing a Mishna where he rules that a person who immersed in a mikveh with doubt is impure for severe impurity, but pure for light impurity, implying he is lenient in some cases. Rabbi Yosei disagrees and declares him impure even for light impurity.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Meir's stringency by asking whether he consistently rules doubtful cases stringently.
The Gemara cites a Mishna where Rabbi Meir rules that a person with doubtful immersion in a mikveh is impure for severe impurity, showing he is stringent in some cases.
The Mishna specifies that for light impurity, Rabbi Meir rules the doubtful case pure, implying leniency.
The Mishna concludes that Rabbi Yosei declares the doubtful case impure even for light impurity.

items.text: Gemara's resolution: Rabbi Meir holds techumin are biblical
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution: Rabbi Meir holds techumin are biblical
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by stating that Rabbi Meir considers techumin to be biblical law, hence he is stringent regarding the eruv.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei declares impure.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's view from a baraita about kudring in mountains
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Meir's view from a baraita about kudring in mountains
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Meir's view that techumin are biblical by citing a baraita where Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai says in Rabbi Meir's name that one may 'kuder' (measure) in mountains for eruv techumin, implying it is rabbinic. The Gemara resolves that the baraita reflects Rabbi Meir's teacher's view, not his own.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Meir's view that techumin are biblical by citing a baraita where Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai reports in Rabbi Meir's name that one may 'kuder' (measure) in mountains for eruv techumin, implying it is rabbinic.

The Gemara objects that if techumin were biblical, one could not 'kuder' (measure) in mountains, citing Rav Nachman's ruling that one does not measure for biblical matters like cities of refuge or the heifer.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita reflects Rabbi Meir's teacher's view, not his own, as indicated by the phrase 'I heard that one may kuder in mountains.'

items.text: Contradiction within Rabbi Meir's biblical rulings on doubt
items.text_en: Contradiction within Rabbi Meir's biblical rulings on doubt
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two biblical rulings of Rabbi Meir: here he is stringent regarding techumin, but in a Mishna about touching a corpse at night, he is lenient and declares purity, while the Sages are stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between two biblical rulings of Rabbi Meir: here he is stringent regarding techumin, but in a Mishna about touching a corpse at night, he is lenient and declares purity, while the Sages are stringent.

items.text: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: the Mishna deals with a carcass present at twilight
items.text_en: Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution: the Mishna deals with a carcass present at twilight
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya resolves the contradiction by explaining that the Mishna about touching a corpse deals with a case where a carcass was present throughout twilight, so the doubt is about the moment of contact, not about the status of the object. This leads to a question: if so, why does Rabbi Yosei consider the eruv valid?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Torah law and Torah law regarding Rabbi Meir: We learned: He touched one at night, not knowing if alive or dead; next morning he found him dead. Rabbi Meir declares pure, and Sages declare impure, because all impurities are at the time of finding.
The Gemara questions: if so, why does Rabbi Yosei consider the eruv valid, given the doubt about the carcass's presence?

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's resolution: two sets of witnesses
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's resolution: two sets of witnesses
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef resolve the difficulty by explaining that the case involves two sets of witnesses: one says the eruv was impure before dark, the other says after dark. Thus, the doubt is about the time of impurity, not the status of the eruv, and Rabbi Yosei's leniency is justified.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yirmeya answers: Our Mishna deals with a reptile that was on it during twilight. If so, then would Rabbi Yosei say a doubtful eiruv is valid?

items.text: Rava's distinction between impurity and eruv
items.text_en: Rava's distinction between impurity and eruv
items.desc_en: Rava explains that in the impurity case there are two lenient presumptions, while in the eruv case there is only one, justifying Rabbi Yosei's different rulings.

sub.desc_en: Rava answers the contradiction by explaining that in the impurity case there are two lenient presumptions, while in the eruv case there is only one.

items.text: Contradiction in Rabbi Yosei's rulings and resolution
items.text_en: Contradiction in Rabbi Yosei's rulings and resolution
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised between Rabbi Yosei's rulings on impurity and eruv. Rav Huna bar Chinana resolves it by noting that impurity has a Torah basis, while eruv boundaries are rabbinic, so Rabbi Yosei is lenient only for rabbinic laws.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction between Rabbi Yosei's rulings on impurity and eruv.
Rav Huna bar Chinana resolves the contradiction by distinguishing impurity, which has a Torah basis, from eruv boundaries, which Rabbi Yosei holds are rabbinic.

items.text: Alternative resolution: different traditions
items.text_en: Alternative resolution: different traditions
items.desc_en: An alternative answer suggests that the two rulings come from different sources—one from Rabbi Yosei himself, the other from his teacher. The baraita supports this by citing Rabbi Yosei in the name of Avtulmos.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the two rulings of Rabbi Yosei come from different sources—one from himself, the other from his teacher Avtulmos—and the baraita supports this by citing Rabbi Yosei in the name of Avtulmos.

items.text: Rava's alternative explanation for impurity
items.text_en: Rava's alternative explanation for impurity
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different explanation: in the impurity case, we place the person on his presumptive status of being impure, and the mikveh on its presumptive status of being full. The Gemara objects that we should instead presume the mikveh is full, but Rava clarifies it is a mikveh that was not measured.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that Rabbi Yosei's ruling in the impurity case is based on placing the impure person on his presumptive status (חזקה) that he did not immerse.
The Gemara objects that one should instead place the mikveh on its presumptive status that it was full and not lacking.
Rava clarifies that the case involves a mikveh that was never measured, so there is no presumptive status of fullness.

items.text: Definition of a valid doubtful eruv
items.text_en: Definition of a valid doubtful eruv
items.desc_en: A baraita defines when Rabbi Yosei considers a doubtful eruv valid: when the doubt is about the timing of an event (e.g., before or after nightfall). But if the doubt is about the food's inherent status (e.g., pure or impure), it is invalid. The Gemara questions why the same logic doesn't apply to produce, and resolves by reinterpreting the case as doubt about mixture.

sub.desc_en: A baraita defines Rabbi Yosei's valid doubtful eruv: when the doubt is about the timing of an event (before or after nightfall), the eruv is valid.
The baraita contrasts: if the doubt is about the food's inherent status (pure or impure), the eruv is invalid.
The Gemara questions why the same logic of 'stand the produce on its presumption' doesn't apply to untithed produce, making the eruv valid.
The Gemara resolves by reinterpreting the case: the doubt is not about tithing but about mixture (דמוע), so the presumption of untithed status is irrelevant.

items.text: Case of two loaves: one pure, one impure
items.text_en: Case of two loaves: one pure, one impure
items.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak asks Rav Huna about a case where one has two loaves, one pure and one impure, and says 'make an eruv for me with the pure one wherever it is.' The Gemara considers whether Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Yosei would validate it, and Rav Huna rules it invalid because we require a meal fit to eat before nightfall.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak asks Rav Huna about a case where one has two loaves, one pure and one impure, and says 'make an eruv for me with the pure one wherever it is.'

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the question's implications
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the question's implications
sub.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the question applies to both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei, analyzing their respective positions regarding the availability of a known pure loaf.
Rav Huna rules that both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei would invalidate the eruv because we require a meal fit to eat before nightfall, and here the pure loaf is unknown.

items.text: Case of a loaf that changes status between weekday and holy day
items.text_en: Case of a loaf that changes status between weekday and holy day
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a loaf that is today profane and tomorrow holy, or vice versa. Rav Nachman rules that in the first case the eruv is valid because sanctity does not take effect on a doubtful basis, but in the second case it is invalid because sanctity does not depart on a doubtful basis.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman about a loaf that is today profane and tomorrow holy, and whether an eruv declared on it is valid.
Rav Nachman rules that the eruv is valid when the loaf is profane today and holy tomorrow.
Rava asks about the reverse case: a loaf that is holy today and profane tomorrow.
Rav Nachman rules that the eruv is invalid when the loaf is holy today and profane tomorrow.
The gemara asks what distinguishes the two cases.
Rav Nachman explains that sanctity does not take effect on a doubtful basis in the first case, and does not depart on a doubtful basis in the second.

items.text: Mishnah about a jug of tevel and Rava's conclusion
items.text_en: Mishnah about a jug of tevel and Rava's conclusion
items.desc_en: A mishnah discusses a jug of tevel from which a tevul yom fills and designates terumah for after nightfall—his words stand, but if he says 'make an eruv with this,' it is invalid. Rava concludes that the end of the day acquires the eruv.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah is cited: a jug of tevul yom filled from a barrel of tevel, where he declares it terumat maaser after nightfall—his words stand.
The mishnah continues: if he said 'make an eruv with this,' his words are void.
Rava concludes from the mishnah that the end of the day acquires the eruv.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says one who says 'mix an eruv for me in this place' says nothing, suggesting that if the beginning of the day acquires the eruv, he should be able to stipulate. Rav Pappa answers that even if the beginning of the day acquires, a meal fit for that time is required, which is lacking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah rules that one who says 'mix an eruv for me in this place' says nothing, given that if the beginning of the day acquires the eruv, he should be able to stipulate.
Rav Pappa answers that even if the beginning of the day acquires the eruv, a meal fit for that time is required, which is lacking.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional eruv based on gentiles or a sage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional eruv based on gentiles or a sage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that one may stipulate conditions on his eruv: if gentiles come from the east, his eruv is for the west; if from the west, for the east; if from both, he goes where he wishes; if none come, he is like the people of his city. Similarly, if a sage comes from the east or west, the eruv is directed accordingly. Rabbi Yehuda adds that if one of them is his teacher, he goes to his teacher; if both are his teachers, he chooses.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a person may stipulate regarding his eruv based on the direction from which gentiles or a sage might come.
The Mishnah presents a parallel case for a sage's arrival, with the same conditional stipulation.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that if one of the sages is his teacher, he goes to his teacher; if both are his teachers, he may choose.

items.text: Gemara resolves contradictions in the Mishnah's versions
items.text_en: Gemara resolves contradictions in the Mishnah's versions
items.desc_en: When Rabbi Yitzchak came, he taught the entire Mishnah in reverse, creating apparent contradictions between the cases of gentiles and sages. The Gemara resolves: the first case of gentiles refers to a governor, the second to a city mayor; the first case of sages refers to one who expounds, the second to one who teaches Shema.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports that when Rabbi Yitzchak came, he taught the entire Mishnah in reverse, creating apparent contradictions between the cases of gentiles and sages.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the gentile cases: the first refers to a governor (פרהגבנא), the second to a city mayor (מרי דמתא).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction between the sage cases: the first refers to one who expounds (מותיב פירקי), the second to one who teaches Shema (מקרי שמע).

items.text: Reason for the Sages' disagreement with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Reason for the Sages' disagreement with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Sages disagree with Rabbi Yehuda: sometimes one prefers his colleague over his teacher.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yehuda because sometimes one prefers his colleague over his teacher.

items.text: Rav's challenge from the baraita of Ayo
items.text_en: Rav's challenge from the baraita of Ayo
items.desc_en: Rav says the Mishnah is not according to the baraita of Ayo, who taught that Rabbi Yehuda says one cannot stipulate on two things at once, only on one direction. The Gemara questions why the case of 'to here and to here' is invalid due to bereirah, but the case of 'to the east, to the west' also lacks bereirah. Rabbi Yochanan answers: 'And the sage already came' (so it is retroactively clarified).

sub.desc_en: Rav declares that the Mishnah does not align with the baraita of Ayo, which teaches that Rabbi Yehuda only allows stipulation for one direction, not two simultaneously.
The Gemara questions why the case of 'to here and to here' is invalid due to lack of בְּרֵירָה (retroactive clarification), while the case of 'to the east, to the west' also lacks such clarification.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that the case of 'to the east, to the west' is valid because the sage has already arrived, providing retroactive clarification.

items.text: Rejection of Rav's claim and proof from Rabbi Yehuda's view
items.text_en: Rejection of Rav's claim and proof from Rabbi Yehuda's view
