items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the opposite: that Ayo's baraita is not according to the Mishnah. But this is rejected because we have heard that Rabbi Yehuda does not accept bereirah, as taught in a mishnah about buying wine from Cutheans.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Ayo's baraita is not supported by the Mishnah, suggesting the opposite.
The Gemara rejects the counter-suggestion because Rabbi Yehuda is known to reject בְּרֵירָה (retroactive designation), as taught in a mishnah about buying wine from Cutheans.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir permits one to separate terumot and ma'asrot by declaring future designations and drinking immediately, relying on ברירה. Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir permits declaring future separation of terumot and ma'asrot and drinking immediately, relying on ברירה (retroactive clarification), while Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon forbid it.

items.text: Ulla's correction of the Mishnah's text
items.text_en: Ulla's correction of the Mishnah's text
items.desc_en: Ulla argues that the Mishnah's version is not precise; he asserts that the correct text pairs Rabbi Meir with Rabbi Yehuda (permitting) and Rabbi Yosei with Rabbi Shimon (forbidding), implying that Rabbi Yehuda actually permits.

sub.desc_en: Ulla asserts that the statement of Ayo should not be accepted because it contradicts the Mishnah, and he notes the Tosefta's ruling that Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Shimon prohibit.

Ulla resolves the contradiction by teaching that the Tosefta's text pairs Rabbi Meir with Rabbi Yehuda (permitting) and Rabbi Yosei with Rabbi Shimon (forbidding), thereby showing that Rabbi Yehuda actually permits.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita on bird offerings
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita on bird offerings
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's version by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei appears to rely on ברירה regarding bird offerings, contradicting the claim that he forbids it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Ulla's version by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yosei appears to rely on ברירה regarding bird offerings, contradicting the claim that he forbids it.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution and Rav Chisda's principle
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution and Rav Chisda's principle
items.desc_en: Rabbah answers that the baraita deals with a case where the women stipulated in advance, so it does not prove Rabbi Yosei's view on ברירה. The Gemara adds that this teaches Rav Chisda's principle that bird offerings are not designated individually.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on Rabbi Yosi's position
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on Rabbi Yosi's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosi can reject bereirah in the context of eruv, given that he seems to accept it in a case of produce acquisition from an am ha'aretz.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosi can reject bereirah in the context of eruv, given that he seems to accept it in a case of produce acquisition from an am ha'aretz.

items.text: Proof from a baraita about an am ha'aretz
items.text_en: Proof from a baraita about an am ha'aretz
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosi exempts an am ha'aretz from tithing when he sends a haver to buy produce, implying bereirah. The Sages disagree. The Gemara suggests flipping the attribution.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how Rabbi Yosi can hold that there is no bereirah (retroactive clarification) given a baraita that seems to require it.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosi exempts an am ha'aretz (ignorant person) from tithing when he sends a haver (associate) to buy produce, implying bereirah.
The Sages disagree with Rabbi Yosi and require tithing, contradicting the assumption that Rabbi Yosi holds bereirah.
The Gemara suggests flipping the attribution of the baraita to resolve the contradiction.

items.text: Proof from a case of redeeming ma'aser on a coin
items.text_en: Proof from a case of redeeming ma'aser on a coin
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita where Rabbi Yosi allows redeeming ma'aser on a coin that will come up from the purse, which seems to accept bereirah. The Gemara flips the text based on the end of the baraita, showing Rabbi Yosi only allows it when the coin is new and unique.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita where Rabbi Yosi allows redeeming ma'aser on a coin that will come up from the purse, which seems to accept bereirah.
The Gemara objects that the baraita should be flipped, making Rabbi Yosi say the redemption is invalid, and questions why one would flip two cases before one.

The Gemara resolves that the baraita is indeed flipped, as the end of the baraita shows Rabbi Yosi only allows redemption when the coin is new and unique, implying that in the first case he does not allow it.

items.text: Analysis of the new coin case
items.text_en: Analysis of the new coin case
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the case of the new coin: if there are multiple coins, it's like the first case; if only one, the term 'will come up' is problematic. The Gemara explains the repetition of 'will come up' as stylistic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what are the circumstances of the new coin case? If there are multiple coins, it's like the first case; if only one, the term 'תעלה' (will come up) is problematic.
The Gemara answers: because the first clause used 'תעלה', the latter clause also used 'תעלה' as a stylistic repetition.

items.text: Rava's question to Rav Nachman about a tanna who rejects bereirah even rabbinically
items.text_en: Rava's question to Rav Nachman about a tanna who rejects bereirah even rabbinically
items.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman who is the tanna that rejects bereirah even in rabbinic matters, citing a baraita about eruv with multiple people. Rav Nachman is silent; the Gemara suggests it is the school of Ayyo, but Rav Nachman didn't know that.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Rav Nachman to identify the tanna who rejects bereirah even in rabbinic matters, citing a baraita about an eruv for multiple people where the choice is made after nightfall.
Rav Nachman remains silent, and the Gemara notes that he could have answered that it is the school of Ayyo, but he simply did not know that tradition.

items.text: Rav Yosef's answer: Tannaim dispute
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's answer: Tannaim dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef says the issue is a dispute among Tannaim, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon accepts bereirah for eruv after dark, while the Sages reject it. The Gemara notes a contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's own views and suggests flipping the text.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef answers that the issue is a dispute among Tannaim, citing a baraita where Rabbi Shimon accepts bereirah (retroactive clarification) for eruv after dark, while the Sages reject it.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Shimon elsewhere rejects bereirah (retroactive clarification), creating a contradiction within his own views.
The Gemara suggests flipping the text of the baraita to resolve the contradiction.

items.text: Distinction between biblical and rabbinic law
items.text_en: Distinction between biblical and rabbinic law
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between biblical and rabbinic law: Rabbi Shimon rejects bereirah biblically but accepts it rabbinically. Rav Yosef holds that one's view on bereirah is consistent across both domains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the contradiction in Rabbi Shimon's positions can be resolved by distinguishing between biblical and rabbinic law: he rejects bereirah (retroactive clarification) for biblical matters but accepts it for rabbinic matters.
Rav Yosef rejects the proposed distinction, holding that one's view on bereirah (retroactive clarification) is consistent across both biblical and rabbinic domains.

items.text: Rava's alternative: Requirement of recognizable remnants
items.text_en: Rava's alternative: Requirement of recognizable remnants
items.desc_en: Rava offers a different explanation: the case of terumah requires that the remnants be recognizable, which is not a matter of bereirah.

sub.desc_en: Rava distinguishes the terumah case from bereirah by invoking the requirement that the remnants of the first portion be recognizable (ראשית ששיריה ניכרין).

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects with a case of two untithed pomegranates where the designation is conditional on rain, which would be invalid. The Gemara cites a mishna where Rabbi Shimon allows designation when the terumah is surrounded by its produce, distinguishing that case.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that if the requirement of 'ראשית ששיריה ניכרין' (a portion whose remnants are recognizable) applies, then a conditional designation of terumah from two untithed pomegranates based on rain would be invalid in all cases.
The Gemara cites a mishna where Rabbi Shimon validates designation of terumah when the terumah is surrounded by its produce, implying that the requirement of recognizable remnants is not absolute.

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing that in the mishna's case, the terumah is surrounded by its produce (סביביו), which satisfies the requirement of recognizable remnants, unlike Abaye's case.

items.text: Alternative answer and conclusion
items.text_en: Alternative answer and conclusion
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer citing the Sages' objection to Rabbi Meir about the possibility of the wine skin bursting, and explains that the requirement of recognizable remnants applies to the Sages but not to Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer by citing the Sages' objection to Rabbi Meir that the wine skin might burst, making him drink untithed wine retroactively.
The Gemara questions what the Sages' objection means according to the initial assumption that recognizable remnants are required.
The Gemara explains that the Sages were saying to Rabbi Meir: 'We require recognizable remnants, but you do not.'

items.text: Opening objection from the previous Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening objection from the previous Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara recalls an objection raised against Rabbi Eliezer: if one relies on a condition that the wine vessel might burst, he would be drinking untithed wine retroactively. Rabbi Eliezer responds that the condition applies only when the vessel bursts.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object to Rabbi Eliezer: if one relies on a condition that the wine vessel might burst, he would retroactively be drinking untithed wine.
Rabbi Eliezer responds that the condition applies only when the vessel actually bursts.

items.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages on eruv for a festival adjacent to Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages on eruv for a festival adjacent to Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Eliezer's opinion that one may prepare two eruvs for a festival adjacent to Shabbat, with various conditional statements. The Sages argue that one may only prepare one eruv for one direction or for two days, not both. Rabbi Eliezer then asks the Sages to admit that the two days are two distinct sanctities.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer states that for a festival adjacent to Shabbat, one may prepare two eruvs, specifying various conditional placements.
The Sages argue that one may only prepare an eruv for one direction or for two days, but not both.
The Mishnah describes the procedure for the Sages' approach: one brings the eruv on the first day, retrieves it, and on the second day uses it again, gaining benefit from both walking and the eruv.
The Mishnah rules that if the eruv was consumed on the first day, it is valid only for the first day and not for the second.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's question to the Sages
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's question to the Sages
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer asks the Sages to admit that the two days are two distinct sanctities.

items.text: Gemara's clarification of the Sages' statement
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification of the Sages' statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the redundancy in the Sages' statement: 'for one direction' and 'for two days' seem to mean the same thing. It clarifies that the Sages were actually addressing Rabbi Eliezer with a logical argument.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the redundancy in the Sages' statement, noting that 'for one direction' and 'for two days' seem to mean the same thing.

The Gemara explains that the Sages were actually addressing Rabbi Eliezer with a logical argument: just as one cannot split a single day between two directions, one cannot split two days between two directions.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes between a single holiness (one day) and two distinct holies (two days), so the analogy fails.

Rabbi Eliezer argues that if one established an עירוב (eruv) by foot on the first day, he can do so on the second day, but if the eruv was eaten on the first day, he cannot go out on the second day — implying two distinct holies.
The Sages concede that these are indeed two distinct holies, but explain that they are uncertain about the status, so they rule stringently in both directions.
The Sages argue that one cannot establish an eruv initially from a festival to Shabbat, implying a single holiness, and Rabbi Eliezer concedes.
Rabbi Eliezer explains that the prohibition there is due to preparation (הכנה) from festival to Shabbat, not because they share a single holiness.

A baraita is cited supporting Rabbi Eliezer's position: if one established an eruv by foot on the first day, he can do so on the second day; if the eruv was eaten on the first day, he cannot go out on the second day — the words of Rabbi.
The baraita begins to cite Rabbi Yehuda's differing opinion, which continues beyond the section.

items.text: First argument: analogy to one day with two directions
items.text_en: First argument: analogy to one day with two directions
items.desc_en: The Sages argue to Rabbi Eliezer that just as one cannot prepare an eruv for one day half to the north and half to the south, so too one cannot prepare for two days one to the east and one to the west. Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes: there it is one sanctity, here it is two sanctities.

sub.desc_en: The Sages argue to Rabbi Eliezer that just as one cannot prepare an eruv for one day half to the north and half to the south, so too one cannot prepare for two days one to the east and one to the west.
Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes: there (one day) it is one sanctity, here (two days) it is two sanctities.

items.text: Second argument: eruv by foot and consumption of eruv
items.text_en: Second argument: eruv by foot and consumption of eruv
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer argues that if one can establish an eruv by foot on the first day and again on the second, and if the eruv is consumed on the first day it does not work for the second, this proves two sanctities. The Sages concede but explain they are uncertain and rule stringently in both cases.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer asks Sages: Do you admit that if one made an eruv by foot on first day, he may also make one by foot on second day?
Sages answer: If the eruv was eaten on first day, one cannot go out on second day.
Rabbi Eliezer objects: Do you admit that if one made an eruv by foot on first day, he may also make one by foot on second day?
Sages answer: If the eruv was eaten on first day, one cannot go out on second day.
Rabbi Eliezer rejects: Do you admit that if one made an eruv by foot on first day, he may also make one by foot on second day?
Sages answer: If the eruv was eaten on first day, one cannot go out on second day.
Rabbi Eliezer resolves: Do you admit that if one made an eruv by foot on first day, he may also make one by foot on second day?
Sages answer: If the eruv was eaten on first day, one cannot go out on second day.
Gemara cites a baraita: If one made an eruv by foot on first day, he may also make one by foot on second day.
Gemara continues the baraita: If the eruv was eaten on first day, one cannot go out on second day.
Gemara notes: These are the words of Rabbi (anonymous).
Rabbi Yehuda says (something).

items.text: Third argument: no eruv from Yom Tov to Shabbat
items.text_en: Third argument: no eruv from Yom Tov to Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Sages argue that one cannot initially prepare an eruv from Yom Tov to Shabbat, indicating one sanctity. Rabbi Eliezer responds that this is due to the prohibition of preparing (הכנה) from Yom Tov to Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Sages object to Rabbi Eliezer that one cannot initially prepare an eruv from Yom Tov to Shabbat, implying the two days share one sanctity.
Rabbi Eliezer concedes the fact but argues that the prohibition is due to the rule of הכנה (preparation) from Yom Tov to Shabbat, not shared sanctity.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer distinguishes the case as being due to the prohibition of הכנה (preparation) from Yom Tov to Shabbat, not because the days share one sanctity.

items.text: Baraita: Rabbi and Rabbi Yehuda on eruv by foot
items.text_en: Baraita: Rabbi and Rabbi Yehuda on eruv by foot
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi states that if one established an eruv by foot on the first day, he may do so on the second; if the eruv was consumed on the first day, it does not work for the second. Rabbi Yehuda's opinion begins but is cut off.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi states that if one established an eruv by foot on the first day, he may do so on the second; if the eruv was consumed on the first day, it does not work for the second. Rabbi Yehuda's opinion begins but is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a case of a חמר גמל (a donkey driver and camel driver). Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael state that if one established an eruv by foot on the first day, he cannot do so on the second; if his eruv was eaten on the first day, he may go out on the second.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the case of a חמר גמל (donkey driver and camel driver) and states the opinion of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael regarding the rules of eruv on consecutive holy days.

items.text: Rav's ruling and identification of the four elders
items.text_en: Rav's ruling and identification of the four elders
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the law follows the four elders, in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer who holds that Shabbat and Yom Tov are two separate sanctities. The Gemara identifies the four elders: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Eliezer ben Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda S'timta'ah; some say one of them is Rabbi Elazar, excluding Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the law follows the four elders, in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer who holds that Shabbat and Yom Tov are two separate sanctities, and identifies the four elders with a dispute about their identity.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's opinion
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: we heard Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael state the opposite elsewhere. The Gemara resolves by reversing their statement. It then questions whether this is the same as Rabbi's opinion, and explains that Rabbi taught the Mishnah but did not hold it, while Rav learned it as a tradition (גמרא).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael were heard elsewhere stating the opposite opinion.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by reversing the attributed statement.
The Gemara asks whether this reversed opinion is identical to Rabbi's position.
The Gemara suggests that the Mishnah should be read as 'and so said Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel etc.' to align with Rabbi.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi himself is not counted among the four elders.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi taught the Mishnah but did not personally hold that opinion.
The Gemara asks whether the other rabbis also taught it without holding it.
The Gemara resolves that Rav learned this tradition as a received tradition (גמרא) from his teachers.

items.text: Rav Huna's death and Rav Chisda's challenge from Rav's own statement
items.text_en: Rav Huna's death and Rav Chisda's challenge from Rav's own statement
items.desc_en: When Rav Huna died, Rav Chisda entered to challenge Rav's ruling: Did Rav say the law follows the four elders in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer? But elsewhere Rav said that regarding Shabbat and Yom Tov, a newborn animal is forbidden on the other day, implying one sanctity. Rav Chisda raises a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that when Rav Huna died, Rav Chisda entered to raise a contradiction from Rav against Rav.
Rav Chisda challenges: Did Rav rule like the four elders in accordance with Rabbi Eliezer who says they are two sanctities?
Rav Chisda raises a contradiction: But it was stated that regarding Shabbat and Yom Tov, Rav said a newborn animal on one day is forbidden on the other, implying one sanctity.

items.text: Rabbah's resolution: the distinction of הכנה (preparation)
items.text_en: Rabbah's resolution: the distinction of הכנה (preparation)
items.desc_en: Rabbah answers that the case of a newborn animal is different due to the prohibition of הכנה (preparation): weekday prepares for Shabbat and Yom Tov, but Yom Tov does not prepare for Shabbat. Abaye objects from a Mishnah that seems to allow preparation from Yom Tov to Shabbat. Rabbah responds that the beginning of the day acquires the eruv, not the end, so Shabbat prepares for itself.

items.text: Further objections and resolutions regarding the eruv and preparation
items.text_en: Further objections and resolutions regarding the eruv and preparation
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, why not establish an eruv with a jug (לגין)? The answer: we need a meal fit for the day before. Another objection from Rabbi Eliezer's Mishnah about two eruvin is resolved by explaining that the eruv is placed at the end of 1000 amot, not 2000, so no preparation occurs.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if so, why not establish an eruv with a jug (לגין)?
The Gemara answers: we need a meal fit for the day before (סעודה הראויה מבעוד יום), and a jug does not qualify.
The Gemara objects from Rabbi Eliezer's Mishnah about two eruvin, which also seems to require preparation from Yom Tov to Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves: the eruv is placed at the end of 1000 amot, not 2000, so no preparation occurs.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement and the resolution via Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement and the resolution via Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said that if one established an eruv by foot on the first day, he may do so on the second; if by bread, similarly. This seems to involve preparation from Yom Tov to Shabbat. Rabbah answers that he goes and sits silently, like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri who says ownerless objects acquire a place of rest. Even the Rabbis agree in the case of one who is awake, as he could speak if he wanted.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah: Rav Yehuda's statement that one may establish an eruv by foot or bread on consecutive days seems to involve preparation from Yom Tov to Shabbat.
Rabbah answers that the person goes and sits silently, without verbally declaring the eruv, thus avoiding preparation.
The gemara identifies that Rabbah's answer aligns with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that ownerless objects acquire a place of rest by being present at the onset of Shabbat.

The gemara resolves that even the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri regarding a sleeping person, would agree here because the person is awake and could speak if he wanted, so his silence is considered as if he spoke.

items.text: Rabbah bar Rav Chanin's question to Abaye
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanin's question to Abaye
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanin asks Abaye whether he has heard the teaching that one should not walk to the end of his field to see what it needs, and a similar case, implying a continuation of the discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanin said to Abaye: If Master had heard this baraita: 'A person should not walk to the end of his field to know what it needs; similarly...'

items.text: Gemara's discussion of the earlier Mishnah about loitering at the city gate
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion of the earlier Mishnah about loitering at the city gate
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially states that one may not loiter at the city gate to enter the bathhouse immediately, but then retracts. It explains that the retraction is not absolute; in some cases it is obvious, in others not. If the person is a Torah scholar, we assume he was preoccupied with his learning; if an ignoramus, we assume he was delayed by wine.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the Mishnah's rule that one may not loiter at the city gate to enter the bathhouse immediately, then retracts it.
The Gemara clarifies that the retraction is not absolute; in some cases the delay is obvious, in others not.
The Gemara distinguishes: if the person is a Torah scholar, we assume he was preoccupied with his learning; if an ignoramus, we assume he was delayed by wine.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on changing the method of eruv from first to second day
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on changing the method of eruv from first to second day
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if one established an eruv by foot on the first day, he may do so by foot on the second; if by bread on the first, by bread on the second. However, if he used bread on the first, he may switch to foot on the second, but not vice versa, because one cannot initiate an eruv with bread on the second day. Shmuel adds that if he used bread on both days, it must be the same loaf. Rav Ashi supports this from the Mishnah. The Gemara suggests that the Rabbis might interpret the Mishnah as merely giving good advice.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one may change the method of eruv from bread to foot on the second day, but not from foot to bread, because one cannot initiate an eruv with bread on the second day.
Shmuel adds that if one used bread on both days, it must be the same loaf.
Rav Ashi supports Shmuel's ruling by citing the Mishnah's description of using the same loaf on both days.
The Rabbis suggest that the Mishnah's description is merely good advice, not a binding requirement.

items.text: Mishnah: Conditional eruvin for Rosh Hashanah and related disputes
items.text_en: Mishnah: Conditional eruvin for Rosh Hashanah and related disputes
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents Rabbi Yehuda's opinion that on Rosh Hashanah, when one fears the month might be intercalated, he may establish two conditional eruvin, one for east and one for west, etc. The Sages did not agree. Rabbi Yehuda further allows stipulating about a basket of produce on the first festival day to eat on the second, and similarly an egg born on the first may be eaten on the second; again the Sages disagreed. Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas rules that the prayer leader on Rosh Hashanah should say 'Grant us, Lord our God, this new month, whether today or tomorrow,' and the next day 'whether today or yesterday'; the Sages did not agree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that on Rosh Hashanah, one may establish two conditional eruvin for different directions, but the Sages did not agree.
The Mishnah adds Rabbi Yehuda's further ruling that one may stipulate about a basket of produce on the first festival day to eat it on the second.
The Mishnah records Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that an egg laid on the first day may be eaten on the second, but the Sages did not agree.
The Mishnah presents Rabbi Dosa ben Horkinas's opinion that the prayer leader on Rosh Hashanah should say a conditional blessing, but the Sages did not agree.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying the Sages who disagreed with Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying the Sages who disagreed with Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who are the 'Sages' who did not agree with Rabbi Yehuda. Rav answers that it is Rabbi Yosei, as a baraita teaches that the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer that one may establish two conditional eruvin on Rosh Hashanah, but Rabbi Yosei forbids it. Rabbi Yosei argues: Do you not agree that if witnesses come from mincha time onward, they treat that day as sacred and the next as sacred?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who are the Sages who did not agree with Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav answers that the Sages are those who follow Rabbi Yosei, citing a baraita where the Sages agree with Rabbi Eliezer about conditional eruvin on Rosh Hashanah, but Rabbi Yosei forbids it.
Rabbi Yosei argues to the Sages that if witnesses come from mincha time onward, they treat both that day and the next as sacred, showing the two days have unified sanctity.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Rabbis' reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yehuda: they are concerned that one might come to treat the sanctity of Yom Tov lightly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Yehuda because they are concerned that one might come to treat the sanctity of Yom Tov lightly.

items.text: The necessity of the Mishnah's three cases
items.text_en: The necessity of the Mishnah's three cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah needed to list all three cases (Rosh Hashanah, basket of untithed produce, and egg) to show that Rabbi Yehuda's leniency applies in each, and that he would not concede to the Rabbis in any of them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that all three cases are necessary, and explains that if only the case of ראש השנה (Rosh Hashanah) were taught, one might think Rabbi Yehuda's leniency is limited there because he does no action, but in the basket case where he appears to be fixing טבל (untithed produce), he would concede to the Rabbis.

The Gemara adds that if only the first two cases were taught, one might think Rabbi Yehuda is lenient because there is no reason to decree, but in the egg case where there is a concern for falling fruits and oozing liquids, he would concede to the Rabbis; therefore all three are necessary.

items.text: Baraita detailing Rabbi Yehuda's conditional separation
items.text_en: Baraita detailing Rabbi Yehuda's conditional separation
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how Rabbi Yehuda permits one to conditionally separate terumah from a basket of untithed produce on the first day of Yom Tov and eat it on the second day, with a specific procedure. Rabbi Yosei prohibits this, and similarly prohibits any leniency on the two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by describing Rabbi Yehuda's procedure for conditionally separating תרומה (priestly portion) from a basket of untithed produce on the first day of Yom Tov.
The baraita details the second day's conditional declaration, where Rabbi Yehuda permits eating the produce after repeating the condition.
Rabbi Yosei prohibits this conditional separation entirely.
The baraita adds that Rabbi Yosei likewise prohibits any leniency on the two days of Yom Tov in the Diaspora.

items.text: The case of the deer and the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: The case of the deer and the dispute between Rav Nachman and Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: A deer was caught on the first day of Yom Tov and slaughtered on the second. Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda ate it, but Rav Sheshet refrained, citing a baraita of Isi that Rabbi Yosei prohibits all two-day Yom Tovs of the Diaspora.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a deer was caught on the first day of Yom Tov of the Diaspora and slaughtered on the second day.
Rav Nachman and Rav Chisda ate the deer, but Rav Sheshet refrained; Rav Nachman asks why Rav Sheshet does not eat deer meat.
Rav Sheshet explains that he cannot eat because Isi taught a baraita that Rabbi Yosei prohibits all two-day Yom Tovs of the Diaspora.

items.text: Rava and Rav Asi's challenges to Rav Sheshet's inference
items.text_en: Rava and Rav Asi's challenges to Rav Sheshet's inference
items.desc_en: Rava questions Rav Sheshet's proof, suggesting that Rabbi Yosei's stringency might only apply to Rosh Hashanah in the Diaspora. Rav Asi offers an alternative interpretation: Rabbi Yosei treats the two days of Diaspora Yom Tov as having the same stringency as Rosh Hashanah for the Rabbis who permit it.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions Rav Sheshet's proof, suggesting that Rabbi Yosei's stringency might only apply to Rosh Hashanah in the Diaspora, but the Gemara rejects this because the text says 'of the Diaspora' (של גליות) not 'in the Diaspora' (בגולה).
Rav Asi offers an alternative interpretation: Rabbi Yosei treats the two days of Diaspora Yom Tov as having the same stringency as Rosh Hashanah for the Rabbis who permit it.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's inquiry and Rabba bar Shmuel's response
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's inquiry and Rabba bar Shmuel's response
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet asks Rabba bar Shmuel if he knows any tradition about the sanctity of the two days. Rabba bar Shmuel cites a baraita that Rabbi Yosei concedes regarding the two days of Diaspora Yom Tov, but Rav Sheshet tells him not to reveal this to others.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet finds Rabba bar Shmuel and asks if he knows any tradition about the sanctity of the two days.
Rabba bar Shmuel cites a baraita that Rabbi Yosei concedes regarding the two days of Diaspora Yom Tov.
Rav Sheshet instructs Rabba bar Shmuel not to reveal this tradition to others.

items.text: Rav Ashi's report from Amemar about the deer
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's report from Amemar about the deer
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that Amemar told him that the deer in question was not actually caught on Yom Tov, implying that the entire dispute might be moot.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi reports that Amemar told him the deer was not actually caught on Yom Tov, implying the entire dispute may be moot.

items.text: Dispute about produce brought from outside the Sabbath limit
items.text_en: Dispute about produce brought from outside the Sabbath limit
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains a disagreement: one who ate assumes that produce brought for one Jew is permitted to another, while one who did not eat assumes that produce brought for the Exilarch is intended for all rabbis.

items.text: Rav Sheshet denies the incident
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet denies the incident
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet encountered Rabbah bar Shmuel and told him that the incident never occurred.

items.text: Rava's ruling about turnips brought to Mahoza
items.text_en: Rava's ruling about turnips brought to Mahoza
items.desc_en: Rava initially permitted buying turnips that were clearly uprooted the previous day, reasoning that produce brought for one Jew is permitted to another, especially when brought for gentiles. Later, when he saw that they were bringing large quantities, he forbade it.

items.text: Ravina permits using myrtle cut on the second day of Yom Tov
items.text_en: Ravina permits using myrtle cut on the second day of Yom Tov
items.desc_en: Ravina permitted using myrtle cut on the second day of Yom Tov for immediate use, but Rava bar Tachlifa objected because the cutters were not Torah scholars. Rav Shemayah challenged this, noting that even Torah scholars would need the myrtle to be prepared in a permissible manner. Rava ruled that it must be prepared in a permissible way.

items.text: Rabbi Dosa's ruling on mentioning Rosh Chodesh in Rosh Hashanah prayer
items.text_en: Rabbi Dosa's ruling on mentioning Rosh Chodesh in Rosh Hashanah prayer
items.desc_en: Rabbah reports a question from Rav Huna's study: may one mention Rosh Chodesh in the Rosh Hashanah prayer? He cites Rabbi Dosa's statement about the prayer leader, which is interpreted as either mentioning or conditioning. The Gemara concludes that it is for conditioning, not mentioning, and explains why both cases (Rosh Hashanah and other Rosh Chodeshs) are needed.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about Rosh Hashanah on Shabbat
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about Rosh Hashanah on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita: if Rosh Hashanah falls on Shabbat, Beit Shammai says one prays ten blessings and Beit Hillel says nine. If one were to mention Rosh Chodesh, Beit Shammai should require eleven blessings.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's distinction for Rosh Chodesh
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's distinction for Rosh Chodesh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that Rosh Chodesh is different because it is mentioned in both the morning and evening prayers, so it is also included in the Musaf prayer.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira distinguishes Rosh Chodesh from other occasions, arguing that since it is included in the morning and evening prayers, it is also included in the Musaf prayer.

items.text: Challenge from Beit Shammai
items.text_en: Challenge from Beit Shammai
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Zeira's reasoning by citing a baraita where Beit Shammai does not include Rosh Chodesh in the Sabbath prayer, contradicting the notion of inclusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Zeira's reasoning by citing a baraita where Beit Shammai does not include Rosh Chodesh in the Sabbath prayer, contradicting the notion of inclusion.

items.text: Resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.text_en: Resolution: Tannaitic dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by presenting a Tannaitic dispute about whether one includes the special occasion in the Amidah. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel hold different views on the structure of the prayer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the challenge by asserting that the issue of whether one includes the special occasion in the Amidah is a Tannaitic dispute.

The baraita presents the first opinion: for Shabbat that falls on Rosh Chodesh or Chol HaMoed, one prays the standard seven blessings for weekday prayers and mentions the special occasion in the 'avodah' blessing; Rabbi Eliezer says to mention it in the 'hoda'ah' blessing, and if one omitted it, they must repeat.
The baraita continues: for the Musaf prayer, one begins and ends with the Shabbat theme and inserts the sanctity of the day in the middle.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yishmael state that whenever one is required to recite seven blessings, they begin and end with the Shabbat theme and insert the sanctity of the day in the middle.

items.text: Rav Chisda and Rabbah's ruling on remembrance
items.text_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah's ruling on remembrance
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda and Rabbah rule that a single remembrance suffices for both Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the practical ruling is regarding the dispute about remembrance in the Musaf prayer.
Rav Chisda rules that a single remembrance (זכרון) suffices for both Shabbat and Rosh Chodesh.
Rabbah concurs with Rav Chisda's ruling that one remembrance covers both occasions.

items.text: Inquiry about reciting Shehecheyanu on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Inquiry about reciting Shehecheyanu on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks whether one recites the blessing of זְמַן on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, given they are not pilgrimage festivals. Rav Yehudah reports that Rav and Shmuel rule it is only said on the three pilgrimage festivals.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks whether one recites the blessing of זְמַן on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, given they are not pilgrimage festivals, and he does not have an answer.
Rav Yehudah reports that Rav and Shmuel rule that the blessing of זְמַן is only recited on the three pilgrimage festivals, not on Rosh Hashanah or Yom Kippur.

items.text: Attempted proof from Ecclesiastes and discussion of cup requirement
items.text_en: Attempted proof from Ecclesiastes and discussion of cup requirement
items.desc_en: The Gemara attempts to prove that זְמַן is said on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur from a verse, but deflects it to a blessing. It then discusses whether a cup is required, supporting Rav Nachman's view that it can be said even in the market.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita interpreting Ecclesiastes 11:2, where Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua debate the meaning of 'seven' and 'eight', and the verse adds 'and also' to include Shavuot, Rosh Hashanah, and Yom Kippur, attempting to prove that זְמַן (the blessing of time) is said on these days.
The Gemara rejects the proof, clarifying that the verse refers to a blessing (ברכה) over the day, not to the blessing of time (זְמַן).

The Gemara provides supporting reasoning: if the verse referred to זְמַן, one could not say it for a seven-day festival since the blessing is said only once, but this is resolved by noting one can say it later.
The Gemara asks whether a cup (כּוֹס) is required for saying זְמַן, and suggests this supports Rav Nachman's view.
Rav Nachman states that זְמַן can be said even in the market, implying no cup is required, but the Gemara deflects that the case involved a cup that happened to be available.

items.text: Practical problem with Yom Kippur
items.text_en: Practical problem with Yom Kippur
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a practical difficulty: on Yom Kippur, one cannot drink the wine after reciting the blessing, and giving it to a child is problematic. It concludes that the ruling of Rav Acha is not followed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how one can recite the blessing of 'זְמַן' on Yom Kippur, since reciting it over wine would require drinking it, which is forbidden.

The Gemara cites a precedent: Rav Yirmeyah bar Abba asked Rav whether he separates (recites Havdalah) on Yom Kippur, and Rav confirmed he does, showing that reciting a blessing over wine on Yom Kippur is problematic.
The Gemara rejects alternatives: one cannot recite the blessing without tasting, nor give the wine to a child (following Rav Acha's ruling), concluding that Rav Acha's opinion is not followed.

items.text: Practical resolution and final halakha
items.text_en: Practical resolution and final halakha
items.desc_en: The rabbis send Rav Yeimar Sava to observe Rav Chisda's practice on Rosh Hashanah eve. Rav Chisda recites Kiddush and says זְמַן. The Gemara concludes that one says זְמַן on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and it can be said even in the market.

sub.text: Narrative: the rabbis send Rav Yeimar Sava
sub.text_en: Narrative: the rabbis send Rav Yeimar Sava
sub.desc_en: The rabbis send Rav Yeimar Sava to observe Rav Chisda's practice on Rosh Hashanah eve; Rav Chisda recites Kiddush and says זְמַן.
The Gemara concludes that one says זְמַן on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, and it can be said even in the market.

items.text: New inquiry: completing a fast on Friday afternoon
items.text_en: New inquiry: completing a fast on Friday afternoon
items.desc_en: Rabbah asks whether a student who fasts on Friday afternoon completes the fast. The matter is unresolved until Rava cites a baraita about Tisha B'Av falling on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asks whether a student who fasts on Friday afternoon completes the fast, and neither he nor Rav Yehudah has an answer.
Rava resolves the inquiry by citing a baraita about Tisha B'Av falling on Shabbat, implying that the fast is completed.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that when Tisha b'Av falls on Shabbat, one may eat freely on Friday; but when it falls on Friday, one eats only an egg to avoid entering Shabbat while still fasting.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for Tisha b'Av falling on Shabbat or Friday.

items.text: Tannaitic dispute about completing the fast
items.text_en: Tannaitic dispute about completing the fast
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda recounts that Rabbi Akiva ate only an egg on such a Friday to teach halakha. Rabbi Yosei argues that one must fast and complete the fast until nightfall, comparing it to Tisha b'Av that falls on Sunday where one must stop eating before Shabbat. The Sages object that entering Shabbat while fasting is different from leaving it.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda recounts that Rabbi Akiva ate only a hard-boiled egg without salt on a Tisha b'Av that fell on Friday, to teach the halakha to his students.
Rabbi Yosei argues that one must fast and complete the fast until nightfall, drawing an analogy to Tisha b'Av that falls on Sunday where one stops eating before Shabbat.
The Sages object that entering Shabbat while fasting is different from leaving it, since on Sunday one has eaten all day before the fast begins.

items.text: Ulla's ruling and a contradiction
items.text_en: Ulla's ruling and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Ulla rules like Rabbi Yosei that one completes the fast. The Gemara questions this practice by citing a baraita where Rabban Gamliel says that if a public fast began on Hanukkah or Purim, one does not stop but does not complete it; Rabbi Meir adds that the same applies to Tisha b'Av on Friday.

sub.desc_en: Ulla rules like Rabbi Yosei, but a contradiction is raised from a baraita where Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Meir discuss completing fasts on festive days.
The Gemara questions whether we actually practice like Rabbi Yosei, and raises a contradiction from a baraita.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabban Gamliel rules that if a public fast began on Hanukkah or Purim, one does not stop but does not complete it, and Rabbi Meir adds that the same applies to Tisha b'Av on Friday.

items.text: Attempt to overturn Rabban Gamliel's ruling
items.text_en: Attempt to overturn Rabban Gamliel's ruling
items.desc_en: After Rabban Gamliel's death, Rabbi Yehoshua tried to overturn his ruling, but Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri objected, stating that the halakha was already established. The Gemara notes that in Rabban Gamliel's generation they followed him, and in Rabbi Yosei's generation they followed him.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that in Rabban Gamliel's generation they followed his ruling, and in Rabbi Yosei's generation they followed his ruling.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok's testimony
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok's testimony
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the claim that in Rabban Gamliel's generation they followed him, citing Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok who said that when Tisha b'Av fell on Shabbat and was postponed, they fasted but did not complete it because it was their festival. This implies that on a festival eve they would complete it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous statement with a baraita where Rabbi Elazar ben Tzadok reports that in Rabban Gamliel's time, they did not complete the fast when Tisha b'Av fell on Shabbat, implying that on a festival eve they would complete it.

items.text: Ravina's distinction
items.text_en: Ravina's distinction
items.desc_en: Ravina explains that a festival (Yom Tov) is different because one may fast part of the day, so completing it is allowed; but Shabbat, on which one may not fast at all, does not allow completion.

sub.desc_en: Ravina distinguishes between a festival day (יום טוב) where one may fast part of the day, and Shabbat where one may not fast at all, explaining the difference in completing the fast.

items.text: Rav Yosef's unfamiliarity and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's unfamiliarity and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef was unfamiliar with the tradition, but Abaye reminded him that Rav Yehuda said in Rav's name that the baraita about not completing fasts is only Rabbi Meir's view, while the Sages say one fasts and completes. The Gemara clarifies that this applies only to Hanukkah and Purim, not to all cases.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that he is unfamiliar with this tradition.

Abaye reminds Rav Yosef that he himself taught the baraita about not decreeing fasts on certain days, and that Rav Yehuda said in Rav's name that this is only Rabbi Meir's view citing Rabban Gamliel, but the Sages say one fasts and completes.
The Gemara asks whether the Sages' position applies to all cases listed in the baraita.
The Gemara answers that the Sages' position applies only to Hanukkah and Purim, not to all cases.
The Gemara concludes that this interpretation is also logically compelling.

items.text: Resolution of contradiction about Rabba's query
items.text_en: Resolution of contradiction about Rabba's query
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves a contradiction between two statements: one where Rabba asked Rav Yehuda about fasting and completing the fast, and another where Mar Zutra taught a halakha that one fasts and completes. The resolution is that one statement was before Rabba heard the teaching, the other after.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: if Rabba had already heard the ruling that one fasts and completes, why did he ask Rav Yehuda and receive no answer?
The Gemara further objects: Mar Zutra taught in the name of Rav Huna that one fasts and completes, yet Rabba asked Rav Huna and received no answer.
The Gemara resolves: one statement was before Rabba heard the teaching, the other after.
Mar Zutra taught in the name of Rav Huna: the הלכה (binding law) is that one fasts and completes the fast.

items.text: Mar Zutra's teaching on fasting
items.text_en: Mar Zutra's teaching on fasting
items.desc_en: Mar Zutra teaches in the name of Rav Huna that the halakha is that one fasts and completes the fast on Yom Kippur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous assumption by noting that Mar Zutra's teaching about fasting and completing was also asked by Rabbah from Rav Huna without resolution.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between before and after hearing the teaching.
Mar Zutra teaches in the name of Rav Huna that the halakha is that one fasts and completes the fast on Yom Kippur.

items.text: Conclusion of the chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the chapter
items.desc_en: The standard formula marking the end of the chapter 'In all things they may establish an eruv'.

sub.desc_en: The standard formula marking the end of the chapter 'In all things they may establish an eruv'.

items.text: Mishnah: One taken beyond the limit
items.text_en: Mishnah: One taken beyond the limit
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that if non-Jews or an evil spirit took someone beyond the Shabbat limit, they have only four cubits. If they returned him, it is as if he never left. If they took him to another city or placed him in a pen or prison, Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya say he may walk the entire city, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva say he has only four cubits. A story is told about a ship that drifted, and Rabban Gamliel permitted them to descend based on his prior observation.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule: if non-Jews or an evil spirit took someone beyond the Shabbat limit, they have only four cubits.
The Mishnah adds that if they returned him, it is as if he never left.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the opinion of Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that one may walk the entire city.

sub.text: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
sub.text_en: Mishnah: Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the opposing opinion of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva that one has only four cubits.
The Mishnah recounts a story where Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya walked the entire city, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva were stringent and stayed within four cubits.
The Mishnah relates that once they arrived after dark and asked Rabban Gamliel whether they may descend.
Rabban Gamliel permits them to descend because he had observed that they were already within the Shabbat limit before dark.

items.text: Three things that remove a person from his mind
items.text_en: Three things that remove a person from his mind
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita listing three things that remove a person from his mind and from his Creator's mind: non-Jews, an evil spirit, and the strictures of poverty. It then discusses three who do not see Gehinnom, three who die while speaking, and the practical implications of these lists.

sub.desc_en: The baraita lists three things that remove a person from his mind and from his Creator's mind: non-Jews, an evil spirit, and the strictures of poverty.
The Gemara asks what practical halachic implication arises from this list, and answers: to pray for mercy regarding these afflictions.
The baraita lists three who do not see Gehinnom: the strictures of poverty, intestinal illness, and the ruling authority; Yesh Omrim adds one who has a bad wife.
The Gemara objects that a bad wife should not be included because it is a mitzvah to divorce her, so she is not a permanent affliction.
The Gemara rejects the objection, noting that sometimes the wife's ketubah is large or he has children from her, preventing divorce.
The Gemara asks the practical implication of the list of those who do not see Gehinnom, and answers: to accept suffering with love.
The baraita lists three who die while speaking: intestinal illness, childbirth, and dropsy.
The Gemara asks the practical implication of the list of those who die while speaking, and answers: to feel their pulse for provisions (i.e., to check if they are still alive).

items.text: Debate about one who left intentionally and was returned
items.text_en: Debate about one who left intentionally and was returned
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quotes Shmuel: one who left the limit intentionally has only four cubits. The Gemara questions this, then suggests alternative versions: one who returned to his senses, or one who left intentionally and was returned by non-Jews. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's case of 'returned him' refers to one who left intentionally and was returned, teaching that even then it is as if he never left.

items.text: One who needs to relieve himself
items.text_en: One who needs to relieve himself
items.desc_en: Rabba is asked about one who needs to relieve himself and is outside the limit. He answers that human dignity overrides a negative commandment of the Torah.

sub.desc_en: Rabba answers that human dignity (כבוד הבריות) overrides a negative commandment of the Torah.

items.text: Fruits that left the limit and returned
items.text_en: Fruits that left the limit and returned
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that fruits that left the limit and returned, even intentionally, did not lose their place because they were forced. An objection is raised from a baraita of Rabbi Nehemya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, and the Gemara resolves that it is a dispute among Tannaim.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa rules that fruits that left the Shabbat limit and returned, even intentionally (במזיד), did not lose their place because they were forced (אנוסין).

Rav Yosef bar Shmaya objects by citing a baraita of Rabbi Nehemya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who say fruits are always forbidden until they return to their place unintentionally (שוגגין), implying that intentionally (במזיד) they remain forbidden.

The Gemara resolves that the dispute is between Tannaim: a baraita states that fruits that left the limit, if unintentionally (בשוגג) they may be eaten, but if intentionally (במזיד) they may not be eaten, supporting Rav Pappa's position that the baraita of Rabbi Nehemya and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is a minority view.

items.text: מחלוקת רבי נחמיה ותנא קמא בפירות שיצאו חוץ לתחום
items.text_en: Resolution of Rabbi Nechemiah's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the meaning of 'in their place' in Rabbi Nechemiah's statement. It initially suggests it refers to intentional violation, but rejects this based on a later baraita. It then reinterprets the Mishnah as missing a clause, concluding that the dispute between the Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Nechemiah is specifically about an unintentional violation outside the boundary.
items.desc: רבי נחמיה אומר שפירות שיצאו חוץ לתחום, אם חזרו למקומן – יאכלו, ואם לא – לא יאכלו. הגמרא מבררת את כוונת הברייתא ומציעה מספר פירושים למחלוקת בין רבי נחמיה לתנא קמא, תוך דיון בשוגג ומזיד.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Nechemiah's statement that fruits that left the boundary may be eaten in their place but not outside their place.
sub.desc: רבי נחמיה פוסק שפירות שיצאו חוץ לתחום נאכלים רק אם חזרו למקומן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'in their place' means, initially suggesting it refers to intentional violation, but rejects this because a later baraita explicitly states that Rabbi Nechemiah and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov permit only for an unintentional violation.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: אם 'במקומן' פירושו במזיד, הרי ברייתא מפורשת אוסרת במזיד.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah as missing a clause: the Tanna Kamma permits fruits that left the boundary unintentionally, but forbids them if done intentionally, and the dispute is only about unintentional cases outside the boundary.
sub.desc: מציע: 'במקומן' פירושו בשוגג, והברייתא חסרה ומלמדת שפירות שיצאו בשוגג נאכלים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that all agree intentional violation in their place is forbidden; the dispute is only about unintentional violation outside the boundary, where the Tanna Kamma permits and Rabbi Nechemiah forbids.
sub.desc: דוחה: במזיד במקומן כולי עלמא לא פליגי שאסור; המחלוקת היא בשוגג שלא במקומן.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proves its resolution from the later baraita, which implies that the Tanna Kamma permits even intentional violation, confirming the dispute is about unintentional cases outside the boundary.
sub.desc: דוחה את הדחייה: מהסיפא מוכח שהתנא קמא מתיר אפילו במזיד, ומסקנת הגמרא כתירוץ הראשון.

items.text: הלכות תחום שבת למי שאינו יודע התחום
items.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: One unaware of the boundary
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Shmuel that a person who is walking and does not know the Sabbath boundary may walk two thousand average paces, and that is his Sabbath boundary.
items.desc: רב נחמן בשם שמואל קובע שאדם שאינו יודע תחום שבת, ילך אלפיים פסיעות בינוניות וזהו תחום שבת.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports in the name of Shmuel that a person walking who does not know the Sabbath boundary may walk two thousand average paces, and that constitutes his Sabbath boundary.
sub.desc: רב נחמן בשם שמואל קובע שמי שאינו יודע את תחום השבת יכול למדוד אלפיים פסיעות בינוניות, שהן כאלפיים אמה.

items.text: מחלוקת בדיני תחום בשדה שהוקפה מחיצה בשבת
items.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Shmuel: Surrounded by a partition on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that if one spent Shabbat in a valley and gentiles surrounded it with a partition on Shabbat, he may walk two thousand cubits and may carry throughout by throwing. Rav Huna limits carrying to four cubits. The Gemara questions why one cannot carry normally within the two thousand cubits, and answers that it is like a breached partition leading to a forbidden area.
items.desc: רב נחמן בשם שמואל ורב הונא נחלקו בדין מי ששבת בבקעה והקיפוה נכרים מחיצה: שמואל מתיר לטלטל בכולה על ידי זריקה, ורב הונא אוסר ומגביל לטלטל ארבע אמות. הגמרא מביאה טעמים לאיסור, מחשש שימשך אחר חפצו ומשום מחיצה שנפרצה במלואה למקום האסור.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites Shmuel's ruling that if one spent Shabbat in a valley and gentiles surrounded it with a partition on Shabbat, he may walk two thousand cubits and may carry throughout by throwing.
Rav Huna objects, limiting carrying to four cubits only.
The Gemara questions why one cannot carry throughout the entire valley by throwing.
The Gemara answers that one might be drawn after his object, violating the Shabbat boundary.
The Gemara questions why one cannot carry normally within the two thousand cubits.
The Gemara resolves that the valley is like a partition breached in its entirety to a forbidden area, so carrying is restricted.

items.text: Chiya bar Rav's opinion and Rav Nachman's challenge
items.text_en: Chiya bar Rav's opinion and Rav Nachman's challenge
items.desc_en: Chiya bar Rav states that one may walk two thousand cubits and carry within two thousand cubits. The Gemara notes this differs from both Rav Nachman and Rav Huna, and emends his statement to say he carries within four cubits, aligning with Rav Huna. Rav Nachman then tells Rav Huna not to dispute Shmuel, as a baraita supports Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Chiya bar Rav states that one may walk two thousand cubits and carry within two thousand cubits.
The Gemara questions whose opinion Chiya bar Rav follows, noting it aligns with neither Rav Nachman nor Rav Huna.
The Gemara emends Chiya bar Rav's statement to say he carries within four cubits.
The Gemara objects that if so, Chiya bar Rav's opinion is identical to Rav Huna's.
The Gemara resolves by rephrasing: Chiya bar Rav said the same as Rav Huna.

sub.text: Rav Nachman's challenge to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's challenge to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman tells Rav Huna not to dispute Shmuel, as a baraita supports Shmuel's position.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one's measurement of the techum ends in the middle of a city, one may carry throughout the entire city, provided one does not walk beyond the boundary. The Gemara asks whether 'carrying' here means by throwing.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one's measurement of the techum ends in the middle of a city, one may carry throughout the entire city, provided one does not walk beyond the boundary.
The Gemara asks whether 'carrying' in the Mishnah means by throwing (זריקה).

items.text: Rav Huna's answer: carrying by pulling
items.text_en: Rav Huna's answer: carrying by pulling
items.desc_en: Rav Huna answers that the carrying is done by pulling, not by throwing, clarifying the Mishnah's intent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna answers that the carrying in the Mishnah is done by pulling (משיכה), not by throwing (זריקה), clarifying the permitted mode of טלטול (moving objects).

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a courtyard and the Gemara's clarification
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a courtyard and the Gemara's clarification
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one's measurement ends in the middle of a courtyard, one only has half the courtyard. The Gemara questions why this is not obvious, and explains that the ruling teaches that one does not have the entire courtyard, countering a concern that one might come to carry throughout.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if one's Shabbat measurement ends in the middle of a courtyard, one only has half the courtyard.
The Gemara objects that the ruling is obvious, and suggests the opposite formulation would be more novel.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is not obvious because it teaches that one does not have the entire courtyard, countering a concern that one might come to carry throughout.

items.text: דין מדידה שהסתיימה על שפת תקרה
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on a roof edge
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Rav Huna agrees that if one's measurement ends at the edge of a roof, one may carry throughout the entire house, because the roof of the house 'strikes' (i.e., serves as a barrier).
items.desc: רב נחמן מביא דין נוסף שרב הונה מסכים לו: אם מדידת התחום הסתיימה על שפת תקרת בית, מותר לטלטל בכל הבית. הטעם הוא שתקרת הבית נחשבת כאילו היא חובטת ויוצרת מחיצה, כך שאין חשש שימשך אחר חפצו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman reports that Rav Huna agrees: if one's measurement ends at the edge of a roof, one may carry throughout the entire house.
sub.desc: רב נחמן מביא בשם רב הונא שכאשר המדידה מסתיימת על שפת התקרה, מותר לטלטל בכל הבית.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains the reason: because the roof of the house 'strikes' (serves as a barrier).
sub.desc: הגמרא מסבירה את טעם ההיתר: התקרה נחשבת כמחיצה החובטת ומונעת חשש שימשך אחר החפץ.

items.text: השוואה למחלוקת תנאים בדיר, סהר וספינה
items.text_en: Connection to the Tannaitic dispute about a pen and stable
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan links the previous ruling to a Tannaitic dispute: if one was taken to another city and placed in a pen or stable, Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permit walking throughout, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva restrict to four cubits. The Gemara analyzes whether the dispute extends to carrying, and considers alternative explanations based on the nature of the place and whether one rested within partitions before Shabbat.
items.desc: רב הונא בר נתן מקשר את מחלוקת האמוראים למחלוקת תנאים במשנה: רבן גמליאל ורבי אלעזר בן עזריה מתירים להלך בכל דיר או סהר, ואילו רבי יהושע ורבי עקיבא מגבילים לארבע אמות. הגמרא מנתחת את טעמי המחלוקת, ומעלה אפשרות שהמחלוקת נוגעת גם לדיני טלטול. עם זאת, הגמרא דוחה את ההשוואה ומציעה הסברים חלופיים, כגון שההיתר תלוי בשביתה באויר מחיצות מבעוד יום.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Rav Nathan introduces a Tannaitic dispute about one placed in a pen or stable, where Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya permit walking throughout, while Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Akiva restrict to four cubits.
sub.desc: רב הונא בריה דרב נתן מקביל את מחלוקת האמוראים למחלוקת תנאים בדיר, סהר וספינה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers that the dispute about walking extends to carrying: the lenient position does not decree walking in a pen against walking in a field, so it also does not decree carrying against walking; the strict position does decree walking in a pen against walking in a field, so it also decrees carrying against walking.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: האם אין ללמוד מדברי רבן גמליאל ורבי אלעזר בן עזריה שאינם גוזרים הלוך אטו הלוך, וממילא אינם גוזרים טלטול אטו הלוך?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: perhaps the lenient position only refrains from decreeing walking in a pen against walking in a field because they are two different places, but regarding carrying against walking in the same place they would decree, lest one be drawn after his object.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה: שמא רבן גמליאל ורבי אלעזר בן עזריה לא גזרו רק משום שמדובר בשני מקומות שונים, אבל בטלטול אטו הלוך שמקום אחד הוא – אפשר שגוזרים.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara further objects: perhaps the strict position's restriction is not due to a decree but because they hold that the rule 'the entire house is like four cubits' applies only when one rested within the airspace of partitions before Shabbat, not when he did not.
sub.desc: הגמרא דוחה גם את הצד השני: שמא רבי יהושע ורבי עקיבא אינם גוזרים, אלא סוברים שכל הבית כארבע אמות נאמר דווקא כששבת באויר מחיצות מבעוד יום, וכאן לא שבת.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's rulings on the halakha, and the reason for the leniency in a ship
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's rulings on the halakha, and the reason for the leniency in a ship
items.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel for a pen, stable, and ship. Shmuel limits this to a ship only. The Gemara explains that all agree the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel for a ship, and debates the reason: Rabbah says because one rested within partitions before Shabbat, while Rabbi Zeira says because the ship carries one from the beginning of four cubits to the end. The difference between them is a case where the ship's sides are breached or one jumps from ship to ship.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel for a pen, stable, and ship.
Shmuel limits the ruling to a ship only, excluding a pen and stable.
The Gemara asks what is the reason that all agree the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel for a ship.
Rabbah explains that the leniency is because one rested within the partitions of the ship before Shabbat.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the leniency is because the ship carries one from the beginning of four cubits to the end, so one never actually walked beyond his permitted area.
The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations.
The Gemara resolves that the difference is a case where the ship's sides are breached, or one jumps from ship to ship.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rabbah's reason
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's objection to Rabbah's reason
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Zeira does not accept Rabbah's reason, and Rabbi Zeira explains that partitions that are not fixed before Shabbat are not considered valid partitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Zeira does not accept Rabbah's reason for the leniency regarding a ship.

items.text: Rabbah's position on the dispute about a moving boat
items.text_en: Rabbah's position on the dispute about a moving boat
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the dispute between Rabbi Zeira and others is only when the boat is stationary, not when it is moving. He clarifies that everyone agrees about a moving boat.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the Mishnah's phrase that boats are made to 'chase away water' (i.e., to move).
Rabbah explains that the dispute between Rabbi Zeira and others applies only when the boat is stationary (עָמְדָה), not when it is moving (מְהַלֶּכֶת), where all agree.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from the Mishnah
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's proof from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak proves from the Mishnah that there is no dispute about a moving boat, because the Sages who were stringent only did so out of concern that the boat might stop.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak asserts that the Mishnah itself proves that there is no dispute regarding a moving boat.
He cites the Mishnah's story of the boat from Plundersin, where the Sages who were stringent did so voluntarily, implying they were not required to be strict.
He explains that the Mishnah's use of 'רצו' (they wanted to be stringent) makes sense only if the dispute is about a stationary boat, not a moving one.
He concludes that if there were a dispute about a moving boat, the Mishnah would have called the stringency an actual prohibition (איסורא), not a voluntary stringency.

items.text: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah's comparison
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's proof from the Mishnah's comparison
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves that the boat is considered fixed like a pen or stable, based on the Mishnah's comparison.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah's comparison of a boat to a pen and stable that the boat is considered fixed (קבוע), just as a pen and stable are fixed.

items.text: דחיית ההוכחה והבאת ברייתא המכריעה במחלוקת
items.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge and the Baraita's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges Rav Ashi, noting that the ruling in favor of Rabban Gamliel implies a dispute. A Baraita confirms that there was a dispute, with Hananiah reporting that the law follows Rabban Gamliel for a boat and Rabbi Akiva for a pen or stable.
items.desc: רב אחא בריה דרבא מקשה על רב אשי: עצם הקביעה שהלכה כרבן גמליאל בספינה מוכיחה שיש מחלוקת. רב אשי משיב שהמחלוקת היא רק בספינה עומדת, והברייתא של חנניא בן אחי רבי יהושע מכריעה שהלכה כרבן גמליאל בספינה מהלכת וכרבי עקיבא בדיר וסהר (וספינה עומדת).

sub.text: Rav Acha's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha challenges Rav Ashi: if the halacha follows Rabban Gamliel regarding a boat, this implies there was a dispute, contradicting the assumption that all agree on a moving boat.
The Gemara cites a Baraita where Hananiah reports that a dispute indeed occurred, and the ruling was that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabban Gamliel for a boat and Rabbi Akiva for a pen or stable.

items.text: שאלת תחומין מעל עשרה טפחים
items.text_en: Rav Chananya's question about techumim above ten handbreadths
items.desc_en: Rav Chananya asks whether there are techumim above ten handbreadths. He clarifies that the question applies to a pillar ten handbreadths high but less than four wide, or when jumping, not to a pillar that is four wide (which is considered ground).
items.desc: רב חנניה מעלה ספק: האם איסור תחומין חל מעל גובה עשרה טפחים? הגמרא מבהירה שהספק אינו בעמוד גבוה עשרה ורחב ארבעה, שנחשב כארץ, אלא בעמוד גבוה עשרה אך אינו רחב ארבעה, או במקרה של קפיצה באוויר.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chananya asks whether the laws of techumim (Sabbath boundaries) apply above ten handbreadths.
Rav Chananya clarifies that a pillar ten handbreadths high and four handbreadths wide is considered ground, so the question does not apply.
Rav Chananya specifies that the question applies to a pillar less than four handbreadths wide, or when one moves by jumping.

items.text: Alternative version: question about a boat and Rav Hoshaya's proof
items.text_en: Alternative version: question about a boat and Rav Hoshaya's proof
items.desc_en: An alternative version asks about a boat. Rav Hoshaya attempts to prove that there are techumim above ten handbreadths from the Mishnah, but Rava deflects by saying the boat was moving on planks.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents an alternative version of the question: what is the law regarding a boat (whether there are techumim above ten handbreadths)?
Rav Hoshaya attempts to prove that there are techumim above ten handbreadths from the Mishnah's story, arguing that if there were no techumim, why would the sages have restricted themselves?
Rava deflects Rav Hoshaya's proof by explaining that the case involved a boat moving on planks (בִּמְהַלֶּכֶת בִּרְקָק), so the restriction was due to the planks, not techumim above ten.

items.text: Second proof from the story of not entering the port
items.text_en: Second proof from the story of not entering the port
items.desc_en: Another proof is brought from a story where they did not enter the port until dark, implying techumim apply. Rava again explains it was a case of moving on planks.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaia says: Hear the story from Plendar — if you say techumim exist, that's why they sought to be strict; if not, why did they?

items.text: Proof from the seven halachot and the Nazirite vow
items.text_en: Proof from the seven halachot and the Nazirite vow
items.desc_en: A proof is attempted from the seven halachot taught in Sura and Pumbedita, suggesting Elijah taught them, indicating no techumim above ten. This is rejected as possibly demons. A final proof from a Nazirite vow is cited but cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara attempts a proof from the seven halachot taught in Sura and Pumbedita, suggesting Elijah taught them, which would imply no techumim above ten.
The Gemara rejects the proof, suggesting the teachings might have been transmitted by Joseph the demon rather than Elijah.
The Gemara begins to cite a case of a Nazirite vow conditioned on the coming of the son of David, which is cut off.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is forbidden to drink wine all the days of the week (as a nazirite).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is forbidden to drink wine all the days of the week (as a nazirite).

items.text: Gemara's discussion on techumin and Elijah's arrival
items.text_en: Gemara's discussion on techumin and Elijah's arrival
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the prohibition is due to techumin (Sabbath boundaries). It argues that if there are no techumin, why is it permitted on Shabbat and Yom Tov? The answer is that Elijah does not come on those days, but the Gemara objects that if so, it should be permitted every day since Elijah hasn't come yet. The resolution is that Elijah comes to the Great Court, but it is already assured that he does not come on Shabbat or Yom Tov eves due to the trouble.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the prohibition is due to techumin (Sabbath boundaries), arguing that if there are no techumin, why is it permitted on Shabbat and Yom Tov?
The Gemara answers that the case is different because Elijah has not come yet, as per the verse.
The Gemara objects that if so, it should be permitted every day since Elijah hasn't come yet, and suggests that Elijah comes to the Great Court.
The Gemara resolves that it is already assured that Elijah does not come on Shabbat or Yom Tov eves due to the trouble.

items.text: דחיית ההיתר בערב שבת וביום ראשון
items.text_en: Discussion on Messiah's arrival and techumin
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers that if Elijah does not come, perhaps the Messiah also does not come, so it should be permitted on Shabbat eve. But it is argued that the Messiah does come, and then all are servants to Israel. The Gemara then questions whether on Sunday it should be permitted, and concludes that this Tanna is uncertain whether there are techumin and rules stringently.
items.desc: הגמרא דוחה את האפשרות להתיר בערב שבת בטענה שהמשיח יכול לבוא גם אז, ומקשה מדוע לא להתיר ביום ראשון. התשובה היא שהתנא מסופק אם יש תחומין מעל עשרה טפחים ומחמיר.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: If one assumes that since Elijah has not come, the Messiah also has not come, then why not permit drinking wine on Shabbat eve?
The Gemara answers that the initial assumption is wrong: though Elijah has not come, the Messiah does come, and then all nations become servants to Israel.

The Gemara asks: then why not permit it on Sunday, and suggests that this would prove there are no techumin, since if there were techumin, Sunday would still be restricted because Elijah does not come on Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves that this Tanna (of the baraita) is uncertain whether techumin exist or not, and therefore rules stringently.

items.text: זמן הנדר של הנזיר
items.text_en: Clarification of the nazirite vow's timing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks when the nazirite vow was taken. If it was on a weekday, once the vow takes effect, how can Shabbat nullify it? Rather, it must have been taken on Shabbat or Yom Tov, and that day is permitted, but from then on it is forbidden.
items.desc: הגמרא מבררת מתי הנזיר נדר: אם נדר בחול, הנזירות חלה ואינה מתבטלת בשבת; לכן יש להניח שנדר בשבת או ביום טוב, ורק אותו יום מותר, ומכאן ואילך אסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: When was the nazirite vow taken? If on a weekday, once the vow takes effect, how can Shabbat nullify it?
The Gemara answers: The vow was taken on Shabbat or Yom Tov, so that day is permitted, but from then on it is forbidden.

items.text: מעשה רבן גמליאל וכללי מדידה
items.text_en: Story of Rabban Gamliel's tube and related teachings
items.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts that once they did not enter the port. A baraita describes Rabban Gamliel's tube for viewing distances, and additional methods for measuring depth and height, and for avoiding wild animals near graves.
items.desc: מובא סיפור מהמשנה על רבן גמליאל שהתיר לרדת מהספינה לאחר שצפה שנכנסו לתחום. לאחר מכן מובאות ברייתא על שפופרת הצפייה של רבן גמליאל, ועוד כללים למדידת עומק גיא, גובה דקל, וצל קבר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah recounts that once they did not enter the port, setting the context for the following baraita.
A baraita teaches that Rabban Gamliel had a tube (שפופרת) through which he could view and measure two thousand amot on land and correspondingly two thousand amot at sea.
