The baraita provides a method for measuring the depth of a valley using a tube (שפופרת).
The baraita teaches how to measure the height of a palm tree by comparing its shadow to the person's height.
The baraita concludes with a method to avoid wild animals near graves by observing the direction of a reed's shadow at the fourth hour of the day.

items.text: מעשה נחמיה שיצא מחוץ לתחום
items.text_en: Nechemya's case and the halakhic question
items.desc_en: Nechemya, son of Rav Chanilai, was drawn by a discussion and went beyond the techum. Rav Chisda asked Rav Nachman to help. Rav Nachman said to make a partition of people for him to enter. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak then asked Rava what Rav Chisda's question was: whether we are dealing with a case where people filled the area, and whether the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
items.desc: מסופר על נחמיה בר חנילאי שיצא מחוץ לתחום בשבת. רב חסדא פנה לרב נחמן, שהציע לעשות מחיצה אנושית כדי להכניסו. רב נחמן בר יצחק ורבא דנים בשאלה האם ההלכה כרבן גמליאל בעניין זה.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Nechemya, son of Rav Chanilai, who was drawn by a discussion and went beyond the techum, and Rav Chisda tells Rav Nachman that his student is in distress.
Rav Nachman instructs Rav Chisda to make a partition of people for Nechemya to enter.

sub.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak, sitting behind Rava, asks Rava what Rav Chisda's question was.
Rava explains that Rav Chisda's question was whether we are dealing with a case where people filled the area, and whether the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.

items.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Eliezer's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the question is about a boat without men filling it, and whether the halakha follows Rabbi Eliezer. It deduces from the language 'yikanes' that the boat lacks a partition.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a double question: whether the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel or Rabbi Eliezer, and clarifies that the issue is about a boat without men filling it.
The Gemara resolves that the question is about a boat without men filling it, because if men filled it, Rav's ruling that the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel would be obvious.
The Gemara deduces from the language 'יִכָּנֵס' (he may enter) that the boat lacks a partition, confirming the interpretation.

items.text: Objection from a baraita about a fallen wall
items.text_en: Objection from a baraita about a fallen wall
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects to Rava with a baraita that prohibits making a temporary tent on Yom Tov. Rava responds with a contradictory baraita that permits using a friend as a wall for eating, drinking, and sleeping.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak objects to Rava by citing a baraita: if a boat's side falls, one may not use animals or vessels as a partition, nor erect a bed to spread a sheet, because one may not make a temporary tent (אוהל עראי) on Yom Tov, and certainly not on Shabbat.
Rava counters by citing a conflicting baraita: one may use a friend as a partition to eat, drink, and sleep, and may erect a bed to spread a sheet to protect a corpse or food from the sun.

items.text: First resolution: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Sages
items.text_en: First resolution: Rabbi Eliezer vs. Sages
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes the contradiction and resolves it by attributing the first baraita to Rabbi Eliezer and the second to the Sages, citing a mishna about a window plug. However, a statement by Rabbi Yochanan says all agree that one does not make a temporary tent initially on Yom Tov, and the dispute is only about adding.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes the contradiction between the two baraitot and resolves it by attributing one to Rabbi Eliezer and the other to the Sages, citing a Mishnah about a window plug (פקק החלון).
The Gemara cites the Mishnah about a window plug: Rabbi Eliezer permits plugging only if tied and hanging, while the Sages permit in all cases.

The Gemara cites Rabbi Yochanan's ruling that all agree one may not make a temporary tent (אוהל עראי) on Yom Tov, and they only dispute about adding to an existing tent: Rabbi Eliezer forbids adding on Yom Tov, while the Sages permit adding on Shabbat.

items.text: Second resolution: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Second resolution: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another resolution, attributing the baraitot to Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, based on a dispute about using an animal as a wall for a sukkah. Rabbi Meir invalidates it, implying it is not a valid partition, so using a person is permitted; Rabbi Yehuda validates it, so using a person is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the conflicting baraitot align with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita where using an animal as a partition for a sukkah is invalid according to Rabbi Meir but valid according to Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir, who invalidates an animal as a partition there, permits using a person here because it is not a significant action.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda, who validates an animal as a partition there, forbids using a person here because it constitutes a significant partition.

items.text: Objections to the second resolution
items.text_en: Objections to the second resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Meir's ruling about an animal does not extend to people and vessels. Moreover, if Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Eliezer, he would prohibit adding; if he follows the Sages, they only permit adding, not initial construction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: Rabbi Meir's ruling about an animal does not necessarily extend to people and vessels.
The Gemara further objects: if Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Eliezer, then Rabbi Meir would also forbid adding to a tent, contradicting the earlier resolution.
The Gemara objects: if Rabbi Meir follows the Sages, the Sages only permit adding to an existing tent, not making one לכתחילה (from scratch), so the resolution fails.

items.text: Final resolution: both baraitot are Sages, distinguishing third vs. fourth wall
items.text_en: Final resolution: both baraitot are Sages, distinguishing third vs. fourth wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that both baraitot follow the Sages, and the contradiction is resolved by distinguishing between a third wall (where adding is permitted) and a fourth wall (where initial construction is prohibited). The language 'its wall fell' supports this, as it refers to a fourth wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves definitively: both baraitot follow the Sages, and the contradiction about vessels is resolved by distinguishing between a third wall (דופן שלישית) and a fourth wall (דופן רביעית).
The Gemara deduces support from the baraita's language 'נָפַל דּוֹפְנָהּ' (its side fell), implying a specific wall, confirming the distinction.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about Rav Chisda and Rabbi Nechemya
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about Rav Chisda and Rabbi Nechemya
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially questions a contradiction between two cases involving a person carrying into a courtyard. It resolves that one case was with knowledge and the other without. It then clarifies that Rabbi Nechemya's case was with knowledge, and Rav Chisda's was not part of the official count.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: one case says a person who carries into a courtyard on Shabbat is liable, while another says he is exempt. It resolves that the first case was with knowledge (the person knew it was Shabbat), the second without knowledge (he thought it was weekday). Then it notes that Rabbi Nechemya's case was with knowledge, and Rav Chisda's was not part of the official count.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on the Ganana children
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on the Ganana children
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Shmuel punished children who brought water into a partition made of people, reasoning that if they did it without knowledge, they might later do it with knowledge.

sub.desc_en: A story: certain people brought water through a partition of human beings. Samuel punished them. He said: If they said it was without knowledge, they should be told it was with knowledge.

items.text: Rava's ruling on the wine skins
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on the wine skins
items.desc_en: Rava was brought wine skins that were lying in the street of Mechoza. He permitted them for that Shabbat but forbade them for the next, as it was considered with knowledge.

sub.desc_en: Another story: certain beams were thrown in the marketplace of Machoza. When Rava came from his session, he brought them in. On the next Shabbat he wanted to bring them in again, but he forbade it, because it was like knowledge — and forbidden.

items.text: Levi, Ze'iri, and Rav Shimi bar Chiyya's cases
items.text_en: Levi, Ze'iri, and Rav Shimi bar Chiyya's cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara briefly mentions that Levi had straw brought in, Ze'iri had a sponge, and Rav Shimi bar Chiyya had water brought in, all related to the same principle.

sub.desc_en: Levi brought straw, Ze'iri brought a basket, and Rav Shimi bar Chiya brought water — all as examples of carrying into a courtyard.

items.text: Mishnah: One who left the boundary and was told the eruv was made
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who left the boundary and was told the eruv was made
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one left the Shabbat boundary and was told the eruv was already made, he has 2000 amot in all directions. If he was within the boundary, it is as if he never left. Those who go out to save lives may return to their place.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who left the Shabbat boundary with permission and was told the eruv was already made, granting him 2000 amot in all directions.
The Mishnah adds that if he was within the boundary, it is as if he never left.
The Mishnah concludes that all who go out to save lives may return to their place.

items.text: Gemara: Rabba and Rav Shimi bar Chiyya dispute the Mishnah's meaning
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabba and Rav Shimi bar Chiyya dispute the Mishnah's meaning
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'if he was within the boundary, it is as if he never left.' Rabba says it means within his own Shabbat boundary, as if he never left his house. Rav Shimi bar Chiyya says it means the boundaries given by the Sages are absorbed into his own boundary. They disagree about the concept of absorption of boundaries.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah's phrase 'if he was within the boundary, it is as if he never left' means, and Rabba answers that it refers to being within his own Shabbat boundary, as if he never left his house.
The Gemara objects that Rabba's explanation is obvious, but resolves that the Mishnah teaches that even though he uprooted himself, he is still considered within his boundary.
Rav Shimi bar Chiyya explains that the Mishnah means the boundaries given by the Sages are absorbed into his own boundary, as if he never left his boundary.
The Gemara resolves the dispute: Rabba holds that the absorption of boundaries (הבלעת תחומין) is not a valid concept, while Rav Shimi bar Chiyya holds that it is.

items.text: Abaye challenges Rabba about absorption of boundaries
items.text_en: Abaye challenges Rabba about absorption of boundaries
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabba if he does not hold that absorption of boundaries is significant, citing a case of a cave with 4000 amot inside and less than 4000 on its roof. Rabba distinguishes between one who rested in the airspace of partitions before Shabbat and one who did not.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabba by asking whether he does not hold that absorption of boundaries (הבלעת תחומין) is significant, citing a case of a cave with 4000 amot inside and less than 4000 on its roof, where one would walk the entire cave and then 2000 amot outside.
Rabba distinguishes between one who rested in the airspace of partitions before Shabbat and one who did not, implying that absorption of boundaries applies only in the former case.
The Gemara confirms Rabba's position: where one did not rest in the airspace of partitions before Shabbat, absorption of boundaries does not apply.

items.text: Gemara's question from Rabbi Eliezer's mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's question from Rabbi Eliezer's mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous assumption by citing a mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that two people may enter the city but three may not, implying that the four cubits given by the Sages are considered absorbed, and thus the concept of absorption of boundaries is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous assumption by citing a mishnah where Rabbi Eliezer rules that two people may enter the city but three may not, implying that the four cubits given by the Sages are considered absorbed, and thus the concept of absorption of boundaries is valid.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana's objection and Abaye's response
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana's objection and Abaye's response
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana asks Abaye if he is challenging Mar (Rav) from Rabbi Eliezer's statement. Abaye responds that he heard from Mar that the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer for optional matters, but for a mitzvah they agree with him.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana objects to Abaye that the challenge from Rabbi Eliezer is invalid, because the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer regarding a voluntary matter, but for a mitzvah they concede to him.
Abaye affirms and explains that he heard from Mar that the Sages only disagree with Rabbi Eliezer for optional matters, but for a mitzvah they agree with him.

items.text: Question on the mishnah about rescuers returning
items.text_en: Question on the mishnah about rescuers returning
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah that says all who go out to save lives return to their place, even if far away, contradicting the earlier statement that they only have 2000 cubits. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that they return with their weapons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the mishnah's statement that all who go out to save lives return to their place, even far away, contradicting the earlier rule of only 2000 cubits.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that they return with their weapons, and the Gemara notes that the case of rescue is different.

items.text: Alternative difficulty from the baraita
items.text_en: Alternative difficulty from the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a different difficulty from a baraita: initially they would not move from there all day, but Rabban Gamliel the Elder instituted that they have 2000 cubits in every direction, and this applies also to a woman giving birth and those rescuing from various dangers.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a different difficulty from the mishnah of Rabban Gamliel the Elder, who instituted that those who go out to rescue have two thousand cubits in every direction.
The baraita reports that Rabban Gamliel the Elder instituted that those who go out to rescue have 2000 cubits in every direction, and this applies also to a woman giving birth and other rescuers.

items.text: Resolution with the baraita about weapons
items.text_en: Resolution with the baraita about weapons
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks again about the contradiction between the mishnah and the baraita. Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that they return with their weapons, as taught in a baraita: initially they left weapons in a house near the wall, but after a tragic incident where they killed each other, they instituted that they return with their weapons.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the mishnah's limit of 2000 amot by citing the baraita that all who go out to save lives return to their place, even many people.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav answers that the baraita means they return with their weapons, not that they may travel freely beyond the 2000 amot limit.

A baraita is cited to support Rav's answer: originally they left weapons near the wall, but after a tragic incident where they killed each other, the institution was made that they return with their weapons.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says there is no difficulty: one case is where Israel defeated the nations, the other where the nations defeated themselves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when Israel defeated the nations and when the nations defeated themselves.

items.text: Laws of going out against gentile attackers
items.text_en: Laws of going out against gentile attackers
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that if gentiles besiege Jewish cities, one does not go out with weapons or desecrate Shabbat. A baraita qualifies: for monetary matters, no; for lives, yes. A border city even for straw and stubble. Rav Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Nachman says Babylonia is like a border city, specifically Nehardea.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav rules that when gentiles besiege Jewish cities, one does not go out with weapons or desecrate Shabbat.
A baraita supports Rav's ruling, qualifying that for monetary matters one does not go out, but for lives one does, and for a border city even for straw and stubble.

sub.text: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef bar Minyumi in the name of Rav Nachman states that Babylonia is like a border city, specifically Nehardea.

items.text: Proof from David and Keilah
items.text_en: Proof from David and Keilah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai of Beirai expounds a verse about David and the Philistines at Keilah, a border city. The Gemara explains that David asked not whether it was permitted (since Shmuel's court existed) but whether he would succeed, as the verse says 'Go and strike the Philistines and save Keilah.'

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Dostai of Beirai expounds the verse about David and the Philistines at Keilah, noting that Keilah was a border city and the Philistines came only for straw and chaff.
A baraita confirms Keilah was a border city, and the verse shows David inquired of God whether to go and save Keilah.
The Gemara asks what David was inquiring about, since he could not have been asking whether it was permitted, because Shmuel's court existed.
The Gemara answers that David was asking whether he would succeed, and the verse confirms this by saying 'Go and strike the Philistines and save Keilah.'

items.text: Mishnah: One who sat on the road and saw he is near the city
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who sat on the road and saw he is near the city
items.desc_en: The mishnah states: If one sat on the road and then stood and saw he is near the city, since he did not intend to enter, he may not enter according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says he may enter, citing a precedent with Rabbi Tarfon who entered unintentionally.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of one who sat on the road and then saw he was near the city; Rabbi Meir rules he may not enter since he lacked intent.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that he may enter, citing a precedent where Rabbi Tarfon entered unintentionally.

items.text: Gemara: The story of Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Gemara: The story of Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates: Rabbi Tarfon was walking, it got dark, and he slept outside. In the morning, shepherds told him the city was before him, so he entered and taught all day. The Gemara questions the proof: perhaps he had it in mind, or the study hall was within his Shabbat boundary.

sub.desc_en: A baraita recounts that Rabbi Tarfon slept outside the city, was told by shepherds that the city was before him, entered, and taught all day.
The Gemara objects that the story does not prove Rabbi Yehuda's position, because Rabbi Tarfon may have had the city in mind or the study hall may have been within his Shabbat boundary.

items.text: Mishnah: One who slept on the road and did not know it got dark
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who slept on the road and did not know it got dark
items.desc_en: The mishnah discusses one who slept on the road and did not realize it got dark: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri says he has 2000 cubits in every direction; the Sages say only four cubits; Rabbi Eliezer says he is in the middle; Rabbi Yehuda says he may go in any direction he chooses, but once he chooses he cannot retract. If two people have overlapping four-cubit areas, they may eat together in the middle.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of one who slept on the road and did not know it got dark, stating Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's position that he has 2000 cubits in every direction.
The Sages rule that he has only four cubits, and Rabbi Eliezer adds that he is considered to be in the middle of those four cubits.
Rabbi Yehuda says he may go in any direction he chooses, but once he chooses he cannot retract.
The mishnah concludes with the case of two people whose four-cubit areas overlap, permitting them to eat together in the middle.

items.text: Mishnah: Three courtyards with a middle one absorbed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Three courtyards with a middle one absorbed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if three courtyards are arranged such that the middle one is absorbed between the two outer ones, the middle is permitted with each outer, but the two outer ones are forbidden with each other. Rabbi Shimon compares this to three courtyards opened to each other and to the public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for three courtyards where the middle one is absorbed: the middle is permitted with each outer, but the two outer ones are forbidden with each other.
Rabbi Shimon compares the case to three courtyards opened to each other and to the public domain, illustrating the same rule.

items.text: Rava's question about Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's reasoning
items.text_en: Rava's question about Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rava questions whether Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that ownerless objects acquire a Sabbath residence, and the dispute with the Rabbis is about vessels, but they argue about a person to show the Rabbis' strength; or perhaps he holds that ownerless objects do not acquire a residence, and the reason here is because an awake person acquires, so a sleeping one also acquires.

sub.desc_en: Rava raises a dilemma: does Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri hold that ownerless objects acquire a Sabbath residence?
The Gemara suggests that according to this view, the dispute should have been about vessels, but they argued about a person to show the Rabbis' strength.

The Gemara offers an alternative: perhaps Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that ownerless objects do not acquire residence, and the reason here is that since an awake person acquires, a sleeping one also acquires.

items.text: Rav Yosef's attempted proof from a baraita about rainwater
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's attempted proof from a baraita about rainwater
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a baraita: rain that fell on the eve of a festival has a limit of 2000 cubits in every direction; on the festival itself, it follows the feet of every person. He argues that if Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that ownerless objects acquire a residence, the baraita aligns with him; if not, it aligns with neither him nor the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a baraita: rain that fell on the eve of a festival has a limit of 2000 cubits in every direction; on the festival itself, it follows the feet of every person.
The Gemara analyzes: if Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that ownerless objects acquire residence, the baraita aligns with him.
The Gemara argues: if Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that ownerless objects do not acquire residence, the baraita aligns with neither him nor the Rabbis.

items.text: Abaye's discussion with Rav Safra and resolution via a contradiction in baraitot
items.text_en: Abaye's discussion with Rav Safra and resolution via a contradiction in baraitot
items.desc_en: Abaye states this teaching, and Rav Safra suggests the baraita deals with rain near a town, where people's minds are on it. Abaye rejects this, citing a contradiction between a baraita about a private well and one about a tribal well, concluding that one follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the other the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra objects to Abaye's teaching, suggesting that the baraita deals with rain near a city, where the residents' intention is upon it.
Abaye rejects the objection, citing a Mishnah about a private cistern following the owner's feet and a public cistern following the city's feet.
A baraita about a cistern of the tribes giving 2000 cubits is cited, creating a contradiction with the previous Mishnah.
The Gemara resolves that one baraita follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the other follows the Rabbis, confirming that he holds ownerless objects acquire a שביתה.
The gemara resolves the contradiction: one baraita follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the other follows the Rabbis.

items.text: Rav Yosef's critique of Abaye's response
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's critique of Abaye's response
items.desc_en: When Abaye came before Rav Yosef and reported the exchange, Rav Yosef asked why he didn't point out from the baraita itself: if it deals with rain near a town, it should say 'like the feet of the people of that town', not '2000 cubits in every direction'.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Abaye why he did not point out from the baraita itself that if it dealt with rain near the city, it should say 'like the feet of the city's people' rather than '2000 cubits'.

items.text: Question about rainwater on a festival and the ocean
items.text_en: Question about rainwater on a festival and the ocean
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: why does rainwater on a festival follow every person's feet? Let it acquire a residence in the ocean! This suggests it is not like Rabbi Eliezer, who says the whole world drinks from the ocean. Rabbi Yitzchak answers that we deal with clouds that formed before the festival, and they have a distinguishing mark.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why rainwater on a festival follows every person's feet, asking why it does not acquire a residence in the ocean.
The Gemara objects that this ruling contradicts Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that the whole world drinks from the ocean, implying rainwater should be considered as originating there.
Rabbi Yitzchak answers that the case involves clouds that formed before the festival, so the water already acquired a residence then.
The Gemara resolves the potential objection that different clouds might be involved by noting that these clouds have a distinguishing mark, ensuring continuity.

items.text: Alternative answers: doubt in rabbinic law and the principle of no techumim above ten
items.text_en: Alternative answers: doubt in rabbinic law and the principle of no techumim above ten
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers alternative answers: it is a doubt in rabbinic law, which is lenient; or, one can prove that there are no techumim above ten handbreadths, since otherwise the rain would acquire a residence in the clouds. The final answer is that there are techumim, but the water is absorbed within the cloud.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative answer: the case is a doubt in rabbinic law (ספק דדבריהם), and such doubts are resolved leniently.
The Gemara asks: why not say that the rain acquires a residence in the clouds, and then infer that there are no techumim above ten handbreadths?
The Gemara resolves: one can still say there are techumim above ten, but the water is absorbed within the cloud and therefore does not acquire a residence.

items.text: Resolving the ocean and river problem
items.text_en: Resolving the ocean and river problem
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier difficulty about the ocean by noting that water in the ocean also moves, and cites a baraita that flowing rivers and springs follow the feet of every person.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the earlier difficulty by noting that water in the ocean also moves, just like water in clouds.
The Gemara cites a baraita that flowing rivers and springs follow the feet of every person, supporting the resolution.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about the ruling
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry about the ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reports that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled like Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri. Rabbi Zeira asks whether he heard this explicitly or inferred it from the general principle that halakha follows the lenient opinion in eruvin.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reports in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that the halakha follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri.
Rabbi Zeira asks Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi whether he heard this ruling explicitly or inferred it from a general principle.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi answers that he heard the ruling explicitly.
The Gemara explains the general principle: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled that the halakha follows the lenient opinion in matters of עירוב (eruv).

items.text: Why both rulings are necessary
items.text_en: Why both rulings are necessary
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that both statements are needed: the specific ruling about Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri might have been thought to apply both leniently and stringently, so the general principle clarifies it is only lenient. The general principle alone might have been thought not to apply when an individual disputes a majority, so the specific ruling is needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why both rulings—the specific one about Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri and the general principle—are necessary.

Rabbi Zeira explains that the specific ruling is needed because without it one might have thought Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's opinion applies both leniently and stringently, so the general principle clarifies it is only lenient.
The Gemara objects that if the general principle suffices, why is the specific ruling about Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri needed at all?

The Gemara resolves that the specific ruling is needed because otherwise one might have thought the lenient principle applies only when an individual disputes another individual, but not when an individual disputes a majority.

items.text: Rava's challenge: eruvin are rabbinic
items.text_en: Rava's challenge: eruvin are rabbinic
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the distinction between individual vs. majority in eruvin, since eruvin are rabbinic. Rav Pappa supports this, questioning whether we differentiate at all in rabbinic matters.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye: since eruvin are rabbinic, why distinguish between an individual against an individual and an individual against a majority?
Rav Pappa supports Rava's challenge, questioning whether we differentiate at all between an individual against an individual and an individual against a majority in rabbinic matters.

items.text: Counterexample from niddah
items.text_en: Counterexample from niddah
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites a mishna where Rabbi Elazar's individual opinion was relied upon only in a time of pressure because the Sages disputed him, showing that in rabbinic law we do distinguish between individual and majority.

sub.text: Rav Pappa's citation of the Mishnah
sub.text_en: Rav Pappa's citation of the Mishnah
sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa cites the Mishnah where רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar) rules that a woman who passed three cycles is only impure from the time of discovery.
A ברייתא (baraita) reports that רבי (Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi) initially ruled like רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar), then upon remembering the dispute, said he is worthy to rely on in exigent circumstances.
The גמרא (Gemara) questions the meaning of 'after he remembered', rejecting the possibility that the הלכה (halakha) was already decided against רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar).

The גמרא (Gemara) resolves that the הלכה (halakha) was not yet decided, and because many sages disputed רבי אלעזר (Rabbi Elazar), he is only relied upon in exigent circumstances, proving that in rabbinic law we distinguish between an individual and a majority.

items.text: Counterexample from mourning and resolution
items.text_en: Counterexample from mourning and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya cites a baraita about mourning where Rabbi Akiva is lenient against the Sages, yet Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Akiva, following Shmuel's principle that in mourning we follow the lenient opinion. The Gemara concludes that mourning is exceptional; elsewhere, even in rabbinic law, we distinguish between individual vs. individual and individual vs. majority.

sub.text: Rav Mesharshiya (or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya (or Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak) to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenges Rava: is there really no distinction in rabbinic law between a single authority versus a single authority and a single authority versus a majority?

A baraita is cited: a proximate report of a relative's death requires seven and thirty days of mourning, while a distant report requires only one day; Rabbi Akiva defines proximate as within thirty days, while the Sages say both require full mourning.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan rules that generally the halakha follows the stringent majority, except in this case where Rabbi Akiva is lenient and the Sages are stringent, yet the halakha follows Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yochanan follows Shmuel's principle that in mourning the halakha follows the lenient opinion.

The Gemara concludes that mourning is exceptional because the Sages were lenient in it; elsewhere, even in rabbinic law, we do distinguish between a single authority versus a single authority and a single authority versus a majority.

items.text: Rav Pappa's necessity for the statement about eiruvei chatzeiros vs. eiruvei techumin
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's necessity for the statement about eiruvei chatzeiros vs. eiruvei techumin
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa argues that the statement was necessary because one might have thought it applies only to eiruvei chatzeiros but not to eiruvei techumin. He supports this with a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between the two types of eiruv.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asserts that the statement was necessary, because one might have thought it applies only to eiruvei chatzeiros (alleyway eiruvin) but not to eiruvei techumin (Sabbath boundary eiruvin).
Rav Pappa cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between eiruvei techumin and eiruvei chatzeiros, supporting the need for the statement.

items.text: Rav Ashi's necessity for the statement about shiyurei eiruv vs. techilas eiruv
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's necessity for the statement about shiyurei eiruv vs. techilas eiruv
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the statement was necessary because one might have thought it applies only to shiyurei eiruv but not to techilas eiruv. He supports this with a baraita where Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between the two, and adds a general principle about eiruvei chatzeiros.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that the statement was necessary, because one might have thought it applies only to shiyurei eiruv (remnants of an eiruv) but not to techilas eiruv (the initial establishment of an eiruv).
Rav Ashi cites a baraita where Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between techilas eiruv and shiyurei eiruv, proving that the distinction is recognized in Tannaitic sources.
Rav Ashi adds a general principle that the rabbis only instituted eiruvei chatzeiros (courtyard eiruvin) to prevent the laws of eiruv from being forgotten by children.

items.text: Rule about halacha following Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi
items.text_en: Rule about halacha following Rabbi Akiva, Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Zerika state a general rule: the halacha follows Rabbi Akiva over his colleague, Rabbi Yosei over his colleagues, and Rabbi over his colleague. The Amoraim then debate the precise meaning of this rule, with Rabbi Assi saying it means 'halacha', Rabbi Chiya bar Abba saying 'mattin' (leaning), and Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina saying 'nir'in' (it seems).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov and Rabbi Zerika state a general rule: the halacha follows Rabbi Akiva over his colleague, Rabbi Yosei over his colleagues, and Rabbi over his colleague.
The Gemara asks: for what practical purpose is this rule stated?
Rabbi Assi answers that the rule means the halacha (binding law) follows those sages.
Rabbi Chiya bar Abba answers that the rule means 'מטין' (one leans toward their opinion).
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina answers that the rule means 'נראין' (their opinion seems correct).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's rule about Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's rule about Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quotes Rabbi Yochanan stating a rule: between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda; between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei; and certainly between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei, the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei. The Gemara questions the redundancy of the last statement.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reports Rabbi Yochanan's rule: between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda; between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei it follows Rabbi Yosei; and certainly between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei it follows Rabbi Yosei.
The Gemara objects that since Rabbi Yehuda is not considered against Rabbi Yosei, the last clause is redundant.

items.text: Rav Assi's extension to Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav Assi's extension to Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Assi adds that the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei over Rabbi Shimon, citing Rabbi Abba quoting Rabbi Yochanan that between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara again questions the redundancy.

sub.desc_en: Rav Assi states that he also learns that the halacha follows Rabbi Yosei over Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rav Assi citing Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Assi citing Rabbi Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Assi supports his ruling by citing Rabbi Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon the halacha follows Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara questions the redundancy: if Rabbi Yehuda is not even considered against Rabbi Yosei, why is it necessary to state that Rabbi Yosei prevails over Rabbi Shimon?

items.text: Unresolved question about Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Unresolved question about Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question (teiku) regarding the halacha when Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon disagree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question (תיקו) about the halacha when Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Shimon disagree.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya challenges the rules with a Mishna
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya challenges the rules with a Mishna
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya claims that these rules are not absolute, citing a Mishna where Rabbi Shimon's opinion is followed as halacha despite a dispute with Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara initially suggests this disproves the rules, but then answers that the rules only apply where explicitly stated.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya declares that these rules (about halachic precedence) are not absolute, and the Gemara asks what his source is.
The Gemara suggests Rav Mesharshiya's source is a Mishna where Rabbi Shimon rules about three courtyards open to each other and to the public domain.
The Gemara notes that Rav ruled like Rabbi Shimon, contradicting the rule that Rabbi Yehuda takes precedence over Rabbi Shimon, proving the rules are not absolute.
The Gemara resolves the challenge: the rules only apply where explicitly stated, and where not stated (as in this Mishna), they do not apply.

items.text: Alternative challenge from a Mishna about a city
items.text_en: Alternative challenge from a Mishna about a city
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings another Mishna about a city that changes from private to public domain, where Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree, to further challenge the rules. The text cuts off at the beginning of Rabbi Shimon's statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces an alternative challenge from a Mishna about a city that changes from private to public domain, citing Rabbi Yehuda's position.
The Mishna begins to cite Rabbi Shimon's dissenting opinion, but the text cuts off at this point.

items.text: First challenge: Rav rules like Rabbi Shimon against Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: First challenge: Rav rules like Rabbi Shimon against Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya cites Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon in a case of three courtyards with two houses each. The Gemara objects: the general rule is that Rabbi Yehuda prevails over Rabbi Shimon. The Gemara deflects: perhaps the rule was stated only where explicitly said, not here.

sub.text: Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya cites Rav that the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon in the case of three courtyards with two houses each.
The Gemara objects: since Rabbi Yehuda disputes Rabbi Shimon, the general rule is that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, contradicting Rav's ruling.
The Gemara deflects: perhaps the general rule applies only where explicitly stated, not in this case.

items.text: Second challenge: Rav rules like Rabbi Shimon in the Mishnah of one who leaves his house
items.text_en: Second challenge: Rav rules like Rabbi Shimon in the Mishnah of one who leaves his house
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Yehuda, Rabbi Yosi, and Rabbi Shimon dispute whether one who leaves his home for Shabbat prohibits the residents. Rav again rules like Rabbi Shimon. The same objection arises: Rabbi Yehuda should prevail. The same deflection is offered.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: one who leaves his house to stay elsewhere for Shabbat — Rabbi Meir says he prohibits the residents, Rabbi Yehuda says he does not, Rabbi Yosi distinguishes between a gentile (prohibits) and an Israelite (does not), and Rabbi Shimon says even if he stays with his daughter in the same city he does not prohibit.

sub.text: Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chama bar Gurya reports that Rav ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon in this Mishnah.

The Gemara objects: since Rabbi Yehuda is the disputant here, and the established rule is that when Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon disagree the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda, why does Rav rule like Rabbi Shimon?

The Gemara deflects: the rule that Rabbi Yehuda prevails over Rabbi Shimon was stated only in contexts where it was explicitly articulated, but here it was not stated, so Rav's ruling is not contradicted.

items.text: Third challenge: Rav rules like Rabbi Yehuda against Rabbi Meir, but the rule already says so
items.text_en: Third challenge: Rav rules like Rabbi Yehuda against Rabbi Meir, but the rule already says so
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah about the poor person making an eiruv by foot. Rav Chiya bar Ashi taught before Rav that both poor and rich may do so, and Rav said the halakha is like Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara objects: the general rule already says Rabbi Yehuda prevails over Rabbi Meir. The Gemara deflects: perhaps Rav does not accept these general rules.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: the poor person makes an eiruv by foot; Rabbi Meir says only the poor may do so, while Rabbi Yehuda says both poor and rich may, as the rule of bread-eiruv was only to ease the rich.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Ashi's teaching before Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi's teaching before Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Ashi taught before Rav that both poor and rich may make an eiruv by foot, and Rav instructed him to also conclude that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara objects: why does Rav need to state the rule here, since the general principle already says that when Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree, the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda?
The Gemara deflects: perhaps Rav does not accept these general rules of precedence, so his explicit ruling is necessary.

items.text: Fourth challenge: Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Yosi against Rabbi Meir, but the rule already says so
items.text_en: Fourth challenge: Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Yosi against Rabbi Meir, but the rule already says so
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a Mishnah about a yevamah waiting three months. Rabbi Yochanan rules like Rabbi Yosi. The Gemara objects: the general rule says Rabbi Yosi prevails over Rabbi Meir. The Gemara deflects: perhaps it was necessary to exclude Rav Nachman's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: a yevamah (widow awaiting levirate marriage) must wait three months before performing חליצה (levirate refusal) or יבום (levirate marriage), and all other women must wait three months before remarrying or betrothal.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that married women may be betrothed immediately, and betrothed women may marry immediately, except for a betrothed woman from Judea, because her husband is familiar with her.
Rabbi Yosi rules that all women may be betrothed immediately, except for a widow, because of the mourning period.

sub.text: Gemara's narrative: Rabbi Eliezer asks Rabbi Asi
sub.text_en: Gemara's narrative: Rabbi Eliezer asks Rabbi Asi
sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbi Eliezer did not enter the study hall; he found Rabbi Asi standing and asked what was said in the study hall.

sub.text: Rabbi Asi's report: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.text_en: Rabbi Asi's report: Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi reports that Rabbi Yochanan ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosi, implying that an individual Tanna (תנא) disputes him.

sub.text: Supporting baraita: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yosi
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yosi
sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited listing various cases where a woman must wait three months according to Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yosi permits immediate betrothal and marriage.
The Gemara objects: why is Rabbi Yochanan's ruling needed, given the general rule that Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosi disagree and the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yosi?
The Gemara deflects: perhaps the ruling was necessary to exclude Rav Nachman's statement in the name of Shmuel, who ruled that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Meir in his decrees (גזירותיו).

items.text: Fifth challenge: Rabbi Yosi permits impurity to learn Torah even when a teacher is available
items.text_en: Fifth challenge: Rabbi Yosi permits impurity to learn Torah even when a teacher is available
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita about a kohen going to a gentile fair and becoming impure. Rabbi Yehuda limits impurity to when no teacher is available; Rabbi Yosi permits it even when one is. The Gemara implies a dispute, but the text breaks off.

sub.desc_en: The baraita permits going to a gentile fair to buy animals, slaves, and property, and writing documents in their courts, as it is like rescuing from them.
The baraita adds that a kohen may become impure outside the land to litigate with them, and similarly may become impure in a cemetery.
The Gemara objects: How can a kohen enter a cemetery, which is a Torah-level impurity?
The Gemara resolves: Rather, it refers to a בית הפרס (a plowed-over grave area), which is only rabbinic impurity.
The baraita permits impurity to marry a woman and to learn Torah; Rabbi Yehuda limits this to when no teacher is available.
Rabbi Yosi permits impurity even when a teacher is available, because of the reason that follows (the text breaks off).

items.text: Opening: Rabbi Yose's story and the rule on learning Torah
items.text_en: Opening: Rabbi Yose's story and the rule on learning Torah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yose recounts a story about Yosef the Kohen going to his rabbi in Tzidan to learn Torah. Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yose. Abaye clarifies that this applies to Mishnaic statements, not baraitas, and that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose agree on the halacha following Rabbi Yose.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yose recounts a story about Yosef the Kohen going to his teacher in Tzidan to learn Torah.

Rabbi Yochanan rules that the halacha follows Rabbi Yose, and the Gemara questions why this ruling is needed given the general principle that in disputes between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose the halacha follows Rabbi Yose.

Abaye explains that the ruling was necessary because one might have thought the principle applies only to Mishnaic disputes, not to baraitas, so Rabbi Yochanan teaches that it applies to baraitas as well.
The Gemara emends Rav Mesharshiya's statement: these principles are not universally accepted, as Rav did not accept them.

items.text: Gemara's first question: Non-Jewish items and Sabbath rest
items.text_en: Gemara's first question: Non-Jewish items and Sabbath rest
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel says non-Jewish items do not acquire shvita. The Gemara questions: if this is for Rabbanan, it's obvious since hefker items (ownerless) don't acquire shvita; non-Jewish items have owners, so why would they? The answer is that it's according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that non-Jewish items can acquire shvita, but only hefker items, not owned ones.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel stating that objects belonging to a gentile do not acquire residence (שביתה).

The Gemara questions the necessity of Shmuel's statement: if it aligns with the Rabbis, it is obvious, since even ownerless objects do not acquire residence, so owned gentile objects certainly should not.
The Gemara answers that Shmuel's statement is according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, teaching that even he only grants residence to ownerless objects, not to owned gentile objects.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita on borrowed items on Yom Tov
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar's baraita on borrowed items on Yom Tov
items.desc_en: A baraita from Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar states: one who borrows a vessel from a non-Jew on Yom Tov, or lends to a non-Jew on Erev Yom Tov and gets it back on Yom Tov, the vessels and storerooms that rested within the techum have 2000 amot each direction. And a non-Jew who brings fruit from outside the techum may not move them from their place. This challenges the view that non-Jewish items acquire shvita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection by citing a baraita of Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar that describes cases where borrowed or lent vessels and storerooms that rested within the techum have 2000 amot in each direction, and a non-Jew who brings fruit from outside the techum may not move them, implying that non-Jewish items do acquire shvita.
The Gemara posits that if Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that non-Jewish items acquire shvita, then the baraita aligns with his view.
The Gemara objects that if Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds that non-Jewish items do not acquire shvita, then the baraita aligns with neither his view nor the Rabbis' view, creating a difficulty.

items.text: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds non-Jewish items acquire shvita, but Shmuel holds like Rabbanan
items.text_en: Resolution: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds non-Jewish items acquire shvita, but Shmuel holds like Rabbanan
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri indeed holds that non-Jewish items acquire shvita, but Shmuel's statement aligns with Rabbanan. The question was whether Rabbanan's simple position (non-Jewish items don't acquire) needed explicit teaching; the answer is that the teaching was needed to counter a possible decree equating non-Jewish owners with Jewish owners.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri holds non-Jewish items acquire shvita, while Shmuel's statement aligns with Rabbanan, and the teaching was needed to counter a possible decree equating non-Jewish owners with Jewish owners.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin reports that Rabbi Yochanan explicitly rules that non-Jewish items acquire shvita, due to a decree equating non-Jewish owners with Jewish owners.

items.text: Rava's ruling on buying from non-Jews in Machoza
items.text_en: Rava's ruling on buying from non-Jews in Machoza
items.desc_en: Rava permits the residents of Machoza to buy produce from non-Jews who brought it from outside the techum, relying on Rabbi Yochanan's view that non-Jewish items acquire shvita. Ravina questions this based on Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel that non-Jewish items don't acquire shvita. Rava responds that Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan disagree, and the halacha follows Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rava permits the residents of Machoza to buy rams brought from outside the techum by non-Jews.
Ravina objects to Rava's ruling, citing Rav Yehuda quoting Shmuel that non-Jewish items do not acquire shvita.

Rava resolves the objection by stating that Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan disagree, and the halacha follows Rabbi Yochanan, who holds that non-Jewish items acquire shvita, as a גזירה (decree) lest one confuse non-Jewish owners with Jewish owners.

items.text: Rava's revised ruling: sell to Benei Mebarekhta
items.text_en: Rava's revised ruling: sell to Benei Mebarekhta
items.desc_en: Rava retracts his earlier permission, now saying to sell only to Benei Mebarekhta (a specific group), because the entire Mebarekhta area is considered like four amot for them (i.e., within their techum). This limits the sale to those who can carry the produce within their own techum.

sub.desc_en: Rava retracts his earlier permission and rules that the rams should be sold only to the residents of Mebarekhta, because for them the entire Mebarekhta area is considered like four amot (their own domain).

items.text: Rabbi Chiya's teaching on cherem between Sabbath techums
items.text_en: Rabbi Chiya's teaching on cherem between Sabbath techums
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya teaches: a cherem (ban) placed between Sabbath techums requires a specific procedure to define the boundary, ensuring that items within it are considered as resting within the techum.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya teaches that a cherem (ban) placed between Sabbath techums requires a specific procedure to define the boundary.

items.text: Opening statement and Rabbi Yosi's laughter
items.text_en: Opening statement and Rabbi Yosi's laughter
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that an iron partition is needed to separate a stream. Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina laughs at this statement, prompting the Gemara to investigate the reason for his laughter.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that an iron partition is needed to separate a stream, and Rabbi Yosi bar Chanina laughs at this statement.

items.text: First explanation rejected: stringency vs leniency
items.text_en: First explanation rejected: stringency vs leniency
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rabbi Yosi laughed because the mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's stringent view, while he holds the lenient view of the Rabbis. But the Gemara rejects this, asking why one would laugh at a stringent opinion just because he holds a lenient one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yosi laughed at the mishnah's ruling, and rejects the first answer that it was because the mishnah follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri's stringent view while he holds the lenient view of the Rabbis.

items.text: Second explanation: rivers are like everyone's feet
items.text_en: Second explanation: rivers are like everyone's feet
items.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yosi laughed because a baraita states that flowing rivers are considered like everyone's feet, meaning they have no fixed domain. But the Gemara objects that this might only apply to gathered waters, not flowing ones.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Rabbi Yosi laughed because a baraita states that flowing rivers and springs are considered like everyone's feet, meaning they have no fixed domain.
The Gemara objects that the baraita might apply only to gathered waters, not to flowing ones.

items.text: Third explanation: iron vs reeds
items.text_en: Third explanation: iron vs reeds
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests Rabbi Yosi laughed because the mishnah requires an iron partition, but reeds would also work since water flows through them. The objection is that the mishnah might mean 'necessary but no remedy'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Rabbi Yosi laughed because the mishnah requires an iron partition, but reeds would also work since water flows through both.
The Gemara objects that perhaps the mishnah means the iron partition is necessary and there is no remedy, so the comparison to reeds is irrelevant.

items.text: Final explanation: leniency regarding water
items.text_en: Final explanation: leniency regarding water
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yosi laughed because the mishnah's requirement is lenient, as the Sages were lenient regarding water. This is supported by Rabbi Tavla's question about a hanging partition in a ruin, where Rav said such a partition only permits in water, due to the leniency regarding water.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that Rabbi Yosi laughed because the Sages were lenient regarding water, so a minimal partition suffices.
Rabbi Tavla asks Rav whether a hanging partition permits carrying in a ruin.
Rav answers that a hanging partition only permits in water, due to the leniency regarding water.

items.text: Dispute about four amot: Rabbi Meir vs Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Dispute about four amot: Rabbi Meir vs Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding the four-ammah limit for carrying on Shabbat. Rava explains that the difference is eight by eight amot, and a baraita supports this. The Gemara then asks where the four amot are derived from, citing a baraita about the verse 'Sit every man under his own' and the difference between the opinions is whether the four amot are exact or include room for taking objects.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion seems identical to the first tanna (the Rabbis), so what is the dispute?
Rava answers: The difference is that the Rabbis grant him eight by eight cubits (four in every direction), and a baraita supports this as the opinion of Rabbi Meir.
Rava adds: The dispute applies only to walking, but for carrying objects, all agree that four cubits are permitted and more is not.
The Gemara asks: Where are these four cubits written in the Torah?

A baraita derives the four cubits from the verse 'Sit every man under his own' — a person's body is three cubits, plus one cubit to spread hands and feet (Rabbi Meir) or to take an object from under his feet (Rabbi Yehuda).
The Gemara concludes: The practical difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda is that Rabbi Yehuda gives exactly four cubits, while Rabbi Meir allows slightly more for spreading limbs.

items.text: Measurement of the amah: personal or sacred
items.text_en: Measurement of the amah: personal or sacred
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya instructs his son to ask Rav Papa whether the four amot are measured by the person's own amah or the sacred amah. Rav Papa responds that if using the sacred amah, Og would have too much space, but if using the person's own amah, why isn't this listed among 'everything according to the person'? Rav Papa concludes that we always give the person's own amah, and the reason it's not listed is because it's not absolute due to dwarves.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya tells his son to ask Rav Papa whether the four amot are given by the person's own amah or the sacred amah.
Rav Mesharshiya anticipates two objections: if sacred amot, what about Og; if personal amot, why isn't this listed among 'everything according to the person'.
Rav Papa says that if we were so precise, we would not have taught the Mishnah at all.
Rav Papa resolves that we always give the person's own amah, and the reason it's not listed is because dwarves make it not absolute.

items.text: Two courtyards with partial amot and the case of three courtyards
items.text_en: Two courtyards with partial amot and the case of three courtyards
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the mishnah about two people whose amot overlap, and Rabbi Shimon's analogy to three courtyards open to each other and to the public domain. The Rabbis distinguish because in that case there are residents, but here not. The Gemara then questions why the outer courtyards are not considered one, and Rav Yehuda and Rav Sheishet offer different explanations: the middle courtyard gave its eruv to each outer one, or the outer ones gave their eruv to the middle one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the mishnah needs to say 'to what is this comparable' when introducing Rabbi Shimon's analogy.

Rabbi Shimon explains to the Rabbis that the case of overlapping amot is analogous to three courtyards open to each other and to the public domain, questioning why they distinguish between the two cases.
The Rabbis respond that in the three-courtyard case there are residents, but here there are no residents, so the analogy does not apply.
The Gemara questions why the outer courtyards are not considered one, since they both gave their eruv to the middle courtyard.
Rav Yehuda explains that the case is where the middle courtyard gave its eruv separately to each outer courtyard, so they are not unified.
Rav Sheishet offers an alternative explanation, that even if the outer courtyards gave their eruv to the middle one, the case is where they placed it in a way that does not unify them.

items.text: Opening statement: Eruv in two houses
items.text_en: Opening statement: Eruv in two houses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an eruv placed in two houses is invalid. This sets up the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an eruv placed in two houses is invalid.

items.text: Gemara's question: Whose opinion?
items.text_en: Gemara's question: Whose opinion?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion this Mishnah follows, suggesting it aligns with Beit Shammai who invalidate an eruv placed in two vessels. However, it clarifies that even Beit Hillel would agree here because they permit two vessels in one house, not two houses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whose opinion the Mishnah follows, suggesting it aligns with Beit Shammai who invalidate an eruv placed in two vessels.
The Gemara clarifies that even Beit Hillel would agree here because they permit two vessels in one house, not two houses.

items.text: Rav Acha bar Avya's challenge to Rav Yehuda and Rav Sheishet
items.text_en: Rav Acha bar Avya's challenge to Rav Yehuda and Rav Sheishet
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya raises a difficulty against Rav Yehuda's explanation (that the middle courtyard gave its eruv to one outer courtyard, then acted as an agent for the other) and against Rav Sheishet's analogy (five residents in one courtyard where one forgot to join).

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Avya raises a difficulty against Rav Yehuda's explanation that the middle courtyard gave its eruv to one outer courtyard and then acted as an agent for the other.
Rav Acha bar Avya raises a difficulty against Rav Sheishet's analogy of five residents in one courtyard where one forgot to join, which would prohibit them all.

items.text: Rav Ashi's resolution of both challenges
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's resolution of both challenges
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves both difficulties: for Rav Yehuda, the middle courtyard's intent is revealed that it only wants to join with one outer courtyard; for Rav Sheishet, the analogy fails because residents can be lenient but not stringent.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the challenge to Rav Yehuda: the middle courtyard's intent is revealed that it only wants to join with one outer courtyard.
Rav Ashi resolves the challenge to Rav Sheishet: the analogy fails because residents can be lenient but not stringent.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Rav: This is Rabbi Shimon's view
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav: This is Rabbi Shimon's view
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Rav that the Mishnah's ruling follows Rabbi Shimon, but the Sages say one domain may serve two domains, though not two domains serving one domain.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's report to Shmuel
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's report to Shmuel
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda relates that when he stated this before Shmuel, Shmuel responded with a teaching.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says: When I said this before Shmuel, he said to me:

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel's view of the three courtyards
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel's view of the three courtyards
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Yehuda's version of Shmuel's opinion. Rabbi Shimon compares the case to three courtyards open to each other and to the public domain, where the two outer ones may carry from their houses into the middle courtyard and eat there, but the Sages forbid all three.

sub.desc_en: The Stam introduces the baraita: this ruling is in accordance with Rabbi Shimon, but the Sages forbid all three courtyards.

The baraita is cited in support of Rav Yehuda's version of Shmuel's opinion: Rabbi Shimon compares the case to three courtyards open to each other and to the public domain, where the two outer ones may carry from their houses into the middle courtyard and eat there.
The Sages state their opposing view: all three courtyards are prohibited from carrying between them.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a courtyard between two alleys
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a courtyard between two alleys
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel follows his own reasoning, as he stated: a courtyard between two alleys that made an eiruv with both is forbidden with both; if it did not make an eiruv with either, it forbids both; if it was accustomed to one but not the other, the one it is accustomed to is forbidden, the other is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel follows his own reasoning, citing his ruling that a courtyard between two alleyways that made an eiruv with both is forbidden with both.
Shmuel adds that if the courtyard did not make an eiruv with either alleyway, it prohibits carrying in both.
Shmuel rules that if the courtyard was accustomed to one alleyway but not the other, the accustomed one is forbidden and the unaccustomed one is permitted.

items.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna's additions to Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna's additions to Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna adds two clarifications: if the courtyard made an eiruv with the alley it is not accustomed to, the accustomed alley becomes permitted for itself; and if the accustomed alley made an eiruv for itself while the other did not and the courtyard itself did not eiruv, we force the courtyard to join the unaccustomed alley, as this is compelling a measure of Sodom.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna's first addition
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna's first addition
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna adds that if the courtyard made an eiruv with the alley it is not accustomed to, the accustomed alley becomes permitted for itself.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Huna's second addition citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna's second addition citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna adds that if the accustomed alley made an eiruv for itself while the other did not and the courtyard itself did not eiruv, we force the courtyard to join the unaccustomed alley, as this is compelling a measure of Sodom.

items.text: Dispute about one who is particular about his eiruv
items.text_en: Dispute about one who is particular about his eiruv
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: one who is particular about his eiruv — his eiruv is not a valid eiruv; but what is it called? It is called an eiruv. Rabbi Chanina says: his eiruv is valid, but he is called one of the people of Vardina (a place known for stinginess).

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that one who is particular about his eiruv — his eiruv is not valid, though it is still called an eiruv.
Rabbi Chanina counters that his eiruv is valid, but he is called one of the people of Vardina (a place known for stinginess).

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on a divided eiruv and its necessity
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on a divided eiruv and its necessity
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: one who divides his eiruv (into two vessels) — it is not a valid eiruv. The Gemara asks: in accordance with whom? It is like Beit Shammai, but even Beit Hillel would agree here because they only permit when the bread fills the vessel and there is extra, but not when it is explicitly divided. The Gemara then explains why both rulings (the particular person and the divided eiruv) are necessary.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Shmuel's name that one who divides his eiruv (into two vessels) has not made a valid eiruv.
The Gemara asks: in accordance with whom does Shmuel rule? It suggests it aligns with Beit Shammai.
A baraita is cited: five people who collected their eiruv and placed it in two vessels — Beit Shammai says it is not a valid eiruv, Beit Hillel says it is.
The Gemara explains that even according to Beit Hillel, they only permit when the bread fills the vessel and there is extra, but not when it is explicitly divided.
The Gemara explains why both rulings (the particular person and the divided eiruv) are necessary, showing that each teaches a distinct case.

items.text: Rabbi Abba's challenge and resolution regarding Shmuel's consistency
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba's challenge and resolution regarding Shmuel's consistency
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba challenges Rav Yehuda: does Shmuel really say that a divided eiruv is invalid? But Shmuel also said that a house where the eiruv is placed does not need to give bread, because placing it in a basket is like placing it there. Rav Yehuda answers: there, even though there is no bread, the reason is that all the residents dwell there (so the eiruv is not divided).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba challenges Rav Yehuda: does Shmuel really say that a divided eiruv is invalid, when he also said that a house where the eiruv is placed does not need to give bread, because placing it in a basket is like placing it there?
Rav Yehuda answers: there, even though there is no bread, the reason is that all the residents dwell there (so the eiruv is not divided).

items.text: Shmuel's rationale: eiruv is due to acquisition
items.text_en: Shmuel's rationale: eiruv is due to acquisition
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that eiruv is due to acquisition (kinyan). The Gemara asks: if so, why not acquire with a coin? Because coins are not commonly available on Friday afternoons. But if one did eiruv with a coin, let it be effective? The Gemara answers: a decree lest people say the coin is primary, and sometimes when no coin is available they will not eiruv with bread, causing the eiruv institution to be undermined.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that the eiruv (Shabbat boundary merger) is effective due to the principle of acquisition (קִנְיָן).
The Gemara asks: if eiruv is based on acquisition, why do we not acquire with a coin (מָעָה)? It answers: because coins are not commonly available on Friday afternoons.
The Gemara asks further: but if one did use a coin for eiruv, let it be effective as an acquisition?

The Gemara answers: it is a decree (גְּזֵירָה) lest people say the coin is the primary means, and sometimes when no coin is available they will not eiruv with bread, causing the institution of eiruv to be undermined.

items.text: Rabba's alternative rationale: eiruv is due to residence
items.text_en: Rabba's alternative rationale: eiruv is due to residence
items.desc_en: Rabba says: eiruv is due to residence (dirah). The Gemara asks: what is the practical difference between them? The difference is a vessel (that is worth less than a perutah) — according to Shmuel, a vessel can be acquired, but according to Rabba, residence is not established by a vessel.

items.text: Abaye's challenge to Rabbah and Shmuel regarding the mishnah of five people collecting an eiruv
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to Rabbah and Shmuel regarding the mishnah of five people collecting an eiruv
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah and Shmuel with a baraita stating that when five people collect an eiruv, only one carries it for all, implying that only that person acquires residence. Rabbah responds that the one carrying acts as their agent.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of the mishnah's final clause
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of the mishnah's final clause
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah's concluding word 'וְקָטָן' (and a minor) as the trigger for the discussion.

sub.text: Abaye's challenge to Rabbah and Shmuel
sub.text_en: Abaye's challenge to Rabbah and Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah and Shmuel by citing a baraita that when five people collect an eiruv, only one carries it for all, implying that only that person acquires residence, contradicting their view.
Rabbah responds that the one carrying the eiruv acts as the agent (שליחות) of all the others, so they all acquire residence through him.

items.text: Rabbah's ruling in the name of Rav
items.text_en: Rabbah's ruling in the name of Rav
items.desc_en: Rabbah states a halakhic ruling in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav: the law follows Rabbi Shimon.

sub.text: Rabbah in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbah in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbah transmits a tradition in the name of Rav Chama bar Gurya in the name of Rav, ruling that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon.

items.text: Mishnah: One who designates a tree or fence for his shvita
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who designates a tree or fence for his shvita
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents cases of one who designates a tree or fence for his shvita, the measurements for one who says 'my shvita is at its root,' and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about who may use the method of eiruv by foot.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the case of one who is on the road at nightfall and designates a tree or fence for his shvita, ruling that his statement is invalid.
The mishnah presents the case of one who says 'my shvita is at its root,' granting him 2000 amot from his place to the root and 2000 from the root to his home, totaling 4000 amot.
The mishnah rules that if one does not recognize a landmark or is not expert in halacha and says 'my shvita is in my place,' his place grants him 2000 amot in every direction.
The mishnah records the dispute between Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonos, who says the 2000 amot are circular, and the Sages, who say they are square like a square tablet to gain the corners.

The mishnah concludes with the principle that a poor person may use the method of eiruv by foot, and the dispute between Rabbi Meir (only the poor) and Rabbi Yehuda (both poor and rich, as the bread method is merely a leniency for the rich).

items.text: Gemara's question and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Gemara's question and the dispute between Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'he said nothing' means. Rav says it means he cannot go even to under the tree, while Shmuel says he cannot go to his house but can go to under the tree.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what the Mishnah means by 'he said nothing'.
Rav says 'he said nothing' means he cannot go even to under the tree.
Shmuel says 'he said nothing' means he cannot go to his house, but he can go to under the tree.

items.text: Discussion of making under the tree a 'chamar gamal' and measuring from the north or south
items.text_en: Discussion of making under the tree a 'chamar gamal' and measuring from the north or south
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether under the tree becomes a 'chamar gamal' (a donkey-driver and camel-driver, i.e., a place with no techum), and the rule for measuring if one comes from the north or south.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether under the tree becomes a 'חמר גמל' (donkey-driver and camel-driver, i.e., a place with no techum), where one cannot move in any direction.
The Gemara answers that if one comes to measure from the north, they measure from the south, and vice versa, indicating that the tree's area is treated as a 'חמר גמל' (a place with no techum).

items.text: Rabbah's two explanations for Rav's position
items.text_en: Rabbah's two explanations for Rav's position
items.desc_en: Rabbah offers two possible reasons for Rav's ruling: either because the location is not defined, or because of the principle that anything not possible sequentially is also not possible simultaneously.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains Rav's ruling: because the location is not defined (לא מסיים אתריה).
Rabbah alternatively explains Rav's ruling: because anything not possible sequentially (זה אחר זה) is also not possible simultaneously (בבת אחת).

items.text: Distinction between the two explanations
items.text_en: Distinction between the two explanations
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations, and answers that it lies in a case where one says 'acquire for me four cubits out of eight'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what practical difference exists between the two explanations of Rav's reasoning.
According to the first explanation (because his place is not demarcated), the case where one says 'acquire for me four cubits out of eight' is invalid because the place is not demarcated.
According to the second explanation (anything not possible sequentially is not possible simultaneously), the case is equivalent to four cubits because the person only said 'four cubits'.

items.text: Abaye's objection from ma'aser
items.text_en: Abaye's objection from ma'aser
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rabbah's principle by citing the case of one who adds to ma'aser, where the produce is fixed but the tithes are invalid, implying the principle does not hold.
