sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbah's principle: anything that cannot be done sequentially cannot be done simultaneously.
Abaye raises an objection from the case of one who adds to ma'aser, where the produce is fixed but the tithes are ruined, implying the principle does not hold.
The Gemara questions why the produce is fixed, given Rabbah's principle that what cannot be done sequentially cannot be done simultaneously.

items.text: Distinction for ma'aser
items.text_en: Distinction for ma'aser
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that ma'aser is different because it can be divided into halves, unlike ma'aser behema which cannot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the case of מעשר (tithe) is different because it can take effect on halves, as if one says 'let half of each grain be consecrated' it is consecrated.
The Gemara contrasts that מעשר בהמה (animal tithe) cannot take effect on halves, setting up the next objection.

items.text: Rabbah's case of ma'aser behema and distinction by error
items.text_en: Rabbah's case of ma'aser behema and distinction by error
items.desc_en: Rabbah cites a case where two animals emerge as tenth and are called tenth, and the Gemara distinguishes because ma'aser behema can apply sequentially in cases of error, as per a mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah presents a case where two animals emerge as the tenth and are called tenth, resulting in the tenth and eleventh being intermingled.
The Gemara distinguishes ma'aser behema because it can apply sequentially in cases of error.
The Gemara cites a mishnah where calling the ninth tenth, the tenth ninth, and the eleventh tenth renders all three consecrated, supporting the sequential application in error.

items.text: Counterexample from todah and resolution
items.text_en: Counterexample from todah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the case of a todah slaughtered for eighty loaves, where Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree, and Rabbi Zeira resolves that all agree when specifying 'forty out of eighty' they are sanctified, but dispute in an unspecified case.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a counterexample from the case of a todah (thanksgiving offering) slaughtered for eighty loaves, where Chizkiyah and Rabbi Yochanan disagree about whether forty loaves are sanctified out of eighty.
Rabbi Zeira resolves that all agree when specifying 'forty out of eighty' they are sanctified, and when saying 'forty shall not be sanctified unless eighty are sanctified' they are not sanctified.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's explanation of the dispute
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's explanation of the dispute
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira explains that the dispute is only in an unspecified case, where one master holds the intent is for backup (אחריות) and the other holds they were brought conditionally.

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the dispute's basis
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the dispute between Rav and Shmuel hinges on whether one intends to designate the entire tree (Rav) or just the area under it (Shmuel) as his residence.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rav holds one intends to designate the entire tree as his residence, while Shmuel holds one intends only the area under the tree.

items.text: Abaye's qualification
items.text_en: Abaye's qualification
items.desc_en: Abaye limits Rav's ruling to a tree whose shade covers exactly twelve amos; otherwise, part of one's house is recognizable, making the designation valid.

sub.desc_en: Abaye limits the dispute to a tree with twelve cubits beneath it; otherwise, part of one's residence is recognizable.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection and alternative
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's objection and alternative
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects to Abaye's assumption that the tree's branches are evenly distributed, and instead proposes a different measurement: the tree must have exactly eight amos of shade underneath for Rav's ruling to apply.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects to Abaye's assumption that the tree's branches are evenly distributed, suggesting the four amos might be on one side and four on the other.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua proposes an alternative measurement: Rav's ruling applies only to a tree with eight amos of shade underneath, not twelve.

items.text: Introduction of supporting baraitot
items.text_en: Introduction of supporting baraitot
items.desc_en: The Gemara announces that there are baraitot supporting both Rav and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara announces that there are baraitot supporting both Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that rules: if one designates a tree or fence as his Shabbos residence, it is invalid; but if he designates a specific place, he may walk there and then have 2000 amos. This is limited to a defined area like a mound or valley of specific dimensions. If two people, one familiar and one not, the unfamiliar one may transfer his residence to the familiar one, who designates a place. This only works if the familiar one has already marked four amos.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that designating a tree or fence as a Shabbos residence is invalid, but designating a specific place allows walking there and then 2000 amos beyond.
The baraita specifies that this leniency applies only to a defined area, such as a mound or valley of specific dimensions.
The baraita adds that an undefined place grants only four amos.
The baraita rules that an unfamiliar person may transfer his residence to a familiar one, who then designates a place.
The baraita concludes that this works only if the familiar one has already marked four amos; otherwise he may not move.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Shmuel's defense
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Shmuel's defense
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the baraita refutes Shmuel, but Shmuel explains it deals with a case where the distance from his feet to the tree's base is 2004 amos, so designating the tree would place him outside the techum. Only if he marks four amos can he go.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges whether the baraita refutes Shmuel's position.
Shmuel explains the baraita deals with a case where the distance from his feet to the tree's base is 2004 amos, so designating the tree would place him outside the techum.
Shmuel concludes that only if he marks four amos can he go; otherwise he cannot.

items.text: Baraita supporting Shmuel
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Shmuel
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Shmuel: if one errs and has eiruvin placed in two directions, or tells two slaves to do so and they do opposite directions, he may walk north as far as his southern eiruv allows and vice versa; if they restrict his techum, he may not move.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supporting Shmuel rules that if one erred and had two eiruvin placed in opposite directions, he may walk north as far as the southern eiruv allows and vice versa, but if the boundaries overlap, he may not move.
The baraita concludes that if the two eiruvin restrict his techum (תחום), he may not move from his place.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and Rav's defense
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and Rav's defense
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests the baraita refutes Rav, but answers that Rav is a tanna and can disagree with the baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the baraita supporting Shmuel constitutes a refutation of Rav.
The Gemara answers that Rav is a Tanna and may dispute the baraita.

items.text: Final ruling: designating the tree's base
items.text_en: Final ruling: designating the tree's base
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if one says 'my residence is at the base of the tree,' he may walk 2000 amos from his feet to the base, and then another 2000 from the base to his home, totaling 4000 amos from nightfall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that if one says 'my residence is at its base,' he may walk from his feet to the base (2000 cubits) and from the base to his home (2000 cubits), totaling 4000 cubits from nightfall.

items.text: Rava's explanation of 'darkness fell for him'
items.text_en: Rava's explanation of 'darkness fell for him'
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's case of 'darkness fell for him' refers to one who can reach the tree's base only by running, but not by walking. Abaye objects that the Mishnah says 'darkness fell for him' implying he cannot reach his home, but Rava clarifies that he can still reach the tree's base. An alternative version of Rava's statement is also presented.

sub.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's case of 'darkness fell for him' refers to one who can reach the tree's base by running but not by walking, and Abaye objects that the Mishnah says 'darkness fell for him' implying he cannot reach his home, but Rava clarifies that he can still reach the tree's base.
An alternative version of Rava's statement is presented: darkness fell for him when walking slowly, but if he runs he can still reach the tree's base.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's journey and the rule of Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's journey and the rule of Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef are traveling, and Rabbah proposes that their shevita be under a certain palm tree. Rav Yosef does not know the tree, so Rabbah relies on the teaching of Rabbi Yosei that one who does not know the place can transfer his shevita to one who does. The Gemara notes that the ruling was not actually taught according to Rabbi Yosei, but was accepted because his reasoning is compelling.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef are traveling, and Rabbah proposes that their shevita (Shabbat residence) be under a specific palm tree.
Rabbah asks Rav Yosef if he knows the tree, and Rav Yosef responds that he does not.

sub.text: Rabbah's reliance on Rabbi Yosei's teaching
sub.text_en: Rabbah's reliance on Rabbi Yosei's teaching
sub.desc_en: Rabbah tells Rav Yosef to rely on him, citing the baraita where Rabbi Yosei rules that one who does not know the place can transfer his shevita to one who does.
The Gemara notes that the ruling was not actually taught according to Rabbi Yosei, but was accepted because his reasoning is compelling.

items.text: Continuation of the Mishnah: if one does not know
items.text_en: Continuation of the Mishnah: if one does not know
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the continuation of the Mishnah: 'If he does not know or is not an expert...' This segment is a single line from the Mishnah, serving as a transition to the next discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the continuation of the Mishnah: 'If he does not know or is not an expert...' as a transition to the next discussion.

items.text: Derivation of the 2000-cubit limit from the Torah
items.text_en: Derivation of the 2000-cubit limit from the Torah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the 2000-cubit limit is written. It cites a baraita that derives four cubits from 'Sit, each man under his place' and 2000 cubits from 'Let no man go out from his place'. Rav Chisda explains the derivation through a series of verbal analogies (gezeirah shavah) from the cities of the Levites. The Gemara then questions why we don't learn from the verse 'from the wall of the city and outward 1000 cubits', and answers that we learn 'outside' from 'outside' (chuts) and not from 'chutsah'. It then cites a principle from the school of Rabbi Yishmael about preferring a similar term.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks where the 2000-cubit limit for Shabbat boundaries is written in the Torah.
A baraita is cited, deriving four cubits from 'Sit, each man under his place' and 2000 cubits from 'Let no man go out from his place'.
The Gemara asks how the derivation of 2000 cubits from the verse is established.
Rav Chisda explains the derivation through a chain of verbal analogies (גזירה שווה) from the cities of the Levites, culminating in the verse 'וּמַדּוֹתֶם מִחוּץ לָעִיר... אַלְפַּיִם בָּאַמָּה'.
The Gemara objects: why not derive the 2000-cubit limit from the verse 'from the wall of the city and outward 1000 cubits' (which gives only 1000 cubits)?
The Gemara answers: we derive 'outside' (חוּץ) from 'outside' (חוּץ), and do not derive 'outside' (חוּץ) from 'outside' (חוּצָה) because the terms differ in form.
The Gemara objects: what difference does this distinction make, since the school of Rabbi Yishmael teaches that similar terms can be derived even if they differ in form?
The school of Rabbi Yishmael is cited, teaching that 'return' (שיבה) and 'coming' (ביאה) are treated as equivalent for verbal analogy despite different forms.
The Gemara resolves: the principle of the school of Rabbi Yishmael applies only when there is no closer term; here, since there is a term 'חוּץ' that is more similar, we prefer it over 'חוּצָה'.

items.text: Dispute about 2000 cubits as a circle vs. square
items.text_en: Dispute about 2000 cubits as a circle vs. square
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the 2000 cubits are measured as a circle. The Gemara questions Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus: if he accepts the gezeirah shavah, the verse says 'corners' (pe'ot) implying a square; if not, how does he derive 2000 cubits? The Gemara answers that he does accept the gezeirah shavah, but the verse 'This shall be for them the open spaces of the cities' teaches that corners are given for the Levites' cities, not for Shabbat boundaries. The Rabbis, however, cite Rabbi Chananya who says that Shabbat boundaries are like the Levites' cities.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara poses a dilemma to Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus: if he accepts the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy), the verse says 'corners' (פיאות) implying a square; if not, from where does he derive the 2000 cubits?

The Gemara answers that Rabbi Chanina ben Antigonus does accept the גזירה שוה (verbal analogy), but the verse 'זֶה יִהְיֶה לָהֶם מִגְרְשֵׁי הֶעָרִים' (This shall be for them the open spaces of the cities) teaches that corners are given for the Levites' cities, not for Shabbat boundaries.
The Rabbis cite a baraita where Rabbi Chananya says that Shabbat boundaries are like the Levites' cities, implying a square measurement.

items.text: The law of carrying four cubits in the public domain
items.text_en: The law of carrying four cubits in the public domain
items.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov states that one who carries an object four cubits in the public domain is not liable unless he carries the object and its diagonal. Rava tested Rav Papa on whether a pillar ten handbreadths high and four wide requires the diagonal measurement. They answered that this is the same as the teaching of Rabbi Chananya, who says that Shabbat boundaries are like the Levites' cities.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov states that one who carries an object four cubits in the public domain is not liable unless he carries the object and its diagonal.
Rava tests Rav Papa whether a pillar ten handbreadths high and four wide in the public domain requires the diagonal measurement for liability.
Rav Papa answers that this is the same as the teaching of Rabbi Chananya, who says that Shabbat boundaries are like the Levites' cities.

items.text: The poor person establishes eiruv by foot and the dispute of Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: The poor person establishes eiruv by foot and the dispute of Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that this is what they said: the poor person establishes eiruv by his feet. Rabbi Meir says: we have only the poor person... The Gemara begins to cite Rav Nachman's explanation of the dispute, noting that the dispute is about the phrase 'in my place', as Rabbi Meir holds that the essence of eiruv is with bread.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the poor person establishes an eiruv by foot, and Rabbi Meir says we have only the poor person.
Rav Nachman explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages concerns the phrase 'in my place', as Rabbi Meir holds that the essence of eiruv is with bread.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's dispute
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the positions of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda: Rabbi Meir holds that only a poor person may rely on a verbal declaration, while a wealthy person must use bread; Rabbi Yehuda holds that the essence of עירוב is by foot, so both poor and wealthy may use a verbal declaration, but for 'in place X' even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that only a poor person may rely on it.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir holds only a poor person may rely on a verbal declaration for עירוב (eruv), not a wealthy person.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Yehuda's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda holds the essence of עירוב (eruv) is by foot, so both poor and wealthy may use a verbal declaration, but for 'in place X' even he agrees only a poor person may rely on it.

items.text: Attribution of Mishnaic statements
items.text_en: Attribution of Mishnaic statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies which Tanna authored each clause of the Mishnah: 'וזו היא שאמרו' is attributed to Rabbi Meir and refers to the case of one who does not know the halacha; 'ולא אמרו מערבין בפת אלא להקל' is attributed to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's attribution
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the Mishnah's attribution
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who teaches the Mishnah's statement 'and this is what they said', and answers it is Rabbi Meir.

sub.text: Gemara's answer about the Mishnah's reference
sub.text_en: Gemara's answer about the Mishnah's reference
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's phrase refers to the case of one who does not recognize or is not expert in the law.

sub.text: Gemara's question about the second Mishnah statement
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about the second Mishnah statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who teaches the Mishnah's statement 'they only said one may make an eruv with bread to be lenient', and answers it is Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rav Chisda's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda reinterprets the dispute: the disagreement is specifically about 'במקום פלוני', where Rabbi Meir distinguishes between poor and wealthy, while Rabbi Yehuda equates them. But regarding 'במקומי', all agree that both poor and wealthy may rely on it, since the essence of עירוב is by foot. He then reattributes the Mishnaic clauses: 'וזו היא שאמרו' refers to the case of one who is overtaken by darkness, and 'ולא אמרו מערבין בפת אלא להקל' is the view of all.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda reinterprets the dispute: the disagreement is specifically about 'במקום פלוני', where Rabbi Meir distinguishes between poor and wealthy, while Rabbi Yehuda equates them; but regarding 'במקומי', all agree that both poor and wealthy may rely on it, since the essence of עירוב is by foot.
The Gemara reattributes the Mishnaic clauses: 'וזו היא שאמרו' refers to the case of one who is overtaken by darkness and is taught by Rabbi Meir; 'ולא אמרו מערבין בפת אלא להקל' is the view of all.

items.text: Baraita supporting Rav Nachman
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rav Nachman
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that supports Rav Nachman's view: both poor and wealthy may use bread for עירוב, but a wealthy person may not rely on a verbal declaration outside the techum, according to Rabbi Meir. Rabbi Yehuda says both may use a verbal declaration, and that is the essence of עירוב; the Sages permitted a householder to send his עירוב via a slave or agent only to be lenient.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states Rabbi Meir's position: both poor and wealthy may use bread for עירוב, but a wealthy person may not rely on a verbal declaration outside the techum.

The baraita states Rabbi Yehuda's position: both poor and wealthy may use a verbal declaration, which is the essence of עירוב; the Sages permitted sending an עירוב via a slave or agent only to be lenient.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's ma'aseh
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's ma'aseh
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda brings a precedent: the people of Beit Memel and Beit Guryon in Aroma would distribute dried figs and raisins to the poor during a famine, and the poor of Kfar Shichin and Kfar Chananya would come and stay overnight at the techum, then enter early in the morning.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda cites a story about the people of Beit Memel and Beit Guryon in Aroma who distributed dried figs and raisins to the poor during a famine, and the poor would come and stay overnight at the boundary.

items.text: Proof from the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Proof from the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi proves from the Mishnah that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda: the case of one who went out but was turned back by a friend—he is permitted, but all other residents are forbidden. The Gemara explains that this is because he is considered poor (having left his house), while the others are wealthy, showing that 'במקום פלוני' distinguishes between poor and wealthy, which aligns with Rabbi Yehuda's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that the Mishnah itself supports the halakha following Rabbi Yehuda, citing the case of one who went out but was turned back.
The Gemara asks why the one who went out is permitted while the other residents are forbidden.
Rav Huna answers that the case involves a person who owns two houses with two Shabbat boundaries between them.
The Gemara explains that the one who went out is considered poor (עָנִי) because he left his house.
The Gemara concludes that the other residents are wealthy, proving that for 'במקום פלוני' (a specific place) only a poor person may rely on it, not a wealthy one, thus confirming Rabbi Yehuda's view.

items.text: Rav's ruling in favor of Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav's ruling in favor of Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi taught before Rav that both poor and wealthy may use bread, and Rav instructed him to conclude that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi's teaching before Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi's teaching before Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi taught Chiyya bar Rav before Rav that both poor and wealthy may make an eruv, and Rav instructed him to also conclude that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Introduction of Rabba bar Rav Chanan's practice
items.text_en: Introduction of Rabba bar Rav Chanan's practice
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabba bar Rav Chanan regularly traveled from Artivna to Pumbedita, setting up the next discussion.

sub.text: Story about Rabbah bar Rav Chanan
sub.text_en: Story about Rabbah bar Rav Chanan
sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbah bar Rav Chanan regularly traveled from Artivna to Pumbedita.

items.text: Abaye's challenge to Rav Nachman's ruling
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to Rav Nachman's ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye questions Rav Nachman's ruling that one who says 'my shvita be-tzinta' is valid, citing the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda and Rav Chisda's statement. Rav Nachman retracts his ruling.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges Rav Nachman's ruling by citing the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda and Rav Chisda's statement that the dispute is about a specific location.
Abaye objects that Rav Nachman's ruling contradicts a baraita that supports the opposing view.
Rav Nachman retracts his ruling in response to Abaye's objection.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about four cubits for the eruv giver
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about four cubits for the eruv giver
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether one who places an eruv has four cubits like one who rests on Shabbat. Rava brings a proof from a baraita about the leniency of bread eruv, but the Gemara rejects it, explaining that the wealthy prefer the convenience.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks whether one who places an עירוב (eruv) has four cubits of movement, analogous to one who merely rests on Shabbat.
Rava answers by citing a baraita that the rule of עירוב (eruv) with bread is only to leniently allow the rich to avoid going out, implying that the eruv does not grant four cubits.
The gemara rejects Rava's proof, arguing that even if the eruv does not grant four cubits, the rich person still prefers it to avoid the trouble of going out.

items.text: Mishnah: One who set out and was turned back
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who set out and was turned back
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Yehuda says that if one set out to establish an eruv and was turned back by a friend, he alone may walk, while all other residents are forbidden. Rabbi Meir says anyone who could have established an eruv and did not is a 'chamar gamal'.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states that one who set out to walk in a city where an eruv is established and was turned back by a friend is permitted to walk, while all other residents are forbidden, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Meir states that anyone who could have established an eruv but did not is considered a חמר גמל (a donkey driver and camel driver, i.e., restricted to both sides).

items.text: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's distinction
items.text_en: Gemara's explanation of the Mishnah's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the one who set out is permitted while others are not. Rav Huna explains that the case involves a person with two houses two techumim apart; he becomes 'poor' (having no eruv) once he sets out, while the others are 'rich' (having an eruv at home).

sub.desc_en: The gemara asks why the one who set out is permitted while the other residents are forbidden.
Rav Huna explains that the case involves a person with two houses separated by two Shabbat boundaries; the traveler becomes poor (עני) by setting out, while the others remain rich (עשירי).

items.text: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose's addition
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose's addition
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Rabbi Yehuda's view that once one sets out, he acquires the eruv. Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda adds that even if a friend tells him to stay due to heat or cold, he may go early the next day.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Rav Huna's explanation, stating that one with two houses separated by two Shabbat boundaries acquires an eruv once he sets out, according to Rabbi Yehuda.
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda adds that even if a friend finds him and invites him to stay due to heat or cold, he may still go early the next morning.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef about 'lomar' and 'lehachzik'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Yosef about 'lomar' and 'lehachzik'
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef debate whether the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda is about 'lomar' (saying) or 'lehachzik' (setting out). Ulla's statement is then analyzed and aligned with Rav Yosef's view in accordance with Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that all agree that 'lomar' (saying) requires a declaration, and the dispute is only about 'lehachzik' (setting out).
Rav Yosef counters that all agree that 'lehachzik' (setting out) is required, and the dispute is only about 'lomar' (saying).
The gemara asks whose view Ulla's statement aligns with, that one who set out and was turned back is 'returned and established'.
The gemara objects that the terms 'returned' and 'established' seem contradictory.
The gemara resolves that Ulla means 'even though he was turned back, he is established,' and aligns this with Rav Yosef's view according to Rabbi Yose bar Yehuda.

items.text: Story of Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata and Rav Natan bar Oshaya
items.text_en: Story of Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata and Rav Natan bar Oshaya
items.desc_en: A story is told: Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata brought a basket of fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya. When he left and descended a step, Rav Natan told him to stay overnight and go early the next day, illustrating the halakha of being turned back.

sub.text: Story about Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata
sub.text_en: Story about Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata
sub.desc_en: A story is told about Rav Yehuda bar Ishtata bringing a basket of fruit to Rav Natan bar Oshaya, who was turned back and told to stay overnight and go early the next day.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's ruling aligns with Rav Yosef's view according to Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda, or with Rabbah's view according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's ruling follows Rav Yosef according to Rabbi Yosi bar Yehuda or Rabbah according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rabbi Meir's ruling and Rav Sheshet's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Meir's ruling and Rav Sheshet's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Meir's statement in the Mishnah seems redundant, as it was already taught elsewhere. Rav Sheshet explains that Rabbi Meir's ruling applies even when one definitely did not establish an eruv, not only in cases of doubt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Rabbi Meir's ruling in the Mishnah is necessary, since it was already taught in a baraita about a case of doubt.
Rav Sheshet explains that Rabbi Meir's ruling applies even when one definitely did not establish an eruv, not only in cases of doubt.

items.text: Mishnah: One who left the boundary
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who left the boundary
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who left the Shabbat boundary even one amah may not re-enter. Rabbi Eliezer says two amot outside permits return, but three does not.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who left the Shabbat boundary even one cubit may not re-enter, with Rabbi Eliezer distinguishing between two and three cubits.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's first version: one foot inside, one outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's first version: one foot inside, one outside
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that if one foot is inside the boundary and one outside, he may not enter, citing the verse 'if you turn back your foot' (singular). A baraita contradicts this, and the Gemara resolves it by attributing the baraita to Acheirim, who follow the majority of the body.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina rules that if one foot is inside the boundary and one outside, he may not enter, citing the verse 'if you turn back your foot' (singular).
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that permits entry when one foot is inside and one outside.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the baraita to Acheirim, who follow the majority of the body.

items.text: Rabbi Chanina's second version: one foot inside, one outside
items.text_en: Rabbi Chanina's second version: one foot inside, one outside
items.desc_en: An alternative version has Rabbi Chanina ruling that one may enter, reading the verse as 'your feet' (plural). A baraita contradicts this, and the Gemara explains that Rabbi Chanina follows Acheirim's view of following the majority.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rabbi Chanina's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version has Rabbi Chanina ruling that one may enter, reading the verse as 'your feet' (plural).
The Gemara objects that a baraita contradicts this, ruling that one may not enter.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Chanina follows Acheirim's view that one follows the location of the majority of the body.

items.text: Reconciling contradictory baraitot of Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Reconciling contradictory baraitot of Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves contradictions between baraitot about Rabbi Eliezer's ruling: one baraita says two amot outside permit return, another says one amah permits return, and a third says even one amah does not. The first two are reconciled by whether he took one step and stood on two, or took two steps and stood on three. The third is explained as referring to a surveyor, who is given 2000 amot even if his measurement ends in a cave.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states Rabbi Eliezer's ruling: one who went two amot outside the Shabbat boundary may re-enter, but three amot prohibits re-entry.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita reports Rabbi Eliezer saying one amah permits re-entry, but two amot forbid it.

The Gemara resolves: the first baraita refers to one who took one step and stood on two amot (so two amot outside is like one step), the second to one who took two steps and stood on three amot (so two amot outside is like two steps).
The Gemara raises another contradiction: a third baraita says Rabbi Eliezer rules that even one amah outside forbids re-entry.
The Gemara explains: that baraita refers to a surveyor (מודד), who is given 2000 amot even if his measurement ends in a cave, so the strict rule applies to him.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: One who became dark outside the boundary
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: One who became dark outside the boundary
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who became dark (i.e., Shabbat began) outside the boundary may not enter even one amah. Rabbi Shimon permits up to fifteen amot because surveyors do not measure precisely. The Gemara clarifies that this is due to measurement errors.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one who became dark outside the boundary may not enter even one amah, while Rabbi Shimon permits up to fifteen amot because surveyors do not measure precisely.
A baraita clarifies that the reason for Rabbi Shimon's leniency is due to measurement errors (טוֹעֵי הַמִּדָּה).

items.text: Conclusion of chapter and beginning of next Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion of chapter and beginning of next Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter 'Mi shehotzi'uhu' and begins the next Mishnah on how cities are extended (ibur) for Shabbat boundaries.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter 'Mi shehotzi'uhu' and begins the next Mishnah on how cities are extended (עיבור) for Shabbat boundaries.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Measuring cities with bridges and domed structures
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Measuring cities with bridges and domed structures
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that bridges and domed structures that have dwelling quarters are included in the measurement of the city, and the city is squared off like a square tablet to gain the corners.

items.text: Gemara's first dispute: 'Me'abrin' vs. 'Me'abbirin'
items.text_en: Gemara's first dispute: 'Me'abrin' vs. 'Me'abbirin'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute the correct reading of the Mishnah's term for squaring the city: one says 'me'abrin' (to square) and the other says 'me'abbirin' (to limb). The explanation connects 'me'abbirin' to limbs (eiver eiver) and 'me'abrin' to a pregnant woman (ishah ubarah).

items.text: Dispute about the Cave of Machpelah and the name 'Kiryat Arba'
items.text_en: Dispute about the Cave of Machpelah and the name 'Kiryat Arba'
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel argue about the structure of the Cave of Machpelah: one says it is two rooms one inside the other, the other says it is a house with an attic. The Gemara explains the name 'Machpelah' and then Rabbi Yitzchak explains 'Kiryat Arba' as the city of the four couples buried there.

items.text: Disputes about Amraphel and the new king of Egypt
items.text_en: Disputes about Amraphel and the new king of Egypt
items.desc_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute whether Amraphel is Nimrod and why he is called by each name, and then dispute whether the new king over Egypt was literally new or just renewed his decrees. The Gemara provides scriptural support for each position.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's studies with Rabbi Oshaya and the resolution of contradictions
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's studies with Rabbi Oshaya and the resolution of contradictions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says he studied eighteen days with Rabbi Oshaya and learned only one thing about squaring cities. The Gemara objects that he also said he learned the heart and wisdom of each of Rabbi Oshaya's twelve students. The Gemara resolves that he learned their wisdom but not the full Gemara, or he learned from them but not from Rabbi Oshaya himself, or he meant only one thing in our Mishnah.

items.text: Decline of generations: from the Ulam to the eye of a fine needle
items.text_en: Decline of generations: from the Ulam to the eye of a fine needle
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan describes how students sat crowded by Rabbi Oshaya and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua, then compares the hearts of earlier generations to the entrance of the Ulam, later generations to the Heikhal, and his own to a needle's eye. Abaye, Rava, and Rav Ashi add further metaphors for their own diminished capacities.

items.text: Why Judeans retained Torah and Galileans did not
items.text_en: Why Judeans retained Torah and Galileans did not
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav says Judeans who were precise with their language retained Torah, while Galileans who were not did not. The Gemara refines this: it was because Judeans were precise in language and used mnemonics, or because they learned from one master, or because they revealed the tractate (gillu masekhta). The section ends with a comparison of David and Saul regarding revealing the tractate.

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from the verse
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's derivation from the verse
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse that God forgave Korach's sin, interpreting 'with Me' as 'in My division'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a verse as the basis for Rabbi Yochanan's statement.
Rabbi Yochanan derives from the verse 'מחר אתה ובניך עמי' (tomorrow you and your sons with Me) that God forgave Korach's sin, interpreting 'עמי' (with Me) as 'במחיצתי' (in My division).

items.text: Rabbi Abba on the precision of the Judeans
items.text_en: Rabbi Abba on the precision of the Judeans
items.desc_en: Rabbi Abba notes that the Judeans, who are precise in language, would know whether the correct reading is 'me'abrin' or 'me'abrin', and 'akkuzo' or 'akkuzo'. He inquired and found that both versions exist.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Abba states that if one asks the Judeans, who are precise in language, they would know whether the correct reading is 'מאברים' or 'מעברים', and 'אכוזו' or 'עכוזו'.
The Gemara reports that when asked, the Judeans said that both versions exist: some teach 'מאברים' and some 'מעברים', some 'אכוזו' and some 'עכוזו'.

items.text: Examples of precise and imprecise language
items.text_en: Examples of precise and imprecise language
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples: a Judean described his cloak as 'like beet leaves on the ground', while a Galilean's ambiguous question led to confusion about whether he meant a donkey for riding or wine, wool or a lamb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for an example of precise language among Judeans, and provides a story where a Judean described his cloak as 'like beet leaves on the ground'.
The Gemara provides an example of imprecise language among Galileans, where a Galilean's ambiguous question led to confusion about whether he meant a donkey for riding or wine, wool or a lamb.

items.text: Anecdotes of women speaking in refined language
items.text_en: Anecdotes of women speaking in refined language
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts stories: a woman who intended to say 'come, I will feed you milk' but said 'my messenger, a lion will eat you'; a woman who spoke to a judge in cryptic terms about a stolen item; and the maidservant of Rabbi's house who spoke in a refined manner about a pot and birds.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara recounts a woman who intended to say 'come, I will feed you milk' but instead said 'my messenger, a lion will eat you', illustrating a slip in refined speech.
The Gemara tells of another woman who spoke cryptically to a judge about a stolen item, using refined language.
The maidservant of Rabbi's house spoke in refined language, saying 'the pot has ascended with the lid, let the birds fly to their nests'.
When she wanted them to eat, she said 'let one take from its fellow, and the pot will be sealed like a ship going in the sea'.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan and Rabbi Avahu speaking in cryptic language
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan and Rabbi Avahu speaking in cryptic language
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan spoke cryptically about a bull in judgment on a poor mountain, and when asking for lodging. Rabbi Avahu spoke cryptically about coals, gold, and two 'magidei ba'alata'.

sub.text: Narrator introducing Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan
sub.text_en: Narrator introducing Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan speaks cryptically, asking for a bull in judgment on a poor mountain.

sub.text: Narrator describing Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan's lodging request
sub.text_en: Narrator describing Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan's lodging request
sub.desc_en: When asking for lodging, Rabbi Yosei bar Asiyan says cryptically: 'A man of this mouth lives, what good is this?'
Rabbi Avahu speaks cryptically, asking to heat coals, refine gold, and make two 'magidei ba'alata' (night lamps).

items.text: The sages ask about the whereabouts of Rabbi Ilai and Rabbi Avahu
items.text_en: The sages ask about the whereabouts of Rabbi Ilai and Rabbi Avahu
items.desc_en: The sages asked Rabbi Avahu where Rabbi Ilai was hidden, and he responded cryptically. Similarly, they asked Rabbi Ilai where Rabbi Avahu was hidden, and he also responded cryptically.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's encounters with a woman, a girl, and a boy
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's encounters with a woman, a girl, and a boy
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya relates three incidents where he was bested: by a woman who criticized him for not leaving a portion in the pot, by a girl who corrected him about the path, and by a boy who gave him misleading directions about the road to the city.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya declares that no one ever defeated him except a woman, a boy, and a girl.
The Gemara asks about the woman incident, and Rabbi Yehoshua relates how a hostess served him beans for three days, salting them on the third day so he stopped eating.
The woman rebukes Rabbi Yehoshua for claiming he already ate, saying he should have withdrawn from bread instead of from the beans.
The woman further rebukes him for not leaving a portion in the pot, citing the rabbinic rule that one leaves a portion in the bowl but not in the pot.
The Gemara asks about the girl incident, and Rabbi Yehoshua relates how a girl corrected him that the path through the field was made by robbers, not a proper road.

The Gemara asks about the boy incident, and Rabbi Yehoshua relates how a boy at a crossroads told him that one road is 'short and long' and the other 'long and short,' and he took the short one only to find it blocked by gardens.
Rabbi Yehoshua returns, the boy explains that he said 'short and long,' and Rabbi Yehoshua kisses him, praising Israel that all are great sages from great to small.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Berurya
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili and Berurya
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili asked Berurya for directions to Lod, and she rebuked him for speaking excessively with a woman, suggesting he should have asked more concisely. The Gemara then mentions Berurya finding a student studying quietly.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili meets Berurya on the road and asks her for directions to Lod, but she rebukes him for speaking excessively with a woman, suggesting he should have asked more concisely.
The Gemara adds that Berurya once found a student studying quietly (in a low voice).

items.text: Story of Rabbi Eliezer's student who studied in a whisper
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Eliezer's student who studied in a whisper
items.desc_en: A story is told about a student of Rabbi Eliezer who studied in a whisper and forgot his learning after three years. His wife rebukes him with a verse about the Torah being 'arranged and guarded' if studied properly.

items.text: Another student of Rabbi Eliezer sentenced to burning
items.text_en: Another student of Rabbi Eliezer sentenced to burning
items.desc_en: A second story is told about a student of Rabbi Eliezer who was sentenced to burning by Heaven, and the Sages comment that he had served a great man (Rabbi Eliezer).

items.text: Advice from Samuel and Rav on Torah study and life
items.text_en: Advice from Samuel and Rav on Torah study and life
items.desc_en: Samuel instructs Rav Yehuda to study aloud to retain Torah and prolong life, citing a verse. Samuel also advises to eat and drink quickly because life is fleeting. Rav advises Rav Hamnuna to enjoy his wealth now, as there is no pleasure in the afterlife.

items.text: Torah as a remedy for various ailments
items.text_en: Torah as a remedy for various ailments
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one who travels without a companion should engage in Torah, which is a 'graceful companion.' He then lists various bodily ailments (head, throat, stomach, bones, entire body) and prescribes Torah study as a cure, citing verses.

items.text: Torah as a universal remedy unlike human medicine
items.text_en: Torah as a universal remedy unlike human medicine
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Rabbi Chiyya contrasts human medicine, which helps one person but harms another, with the Torah given by God, which is a life-giving remedy for the entire body.

items.text: Expositions on the condition for Torah retention
items.text_en: Expositions on the condition for Torah retention
items.desc_en: Multiple Amoraim (Rav Ami, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbi Yitzchak, Rava) derive from verses that Torah is retained only when it is spoken aloud. Rava resolves a contradiction between two verses: one who merits receives his heart's desire, otherwise only the request of his lips is granted.

items.text: Eternal terms in Scripture
items.text_en: Eternal terms in Scripture
items.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov teaches that the words 'netzach,' 'selah,' and 'va'ed' indicate eternity without end, and provides scriptural proofs for each.

items.text: Conditions for Torah retention: humility and dedication
items.text_en: Conditions for Torah retention: humility and dedication
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer and others expound verses to teach that Torah endures only when one makes oneself like an anklet (visible yet not visible), like a garden bed (trodden upon), like stone (hard), and like a desert (open to all). Rabbi Acha bar Yaakov adds that the tablets were 'charut' (engraved) implying 'cherut' (freedom) from foreign domination.

items.text: Story of Rava bar Rav Yosef and Rav Yosef: the progression from humility to greatness
items.text_en: Story of Rava bar Rav Yosef and Rav Yosef: the progression from humility to greatness
items.desc_en: Rava bar Rav Yosef goes to appease Rav Yosef before Yom Kippur. Rav Yosef, not recognizing him, asks him to explain verses about the journey from 'midbar' (desert) to 'matana' (gift) to 'nachaliel' (inheritance of God) to 'bamot' (high places) to 'gai' (valley). Rava explains that one who makes himself like a desert receives Torah as a gift, then inherits it, rises to greatness, but if haughty, God lowers him; if he repents, God raises him.

items.text: Torah study likened to a beast and a fig tree
items.text_en: Torah study likened to a beast and a fig tree
items.desc_en: Rav Huna teaches that one must make himself like a beast that tears and eats (or rots and eats) for Torah to endure, and God prepares a feast for him. Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan asks why Torah is compared to a fig tree, beginning an explanation.

items.text: Metaphors for Torah: fig, doe, and breast
items.text_en: Metaphors for Torah: fig, doe, and breast
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a mashal comparing Torah to a fig tree that yields fruit each time one touches it. Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani then explains why Torah is likened to a doe (its womb is narrow, yet it is beloved each time) and to a breast (the infant always finds milk).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a mashal comparing Torah to a fig tree that yields fruit each time one touches it.
Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani explains why Torah is likened to a doe: just as a doe's womb is narrow yet it is cherished each time, so too Torah is cherished by its students each hour like the first.

Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani continues, explaining that Torah is called 'graceful roe' because it bestows grace on its students, and is compared to a breast because the infant always finds milk, so too one always finds new meaning in Torah.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer ben Pedat's devotion
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Pedat's devotion
items.desc_en: The verse 'In her love you will stray constantly' is applied to Rabbi Eliezer ben Pedat, who was so absorbed in Torah study that a snake guarded his cloak left in the upper market.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara applies the verse 'In her love you will stray constantly' to the example of Rabbi Eliezer ben Pedat.
A baraita relates that Rabbi Eliezer ben Pedat was so absorbed in Torah study in the lower marketplace that a snake guarded his cloak left in the upper marketplace.

items.text: Interpretation of Judges 5:10
items.text_en: Interpretation of Judges 5:10
items.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rav Anan interprets the verse about riders on white donkeys as referring to Torah scholars who travel to learn, making Torah clear as noon, judging truth, and distinguishing between Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud.

sub.text: Tanna of the school of Rav Anan
sub.text_en: Tanna of the school of Rav Anan
sub.desc_en: The Tanna of the school of Rav Anan interprets the verse about riders on white donkeys as referring to Torah scholars who travel to learn, making Torah clear as noon, judging truth, and distinguishing between Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud.

items.text: The deceitful hunter
items.text_en: The deceitful hunter
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi cites Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya that a deceitful hunter will not live long. Rav Sheshet questions this, and Rav Dimi explains with a parable: a hunter who breaks the wings of each bird caught prevents escape, but if not, the birds learn to avoid him.

sub.text: Rav Sheizvi citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.text_en: Rav Sheizvi citing Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi cites Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya interpreting the verse 'לֹא יַחֲרוֹךְ רְמִיָּה צֵידוֹ' to mean that a deceitful hunter will not live long.
Rav Sheshet questions the interpretation, asking whether the deceitful hunter will indeed 'scorch' (live long).
Rav Dimi explains with a parable: a hunter who breaks the wings of each bird caught prevents escape, but if not, the birds learn to avoid him.

items.text: Torah studied in bundles diminishes
items.text_en: Torah studied in bundles diminishes
items.desc_en: Rav Huna teaches that if one studies Torah in bundles (superficially), it diminishes; if not, it increases. Rabba notes that the rabbis know this but violate it, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says he observed it and it was fulfilled for him.

sub.text: Rav Huna (via Rabba and Rav Sehora)
sub.text_en: Rav Huna (via Rabba and Rav Sehora)
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna interprets a verse to teach that studying Torah in bundles (superficially) diminishes it, while not doing so increases it.
Rabba notes that the rabbis know this principle but violate it.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak testifies that he observed the teaching and it was fulfilled for him.

items.text: The order of Mishnah transmission from Moses
items.text_en: The order of Mishnah transmission from Moses
items.desc_en: A baraita describes how Moses taught the Torah to Aaron, his sons, the elders, and all the people, each group receiving a different number of repetitions. Rabbi Eliezer deduces that a teacher must repeat a lesson four times, and Rabbi Akiva derives from verses that one must teach until the student knows it and it is arranged in their mouth, and even show them the 'faces' of the law. The Gemara explains why not all learned directly from Moses: to honor Aaron, his sons, and the elders.

sub.desc_en: The baraita describes the order of Mishnah transmission: Moses learned from God, then taught Aaron, his sons, the elders, and all the people, each with decreasing repetitions.
The baraita continues: after Moses departed, Aaron, his sons, and the elders each taught their own lesson, so that everyone ended up with four repetitions.
Rabbi Eliezer deduces from the baraita that a teacher must repeat a lesson four times, using a קל וחומר (a fortiori argument) from Aaron learning from Moses who learned from God.
Rabbi Akiva derives from verses that a teacher must teach until the student knows it, it is arranged in their mouth, and even show them the 'faces' of the law.
The Gemara asks why all the people did not learn directly from Moses, and answers that it was to honor Aaron, his sons, and the elders.

items.text: Why not learn from Moses directly? And seating arrangement
items.text_en: Why not learn from Moses directly? And seating arrangement
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Aaron and his sons did not learn directly from Moses, and answers that Moses' teaching was more effective since he learned from the Almighty. It then discusses Rabbi Yehuda's view that Aaron always returned to Moses' right, and relates this to a baraita about three walking on a road.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why Aaron, his sons, and the elders did not all learn directly from Moses instead of through the chain described in the baraita.
The Gemara answers that the chain was established to honor Aaron, his sons, and the elders by having them receive the Torah directly from Moses.
The Gemara asks why Aaron could not then teach his sons, and they the elders, and so on, rather than having Moses teach each group separately.
The Gemara answers that Moses' teaching was more effective because he learned directly from the Almighty, so his transmission was uniquely authoritative.

sub.text: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's view
sub.text_en: Gemara's question about Rabbi Yehuda's view
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita's report that Rabbi Yehuda says Aaron always returned to Moses' right, and asks whether a baraita about three walking on a road (with the greatest on the right) follows Rabbi Yehuda and not the Sages.
The Gemara resolves that even the Sages could agree with the baraita about the road, because Aaron's position at Moses' right was due to the burden of his role, not a general rule.

items.text: Rabbi Perida's four hundred repetitions
items.text_en: Rabbi Perida's four hundred repetitions
items.desc_en: Rabbi Perida had a student who learned after four hundred repetitions, but one day was distracted by a mitzvah matter. Rabbi Perida repeated the lesson another four hundred times. A heavenly voice offered him either four hundred years of life or the World to Come; he chose the latter, and God granted both.

sub.desc_en: Introduces Rabbi Perida's student who learned after four hundred repetitions but failed to learn one day due to a mitzvah matter.
Rabbi Perida asks the student why he failed to learn today, and the student explains his distraction.
The student explains that since he was told about a mitzvah matter, he was distracted, constantly expecting Rabbi Perida to leave.
Rabbi Perida tells the student to focus and repeats the lesson another four hundred times.
A heavenly voice offers Rabbi Perida either four hundred years of life or the World to Come; he chooses the latter, and God grants both.

items.text: Torah is acquired through mnemonic signs
items.text_en: Torah is acquired through mnemonic signs
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda teaches that Torah is acquired only through simanim (mnemonic signs), based on a play on the word 'simah'. Rav Tachlifa from the West reports this to Rabbi Avahu, who cites a different verse about making 'ziyunim' (markers) for Torah. Rabbi Eliezer and Rava offer additional derivations.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda states that Torah is acquired only through mnemonic signs (סִימָנִין), deriving this from a wordplay on the verse 'שִׂימָהּ בְּפִיהֶם' (place it in their mouth), reading it as 'סַיְּמֶנָּהּ' (make it distinct).

Rav Tachlifa from the West reports Rav Chisda's teaching to Rabbi Avahu, who responds that they derive the same principle from a different verse: 'הַצִּיבִי לָךְ צִיּוּנִים' (set up markers), proving that 'צִיּוּן' means a sign from the verse about a bone marker.
Rabbi Eliezer derives the same lesson from the verse 'אֱמוֹר לַחׇכְמָה אֲחוֹתִי אָתְּ' (say to wisdom: you are my sister), interpreting it as making acquaintances (מוֹדָעִים) for Torah.
Rava offers a different interpretation: make festivals (מוֹעֲדִים) for Torah, implying designated times for study.

items.text: Homiletical interpretations of 'It is not in heaven'
items.text_en: Homiletical interpretations of 'It is not in heaven'
items.desc_en: Three amoraim (Avdimi bar Hama bar Dosa, Rava, and Rabbi Yochanan) offer different homiletical readings of the verse 'It is not in heaven, nor beyond the sea,' each explaining that Torah is not found in those who are arrogant or overly expansive in spirit.

sub.desc_en: Avdimi bar Hama bar Dosa interprets the verse 'It is not in heaven, nor beyond the sea' literally: if Torah were in heaven one would need to ascend, and if beyond the sea one would need to cross.
Rava interprets the verse homiletically: Torah is not found in one who raises his mind over it like heaven or expands his mind over it like the sea.
Rabbi Yochanan interprets the verse: Torah is not found in the arrogant (גסי רוח) nor in merchants or traders.

items.text: Baraita on how to extend cities for Shabbat boundaries
items.text_en: Baraita on how to extend cities for Shabbat boundaries
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches the rules for measuring the Shabbat boundary (techum) for cities of various shapes: an elongated city is measured as is, a round city is squared, a square city is not further squared, and a city with protruding houses or an irregular shape is measured as if a string were stretched across the protrusions.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by asking how to extend cities for Shabbat boundaries and gives the rule for an elongated city: it is measured as is.
The baraita continues: a round city is squared, but a square city is not further squared.
The baraita concludes: for a city with protruding houses or an irregular shape, one measures as if a string were stretched across the protrusions.

items.text: Gemara clarifies the baraita on elongated and square cities
items.text_en: Gemara clarifies the baraita on elongated and square cities
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita states the obvious: an elongated city is measured as is, and a square city is not squared. It explains that the baraita is necessary to teach that even if the city is long and narrow, we do not give it width along its length, and if it is square but not aligned with the cardinal directions, we do not re-square it to align with the world's directions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita states the obvious that an elongated city is measured as is.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is necessary to teach that even if the city is long and narrow, we do not give it width along its length.
The Gemara questions why the baraita states the obvious that a square city is not squared.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is necessary to teach that if the city is square but not aligned with the cardinal directions, we do not re-square it to align with the world's directions.

items.text: Gemara clarifies the case of protruding houses
items.text_en: Gemara clarifies the case of protruding houses
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions both one house and two houses protruding like a 'pigum' (notch), since if one house is considered, two houses should certainly be. It answers that the baraita is necessary to teach that even if the two houses protrude from two different sides of the city, we still consider them as if a string is stretched across them.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the baraita mentions both one house and two houses protruding like a 'פיגום' (notch), since if one house is considered, two houses should certainly be.
The Gemara answers that the baraita is necessary to teach that even if the two houses protrude from two different sides of the city, we still consider them as if a string is stretched across them.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a bow-shaped city and a contradiction resolved
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a bow-shaped city and a contradiction resolved
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that for a city shaped like a bow, if the distance between its two ends is less than 4000 amot, we measure the boundary from the imaginary string (the chord); otherwise, we measure from the bow itself. The Gemara raises a contradiction from another ruling of Rav Huna about a breached city wall, and Rabba bar Ulla resolves it by distinguishing between a breach on one side versus two sides.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that for a bow-shaped city, if the distance between its two ends is less than 4000 amot, we measure the boundary from the imaginary string (the chord); otherwise, we measure from the bow itself.
The Gemara raises a contradiction from another ruling of Rav Huna about a breached city wall, implying a different standard.
Rabba bar Ulla resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a breach on one side versus two sides.

items.text: Gemara questions the novelty of Rav Huna's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara questions the novelty of Rav Huna's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Rabba bar Ulla's resolution adds, since Rav Huna had already stated the principle of giving a karpaf (an area outside the city) to each side in a mishnah. This sets up the continuation of the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions what Rabba bar Ulla's resolution adds, since Rav Huna had already stated the principle of giving a karpaf (an area outside the city) to each side in a mishnah.

items.text: Dispute on adding a karpaf to a city
items.text_en: Dispute on adding a karpaf to a city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir allows adding a karpaf to a city, while the Sages limit it to between two cities. The Gemara cites a dispute between Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav: Rav Huna says each city gets its own karpaf, while Chiyya bar Rav says only one karpaf is given for both.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Meir allows adding a karpaf to a city, while the Sages limit it to between two cities.
The Gemara cites a dispute: Rav Huna says each city gets its own karpaf, while Chiyya bar Rav says only one karpaf is given for both.

items.text: Need for both cases
items.text_en: Need for both cases
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why both cases (the Mishnah and the dispute) are necessary: each case has a unique factor that would not apply to the other, so both must be stated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that both cases are necessary, explaining that if only the first case were taught, one might think it applies only there because it had a leniency from the outset, but not in the second case.

The Gemara completes the explanation by noting that if only the second case were taught, one might think it applies only there because their space is cramped, but not in the first case, so both are necessary.

items.text: Distance between the bow and the string
items.text_en: Distance between the bow and the string
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much distance can be between the bow-shaped city and the string (the straight line). Rabbah bar Rav Huna says up to 2000 amot, while Rava his son says even more than 2000 amot. Abaye supports Rava's view because one can return via houses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much distance can be between the bow-shaped city and the string (the straight line).
Rabbah bar Rav Huna says the distance is up to 2000 amot.

sub.text: Rava brei d'Rabbah bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.text_en: Rava brei d'Rabbah bar Rav Huna's answer
sub.desc_en: Rava his son says even more than 2000 amot is permitted.
Abaye supports Rava's view because one can return via houses.

items.text: Structures that are included with the city
items.text_en: Structures that are included with the city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah mentions 'gedudiyot' (high partitions). Rav Yehudah defines them as three walls without a roof. A question arises about two walls with a roof. The Gemara cites a baraita listing structures that are or are not included with the city for measurement, and analyzes the case of a 'nefesh' (mausoleum) that is breached on two sides.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'gedudiyot' (high partitions) are.
Rav Yehudah defines 'gedudiyot' as three walls without a roof.
The Gemara raises a question about two walls with a roof.
The Gemara cites a baraita listing structures that are or are not included with the city for measurement.

The Gemara infers from the baraita that a 'nefesh' (mausoleum) breached on two sides is excluded, and concludes that this implies it has a roof, but the answer rejects that inference, saying it has no roof.

items.text: House in the sea and cave
items.text_en: House in the sea and cave
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa explains that a 'house in the sea' is used for storing ship utensils. The Gemara notes a contradiction about a cave: a baraita says it is included, but the Mishnah says it is not. Abaye resolves that it is included when there is a building at its entrance, and the building itself is needed to complete the measurement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what purpose a 'house in the sea' serves, since it is not a normal dwelling.
Rav Pappa answers that it is a house made for storing ship utensils.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah lists a cave as not being included, but a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya says a cave is included.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by explaining that the cave is included only when there is a building at its entrance.
The Gemara objects that the building itself should already count for the measurement, so why mention the cave?
Abaye clarifies that the building alone is insufficient for the full measurement, and the cave is needed to complete (להשלים) the required area.

items.text: Dwellers of huts and the camp in the desert
items.text_en: Dwellers of huts and the camp in the desert
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that dwellers of huts (succah-like dwellings) measure Shabbat limits from the door of their permanent houses. Rav Chisda challenges this from the camp of Israel in the desert, which was three parasangs square and had a designated area for relieving oneself. Rava distinguishes the desert camp because it was fixed by God's command.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that dwellers of huts (צְרִיפִין) measure their Shabbat limit only from the door of their permanent houses.

Rav Chisda challenges Rav Huna from the camp of Israel in the desert, which was three parasangs square and had a designated area for relieving oneself behind the camp, implying that even temporary dwellers measure from their dwelling.
Rava distinguishes the desert camp because it was fixed by God's command ('עַל פִּי ה׳'), making it like a permanent settlement, unlike ordinary hut dwellers.

items.text: Establishing a settlement and the condition of hut dwellers
items.text_en: Establishing a settlement and the condition of hut dwellers
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana says that if there are three courtyards each with two houses, the place is established as a settlement. Rav Yehudah says hut dwellers and desert travelers have no life. A baraita compares them to those who sleep with animals. Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan dispute the reason: lack of bathhouses or feeling each other during immersion. The difference is a river near the house.

sub.text: Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana citing Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana citing Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Rav Kahana citing Rav Ashi rules that if there are three courtyards each with two houses, the place is established as a settlement.
Rav Yehudah citing Rav states that hut dwellers and desert travelers have no life, and their wives and children are not truly theirs.
A baraita supports Rav Yehudah: Eliezer Ish Biriya compares hut dwellers to those who sleep in graves, and applies the verse 'cursed is one who lies with any animal' to their daughters.
The gemara asks for the reason behind the harsh assessment of hut dwellers.
Ulla answers that it is because they lack bathhouses.
Rabbi Yochanan answers that it is because they feel each other during immersion.
The gemara resolves the dispute: the practical difference between Ulla and Rabbi Yochanan is a river near the house, which provides bathing but does not prevent feeling each other during immersion.

items.text: City without vegetables
items.text_en: City without vegetables
items.desc_en: Rav Huna states that a Torah scholar may not live in a city without vegetables. The Gemara questions whether vegetables are beneficial, citing a baraita that lists three things that increase waste, bend the stature, and take one five-hundredth of eyesight.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a Torah scholar may not reside in a city that lacks vegetables.
The Gemara questions whether vegetables are indeed beneficial, given the baraita that follows.
The Gemara cites a baraita listing three things that increase waste, bend the stature, and take one five-hundredth of eyesight, implying vegetables are harmful.

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about radish
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about radish
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one says radish is a life-giving drug, the other says it is a deadly drug. It resolves by distinguishing between leaves (dangerous) and roots (beneficial), and between summer (leaves harmful) and rainy season (leaves beneficial).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: one baraita states that radish (צְנוֹן) is a life-giving drug (סַם חַיִּים), while another baraita calls it a deadly drug (סַם הַמָּוֶת).
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between the leaves (עָלִין) of the radish, which are dangerous, and the roots (אִמָּהוֹת), which are beneficial.
The Gemara adds a further distinction: in summer (ימוֹת הַחַמָּה) the leaves are harmful, but in the rainy season (ימוֹת הַגְּשָׁמִים) they are beneficial.

items.text: Teaching about cities with slopes
items.text_en: Teaching about cities with slopes
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav that any city with ascents and descents causes its people and animals to age prematurely. The Gemara corrects 'die' to 'age'. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that the people of the valleys of Bei Beirei and Bei Naresh aged early.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in Rav's name that any city with ascents and descents causes its people and animals to die at half their normal lifespan.
The Gemara objects: can it really enter your mind that they die at half their days?
The Gemara corrects the statement: rather, say they age at half their days.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that the people of the valleys of Bei Beirei and Bei Naresh aged early, supporting the corrected teaching.

items.text: Squaring the city for Shabbat limits
items.text_en: Squaring the city for Shabbat limits
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that to square a city for Shabbat limits, one aligns it with the cardinal directions: north to north, south to south, using the wagon (Ursa Major) in the north and Scorpio in the south. Rabbi Yosei offers an alternative: if one cannot do that, square it like a tekufah, using the sun's path. The Gemara cites a verse from Ecclesiastes to support the directions.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the Tanna Kamma's method: to square a city for Shabbat limits, align it with the cardinal directions using the wagon (Ursa Major) in the north and Scorpio in the south.
Rabbi Yosei offers an alternative: if one cannot align with the celestial wagon and scorpion, square the city like a tekufah (seasonal solstice/equinox) using the sun's path.
The Gemara cites Ecclesiastes 1:6 to support the identification of the sun's path with the cardinal directions.

items.text: Rav Mesharshiya's objection to the rules
items.text_en: Rav Mesharshiya's objection to the rules
items.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to the previous rules about the sun's path, citing a baraita that the sun never emerges from the northeastern corner and sets in the northwestern corner, nor from the southeastern corner and sets in the southwestern corner, implying the sun's path is always in the southern half of the sky.

sub.desc_en: Rav Mesharshiya objects to the previous rules about the sun's path, citing a baraita that the sun never emerges from the northeastern corner and sets in the northwestern corner, nor from the southeastern corner and sets in the southwestern corner, implying the sun's path is always in the southern half of the sky.

items.text: Shmuel's rules about the tekufot
items.text_en: Shmuel's rules about the tekufot
items.desc_en: Shmuel states that the tekufah of Nisan falls only at one of four times: beginning of day, beginning of night, midday, or midnight. Similarly, the tekufot of Tammuz, Tishrei, and Tevet fall at specific half-hour intervals. He also gives the interval between tekufot as 91 days, 7.5 hours, and that each tekufah is half an hour later than the previous one.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel opens by stating that the tekufah of Nisan falls only at one of four quarter-day times: beginning of day, beginning of night, midday, or midnight.
Shmuel extends the rule to the tekufot of Tammuz, Tishrei, and Tevet, each falling at specific half-hour intervals.
Shmuel gives the interval between tekufot as 91 days and 7.5 hours, and states that each tekufah is half an hour later than the previous one.

items.text: Shmuel's teaching about tekufah in Jupiter
items.text_en: Shmuel's teaching about tekufah in Jupiter
items.desc_en: Shmuel further teaches that any tekufah of Nisan that falls in Jupiter (Tzedek) breaks the trees, and any tekufah of Tevet that falls in Jupiter dries the seeds. This applies only when the moon is born in or in conjunction with Jupiter.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states that any Nisan tekufah (seasonal equinox) that falls in the planet Jupiter (Tzedek) breaks the trees.
Shmuel adds that any Tevet tekufah that falls in Jupiter dries the seeds.
The gemara qualifies that this effect applies only when the moon is born in or in conjunction with Jupiter.

items.text: The baraita on squaring the city and boundaries
items.text_en: The baraita on squaring the city and boundaries
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that when measuring the Shabbat boundary, one squares the city like a square tablet, then squares the boundaries. To avoid losing the corners, one places a 2000-ama square diagonally at each corner, resulting in the city gaining 400 amot on each side and the boundaries gaining 800 amot on each side.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that one squares the city like a square tablet, then squares the boundaries likewise.
The baraita explains that to avoid losing the corners, one places a 2000-ama square diagonally at each corner.
The baraita concludes that the city gains 400 amot on each side, the boundaries gain 800 amot on each side, and together they gain 1200 amot on each side.

items.text: Abaye's condition for the calculation
items.text_en: Abaye's condition for the calculation
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that this calculation applies only to a city that is 2000 by 2000 amot, as only then do the numbers work out as described.

sub.desc_en: Abaye notes that this calculation is found in a city that is 2000 by 2000 amot.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's statement on the Levite cities and Rava's derivation
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's statement on the Levite cities and Rava's derivation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Yosi states that the techum of Levite cities is 2000 amot, from which 1000 amot are taken for the migrash (pasture), leaving a quarter of the area as migrash and the rest for fields and vineyards. Rava derives this from the verse 'from the wall of the city and outward 1000 amot around,' interpreting that the Torah surrounds the city with 1000 amot, resulting in a quarter of the area being migrash.

sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer bar Rabbi Yosi stating that the techum of Levite cities is 2000 amot, from which 1000 amot are taken for the migrash, leaving a quarter of the area as migrash and the rest for fields and vineyards.
The Gemara asks: From where are these matters derived?

Rava answers by citing the verse 'from the wall of the city and outward 1000 amot around' (Numbers 35:4), interpreting that the Torah surrounds the city with 1000 amot, resulting in a quarter of the area being migrash.

items.text: The Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the quarter calculation
items.text_en: The Gemara's objection and resolution regarding the quarter calculation
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the migrash should be half, not a quarter. Rava explains, citing Bar Adda the surveyor, that for a 2000x2000 city, the techum area is 16 (square units), and the corners are also 16. After subtracting 8 for the techum and 4 for the corners, 12 remain, which is more than a third. The Gemara then adds the city's 4 units, making it a third. The resolution is that the calculation is based on a circle, not a square: since a square exceeds a circle by a quarter, deducting a quarter from the 12 leaves 9, which is a quarter of 36. Thus, the migrash is indeed a quarter of the total area.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the open space (מִגְרָשׁ) should be half of the total area, not a quarter.

sub.text: Rava's answer citing Bar Adda the surveyor
sub.text_en: Rava's answer citing Bar Adda the surveyor
sub.desc_en: Rava explains, citing Bar Adda the surveyor, that for a 2000x2000 city, the techum area is 16 (square units), the corners are also 16, and after subtracting 8 for the techum and 4 for the corners, 12 remain.
The Gemara objects that the remaining 12 units are more than a third of the total, not a quarter.
The Gemara suggests adding the city's 4 units to the total, but then the open space becomes exactly a third.
The Gemara resolves that the calculation is based on a round city, not a square one.
The Gemara calculates that since a square exceeds a circle by a quarter, deducting a quarter from the 12 leaves 9, which is exactly a quarter of 36, confirming the open space is a quarter.

items.text: Abaye's alternative calculation for a 1000x1000 city
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative calculation for a 1000x1000 city
items.desc_en: Abaye notes that the same result can be found with a city of 1000 by 1000 amot, where the techumim are 8 and the corners are 16, leading to the same proportional outcome.

sub.desc_en: Abaye adds that the same calculation applies to a city of 1000 by 1000 amot, where the boundaries are 8 and the corners are 16.

items.text: Calculating the techum for a circular city
items.text_en: Calculating the techum for a circular city
