items.desc_en: The Gemara calculates the area of a circular city's techum, subtracting the corners and the city itself, and determines that the remaining area is a quarter of the total. It explains that the calculation is based on a circle, not a square, and uses the principle that a square exceeds a circle by a quarter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks to subtract four techum areas and four corner areas, totaling eight, from the total area.
The Gemara objects that eight out of twenty-four is a third, not a quarter.
The Gemara explains that the calculation is for a circle, not a square, and since a square exceeds a circle by a quarter, subtracting that quarter leaves six, which is a quarter of twenty-four.

items.text: Ravina and Rav Ashi interpret 'quarter'
items.text_en: Ravina and Rav Ashi interpret 'quarter'
items.desc_en: Ravina and Rav Ashi offer different interpretations of what 'quarter' refers to: Ravina says it is a quarter of the techum, while Rav Ashi says it is a quarter of the corners.

sub.desc_en: Ravina states that the 'quarter' mentioned in the calculation refers to a quarter of the techum (the Sabbath boundary).
Rav Ashi counters that the 'quarter' refers to a quarter of the corners (the diagonal projections of the city).

items.text: Ravina questions Rav Ashi from the verse 'saviv'
items.text_en: Ravina questions Rav Ashi from the verse 'saviv'
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rav Ashi by citing the verse that says 'saviv' (around), implying the entire circumference. Rav Ashi responds that 'saviv' refers to the corners, as in the case of the altar where 'saviv' means the corners, not the literal circumference.

sub.desc_en: Ravina objects to Rav Ashi that the verse says 'סָבִיב' (around), implying the entire circumference, not just the corners.
Rav Ashi answers that 'סָבִיב' here means around the corners, citing a parallel from the burnt offering where 'סָבִיב' also refers to the corners of the altar.

items.text: Rav Chavivi's question about the protrusion of the corners
items.text_en: Rav Chavivi's question about the protrusion of the corners
items.desc_en: Rav Chavivi asks Rav Ashi about the protrusion of the corners (mursha d'karnata) that would add area. Rav Ashi answers that the city is circular, and although we consider it as if it were squared, we do not actually square it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chavivi objects that there are the pointed tips of the corners that are not accounted for.
Rav Ashi answers that the city is circular, and while we consider it as if it were squared for measurement, we do not actually square it, so the tips are not a concern.

items.text: Rav Chanilai's calculation and Rav Ashi's response about the diagonal
items.text_en: Rav Chanilai's calculation and Rav Ashi's response about the diagonal
items.desc_en: Rav Chanilai calculates that 800 cubits minus a quarter should be 600 and two-thirds, not the previously stated amount. Rav Ashi explains that the quarter ratio applies only to a circle within a square, but for the diagonal, more is needed, as per the rule that a square's diagonal is 1.4 times its side.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanilai objects that if a square exceeds a circle by a quarter, then the calculation for eight hundred cubits should yield six hundred sixty-seven and a third, not a quarter.
Rav Ashi answers that the quarter ratio applies only to a circle inscribed within a square, but for the diagonal, more is needed, as a square's diagonal is one and two-fifths times its side.

items.text: Mishnah: Adding a karpaf to a city
items.text_en: Mishnah: Adding a karpaf to a city
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir says a karpaf (an area of 70 cubits and a bit) is added to a city for Shabbat boundaries. The Sages say a karpaf is only between two cities, and if each has 70 cubits and a bit, the karpaf joins them. Similarly, three villages in a triangle with 141⅓ cubits between the outer two are joined by the middle one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a קרפף (an additional area) is given to a city according to Rabbi Meir, but the Sages say it is only given between two cities, and similarly for three villages arranged in a triangle.
Rabbi Meir holds that a karpaf is added to a single city.
The Sages argue that a karpaf is only applied between two cities, joining them if each has 70 cubits and a bit.
The Mishnah adds that three villages in a triangle are joined by the middle one if the outer two are 141⅓ cubits apart.

items.text: Gemara: Source for adding a karpaf
items.text_en: Gemara: Source for adding a karpaf
items.desc_en: Rava derives the source for adding a karpaf from the verse 'from the wall of the city and outward', meaning the Torah says to give an outer area and then measure.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks the scriptural source for the rule of giving a קרפף.
Rava answers that the verse 'מִקִּיר הָעִיר וָחוּצָה' (from the wall of the city and outward) teaches that one must first give an outer area and then measure.

items.text: Dispute between Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav about the karpaf
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav about the karpaf
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the dispute between Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav: Rav Huna says a karpaf is given to each city separately, while Chiyya bar Rav says one karpaf serves both. The Mishnah's wording supports Chiyya bar Rav, but Rav Huna explains that 'karpaf' means the law of karpaf, not a single area. The Gemara concludes that the Mishnah's continuation supports Chiyya bar Rav.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the dispute: Rav Huna says each city receives its own karpaf, while Chiyya bar Rav says one karpaf serves both cities.
The Gemara raises an objection from the Mishnah, which states that the sages said a karpaf is only given between two cities, implying a single karpaf, which contradicts Rav Huna's position.
Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah's term 'karpaf' refers to the law of karpaf (תורת קרפף), not a single physical area, so each city still gets its own karpaf.
The Gemara notes that the Mishnah's continuation, which says 'makes the karpaf for both to be one,' supports Chiyya bar Rav's view that a single karpaf serves both cities.
The Gemara raises a potential objection against Chiyya bar Rav from the same continuation, but then cuts off as Chiyya bar Rav begins to respond.

items.text: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's position on courtyards
items.text_en: Clarification of Rabbi Meir's position on courtyards
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the mishnah's ruling about giving a courtyard to a city is attributed to Rabbi Meir, and why it is necessary to state both this and the earlier ruling about a single courtyard for two houses.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by questioning the attribution of the mishnah's ruling about giving a courtyard to a city, suggesting it is Rabbi Meir's, and then explains why both this and the earlier ruling about a single courtyard for two houses are necessary.

The Gemara answers that both rulings are needed: from the first we might think only one courtyard per two houses, but the second teaches we give two courtyards per two houses; and from the second we might think only when cramped, but the first teaches even when not cramped.

items.text: Challenge to Rav Huna from the mishnah
items.text_en: Challenge to Rav Huna from the mishnah
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that three villages in a triangle can be combined only if there is a middle village, implying that without a middle village they cannot be combined, which contradicts Rav Huna's ruling.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: three triangular villages, if the distance between the outer two is 141⅓ amos, the middle one makes them all one.

items.text: Rav Huna's response via Rabba bar Rav Idi
items.text_en: Rav Huna's response via Rabba bar Rav Idi
items.desc_en: Rav Huna responds that the mishnah's 'triangular' villages are not literally triangular; rather, we consider them as if a middle village were placed between them, and if the distance between the outer villages is only 141⅓ amot, they are combined.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna objects: the baraita only works when there IS a middle village; if not, it fails. This is a refutation of Rav Huna's earlier position.

items.text: Rava's question to Abaye about the distance between outer and middle villages
items.text_en: Rava's question to Abaye about the distance between outer and middle villages
items.desc_en: Rava asks Abaye how far the outer village can be from the middle village, and Abaye answers 2000 amot. Rava objects based on his own earlier opinion that it can be more than 2000 amot, but Abaye distinguishes between cases with houses (where more is allowed) and without houses.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Abaye how far the outer village can be from the middle village, and Abaye answers 2000 amot.
Rava objects that Abaye himself previously ruled like Rava bar Rabba bar Rav Huna, who allows more than 2000 amot.
Abaye distinguishes: there, houses exist between the villages, allowing more distance; here, there are no houses, so only 2000 amot are permitted.

items.text: Rava's question about the distance between outer villages
items.text_en: Rava's question about the distance between outer villages
items.desc_en: Rava asks Abaye about the maximum distance between the two outer villages, and Abaye says it can be up to 4000 amot, based on the principle of filling in the middle. Rava objects citing Rav Huna's ruling about a bow-shaped city, but Abaye distinguishes because there is no possibility of filling in that case.

sub.desc_en: Rava asks Abaye what is the maximum distance between the two outer villages, and Abaye responds that it is irrelevant as long as inserting a middle village would leave only 141⅓ amot between them.
Rava objects: even if the distance is 4000 amot? He cites Rav Huna's ruling about a bow-shaped city, where if the gap between the ends exceeds 4000 amot, the city is measured from the bow itself.
Abaye distinguishes: in the bow-shaped city case there is no possibility of 'filling in' (מלי) the gap with houses, but here there is, so the distance can be up to 4000 amot.

items.text: Rav Safra's challenge and resolution regarding the Tigris
items.text_en: Rav Safra's challenge and resolution regarding the Tigris
items.desc_en: Rav Safra asks Rava about the cities of Akistafon and Ardashir, which are separated by the Tigris river wider than 141⅓ amot, yet they measure boundaries from each other. Rava shows him the river's banks that narrow the gap to 70 amot and a remainder.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra challenges Rava: the cities of Akistafon and Ardashir are separated by the Tigris river wider than 141⅓ amot, yet they measure boundaries from each other — how is this possible?
Rava goes out and shows Rav Safra the river's banks that narrow the gap to 70 amot and a remainder, resolving the challenge.

items.text: Mishnah: Rules for measuring Shabbat boundaries
items.text_en: Mishnah: Rules for measuring Shabbat boundaries
items.desc_en: The mishnah states that measurement must be done with a 50-amah rope, measured opposite the measurer's heart, and that when encountering a valley or fence, the measurer 'swallows' it and continues; similarly for a mountain.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens by stating that Shabbat boundary measurement must be done with a 50-amah rope, no less and no more.
The mishnah adds that the measurer must measure opposite his heart.
The mishnah rules that when encountering a valley or fence, the measurer 'swallows' it and continues the measurement.
The mishnah similarly rules that when encountering a mountain, the measurer 'swallows' it and continues the measurement.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may measure the techum with a rope of fifty cubits, provided one does not go outside the boundary. If one cannot span a valley, Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai in the name of Rabbi Meir says one may 'bore holes' (measure by stepping) in the mountains.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the basic rule that one may measure the techum with a fifty-cubit rope provided one does not go outside the boundary.

sub.text: Mishnah citing Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.text_en: Mishnah citing Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai in the name of Rabbi Meir
sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that if one cannot span a valley, Rabbi Dostai bar Yannai in the name of Rabbi Meir says one may 'bore holes' (measure by stepping) in the mountains.

items.text: Gemara's derivation of the fifty-cubit rope
items.text_en: Gemara's derivation of the fifty-cubit rope
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav derives from the verse about the courtyard (Exodus 27:18) that the measuring rope must be fifty cubits long. The Gemara explains that the verse implies both a minimum and maximum length, as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the scriptural source of the fifty-cubit rope requirement.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav cites the verse about the courtyard (Exodus 27:18) to derive that the measuring rope must be fifty cubits.
The Gemara objects that the verse might be needed to teach a different halacha — to take fifty cubits and surround fifty cubits — rather than the rope length.
The Gemara resolves that the verse's unique phrasing 'חמישים בחמישים' (fifty by fifty) implies two teachings: both the rope length and the measurement method.
A baraita explicitly states that the rope must be neither less nor more than fifty cubits, confirming the derivation.

items.text: The material of the measuring rope
items.text_en: The material of the measuring rope
items.desc_en: Rabbi Asi rules that one may only measure with a rope of 'afsekima'. Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yaakov explain that this refers to a palm branch (nargila) or a single-branched palm tree. An alternative version attributes the explanation to Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Asi rules that one may only measure with a rope of אפסקימא (a specific type of rope).
The Gemara asks: what is אפסקימא?
Rabbi Abba answers: it is נרגילא (a type of palm fiber).
The Gemara asks: what is נרגילא?
Rabbi Yaakov answers: it is a palm tree of a single branch (a young palm).
An alternative version reports: Rabbi Abba said it is נרגילא, and Rabbi Yaakov said it is a palm tree of a single branch.

items.text: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's preference for iron chains
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya's preference for iron chains
items.desc_en: A baraita quotes Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya saying that iron chains are best for measurement, but the Torah requires a rope (as per the verse). The Gemara notes that another verse mentions a 'measuring rod' (kaneh), but that is for measuring gates.

sub.text: Baraita quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.text_en: Baraita quoting Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya
sub.desc_en: A baraita cites Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya stating that iron chains are best for measurement, but the Torah requires a rope (חבל מדה).
The Gemara objects by citing a verse that mentions a measuring rod (קנה המדה), not a rope.
The Gemara resolves that the rod is used specifically for measuring gates, not for general Shabbat boundaries.

items.text: Three types of ropes
items.text_en: Three types of ropes
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches a baraita listing three types of ropes: magag (for the red heifer), netzer (for the sotah), and pishtan (flax, for measurement). The Gemara cites Mishnayot to support each use.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef teaches a baraita: there are three types of ropes — of מגג (flax waste), of נצר (bast), and of פשתן (linen).
The baraita explains: the מגג rope is for the red heifer, the נצר rope is for the sotah (suspected adulteress), and the linen rope is for measurement.

items.text: The rule of 'mablio' (spanning) for valleys and walls
items.text_en: The rule of 'mablio' (spanning) for valleys and walls
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that if one cannot span a valley with a fifty-cubit rope, one goes to a place where one can span, spans, and then returns to the original measurement point. A baraita adds that for a winding valley, one 'bores holes' (measures by stepping) up and down. For a wall, one estimates. The Gemara resolves a contradiction between the Mishnah and the baraita regarding returning to the measurement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'returns to his measurement' that if one cannot span a valley, one goes to a place where one can span, spans, and then returns to the original measurement point.

A baraita is cited that explicitly states the same rule: if one reaches a valley and cannot span it with a fifty-cubit rope, one goes to a place where one can span, spans, and returns to the measurement.
The baraita adds that for a winding valley one 'bores holes' (measures by stepping) up and down, and for a wall one estimates rather than piercing through.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: the Mishnah says 'spans and returns to his measurement' without mentioning the need to go elsewhere, while the baraita says one goes to a place where one can span.
The Gemara resolves: there (in the Mishnah) the terrain is convenient for use, so one can span directly; here (in the baraita) it is not convenient, so one must go to a suitable spot.

items.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel's qualification
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel's qualification
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states that the rule of spanning (mablio) only applies when the plumb line does not descend directly opposite the measurement point.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel states: they only taught (the rule of spanning) when the plumb line does not descend opposite him (i.e., the valley is not sheer).

items.text: Opening statement on measuring with a plumb line
items.text_en: Opening statement on measuring with a plumb line
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that when a plumb line descends straight down opposite a valley, one measures it properly (i.e., the valley is not 'blended' into the measurement).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that when a plumb line descends straight opposite a valley, one measures it properly.

items.text: Depth of a valley and the dispute of Rav Yosef
items.text_en: Depth of a valley and the dispute of Rav Yosef
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that a valley's depth is up to 2000 cubits. Abaye objects with a baraita that says a valley 100 deep and 50 wide is blended, but if not, it is not blended. The Gemara explains that Rav Yosef follows the opinion of Acheirim, who say even 2000 deep and 50 wide is blended. An alternative version says Rav Yosef allows even more than 2000, which would contradict both the first Tanna and Acheirim; the Gemara resolves this by distinguishing cases where the plumb line does or does not descend.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what is the maximum depth of a valley that can be blended into the measurement.
Rav Yosef answers that a valley up to 2000 cubits deep is blended.
Abaye objects with a baraita that only a valley 100 deep and 50 wide is blended, contradicting Rav Yosef's 2000.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Yosef follows the opinion of Acheirim, who allow even a valley 2000 deep and 50 wide to be blended.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Yosef's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version says Rav Yosef allows even more than 2000, which contradicts both the first Tanna and Acheirim.

sub.text: Gemara's resolution of the alternative version
sub.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the alternative version
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing cases where the plumb line (חוט המשקולת) does or does not descend straight down.

items.text: Maximum width when plumb line does not descend
items.text_en: Maximum width when plumb line does not descend
items.desc_en: When the plumb line does not descend straight down, Avimi and Rami bar Yechezkel state that the maximum width for blending is four cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how much of a slope is needed for the plumb line not to descend opposite, and Avimi answers: four cubits.
Rami bar Yechezkel teaches a baraita that also states the measure is four cubits.

sub.text: Supporting baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel
sub.text_en: Supporting baraita of Rami bar Yechezkel
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel's baraita supports Avimi's ruling, also stating four cubits.

items.text: Blending a hill and the dispute between Rava and Rav Huna
items.text_en: Blending a hill and the dispute between Rava and Rav Huna
items.desc_en: When reaching a hill, one blends it and returns to the measurement. Rava says this applies only to a hill that rises 10 cubits within 4 cubits, but if it rises 10 within 5, one measures properly. Rav Huna bar Rav Natan teaches leniently: the leniency applies to a hill rising 10 within 5, but for 10 within 4, one estimates and proceeds.

sub.desc_en: Resolution: When reaching a hill, one blends it and returns to its measure. Rava said: They taught only for a hill that gathers 10 from 4, but for a hill that gathers 10 from 5 — one measures a fine measurement.

items.text: Condition not to exit the boundary
items.text_en: Condition not to exit the boundary
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that one may only blend provided that one does not exit the Sabbath boundary. Rav Kahana explains the reason: a decree lest people say that the measure of the boundary came here.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that one may not go outside the Shabbat boundary, and Rav Kahana explains the reason is a decree lest people say the boundary measurement came here.
The Gemara asks for the reason behind this condition.
Rav Kahana explains that the condition is a decree lest people mistakenly think that the measure of the boundary came to this point.

items.text: Method of קידור (arching) and its limitations
items.text_en: Method of קידור (arching) and its limitations
items.desc_en: The Sages taught how to arch: the lower end opposite the heart, the upper end opposite the feet. Abaye states that we hold that one may only arch with a rope of four cubits. Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh adds that one may not arch for the עגלה ערופה or for cities of refuge, because they are Torah laws.

sub.desc_en: The Sages taught the method of קידור (arching): the lower end of the rope is placed opposite the heart, the upper end opposite the feet.
Abaye states that the accepted tradition is that one may only arch with a rope of four cubits.

sub.text: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman citing Rabbah bar Avuh
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuh adds that one may not arch for the עגלה ערופה (broken-necked heifer) or for cities of refuge, because they are Torah laws.

items.text: Mishnah: Measuring from an expert and trustworthiness
items.text_en: Mishnah: Measuring from an expert and trustworthiness
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one measures only from an expert. If one added to one place and reduced from another, we listen to the place that was added. If one added to one and reduced to one, we listen to the one that was increased. Even a slave or maidservant is believed to say 'up to here is the Sabbath boundary', because the Sages only said the matter to be lenient, not stringent.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that one measures the Sabbath boundary only from an expert, and if one added to one place and reduced from another, we listen to the place that was increased.
The Mishnah adds that even a slave or maidservant is believed to say 'up to here is the Sabbath boundary', because the Sages only said the matter to be lenient, not stringent.

items.text: Clarifying the Mishnah's language on expansion and contraction
items.text_en: Clarifying the Mishnah's language on expansion and contraction
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's phrasing, suggesting that the phrase 'to a place that expanded' implies only expansion, not contraction. It then reinterprets the Mishnah to mean that one listens to the one who expanded, even if another contracted.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's phrase 'to a place that expanded' implies that only expansion is considered, not contraction.
The Gemara reinterprets the Mishnah to mean that one listens to the one who expanded, even if another contracted.

items.text: Abaye's condition on expansion
items.text_en: Abaye's condition on expansion
items.desc_en: Abaye adds a condition: the expansion must not exceed the diagonal measure of the city, ensuring it does not become overly lenient.

sub.desc_en: Abaye adds a condition that the expansion must not exceed the city's diagonal measure.

items.text: Resolving a contradiction about leniency and stringency
items.text_en: Resolving a contradiction about leniency and stringency
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two statements: one says the Sages only ruled leniently, another says they only ruled stringently. Ravina resolves this by explaining that the first refers to leniency regarding Torah law but stringency regarding rabbinic laws, and Sabbath boundaries are rabbinic.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a statement that the Sages only ruled leniently, not stringently.
The Gemara raises a contradiction by citing a baraita that says the Sages only ruled stringently, not leniently.
Ravina resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first statement refers to leniency regarding Torah law but stringency regarding rabbinic laws, and Sabbath boundaries (תחומין) are rabbinic.

items.text: Mishnah: City of an individual becomes of many
items.text_en: Mishnah: City of an individual becomes of many
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a city originally belonging to one individual becomes public, the entire city can be joined for an eruv. Conversely, if a public city becomes private, it cannot be joined unless an outer area is made. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon debate the definition of a 'new city in Judea' with fifty residents versus three courtyards with two houses each.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a city of an individual that becomes public can be fully joined for an eruv.
The Mishnah states the converse rule: a public city that becomes private cannot be fully joined unless an outer area is made.
Rabbi Yehuda defines a 'new city in Judea' as one with fifty residents.
Rabbi Shimon defines a 'new city in Judea' as three courtyards each with two houses.

items.text: Gemara: Examples of a city of an individual becoming public
items.text_en: Gemara: Examples of a city of an individual becoming public
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks for an example of such a city. Rav Yehuda suggests the island of the Exilarch. Rav Nachman questions this, noting that all Jews gather on Shabbat morning. He instead proposes the island of Nattzua.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for an example of a city of an individual that becomes a city of the public.
Rav Yehuda proposes the island of the Exilarch as an example.
Rav Nachman objects, arguing that all Jews gather together on Shabbat morning, so the Exilarch's island is not unique.
Rav Nachman instead proposes the island of Nattzua as a proper example.

items.text: Baraita: How to join a city with a public domain
items.text_en: Baraita: How to join a city with a public domain
items.desc_en: A baraita explains that if a city of an individual becomes public and a public domain passes through it, one can join it by placing a side post or beam on each side, allowing carrying in the middle. It cannot be joined in halves, but only as a whole or each alleyway separately.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by presenting the case of a private city that became public with a public domain passing through it, and prescribes placing a side post or beam on each side to permit carrying in the middle.
The baraita concludes by ruling that the city cannot be joined in halves, but only as a whole or each alleyway separately.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an alleyway has only one opening, it can be merged as a whole; if it has multiple openings, it must be divided into separate alleyways.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if an alleyway has only one opening, it can be merged as a whole.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that a public domain can be merged. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua identifies it as Rabbi Yehuda, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits using a public domain with a side post or beam, while the Sages forbid it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks which Tanna holds that a public domain can be merged.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua identifies the Tanna as Rabbi Yehuda.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yehuda permits using a public domain with a side post or beam, while the Sages forbid it.

items.text: Dividing the alleyway lengthwise vs. widthwise
items.text_en: Dividing the alleyway lengthwise vs. widthwise
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa states that the Mishnah's prohibition on dividing the alleyway applies only lengthwise, but widthwise it is permitted. The Gemara considers whether this aligns with Rabbi Akiva's view, but suggests that even Rabbi Akiva would permit here because each side has its own opening.

sub.desc_en: Mar states that the alleyway may not be divided in half for the purpose of an עירוב (eruv).
Rav Pappa clarifies that the prohibition applies only when dividing lengthwise, but widthwise it is permitted.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Pappa's ruling aligns with Rabbi Akiva's view or not.
The Gemara objects that if Rav Pappa followed Rabbi Akiva, the principle of 'a permitted foot in its place forbids even elsewhere' would prohibit widthwise division.
The Gemara resolves that even Rabbi Akiva would permit widthwise division here because each side has its own opening, unlike the case of two courtyards one inside the other.

items.text: Alternative version: even widthwise is prohibited
items.text_en: Alternative version: even widthwise is prohibited
items.desc_en: An alternative version of Rav Pappa's statement says that even widthwise division is prohibited. The Gemara explains that this aligns with Rabbi Akiva, but even the Rabbis would agree because the public domain cannot be removed from the alleyway.

sub.text: Alternative version of Rav Pappa's statement
sub.text_en: Alternative version of Rav Pappa's statement
sub.desc_en: An alternative version reports Rav Pappa's statement that even widthwise division of the alleyway is prohibited, not just lengthwise.
The Gemara asks whose opinion this alternative version follows, suggesting it aligns with Rabbi Akiva.
The Gemara answers that even the Rabbis would agree here, because unlike the case of two courtyards one within the other, here the public domain cannot be removed from the alleyway.

items.text: Distinction between dividing into halves and separate alleyways
items.text_en: Distinction between dividing into halves and separate alleyways
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why dividing into halves is prohibited but dividing into separate alleyways is permitted, since both involve mutual restriction. The answer is that the case involves a small partition (דקה), and Rav Idi bar Avin cites Rav Chisda that a resident who makes a small partition at his entrance does not restrict the alleyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why dividing the alleyway into halves is prohibited but dividing it into separate alleyways is permitted, since in both cases the residents restrict each other.

The Gemara answers that the case involves a small partition (דקה), and cites Rav Idi bar Avin quoting Rav Chisda that a resident who makes such a partition at his entrance does not restrict the alleyway.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's practice and the dispute with Abaye
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's practice and the dispute with Abaye
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira merged the entire city of Bei Rabbi Chiyya without leaving a remnant. Abaye questions this, and Rabbi Zeira explains that the city's elders told him Rabbi Chiyya bar Asi did the same, implying it was a city of individuals that became public. Abaye counters that the elders told him the city had a garbage dump on one side, and now that it's gone, it has two openings and is prohibited. Rabbi Zeira admits he was unaware.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Zeira merged the entire city of Bei Rabbi Chiyya without leaving a remnant.
Abaye asks Rabbi Zeira why he performed the merging in this manner.
Rabbi Zeira explains that the city's elders told him Rabbi Chiyya bar Asi merged the entire city, implying it was originally a private city that became public.
Abaye counters that the elders told him the city had a garbage dump on one side, and now that it is gone, the city has two openings and is prohibited.
Rabbi Zeira admits he was unaware of this fact.

items.text: The status of a ladder as an opening
items.text_en: The status of a ladder as an opening
items.desc_en: Rav Ami bar Adda asks Rabbah whether a ladder on one side and a door on the other constitutes two openings. Rabbah cites Rav that a ladder has the status of an opening. Rav Nachman adds that a ladder has both the status of an opening and a partition, explaining the latter in the context of two courtyards.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ami bar Adda asks Rabbah whether a ladder on one side and a door on the other constitute two openings for the purpose of eruv.
Rabbah answers that Rav ruled: a ladder has the status of an opening (תורת פתח).
Rav Nachman objects to Rabbah's partial citation, correcting that Rav Adda said in Rav's name that a ladder has both the status of an opening and the status of a partition (תורת מחיצה).

sub.text: Rav Nachman's explanation of the dual status
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman's explanation of the dual status
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman explains that the status of an opening applies to a ladder between two courtyards, allowing them to either join as one eruv or remain separate.

items.text: Questioning Rav Nachman's consistency
items.text_en: Questioning Rav Nachman's consistency
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rav Nachman actually holds this view, citing a contradiction with his statement in the name of Shmuel regarding residents of a courtyard and a gallery who forgot to merge.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rav Nachman's consistency by citing his own statement in the name of Shmuel regarding residents of a courtyard and a gallery who forgot to merge.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling about a mirpeset
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's ruling about a mirpeset
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's case where a mirpeset is less than ten handbreadths high, and the residents forgot to join. If there is a small partition (dakka) of four handbreadths, it does not prohibit; otherwise it does. The Gemara clarifies that the mirpeset is not ten high, and the dakka is effective because the mirpeset is enclosed up to ten cubits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by quoting the Mishnah: if they did not merge (עירוב), and there is a small partition (דקה) of four handbreadths in front of them, it does not prohibit; if not, it prohibits.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's statement about a wall with ladders and a contradiction
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's statement about a wall with ladders and a contradiction
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that a wall which is scaled with ladders, even more than ten handbreadths, has the status of a partition. Rav Berona raises a contradiction from another statement of Shmuel regarding the mirpeset, and the Gemara resolves it by applying the same explanation as before.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states in the name of Shmuel that a wall scaled with ladders, even more than ten handbreadths high, has the status of a partition.

sub.text: Rav Berona's challenge to Rav Yehuda
sub.text_en: Rav Berona's challenge to Rav Yehuda
sub.desc_en: Rav Berona raises a contradiction from another statement of Shmuel, reported by Rav Nachman, regarding the mirpeset (balcony) and the requirement of a four-handbreadth partition.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by applying the same explanation as before: the case of the mirpeset involves a balcony less than ten handbreadths high, and the four-handbreadth partition effectively removes it from consideration.

items.text: The story of the people of Kakunai and Abaye's deliberation about a shiur
items.text_en: The story of the people of Kakunai and Abaye's deliberation about a shiur
items.desc_en: The people of Kakunai ask Rav Yosef for someone to make an eruv for their city. He sends Abaye, who considers various options: using houses opening to the river as a shiur, then making windows, then relying on the precedent of Rabbah bar Avuh who used separate alleyways, and finally citing the case of Mar bar Pofidta's hayloft. Abaye concludes that no shiur is needed, realizing this is what Rav Yosef meant by not causing an outcry.

sub.desc_en: The people of Kakunai come to רב יוסף (Rav Yosef) asking for someone to make an עירוב (eiruv) for their city; he sends אביי (Abaye), who initially proposes using houses opening to the river as the שיור (excluded section).

אביי (Abaye) retracts, arguing that the houses opening to the river cannot serve as a שיור (excluded section) because they could not have joined the עירוב (eiruv) in the first place, and instead proposes creating windows so they could join if needed.

אביי (Abaye) retracts again, citing the precedent of רבה בר אבוה (Rabbah bar Avuh) who made separate עירובין (eiruvin) for neighborhoods of מחוזא (Meḥoza) using alleyways as שיור (excluded sections) even though they could not join together.
אביי (Abaye) retracts yet again, distinguishing the case of מחוזא (Meḥoza) where roofs could connect neighborhoods, whereas here the houses cannot join, so windows are still needed.

אביי (Abaye) retracts a fourth time, citing the case of מר בר פופידתא (Mar bar Pofidta) whose straw storehouse served as a שיור (excluded section) for פומבדיתא (Pumbedita), showing that windows are unnecessary.
אביי (Abaye) concludes that this is what רב יוסף (Rav Yosef) meant by warning him not to cause an outcry in the study hall, realizing the complexity of the issue.

items.text: The baraita about the city of Chadasha
items.text_en: The baraita about the city of Chadasha
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda says there was a city in Judea named Chadasha with fifty residents, and the Sages used it as a standard for a shiur (a remnant) for a large city.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is cited: Rabbi Yehuda reports that there was a city in Judea named Chadasha with fifty residents, and the Sages used it as a standard for a shiur (a remnant) for a large city.

items.text: Inquiry about the status of Chadasha and a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Inquiry about the status of Chadasha and a dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara inquires: does Chadasha itself serve as a shiur for a larger city, and does a larger city serve as a shiur for a smaller one? Then it asks about a city 'like Chadasha' (i.e., of similar size). Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute whether such a city requires a shiur.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Chadasha itself serves as a shiur for a larger city, and whether a larger city serves as a shiur for a smaller one.
The Gemara then asks about a city 'like Chadasha' (of similar size) whether it requires a shiur.

sub.text: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda's dispute
sub.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda's dispute
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute: one says such a city requires a shiur, the other says it does not.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's ruling and the dispute between Rav and Rabbi Yitzchak
items.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Shimon requiring three courtyards. Rav says the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon. Rabbi Yitzchak says even one house in one courtyard suffices. Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether this is a tradition or logic, and Rav Yosef dismisses the question.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah cites Rabbi Shimon's ruling that three courtyards are required for the shiur (measure) of a city's shiur (remnant).
Rav, transmitted by Rav Chama bar Guria, rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon's position.
Rabbi Yitzchak argues that even a single house in one courtyard suffices as a shiur (remnant), and the Gemara corrects the phrasing from 'courtyard' to 'house in a courtyard'.
Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether Rabbi Yitzchak's statement is a received tradition (גמרא) or derived by logic (סברא).
Rav Yosef dismisses the question as irrelevant, saying 'What difference does it make to us? — either way, it is a tradition; should it be a mere twig?'

items.text: Mishnah: A person who instructs his son to place an eruv in a different direction
items.text_en: Mishnah: A person who instructs his son to place an eruv in a different direction
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents cases where a person is in the east and tells his son to place an eruv in the west, or vice versa. If the distance from the person to his house is 2000 cubits but to the eruv is more, he is permitted to his house but forbidden to the eruv. If the opposite, he is forbidden to his house but permitted to the eruv. Placing the eruv in the city's outskirts is invalid, and placing it outside the techum even one cubit is also invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the first case: a person in the east tells his son to place an eruv in the west; if the distance to his house is 2000 cubits but to the eruv is more, he is permitted to his house but forbidden to the eruv.
The Mishnah presents the second case: if the distance to the eruv is 2000 cubits but to the house is more, he is forbidden to his house but permitted to the eruv.
The Mishnah rules that placing the eruv in the city's outskirts (עיבור העיר) is invalid.
The Mishnah states that placing the eruv outside the techum (Shabbat boundary), even one cubit, is also invalid.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who places an eruv gains some distance but loses others, implying a trade-off.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one who places an eruv gains some distance but loses others, implying a trade-off.

items.text: Gemara's question and answers on 'east' and 'west'
items.text_en: Gemara's question and answers on 'east' and 'west'
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes 'east' means east of his house and 'west' means west of his house, then questions how the Mishnah's cases are possible. Rabbi Yitzchak reinterprets 'east' and 'west' as referring to his son's house, and Rava bar Rav Sheila offers an alternative resolution involving a diagonal placement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that 'east' and 'west' in the Mishnah refer to the east and west of the speaker's own house.
The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's second case is possible, where the distance to the eruv is 2000 amos but the distance to the house is greater.
Rabbi Yitzchak reinterprets 'east' and 'west' as referring to the east and west of his son's house, not his own.
Rava bar Rav Sheila offers an alternative resolution: even if 'east' and 'west' refer to the speaker's own house, the Mishnah's case is possible when the house is positioned diagonally (באלכסונא).

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's phrase 'within its built-up area'
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's phrase 'within its built-up area'
items.desc_en: The Gemara corrects a potential misunderstanding: the Mishnah's phrase 'within its built-up area' is not 'within the techum' but 'within the city's built-up area'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah's phrase 'outside its built-up area' could possibly mean 'outside the techum'.
The Gemara corrects the phrase to mean 'outside the city's built-up area' (עיבור), not outside the techum.

items.text: Challenge from a baraitha
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraitha
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the Mishnah's statement that one only gains and loses, citing a baraitha that adds more details: placing the eruv outside the built-up area even by one cubit gains that cubit but loses the entire city.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: No difficulty: here where his measure ended in the middle of the city; there where his measure ended at the end of the city.

items.text: Resolution via Rabbi Idi's distinction
items.text_en: Resolution via Rabbi Idi's distinction
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when his measurement ended in the middle of the city versus at the end of the city, citing Rabbi Idi's ruling in the name of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when his measurement ended in the middle of the city versus at the end of the city.

sub.text: Rabbi Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Idi citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Idi, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, provides the supporting ruling: if the measurement ended in the middle of the city, he gets only half the city; if at the end, the entire city counts as four cubits and he completes the rest.

items.text: Rabbi Idi's objection and Rava's support
items.text_en: Rabbi Idi's objection and Rava's support
items.desc_en: Rabbi Idi questions the distinction as prophetic nonsense, but Rava supports it by citing a Mishnah about residents of a large city walking through a small city.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Idi objects that the distinction between measuring to the middle vs. the end of the city is prophetic nonsense, questioning why the outcome should differ.
Rava supports the distinction by citing a Mishnah that residents of a large city may walk through the entire small city, implying that the city's size relative to the measurement endpoint matters.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah states that residents of a small town may not walk through the entire large town. It suggests the reason is that the Shabbat limit of the small town residents ends at the midpoint of the large town, while the limit of the large town residents ends at the edge of the small town.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah prohibits residents of a small town from walking through the entire large town, and suggests the reason is that their Shabbat limit ends at the midpoint of the large town while the large town residents' limit ends at the edge of the small town.

items.text: Rabbi Idi's resolution and the Gemara's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Idi's resolution and the Gemara's objection
items.desc_en: Rabbi Idi explains that the version of the Mishnah that reads 'residents of a small town' (אַנְשֵׁי) refers to one who places an eruv, not one who measures. The Gemara objects, citing a Mishnah that explicitly mentions the one who measures, but Rabbi Idi clarifies that the phrase 'end of the city' is needed only for the one who places an eruv, not for the one who measures.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Idi resolves the contradiction by asserting that the version of the Mishnah reading 'אַנְשֵׁי' (residents of a small town) refers to one who places an eruv, not to one who measures.
The Gemara objects, citing a Mishnah that explicitly mentions the one who measures, implying that the Mishnah indeed discusses the measurer.
Rabbi Idi clarifies that the phrase 'end of the city' is needed only for the one who places an eruv, not for the one who measures, thereby resolving the objection.

items.text: Rav Nachman's resolution of the two versions
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's resolution of the two versions
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that both versions of the Mishnah are correct: one who teaches 'residents of a small town' (אַנְשֵׁי) is not mistaken, as it refers to one who places an eruv; one who teaches 'no, residents of a small town' (אֵין אַנְשֵׁי) is also not mistaken, as it refers to one who measures. He then explains that the Mishnah is missing a clause and should read: residents of a large town may walk through the entire small town, but not vice versa, and this applies to the one who measures; however, one who places an eruv may walk through the entire town and beyond.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman opens by declaring that both versions of the Mishnah—one teaching 'residents of a small town' (אַנְשֵׁי) and one teaching 'no, residents of a small town' (אֵין אַנְשֵׁי)—are correct and not mistaken.

Rav Nachman explains that the version 'residents of a small town' (אַנְשֵׁי) refers to one who places an eruv (נוֹתֵן), while the version 'no, residents of a small town' (אֵין אַנְשֵׁי) refers to one who measures (מוֹדֵד).

Rav Nachman resolves the contradiction by emending the Mishnah: it is missing a clause and should read that residents of a large town may walk through the entire small town, but not vice versa, for the one who measures; however, one who places an eruv may walk through the entire town and beyond.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a city by a river and Abaye's question
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a city by a river and Abaye's question
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that if a city is situated on the bank of a river and has a bank (דַּקָּה) of four cubits in front of it, the Shabbat limit is measured from the riverbank; otherwise, it is measured from the entrance of each house. Abaye questions why the bank must be specifically four cubits, and Rav Huna explains that elsewhere a bank of four cubits is not needed for use, but here it is needed for use.

sub.text: Rav Yosef citing Rami bar Abba citing Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rav Yosef citing Rami bar Abba citing Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that for a city on a riverbank, if there is a bank (דַּקָּה) of four cubits, the Shabbat limit is measured from the riverbank; otherwise, from each house's entrance.
Abaye questions why the bank must be specifically four cubits, unlike other banks of four cubits elsewhere.
Rav Huna explains that elsewhere a four-cubit bank is not needed for use, but here it is needed for use.

items.text: Rav Yosef's proof from the Gader and Chamtan dispute
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's proof from the Gader and Chamtan dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted the residents of Gader to go down to Chamtan but not vice versa, suggesting the reason is that the residents of Gader had a bank (דַּקָּה) while those of Chamtan did not. Rav Dimi challenges this, explaining that the residents of Gader would harass the residents of Chamtan, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi instituted the restriction to prevent violence on Shabbat due to drunkenness. The Gemara questions why the harassment would not occur when the residents of Chamtan go to Gader, and answers that a dog in a foreign town does not bark for seven years, meaning they are submissive.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks for a source for his position, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi permitted the residents of Gader to go down to Chamtan but not vice versa, and suggests the reason is that the residents of Gader had a bank (דַּקָּה) while those of Chamtan did not.

Rav Dimi challenges Rav Yosef's proof, explaining that the residents of Gader would harass the residents of Chamtan, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling was a תקנה (enactment) to prevent violence, not based on the presence of a bank.
The Gemara asks why the restriction was specifically instituted for Shabbat, and answers that drunkenness is common on Shabbat, leading to potential violence.

The Gemara questions why the harassment would not occur when the residents of Chamtan go to Gader, and answers with a proverb: a dog in a foreign town does not bark for seven years, meaning they are submissive.
The Gemara objects that even now the residents of Chamtan harass the residents of Gader, and answers that they are not submissive to that extent.

items.text: Rav Safra and Rav Dimi bar Chinana's alternative explanations
items.text_en: Rav Safra and Rav Dimi bar Chinana's alternative explanations
items.desc_en: Rav Safra explains that the case involves a city shaped like a bow, while Rav Dimi bar Chinana explains it involves residents of a large city and a small city. The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyomei taught these explanations differently, with one saying the dispute is between Rav Safra and Rav Dimi bar Chinana over whether it is a bow-shaped city or a large and small city.

sub.desc_en: Rav Safra explains that the case involves a city shaped like a bow (עיר העשויה כקשת).
Rav Dimi bar Chinana explains that the case involves residents of a large city and a small city (אנשי עיר גדולה ואנשי עיר קטנה).

The Gemara notes that Rav Kahana and Rav Tavyomei taught these explanations differently, with one presenting them as a dispute between Rav Safra and Rav Dimi bar Chinana over whether it is a bow-shaped city or a large and small city.

items.text: The Mishnah and Rabbi Akiva's dispute
items.text_en: The Mishnah and Rabbi Akiva's dispute
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that residents of a large city may walk through the entire small city and vice versa, and explains that one who places an eruv in the other city may walk through the entire city and beyond. Rabbi Akiva disagrees, arguing that one may only walk 2000 cubits from the place of the eruv. The Sages respond that this applies only when the city has no residents, but if it has residents, one may walk through the entire city and beyond, making the inside of the city more lenient than its roof.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that residents of a large city may walk through the entire small city and vice versa, and explains that one who places an eruv in the other city may walk through the entire city and beyond.
Rabbi Akiva objects, arguing that one may only walk 2000 cubits from the place of the eruv, and challenges the Sages with the case of placing an eruv in a cave.

The Sages respond that Rabbi Akiva's cave case applies only when the city has no residents, but if it has residents, one may walk through the entire city and beyond, making the inside of the city more lenient than its roof.
The Mishnah adds a supporting rule that for one who measures, they are given 2000 cubits, even if the end of their measurement ends in a cave.

items.text: Dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Elazar regarding a ruined city
items.text_en: Dispute between Shmuel and Rabbi Elazar regarding a ruined city
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel: If one rested (shavat) in a ruined city, according to the Rabbis he may walk the entire city and 2000 cubits outside it; if he placed his eruv there, he only has 2000 cubits from the eruv. Rabbi Elazar says that whether he rested or placed the eruv, he may walk the entire city and 2000 cubits outside.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Shmuel's ruling: if one rested in a ruined city, he may walk the entire city plus 2000 cubits outside; if he placed his eruv there, he only has 2000 cubits from the eruv.
Rabbi Elazar disputes Shmuel, ruling that whether one rested or placed the eruv, he may walk the entire city and 2000 cubits outside.

items.text: Challenge from Rabbi Akiva's statement about a cave
items.text_en: Challenge from Rabbi Akiva's statement about a cave
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from Rabbi Akiva, who asked the Sages: Do you not agree that one who places his eruv in a cave only has 2000 cubits from the eruv? They replied: When? When there are no residents. The Gemara infers that in a cave without residents, they agree with Rabbi Akiva. It then clarifies that 'no residents' means it is unfit for dwelling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection by citing Rabbi Akiva's question to the Sages about one who places his eruv in a cave, implying that even the Sages agree that in a cave without residents, the eruv limits movement to 2000 cubits.
The Sages respond to Rabbi Akiva that his ruling applies only when the cave has no residents.
The Gemara infers that when there are no residents, the Sages agree with Rabbi Akiva, challenging the earlier position.
The Gemara clarifies that 'no residents' means the cave is unfit for dwelling, thereby resolving the objection.

items.text: Supporting baraita about a city and a cave
items.text_en: Supporting baraita about a city and a cave
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: If one rested in a city, even as large as Antioch, or in a cave, even as large as King Zedekiah's cave, he may walk the entire area and 2000 cubits outside. The baraita compares the city to the cave: just as the cave is ruined, so too the city is ruined. This implies that only if he rested (shavat) does he have this right, but if he placed an eruv (hiniach), he does not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita: one who rested in a city (even large) or a cave (even large) may walk the entire area plus 2000 cubits, implying that only resting (not placing an eruv) grants this leniency, supporting Shmuel.

items.text: Analysis of the baraita's authorship
items.text_en: Analysis of the baraita's authorship
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita: If it is Rabbi Akiva, why specify a ruined city? Even a settled one would be the same! Rather, it must be the Rabbis, and the reason is that resting (shavat) is different from placing an eruv (hiniach).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita: if it follows Rabbi Akiva, why specify a ruined city? Even an inhabited city would be the same; therefore it must follow the Rabbis, proving that only resting (not placing an eruv) grants the leniency.
The Gemara concludes that the baraita must follow the Rabbis, who distinguish between resting (שבת) and placing an eruv (הניח).

items.text: Alternative interpretation of the baraita
items.text_en: Alternative interpretation of the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets: Do not say the city is compared to the cave, but rather the cave is compared to the city. Just as the city is settled, so too the cave is settled. This aligns with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one only has 2000 cubits from the eruv, but he agrees regarding resting (shavat). The Gemara addresses the mention of Zedekiah's cave: it is like it in size but not in being ruined; here it is settled.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reinterprets the baraita: do not say the city is compared to the cave, but rather the cave is compared to the city, so just as the city is settled, the cave is also settled.
The Gemara identifies this reinterpretation as aligning with Rabbi Akiva, who holds that one only has 2000 cubits from the eruv, but agrees regarding resting (shavat).
The Gemara objects: the baraita mentions Zedekiah's cave, which is ruined, not settled.
The Gemara resolves: it is like Zedekiah's cave in size but not in being ruined; here the cave is settled.

items.text: Practical ruling by Mar Yehuda and Rava
items.text_en: Practical ruling by Mar Yehuda and Rava
items.desc_en: Mar Yehuda found the people of Mevarkhta placing their eruv in the synagogue of Bei Agobar and told them to include more space in the eruv to permit more. Rava commented that in eruv matters, no one follows Rabbi Akiva's opinion.

sub.desc_en: Rava told them: No one follows Rabbi Akiva's opinion on eruv matters, as we find no one who says like him.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter 'How do we extend the borders' (Keitzad Me'abrin).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the chapter with the standard formula 'we return to you, How to extend cities'.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: A Jew living with a non-Jew or one who does not believe in eruv
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: A Jew living with a non-Jew or one who does not believe in eruv
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states: One who lives with a non-Jew in a courtyard, or with someone who does not believe in eruv, that person prohibits him (from carrying). Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says he never prohibits unless there are two Jews who prohibit each other. Rabban Gamliel relates a story about a Sadducee living with them in an alley in Jerusalem, and his father told them to hurry and take out vessels to the alley before the Sadducee takes out and prohibits them. Rabbi Yehuda reports a different version: hurry and do your needs in the alley.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the ruling that a Jew living with a non-Jew or one who does not accept eiruv in a courtyard prohibits carrying.
רבי אליעזר בן יעקב (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov) states that a non-Jew never prohibits unless there are two Jews who would prohibit each other.

רבן גמליאל (Rabban Gamliel) relates a story about a Sadducee living with them in an alley in Jerusalem, and his father instructed them to hurry and take out vessels to the alley before the Sadducee takes out and prohibits them.
רבי יהודה (Rabbi Yehuda) reports a different version of the story: his father said to hurry and do their needs in the alley before the Sadducee takes out and prohibits them.

items.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chinana bar Avin's initial question
items.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chinana bar Avin's initial question
items.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chinana bar Avin, with Abaye present, question the logic of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position: if a gentile's residence is considered a residence, even one gentile should prohibit; if not, even two should not prohibit.

sub.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chinana bar Avin's question
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chinana bar Avin's question
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chinana bar Avin, with Abaye present, question the logic of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position: if a gentile's residence is considered a residence, even one gentile should prohibit; if not, even two should not prohibit.

items.text: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Abaye's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to the premise that Rabbi Meir considers a gentile's residence a residence, citing a baraita that compares a gentile's courtyard to an animal pen. He then resolves that both agree it is not a residence, and they dispute only about a decree lest one learn from the gentile's ways.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to the premise that Rabbi Meir considers a gentile's residence a residence, citing a baraita that compares a gentile's courtyard to an animal pen.
Abaye resolves that both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov agree a gentile's residence is not a residence, and they dispute only about a decree lest one learn from the gentile's ways.

items.text: Explanation of the dispute: concern for bloodshed and sorcery
items.text_en: Explanation of the dispute: concern for bloodshed and sorcery
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that since a gentile is suspected of bloodshed, the Sages decreed only for two gentiles who commonly dwell together, but not for one. Rabbi Meir holds that sometimes a single gentile might come to dwell, and the Sages stated that eruv and bitul reshus are ineffective without renting from the gentile, who will not rent.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov holds that since a gentile is suspected of bloodshed, the Sages decreed only for two gentiles who commonly dwell together, but not for one.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Meir's position
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Meir holds that sometimes a single gentile might come to dwell, and the Sages stated that eruv and bitul reshus are ineffective without renting from the gentile, who will not rent.

items.text: Gemara's question about the reason the gentile will not rent
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the reason the gentile will not rent
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the gentile will not rent. If it is because he might strengthen his hold, that works for the opinion that requires a strong rental. But for the opinion that requires a weak rental, what can be said? It cites Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet who dispute this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the gentile will not rent, and considers the possibility that it is because he might strengthen his hold, which works for the opinion requiring a strong rental but not for the opinion requiring a weak rental.

sub.text: Citation of dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Citation of dispute between Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the dispute between Rav Chisda, who requires a strong rental (שְׂכִירוּת בְּרִיאָה), and Rav Sheshet, who requires a weak rental (שְׂכִירוּת רְעוּעָה).

items.text: Clarification of 'strong' and 'weak' rental
items.text_en: Clarification of 'strong' and 'weak' rental
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers defining 'strong' as a perutah and 'weak' as less than a perutah, but rejects this because Rabbi Yochanan ruled that one may rent from a gentile even for less than a perutah. Additionally, Rabbi Yochanan said a Noahide is executed for stealing less than a perutah and it is not subject to return.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what 'strong' and 'weak' rental mean, proposing that 'strong' means a perutah and 'weak' means less than a perutah.
The Gemara objects: is there anyone who says one may not rent from a gentile for less than a perutah?

sub.text: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyorei in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyorei in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Yaakov bar Giyorei sent in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that one may rent from a gentile even for less than a perutah, refuting the proposed definition.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a Noahide is executed for stealing less than a perutah and it is not subject to return, further undermining the proposed definition.

items.text: Alternative definition and resolution regarding sorcery
items.text_en: Alternative definition and resolution regarding sorcery
items.desc_en: The Gemara redefines 'strong' as with a signed document and 'weak' as without. For the opinion requiring a weak rental, the Gemara explains that even so, the gentile fears sorcery and will not rent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara redefines 'strong' rental as one with a signed document (מוהרקי ואבורגני) and 'weak' rental as one without such documentation.
The Gemara explains that even for the opinion requiring only a weak rental, the gentile fears sorcery and will not rent.

items.text: Baraita citation and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Baraita citation and the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita: a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen, and it is permitted to carry from the courtyard to the houses and vice versa. Rabbi Meir says if there is one Israelite, he prohibits. Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says it never prohibits unless there are two Israelites who prohibit each other.

sub.desc_en: The baraita establishes the general rule: a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen, permitting carrying between the courtyard and houses.
Rabbi Meir states that if there is one Israelite in the courtyard, he prohibits carrying.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov rules that a gentile's courtyard never prohibits carrying unless there are two Israelites who prohibit each other.

items.text: Contradiction between the Mishnah and the earlier statement
items.text_en: Contradiction between the Mishnah and the earlier statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Mar said a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen (not requiring eiruv), but the Mishnah states that a Jew living with a gentile in a courtyard prohibits carrying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: Mar said a gentile's courtyard is like an animal pen (not requiring eiruv), but the Mishnah states that a Jew living with a gentile in a courtyard prohibits carrying.
The Gemara resolves: the two statements refer to different cases — one where the gentile is present, the other where he is absent.
The Gemara objects: what is the underlying principle? If residence without the owner is considered residence, then even a gentile should prohibit; if not, even a Jew should not prohibit.
The Gemara answers: the principle is that residence without the owner is not considered residence; for a Jew, the Rabbis decreed a prohibition even when absent.
The Gemara explains: for a gentile, when present he prohibits due to a decree lest the Jew learn from his actions; when absent, he does not prohibit.

The Gemara objects: is it true that when absent he does not prohibit? But we learned in a baraita: one who leaves his home and goes to stay in another city, both a gentile and a Jew prohibit, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara resolves: that case is different because he returns on the same day (so he is considered present).

items.text: Resolution: presence vs. absence
items.text_en: Resolution: presence vs. absence
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the gentile is present (he prohibits) and when he is absent (his courtyard is like an animal pen).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the gentile is present (he prohibits) and when he is absent (his courtyard is like an animal pen).

items.text: Question on the underlying principle
items.text_en: Question on the underlying principle
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the underlying principle: if residence without the owner is considered residence, then even a gentile should prohibit; if not, even a Jew should not prohibit.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the underlying principle: if residence without the owner is considered residence, then even a gentile should prohibit; if not, even a Jew should not prohibit.

items.text: Answer: distinction between Jew and gentile
items.text_en: Answer: distinction between Jew and gentile
items.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the principle is that residence without the owner is not considered residence. For a Jew, the Sages decreed that when he is absent he still prohibits (due to his presence when present). For a gentile, when he is absent he does not prohibit, because the concern is only that one might learn from his actions when he is present.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by asserting that the principle is that residence without the owner is not considered residence, and then distinguishes between a Jew, for whom the Sages decreed a prohibition even when absent, and a gentile, for whom the prohibition applies only when present due to concern about learning from his actions.

items.text: Challenge from a Mishnah and resolution
items.text_en: Challenge from a Mishnah and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the ruling that a gentile does not prohibit when absent, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir says both a gentile and a Jew who leave for Shabbat prohibit. The Gemara resolves that the case there is where the gentile returns on the same day.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the ruling that a gentile does not prohibit when absent, citing a Mishnah where Rabbi Meir says both a gentile and a Jew who leave for Shabbat prohibit.
The Gemara resolves that the case there is where the gentile returns on the same day.

items.text: Statements about the halakha following Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.text_en: Statements about the halakha following Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel says the halakha is like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. Rav Huna says it is the custom, and Rabbi Yochanan says the people practice accordingly.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel: the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Rav Huna says: the custom (מנהג) follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Rabbi Yochanan says: the people have adopted the practice (נהגו העם) like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: Inquiry about ruling in the presence of one's teacher
items.text_en: Inquiry about ruling in the presence of one's teacher
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef whether one may issue a ruling in the place of one's teacher, given that the Mishnah of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is clear. Rav Yosef responds that even for a trivial matter like an egg in vinegar, they asked Rav Chisda during Rav Huna's lifetime and he did not rule. Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba then asks Abaye about a written text like Megillat Ta'anit, and receives the same answer. The Gemara notes that Rav Chisda did rule in Kafri during Rav Huna's time.

sub.desc_en: Abaye opens by stating that the Mishnah of Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov is clear and that Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel that the halacha follows him.
Abaye asks whether one may issue a ruling in the place of one's teacher.
Rav Yosef answers that even for a trivial matter like an egg in vinegar, they asked Rav Chisda during Rav Huna's lifetime and he did not rule.

sub.text: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yaakov bar Abba asks Abaye whether one may rule based on a written text like Megillat Ta'anit in the place of one's teacher.
Abaye answers by citing Rav Yosef's same ruling that even for a trivial matter they asked Rav Chisda and he did not rule.
The Gemara notes that Rav Chisda did issue a ruling in Kafri during Rav Huna's lifetime, seemingly contradicting the earlier claim.

items.text: Rav Hamnuna and Ravina's actions in their teachers' domains
items.text_en: Rav Hamnuna and Ravina's actions in their teachers' domains
items.desc_en: Rav Hamnuna ruled on a halakha in the courtyard of the Exilarch during Rav Chisda's tenure, and Ravina sharpened a knife in Babylonia. Rav Ashi questions Ravina, who cites Rav Hamnuna's precedent. Rav Ashi clarifies that there is a dispute about whether Rav Hamnuna actually ruled, and Ravina explains that Rav Hamnuna did not rule in the presence of his teacher Rav Huna, but did so before Rav Chisda, who was his colleague-student, and Ravina considers himself a colleague-student of Rav Ashi.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rav Hamnuna ruled on a halakha in the Exilarch's courtyard during Rav Chisda's tenure.
The gemara reports that Ravina sharpened a knife in Babylonia.
Rav Ashi asks Ravina why he acted in this manner.
Ravina defends his action by citing Rav Hamnuna's precedent of ruling in the Exilarch's courtyard during Rav Chisda's tenure.
Rav Ashi objects that there is a version of the tradition that Rav Hamnuna did not actually rule.

Ravina resolves the dispute by explaining that Rav Hamnuna did not rule in the presence of his teacher Rav Huna, but did rule before Rav Chisda who was his colleague-student, and Ravina considers himself a colleague-student of Rav Ashi.

items.text: Rava's ruling: a scholar may act for himself
items.text_en: Rava's ruling: a scholar may act for himself
items.desc_en: Rava states that a Torah scholar may act for himself (i.e., perform a permitted action without consulting his teacher). Ravina arrived at Mechoza, and his host brought a knife and showed it to him (to slaughter an animal). Ravina told him to take it to Rava. The host questioned why, citing Rava's own ruling, and Ravina replied that he was buying it (not slaughtering).

sub.desc_en: Rava states that a Torah scholar may act for himself (i.e., rule on his own behalf without consulting his teacher).
The gemara recounts that Ravina arrived at Mechoza, and his host brought a knife and showed it to him (to slaughter an animal).
Ravina tells the host to take the knife to Rava (to slaughter the animal).
The host objects, citing Rava's own ruling that a scholar may act for himself.
Ravina explains that he is buying the knife (not slaughtering), so the ruling does not apply.

items.text: Story of Rabbi Elazar and Rav Abba bar Tachlifa at Rav Acha's house
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Elazar and Rav Abba bar Tachlifa at Rav Acha's house
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya and Rav Abba bar Tachlifa visited the place of Rav Acha bar Yaakov. Rav Acha bar Ika wanted to prepare a third calf for them and showed them a knife. Rav Abba bar Tachlifa questioned whether they should disregard the elder (Rav Acha bar Yaakov). Rabbi Elazar cited Rava's ruling that a scholar may act for himself, but he was punished. The Gemara explains that the case is different because the host had already begun to honor them, or because Rav Acha bar Yaakov was an outstanding scholar.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a mnemonic and recounts that Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya and Rav Abba bar Tachlifa visited the place of Rav Acha bar Yaakov, and Rav Acha bar Ika wanted to prepare a third calf for them, showing them a knife.
Rav Abba bar Tachlifa asks whether they should disregard the elder (Rav Acha bar Yaakov) by performing the slaughter themselves.
Rabbi Elazar of Hagronya cites Rava's ruling that a scholar may act for himself (perform the slaughter) in the presence of his teacher.
Rabbi Elazar acted on Rava's ruling but was punished, showing that the ruling did not apply in this case.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Elazar was punished, given Rava's explicit ruling that a scholar may act for himself.
The Gemara answers that the case is different because the host had already begun to honor them, so the scholar's action was a slight to the elder.
Alternatively, the Gemara answers that Rav Acha bar Yaakov was an outstanding scholar (מופלג), so the ruling does not apply to him.

items.text: Ravina excommunicates a man for desecrating Shabbat
items.text_en: Ravina excommunicates a man for desecrating Shabbat
items.desc_en: Ravina was sitting before Rav Ashi and saw a man tying his donkey to a palm tree on Shabbat. Ravina called out to him but he ignored him, so Ravina placed him under a ban. Rav Ashi questioned whether this appeared disrespectful to his teacher. Ravina replied that where there is a desecration of God's name, no honor is paid to the teacher.

sub.desc_en: Rava rules that to prevent a transgression, a student may rule even in his teacher's presence.
Ravina, sitting before Rav Ashi, sees a man tying his donkey on Shabbat and excommunicates him after the man ignores his call.
Rav Ashi questions whether Ravina's action appears disrespectful to his teacher.
Ravina cites the verse that where there is חילול השם (desecration of God's name), no honor is paid to the teacher.

items.text: The prohibition of ruling in front of one's teacher and the story of Nadav and Avihu
items.text_en: The prohibition of ruling in front of one's teacher and the story of Nadav and Avihu
items.desc_en: Rava states that ruling in front of one's teacher is forbidden and carries a death penalty. The Gemara questions whether this applies only in his presence, citing a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer says the sons of Aaron died because they ruled in front of Moses.
