Another story tells of a student of Rabbi Eliezer who ruled in his presence and died within the year. Rabbi Yochanan identifies the student as Yehuda ben Guria, who was three parasangs away, but the Gemara resolves that it was still considered 'in his presence' because the distance did not negate the prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that ruling halacha in front of one's teacher is forbidden and carries a death penalty, but ruling not in his presence is forbidden without the death penalty.
The Gemara questions whether the prohibition applies even not in his presence, citing a baraita about Nadav and Avihu.

The baraita cites Rabbi Eliezer who says that the sons of Aaron died because they ruled halacha in front of Moses their teacher, using a דרשה (exegetical derivation) from the verse about bringing fire.
The baraita recounts that a student of Rabbi Eliezer ruled halacha in his presence, and Rabbi Eliezer predicted he would not survive the year, which came true.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer's statement to his wife
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's statement to his wife
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer tells his wife Imma Shalom that he is not a prophet but has a tradition that anyone who rules halacha in front of his teacher is liable to death.
Rabbi Yochanan identifies the student as Yehuda ben Guria, who was three parasangs away from Rabbi Eliezer, challenging the notion that this was 'in his presence'.

The Gemara resolves that it was still considered 'in his presence' because the distance did not negate the prohibition, and the mention of his name and father's name was to prevent the story from being dismissed as a parable.

items.text: Additional punishments for ruling before one's teacher and related teachings
items.text_en: Additional punishments for ruling before one's teacher and related teachings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan says one who rules before his teacher deserves to be bitten by a snake. Ze'iri says he is called a sinner. Rav Hamnuna resolves a contradiction between hiding and proclaiming God's word, depending on the presence of a great sage like Ira the Yairite. Rabbi Abba bar Zavda says giving all priestly gifts to one priest brings famine. Rabbi Eliezer says such a person is removed from greatness, citing Eleazar the priest. Rabbi Levi says one who states a ruling before his teacher goes to Gehenna without children.

sub.text: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan states that one who rules halacha before his teacher deserves to be bitten by a snake, citing verses about Elihu and the serpent.
Ze'iri adds that such a person is called a sinner, citing the verse 'I hid Your word in my heart so that I would not sin against You.'
Rav Hamnuna resolves the apparent contradiction between hiding God's word and proclaiming it, depending on whether a great sage like Ira the Yairite is present.
Rabbi Abba bar Zavda says that giving all priestly gifts to one priest brings famine, citing the case of Ira the Yairite and the subsequent famine in David's days.
Rabbi Eliezer says such a person is removed from greatness, citing Eleazar the priest who was punished despite deferring to Joshua.
Rabbi Levi says one who states a ruling before his teacher goes to Gehenna without children, citing Joshua's plea to Moses to imprison the offenders.

items.text: Joshua's sin and the angel's rebuke
items.text_en: Joshua's sin and the angel's rebuke
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites verses showing that Joshua was punished for causing Israel to neglect procreation for one night. The angel of the Lord rebukes him for both neglecting the daily offering and Torah study, and Joshua goes into the depth of halakha.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the verse establishing Joshua's lineage.
Rabbi Abba bar Pappa states that Joshua was punished only for causing Israel to neglect procreation for one night.
The Gemara cites the verse where the angel appears to Joshua in Jericho.
The angel rebukes Joshua for neglecting both the daily offering and Torah study, asking which transgression he came for.
Rabbi Yochanan explains that Joshua's going into the valley that night teaches that he delved into the depth of halakha.

items.text: Prohibition of marital relations when the Ark is not in its place
items.text_en: Prohibition of marital relations when the Ark is not in its place
items.desc_en: A tradition is cited that when the Ark and the Divine Presence are not in their proper place, marital relations are forbidden.

sub.desc_en: A tradition is cited that when the Ark and the Divine Presence are not in their proper place, marital relations are forbidden.

items.text: Torah study is greater than the daily offerings
items.text_en: Torah study is greater than the daily offerings
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Inya in the name of Rav derives from the angel's words that Torah study is greater than the daily offerings, as the angel said 'now I have come' (for Torah study).

sub.text: Rabbi Shmuel bar Inya citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Inya citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Inya in the name of Rav declares that Torah study is greater than the daily offerings, citing the angel's words 'now I have come' as proof.

items.text: Sleeping in a room where a couple is present
items.text_en: Sleeping in a room where a couple is present
items.desc_en: Rav Berona in the name of Rav says that one who sleeps in a room where a husband and wife are present is condemned by Scripture. Rav Yosef adds that this applies even if the wife is a niddah. Rava says that if the wife is a niddah, it is a blessing, but the Gemara questions this.

sub.text: Rav Berona in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Berona in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Berona in the name of Rav states that one who sleeps in a room where a husband and wife are present is condemned by the verse 'נְשֵׁי עַמִּי תְּגָרְשׁוּן מִבֵּית תַּעֲנוּגֶיהָ' (the wives of My people you drive out from their pleasant house).
Rav Yosef adds that the condemnation applies even if the wife is a נִדָּה (menstruant), where marital relations are forbidden.
Rava objects that if the wife is a נִדָּה (menstruant), the sleeper is blessed, because the couple is prevented from sin.
The Gemara rejects Rava's blessing, asking: until now, who guarded the couple from sin? (implying the sleeper's presence is not a reliable safeguard).

items.text: Abaye's ruling on a non-Jewish neighbor
items.text_en: Abaye's ruling on a non-Jewish neighbor
items.desc_en: The residents of a courtyard asked a non-Jew named Lachman bar Ristak to rent them his rights, but he refused. They came to Abaye, who advised them to nullify their rights to one person, making him a single person in the place of a non-Jew, which does not prohibit. They objected that the non-Jew actually lives there, but Abaye responded that nullifying rights to one person is uncommon, and the Sages did not decree in uncommon cases.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces a case: a courtyard where a non-Jew named Lachman bar Ristak lived; the residents asked him to rent them his rights but he refused.
The residents came to Abaye, who advised them to nullify their rights to one person, making him a single person in the place of a non-Jew, which does not prohibit.
The residents objected that the reason for the leniency is when the non-Jew does not actually live there, but here the non-Jew does live there.
Abaye responded that nullifying rights to one person is uncommon, and the Sages did not decree in uncommon cases.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua reports the ruling to Rava
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua reports the ruling to Rava
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua went and stated this halakha before Rava.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua goes and reports the halakhic ruling to Rava.

items.text: Objection to the previous solution regarding a gentile's courtyard
items.text_en: Objection to the previous solution regarding a gentile's courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the gentile is treated as a resident, the law of eruv would be nullified for that alley, as people would say eruv is effective in a place with a gentile. The Gemara responds that this is publicized.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the gentile is treated as a resident, the law of eruv would be nullified for that alley, as people would say eruv is effective in a place with a gentile. The Gemara responds that this is publicized.

items.text: Question about the publicity
items.text_en: Question about the publicity
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the publicity is effective for children (dardekei).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the public announcement (אכרזתא) is effective for children (דרדקי), implying that children may not understand or be bound by it.

items.text: Rava's alternative solution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative solution
items.desc_en: Rava proposes that one of the residents should approach the gentile, rent a place from him, and deposit something there, making the gentile like a hired worker or day-laborer. He cites Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that even a hired worker or day-laborer may place his eruv and it suffices.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes that one resident approach the gentile, rent a spot, and deposit something, making the gentile like a hired worker or day-laborer.
Rava supports his proposal by citing Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel that even a hired worker or day-laborer may place his eruv and it suffices.

items.text: Abaye's question about multiple hired workers
items.text_en: Abaye's question about multiple hired workers
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef: if there are five hired workers and five day-laborers, what is the law? Rav Yosef responds that if the leniency of hired worker/day-laborer was stated, would they say it to be stringent?

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rav Yosef: if there are five hired workers and five day-laborers, what is the law?
Rav Yosef responds that if the leniency of hired worker/day-laborer was stated, would they say it to be stringent?

items.text: Rav Nachman's praise of the ruling
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's praise of the ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara repeats Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel's ruling about a hired worker or day-laborer, and Rav Nachman praises it as excellent.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara repeats the ruling of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel that even a hired worker or day-laborer may place an עירוב (eruv) and it suffices.
Rav Nachman praises the ruling, calling it excellent.

items.text: Rav Nachman's criticism of a ruling about drinking wine and teaching
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's criticism of a ruling about drinking wine and teaching
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel rules that one who drank a quarter-log of wine should not teach. Rav Nachman criticizes this, saying his own mind is not clear without drinking wine. Rava objects, citing Rabbi Acha bar Chanina that praising one teaching and disparaging another wastes Torah. Rav Nachman retracts.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel says even a hired or leased worker gives his eruv and it suffices. Rav Nachman praises this ruling.
Rav Nachman criticizes the ruling, saying that without drinking a quarter-log of wine his own mind is not clear.

sub.text: Rava citing Rabbi Acha bar Chanina
sub.text_en: Rava citing Rabbi Acha bar Chanina
sub.desc_en: Rava objects to Rav Nachman's criticism, citing Rabbi Acha bar Chanina that praising one teaching and disparaging another wastes the wealth of Torah.
Rav Nachman retracts his criticism, saying 'I take it back' (הדרי בי).

items.text: Distinction between shatuy and shikor regarding prayer
items.text_en: Distinction between shatuy and shikor regarding prayer
items.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that one who has drunk (shatuy) may not pray, but if he prayed, his prayer is valid; one who is drunk (shikor) may not pray, and if he prayed, his prayer is an abomination. The Gemara then defines the difference: shatuy is one who can speak before a king, shikor is one who cannot.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Huna rules that a shatuy (one who has drunk) should not pray, but if he prayed his prayer is valid; a shikor (drunkard) should not pray, and if he prayed his prayer is an abomination.
The Gemara asks for the definition of shatuy and shikor, and introduces a story of Rabbi Abba bar Shumni and Rav Menashya bar Yirmeya who parted with a halachic statement.
One of the rabbis defines shatuy as one who can speak before a king, and shikor as one who cannot.

items.text: Story of two sages and a halachic teaching about a convert's property
items.text_en: Story of two sages and a halachic teaching about a convert's property
items.desc_en: The second sage teaches that one who takes possession of a convert's property should buy a Torah scroll with it to ensure it remains in his possession. Rav Sheshet adds that even a Torah scroll is not necessary.

sub.desc_en: The second sage opens with a teaching: one who takes possession of a convert's property should buy a Torah scroll with it to ensure the property remains in his possession.
Rav Sheshet adds that even a Torah scroll is not necessary for the property to remain in the possessor's hands.

items.text: Husband's profit from wife's property
items.text_en: Husband's profit from wife's property
items.desc_en: Rava, Rav Pappa, and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak debate the extent to which a husband's profit from his wife's property is considered his own, with examples including business profit, found objects, and even writing tefillin.

sub.desc_en: The gemara opens the discussion with the general principle of a husband's rights over his wife's property.
Rava states that a husband's profit from his wife's property includes even business profit.
Rav Pappa adds that even a found object belongs to the husband.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak extends the principle to include even writing tefillin with the wife's property.

items.text: Scriptural support for the husband's rights
items.text_en: Scriptural support for the husband's rights
items.desc_en: Rav Chanin or Rabbi Chanina cites a verse to support the idea that a husband has rights over his wife's property.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chanin or Rabbi Chanina cites the verse 'וַיִּדַּר יִשְׂרָאֵל נֶדֶר' (And Israel vowed a vow) as scriptural support for the husband's rights over his wife's property.

items.text: Walking and sleep dispel wine
items.text_en: Walking and sleep dispel wine
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba states that a mil of walking or any sleep dispels wine, but Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha qualifies that this applies only to a revi'is; more than that, walking disturbs and sleep intoxicates.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Abba states that a mil of walking or any sleep dispels wine.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avuha qualifies that the rule applies only to a revi'is; more than that, walking disturbs and sleep intoxicates.

items.text: Story of Rabban Gamliel and the annulment of vows
items.text_en: Story of Rabban Gamliel and the annulment of vows
items.desc_en: A story is brought to challenge the claim that a mil of walking dispels wine: Rabban Gamliel, after drinking a revi'is of Italian wine, walked three mil before annulling a vow, implying more walking was needed. The story also teaches several halachot, including that one does not pass over food, follows the majority of travelers, and that a drunk may not teach.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the claim that a mil of walking dispels wine, citing a baraita about Rabban Gamliel.
The baraita recounts Rabban Gamliel riding from Acco to Keziv, finding food on the road, and instructing Rabbi Ila'i and Mavgai.
Rabbi Ila'i questions Mavgai about his origin and whether Rabban Gamliel knew him.

The Gemara notes that Rabban Gamliel acted with divine inspiration, and three halachot are derived: one does not pass over food, follows the majority of travelers, and a gentile's chametz after Passover is permitted for benefit.
When Rabban Gamliel reached Keziv, a man came to annul his vow; Rabban Gamliel asked if they had drunk a revi'is of Italian wine and decided to walk until the wine dissipated.
They walked three mil to the ladder of Tyre, where Rabban Gamliel dismounted, wrapped himself, sat, and annulled the man's vow.
The Gemara lists additional halachot learned: a revi'is of Italian wine intoxicates, a drunk may not teach, walking dispels wine, and vows are annulled only while sitting.

items.text: Resolution: Italian wine is stronger
items.text_en: Resolution: Italian wine is stronger
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that Italian wine is more intoxicating, so it requires more walking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the contradiction by noting that Italian wine is more intoxicating, so it requires more walking.

items.text: Further challenge and resolution: Riding is different
items.text_en: Further challenge and resolution: Riding is different
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the resolution with Rav Nachman's statement, and answers that riding is different from walking, so the case of Rabban Gamliel (who was riding) does not contradict the rule.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous resolution by citing Rav Nachman's statement that drinking more than a quarter-log only increases the effect of walking and sleep.
The Gemara answers that riding is different from walking, so the case of Rabban Gamliel (who was riding) does not contradict the rule.

items.text: Dispute about annulling vows while riding
items.text_en: Dispute about annulling vows while riding
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that vows can be annulled while walking, standing, or riding, but the Gemara resolves this as a dispute between Tannaim regarding whether one opens with regret.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the previous resolution by citing Rav Nachman's explicit statement that vows may be annulled while walking, standing, or riding.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction by attributing the positions to a Tannaic dispute: one Tanna holds that one opens with regret (allowing annulment while riding), and the other holds that one does not open with regret (requiring sitting).

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's opening for annulment
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's opening for annulment
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan explains that Rabban Gamliel opened the annulment with a verse about the tongue of the wise being healing.

sub.text: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar bar Chanah quoting Rabbi Yochanan explains: What did Rabban Gamliel open for that man? — 'There is a boteh like sword thrusts, but the tongue of the wise is healing.' Everyone who boteh (speaks rashly) deserves to be stabbed, but the tongue of the wise heals.

items.text: Passing over food and witchcraft
items.text_en: Passing over food and witchcraft
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai distinguishes between earlier generations where one does not pass over food and later generations where one does, due to witchcraft. A baraisa adds that whole loaves are passed over but not pieces, with a scriptural support.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the earlier statement from the baraisa that one does not pass over food.

sub.text: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan citing Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai distinguishes between earlier generations, where one does not pass over food because Jewish women were not prone to witchcraft, and later generations, where they are prone and one does pass over.
A baraisa teaches that whole loaves are passed over but pieces are not.

Rav Asi objects to Rav Ashi that pieces are indeed used for witchcraft, citing the verse 'ותחללנה אותי אל עמי בשעלי שעורים ובפתותי לחם' (they profaned Me among My people for handfuls of barley and for pieces of bread).
The Gemara resolves that the verse refers to witches who take pieces in their hands (i.e., as payment), not for sorcery itself.

items.text: Beginning of a new statement
items.text_en: Beginning of a new statement
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet begins a statement in the name of Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, which is cut off at the end of the daf.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers (citing Rav Sheshet quoting Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya):

items.text: Opening statement and challenge
items.text_en: Opening statement and challenge
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a statement that one could exempt the entire world from judgment since the Temple's destruction, citing a verse about a drunken and afflicted woman. A challenge is raised from a baraita that a drunk person's transactions are valid, and he is liable for capital and corporal punishment, except that he is exempt from prayer. The Gemara clarifies that the original statement referred only to exemption from prayer.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a claim that one could exempt the entire world from judgment since the Temple's destruction, citing the verse about a drunken and afflicted woman.
A baraita is cited as a challenge, stating that a drunk person's transactions are valid and he is liable for capital and corporal punishment, except that he is exempt from prayer.
The Gemara clarifies that the original statement referred only to exemption from prayer, not from all judgment.

items.text: Distinction by level of drunkenness
items.text_en: Distinction by level of drunkenness
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina distinguishes between two levels of drunkenness: one who has not reached Lot's level of intoxication is liable for all matters except prayer, but one who has reached Lot's level is exempt from all obligations.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between one who has not reached Lot's level of drunkenness (liable for all matters except prayer) and one who has reached it (exempt from all obligations).

items.text: Interpretation of a verse about shields and troubles
items.text_en: Interpretation of a verse about shields and troubles
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina interprets a verse about those who 'remove shields' in times of pride, saying that troubles are sealed against them. The Gemara debates the meaning of the word 'afik' – whether it means 'remove' (as in a wadi) or 'reveal' (as in channels of water). Rabbi Yochanan says the verse refers to one who does not 'remove' (i.e., reveal his troubles). The difference between them is illustrated by the practice of Rav Sheshet, who would entrust his sleep to his attendant.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that anyone who 'removes shields' in a time of pride has troubles sealed against them, citing a verse.
The Gemara asks how the word 'אפיק' (afik) in the verse is understood as meaning 'remove', and cites a proof from another verse where 'אפיק' refers to a wadi that passes through.
Rabbi Yochanan asserts that the verse actually means 'one who does not reveal' (his troubles), interpreting 'מפיק' as 'reveal'.
The Gemara asks how the word 'מפיק' (mefik) can mean 'reveal', and cites a verse where 'אפיקי מים' (channels of water) are revealed.

The Gemara resolves the dispute by noting that both interpretations are supported by verses, and the practical difference lies in the practice of Rav Sheshet, who entrusted his sleep to his attendant — one opinion accepts this practice, the other does not.

items.text: Conditions for prayer: mental composure and distractions
items.text_en: Conditions for prayer: mental composure and distractions
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav states that one whose mind is not settled should not pray, citing a verse. Rabbi Chanina would not pray on a day he was angry, and Mar Ukva would not go to court on a day of strong wind. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says that halakha requires clarity like a day of danger. Abaye and Rava give examples of minor distractions that would invalidate prayer, and Mar bar Ravina's mother would prepare seven garments for seven days.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi quotes Rav stating that one whose mind is unsettled should not pray, citing the verse 'בְּצָר אַל יוֹרֶה' (in distress do not pour forth).
Rabbi Chanina would not pray on a day he was angry, citing the same verse 'בְּצָר אַל יוֹרֶה'.
Mar Ukva would not go to court on a day of strong wind (a distraction).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak rules that the הלכה (binding law) requires clarity of mind like a day of danger (when one is alert).
Abaye gives an example of a minor distraction (his mother asking him to bring a condiment) that would invalidate prayer.
Rava gives another example of a minor distraction (a louse bite) that would invalidate prayer.
Mar bar Ravina's mother would prepare seven garments for seven days to ensure he had no distraction from clothing concerns.

items.text: The purpose of night and day for sleep and study
items.text_en: The purpose of night and day for sleep and study
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says night was created only for sleep, while Reish Lakish says the moon was created only for study. Rabbi Zeira is told his teachings are sharp, and he attributes this to daytime study. The daughter of Rav Chisda asks her father if he doesn't need to sleep a little, and he responds that the days are long and short (i.e., there is time to sleep later). Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak says they are daytime workers, and Rav Acha bar Yaakov would borrow and repay (i.e., sleep during the day to study at night).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda states that night was created only for sleep.
Reish Lakish counters that the moon was created only for study.
Rabbi Zeira is told his teachings are sharp, and he attributes this to daytime study.
The daughter of Rav Chisda asks her father if he does not need to sleep a little.
Rav Chisda responds that the days are long and short (i.e., there will be time to sleep later).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak states that they are daytime workers (i.e., they study during the day and sleep at night).
Rav Acha bar Yaakov would borrow sleep during the day and repay at night (i.e., sleep during the day to study at night).

items.text: One who returns from a journey should not pray for three days
items.text_en: One who returns from a journey should not pray for three days
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar states that one who returns from a journey should not pray for three days, citing the verse about Ezra gathering the people by the river. The father of Shmuel would not pray for three days after returning from a journey. Shmuel would not pray in a house that had beer, and Rav Pappa would not pray in a house that had a type of strong drink.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that one who returns from a journey should not pray for three days, citing the verse about Ezra gathering the people by the river.
The father of Shmuel would not pray for three days after returning from a journey, supporting Rabbi Elazar's ruling.
Shmuel would not pray in a house that had beer, adding a related restriction about prayer environment.
Rav Pappa would not pray in a house that had a type of strong drink (הרסנא), further illustrating the principle of avoiding prayer in distracting or impure environments.

items.text: Wine, wisdom, and blessing
items.text_en: Wine, wisdom, and blessing
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina says that one who is appeased by his wine has the knowledge of his Creator. Rabbi Chiya says that one who is settled by his wine has the wisdom of seventy elders, as the word 'yayin' (wine) has the numerical value of seventy, and 'sod' (secret) also has seventy – when wine enters, secrets emerge. Rabbi Chanin says wine was created only to comfort mourners and reward the wicked. Rabbi Chanin bar Pappa says that one whose house does not have wine flowing like water is not included in blessing, based on a verse comparing wine to water.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina states that one who is appeased by his wine has the knowledge of his Creator, citing the verse about Noah's sacrifice.
Rabbi Chiya adds that one who is settled by his wine has the wisdom of seventy elders, based on the numerical equivalence of 'yayin' (wine) and 'sod' (secret), both equaling seventy.
Rabbi Chanin states that wine was created only to comfort mourners and reward the wicked, citing a verse.
Rabbi Chanin bar Pappa rules that one whose house lacks wine flowing like water is not included in blessing, deriving from a verse that equates wine with water.

items.text: Opening aphorism about blessing in the home
items.text_en: Opening aphorism about blessing in the home
items.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a folk saying: if water spills in one's house like water, there is blessing; if not, not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens with a folk saying: if water spills in one's house like water, there is blessing; if not, not.

items.text: Rabbi Ila'i's statement on character indicators
items.text_en: Rabbi Ila'i's statement on character indicators
items.desc_en: Rabbi Ila'i says a person is known by three things: his cup (koso), his pocket (kiso), and his anger (ka'aso); some add also his laughter (sachako).

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Il'ai states that a person is known through three things: his cup, his pocket, and his anger; some add also his laughter.
Some add that a person is also known by his laughter (שחוקו).

items.text: Rav's ruling on a Jew and non-Jew in a courtyard
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on a Jew and non-Jew in a courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav rules: if a Jew and non-Jew live in the inner courtyard and a Jew in the outer, it is prohibited. This case came before Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya, and both prohibited.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports Rav's ruling: a Jew and a gentile in the inner courtyard and a Jew in the outer courtyard; a case came before Rabbi and he forbade, and before Rabbi Chiyya and he forbade.
The case was brought before Rabbi and Rabbi Chiyya, and both prohibited, supporting Rav's ruling.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of Rav's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of Rav's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef sit before Rav Sheshet, who suggests Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Meir. Rabbah shakes his head in dissent. Rav Yosef objects: if it's Rabbi Meir, why need a Jew in the outer courtyard? The Gemara considers other Tannaim (Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, Rabbi Akiva) and raises difficulties until Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves it by combining both opinions.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef sit before Rav Sheshet, who suggests Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Meir; Rabbah shakes his head in dissent.
Rav Yosef objects: if Rav follows Rabbi Meir, why require a Jew in the outer courtyard?
The Gemara notes that when asked about an inner Jew in his place, Rav ruled it permitted, contradicting the idea that the case was unique.
The Gemara considers Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's position, which requires two Jews to prohibit each other.
The Gemara considers Rabbi Akiva's position, but objects that then a gentile would be unnecessary — even a Jew would suffice.

Rav Huna bar Yehoshua resolves the difficulty by combining both opinions: the case involves an eruv, and the gentile's presence prohibits the Jew from carrying, but without the gentile there is no prohibition.

items.text: Rabbi Eliezer's inquiry about a different configuration
items.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer's inquiry about a different configuration
items.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer asks Rav: what if a Jew and non-Jew are in the outer courtyard and a Jew in the inner? Rav responds cryptically: 'Give to the wise and he will become wiser.' The Gemara explores the reasoning: in the first case the non-Jew fears the Jew will ask about the other Jew, but here he might think the Jew left or might see him.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer asks Rav about a new configuration: a Jew and a non-Jew in the outer courtyard and a Jew in the inner one.

sub.text: Gemara's analysis of the first case's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the first case's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that in the first case (Jew and non-Jew in inner courtyard), the non-Jew fears the Jew will ask about the other Jew.

sub.text: Gemara's first possible reasoning for the new case
sub.text_en: Gemara's first possible reasoning for the new case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that in the new case, the non-Jew might think the inner Jew has left, so he is not afraid.

sub.text: Gemara's second possible reasoning for the new case
sub.text_en: Gemara's second possible reasoning for the new case
sub.desc_en: The Gemara alternatively suggests that the non-Jew might still fear, thinking the inner Jew might see him.
Rav responds cryptically with the verse 'Give to the wise and he will become wiser,' implying the answer is obvious.

items.text: Rav's response to Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Rav's response to Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: Rav answers Rabbi Eliezer with the verse: 'Give to the wise and he will become wiser,' implying the answer is obvious.

sub.desc_en: Rav answers with a verse: 'Give to the wise and he will become wiser' (Proverbs 9:9), implying that Rabbi Eliezer already knows the answer.

items.text: First story: Reish Lakish and students at an inn
items.text_en: First story: Reish Lakish and students at an inn
items.desc_en: Reish Lakish and Rabbi Chanina's students arrive at an inn where the non-Jewish owner does not rent but leases. They debate whether they may rent from him on Shabbat when he can evict them. Reish Lakish advises to rent and later ask the sages of the South. They ask Rabbi Apas, who approves.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces Reish Lakish and Rabbi Chanina's students arriving at an inn where the non-Jewish owner does not rent but leases.
The students ask whether they may rent from the owner on Shabbat, distinguishing between cases where the owner can evict them and where he cannot.
The students debate whether the possibility of eviction permits renting now, or whether the fact that eviction has not yet occurred forbids it.

sub.text: Reish Lakish's advice and Rabbi Apas's approval
sub.text_en: Reish Lakish's advice and Rabbi Apas's approval
sub.desc_en: Reish Lakish advises them to rent and later ask the sages of the South; they ask Rabbi Apas, who approves their action.

items.text: Second story: Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef and colleagues at an inn
items.text_en: Second story: Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef and colleagues at an inn
items.desc_en: Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, and Rabbi Asi arrive at an inn where the non-Jewish owner comes on Shabbat. They debate whether renting is like merging (must be before Shabbat) or like nullifying (can be on Shabbat). Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef permits, Rabbi Asi prohibits; Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba suggests following the elder. They ask Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: The narrative introduces Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef, Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba, and Rabbi Asi arriving at an inn whose non-Jewish owner came on Shabbat, and they ask whether they may rent from him.
The gemara presents the dilemma: is renting analogous to merging (עירוב), which must be done before Shabbat, or to nullifying a domain (ביטול רשות), which can be done even on Shabbat?
Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef permits renting, while Rabbi Asi prohibits it.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba suggests following the elder (Rabbi Chanina bar Yosef) and renting, and they go to ask Rabbi Yochanan for a ruling.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yochanan's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's praise of the Nehardeans implies that hiring a gentile must be done before Shabbat, based on his earlier statement that hiring is like an eruv.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yochanan's praise of the Nehardeans implies that hiring a gentile must be done before Shabbat, based on his earlier statement that hiring is like an eruv.

items.text: Gemara's answer: three parallels between hiring and eruv
items.text_en: Gemara's answer: three parallels between hiring and eruv
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference, explaining that the comparison to eruv is not about timing but about three other halachic aspects: even less than a perutah, even a hired hand or day-laborer, and one person can hire for all five residents of a courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the inference from Rabbi Yochanan's statement, explaining that the comparison to eruv is about three halachic aspects: even less than a perutah, even a hired hand or day-laborer, and one person can hire for all five residents of a courtyard.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's difficulty and Rabbi Zeira's confusion
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's difficulty and Rabbi Zeira's confusion
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar expresses difficulty with the previous discussion, and Rabbi Zeira wonders what that difficulty is. Rabbi Sheshet rebukes Rabbi Zeira for not understanding that the difficulty relates to Shmuel, Rabbi Elazar's teacher.

sub.desc_en: The gemara reports that Rabbi Elazar expressed difficulty (תִּהְיָא) with the preceding discussion.
Rabbi Zeira asks what exactly Rabbi Elazar's difficulty is.
Rabbi Sheshet rebukes Rabbi Zeira for not understanding that the difficulty relates to Shmuel, Rabbi Elazar's teacher.

items.text: Shmuel's principle about nullification
items.text_en: Shmuel's principle about nullification
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's rule: wherever a gentile both prohibits and requires an eruv, one may nullify his domain; but if he only prohibits or only requires an eruv, one may not nullify.

sub.desc_en: Shmuel states a general rule: wherever a gentile both prohibits and requires an eruv, one may nullify his domain; if he only prohibits or only requires an eruv, one may not nullify.

items.text: Examples of Shmuel's categories
items.text_en: Examples of Shmuel's categories
items.desc_en: The Gemara provides examples: two courtyards one inside the other (both prohibit and require eruv, so nullification works); two courtyards with one door (require eruv but do not prohibit, so no nullification); and the case of a gentile (prohibits but does not require eruv, so no nullification).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara gives the example of two courtyards one inside the other as a case where both prohibition and eruv apply, so nullification works.
The Gemara gives the example of two courtyards with one door between them as a case where eruv applies but no prohibition, so nullification does not work.
The Gemara gives the example of a gentile as a case where prohibition applies but no eruv, so nullification does not work.

items.text: Conclusion: the gentile must have arrived before Shabbat
items.text_en: Conclusion: the gentile must have arrived before Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the case of a gentile who arrived on Shabbat is different, as he would need to hire from before Shabbat, resolving Rabbi Elazar's difficulty.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves Rabbi Elazar's difficulty by concluding that the gentile must have arrived before Shabbat, so hiring him from before Shabbat is possible.

items.text: Conclusion from the earlier Mishnah
items.text_en: Conclusion from the earlier Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that if a non-resident came on Shabbat, the ruling is that they prohibit but do not join, and do not nullify, concluding that bitul reshus is not possible from one courtyard to another.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Abaye's discussion on Shmuel's statement
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Abaye's discussion on Shmuel's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef admits he did not hear the tradition about bitul reshus between courtyards. Abaye reminds him that he himself taught that Shmuel's rule applies only to two courtyards with one opening, but for nested courtyards, bitul is possible. Rav Yosef denies saying that, citing Shmuel's principle that we only have the language of the Mishnah. Abaye clarifies that Shmuel's statement was about the alleyway relative to courtyards.

items.text: Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute on bitul reshus
items.text_en: Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan's dispute on bitul reshus
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the core dispute: Shmuel says there is no bitul reshus from courtyard to courtyard or in a ruin, while Rabbi Yochanan permits it. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary to state, as each might have been conceded in the other case.

items.text: Abaye's qualification of Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Abaye's qualification of Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye states that Shmuel's rule applies only to two courtyards with one opening between them, but for nested courtyards, since they prohibit each other, they may nullify.

items.text: Rava's detailed analysis of nested courtyards
items.text_en: Rava's detailed analysis of nested courtyards
items.desc_en: Rava disagrees with Abaye, arguing that even for nested courtyards, sometimes bitul is possible and sometimes not, depending on where the eruv was placed and who forgot. He analyzes various scenarios: when the eruv is in the outer courtyard, the inner one, and who forgot, concluding that bitul is often impossible due to the prohibition of bitul between courtyards.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one from the outer courtyard forgot to join, the inner courtyard is permitted (since it has its own door) and the outer is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: if one from the outer courtyard forgot to join, the inner courtyard is permitted and the outer is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua asks Rava: why, if one from the inner courtyard forgot, are both forbidden? Let the inner resident nullify to the inner residents, and the outer courtyard be permitted with them? Rava answers that this follows Rabbi Eliezer, but he was speaking to the Rabbis who require nullification to each individual.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's question to Rava
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua's question to Rava
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua asks Rava: if one from the inner courtyard forgot, why are both forbidden? Let the inner resident nullify to the inner residents, and the outer courtyard be permitted with them.
Rava answers that this follows Rabbi Eliezer, but he was speaking to the Rabbis who require nullification to each individual.

items.text: Introduction of Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet
items.text_en: Introduction of Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet
items.desc_en: A brief narrative describes the mutual fear between Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet: Rav Chisda trembles at Rav Sheshet's traditions, and Rav Sheshet trembles at Rav Chisda's dialectics.

sub.desc_en: The gemara describes the mutual fear between Rav Chisda and Rav Sheshet: Rav Chisda trembles at Rav Sheshet's traditions, and Rav Sheshet trembles at Rav Chisda's dialectics.

items.text: Inquiry about two houses on opposite sides of public domain surrounded by a partition on Shabbat
items.text_en: Inquiry about two houses on opposite sides of public domain surrounded by a partition on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Sheshet: two houses on opposite sides of public domain, and gentiles came and surrounded them with a partition on Shabbat — what is the law? The Gemara analyzes the case according to the dispute about nullification from courtyard to courtyard, concluding that nullification is not possible.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks Rav Sheshet about two houses on opposite sides of the public domain that gentiles surrounded with a partition on Shabbat.

The Gemara argues that according to the view that there is no nullification of domain from courtyard to courtyard, the case is obviously forbidden, since even if they could have joined yesterday they cannot nullify now.
The Gemara reframes the question according to the view that nullification is possible, suggesting that here, where they could not have joined yesterday, nullification might also be impossible.
Rav Sheshet answers that they cannot nullify domain in this case.

items.text: Inquiry about a gentile who died on Shabbat
items.text_en: Inquiry about a gentile who died on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks: if a gentile died on Shabbat, what is the law regarding nullification? The Gemara distinguishes between the opinion that one may rent from a gentile and the opinion that one may not. Rav Sheshet says one may nullify, but Hamnuna says one may not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda asks: if a gentile died on Shabbat, what is the law regarding nullification of his domain?
The Gemara clarifies that according to the opinion that one may rent from a gentile, the question is unnecessary since performing two actions (renting and nullifying) is more stringent than one.
The Gemara reframes the question according to the opinion that one may not rent from a gentile: is nullification alone permitted, or is it also forbidden?
Rav Sheshet answers that one may nullify the gentile's domain.
Hamnuna states that one may not nullify the gentile's domain.

items.text: A gentile with a four-by-four opening to a valley
items.text_en: A gentile with a four-by-four opening to a valley
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a gentile with a four-by-four opening to a valley does not forbid the alley, even if he brings in camels and wagons all day. The Gemara then inquires about an opening to a karpaf, and Rav Nachman bar Ami cites a tradition from the academy.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a gentile with a four-by-four opening to a valley does not forbid the alley, even if he brings in camels and wagons all day.
The Gemara explains the reason: the gentile is satisfied with the opening designated for him, so he does not use the alley entrance.
The Gemara raises an inquiry about an opening to a karpaf, and Rav Nachman bar Ami cites a tradition from the academy.

items.text: Opening statement about a karpaf
items.text_en: Opening statement about a karpaf
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by stating that even if a karpaf is open to another karpaf, the laws of carrying still apply. This sets the stage for the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that even if a karpaf is open to another karpaf, the laws of carrying still apply.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's ruling on a gentile's karpaf
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef's ruling on a gentile's karpaf
items.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef state that a gentile's karpaf of beit se'atayim prohibits carrying, but larger than that does not. For a Jew, a karpaf of beit se'atayim does not prohibit, but larger than that does.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef both state that a gentile's residence of two se'ah (בית סאתים) prohibits carrying, while more than that does not; for an Israelite, two se'ah does not prohibit, but more than that does.
They add that for a Jew, a karpaf of beit se'atayim does not prohibit carrying.
They conclude that for a Jew, a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim does prohibit carrying.

items.text: Rava bar Chaklai's question to Rav Huna
items.text_en: Rava bar Chaklai's question to Rav Huna
items.desc_en: Rava bar Chaklai asks Rav Huna about the status of a karpaf open to another karpaf. Rav Huna responds with the same ruling as Rabbah and Rav Yosef.

sub.text: Rava bar Chaklai's question to Rav Huna
sub.text_en: Rava bar Chaklai's question to Rav Huna
sub.desc_en: Rava bar Chaklai asks Rav Huna: what is the law if a karpaf is open to another karpaf?
Rav Huna answers by citing the earlier ruling: a karpaf of two se'ah (בית סאתים) prohibits, more than that does not.

items.text: Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan on a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim
items.text_en: Ulla citing Rabbi Yochanan on a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim
items.desc_en: Ulla says in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim not enclosed for dwelling is considered a partition, and one who throws into it is liable, because it is a partition lacking inhabitants.

sub.desc_en: Ulla reports in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that a karpaf larger than two se'ah (בית סאתים) that was not enclosed for dwelling is considered a partition (מחיצה) lacking inhabitants, so one who throws into it is liable.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Chinana's objection from a rock in the sea
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana's objection from a rock in the sea
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana raises an objection from a baraita about a rock in the sea that is ten handbreadths high and four wide, where one may not carry from it to the sea or vice versa. The Gemara analyzes whether this applies to the first or last clause, concluding it is a refutation of Rabbi Yochanan.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Chinana raises an objection by citing a baraita about a rock in the sea that is ten handbreadths high and four wide, where one may not carry from it to the sea or vice versa, and the limit for leniency is up to a בית סאתים (two se'ah space).

The Gemara asks which clause of the baraita the limit of בית סאתים applies to, and rejects the possibility that it applies to the latter clause because that would permit carrying from one כרמלית (karmelit) to another.

The Gemara concludes that the limit applies to the first clause, meaning a rock larger than בית סאתים is treated as a כרמלית (karmelit), which refutes Rabbi Yochanan's statement that a large karpaf is a full-fledged private domain.

items.text: Rava's resolution of the baraita
items.text_en: Rava's resolution of the baraita
items.desc_en: Rava says that one who does not know how to resolve baraitot would raise a refutation against Rabbi Yochanan. He explains that the baraita always refers to the first clause, and the measure of beit se'atayim applies to carrying within the rock.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to the first part and means that within the rock, carrying is permitted up to two se'ah (בית סאתים).

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi says the baraita always refers to the first clause, and the Sages said two things: a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim not enclosed for dwelling is only permitted within four cubits, and one may not carry from a private domain to a karmelit. He explains the distinction between a rock of beit se'atayim and larger than that.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves the contradiction by explaining that the baraita refers to the first part and that the Sages made two statements: one about a karpaf larger than two se'ah (בית סאתים) and one about carrying from a private domain to a karmelit (כרמלית), with the distinction based on common occurrence.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's first statement of the Sages
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's first statement of the Sages
sub.desc_en: The Sages said that a karpaf larger than beit se'atayim not enclosed for dwelling is only permitted within four cubits.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's second statement of the Sages
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's second statement of the Sages
sub.desc_en: The Sages also said that one may not carry from a private domain to a karmelit.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's explanation for a rock of beit se'atayim
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation for a rock of beit se'atayim
sub.desc_en: For a rock of beit se'atayim, which is permitted to carry throughout, the Sages prohibited carrying from the sea to it or from it to the sea because it is a complete private domain.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's explanation for a rock larger than beit se'atayim
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's explanation for a rock larger than beit se'atayim
sub.desc_en: For a rock larger than beit se'atayim, which is prohibited to carry throughout, the Sages permitted carrying from it to the sea and from the sea to it, lest people mistakenly think it is a complete private domain and come to carry throughout.

Rav Ashi explains the distinction: carrying within the rock is common, but carrying from the rock to the sea or from the sea to the rock is uncommon, so the Sages were more lenient in the latter case.

items.text: Story of the baby whose hot water spilled
items.text_en: Story of the baby whose hot water spilled
items.desc_en: Rabbah instructs to bring hot water from his house for a baby, but Abaye objects because they did not establish an eruv. Rabbah suggests relying on a shituf, but they did not make one. Abaye wanted to object but Rav Yosef stopped him, citing a principle about rabbinic laws. Later, Abaye explains his objection based on a baraita about asking a gentile to perform a shevut.

sub.desc_en: The story opens with a baby whose hot water spilled, and Rabbah instructs to bring hot water from his house.
Abaye objects that they did not establish an עירוב (eruv) to permit carrying.
Rabbah suggests relying on a שיתוף (shituf) or asking a gentile to bring the water.
Abaye objects that they did not make a shituf either, and the suggestion to ask a gentile remains.

sub.text: Abaye's narration and Rav Yosef's principle
sub.text_en: Abaye's narration and Rav Yosef's principle
sub.desc_en: Abaye recounts that he wanted to object but Rav Yosef stopped him, citing a principle from Rav Yehuda that for rabbinic laws one acts first and then raises objections.

Afterward, Abaye explains that his intended objection was based on a ברייתא (baraita) that both sprinkling (for purification) and asking a gentile to perform a מלאכה (forbidden labor) are considered שבות (rabbinic prohibitions).

items.text: Comparison of shevut with and without action
items.text_en: Comparison of shevut with and without action
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the prohibition of asking a non-Jew to perform an action (shevut) to the prohibition of sprinkling water (haza'ah) which is also shevut. It questions whether there is a difference between shevut that involves an action and shevut that does not, citing the example of not telling a non-Jew to heat something.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the prohibition of asking a non-Jew to perform an action (אמירה לגוי) is comparable to the prohibition of sprinkling water (הזאה), both being שבות (rabbinic prohibitions) that do not override the Sabbath.

The Gemara responds that there is a distinction between a שבות that involves an action (הזאה) and one that does not (אמירה לגוי), citing the precedent that the master (Mar) did not tell a non-Jew to heat something.

items.text: Problem of a mevo'ah with two great men
items.text_en: Problem of a mevo'ah with two great men
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye about a mevo'ah (alley) that has two great men like the rabbis, where neither can make an eruv or shituf. Abaye suggests that if he gives them bread in a basket, but since they might ask for it and he cannot give it, the shituf is invalid, as taught in a baraita.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Chanan asks Abaye about a mevo'ah (alley) with two great men like the rabbis, where neither can make an eruv or shituf.
Abaye explains that if he gives them bread in a basket, but since they might ask for it and he cannot give it, the shituf is invalid.
A baraita is cited to support that if one resident requests wine or oil and is not given, the shituf is void.

items.text: Suggestion to give a quarter-log of challah
items.text_en: Suggestion to give a quarter-log of challah
items.desc_en: Abaye suggests that the master (Rabbah bar Rav Chanan) should give them a quarter-log of challah in a barrel, but a baraita states that one does not join in an otzar (storehouse).

sub.desc_en: Abaye suggests giving a quarter-log of challah in a barrel, but a baraita rules that one does not join in an otzar (storehouse).

items.text: Contradiction resolved by Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.text_en: Contradiction resolved by Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
items.desc_en: A contradiction is noted between two baraitot about joining in an otzar. Rav Oshaya resolves it by attributing one to Beit Shammai and the other to Beit Hillel, citing a Mishnah about a corpse in a house with many doors.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one says one may not join in an otzar, the other says one may.
Rav Oshaya resolves the contradiction by attributing one baraita to Beit Shammai and the other to Beit Hillel.

The Gemara cites a Mishnah about a corpse in a house with many doors, establishing the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding when planning to remove the corpse through a specific opening renders the other openings clean.

sub.text: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's positions
sub.text_en: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel's positions
sub.desc_en: Beit Shammai require planning before the death, while Beit Hillel allow planning even after death, paralleling the dispute about joining in an otzar.

items.text: Case of a child whose hot water spilled
items.text_en: Case of a child whose hot water spilled
items.desc_en: Rava instructs to ask the mother if she needs heating, and then a non-Jew can heat on her behalf. Rav Mesharshiya objects that the mother is eating dates, implying she doesn't need heating, but Rava says it's just a minor ailment.

sub.desc_en: Rava instructs to ask the mother if she needs heating, and then a non-Jew can heat on her behalf.
Rav Mesharshiya objects that the mother is eating dates, implying she doesn't need heating.
Rava responds that the mother's eating dates is merely a minor ailment, not a sign she doesn't need heating.

items.text: Bitul reshus from courtyard to courtyard
items.text_en: Bitul reshus from courtyard to courtyard
items.desc_en: Rava plans to move vessels and sit in another courtyard to nullify his domain for the child. Ravina objects based on Shmuel's ruling that there is no bitul reshus from courtyard to courtyard. Rava responds that he follows Rabbi Yochanan who permits it, and questions whether the master holds like Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rava proposes to move vessels from the men's to the women's courtyard and sit there to nullify his domain (בטול רשות) for the child.
Ravina objects, citing Shmuel's ruling that there is no bitul reshus (בטול רשות) from one courtyard to another.
Rava responds that he follows Rabbi Yochanan who permits bitul reshus (בטול רשות) from courtyard to courtyard, and questions whether Ravina holds like Shmuel.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution regarding Rav's position
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution regarding Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the master (Rav) did not simply nullify his domain and have the others nullify theirs in return, given that Rav allows repeated nullification. It answers that Rav actually holds like Shmuel that one cannot nullify and retract, and explains the reason: once one nullifies, he is completely removed from the domain, like a resident of another courtyard, and nullification between courtyards is invalid. The Gemara then gives a different reason for the ruling: to prevent rabbinic law from becoming a mockery.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the master (Rav) did not simply nullify his domain and have the others nullify theirs in return, given that Rav allows repeated nullification.
Rav answers that he actually holds like Shmuel that one cannot nullify and retract.
The Gemara objects that the same reasoning (once nullified, one is removed like a resident of another courtyard) would apply to Rav as well, so why does Rav not nullify?
The Gemara gives a different reason for Rav's ruling: to prevent rabbinic law from becoming a mockery.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel's dispute linked to Tannaim
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel's dispute linked to Tannaim
items.desc_en: The Gemara states the core dispute: Rav permits repeated nullification, Shmuel forbids it. It suggests they argue over the same issue as the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer. Rav defends his view even according to Rabbi Eliezer, arguing that Rabbi Eliezer only limited nullification to the house, not to complete removal. Shmuel defends his view even according to the Sages, arguing that they only said that what was not nullified remains, but what was nullified is completely removed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the core dispute: Rav permits repeated nullification, Shmuel forbids it.
The Gemara suggests that Rav and Shmuel's dispute aligns with the Tannaitic dispute between the Sages and Rabbi Eliezer.
Rav defends his view even according to Rabbi Eliezer, arguing that Rabbi Eliezer only limited nullification to the house, not to complete removal.
Shmuel defends his view even according to the Sages, arguing that they only said that what was not nullified remains, but what was nullified is completely removed.

items.text: Dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about one who nullified and then carried
items.text_en: Dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda about one who nullified and then carried
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Chana cites a Tannaitic dispute: if one nullified his domain and then carried out, Rabbi Meir says he prohibits whether intentionally or unintentionally, while Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes. The Gemara initially suggests this reflects the dispute about repeated nullification. Rava rejects this, explaining that all agree one cannot retract nullification; the dispute is about penalizing the unintentional case to prevent intentional violations.

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Chana citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Chana citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Chana cites a Tannaitic dispute: if one nullified his domain and then carried out, Rabbi Meir prohibits whether intentionally or unintentionally, while Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes.
The Gemara suggests that the dispute reflects the earlier disagreement about whether one can retract nullification (רב (Rav) permits, שמואל (Shmuel) forbids).
Rava rejects the suggestion, explaining that all agree one cannot retract nullification; the dispute is about penalizing the unintentional case to prevent intentional violations.

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi states that Rav and Shmuel's dispute is directly about the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, without the earlier qualifications.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi resolves that Rav and Shmuel's dispute is directly about the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages, without the earlier qualifications.

items.text: Baraita about a Sadducee neighbor and the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Baraita about a Sadducee neighbor and the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a baraita about a Sadducee living with Rabban Gamliel. It clarifies that the Sadducee is considered like a gentile, but Rabban Gamliel disagrees. The baraita recounts that Rabban Gamliel told his sons to hurry and carry out their items before the Sadducee carries out and prohibits them, since he had nullified his domain. Rabbi Yehuda reports a different version. The Gemara questions whether the Sadducee's carrying after the others would not prohibit, implying a dispute about the effect of nullification.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with Rabban Gamliel's story about a Sadducee neighbor, and the Gemara immediately questions the Sadducee's identity.
The Gemara asks: 'Who mentioned a Sadducee?' — implying the baraita is missing context.
The Gemara explains that the baraita is missing a clause: it originally stated that a Sadducee is like a gentile, but Rabban Gamliel disagrees and says a Sadducee is not like a gentile.

A supporting baraita is cited: one who lives with a gentile, Sadducee, or Boethusian — they prohibit; Rabban Gamliel says they do not prohibit, and the story is told with Rabban Gamliel telling his sons to hurry before the 'abomination' carries out, since he nullified his domain to them — the words of Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yehuda reports a different version: Rabban Gamliel told his sons to hurry and do their needs in the alleyway before dark, lest the Sadducee carry out and prohibit.
The Gemara questions: Does this imply that if they carry out first and then he carries out, he does not prohibit? — raising a dispute about the effect of nullification after carrying.

items.text: Opening Mishnah citation
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah citation
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that one who gave his rights and then carried, whether inadvertently or intentionally, prohibits (the alleyway) — according to Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah stating that one who gave his rights and then carried, whether inadvertently or intentionally, prohibits the alleyway — according to Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Rav Yosef and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Rav Yosef and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef suggests the Mishnah should read 'does not prohibit,' but Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the alleyway residents have taken possession and when they have not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef proposes emending the Mishnah to read 'does not prohibit' instead of 'prohibits' to resolve the contradiction.
Abaye resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between when the alleyway residents have taken possession of the alley and when they have not.

items.text: Baraita with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Baraita with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited: before giving his rights, one who carried can nullify — Rabbi Meir says even if intentional; Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes. After giving rights, Rabbi Meir says he prohibits; Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes, and the baraita concludes that if the residents took possession, he does not prohibit.

sub.desc_en: The baraita cites Rabbi Meir's position that before giving rights, one who carried can nullify whether intentionally or unintentionally, and Rabbi Yehuda's distinction that only unintentional carrying allows nullification.

The baraita continues with the case after giving rights: Rabbi Meir says he prohibits whether intentional or unintentional, Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes, and concludes that if residents took possession, he does not prohibit at all.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's language
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Yehuda's language
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Rabbi Yehuda says in another formulation: 'Hurry and do your needs in the alleyway before it gets dark and he prohibits you,' implying the resident is a gentile. But we learned 'until he carries' — a contradiction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara points out a contradiction: Rabbi Yehuda's alternative formulation implies the resident is a gentile, but the Mishnah says 'until he carries out' (implying a Jew).

items.text: Two answers to the contradiction
items.text_en: Two answers to the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers two answers: either read 'until he carries out the day,' or distinguish between an apostate who desecrates Shabbat privately versus publicly.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers the first answer: read the Mishnah's phrase as 'until he carries out the day' (i.e., until sunset), not 'until he carries out an object.'
The Gemara offers the second answer: distinguish between an apostate who desecrates Shabbat privately (צנעא) — who can nullify his domain — versus one who does so publicly (פרהסיא) — who cannot.

items.text: Identifying the Tanna of a baraita
items.text_en: Identifying the Tanna of a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to whom is the baraita that an apostate with 'gillui panim' cannot nullify rights? It concludes it follows Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: according to which Tanna does the baraita go that an apostate with 'gillui panim' (public face) cannot nullify rights, and questions whether 'gillui panim' itself constitutes an apostate.
The Gemara resolves: the baraita means an apostate with public face (gillui panim) cannot nullify rights, and it follows Rabbi Yehuda's position.

items.text: Anecdote about a threshing-shed apostate
items.text_en: Anecdote about a threshing-shed apostate
items.desc_en: A story: one who went out with a threshing-shed burden covered it upon seeing Rabbi Yehuda Nasi'a, and the Gemara comments that such a person can nullify rights according to Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates a story about a man who went out with a threshing-shed burden and covered it upon seeing Rabbi Yehuda Nasi'a, and comments that such a person can nullify rights according to Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on the definition of a Jewish apostate
items.text_en: Rav Huna and Rav Nachman on the definition of a Jewish apostate
items.desc_en: Rav Huna defines a Jewish apostate as one who publicly desecrates Shabbat. Rav Nachman questions this: according to Rabbi Meir, who holds one suspected of one sin is suspected of all, even any other prohibition would suffice; according to the Rabbis, they hold one is not suspected of all.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna defines a Jewish apostate (מומר) as one who publicly desecrates Shabbat.
Rav Nachman asks Rav Huna: according to which authority is this definition?
Rav Nachman objects: if according to Rabbi Meir, who holds that one suspected of one sin is suspected of all, even any other prohibition would suffice.
Rav Nachman objects: if according to the Rabbis, who hold that one suspected of one sin is not suspected of all, the definition is also problematic.

items.text: Gemara's clarification on the mumar's ability to nullify reshus
items.text_en: Gemara's clarification on the mumar's ability to nullify reshus
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the earlier statement refers to a mumar who gives or nullifies reshus, citing a baraita that distinguishes between a mumar who observes Shabbat in public and one who does not. The baraita further explains that a Jew can take and give reshus, while a gentile must rent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the earlier statement refers to a mumar (apostate) for idolatry (עבודה זרה).
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak explains that the statement refers to giving or nullifying reshus (domain rights).
A baraita is cited distinguishing between a mumar who observes Shabbat in public (משמר שבתו בשוק) and one who does not, regarding nullification of reshus.
The baraita explains that a Jew can take and give reshus, while a gentile must rent (משכיר), and that a verbal declaration suffices without formal acquisition (זכייה).

items.text: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and the baraita about mumar
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's alternative explanation and the baraita about mumar
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi argues that the earlier tanna equates Shabbat with idolatry in severity. He cites a baraita that excludes a mumar from certain laws but accepts offerings from other sinners. The Gemara resolves contradictions in the baraita by distinguishing between a mumar for the entire Torah and one for a single matter, concluding that the baraita refers to a mumar for idolatry and public Shabbat desecration.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi asserts that the earlier tanna equates Shabbat with idolatry in severity.
A baraita is cited that excludes a mumar from offerings, but accepts offerings from other sinners except a mumar, one who pours wine for idolatry, and one who publicly desecrates Shabbat.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: the baraita first excludes a mumar, then says offerings are accepted from sinners.
The Gemara resolves: the first clause refers to a mumar for the entire Torah, the middle clause to a mumar for a single matter.
The Gemara questions the final clause: if the mumar there is for the whole Torah it repeats the first clause; if for one matter it contradicts the middle clause.
The Gemara resolves that the baraita refers to a mumar for idolatry and public Shabbat desecration, concluding that idolatry and Shabbat are equivalent.

items.text: Mishnah: Laws of a courtyard where one forgot to join the eiruv
items.text_en: Mishnah: Laws of a courtyard where one forgot to join the eiruv
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one resident forgot to join the eiruv, his house is forbidden for carrying in and out for him and others, while their houses are permitted. If they gave him their reshus, he is permitted but they are forbidden. If there were two such residents, they forbid each other. Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel dispute when reshus can be given, and Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah dispute whether one who gave reshus and then carried out forbids.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of a courtyard where one resident forgot to join the eiruv, stating that his house is forbidden for carrying in and out for him and others, while their houses are permitted.
The Mishnah continues: if they gave him their reshus (domain), he is permitted but they are forbidden.
The Mishnah states that if there were two such residents, they forbid each other, and explains the principle: one gives and takes reshus, two give but do not take reshus.
The Mishnah records the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel regarding when reshus can be given: Beit Shammai says from before nightfall, Beit Hillel says after dark.
Rabbi Meir states that one who gave his reshus and then carried out, whether inadvertently or intentionally, forbids.
Rabbi Yehudah disputes: if done intentionally he forbids, if inadvertently he does not forbid.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's first case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah says his house is forbidden but his courtyard is permitted. It explains that the case is where he nullified reshus of his courtyard but not his house, as one can dwell in a house without a courtyard. It then explains that their houses are permitted to him because he is considered a guest.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's distinction between the house being forbidden and the courtyard being permitted, asking how this is possible.
The Gemara answers that the case is where he nullified the reshus of his courtyard but not his house, since one can dwell in a house without a courtyard.
The Gemara explains that their houses are permitted to him because he is considered a guest (אורח) relative to them.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's second case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's second case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why when they give him reshus, he is permitted and they are forbidden, suggesting they should be considered guests. It answers that one person among five is a guest, but five among one are not. It then infers that one can nullify and then nullify again, and clarifies that the Mishnah refers to giving reshus from the outset.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why when they give him reshus, he is permitted and they are forbidden, suggesting they should be considered guests.
The Gemara answers that one person among five is a guest, but five among one are not.
The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that one can nullify and then nullify again.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah refers to giving reshus from the outset, not after the fact.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's third case and the principle of one giving reshus
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's third case and the principle of one giving reshus
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the case of two residents forbidding each other is necessary even if one later nullifies his reshus to the other, because at the time of nullification he had no permission in the courtyard. It then questions why the Mishnah states that one gives reshus, as this is obvious, and explains that the latter clause about two giving reshus is necessary to teach that they cannot take reshus.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's case that one may nullify and then re-nullify his reshus.
The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's phrase 'they gave him their reshus' refers to an initial grant, not a repeated one.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states the obvious case of two residents forbidding each other.
The Gemara explains that the case is necessary even if one later nullifies his reshus to the other, because at the time of nullification he had no permission in the courtyard.
The Gemara questions why the Mishnah states that one gives reshus, as this is obvious from earlier clauses.
The Gemara explains that the latter clause about two giving reshus is necessary to teach that they cannot take reshus.

items.text: Gemara's initial clarification of the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial clarification of the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains why the Mishnah states that one does not take permission, teaching that even if they say 'acquire on condition to transfer,' it is ineffective.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why the Mishnah teaches that one does not take permission, suggesting a concern that one might come to nullify the eruv.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that even if the residents say 'acquire on condition to transfer,' the permission is ineffective.

items.text: Abaye's question to Rabbah about nullifying to each individual
items.text_en: Abaye's question to Rabbah about nullifying to each individual
items.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one who forgot to join the eruv must nullify his rights to each of the five residents individually. Rabbah answers that he must nullify to each one.

sub.desc_en: Abaye asks Rabbah whether one who forgot to join the eruv must nullify his rights to each of the five residents individually.
Rabbah answers that he must nullify to each one.

items.text: Objection from the Mishnah and Rabbah's resolution
items.text_en: Objection from the Mishnah and Rabbah's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that seems to contradict Rabbah, showing that one who did not join the eruv gives his rights to one who did, implying no need to nullify to each. Rabbah resolves that the case involves a resident who died, so only one remains.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that seems to contradict Rabbah, showing that one who did not join the eruv gives his rights to one who did, implying no need to nullify to each.
The Gemara continues citing the Mishnah, listing further restrictions on transferring rights.
The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's first clause, questioning how it can apply if there is only one resident who joined the eruv.
Rabbah resolves the objection by explaining that the Mishnah's case involves a resident who died, so only one remains to give rights.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbah's resolution from the Mishnah's latter clauses
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbah's resolution from the Mishnah's latter clauses
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbah: if the resident died, why does the Mishnah forbid one who joined the eruv from giving rights to one who did not? It concludes that the Mishnah's cases are distinct: one with a living resident and one with a deceased.
