It explains that Rabbi Yochanan refers to a case where the partition lacks four by four handbreadths, allowing both sides to bring up food, while the Mishnah refers to a case where it has four by four, allowing only ascending.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan said 'bring up' (מעלין) but the Mishnah says 'ascend' (עולין), implying only ascending is allowed.
The Gemara resolves: the Mishnah refers to a partition with four by four handbreadths (only ascending), while Rabbi Yochanan refers to one without (both sides may bring up food).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and Rav's objection
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan's principle and Rav's objection
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Dimi's report that Rabbi Yochanan permits both public and private domain residents to use a place lacking four by four handbreadths, provided they do not exchange items. Rav disagrees in rabbinic domains because the Sages strengthened their decrees more than Torah law.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Dimi's report
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Dimi's report
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Dimi's report that Rabbi Yochanan permits both public and private domain residents to use a place lacking four by four handbreadths, provided they do not exchange items.
The Gemara asks whether Rav disagrees with Rav Dimi's report.
The Gemara answers that in Torah-level domains, Rav would agree.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves rabbinic domains, where the Sages strengthened their decrees more than Torah law.

items.text: Wall between two courtyards: giving to the easier side
items.text_en: Wall between two courtyards: giving to the easier side
items.desc_en: Rabbah citing Rav Huna citing Rav Nachman rules: a wall between two courtyards, one side ten handbreadths high and the other level with the ground, is given to the side level with the ground because its use is easy for that side and difficult for the other.

sub.text: Rabbah citing Rav Huna citing Rav Nachman
sub.text_en: Rabbah citing Rav Huna citing Rav Nachman
sub.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rav Huna citing Rav Nachman rules that a wall between two courtyards, with one side ten handbreadths high and the other level with the ground, is given to the side level with the ground.
The gemara explains the rationale: the wall is given to the side for which its use is easy (בנחת) and difficult for the other, and the rule is to give it to the side with easy access.

items.text: Trench between two courtyards: similar ruling and necessity
items.text_en: Trench between two courtyards: similar ruling and necessity
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi citing Rav Nachman gives a parallel ruling for a trench: it is given to the side level with the ground. The Gemara explains why both cases are necessary: a wall might be considered easier to use due to height, and a trench due to lack of fear, so each ruling is needed.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rav Nachman rules that a trench between two courtyards, with one side ten handbreadths deep and the other level with the ground, is given to the side level with the ground because that side uses it with ease.

The Gemara asks why both the wall case and the trench case are necessary, suggesting that without both, one might mistakenly think the trench is not given to the side level with the ground because people do not use deep spaces.

The Gemara resolves that both rulings are necessary: the trench case is needed because using it lacks fear, and the wall case is needed because using it involves fear, so each ruling teaches a distinct point.

items.text: Diminishing the wall's height and its effect
items.text_en: Diminishing the wall's height and its effect
items.desc_en: If one reduces the wall's height, and the reduced part has four handbreadths, one may use the entire wall; otherwise only opposite the reduction. The Gemara questions this, and Ravina explains it refers to removing a brick from the top.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states a rule: if one reduces the wall's height and the reduced part has four handbreadths, one may use the entire wall; otherwise only opposite the reduction.
The Gemara questions the logic: if the reduction is effective, why not use the entire wall; if ineffective, why even use opposite the reduction?
Ravina explains that the case is where one removed a brick from the top of the wall, so the reduction is partial and the wall remains usable opposite the removed brick.

items.text: Placing a cup to diminish and the issue of a movable object
items.text_en: Placing a cup to diminish and the issue of a movable object
items.desc_en: Rav Yechiel says placing a cup reduces the height. The Gemara objects that a movable object does not diminish. It answers that the cup is attached to the ground. Further objection from a baraita about a cake in coals is answered by saying the cup has handles (אוגניים).

sub.desc_en: Rav Yechiel states that placing a cup upside down reduces the height of a wall for the purpose of allowing use.
The Gemara objects that a cup is a movable object (דבר הניטל בשבת) and such an object cannot diminish a partition.
The Gemara answers that the case is where the cup is attached to the ground, making it immovable.
The Gemara objects further by citing a baraita about a cake (חררה) buried in coals that is still considered movable even when partially covered, implying attachment does not help.
The Gemara resolves the objection by explaining that the cup has handles (אוגניים), which make it unsuitable for use as a vessel and thus it is considered attached.

items.text: Opening statement about leaves and the need for tools
items.text_en: Opening statement about leaves and the need for tools
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita stating that leaves partially exposed are not subject to kilayim, tithes, or Sabbatical year laws, and may be taken on Shabbat. It clarifies that this applies only when a pick and ax are needed to detach them.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states that partially exposed leaves are not subject to kilayim, tithes, or Sabbatical year laws, and may be taken on Shabbat.
The Gemara clarifies that the leniency applies only when a pick and ax are needed to detach the leaves.

items.text: Egyptian vs. Tyrian ladder and the principle of movability
items.text_en: Egyptian vs. Tyrian ladder and the principle of movability
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that an Egyptian ladder does not reduce the required height, while a Tyrian ladder does. Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi for the reason, and Rav Ashi cites Rav Hamnuna quoting Rav: because an Egyptian ladder is movable on Shabbat, and anything movable on Shabbat does not reduce. The Gemara objects that a Tyrian ladder is also movable, but answers that its weight fixes it in place.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that an Egyptian ladder does not reduce the required height, while a Tyrian ladder does, and Beit Rabbi Yannai defines an Egyptian ladder as one without four rungs.
Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi for the reason why an Egyptian ladder does not reduce the required height.

sub.text: Rav Ashi's answer citing Rav Hamnuna citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer citing Rav Hamnuna citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi answers that an Egyptian ladder is a movable object (דבר שנטל בשבת) on Shabbat, and anything movable on Shabbat does not reduce the required height.
The Gemara objects that a Tyrian ladder is also movable on Shabbat, so it should also not reduce.
The Gemara answers that the Tyrian ladder's weight fixes it in place (כובדו קובעו), so it is not considered movable on Shabbat.

items.text: Abaye's case of two ladders on opposite sides of a wall
items.text_en: Abaye's case of two ladders on opposite sides of a wall
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if a wall between two courtyards is ten handbreadths high, and a ladder four handbreadths wide is placed on each side, with less than three handbreadths between them, the ladders reduce the wall's height. If the gap is three handbreadths or more, they do not. However, if the wall itself is four handbreadths wide, even a large gap does not prevent reduction.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that a wall ten handbreadths high between two courtyards is reduced by ladders four handbreadths wide on each side if the gap between them is less than three handbreadths, but not if the gap is three or more.
Abaye qualifies that if the wall itself is four handbreadths wide, even a large gap between ladders does not prevent reduction.

items.text: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's case of stacked platforms
items.text_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye's case of stacked platforms
items.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye rules that if one builds a platform on top of another, and the lower platform is four handbreadths wide, it reduces the height. Alternatively, if the lower is less than four but the upper is four, and there is less than three handbreadths between them, it also reduces.

sub.desc_en: Rav Beivai bar Abaye rules that stacked platforms reduce the height if the lower is four handbreadths wide, or if the upper is four and the gap is less than three.

items.text: Rav Nachman's case of a ladder with projecting rungs
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's case of a ladder with projecting rungs
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha rules that a ladder whose rungs project outward reduces the height if the lowest rung is four handbreadths wide. Alternatively, if the lowest rung is less than four but the upper rung is four, and there is less than three handbreadths between them, it also reduces.

sub.text: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuha
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that a ladder with projecting rungs reduces the partition height if the lowest rung is four handbreadths wide, or if the lowest is less than four but the upper is four and there is less than three handbreadths between them.

items.text: Opening rule about a ziz and ladder
items.text_en: Opening rule about a ziz and ladder
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a projection (ziz) extending four by four handbreadths from a wall, upon which a ladder of any size is placed, reduces the wall's height. This applies only if the ladder is placed on top of the ziz, not alongside it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the rule that a ziz (projection) of four by four handbreadths with any ladder placed on top reduces the wall's height, but only if the ladder is on the ziz, not alongside it.

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on walls of 19 and 20 cubits
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on walls of 19 and 20 cubits
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh states that a wall of 19 cubits requires one ziz to permit it, while a wall of 20 cubits requires two zizim. Rav Chisda adds that the two zizim must be placed not directly opposite each other.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Avuh rules that a wall of 19 cubits requires one ziz (projection) to permit carrying.
Rav Nachman bar Avuh adds that a wall of 20 cubits requires two zizim to permit it.
Rav Chisda qualifies that the two zizim must be placed not directly opposite each other.

items.text: Rav Huna's ruling on a pillar with a peg
items.text_en: Rav Huna's ruling on a pillar with a peg
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a pillar in the public domain, ten handbreadths high and four wide, can be reduced by inserting any peg. Rav Adda bar Ahavah limits this to a peg at least three handbreadths high, while Abaye and Rava disagree. Rav Ashi argues that even a peg three handbreadths high is effective because one might hang something on it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that a pillar in the public domain, ten handbreadths high and four wide, can be reduced by inserting any peg.
Rav Adda bar Ahavah limits the ruling to a peg at least three handbreadths high.
Abaye and Rava disagree, arguing that even a peg less than three handbreadths high is effective.

sub.text: Gemara's explanation of Abaye and Rava's reasoning
sub.text_en: Gemara's explanation of Abaye and Rava's reasoning
sub.desc_en: The gemara explains that Abaye and Rava hold that a peg less than three handbreadths is not usable for hanging anything.
Rav Ashi argues that even a peg three handbreadths high is effective because one might hang something on it.

items.text: Rav Acha's question about filling the pillar with pegs
items.text_en: Rav Acha's question about filling the pillar with pegs
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi about a pillar filled entirely with pegs. Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yochanan's principle that a pit and its rim combine to ten handbreadths, and applies the same logic here: one can place something on the pegs and use them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if a pillar in the public domain is filled entirely with pegs, does it still constitute a valid partition for an alleyway?
Rav Ashi cites Rabbi Yochanan's principle that a pit and its rim combine to ten handbreadths, implying the same logic applies here.
The gemara objects: how can the pillar be used if it is filled with pegs and one cannot stand on it?
The gemara resolves: just as in the pit case one can place something on the rim and use it, here too one can place something on the pegs and use them.

items.text: Debate on ladder length for a ten-cubit wall
items.text_en: Debate on ladder length for a ten-cubit wall
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a ten-cubit wall requires a fourteen-cubit ladder. Rav Yosef says even thirteen and a bit, Abaye says even eleven and a bit, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua says even seven and a bit.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that a ten-cubit wall requires a fourteen-cubit ladder to permit carrying.
Rav Yosef says even a ladder of thirteen cubits and a bit suffices.
Abaye says even a ladder of eleven cubits and a bit suffices.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua says even a ladder of seven cubits and a bit suffices.

items.text: Rav's statement about a vertical ladder and Shmuel's explanation
items.text_en: Rav's statement about a vertical ladder and Shmuel's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav states that a vertical ladder reduces the wall, but he does not know the reason. Shmuel explains that Rav's reasoning is based on the case of a bench placed on another bench, where the combined height is usable.

sub.desc_en: Rav states that a vertical ladder reduces the wall, but admits he does not know the reason.
Shmuel explains that Rav's reasoning is based on the case of a bench placed on another bench, where the combined height is usable.

items.text: Rabbah and Rav Yosef on palm trees and ladders in Babylonia
items.text_en: Rabbah and Rav Yosef on palm trees and ladders in Babylonia
items.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Chiyya says that palm trees in Babylonia do not require fixing (keva) because their weight fixes them. Rav Yosef in the name of Rabbi Oshaya says the same about ladders. The Gemara notes that the one who says ladders certainly includes palm trees, but the one who says palm trees excludes ladders.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah in the name of Rabbi Chiyya states that palm trees in Babylonia do not require fixing (קֶבַע) because their weight fixes them.
Rav Yosef in the name of Rabbi Oshaya states the same principle regarding ladders in Babylonia.
The Gemara clarifies that the one who says ladders certainly includes palm trees, but the one who says palm trees excludes ladders.

items.text: Rav Yosef's query about ladders and reeds
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's query about ladders and reeds
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rabbah about a case with a ladder on each side and reeds in the middle, and Rabbah responds that the foot cannot ascend. He then asks about reeds on each side with a ladder in the middle, and Rabbah says the foot can ascend.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rabbah about a case with a ladder on each side and reeds in the middle, whether the combined width of four handbreadths is valid.
Rabbah answers that the sole of the foot cannot ascend on the reeds, so the ladder is invalid.
Rav Yosef asks about the reverse case: reeds on each side and a ladder in the middle.
Rabbah answers that the sole of the foot can ascend on the ladder in the middle, so the combined width is valid.

items.text: Initial inquiry about a groove in the wall
items.text_en: Initial inquiry about a groove in the wall
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the dimensions needed for a groove carved in a wall to complete an eruv. The answer distinguishes between a groove that is entirely in the wall and one that is partially carved, based on whether the person can stand upright.

items.text: Rav Yosef's inquiry about a tree as a ladder
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's inquiry about a tree as a ladder
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef asks Rav Sheshet whether a tree used as a ladder for an eruv is permitted. The Gemara considers the opinions of Rabbi and the Rabbis, questioning whether the leniency for a tree applies only at twilight or all day, and whether the Rabbis would permit it as a mere opening.

items.text: Inquiry about an asherah as a ladder
items.text_en: Inquiry about an asherah as a ladder
items.desc_en: The Gemara similarly asks about using an asherah (idolatrous tree) as a ladder. It considers the view of Rabbi Yehuda, who permits purchasing a house with forbidden benefit, and the Rabbis, again suggesting it might be considered a mere opening.

items.text: Rav Chisda's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to the previous ruling, arguing that a tree, whose prohibition stems from Shabbat, should be forbidden, while an asherah, prohibited for other reasons, should be permitted. The Gemara cites a tradition from Rabbi Elazar or Rabbi Avahu in the name of Rabbi Yochanan that supports this distinction.

items.text: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
items.text_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak's alternative version
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak presents a different version of the dispute: the tree case is a disagreement between Rabbi and the Rabbis, while the asherah case is between Rabbi Yehuda and the Rabbis.

items.text: Mishnah: Trench between two courtyards
items.text_en: Mishnah: Trench between two courtyards
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a trench ten handbreadths deep and four wide between two courtyards. If filled with straw or stubble, it does not separate them; if filled with earth or pebbles, it does. A board four handbreadths wide placed over it allows them to merge.

items.text: Gemara: Straw as a partition or barrier
items.text_en: Gemara: Straw as a partition or barrier
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why straw does not separate, citing a baraita where a straw heap ten handbreadths high does separate. Abaye explains that for a partition, straw is effective, but for blocking a trench, it only works if nullified. The Gemara then questions whether earth always blocks, citing a case where nullification is required.

items.text: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question on the Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a pile of straw between two courtyards that is ten handbreadths high allows separate eruvin. Rav Huna suggests the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yosi's view on nullification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that a pile of straw between two courtyards that is ten handbreadths high allows separate eruvin, implying that if not nullified, it is not considered nullified.
Rav Huna answers that the Mishnah's ruling follows Rabbi Yosi's view on nullification of straw.

items.text: Objection to Rav Huna from a baraita
items.text_en: Objection to Rav Huna from a baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosi's position in a baraita is the opposite of what Rav Huna claims, as Rabbi Yosi says straw that will not be removed is like dirt and nullified, while dirt that will be removed is like straw and not nullified.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yosi's position in a baraita contradicts Rav Huna's claim, as Rabbi Yosi rules that straw not destined for removal is like dirt and nullified, while dirt destined for removal is like straw and not nullified.

items.text: Rav Asi's alternative attribution
items.text_en: Rav Asi's alternative attribution
items.desc_en: Rav Asi suggests that the Mishnah in Eruvin follows Rabbi Yosi, not the Mishnah in Ohalot, resolving the contradiction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi resolves the contradiction by attributing the Mishnah in Eruvin to Rabbi Yosi, not the Mishnah in Ohalot.

items.text: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua and Rav Ashi's rejections
items.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua and Rav Ashi's rejections
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua rejects the comparison to impurity laws, noting that even a money belt is nullified on Shabbat. Rav Ashi rejects the comparison to a trench, as a trench is meant for filling but a house is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua objects to the comparison between impurity and Shabbat, arguing that on Shabbat even a money belt is nullified.
Rav Ashi objects to the comparison between a house and a trench, noting that a trench is meant for filling but a house is not.

items.text: Rava's rulings on the board and balconies
items.text_en: Rava's rulings on the board and balconies
items.desc_en: Rava rules that a board placed widthwise is effective only if four handbreadths wide, but lengthwise any width suffices. He also discusses two balconies opposite each other, requiring a gap of less than three handbreadths to be considered a curved wall.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if one placed a board four handbreadths wide on a balcony, it permits carrying.

Rava rules that the Mishnah's requirement of four handbreadths applies only when the board is placed widthwise, but lengthwise any width suffices because it reduces the opening to less than four handbreadths.
Rava further rules that two balconies opposite each other are considered a curved wall (גזוזטרא עקומה) if the gap between them is less than three handbreadths, permitting carrying between them.

items.text: Mishnah: Straw pile between two courtyards
items.text_en: Mishnah: Straw pile between two courtyards
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a straw pile ten handbreadths high between two courtyards allows each to make a separate eruv, but if it is less than ten, they must make one eruv together.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a straw pile ten handbreadths high between two courtyards allows each to make a separate eruv, but if it is less than ten, they must make one eruv together.

items.text: Gemara on feeding from the straw and the baraita
items.text_en: Gemara on feeding from the straw and the baraita
items.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one may not put straw into his basket to feed his animal, but the Gemara questions this from a baraita that permits it. The resolution distinguishes between a house with a roof, where the reduction is noticeable, and an open pile, where it is not.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna rules that one may not put straw into his basket to feed his animal on Shabbat.
The Gemara questions Rav Huna's ruling by citing his own statement that one may stand an animal on grass but not on מוקצה (set-aside items), implying that straw is מוקצה and thus forbidden.
The Gemara resolves that Rav Huna's ruling refers to standing the animal in front of the straw so it eats on its own, not actively placing straw into a basket.
The Gemara objects by citing a baraita that explicitly permits putting straw into one's basket to feed an animal in a house between two courtyards.

The Gemara resolves that in a house with walls and a ceiling, the reduction in straw is noticeable, but in an open pile between courtyards it is not, so the baraita's permission does not apply to Rav Huna's case.

items.text: Inference about partitions and Abaye's explanation
items.text_en: Inference about partitions and Abaye's explanation
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that even if the roof is high, a ten-handbreadth partition is valid, proving that partitions need not reach the ceiling. Abaye explains the case involves a house of slightly less than thirteen handbreadths with ten of straw, and Rav Huna bar Yehoshua allows even a ten-handbreadth house.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah that a partition of ten handbreadths is valid even if the roof is high, proving that partitions need not reach the ceiling.
Abaye explains that the case involves a house of slightly less than thirteen handbreadths with ten handbreadths of straw, so the partition effectively reaches the ceiling.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua allows the inference even in a house of exactly ten handbreadths, arguing that the partition is valid without reaching the ceiling.

items.text: Minimum measure of straw for a partition
items.text_en: Minimum measure of straw for a partition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah stated that a partition of straw requires seven handbreadths and a bit. The Gemara explains that this is because any gap less than three handbreadths is considered closed (lavud).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's measure of seven handbreadths and a bit for a straw partition is because any gap less than three handbreadths is considered closed (lavud).

items.text: Reconciling the Mishnah's 'from ten' with Rav Huna's view
items.text_en: Reconciling the Mishnah's 'from ten' with Rav Huna's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah's phrase 'from ten' fits with Rav Huna's opinion that a partition must be ten handbreadths. It answers that 'from ten' means 'by virtue of ten' (i.e., the partition is considered as if it were ten).

items.text: Are new residents on Shabbat prohibited?
items.text_en: Are new residents on Shabbat prohibited?
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both are prohibited, implying that new residents arriving on Shabbat are prohibited. The Gemara deflects this by suggesting that the case involves residents who moved in yesterday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's statement that both are prohibited that new residents arriving on Shabbat are prohibited.
The Gemara deflects the inference by suggesting that the case involves residents who moved in yesterday, not today.

items.text: The remedy: locking or nullifying
items.text_en: The remedy: locking or nullifying
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says one locks his house and nullifies his domain. The Gemara notes the redundancy and explains that the Mishnah means either locking or nullifying. Alternatively, both are needed because if he only locks, he might come to carry.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the remedy: one locks his house and nullifies his domain.
The Gemara asks why the Mishnah mentions two actions (locking and nullifying) when one would suffice.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah means either locking or nullifying, not both.
Alternatively, both are needed because if he only locks, he might come to carry.

items.text: One is prohibited, his friend is permitted
items.text_en: One is prohibited, his friend is permitted
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one is prohibited while his friend is permitted. The Gemara explains that this teaches that one cannot nullify his domain and then retract the nullification.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: Alternatively, perhaps it means both, since he entered the alleyway, he comes to carry.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the Mishnah teaches that one cannot nullify his domain and then retract the nullification.

items.text: The case of a straw heap between two Shabbat boundaries
items.text_en: The case of a straw heap between two Shabbat boundaries
items.desc_en: The Mishnah applies the same rule to a straw heap between two Shabbat boundaries. The Gemara notes that this is obvious, but it is necessary according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that Shabbat boundaries are biblical, to prevent confusion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers: He is prohibited and his friend is permitted, teaching that one cannot nullify and then re-nullify.
The Gemara asks why this ruling is not obvious.
The Gemara explains that the ruling is necessary according to Rabbi Akiva, who holds that Shabbat boundaries are biblical.
The Gemara resolves that without the Mishnah's ruling, one might have feared a decree due to confusion, but the Mishnah teaches that no such decree is needed.

items.text: Mishnah: How to establish a shituf in a mavoi
items.text_en: Mishnah: How to establish a shituf in a mavoi
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes the procedure for shituf in a mavoi: one places a barrel and declares it for all residents, acquiring it on their behalf through his adult son, daughter, Hebrew slave, or wife, but not through minors or Canaanite slaves, as their hand is like his.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by describing the procedure for establishing a shituf in a mavoi: one places a barrel and declares it for all residents, acquiring it on their behalf through his adult son, daughter, Hebrew slave, or wife.
The Mishnah adds the restriction that one may not acquire through minors or Canaanite slaves, because their hand is considered like his own (i.e., they cannot acquire for others).

items.text: Gemara: Rulings of the elders of Pumpedita
items.text_en: Gemara: Rulings of the elders of Pumpedita
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda requires the barrel for shituf to be lifted a handbreadth off the ground. Rava notes that the elders of Pumpedita said two things: this, and that one who sanctifies wine must taste a cheekful. Rav Chaviva adds that they also said one may make a bonfire for an animal on Shabbat, but not for a sick person except in cold weather. Rav Chiya bar Avin permits a bonfire for one who bled and became chilled, even in summer. Amemar adds that they also discussed the definition of an asherah tree.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that the barrel for shituf of alleyways must be lifted a handbreadth off the ground.
Rava reports that the elders of Pumpedita said two things: this ruling about the barrel, and that one who sanctifies wine must taste a cheekful to fulfill the obligation.

sub.text: Rav Chaviva citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chaviva citing Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chaviva adds that the elders also said, in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel, that one may make a bonfire for an animal on Shabbat.
The Gemara infers from the statement that a bonfire is permitted for an animal but not for a sick person, and in rainy season but not in summer.

sub.text: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Avin citing Shmuel permits a bonfire for one who bled and became chilled, even in the summer solstice.
Amemar adds that the elders also discussed the definition of an asherah tree (idolatrous tree).
Rav defines an asherah tree as any tree that priests guard.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on dates for beer
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on dates for beer
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Shmuel's statement that the mishnah refers to a case where the residents say these dates are for the beer of the house of Nitzrefei which they drink on their holiday. Amemar adds that the elders of Pumbedita said the halakha follows Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the mishnah's rule that one may not taste the fruits of the partnership.
Shmuel explains that the mishnah refers to dates designated for the beer of the house of Nitzrefei, which they drink on their holiday.
Amemar reports that the elders of Pumbedita ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Shmuel.

items.text: Baraita on shittufei mavo'ot
items.text_en: Baraita on shittufei mavo'ot
items.desc_en: A baraita is brought describing how to establish a shittuf in a mavoy: one brings a barrel of wine, oil, dates, dried figs, or other fruits. If from his own, he must formally transfer ownership (zikkui); if from theirs, he must inform them. He lifts a handbreadth from the ground.

sub.desc_en: A baraita is brought describing the procedure for establishing a shittuf in a mavoy: one brings a barrel of wine, oil, dates, dried figs, or other fruits; if from his own, he must formally transfer ownership (zikkui); if from theirs, he must inform them; and he lifts a handbreadth from the ground.

items.text: Rav and Shmuel dispute zikkui for eiruvin
items.text_en: Rav and Shmuel dispute zikkui for eiruvin
items.desc_en: An explicit dispute is recorded: for shittufei mavo'ot, Rav says no zikkui needed, Shmuel says yes; for eiruvei techumin, Rav says zikkui needed, Shmuel says no. The Gemara questions Rav's consistency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara records an explicit dispute: for shittufei mavo'ot, Rav says no zikkui needed, Shmuel says yes; for eiruvei techumin, Rav says zikkui needed, Shmuel says no.
The Gemara questions Rav's consistency: Shmuel's positions align with the respective mishnayot, but what is Rav's reasoning for reversing the requirement of zikkui between the two types of eiruv?

items.text: Story of Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law
items.text_en: Story of Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav recounts a case where Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law went to the bathhouse and it got dark; her mother-in-law made an eiruv for her. Rabbi Chiya forbade it, but Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei challenged him, citing his father's principle to be lenient in eiruvin. The Gemara questions whether the eiruv was from the mother-in-law's food without zikkui, or from her own food without her knowledge. A certain rabbi named Rabbi Yaakov clarifies from Rabbi Yochanan that it was from the mother-in-law's food without zikkui.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav introduces a story about Rabbi Oshaya's daughter-in-law who went to the bathhouse and it got dark, and her mother-in-law made an eiruv for her.
Rabbi Chiya forbade the eiruv when the case was brought before him.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei challenged Rabbi Chiya, citing his father's principle to be lenient in matters of eiruvin.
The Gemara raises a question: was the eiruv made from the mother-in-law's food without proper zikkui (acquisition), or from the daughter-in-law's own food without her knowledge?
A certain rabbi named Rabbi Yaakov clarifies from Rabbi Yochanan that the eiruv was from the mother-in-law's food and the problem was lack of zikkui.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry to Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's inquiry to Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira instructs Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi to ask Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi about the same question. The answer is confirmed: it was from the mother-in-law's food without zikkui.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira's instruction to Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's instruction to Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira instructs Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi to go to Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi and ask him the same question about the daughter-in-law's eruv.

Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi asks Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi whether the daughter-in-law's eruv was invalid because it was from the mother-in-law's food without zikkui (formal acquisition) or because it was from her own food without her knowledge.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi answers that the eruv was invalid because it was from the mother-in-law's food without zikkui (formal acquisition).

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling and query on eiruvei tavshilin
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling and query on eiruvei tavshilin
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman states that eiruvei techumin, eiruvei chatzeirot, and shittufei mavo'ot all require zikkui. He then queries whether eiruvei tavshilin require zikkui. Rav Yosef and Abaye debate whether Rav Nachman heard Shmuel's ruling that eiruvei tavshilin require zikkui. The Gemara distinguishes this from the earlier dispute between Rav and Shmuel.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman states a fixed tradition that eiruvei techumin, eiruvei chatzeirot, and shittufei mavo'ot all require zikkui.
Rav Nachman raises a query whether eiruvei tavshilin require zikkui or not.
Rav Yosef questions why Rav Nachman is uncertain, citing Shmuel's explicit ruling that eiruvei tavshilin require zikkui.
Abaye objects that it is obvious Rav Nachman had not heard Shmuel's ruling, for otherwise he would not have asked the question.

Rav Yosef rejects Abaye's objection, noting that regarding eiruvei techumin, Shmuel said no zikkui is needed, yet Rav Nachman ruled that it is required, so he could still ask despite knowing Shmuel's view.

The Gemara resolves the debate by distinguishing the cases: in eiruvei techumin, Rav and Shmuel disputed, so Rav Nachman could rule stringently; but regarding eiruvei tavshilin, if Shmuel ruled it requires zikkui, no one disputes it, so Rav Nachman would not have asked.

items.text: Wife's ability to grant permission without husband's knowledge
items.text_en: Wife's ability to grant permission without husband's knowledge
items.desc_en: Two stories are told: one with a neighbor of Rabbi Zeira who refused to grant permission, and Rabbi Zeira ruled that a wife can grant permission without her husband's knowledge, citing Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chanina. Another similar case came before Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya and Rav Mattana, who had no answer, but Rav Yehuda ruled in the name of Shmuel that a wife can do so.

sub.desc_en: A story is told about a gentile superintendent in Rabbi Zeira's neighborhood who refused to rent his domain to the neighbors; they ask Rabbi Zeira whether they can rent from his wife.
Rabbi Zeira rules that a wife can grant permission without her husband's knowledge, citing Resh Lakish in the name of Rabbi Chanina.

A similar story is told about a superintendent in Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya's neighborhood; after Rav Yehuda bar Oshaya and Rav Mattana had no answer, Rav Yehuda rules in the name of Shmuel that a wife can grant permission without her husband's knowledge.

items.text: Contradiction and resolution regarding wife's eiruv
items.text_en: Contradiction and resolution regarding wife's eiruv
items.desc_en: A baraita states that women who make an eiruv or shittuf without their husbands' knowledge is invalid. The Gemara resolves that it depends on whether the husband forbids it. This is supported by Shmuel's own ruling that a regular participant's shittuf can be taken by force, implying that only a regular participant, not a non-regular one, can be forced. A supporting baraita about forcing a resident to contribute to a lechi or korah is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita stating that women who make an eiruv or shittuf without their husbands' knowledge are invalid.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the husband forbids carrying (the wife may act) and where he does not (she may not).
The Gemara argues that this resolution is reasonable, because otherwise Shmuel's own ruling that a regular participant's shittuf can be taken by force would contradict the baraita.
The Gemara infers from Shmuel's statement that only a regular participant can be forced, not a non-regular one.
The Gemara suggests that a baraita about compelling a resident to contribute to a lechi and korah supports the idea that Shabbat enactments can be enforced against one's will.

items.text: Dispute about using an asheirah for lechi or korah
items.text_en: Dispute about using an asheirah for lechi or korah
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents two versions of a dispute between Rav Chiyya bar Ashi and Reish Lakish: one says one may make a lechi from an asheirah, the other says one may make a korah. The Gemara explains the logic of each position.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a first version of the dispute, stating that the case of an asheirah is different because it lacks partitions.
The Gemara presents a second version of the dispute, noting that the case of a צד (side alley) is different.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi and Reish Lakish
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi and Reish Lakish
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Ashi says one may make a lechi from an asheirah, while Reish Lakish says one may make a korah from an asheirah.
The Gemara explains the logic: the one who permits a korah certainly permits a lechi, but the one who permits a lechi forbids a korah because the korah's measure is broken into pieces.

items.text: Mishnah: Adding or reducing food in an eruv
items.text_en: Mishnah: Adding or reducing food in an eruv
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if the food of an eruv is reduced, one may add and acquire for others without notifying them; if food is added, one must notify. It defines the measure for many as two meals for all, and for few as a k'grogeret per person. Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between the initial eruv and its remnants.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the rule for adding or reducing food in an eruv: if reduced, one may add and acquire without notifying; if added, one must notify.
The Mishnah defines the measure: for many, two meals for all; for few, a k'grogeret per person.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between the initial eruv, which requires the stated measure, and remnants, which require any amount.
The Mishnah concludes that the rule of eruv in courtyards was instituted only so that children should not forget the laws of eruv.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah deals with one type of food or two. If one type, even if it is entirely gone, no notification is needed; if two types, even reduction requires notification. Two answers are given: either it is one type and 'reduced' means diminished, or it is two types and total depletion is different.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah deals with one type of food or two, arguing that if it is one type, even total depletion should not require notification.
The Gemara objects that if it is two types, even reduction should require notification, citing a baraita that distinguishes between one type and two types.
One answer suggests it is one type, and 'reduced' means diminished (not totally gone), so the Mishnah's case is about reduction, not depletion.
Another answer suggests it is two types, but total depletion is different from mere reduction, so the Mishnah's rule stands.

items.text: Rav Sheizvi's statement about Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Rav Sheizvi's statement about Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi says in the name of Rav Chisda that the Mishnah implies Rabbi Yehuda's colleagues disagree with him. The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between eruvei techumin and eruvei chatzeirot. The Gemara clarifies that this is obvious, but the teaching is needed for a specific case of a courtyard between two alleyways.

sub.text: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi states in the name of Rav Chisda that the Mishnah implies Rabbi Yehuda's colleagues disagree with him.

The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between עירובי תחומין (Sabbath boundary mixtures) and עירובי חצירות (courtyard mixtures), stating that the latter can be done even without the residents' knowledge.
The Gemara objects that it is obvious that Rabbi Yehuda's colleagues disagree with him, questioning why Rav Sheizvi's statement is necessary.

The Gemara clarifies that the teaching is needed for a specific case of a courtyard between two alleyways, where one might think Rabbi Yehuda's leniency does not apply; therefore, the baraita teaches that it does.

items.text: Definition of 'many' for the measure of an eruv
items.text_en: Definition of 'many' for the measure of an eruv
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that 'many' means eighteen people. Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda explains that this means if dividing two meals among them yields less than a k'grogeret per person, they are 'many' and two meals suffice; otherwise they are 'few'. The Gemara notes that this implies two meals are eighteen k'grogerot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of 'many' in the Mishnah, and Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel answers that it means eighteen people.
The Gemara objects that the number eighteen seems arbitrary, suggesting it means from eighteen onward.

sub.text: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda's explanation
sub.text_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda's explanation
sub.desc_en: Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda explains that his father taught him the criterion: if dividing two meals among them yields less than a k'grogeret per person, they are 'many' and two meals suffice; otherwise they are 'few'.
The Gemara infers incidentally that two meals consist of eighteen k'grogerot (dried fig-bulks).

items.text: Mishnah: What may be used for an eruv
items.text_en: Mishnah: What may be used for an eruv
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may use anything for an eruv or shituf except water and salt, according to Rabbi Eliezer. Rabbi Yehoshua says a loaf is an eruv; even a loaf of a se'ah if it is whole, but a broken piece is invalid; a loaf worth an issar if whole is valid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the general rule that anything may be used for an eruv or shituf except water and salt, according to Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Yehoshua states that a loaf serves as an eruv, even a large loaf of a se'ah if whole, but a broken piece is invalid.
Rabbi Yehoshua adds that even a small loaf worth an issar is valid for an eruv if it is whole.

items.text: Gemara's initial question and Rava's answer
items.text_en: Gemara's initial question and Rava's answer
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah already taught 'with anything one may establish an eiruv' and asks why it is repeated. Rava explains it excludes Rabbi Yehoshua's view that only a loaf works, not other items.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah already taught 'with anything one may establish an eiruv' and asks why it is repeated.
Rava explains that the repetition excludes Rabbi Yehoshua's view that only a loaf works, not other items.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rava
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rava
items.desc_en: Abaye objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'with anything' for alleyway partnerships, and Rabbi Yehoshua is the one who limits to bread, yet the Mishnah still says 'with anything'.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'with anything' for alleyway partnerships, and Rabbi Yehoshua is the one who limits to bread, yet the Mishnah still says 'with anything'.

items.text: Rava bar bar Chana's alternative answer and discussion of broken bread
items.text_en: Rava bar bar Chana's alternative answer and discussion of broken bread
items.desc_en: Rava bar bar Chana explains that the Mishnah excludes Rabbi Yehoshua's view that only a whole loaf works, not a broken one. The Gemara explains the reason is enmity, and Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi about using all broken loaves.

sub.desc_en: Rava bar bar Chana offers an alternative answer: the Mishnah's 'בכל' (with anything) excludes Rabbi Yehoshua's view that only a whole loaf works, not a broken one.
The Gemara asks why a broken loaf (פרוסה) is invalid for an עירוב (eruv).

sub.text: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul quoting Rabbi
sub.text_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul quoting Rabbi
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul reports in the name of Rabbi that the reason is משום איבה (to avoid enmity between neighbors).

sub.text: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha bar Rava to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava asks Rav Ashi: if all the neighbors contribute broken loaves (פרוסות), what is the ruling?
Rav Ashi answers that it is invalid, because the practice might revert to its flawed state (שמא יחזור דבר לקלקולו).

items.text: Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul on bread with challah or terumah removed
items.text_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul on bread with challah or terumah removed
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan ben Shaul rules that bread from which the challah portion or terumah mixture was removed may be used for eiruv. A contradiction is resolved by distinguishing between a baker's challah and a homeowner's challah, citing the Mishnah on challah proportions.

items.text: Rav Chisda on sewing a broken loaf together
items.text_en: Rav Chisda on sewing a broken loaf together
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda rules that if one sewed a broken loaf together with a splinter, it may be used for eiruv. A contradiction is resolved by distinguishing whether the sewing is noticeable or not.

sub.desc_en: The gemara cites the mishna on challah proportions: one makes dough for himself or his son's wedding — one twenty-fourth; a baker selling in the market, and similarly a woman selling in the market — one forty-eighth.
The gemara objects by citing a baraita that contradicts Rav Chisda, stating that such a loaf may not be used for eiruv.
The gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the sewing is noticeable (דידיע תפרה) and one where it is not (דלא ידיע תפרה).

items.text: Disputes about bread from rice, millet, lentils, and other grains
items.text_en: Disputes about bread from rice, millet, lentils, and other grains
items.desc_en: Shmuel permits eiruv with rice bread but Mar Ukva reports he forbids millet bread. Rav permits lentil bread, but a story about Shmuel's dog refusing it raises a contradiction, resolved by identifying the bread as mixed grains or baked in human excrement. The verse about barley cakes is interpreted for measurements and texture.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira reports that Shmuel permits an eiruv with bread from rice (אורז) and from millet (דוחן).
Mar Ukva objects, reporting that he heard directly from Shmuel that rice bread is permitted but millet bread is not.

sub.text: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav
sub.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Avin cites Rav, who permits an eiruv with lentil bread.
The Gemara questions Rav's ruling, citing a story where Shmuel's dog refused to eat lentil bread.
The Gemara resolves that the rejected bread was made from mixed grains, citing the verse listing various grains.
Rav Pappa offers an alternative resolution: the bread was baked in human excrement, citing the verse about cakes baked on human dung.

sub.text: Gemara's question and Rav Chisda and Rav Pappa
sub.text_en: Gemara's question and Rav Chisda and Rav Pappa
sub.desc_en: The Gemara interprets the verse 'and you shall eat a barley cake' — Rav Chisda says it teaches about measurements, and Rav Pappa says it teaches about the texture of the dough being like barley, not wheat.

items.text: Mishnah: Giving money to a storekeeper for eiruv
items.text_en: Mishnah: Giving money to a storekeeper for eiruv
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says one may give a coin to a storekeeper or baker to acquire an eiruv for him, while the Sages say his money does not acquire it for him.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Eliezer's position: one may give a coin to a storekeeper or baker to acquire an eiruv for him.
The Sages dispute Rabbi Eliezer, stating that his money does not acquire the eiruv for him.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for all other people, their money acquires for them, because an eruv can only be made with a person's knowledge. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between eruv techumin, where knowledge is required, and eruv chatzeirot, where it is not, based on the principle of זכין (benefiting) versus חבין (harming).

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that for all other people, their money acquires for them, because an eruv can only be made with a person's knowledge.

Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between עירובי תחומין (eruv techumin), where knowledge is required, and עירובי חצירות (eruv chatzeirot), where it is not, based on the principle of זכין (benefiting) versus חבין (harming).

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Eliezer
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Eliezer
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: What is Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning? After all, the person did not perform meshichah (pulling)!

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what Rabbi Eliezer's reasoning is, given that the person did not perform meshichah (pulling).

items.text: First answer: analogy to the four festival periods
items.text_en: First answer: analogy to the four festival periods
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avahu explains that Rabbi Eliezer treats this case like the four festival periods where the Sages force a butcher to slaughter even without payment. The Gemara raises an objection: if the animal dies, it is a loss for the buyer, but he did not pull! Rav Huna answers that he did pull. The Gemara then questions the other side of the ruling, and Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak resolves it by saying the acquisition was through a third party (zichui).

sub.text: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avahu
sub.text_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avahu
sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Rabbah bar Avahu answers that Rabbi Eliezer treats this case like the four festival periods where the Sages force a butcher to slaughter even without payment.
The Gemara objects: if the animal dies, it is a loss for the buyer, but he did not pull the animal to acquire it.
Rav Huna answers that the case is where the buyer did pull the animal.
The Gemara objects to the other side of the ruling: if the buyer pulled, why does the animal belong to the seller in the rest of the year?

Rabbi Shmuel bar Yitzchak resolves that the acquisition was through a third party (זיכוי), so in the four festival periods it is a benefit (זכות) acquired even without the buyer's presence, but in the rest of the year it is a detriment (חוב) and requires the buyer's presence.

items.text: Second answer: Sages overrode Torah law
items.text_en: Second answer: Sages overrode Torah law
items.desc_en: Rav Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan says that during the four festival periods, the Sages established their words over Torah law, because by Torah law money acquires, but the Sages instituted meshichah to prevent disputes.

sub.text: Rav Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rav Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rav Ila in the name of Rabbi Yochanan explains that during the four festival periods, the Sages overrode Torah law (דבר תורה, מעות קונות) and instituted meshichah (משיכה) as the mode of acquisition to prevent disputes, as a גזירה (precautionary decree) lest the seller say 'your wheat burned in the attic'.

items.text: Clarification of 'all other people'
items.text_en: Clarification of 'all other people'
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'all other people' refers to the homeowner (ba'al habayit). Shmuel adds distinctions: a baker is different, a utensil acquires, and if the person said 'arev li' (mix for me) it is considered appointing an agent.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who 'all other people' refers to in the Mishnah.
Rav answers that 'all other people' refers to the homeowner (בעל הבית).
Shmuel agrees that it is the homeowner, and adds that the Mishnah's rule applies only to a baker (נחתום), but a homeowner acquires.
Shmuel adds that the Mishnah's rule applies only to a coin (מעה), but a utensil (כלי) acquires.
Shmuel adds that if the person said 'ערב לי' (mix for me), it is considered appointing an agent, and the agent acquires.

items.text: Ruling on Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Ruling on Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and wherever Rabbi Yehuda teaches in Eruvin, the halakha follows him. Rav Chana of Baghdad asks if this applies even to a mavoy whose beams or side-posts were removed, and Rav Yehuda clarifies it applies only to eruvin, not partitions.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel rules the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and wherever Rabbi Yehuda teaches in Eruvin, the halakha follows him.
Rav Chana of Baghdad asks Rav Yehuda whether Shmuel's ruling applies even to a mavoy (alley) whose beams or side-posts were removed.
Rav Yehuda clarifies that Shmuel's statement applies only to eruvin (eruv matters), not to partitions (mechitzot).

items.text: Challenge: Is Rabbi Yehuda merely explaining?
items.text_en: Challenge: Is Rabbi Yehuda merely explaining?
items.desc_en: Rav Acha bar Rava challenges Rav Ashi: The word 'halakha' implies there is a dispute, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said that whenever Rabbi Yehuda says 'eimatai' or 'bameh' in the Mishnah, he is only explaining the Sages' words. The Gemara brings a Mishnah that seems to show a dispute, but resolves it by distinguishing a courtyard between two alleyways. Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rav Chisda asserts that the colleagues disagree with Rabbi Yehuda, but the Gemara cuts off with 'ela' (rather), leaving the conclusion implicit.

sub.text: Rav Acha brei d'Rava's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rava's challenge to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Rav Acha brei d'Rava challenges Rav Ashi: the word 'halakha' implies a dispute, but Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said that whenever Rabbi Yehuda says 'eimatai' or 'bameh' in the Mishnah, he is only explaining the Sages' words.
The Gemara objects: but we learned a Mishnah that seems to show a dispute, as it says 'one adds and grants possession, and must inform'.
The Gemara resolves: that Mishnah refers to a courtyard between two alleyways, where the dispute is real.

sub.text: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheizvi in the name of Rav Chisda asserts that this Mishnah shows the colleagues disagree with Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara cuts off with 'ela' (rather), leaving the conclusion implicit.

items.text: Gemara's objection to the contradiction between two statements
items.text_en: Gemara's objection to the contradiction between two statements
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects to a contradiction between two statements about whether Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'Eimatai' is for explanation or dispute, noting that one master holds they disagree and another holds they do not.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the two masters' statements about Rabbi Yehuda's use of 'Eimatai' contradict each other, as one holds they disagree and the other holds they do not.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan on 'Eimatai' and 'Bameh'
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Yochanan on 'Eimatai' and 'Bameh'
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi states that whenever Rabbi Yehuda says 'Eimatai' or 'Bameh' in the Mishnah, it is only to explain the Sages' words. Rabbi Yochanan says 'Eimatai' is for explanation, but 'Bameh' is for dispute. The Gemara challenges this with a Mishnah where Rabbi Yehuda says 'Eimatai' and the Sages disagree, showing it is for dispute.

sub.desc_en: He states: Whenever Rabbi Yehuda says 'Eimatai' or 'Bameh' in our Mishnah, it is only to explain the Sages' words.
Rabbi Yochanan responds: 'Eimatai' is for explanation, but 'Bameh' is for dispute.

items.text: Resolution: The Mishnah is from Rabbi Tarfon
items.text_en: Resolution: The Mishnah is from Rabbi Tarfon
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by identifying the Mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the name of Rabbi Tarfon, who holds that uncertainty prevents a person from committing to a nazirite vow. Similarly, in the case of eruv, since the person does not know if he acquires, he does not intend to acquire.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara identifies the Mishnah as Rabbi Yehuda's statement in the name of Rabbi Tarfon.
The Gemara cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda says in Rabbi Tarfon's name that one never becomes a nazir when uncertain, because nazirite vows require explicit designation.

The Gemara concludes that just as uncertainty prevents a person from committing to a nazirite vow, so too in the case of eruv, since the person does not know if he acquires, he does not intend to acquire.

items.text: Mishnah: How to establish an eruv techumin
items.text_en: Mishnah: How to establish an eruv techumin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches how to establish an eruv techumin: one places a barrel and declares it for all the residents of his city, especially for those going to a house of mourning or a wedding. One who accepts the eruv before nightfall is permitted; after nightfall, it is forbidden, as eruv cannot be made after dark.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches how to establish an eruv techumin: one places a barrel and declares it for all the residents of his city, especially for those going to a house of mourning or a wedding; one who accepts the eruv before nightfall is permitted, after nightfall it is forbidden.

items.text: Gemara: Eruv is only for a mitzvah
items.text_en: Gemara: Eruv is only for a mitzvah
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that eruv is only established for a mitzvah. The Gemara questions what he teaches, as the Mishnah already mentions going to a house of mourning or wedding. Rav Yosef clarifies that one might think the Mishnah merely describes the common practice, so he teaches that it is specifically for a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that one establishes an עירוב (eruv) only for a מצוה (commandment).
The Gemara asks what novel point Rav Yosef teaches, since the Mishnah already mentions going to a house of mourning or a wedding feast.
The Gemara explains that Rav Yosef teaches that one might think the Mishnah merely describes the common practice, so he clarifies that it is specifically for a מצוה (commandment).

items.text: דין 'מבעוד יום' ושאלת הברירה
items.text_en: Proof that there is no bereira
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'who accepted upon himself before nightfall' that there is no retroactive clarification (bereira), because if there were, the matter would be clarified retroactively that he was satisfied before nightfall. Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah discusses cases where he was informed or not informed.
items.desc: הגמרא לומדת מהמשנה שאין ברירה, שאם היה ברירה היה העירוב חל גם למי שקיבל לאחר החשיכה. רב אשי מתרץ שהמשנה עוסקת במקרה שלא הודיעוהו על העירוב מבעוד יום.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'who accepted upon himself before nightfall' that there is no retroactive clarification (bereira), because if there were, the matter would be clarified retroactively that he was satisfied before nightfall.
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה מהמשנה: מכך שנדרשת קבלה מבעוד יום, משמע שאין ברירה, שאם יש ברירה היה יכול להיגלות למפרע שרצה בכך מבעוד יום.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah discusses cases where he was informed or not informed, resolving the difficulty.
sub.desc: רב אשי מתרץ: המשנה עוסקת במקרה שלא הודיעו לו, ולכן אין כאן ראיה נגד עקרון הברירה.

items.text: דין קטן היוצא בעירוב אמו
items.text_en: A child's eligibility for his mother's eruv and the age of independence
items.desc_en: Rav Asi says a child of six goes out with his mother's eruv. The Gemara challenges this with a baraita that distinguishes between a child who needs his mother and one who does not. It then discusses the age at which a child no longer needs his mother, with opinions from the school of Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, concluding with ages four or five.
items.desc: רב אסי אומר שקטן בן שש יוצא בעירוב אמו. הגמרא מקשה מברייתא המבחינה בין קטן שצריך לאמו לקטן שאינו צריך. מובאת הגדרה של 'קטן שאינו צריך לאמו' מבית רבי ינאי ומריש לקיש, והגיל המשוער הוא ארבע או חמש.

sub.desc_en: Rav Asi states that a child of six may go out with his mother's eruv.
sub.desc: רב אסי קובע שילד בן שש יוצא בעירוב אמו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rav Asi with a baraita that distinguishes between a child who needs his mother and one who does not, implying that age alone is not the criterion.
sub.desc: רב אסי קובע שילד בן שש יוצא בעירוב אמו.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a parallel baraita regarding סוכה (sukkah) that similarly conditions the child's obligation on whether he needs his mother.
sub.desc: הגמרא מביאה ראיה דומה מסוכה: ילד שאינו צריך לאמו חייב בסוכה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definition of a child who does not need his mother.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו ילד שאינו צריך לאמו, ומביאה את תשובת בית רבי ינאי.

sub.desc_en: The school of Rabbi Yannai defines the child as one who defecates without needing his mother to clean him.
sub.desc: הגמרא שואלת מהו ילד שאינו צריך לאמו, ומביאה את תשובת בית רבי ינאי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish defines the child as one who wakes up without calling 'mother'.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש מגדיר ילד שאינו צריך לאמו כמי שאינו קורא 'אמא' בהתעוררו, ומתקן את דבריו למי שאינו קורא 'אמא, אמא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even adults call 'mother', so the criterion is insufficient.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש מגדיר ילד שאינו צריך לאמו כמי שאינו קורא 'אמא' בהתעוררו, ומתקן את דבריו למי שאינו קורא 'אמא, אמא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara corrects the definition to a child who does not call 'mother, mother' repeatedly upon waking.
sub.desc: ריש לקיש מגדיר ילד שאינו צריך לאמו כמי שאינו קורא 'אמא' בהתעוררו, ומתקן את דבריו למי שאינו קורא 'אמא, אמא'.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes with the age range of four or five for this independence.
sub.desc: הגמרא מסכמת שגיל הילד שאינו צריך לאמו הוא כארבע או חמש שנים, מה שמקשה על רב אסי.

items.text: Rebbi Yehoshua's distinction and its refutation
items.text_en: Rebbi Yehoshua's distinction and its refutation
items.desc_en: Rebbi Yehoshua bar Rav Idi explains Rav Asi's ruling that a minor follows his mother's eiruv even at age 6, but this is refuted by a beraisa stating that a child who needs his mother only goes out on his mother's eiruv until age 6, excluding age 6 itself.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehoshua bar Rav Idi explains that Rav Asi's ruling applies specifically when the father and mother placed eiruvin in opposite directions, and even a six-year-old prefers his mother's company.

The Gemara raises an objection from a beraisa stating that a child who needs his mother goes out on his mother's eiruv only until age six, excluding age six itself, thereby refuting Rav Yehoshua bar Rav Idi.

items.text: Defense of Rav Asi and resolution of Rabbi Yannai and Reish Lakish
items.text_en: Defense of Rav Asi and resolution of Rabbi Yannai and Reish Lakish
items.desc_en: The Gemara first considers whether Rav Asi is also refuted, but he is saved by interpreting 'ad' as inclusive. The contradiction between Rabbi Yannai/Reish Lakish and the beraisa is resolved by distinguishing whether the father is in town.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether Rav Asi is also refuted by the baraita that limits the child's dependency to age six.
Rav Asi defends himself by interpreting the word 'עד' (until) in the baraita as inclusive, so that a child up to and including age six is dependent.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yannai and Reish Lakish are also refuted by the baraita.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between a case where the father is in town (the baraita applies) and where he is not (Rabbi Yannai and Reish Lakish apply).

items.text: Baraisa rules for appointing agents for eiruv
items.text_en: Baraisa rules for appointing agents for eiruv
items.desc_en: Two baraisos detail the rules: a person may establish an eiruv through his minor children or Canaanite slaves whether or not they consent, but not through adult children, Hebrew slaves, or his wife without their consent. If the rabbi (husband/expert) also establishes an eiruv for them, they go by his eiruv, except for a wife who can veto.

sub.desc_en: The first baraisa rules that a person may establish an eiruv through his minor children or Canaanite slaves regardless of consent, but not through adult children, Hebrew slaves, or his wife without their consent.
The second baraisa repeats the same rules, adding the reason that the hand of minors and Canaanite slaves is like the hand of the master.
The baraisa concludes that if both the dependent and the rabbi (husband/expert) established an eiruv, they follow the rabbi's eiruv, except for a wife who can veto.

items.text: The wife's veto power and the meaning of 'consent'
items.text_en: The wife's veto power and the meaning of 'consent'
items.desc_en: Rabba explains why a wife is singled out: her power to object applies to anyone similar. The Gemara then clarifies that the beraisa's 'only with their consent' means silence, not explicit agreement, and that if the wife had already made her own eiruv that is an implicit veto, as Rava notes.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the wife is singled out as able to veto her husband's eiruv.
Rabba answers that the wife is singled out as an example, and the same rule applies to anyone similar (e.g., adult son or daughter).
The Gemara questions the beraisa: if the wife's veto is explicit, then silence would mean she goes out by her husband's eiruv, but the earlier clause requires consent, implying explicit agreement.
The Gemara answers that 'consent' in the beraisa means silence, not explicit agreement, excluding only cases where they say 'no'.
The Gemara objects: the beraisa says that if the wife made her own eiruv and the husband also made one for her, she goes out by her own, even though she was silent, showing silence is not consent.
Rava resolves that when the wife made her own eiruv, that act itself is the greatest possible veto, so silence is irrelevant.

items.text: Mishnah: Shiur of two meals for eiruv
items.text_en: Mishnah: Shiur of two meals for eiruv
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir says the shiur is weekday food for two meals, Rabbi Yehuda says Shabbos food for two meals, and both intend to be lenient. Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka defines a precise measure (one loaf from a pound, i.e., 4 se'ah per sela), and Rabbi Shimon also defines a measure (two-thirds of a loaf from three per kav). The Mishnah concludes with halachic applications of these measures.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule: the shiur (measure) for an eiruv is food for two meals per person.
Rabbi Meir rules that the measure is weekday food for two meals, not Shabbos food.
Rabbi Yehuda rules that the measure is Shabbos food for two meals, and both opinions intend to be lenient.
Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka defines a precise measure: one loaf from a pound, i.e., 4 se'ah per sela.
Rabbi Shimon defines a measure: two-thirds of a loaf from three loaves per kav.
The Mishnah concludes by applying these measures: half of the loaf is used for the metzora's house, and half of that half is used to disqualify the body (of a corpse).

items.text: Amoraim define the 'two meals' and Rav Yosef's opinion
items.text_en: Amoraim define the 'two meals' and Rav Yosef's opinion
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda citing Rav says two meals are two Artichoke or Nachar-Pappa loaves. Rav Yosef reports that his father Rava held like Rabbi Meir (weekday food), and he also holds like Rabbi Meir because otherwise the popular saying 'gaining an appetite is common' contradicts Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the precise quantity of food that constitutes two meals for an eruv.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav defines two meals as two Artichoke loaves.
Rav Adda bar Ahava defines two meals as two Nachar-Pappa loaves.
Rav Yosef asks his son which Tanna his father Rava followed regarding the measure of two meals.
The son reports that Rava held like Rabbi Meir, who defines the meals by weekday food.
Rav Yosef states that he too holds like Rabbi Meir, because the popular saying 'gaining an appetite is common' contradicts Rabbi Yehuda's position.

items.text: Reconciling Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Reconciling Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka's shiur is 4 meals per kav while Rabbi Shimon's is 9 per kav. Rav Chisda suggests two interpretations (deduct a third for the baker, or deduct half), and though a numerical gap remains (9 vs. 8), they are near enough to be considered equal. Another contradiction in Rav Chisda's statements is resolved by whether the homeowner provides wood for baking.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that states the opinions of Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Shimon are close to being equal.
The Gemara objects that the two opinions are far apart: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka holds 4 meals per kav, while Rabbi Shimon holds 9 per kav.
Rav Chisda answers that one must deduct a third from the kav for the baker's profit, reducing the gap.
The Gemara objects that even after deducting a third, the gap remains: 9 vs. 6 meals per kav.
Rav Chisda offers a second interpretation: deduct half from the kav for the baker's profit.
The Gemara objects that even with half deducted, the gap is 9 vs. 8 meals per kav.
The Gemara resolves that the remaining gap is small enough to justify the baraita's claim that their opinions are close to equal.
The Gemara notes an internal contradiction in Rav Chisda's two statements (deduct a third vs. deduct half).
The Gemara resolves that the two statements refer to different cases: one where the homeowner provides wood for baking, and one where he does not.
The Gemara cites the continuation of the Mishnah regarding the half-loaf for the leprous house and the quarter-loaf for disqualifying the body.

items.text: Opening question about טומאת אוכלין
items.text_en: Opening question about טומאת אוכלין
items.desc_en: The Tanna of our Mishnah did not include the law of טומאת אוכלין regarding the half-פרס measure. The Gemara asks why, and answers that the shiurim for half-פרס and טומאת אוכלין are not the same.

sub.desc_en: A Tosefta teaches that one-eighth of a loaf is the minimum measure for טומאת אוכלין (impurity of foods).
The Gemara asks why our Mishnah's tanna did not teach the law of טומאת אוכלין (impurity of foods) in this context.
The Gemara answers that the measures for half-פרס and טומאת אוכלין (impurity of foods) are not identical.

items.text: Dispute over the shiur of half-פרס and טומאת אוכלין
items.text_en: Dispute over the shiur of half-פרס and טומאת אוכלין
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita with three opinions on the size of half-פרס: Rabbi Yehuda says two eggs minus a little, Rabbi Yosei says two 'loose' eggs, and Rebbi says two eggs plus an 'עוד'. Then it cites a dispute about the shiur for טומאת אוכלין: Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Dosa say it is like an egg with its peel, while the Sages say without the peel.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the question of the measure of half-פרס and presents three opinions: Rabbi Yehuda says two eggs minus a little, Rabbi Yosei says two 'loose' eggs, and Rebbi says two eggs plus an 'עוד' (one-twentieth of an egg).
The baraita then cites a dispute about the measure for טומאת אוכלין: Rabbi Natan and Rabbi Dosa say it is like an egg with its peel, while the Sages say without the peel.

items.text: Rafram bar Pappa's statement and clarification
items.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa's statement and clarification
items.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda says that the earlier dispute (about half-פרס) is according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei, but the Sages say it is one and a half 'loose' eggs, and who are these Sages? Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka. The Gemara then notes that the term 'loose' is obvious and was taught to inform us of something.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa in the name of Rav Chisda states that the earlier dispute about half-פרס (half a loaf) is according to Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.

sub.text: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.text_en: Rafram bar Pappa citing Rav Chisda
sub.desc_en: Rafram bar Pappa adds that the Sages say the measure is one and a half 'loose' eggs, and identifies these Sages as Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka.
The Gemara objects that the term 'loose' is obvious, and notes that the teaching came to inform us of something else.

items.text: Rebbi's measurement of eggs in a se'a
items.text_en: Rebbi's measurement of eggs in a se'a
items.desc_en: When Rav Dimi came, he reported that Bonyos sent to Rebbi a measure from Modi'a of Kondes of Neusa, and Rebbi measured it as 217 eggs. The Gemara questions which se'a this refers to (Midbarit, Yerushalmit, or Tzipporit) and concludes it is Tzipporit, but then adds the challah portion and the 'עוד' of Rebbi, leading to a calculation that the excess is less than an egg and thus not counted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Dimi reports that Bonyos sent Rebbi a measure from Modi'a of Kondes of Neusa, and Rebbi measured it as 217 eggs.
The Gemara questions which se'a this refers to, listing the egg counts for Midbarit (144), Yerushalmit (173), and Tzipporit (207).
The Gemara answers that it is based on the Tzipporit se'a, and one must add the challah portion to it.
The Gemara objects that the challah portion is only about eight eggs, so even with it the total is still less than 217.
The Gemara resolves that one must add the excess amounts (עוֹדוֹת) of Rebbi to the calculation.
The Gemara rejects that even with the excess it is slightly more than 217, but since it is less than a whole egg, Rebbi did not count it.

items.text: Baraita on se'a measures and Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution
items.text_en: Baraita on se'a measures and Rabbi Yirmeya's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a Yerushalmit se'a is a sixth larger than a Midbarit, and a Tzipporit se'a is a sixth larger than a Yerushalmit, making Tzipporit a third larger than Midbarit. The Gemara questions the precise calculation, and Rabbi Yirmeya explains that it means 'close to a third', and Ravina further refines that the third of Tzipporit with Rebbi's 'עוד' is a third of an egg more than half of Midbarit.

sub.desc_en: The baraita states the proportional relationships between the wilderness, Jerusalem, and Tzippori se'a measures.
The Gemara questions which measure the 'third' refers to, and calculates that if it is a third of a wilderness se'a (48 eggs), the actual difference is 63 eggs, not 48.
The Gemara continues questioning, testing if the 'third' refers to a Jerusalem se'a (58 2/3 eggs) or a Tzippori se'a (69 2/3 eggs), and shows neither matches the actual difference of 63 eggs.
Rabbi Yirmeya resolves that the baraita means the Tzippori se'a is 'close to a third' larger than the wilderness se'a, and that third is 'close to half' of the wilderness se'a.

Ravina objects that the baraita does not say 'close to', and offers a precise calculation: a third of a Tzippori se'a with Rebbi's excess amounts is exactly a third of an egg more than half of a wilderness se'a.

items.text: Beginning of a baraita on חלה
items.text_en: Beginning of a baraita on חלה
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita about the verse 'ראשית עריסותיכם' regarding the separation of חלה.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a baraita about the verse 'ראשית עריסותיכם' regarding the separation of חלה.

items.text: The 'omer measure and its halachic and health implications
items.text_en: The 'omer measure and its halachic and health implications
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that 'your dough' refers to the dough of the wilderness, which is the 'omer, a tenth of an ephah. From this, the Sages derived that seven quarters of flour plus a little more obligate in challah, and that eating this measure is healthy, while more or less is harmful.
