sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: what is the measure of 'your dough' in the verse, and answers that it is the dough of the wilderness.
The Gemara cites the verse that the 'omer is a tenth of an ephah, establishing the measure.
The Gemara derives that seven quarters of flour plus a little more obligate in challah, with conversions to Jerusalem and Tzippori measures.
The Gemara states that eating this measure is healthy and blessed, while more causes gluttony and less causes digestive trouble.

items.text: Mishnah: Division between courtyard and roof-gallery
items.text_en: Mishnah: Division between courtyard and roof-gallery
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if residents of a courtyard and a roof-gallery forgot to make an eruv, any object ten handbreadths high belongs to the gallery, and lower objects belong to the courtyard. This applies to a well's surround and a rock, and when the gallery is close (within four handbreadths), but if it is far, even a high object belongs to the courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating the general rule: if residents of a courtyard and a roof-gallery forgot to make an eruv, objects ten handbreadths high belong to the gallery, lower ones to the courtyard.
The Mishnah applies the same rule to a well's surround and a rock.
The Mishnah qualifies the rule: it applies only when the gallery is close (within four handbreadths); if far, even a high object belongs to the courtyard.

items.text: Gemara: Identifying cases of shared access
items.text_en: Gemara: Identifying cases of shared access
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that various scenarios of access between two courtyards correspond to known cases: both through a door is a window, both through throwing is a wall, both through lowering is a trench, and mixed access (door and throwing, or door and lowering) are cases cited by Rav Nachman.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that the case where both courtyards access the shared space through a door is simply the known case of a window between two courtyards.
The Gemara clarifies that both accessing by throwing corresponds to a wall between courtyards, and both accessing by lowering corresponds to a trench between courtyards.
The Gemara identifies the mixed cases: door and throwing corresponds to Rabbah bar Rav Huna citing Rav Nachman, and door and lowering corresponds to Rav Sheizvi citing Rav Nachman.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on mixed lowering and throwing
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on mixed lowering and throwing
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where one courtyard accesses via lowering and the other via throwing. Rav rules both are forbidden, while Shmuel gives it to the one who uses lowering, since his use is easier, and anything with easier use is given to that party.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks about a case where one courtyard accesses via lowering (שילוש) and the other via throwing (זריקה), and what the law is.
Rav rules that both are forbidden, as neither has exclusive access.
Shmuel rules that the shared space is given to the one who uses lowering (שילוש), since his use is easier, and anything with easier use is given to that party.

items.text: Gemara's initial assumption about the Mishnah's 'mirpeset'
items.text_en: Gemara's initial assumption about the Mishnah's 'mirpeset'
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to analyze the Mishnah, raising an initial assumption about what 'mirpeset' (roof-gallery) means, setting up a forthcoming discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's ruling about a courtyard and a roof-gallery (mirpeset) that forgot to establish an עירוב (eruv).
The Gemara raises its initial assumption, questioning what 'mirpeset' (roof-gallery) means in this context.

items.text: Gemara's initial inference from the term mirpeset
items.text_en: Gemara's initial inference from the term mirpeset
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the name 'mirpeset' (from the root 'to tread') that the balcony dwellers ascend via a ladder, implying that when one accesses via a ladder (shilshul) and the other via throwing (zerikah), the space is given to the one who uses a ladder. This is supported by Rav Huna's statement that the Mishnah refers to those who live on the mirpeset.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the balcony is called 'mirpeset' (from the root 'to tread'), implying that the dwellers ascend via a ladder.
The Gemara infers that when one accesses via a ladder (שילוש) and the other via throwing (זריקה), the space is given to the one who uses a ladder.
Rav Huna supports the inference by stating that the Mishnah refers to those who live on the mirpeset.

items.text: Challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah's 'to the courtyard'
items.text_en: Challenge and resolution regarding the Mishnah's 'to the courtyard'
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous inference: if the space is less than ten handbreadths, the Mishnah says 'to the courtyard,' but why? Both have door-level access. The Gemara reinterprets 'to the courtyard' as 'also to the courtyard,' meaning both are prohibited. This is supported by the later clause about a distant wall, where 'to the courtyard' must also mean both are prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the previous inference: if the space is less than ten handbreadths, the Mishnah says 'to the courtyard,' but why, since both have door-level access?
The Gemara reinterprets 'to the courtyard' as 'also to the courtyard,' meaning both are prohibited.
The Gemara supports this by citing the later clause about a distant wall, where 'to the courtyard' must also mean both are prohibited.

items.text: Mishnah citation and Rav Huna's explanation
items.text_en: Mishnah citation and Rav Huna's explanation
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a well or rock ten handbreadths high belongs to the mirpeset; less than that belongs to the courtyard. Rav Huna explains this refers to those who live on the mirpeset.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a well or rock ten handbreadths high belongs to the mirpeset (balcony), and less than that belongs to the courtyard.
Rav Huna explains that the Mishnah's ruling refers to those who live on the mirpeset (balcony).

items.text: Discussion of the well case: water or fruit?
items.text_en: Discussion of the well case: water or fruit?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the well case: if it is filled with water, it is subject to loss (when water is drawn), so it might be prohibited. Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda says the well is filled with water, but the Gemara objects that it can become empty. Abaye then says the well is filled with fruit, specifically untithed produce (tivla), which is not subject to loss. This is supported by the parallel to a rock.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the well case: if a rock is understandable, what can be said about a well?
Rav Yitzchak bar Rav Yehuda answers that the case deals with a well filled with water.
The Gemara objects that the well can become empty, and argues that if it is prohibited when empty, it should also be prohibited when full.
Abaye answers that the case deals with a well filled with fruit, specifically untithed produce (טיבלא), which is not subject to loss.
The Gemara supports Abaye's answer by noting that the mishnah pairs the well with a rock, implying a parallel.

items.text: Why both well and rock are needed
items.text_en: Why both well and rock are needed
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that both cases are necessary: if only rock were taught, one might think it is permitted because there is no concern for a decree, but with a well, one might decree due to times when it is filled with prepared fruit; thus both are needed.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why both the case of a well (בור) and a rock (סלע) are necessary in the Mishnah.

The Gemara answers that both are needed: if only rock were taught, one might think it is permitted because there is no concern for a decree, but with a well, one might decree due to times when it is filled with prepared fruit; thus both are necessary.

items.text: Baraita about a courtyard and upper story, and Rav Nachman's resolution
items.text_en: Baraita about a courtyard and upper story, and Rav Nachman's resolution
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a case where people of the courtyard and upper story forgot to make an eiruv: they use the lower ten handbreadths and upper ten handbreadths respectively. The Gemara notes that the middle space is prohibited. Rav Nachman explains the case involves a wall of nineteen handbreadths with a ledge (ziz): below ten, one accesses via a door and the other via a ladder; above ten, one via a door and the other via throwing.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings a baraita about a courtyard and upper story that forgot to make an eiruv, stating they use the lower ten handbreadths and upper ten handbreadths respectively, with a ledge (ziz) determining access.
The Gemara infers that the middle space between the lower and upper ten handbreadths is prohibited for both parties.

Rav Nachman resolves the baraita by explaining it involves a wall of nineteen handbreadths with a ledge (ziz): below ten, one accesses via a door and the other via a ladder; above ten, one via a door and the other via throwing.

items.text: Opening baraita
items.text_en: Opening baraita
items.desc_en: The baraita presents a case of two balconies, one above the other. If the upper balcony made an eruv but the lower did not, both are prohibited from carrying until they make a joint eruv.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a case of two balconies, one above the other, where only the upper made an eruv, and rules both are prohibited until they jointly make an eruv.

items.text: Rav Ada bar Ahava's explanation
items.text_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava's explanation
items.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava explains that the baraita refers to a situation where the lower balcony's residents pass through the upper balcony to draw water, thus the upper balcony's eruv does not permit them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ada bar Ahava explains that the baraita refers to a case where the lower balcony's residents pass through the upper balcony to draw water, so the upper balcony's eruv does not permit them.

items.text: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative explanation
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the balconies are within ten handbreadths of each other, so they restrict each other. He clarifies that even if only the upper balcony made an eruv, one might think the lower balcony's residents, who have easier access, should be permitted, but the baraita teaches that they are still prohibited because they are within ten handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the case involves balconies within ten handbreadths of each other, and the baraita uses a 'no need' style: obviously if only the lower balcony made an eruv, both are prohibited because they are within ten handbreadths.

Abaye clarifies that even if only the upper balcony made an eruv, one might think the lower balcony's easier access should permit it, but the baraita teaches that since they are within ten handbreadths, they still prohibit each other.

items.text: Support from Shmuel's ruling
items.text_en: Support from Shmuel's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara brings a statement by Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel: a roof adjacent to public domain requires a permanent ladder to permit carrying. The Gemara suggests this supports Abaye's reasoning that proximity within ten handbreadths creates restriction.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman in the name of Shmuel rules that a roof adjacent to public domain requires a fixed ladder to permit its use, and the Gemara infers that this is because proximity within ten handbreadths causes mutual restriction.

items.text: Rav Pappa's objection
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's objection
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects, suggesting that Shmuel's ruling might refer to a case where many people use the roof for carrying burdens like beams and scarves, not necessarily due to proximity within ten handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa objects to Shmuel's ruling, suggesting it might apply only when many people carry burdens like beams and scarves on the roof, not due to proximity within ten handbreadths.

items.text: Introduction of a new statement
items.text_en: Introduction of a new statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins a new statement from Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, which will continue the discussion.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel's new statement
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel's new statement
sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a new statement from Rav Yehuda in the name of Shmuel, continuing the discussion.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rav Yehuda's addition
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rav Yehuda's addition
items.desc_en: The Mishnah describes a cistern between two courtyards, each four cubits from its wall, where each may extend a small ledge and draw water. Rav Yehuda adds that even a reed suffices.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the law: a cistern between two courtyards, each four cubits from its wall, allows each to extend a small ledge and draw water.
Rav Yehuda adds that even a reed suffices as a ledge.

items.text: Abaye's identification of Rav Yehuda's source
items.text_en: Abaye's identification of Rav Yehuda's source
items.desc_en: Abaye tells Rav Yosef that Rav Yehuda's statement follows Shmuel, not Rav, because Rav holds that a person does not forbid another through airspace.

sub.desc_en: Abaye tells Rav Yosef that Rav Yehuda's statement follows Shmuel, not Rav, because Rav holds that a person does not forbid another through airspace.

items.text: Gemara's search for Shmuel's source
items.text_en: Gemara's search for Shmuel's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether Shmuel's view derives from his ruling about a roof near public domain, but rejects it due to Rav Pappa's distinction. It then finds support from the Mishnah's implication that without a ledge, one forbids through airspace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: From where does Shmuel derive his view that one can forbid a neighbor through airspace?
The Gemara proposes that Shmuel's view might come from his ruling about a roof near public domain requiring a fixed ladder.
The Gemara rejects this, noting that Rav Pappa's distinction might apply there.
The Gemara concludes that Shmuel's view derives from the Mishnah's implication that without a ledge, one forbids a neighbor through airspace.

items.text: Gemara's search for Rav's source
items.text_en: Gemara's search for Rav's source
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers Rav's ruling about two balconies, where Rav Huna says the upper is permitted if separated by four cubits. It rejects this as proof because the case is different: one uses throwing and lowering, the other only lowering, akin to throwing and a doorway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks from where Rav derives his ruling that one person does not prohibit another through the airspace.
Rav Huna cites Rav's ruling that in the case of two balconies, if the upper is separated by four cubits it is permitted, implying that airspace prohibition applies only when close.
The Gemara rejects this proof because the balcony case is different: one uses throwing and lowering, the other only lowering, analogous to throwing and a doorway.

items.text: Alternative source for Rav's view
items.text_en: Alternative source for Rav's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh quoting Rav about two houses with three ruins between them, where each uses the nearest ruin by throwing, implying Rav's view that airspace does not forbid.

sub.text: Gemara's citation of Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh quoting Rav
sub.text_en: Gemara's citation of Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh quoting Rav
sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites an alternative source for Rav's view: Rav Nachman quoting Rabbah bar Avuh quoting Rav about two houses with three ruins between them, where each uses the nearest ruin by throwing, implying that airspace does not forbid.

items.text: Rav's ruling on the middle house and the dispute with Rav Berona
items.text_en: Rav's ruling on the middle house and the dispute with Rav Berona
items.desc_en: Rav Berona teaches that the middle house is forbidden. Rabbi Eliezer bar Bei Rav questions whether Rav said this, and Rav Berona confirms. When Rabbi Eliezer reports to Rav, Rav clarifies that the houses are arranged as a חצובה, not a שורה, so the ruling differs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Berona teaches that the middle house is forbidden.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer bar Bei Rav's question
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Bei Rav's question
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Bei Rav asks Rav Berona whether Rav actually said this ruling.
Rav Berona confirms and shows Rabbi Eliezer his lodging.

sub.text: Rabbi Eliezer bar Bei Rav's objection to Rav
sub.text_en: Rabbi Eliezer bar Bei Rav's objection to Rav
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer reports to Rav and objects that Rav himself previously ruled that when one throws from a side house and the other throws from the other side, both are forbidden.
Rav clarifies that the houses are arranged as a חצובה (tripod), not a שורה (row), so the ruling differs.

items.text: Rav Pappa's question about Shmuel and Rav Dimi's ruling
items.text_en: Rav Pappa's question about Shmuel and Rav Dimi's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava whether Shmuel rejects Rav Dimi's ruling that a place less than four by four handbreadths may be used for transferring between domains. Rava distinguishes: Rav Dimi's case involves biblical domains, while here the domains are rabbinic, and the Sages strengthened their decrees.

sub.desc_en: Rav Pappa asks Rava whether Shmuel rejects Rav Dimi's ruling, citing Rabbi Yochanan's statement that a place less than four by four handbreadths may be used for transferring between domains.
Rava distinguishes: Rav Dimi's case involves biblical domains, while here the domains are rabbinic, and the Sages strengthened their decrees more than Torah law.

items.text: Ravina's challenge and Rava's resolution about two houses
items.text_en: Ravina's challenge and Rava's resolution about two houses
items.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rava, citing a dispute between Rabbah bar Rav Huna (citing Rav) and Shmuel about throwing between two houses across a public domain. Rava explains that the concern is that one might lift and lower, leading to carrying, so it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: Ravina challenges Rava by citing a dispute between Rabbah bar Rav Huna (citing Rav) and Shmuel about throwing between two houses across a public domain, implying Rav's position contradicts Rava's earlier ruling.
Rava explains that the concern is that one might lift and lower, leading to carrying, so it is forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah: Where an eruv may not be placed
items.text_en: Mishnah: Where an eruv may not be placed
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if one places an eruv in a gatehouse, portico, or balcony, it is invalid, and a resident there does not restrict. However, in a barn, cattle shed, woodshed, or storeroom, the eruv is valid and the resident restricts. Rabbi Yehuda adds an exception if the owner has a hold on the place.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that placing an עירוב (eiruv) in a gatehouse, portico, or balcony is invalid, and a resident there does not restrict carrying.
The Mishnah continues that in a hay shed, cattle shed, woodshed, or storeroom, the עירוב (eiruv) is valid and the resident restricts.
Rabbi Yehuda adds an exception: if the homeowner has a right of usage there, the resident does not restrict.

items.text: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rules and exceptions
items.text_en: Gemara: Clarifying the Mishnah's rules and exceptions
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat states a general principle: wherever a resident does not restrict, an eruv placed there is invalid, except for a private gatehouse. He adds that where an eruv may not be placed, a shituf may be placed, except in the airspace of an alley. The Gemara questions what is new, and resolves that the exceptions of a private gatehouse and alley airspace are needed. A baraita is cited and reconciled with the Mishnah.

sub.text: Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.text_en: Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat
sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda bar Shmuel bar Shilat states a general principle: wherever a resident does not restrict, an eruv placed there is invalid, except for a private gatehouse; and wherever an eruv may not be placed, a shituf may be placed, except in the airspace of an alley.
The Gemara questions what is new in this statement, noting that the Mishnah already implies that an eruv is invalid in these places but a shituf might be valid.

The Gemara answers that the exceptions of a private gatehouse and alley airspace are needed, as they were not taught in the Mishnah. A baraita is cited and reconciled with the Mishnah by reading it as referring to a shituf.
The Gemara objects that a shituf placed in an alley is not properly guarded, and resolves that the baraita refers to a courtyard in the alley.

items.text: Shmuel's ruling on bread for eruv and the dispute resolved
items.text_en: Shmuel's ruling on bread for eruv and the dispute resolved
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: if a group is dining and the day becomes sanctified, they may rely on the bread on the table for an eruv or shituf. Rabbah says there is no dispute: one refers to dining indoors (eruv), the other in the courtyard (shituf). Abaye supports this with a baraita, which is then reconciled with the Mishnah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda cites Shmuel: a group dining when the day becomes sanctified may rely on the bread on the table for an eruv or shituf.
Rabbah resolves the dispute: the two versions refer to different locations — indoors for eruv, in the courtyard for shituf.
Abaye supports Rabbah with a baraita that distinguishes between eruv in the house within the courtyard and shituf in the courtyard within the alleyway.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's condition and the story of Ben Bonyas
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's condition and the story of Ben Bonyas
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains Rabbi Yehuda's condition of תפיסת יד with the example of Bonyas's courtyard. Ben Bonyas came before Rabbi, who asked the people to make room for a man worth a hundred maneh. Another person then came and asked them to make room.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what constitutes Rabbi Yehuda's condition of תפיסת יד (a resident's grasp on the property).
The Gemara answers with the example of Bonyas's courtyard, where the owner maintained a grasp.
The story relates that Ben Bonyas came before Rabbi, who instructed the people to make room for a man worth a hundred maneh.
Another person then came and asked the people to make room.

items.text: Opening anecdote about honoring the wealthy
items.text_en: Opening anecdote about honoring the wealthy
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi honored wealthy individuals, and Rabbi Akiva did as well, citing a verse about the world enduring through kindness and truth.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi instructed people to make room for a wealthy man worth 200 maneh, and Rabbi Yishmael beRabbi Yosei noted the man's father's immense wealth, to which Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi replied to tell the father not to send him in those vessels.
The Gemara states that both Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Akiva honored the wealthy, citing Rava bar Mari's homily that the world endures only when kindness and truth are present.

items.text: Rabba bar bar Chana's analogy
items.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana's analogy
items.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana compares the matter to a plowshare peg, illustrating a point about movable objects.

sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana compares the matter to a plowshare peg, illustrating a point about movable objects.

items.text: Rav Nachman's principle about movable objects
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's principle about movable objects
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites a teaching from the school of Shmuel: an object that may be moved on Shabbat prohibits eiruv, while one that may not be moved does not. A baraita supports this.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman cites the school of Shmuel's principle: an object that may be moved on Shabbat prohibits eiruv, while one that may not be moved does not.
A baraita supports Rav Nachman's principle, adding examples of tevel and a glass lamp.

items.text: Mishnah: One who leaves home for Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: One who leaves home for Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about whether a person who leaves his home to stay elsewhere for Shabbat prohibits his original house from being included in the eiruv. Rabbi Meir says he does, Rabbi Yehuda says he does not, Rabbi Yosei distinguishes between a Jew and a gentile, and Rabbi Shimon says even if he stays with his daughter in the same city he does not prohibit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of one who leaves his home to stay elsewhere for Shabbat, and presents Rabbi Meir's position that both a gentile and a Jew prohibit their original house from being included in the eiruv.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the person does not prohibit his original house from being included in the eiruv.
Rabbi Yosei distinguishes: a gentile prohibits, but a Jew does not, because it is not the way of a Jew to come on Shabbat.
Rabbi Shimon adds that even if he stays with his daughter in the same city, he does not prohibit, because he has already removed his residence from his mind.

items.text: Gemara: Rav rules like Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Gemara: Rav rules like Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav rules the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, specifically only when he goes to his daughter, not his son, citing a folk saying about dogs barking.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon's position.
Rav specifies that Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies only when one goes to his daughter, not to his son.
Rav supports his distinction by citing a folk saying: if a dog barks at you, enter; if a puppy barks at you, leave — implying a daughter's home is more welcoming than a son's.

items.text: Mishnah: A well between two courtyards
items.text_en: Mishnah: A well between two courtyards
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a well situated between two courtyards: one may not draw water from it on Shabbat unless a partition ten handbreadths high is made, either below, within the well's rim, or above. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel cites Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, and Rabbi Yehuda comments that the partition should not be greater than the wall between them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that a well between two courtyards requires a partition ten handbreadths high, placed below, within the rim, or above, to permit drawing water on Shabbat.

sub.text: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.text_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel citing Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel
sub.desc_en: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel reports that Beit Shammai say the partition is placed below the water and Beit Hillel say it is placed above the water.
Rabbi Yehuda comments that the partition should not be taller than the wall between the two courtyards.

items.text: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Gemara: Dispute between Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda dispute the meaning of 'below' and 'above' in the Mishnah. Rav Huna says literally below or above the well, while Rav Yehuda says below or above the water. Rabba bar Rav Chanan questions Rav Yehuda's view, and Abaye answers with teachings about reeds needing to be visible or submerged.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna explains that 'below' and 'above' in the Mishnah refer literally to below or above the well.
Rav Yehuda counters that 'below' and 'above' refer to below or above the water level.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan questions Abaye: if Rav Yehuda's 'below the water' still has water mixing, why not allow literal 'below' which also has mixing?

sub.text: Abaye's answer citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.text_en: Abaye's answer citing Rav Yehuda citing Rav
sub.desc_en: Abaye answers that Rav Yehuda's view requires the tops of reeds to be visible one handbreadth above the water, preventing mixing.

sub.text: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's second question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan's second question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar Rav Chanan similarly questions Rav Yehuda's 'above the water' view, asking why literal 'above' is rejected if water still mixes.
Abaye answers that Rav Yehuda's 'above the water' requires submerging the tops of reeds one handbreadth into the water, preventing mixing.

items.text: Transition to another teaching of Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Transition to another teaching of Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite another statement of Rav Yehuda about a beam permitting use of a ruin, but the discussion is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite Rav Yehuda's statement about a beam of four cubits permitting use of a ruin, and notes that Rav Nachman said it in the name of Rabba bar Avuh.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's first question
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Gemara's first question
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a beam of four handbreadths permits water. The Gemara questions how a bucket can go to the other side and bring water, and answers that the Sages established that a bucket does not travel more than four handbreadths.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a beam of four handbreadths permits the use of water in a courtyard.
The Gemara asks how a bucket can go to the other side of the beam and bring water, given the beam's limitation.
The Gemara resolves that the Sages established a bucket does not travel more than four handbreadths, so it never exits the beam's coverage.

items.text: Gemara's second question and Rabbi Tavla's inquiry
items.text_en: Gemara's second question and Rabbi Tavla's inquiry
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about water mixing under the beam, and answers that it is a leniency the Sages applied to water. Rabbi Tavla asks Rav about a suspended partition in a ruin, and Rav replies that a suspended partition only permits water, as a leniency.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that mixing of water under the beam should still be a problem, as the bucket splashes water across the sides.
The Gemara answers that the leniency is because water is קל (considered light), and the Sages were lenient regarding water.
The Gemara cites the precedent where Rabbi Tavla asked Rav about a hanging partition, and Rav ruled that only water permits it due to the leniency for water.
Rabbi Yehuda objects that a hanging partition should not be considered a valid partition at all.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports in Rabbi Yochanan's name that Rabbi Yehuda's position aligns with Rabbi Yossi, who permits a hanging partition even on dry land.

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's statement and Rabbi Yochanan's explanation
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda says a suspended partition should not be permitted. Rabba bar bar Chana says Rabbi Yochanan taught that Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Yosei's view, who permits a suspended partition even on dry land. A Mishnah about a sukka with dangling walls is cited, where Rabbi Yosei requires ten handbreadths from above to below as well.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda states that a suspended partition (מחיצה תלויה) should not be permitted.

sub.text: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.text_en: Rabba bar bar Chana citing Rabbi Yochanan
sub.desc_en: Rabba bar bar Chana reports that Rabbi Yochanan explained Rabbi Yehuda's statement as following Rabbi Yosei's view, who permits a suspended partition even on dry land.
A Mishnah is cited about a sukka with dangling walls, where Rabbi Yosei requires ten handbreadths from above to below as well, supporting the view that a suspended partition is valid.

items.text: Distinction between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Distinction between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that Rabbi Yehuda does not fully hold like Rabbi Yosei, because Rabbi Yehuda only permits a suspended partition for the rabbinic matter of eiruv chatzeiros, not for the Torah-mandated sukka. Conversely, Rabbi Yosei does not hold like Rabbi Yehuda, because Rabbi Yosei only permits it for sukka, which involves a positive commandment, not for Shabbat, which carries the penalty of stoning.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that Rabbi Yehuda does not fully adopt Rabbi Yosei's view, nor does Rabbi Yosei adopt Rabbi Yehuda's view.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehuda only permits a suspended partition for the rabbinic matter of עירוב חצרות (eiruv chatzeiros), not for the Torah-mandated סוכה (sukka).
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Yosei only permits a suspended partition for סוכה (sukka), which involves a positive commandment, not for שבת (Shabbat), which carries the penalty of stoning.

items.text: The incident in Tzippori and the question about a tent
items.text_en: The incident in Tzippori and the question about a tent
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authorized the incident in Tzippori, and answers it was Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei, not Rabbi Yosei himself. Rav Dimi relates that they once forgot a Torah scroll and spread a sheet on pillars to bring it, but the Gemara objects that one may not make a temporary tent on Shabbat. The story is corrected: they found sheets already spread.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who authorized the incident in Tzippori where a suspended partition was used on land on Shabbat.
The Gemara answers that the incident was performed on the authority of Rabbi Yishmael ben Rabbi Yosei, not Rabbi Yosei himself.
Rav Dimi relates a story where people forgot a Torah scroll and spread a sheet on pillars to bring it on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that spreading a sheet on Shabbat is forbidden because one may not make a temporary tent on Shabbat.
The Gemara corrects the story: they found sheets already spread on the pillars, so no tent was made on Shabbat.

items.text: Rabba equates Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya
items.text_en: Rabba equates Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya
items.desc_en: Rabba states that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya said the same thing. He cites Rabbi Yehuda's view as mentioned, and then begins to cite Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's ruling about a balcony (גזוזטרא) of four by four amot.

sub.desc_en: Rabba opens by stating that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya said the same thing, referencing Rabbi Yehuda's previously mentioned view.

sub.text: Rabba citing Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya
sub.text_en: Rabba citing Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya
sub.desc_en: Rabba begins citing Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's ruling about a balcony (גזוזטרא) of four by four amot to support the equivalence.

items.text: Continuation of the previous discussion: hollowing out a space in a balcony
items.text_en: Continuation of the previous discussion: hollowing out a space in a balcony
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues the previous discussion about a balcony (גזוזטרא) that has four by four cubits, where one may hollow out a four by four handbreadth space and fill it with water. This segment states the halakha without further elaboration.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the halakha that one may hollow out a four-by-four handbreadth space in a balcony and fill it with water.

items.text: Abaye's challenge to the previous ruling
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to the previous ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye challenges the application of the previous ruling, arguing that Rabbi Yehuda's principle of 'Gud Achit Mechitzta' (extend the partition downward) does not apply here, and Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's leniency was specific to the Sea of Tiberias due to its banks and surrounding towns and enclosures, not to other bodies of water.

sub.desc_en: Abaye challenges the previous ruling, arguing that Rabbi Yehuda's principle of 'Gud Achit Mechitzta' (extend the partition downward) does not apply here, and the combination of 'Kof' (bend) and 'Gud' (extend) is not accepted.
Abaye explains that Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya's leniency was specific to the Sea of Tiberias due to its banks, towns, and enclosures, but not to other bodies of water.

items.text: Abaye and Rav Huna's rulings on the dimensions of the balcony
items.text_en: Abaye and Rav Huna's rulings on the dimensions of the balcony
items.desc_en: Abaye rules that if the balcony is close to the wall (within three handbreadths), it needs specific dimensions: length four cubits, width eleven and a bit. If it is upright, height ten handbreadths and width six and two bits. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that if it stands in a corner, height ten handbreadths and width two and two bits.

sub.desc_en: Abaye rules that according to Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya, if the balcony is within three handbreadths of the wall, it must be four cubits long and eleven and a bit handbreadths wide.
Abaye adds that if the balcony is upright, it must be ten handbreadths high and six and two bits handbreadths wide.
Rav Huna bar Yehoshua adds that if the balcony stands in a corner, it must be ten handbreadths high and two and two bits handbreadths wide.

items.text: Clarification of the baraita about the balcony
items.text_en: Clarification of the baraita about the balcony
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baraita of Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya, which requires a balcony of four by four cubits to hollow out four by four handbreadths, can be fulfilled. It answers that the balcony is made like a pillar (אסיתא), i.e., it is narrow at the top and wide at the bottom.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks how the baraita of Rabbi Chananya ben Akavya, requiring a balcony of four by four cubits to hollow out four by four handbreadths, can be fulfilled.
The Gemara answers that the balcony is made like a pillar (אסיתא), i.e., narrow at the top and wide at the bottom, so the hollowed space is at the top.

items.text: Mishnah: Water channel in a courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: Water channel in a courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that if a water channel (אמת המים) passes through a courtyard, one may not draw water from it on Shabbat unless a partition ten handbreadths high is made at its entrance and exit. Rabbi Yehuda says the wall above the channel is considered a partition. He brings a precedent from the channel of Abel, but the Sages reject it because the channel was less than the required measure.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one may not draw water from a water channel passing through a courtyard on Shabbat unless a partition ten handbreadths high is made at its entrance and exit.
Rabbi Yehuda states that the wall above the channel is considered a partition, obviating the need for a separate one.
Rabbi Yehuda brings a precedent from the channel of Abel, where the elders permitted drawing water on Shabbat, implying the wall served as a partition.

The Sages reject the precedent, explaining that the channel of Abel was less than the required measure (ten handbreadths deep and four wide), so it never constituted a biblical domain requiring a partition.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on the channel and Rabbi Yehuda's precedent
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on the channel and Rabbi Yehuda's precedent
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita that elaborates on the Mishnah: a partition is needed at both entrance and exit. Rabbi Yehuda again argues that the wall above suffices, and brings a precedent from the channel from Abel to Tzippori. The Sages reject it, saying the channel was not ten handbreadths deep and four wide.

sub.desc_en: The baraita restates the Mishnah's rule that a partition is required at both entrance and exit, and records Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting opinion that the wall above the channel suffices as a partition.
Rabbi Yehuda brings a precedent from the channel that ran from Abel to Tzippori, where the elders permitted drawing water on שבת (the Sabbath) relying on the wall above.
The Sages reject the precedent, arguing that the channel was not ten handbreadths deep and four wide, so it never constituted a biblical domain requiring a partition.

items.text: Baraita on a channel between windows and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Baraita on a channel between windows and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: A baraita discusses a water channel passing between windows: if the gap is less than three handbreadths, one may lower a bucket and draw water; if three, not. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says less than four is permitted. The Gemara questions the context, considering whether it refers to the channel itself or its banks, and cites Rav Dimi's statement about a place less than four by four handbreadths being permissible for carrying between domains, provided one does not exchange. The Gemara concludes the discussion is about the channel's banks, and the ruling is to prevent exchange.

sub.desc_en: A baraita rules on a water channel between windows: if the gap is less than three handbreadths one may lower a bucket and draw water; if three, not; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says less than four is permitted.

The Gemara asks what the baraita refers to: if it is the channel itself, then Rav Dimi's statement that a כרמלית (a karmelit) cannot be less than four handbreadths would conflict with the baraita's three-handbreadth threshold.
The Gemara objects: would Rav Dimi's statement then be a dispute between Tannaim (the Tanna Kamma and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel)?
The Gemara answers that the baraita refers to the banks (אגפיה) of the channel, and the ruling is to prevent exchange (להחליף) of objects between domains.
The Gemara cites Rav Dimi's statement in the name of Rabbi Yochanan: a place less than four by four handbreadths is permitted for carrying between domains, provided one does not exchange.
The Gemara resolves that the case there involves domains that are de-oraita (biblical), distinguishing it from the present discussion.

items.text: Introduction to the dispute: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on a wall without four handbreadths
items.text_en: Introduction to the dispute: Rav and Rabbi Yochanan on a wall without four handbreadths
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the previous discussion involved Rabbinic domains, and Rabbi Yochanan also rules leniently in Rabbinic domains, as cited in a baraita about a wall between two courtyards. The baraita details the laws of a wall ten handbreadths high and four wide, and what happens if it is breached.

items.text: The dispute over a wall lacking four handbreadths
items.text_en: The dispute over a wall lacking four handbreadths
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises the question: what if the wall has no four handbreadths width? Rav says the air of two domains controls it, and one may not move even a hair's breadth there. Rabbi Yochanan says each side may bring up and eat. This follows Rabbi Yochanan's consistent view, as reported by Rav Dimi: a place lacking four by four handbreadths is permitted for both public and private domain residents to rest items on it, provided they do not exchange.

items.text: Reconciliation of Ze'iri and Rav Dimi's positions
items.text_en: Reconciliation of Ze'iri and Rav Dimi's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the statement about a place lacking four by four was said by Ze'iri, but it is difficult for Ze'iri because of the baraita. Ze'iri establishes the baraita as referring to the water channel itself. Rav Dimi says it is a dispute between Tannaim. The Gemara raises an objection about the holes of a karmelit, and Abaye bar Avin and Rav Chanina bar Avin say there are no holes for a karmelit. Rav Ashi says even if there are, it is when the hole is adjacent, but here it is distant. Ravina says it is like one made outlets at its mouth.

items.text: Conclusion: the Sages and Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel follow their reasoning
items.text_en: Conclusion: the Sages and Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel follow their reasoning
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the Sages and Rabbi Shimon ben Gamliel follow their respective reasoning, referencing earlier disputes.

items.text: Mishnah: Balcony over water and two balconies
items.text_en: Mishnah: Balcony over water and two balconies
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a balcony over water may not be used to draw water on Shabbat unless a partition ten handbreadths high is made, either above or below. Similarly, if there are two balconies one above the other, and a partition is made for the upper but not the lower, both are prohibited unless they establish an eruv.

items.text: Gemara: Chananya ben Akavya's leniency for Tiberias
items.text_en: Gemara: Chananya ben Akavya's leniency for Tiberias
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Chananya ben Akavya, who permits drawing water from a balcony if it has four by four amot, by hollowing out four by four. Rabbi Yochanan in the name of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra limits this to the Sea of Tiberias because it has banks, towns, and enclosures surrounding it, but not for other waters. A baraita lists three leniencies Chananya ben Akavya permitted for the people of Tiberias: drawing water from a balcony, insulating with wood chips, and bathing in aluntit. The Gemara elaborates on the insulation leniency regarding the laws of 'ki yutan' (if water is placed on produce).

items.text: Opening statement about the people of Tiberias
items.text_en: Opening statement about the people of Tiberias
items.desc_en: The Gemara compares the people of Tiberias to someone who has not nullified their work, introducing the concept of using a towel (aluntit) on Shabbat.

items.text: Baraita about drying with a towel
items.text_en: Baraita about drying with a towel
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited about drying oneself with a towel (aluntit) and leaving it in a window, with a dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Sages about bringing it into the house.

items.text: Dispute about filling vs. pouring water
items.text_en: Dispute about filling vs. pouring water
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Rav Huna distinguishes between filling water (permitted) and pouring it (forbidden) in a courtyard. Rav Sheizvi objects, comparing it to a drain (uka). A second version permits pouring as well, with Rav Sheizvi noting the distinction about the water's flow.

items.text: Two balconies and the principle of airspace
items.text_en: Two balconies and the principle of airspace
items.desc_en: Rav Huna citing Rav rules that the Mishnah's case of two balconies applies only when they are close, but if far apart, the upper one is permitted. This aligns with Rav's principle that a person does not prohibit another through airspace.

items.text: Theft on Shabbat and returning a ruin
items.text_en: Theft on Shabbat and returning a ruin
items.desc_en: Rabbah citing Rabbi Chiyya and Rav Yosef citing Rabbi Oshaya state that there is theft on Shabbat, and a ruin is returned to its owners. The Gemara questions the contradiction: if acquisition occurs, why return it? The answer clarifies that it means there is a law of theft on Shabbat, i.e., the ruin is returned.

items.text: Challenge from the Mishnah about two balconies
items.text_en: Challenge from the Mishnah about two balconies
items.desc_en: Rabbah challenges the ruling about theft on Shabbat from the Mishnah: if there is a law of theft, why are the balconies prohibited? Rav Sheshet answers that the case involves a partition made in partnership. The Gemara objects that if so, the lower balcony should also be permitted, and explains that building the lower balcony reveals the owner's intent to exclude the other.

items.text: Mishnah: Courtyard less than four cubits
items.text_en: Mishnah: Courtyard less than four cubits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a courtyard less than four cubits requires a drain (uka) holding two se'ah for pouring water on Shabbat. It discusses the drain's placement, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's opinion about a covered drain, and the Sages' view. It also addresses combining a courtyard and portico, and two rows of houses where some made a drain and others did not.

items.text: Gemara: Reason for the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara: Reason for the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains the rationale: a person typically uses two se'ah of water daily, and in a four-cubit area, one wants to sprinkle it, so the drain prevents the water from spreading into the public domain.

items.text: Opening dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbah
items.text_en: Opening dispute between Rabbi Zeira and Rabbah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a courtyard less than four cubits requires pouring water into a pit. Rabbi Zeira says that four cubits is a requirement (תיימי), while less than four is not. Abaye explains the difference between them is a case of a long and narrow courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a courtyard less than four cubits requires pouring water into a pit; otherwise it is forbidden.
Rabbi Zeira explains that four cubits is a requirement (תיימי), while less than four is not.
Abaye clarifies that the practical difference between the two positions is a case of a long and narrow courtyard.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbah from the Mishnah of courtyard and porch
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbah from the Mishnah of courtyard and porch
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a courtyard and porch combine for four cubits. This is consistent with Rabbi Zeira but challenges Rabbah. Rabbi Zeira resolves it by explaining that the porch runs along the entire courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites a Mishnah that a courtyard and porch combine for four cubits, which is consistent with Rabbi Zeira but challenges Rabbah.
Rabbi Zeira resolves the challenge by explaining that the Mishnah refers to a porch that runs along the entire length of the courtyard.

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Zeira from a baraita
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Zeira from a baraita
items.desc_en: A baraita states that a courtyard without four by four cubits cannot have water poured into it. This supports Rabbah but challenges Rabbi Zeira. Rabbi Zeira responds that the baraita follows the Sages, while the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Zeira by citing a baraita that a courtyard lacking four by four cubits cannot have water poured into it on Shabbat, which supports Rabbah but contradicts Rabbi Zeira.
Rabbi Zeira responds that the baraita follows the Sages, while the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, thereby resolving the contradiction.

items.text: Rava's support for Rabbi Zeira's interpretation
items.text_en: Rava's support for Rabbi Zeira's interpretation
items.desc_en: Rava explains why Rabbi Zeira was forced to interpret the Mishnah as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov: the Mishnah's wording 'courtyard that is less than four' implies a minimum of four, which aligns with Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov's view. The Gemara concludes that this is conclusive.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks what forced Rabbi Zeira to interpret the Mishnah as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.
Rava explains that the Mishnah's wording 'courtyard that is less than four' implies a minimum of four, which forced Rabbi Zeira's interpretation.
The Gemara concludes that this reasoning is conclusive proof that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov.

items.text: Resolution of the contradiction within the baraita
items.text_en: Resolution of the contradiction within the baraita
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the latter part of the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but the first part does not. It resolves by saying the entire baraita is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but it is missing text: it should read that a courtyard less than four cubits is forbidden, but one of four cubits is permitted, as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that the latter part of the baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but the first part does not, creating a contradiction.

The Gemara resolves that the entire baraita is Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, but it is missing text: it should read that a courtyard less than four cubits is forbidden, but one of four cubits is permitted, as Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov says.

items.text: The Mishnah disagrees with Chananya
items.text_en: The Mishnah disagrees with Chananya
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah does not follow Chananya, who says that even a roof of one hundred cubits cannot be used for pouring, because a roof is designed to drain, not absorb.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the Mishnah does not follow Chananya's opinion.
A baraita is cited where Chananya rules that even a roof of one hundred cubits cannot be used for pouring, because a roof is designed to drain, not absorb.

items.text: Distinction between summer and winter
items.text_en: Distinction between summer and winter
items.desc_en: A Tanna states that the prohibition applies only in summer, but in winter one may pour repeatedly. Rava explains that in winter, people want the water to be absorbed in place. Abaye challenges from the case of gutters, and Rava responds that there is no concern for damage or suspicion.

sub.desc_en: A Tanna states that the prohibition against pouring water applies only in summer, but in winter one may pour repeatedly without restriction.
Rava explains that in winter, people want the water to be absorbed in place, so there is no concern about spillage.
Abaye challenges Rava by citing the case of gutters (שופכין), where people also want absorption, yet the mishnah prohibits pouring.
Rava responds that in the gutter case, there is no concern for damage (since the courtyard is already damaged) or for suspicion (since gutters normally spill water anyway).

items.text: Rav Nachman's ruling on pit capacity
items.text_en: Rav Nachman's ruling on pit capacity
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that in winter, one may give water according to the pit's capacity; in summer, only if it holds two se'ah. The Gemara questions why not give one se'ah in summer, and answers due to a decree lest one give two. The same reasoning applies as before.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that in winter, water is given according to the pit's capacity; in summer, only if it holds two se'ah, otherwise none at all.
The Gemara questions why in summer, if the pit holds one se'ah, one may not give even one se'ah.
The Gemara answers that it is a decree lest one come to give two se'ah.
The Gemara objects that the same decree should apply in winter as well.
The Gemara resolves that in winter there is no concern for damage or false rumors, so the decree does not apply.

items.text: Abaye and Rava on large quantities and multiple stories
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava on large quantities and multiple stories
items.desc_en: Abaye concludes that even a kor or two kor may be poured. Rava adds that even if two apartments face each other, it is permitted. Abaye questions the reason, citing a baraita that allows pouring into various containers. The Gemara concludes with Rava's corrected statement.

sub.desc_en: Abaye concludes that in the rainy season, one may pour even a kor or two kor of water into a small pit.
The Gemara cites the mishna's rule about two upper stories facing each other.
Rava states that this halakha applies even if the residents of the two stories established an עירוב (eiruv) together.
Abaye asks Rava for the reason behind his ruling.
Abaye objects that if the reason is the increase in water, a baraita shows that even full containers may receive more water on שבת (Shabbat).
The Gemara concludes that Rava's statement was actually transmitted in a different version, which is then implied to follow.

items.text: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about an alleyway
items.text_en: Gemara's question on the Mishnah's ruling about an alleyway
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, if the residents did not establish an eruv, they are prohibited from carrying from the alleyway into the courtyards. Rav Ashi explains it is a decree lest one come to carry items from the houses into the alleyway.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, if the residents did not establish an eruv, they are prohibited from carrying from the alleyway into the courtyards.
The Mishnah states that the prohibition of carrying from roofs to courtyards applies only when the residents did not make an עירוב (merger of courtyards), but if they did, it is permitted.
Rav Ashi explains that the prohibition is a decree lest one come to carry items from the houses into the alleyway.

items.text: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.text_en: Conclusion of the previous chapter
items.desc_en: This segment marks the formal conclusion of the previous chapter, with the phrase 'הדרן עלך' indicating the return to the study of the chapter.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the previous chapter with the formulaic phrase 'הדרן עלך' (we return to you).

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Rooftops as a single domain
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Rooftops as a single domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute: Rabbi Meir considers all rooftops of a city a single domain, provided no roof is ten handbreadths higher or lower. The Sages say each roof is its own domain. Rabbi Shimon adds that rooftops, courtyards, and enclosed areas are a single domain only for vessels that rested within them, not for those that rested in the house.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that all roofs of a city are a single domain, provided no roof is ten handbreadths higher or lower, according to Rabbi Meir.
The Mishnah opens with Rabbi Meir's ruling that all roofs of a city are a single domain, provided no roof is ten handbreadths higher or lower.
The Sages argue that each roof is its own domain.
Rabbi Shimon rules that roofs, courtyards, and enclosures are a single domain for vessels that rested within them, but not for vessels that rested in the house.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rabbi Meir's reasoning
items.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin, with Abaye present, question Rabbi Meir's position. If he holds that dwellings are divided below, they should be divided above as well, so why are roofs a single domain? If he holds they are not divided, even a roof ten handbreadths high or low should be included.

sub.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin's discussion
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin's discussion
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin explain that the Sages hold that just as dwellings are divided below, so too are they divided above.

sub.text: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin's question
sub.text_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin's question
sub.desc_en: Abaye bar Avin and Rabbi Chanina bar Avin, with Abaye present, question the rationale of the Sages, who hold that just as dwellings are divided below, so they are divided above.

They question what Rabbi Meir holds: if he agrees that dwellings are divided above, why are roofs a single domain; if he holds they are not divided, why does he make an exception for a roof ten handbreadths high or low?

sub.text: Abaye's answer citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.text_en: Abaye's answer citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi
sub.desc_en: Abaye answers by citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi, who reports that Rabbi Meir's distinction is a decree: just as a pillar in a private domain that is ten handbreadths high and four wide is forbidden for use lest one come to use a mound in the public domain, so too a high roof is forbidden.

items.text: Abaye's answer: Decree due to a mound in the public domain
items.text_en: Abaye's answer: Decree due to a mound in the public domain
items.desc_en: Abaye cites Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi who reported that Rabbi Meir's reasoning is a decree: just as a pillar in a private domain that is ten handbreadths high and four wide is prohibited for use lest one come to use a mound in the public domain, so too a high roof is prohibited. The Sages initially thought this applied even to a mortar or vat, but Abaye clarifies it applies only to a pillar and a millstone, which are fixed.

sub.desc_en: Abaye answers the earlier question by citing Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's report that Rabbi Meir's ruling is a decree: just as a pillar in a private domain is prohibited for use lest one come to use a mound in the public domain, so too a high roof is prohibited.
The Sages initially thought Rabbi Meir's decree applies even to a mortar or a vat.
Abaye clarifies that Rabbi Meir's decree applies only to a pillar and a millstone, which are fixed in place.

items.text: Challenge from a wall between two courtyards
items.text_en: Challenge from a wall between two courtyards
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Abaye's explanation: a wall between two courtyards is fixed, yet Rav Yehuda said that according to Rabbi Meir, roofs, courtyards, and enclosed areas are each separate domains. Does this not imply that one may carry via the wall? Rav Huna bar Yehuda in the name of Rav Sheshet explains it refers to carrying through doorways, not via the wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: consider a wall between two courtyards, which is fixed, yet Rav Yehuda said that according to Rabbi Meir, roofs, courtyards, and enclosures are each their own domain.

The Gemara challenges Abaye's explanation by citing a fixed wall between two courtyards and Rav Yehuda's statement that according to Rabbi Meir, roofs, courtyards, and enclosed areas are each separate domains.
The Gemara infers that this means it is permitted to carry via the wall.

sub.text: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.text_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet
sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehuda citing Rav Sheshet rejects this, explaining that it refers to bringing in and taking out through doorways.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on carrying on a roof
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel on carrying on a roof
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the Sages' view that each roof is its own domain. Rav says one may only carry within four cubits, while Shmuel permits carrying throughout. The dispute hinges on whether we apply the principle of 'gud aseik mechitzta' (extend the partition upward) when the partitions are not noticeable. The Mishnah is cited as support.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the Sages' view that each roof is its own domain.
The Gemara introduces the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding carrying on a roof: Rav restricts to four cubits, Shmuel permits throughout.
The Gemara clarifies that the dispute applies only when the partitions are not noticeable; when they are noticeable, all agree.
The Gemara explains that Rav rejects the principle of 'gud aseik mechitzta' (extend the partition upward), while Shmuel accepts it.

items.text: Gemara's question on Rav's position
items.text_en: Gemara's question on Rav's position
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel's ruling is consistent, but Rav's ruling is difficult. It sets up the need to explain Rav's view.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that Shmuel's ruling is consistent, but Rav's ruling is difficult, setting up the need to explain Rav's view.

items.text: Explanation of Rav's ruling and objection
items.text_en: Explanation of Rav's ruling and objection
items.desc_en: The school of Rav explains that the Mishnah's ruling is to prevent carrying two cubits on one roof and two on another. The Gemara objects based on Rabbi Elazar's report that the school of Rav said one may only carry within four cubits, while the school of Shmuel taught they have only their roof. The Gemara resolves that the school of Shmuel also meant two cubits on each roof.

sub.text: School of Rav in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: School of Rav in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: The school of Rav explains that the Mishnah's ruling is to prevent carrying two cubits on one roof and two on another.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Elazar reported the school of Rav said one may only carry within four cubits, while the school of Shmuel taught they have only their roof.
The Gemara resolves that the school of Shmuel also meant two cubits on each roof, consistent with the Mishnah.

items.text: Rav Yosef's unfamiliarity with the tradition
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's unfamiliarity with the tradition
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef states he has not heard this tradition. Abaye reminds him that he himself taught a related ruling about a large roof adjacent to a small one.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef states that he has not heard this tradition about the large roof adjacent to a small one.
Abaye reminds Rav Yosef that he himself taught the ruling: a large roof adjacent to a small one — the large is permitted, the small is forbidden.

items.text: Abaye's recollection of Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.text_en: Abaye's recollection of Rav Yehuda's ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye recalls that Rav Yosef taught them a ruling in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: the Mishnah's case is only when there are dwellings on both roofs, making the small roof's partition trampled; but if there are no dwellings, both are permitted.

sub.desc_en: Abaye recalls that Rav Yosef taught them a ruling in the name of Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: the Mishnah's restriction applies only when there are dwellings on both roofs, making the small roof's partition trampled; but if there are no dwellings, both are permitted.

items.text: Rav Yosef's correction: partitions, not dwellings
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's correction: partitions, not dwellings
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef corrects Abaye, saying he actually taught that the ruling applies when there are partitions on both roofs; the large roof is permitted via its own parapet, while the small one is breached fully. If there are no partitions, both are forbidden. He then clarifies that he meant partitions fit for dwelling.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef corrects Abaye, stating that the ruling applies only when there are partitions on both roofs; the large roof is permitted via its parapet remnants, while the small one is fully breached, and without partitions both are forbidden.
Rav Yosef clarifies that when he spoke of 'residents', he meant partitions fit for dwelling, reiterating the same halakhic distinction.

items.text: Exception when partition is only on the large roof
items.text_en: Exception when partition is only on the large roof
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef adds that if there is a partition fit for dwelling only on the large roof, even the small roof is permitted for the residents of the large one, because they disregard the partition.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that if a partition fit for dwelling exists only on the large roof, even the small roof is permitted for the residents of the large one, because the residents of the small roof have removed themselves from their domain.

items.text: Rav Nachman and Abaye's rulings on permanent structures
items.text_en: Rav Nachman and Abaye's rulings on permanent structures
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that if one made a permanent ladder to his roof, he is permitted to use all the roofs. Abaye adds that if one built an upper story and made a four-cubit balcony in front of it, he is permitted to use all the roofs.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman rules that if one affixed a permanent ladder to his roof, he is permitted to carry on all the roofs.
Abaye adds that if one built an upper story and erected a four-cubit balcony before it, he is permitted to carry on all the roofs.

items.text: Rava's qualification: balcony can be for prohibition
items.text_en: Rava's qualification: balcony can be for prohibition
items.desc_en: Rava notes that sometimes the balcony can be for prohibition, specifically when it is built facing the courtyard of his house, as it then serves as a partition that restricts.

sub.desc_en: Rava states that sometimes the small partition (דקה) leads to prohibition, specifically when it is built facing the garden of his house.

items.text: Clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.text_en: Clarification of the Mishnah's intent
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah's ruling about a roof and a courtyard is specifically for guarding the courtyard, not for general carrying.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that the Mishnah's ruling about a roof and a courtyard is specifically for guarding the courtyard, not for general carrying.

items.text: Rami bar Chama's question about two amot on roof and porch
items.text_en: Rami bar Chama's question about two amot on roof and porch
items.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks about the status of two amot on a roof and two amot on a porch. Rabba initially misunderstands, but Rami bar Chama clarifies: since neither is fit for dwelling, perhaps they form one domain, or perhaps the prohibition between roofs applies.

sub.desc_en: Rami bar Chama asks about the status of two amot on a roof and two amot on a pillar; Rabba misunderstands, thinking the question is about a כרמלית (neutral domain) and a רשות היחיד (private domain).
The gemara clarifies that Rami bar Chama, due to his sharpness, did not examine the matter carefully; his actual question is about two amot on a roof and two amot on a porch (אכסדרה).

The gemara presents the two sides of the question: since neither the roof nor the porch is fit for dwelling, perhaps they form one domain, or perhaps the prohibition between roofs applies, making it forbidden to carry from roof to porch.

items.text: Rav Bivi bar Abaye's question about two amot on roof and ruin
items.text_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye's question about two amot on roof and ruin
items.desc_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye asks about two amot on a roof and two amot on a ruin. Rav Kahana objects that this is like Rami bar Chama's question, but Rav Bivi distinguishes: a ruin is fit for dwelling, unlike a porch. The Gemara then presents an 'if you say' scenario, concluding with teiku.

sub.desc_en: Rav Bivi bar Abaye asks about the status of two amot on a roof and two amot on a ruin.
Rav Kahana objects that this is the same question as Rami bar Chama's.
Rav Bivi bar Abaye distinguishes: a ruin is fit for dwelling, unlike a porch.
The Gemara presents an 'if you say' scenario: even if a porch is unfit, a ruin is fit, but perhaps since it currently lacks dwellers it is different.
The Gemara concludes with teiku (the question remains unresolved).

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding roofs
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding roofs
items.desc_en: Rav permits carrying throughout a roof that is level (like Rabbi Meir's view) or a single roof (like the Sages), while Shmuel restricts carrying to four amot. The Gemara resolves apparent contradictions in each opinion: Rav's leniency applies where the partition is not noticeable, and Shmuel's stringency applies to a roof larger than beit se'atayim without proper partitions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara presents the dispute: regarding roofs that are level (according to Rabbi Meir) or an isolated roof (according to the Sages), Rav permits carrying throughout the entire roof, while Shmuel restricts carrying to four cubits.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: Rav's lenient ruling here seems to conflict with his earlier position that on a roof among roofs one may carry only within four cubits.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: there, in the case of multiple roofs, the inner partitions are not conspicuous, so they are not considered; here, the outer partitions of a single roof are conspicuous and are regarded as extending upward.
The Gemara raises a contradiction: Shmuel's restrictive ruling here seems to conflict with his earlier position that on level roofs one may carry throughout each separate roof.

The Gemara resolves the contradiction: there, the roof area is no more than two בית סאתים (beit se'atayim), so the partitions are effective; here, the roof is larger than two בית סאתים, and the partitions were made for below, not for above, so it is like an enclosure larger than two בית סאתים that was not enclosed for residence, in which one may carry only within four cubits.

items.text: Dispute regarding a boat
items.text_en: Dispute regarding a boat
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a parallel dispute between Rav and Shmuel about carrying on a boat: Rav permits carrying throughout, while Shmuel restricts to four amot.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute regarding a boat.
Rav rules that one may carry throughout the entire boat.
Shmuel restricts carrying on the boat to only four cubits.
The Gemara begins to clarify Rav's reasoning, repeating his ruling.

items.text: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a boat
items.text_en: Dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding a boat
items.desc_en: Rav permits carrying throughout the boat because its walls serve as partitions, while Shmuel restricts carrying to four cubits because the walls are only for keeping out water.

sub.desc_en: Rav permits carrying throughout the boat because its walls serve as partitions, while Shmuel restricts carrying to four cubits because the walls are only for keeping out water.

items.text: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel about the halakha
items.text_en: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel about the halakha
items.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel whether the halakha follows him or Rav, and Shmuel replies that the halakha follows Rav.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel whether the halakha follows him or Rav, and Shmuel replies that the halakha follows Rav.

items.text: Rav Giddel's statement about Rav's concession
items.text_en: Rav Giddel's statement about Rav's concession
items.desc_en: Rav Giddel reports that Rav concedes that if one overturns the boat, carrying is limited to four cubits. The Gemara questions the purpose of overturning it, and explains it is for tarring.

sub.text: Rav Giddel citing Rav Chiyya bar Yosef
sub.text_en: Rav Giddel citing Rav Chiyya bar Yosef
sub.desc_en: Rav Giddel reports that Rav concedes that if one overturns the boat on its mouth, carrying is limited to four cubits.
The Gemara questions the purpose of overturning the boat, asking why it differs from a private roof.
The Gemara explains that the boat was overturned specifically for tarring, not for dwelling.

items.text: Dispute about a porch in a field
items.text_en: Dispute about a porch in a field
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi and Rav Acha bar Rava teach the dispute regarding a porch in a field: Rav permits carrying throughout, applying the principle of 'the edge of the roof descends and seals', while Shmuel restricts to four cubits, rejecting that principle.

sub.desc_en: Rav permits moving throughout because he applies the principle that the edge of the roof descends and seals.
Shmuel restricts to four cubits because he does not apply that principle.

items.text: Question on Rav's position according to Rabbi Meir
items.text_en: Question on Rav's position according to Rabbi Meir
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, according to Rav's view aligned with Rabbi Meir, one may not carry from a roof to a courtyard, and explains it is a decree due to Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi's concern.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara answers that the prohibition is a decree (גזירה) due to the concern of Rav Yitzchak bar Avdimi, who forbids carrying from a roof to a courtyard lest one come to carry from a roof to a public domain.

items.text: Shmuel's position according to the Rabbis and Rava bar Ulla's decree
items.text_en: Shmuel's position according to the Rabbis and Rava bar Ulla's decree
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why, according to Shmuel's view aligned with the Rabbis, one may not carry from a roof to a courtyard, and Rava bar Ulla explains it is a decree lest the roof collapse. The Gemara distinguishes this from a case where the collapse would be noticeable.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why, according to Shmuel's view aligned with the Rabbis, one may not carry from a roof to a קרפף (enclosed area).
The Gemara objects: if so, moving from karpaf to karpaf should also be forbidden lest one collapse and then move.
Rava bar Ulla explains that it is a decree (גזירה) lest the roof collapse, causing one to inadvertently carry from the collapsed area.
Rava bar Ulla distinguishes: there (from roof to karpaf) if it collapses it is noticeable; here (karpaf to karpaf) if it collapses it is not noticeable.
The Gemara objects that if the concern is collapse, then one should also be prohibited from carrying between two קרפף (enclosed areas), where the same risk applies.
The Gemara resolves that in the case of two קרפף, a collapse would be noticeable (מינכרא מילתא), but from a roof to a קרפף, the collapse is not noticeable, so the decree applies only there.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's summary of the dispute
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's summary of the dispute
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda concludes that according to Rabbi Meir, roofs are a domain unto themselves and courtyards are a domain unto themselves, implying no carrying between them.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda concludes that according to Rabbi Meir, roofs are a domain unto themselves and courtyards are a domain unto themselves, implying no carrying between them.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that according to the Sages, roofs and courtyards are one domain, and enclosures are a separate domain; according to Rabbi Shimon, all are one domain.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: according to the Sages, roofs and courtyards are one domain while enclosures are a separate domain; according to Rabbi Shimon, all are one domain.

items.text: Supporting Baraitot for Rav and Rav Yehuda
items.text_en: Supporting Baraitot for Rav and Rav Yehuda
items.desc_en: Two baraitot are cited: one supports Rav's view that roofs are a single domain but carrying between roof and courtyard is forbidden; another supports Rav Yehuda's view that carrying between domains was permitted in Rabbi Shimon's academy, though the Sages reject a proof from a time of danger.

sub.desc_en: The gemara announces that two baraitot are cited: one supporting Rav and one supporting Rav Yehuda.
A baraita states that all roofs of a city are a single domain, but carrying between roofs and courtyards is forbidden, with Rabbi Meir and the Sages disputing the details.
A baraita reports that in Rabbi Shimon's academy in Tekoa, they carried oil and olives from roof to roof, roof to courtyard, etc., all the way to the spring.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that during a time of danger, they carried a Torah scroll from courtyard to roof, roof to courtyard, and courtyard to karpaf to read from it.
The Sages reject Rabbi Yehuda's proof, arguing that a time of danger is not a valid halachic precedent.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's Statement
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's Statement
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon reiterates his view that roofs, courtyards, and enclosures are all one domain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Shimon reiterates his position that roofs, courtyards, and enclosures are all one domain.

items.text: Rav vs. Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Rav vs. Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan
