items.desc_en: Rav rules that Rabbi Shimon's leniency applies only when no eiruv was made, due to a decree lest one bring vessels from houses to the courtyard. Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan disagree, allowing it even when an eiruv was made.

sub.desc_en: Rav rules that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Shimon, but only when no עירוב (eiruv) was made, because of a decree lest one bring vessels from houses to the courtyard.
Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan disagree with Rav, allowing the leniency both when an עירוב (eiruv) was made and when it was not.

items.text: Rav Chisda's Objection and Defense of Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's Objection and Defense of Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan: if an eiruv was made, vessels from the house would be permitted in the courtyard while those that rested in the courtyard would be forbidden, creating an inconsistency. The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon does not decree lest vessels be brought from houses, just as he does not decree in the case of three courtyards.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda objects to Shmuel and Rabbi Yochanan: if an eiruv was made, vessels from the house would be permitted in the courtyard while those that rested in the courtyard would be forbidden, creating an inconsistency.
The Gemara explains that Rabbi Shimon does not decree lest vessels be brought from houses, just as he does not decree in the case of three courtyards.
The Gemara concludes that just as Rabbi Shimon does not decree in the three-courtyard case, so too here he does not decree lest vessels be brought from houses to the courtyard.

items.text: Rav Sheshet's Challenge and Resolution
items.text_en: Rav Sheshet's Challenge and Resolution
items.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Rav's position from a Mishnah stating that Rabbi Shimon's ruling applies only to vessels that rested within the domains, not to vessels from the house. If no eiruv was made, how would vessels from the house be found in the courtyard? He answers that it refers to a cloak and a scarf that one wears out.

sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet challenges Rav's position by citing the Mishnah that Rabbi Shimon's ruling applies only to vessels that rested within the domains, not to vessels from the house, and argues that if no eiruv was made, vessels from the house would not be found in the courtyard.
Rav Sheshet resolves his own challenge by explaining that the vessels from the house refer to a cloak and scarf that one wears out, which can be found in the courtyard even without an eiruv.

items.text: First baraita: people of a courtyard and people of a roof-gallery
items.text_en: First baraita: people of a courtyard and people of a roof-gallery
items.desc_en: The baraita rules that if residents of a courtyard and a roof-gallery forgot to make an eruv, areas ten handbreadths high belong to the gallery, lower areas to the courtyard. This applies when each group is many and made its own eruv, or when they are individuals who need no eruv. But if they are many and forgot to make an eruv, roof, courtyard, portico, and gallery are all a single domain.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that if residents of a courtyard and a roof-gallery forgot to make an eruv, areas ten handbreadths high belong to the gallery, lower areas to the courtyard. This applies when each group is many and made its own eruv, or when they are individuals who need no eruv. But if they are many and forgot to make an eruv, roof, courtyard, portico, and gallery are all a single domain.

items.text: Gemara's inference and identification
items.text_en: Gemara's inference and identification
items.desc_en: The Gemara infers that only when they did not make an eruv are they a single domain, but if they did make an eruv they are not. It identifies the baraita as following the Rabbis, and notes that it does not mention קרפף (enclosure) or מבוי (alley), confirming this.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita that only when they did not make an eruv are they a single domain, but if they did make an eruv they are not.
The Gemara identifies the baraita as following the Rabbis, and notes that it does not mention קרפף (enclosure) or מבוי (alley), confirming this.

items.text: Second baraita: five courtyards opening into an alley
items.text_en: Second baraita: five courtyards opening into an alley
items.desc_en: The baraita states that if five courtyards open into an alley and all forgot to make an eruv, it is forbidden to carry between courtyard and alley, but vessels that rested in the courtyard may be moved within it, while in the alley it is forbidden. Rabbi Shimon permits, ruling that when they are many and forgot to make an eruv, roof, courtyard, portico, gallery, enclosure, and alley are all a single domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara brings another baraita: Five courtyards open to each other and to a mavoi; all forgot to make an eruv — it is forbidden to carry from courtyard to mavoi and from mavoi to courtyard. Vessels that rested in the courtyard may be carried within the courtyard, but in the mavoi it is forbidden.
Rabbi Shimon permits, ruling that when many courtyards forgot to make an eruv, all these areas constitute a single domain.

items.text: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the baraita implies only when they did not make an eruv, but if they did, they are not a single domain. It resolves that 'did not make an eruv' means the courtyards did not make an eruv with each other, but the courtyards and houses did make an eruv. Alternatively, 'did not make an eruv' means they did not join together (שיתוף).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges that the baraita implies only when they did not make an eruv, but if they did, they are not a single domain.
The first answer explains that 'did not make an eruv' means the courtyards did not make an eruv with each other, but the courtyards and houses did make an eruv.
The Gemara objects that the baraita explicitly says 'did not make an eruv' without qualification.
The second answer explains that 'did not make an eruv' means they did not join together (שיתוף).

items.text: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon's response to the Rabbis
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon's response to the Rabbis
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another explanation: Rabbi Shimon said to the Rabbis, 'For me, it makes no difference whether they made an eruv or not; but according to you, at least admit that where they did not make an eruv, it is a single domain.' The Rabbis replied, 'No, they are two domains.'

sub.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation: Rabbi Shimon said to the Rabbis, 'For me, it makes no difference whether they made an eruv or not; but according to you, at least admit that where they did not make an eruv, it is a single domain.'
The Rabbis replied to Rabbi Shimon, 'No, they are two domains.'

items.text: Support for Rabbi Zeira and clarification of the mishnah
items.text_en: Support for Rabbi Zeira and clarification of the mishnah
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's statement 'in the alley it is forbidden' supports Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav that in an alley without a שיתוף one may only move within four cubits. It clarifies that the mishnah is redundant to teach that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Shimon even where they did not make an eruv.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the baraita's statement 'in the alley it is forbidden' supports Rabbi Zeira quoting Rav that in an alley without a שיתוף (partnership) one may only move within four cubits.
The Gemara clarifies that the mishnah is redundant to teach that the Rabbis disagree with Rabbi Shimon even where they did not make an eruv.

items.text: Transition to next discussion
items.text_en: Transition to next discussion
items.desc_en: Ravina addresses Rav Ashi, beginning a new line of inquiry.

sub.desc_en: Ravina says to Rav Ashi: (This is a framing statement for the following discussion.)

items.text: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.text_en: Challenge to Rabbi Yochanan's ruling
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yochanan's statement by citing his own principle that the law follows an anonymous Mishnah, and then quotes a Mishnah about a wall between two courtyards that seems to contradict him. The Gemara further cites a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya that adds a restriction.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara challenges Rabbi Yochanan's statement by citing his own principle that the law follows an anonymous Mishnah (הלכה כסתם משנה), and then quotes a Mishnah about a wall between two courtyards that seems to contradict him.
The Gemara clarifies the Mishnah's phrase 'below' and then cites a baraita of Rabbi Chiyya that adds a further restriction: each person may not eat while standing in his own place.

items.text: Defense of Rabbi Yochanan
items.text_en: Defense of Rabbi Yochanan
items.desc_en: A response is given: if Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not teach that baraita, how would Rabbi Chiyya know it? This implies that the baraita is not authoritative.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara responds that if Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi did not teach that baraita, how would Rabbi Chiyya know it? This implies the baraita is not authoritative.

items.text: Dispute about a ruin between two courtyards
items.text_en: Dispute about a ruin between two courtyards
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses a case of two courtyards with a ruin between them, where one courtyard made an eruv and the other did not. Rav Huna rules that the ruin is given to the one that did not make an eruv, but not to the one that did, due to concern of carrying items from the houses into the ruin. Chiyya bar Rav argues that even the one that made an eruv is forbidden, and both are prohibited, explaining the difference between a ruin and a courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a case of two courtyards with a ruin between them, where one made an eruv and the other did not.
Rav Huna rules that the ruin is given to the courtyard that did not make an eruv, but not to the one that did, due to concern that one might carry items from the houses into the ruin.
Chiyya bar Rav objects, arguing that even the courtyard that made an eruv is forbidden, and both are prohibited, questioning why a courtyard that did not make an eruv is not given to one that did.

The Gemara resolves the objection by distinguishing between a courtyard, where items from houses are guarded and one might carry them out, and a ruin, where items are not guarded and one will not come to carry them out.

items.text: Alternative version of Chiyya bar Rav's opinion
items.text_en: Alternative version of Chiyya bar Rav's opinion
items.desc_en: An alternative version states that Chiyya bar Rav ruled that both courtyards are permitted, and explains why the case of a ruin differs from that of a courtyard.

sub.desc_en: An alternative version states that Chiyya bar Rav ruled that both courtyards are permitted.
The gemara raises an objection: if both are forbidden, why is the courtyard that did not prepare an עירוב (eruv) not given to the one that did?
The gemara explains that in a courtyard, vessels are guarded, so the rabbis prohibited use to prevent carrying out; but in a ruin, vessels are not guarded, so the concern does not apply.

items.text: Mishnah: Large roof and large courtyard
items.text_en: Mishnah: Large roof and large courtyard
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a large roof adjacent to a small one is permitted for the large one but forbidden for the small one. Similarly, a large courtyard breached into a small one is permitted for the large one but forbidden for the small one, because the small one is like an entrance to the large one.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule: a large roof adjacent to a small one is permitted for the large but forbidden for the small, and similarly a large courtyard breached into a small one is permitted for the large but forbidden for the small, because the small is like an entrance to the large.

items.text: Gemara: Why teach both cases?
items.text_en: Gemara: Why teach both cases?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah teaches both the case of roofs and courtyards. It explains that according to Rav, the roof is analogous to the courtyard in that the partition is recognizable; according to Shmuel, the roof is analogous to the courtyard in that the public treads upon it.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why the Mishnah needs to teach both the case of roofs and the case of courtyards.
According to Rav, the Mishnah teaches the roof case as analogous to the courtyard: just as the courtyard's partition is recognizable, so too the roof's partition is recognizable.
According to Shmuel, the roof is analogous to the courtyard in that the public treads upon it.

items.text: Inference about residents of large and small courtyards
items.text_en: Inference about residents of large and small courtyards
items.desc_en: Rabbah, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbah bar Rav Chanan, and Abaye infer from the Mishnah that residents of the large courtyard affect the small one, but not vice versa. They illustrate with a case of vines in the large courtyard prohibiting sowing in the small one.

sub.text: Rabbah, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbah bar Rav Chanan, and Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabbah, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbah bar Rav Chanan, and Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rabbah, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbah bar Rav Chanan, and Abaye infer from the Mishnah that residents of the large courtyard affect the small one, but not vice versa.

sub.text: Rabbah, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbah bar Rav Chanan, and Abaye
sub.text_en: Rabbah, Rabbi Zeira, Rabbah bar Rav Chanan, and Abaye
sub.desc_en: They illustrate the inference with a case of vines in the large courtyard prohibiting sowing in the small one, and if one sowed, the plants are forbidden.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Cases of large and small courtyards
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Cases of large and small courtyards
items.desc_en: The mishnah presents a series of cases involving a large and a small courtyard, where the presence of a partition between them determines the permissibility of various actions: planting vines, giving a get, fulfilling the obligation of prayer, joining a quorum, and reciting Shema near excrement.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah opens with the first case: vines in the small courtyard permit planting in the large one.
The mishnah presents the second case: a woman in the large courtyard and a get in the small one — she is divorced; the reverse — she is not.
The mishnah presents the third case: the congregation in the large courtyard and the prayer leader in the small one — they fulfill their obligation; the reverse — they do not.
The mishnah presents the fourth case: nine in the large courtyard and one in the small one — they join for a quorum; the reverse — they do not.
The mishnah presents the fifth case: excrement in the large courtyard forbids reciting Shema in the small one; excrement in the small one permits reciting Shema in the large one.

items.text: Abaye's challenge: A partition that creates a prohibition
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge: A partition that creates a prohibition
items.desc_en: Abaye objects to the mishnah's ruling about vines, arguing that the partition creates a prohibition where none existed before, since without it one could simply distance four cubits and plant.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to the mishnah's ruling about vines, arguing that the partition creates a prohibition where none existed before, since without it one could simply distance four cubits and plant.

items.text: Rabbi Zeira's counterexample from a different mishnah
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's counterexample from a different mishnah
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges Abaye's assumption by citing a mishnah about a large courtyard breached into a small one, where the partition itself prohibits the small courtyard, showing that a partition can indeed create a prohibition.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira challenges Abaye by citing a mishnah about a large courtyard breached into a small one, where the partition itself prohibits the small courtyard.
Rabbi Zeira adds that if one levels the small courtyard's partitions, even the large courtyard becomes prohibited, showing the partition creates a prohibition.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: Removal of partitions
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: Removal of partitions
items.desc_en: Abaye responds that the case of the breached courtyard is different because there the prohibition results from the removal of the partition, not its existence.

sub.desc_en: Abaye responds to Rabbi Zeira's objection by distinguishing that the breached courtyard case involves סילוק מחיצות (removal of partitions), not the existence of a partition causing a prohibition.

items.text: Rava's further challenge: Another case of a partition creating a prohibition
items.text_en: Rava's further challenge: Another case of a partition creating a prohibition
items.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye by citing a tradition that also demonstrates a partition creating a prohibition, setting up the continuation of the discussion.

sub.desc_en: Rava challenges Abaye by asking whether we do not indeed find a partition that creates a prohibition, citing an additional tradition.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukkah placed over a portico with partitions is valid, but if one filled in the partitions, it becomes invalid.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a sukkah placed over a portico with partitions is valid, but if one filled in the partitions, it becomes invalid.

items.text: Abaye's distinction and Rava's objection
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction and Rava's objection
items.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes between his own view and that of his teacher, calling the filled-in case 'removing partitions'. Rabba bar Rav Chanan objects, citing a baraita about a half-roofed house where filling in the roof prohibits planting, but Abaye maintains that is also a case of removing partitions.

sub.desc_en: Abaye distinguishes between his own view (the sukkah is kosher) and his teacher's view (it is a removal of partitions).
Rabba bar Rav Chanan objects, citing a baraita about a half-roofed house where filling in the roof prohibits planting, to challenge Abaye's concept of 'removing partitions'.
Abaye responds that the baraita's case is also a removal of partitions, not a new prohibition.

items.text: Rava's objection and resolution
items.text_en: Rava's objection and resolution
items.desc_en: Rava sends another objection via Rav Shemaya bar Zeira, citing a baraita about vineyard partitions that can be lenient or stringent. Abaye responds by citing a Mishnah about a bald spot in a vineyard, and the Gemara explains that the leniency is due to the four cubits being considered work of the vineyard, and the area between is ownerless.

sub.text: Rava's question via Rav Shemaya bar Zeira
sub.text_en: Rava's question via Rav Shemaya bar Zeira
sub.desc_en: Rava sends an objection to Abaye via Rav Shemaya bar Zeira, citing a baraita that vineyard partitions can be lenient or stringent, beginning with the lenient case.
The baraita continues with the stringent case of vineyard partitions.
Abaye responds by citing a Mishnah about a bald spot in a vineyard (קרחת הכרם) and the space between the vineyard and the fence (מחול הכרם), with the opinions of Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel.
The Mishnah defines קרחת הכרם as a vineyard whose middle was destroyed, with rules for planting based on the remaining space.
The Mishnah defines מחול הכרם as the area between the vineyard and the fence, with similar rules for planting.

The Gemara explains that the leniency is because the four cubits adjacent to the vineyard are considered work of the vineyard, the area next to the fence is ownerless, and the middle area is significant only if it is at least four cubits.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on three courtyards
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on three courtyards
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that if three courtyards are adjacent, with the outer two enclosed and the middle one open, and one person in each outer courtyard, they are considered a caravan and each gets their full needs. If the middle is enclosed and the outer are open, they only get a bet se'ah each.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that when three courtyards are adjacent, the outer two enclosed and the middle open, with one person in each outer courtyard, they are considered a caravan (שיירה) and each receives their full needs.
Rav Yehuda rules that if the middle courtyard is enclosed and the outer ones are open, with one person in each, they only receive a bet se'ah (בית שש) each.

items.text: Unresolved questions about distribution
items.text_en: Unresolved questions about distribution
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a question: if there is one person in each outer courtyard and two in the middle, how do they distribute? It then asks about two in each outer and one in the middle. The conclusion is that the halakha is lenient in these questions.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an unresolved question: if there is one person in each outer courtyard and two in the middle, how do they distribute — perhaps each outer pair plus the middle person forms three, regardless of which outer they join?
The Gemara considers an alternative: perhaps one of the middle two goes to each outer courtyard, leaving one in the middle.

Assuming the first question is resolved, the Gemara asks a second question: if there are two in each outer courtyard and one in the middle, does the middle one join one outer to form three, or is it uncertain which outer he joins?
The Gemara concludes that the halakha (הלכה) in these unresolved questions is lenient (לכתחילה (the ideal standard) or בדיעבד (after the fact)).

items.text: Rav Chisda's statement
items.text_en: Rav Chisda's statement
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda begins a statement, but the text cuts off.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda says: (unfinished — likely a continuation)

items.text: Opening statement: Gedud and mechitzah do not combine
items.text_en: Opening statement: Gedud and mechitzah do not combine
items.desc_en: The Gemara states that a gedud of five handbreadths and a mechitzah of five handbreadths do not combine to form a valid partition unless the entire partition is either all gedud or all mechitzah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a gedud of five handbreadths and a mechitzah of five handbreadths do not combine to form a valid partition unless the entire partition is either all gedud or all mechitzah.

items.text: Challenge from a baraita about two courtyards
items.text_en: Challenge from a baraita about two courtyards
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited that describes two courtyards, one above the other, where the upper is ten handbreadths higher than the lower, or where there is a gedud of five and a mechitzah of five; in such cases they may join separately but not together, contradicting the earlier statement.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises an objection from a baraita that describes two courtyards one above the other, where a gedud of five and a mechitzah of five combine to allow separate eiruvin, contradicting the opening statement.

items.text: Rav's resolution: Rav Chisda admits regarding the lower courtyard
items.text_en: Rav's resolution: Rav Chisda admits regarding the lower courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav says that Rav Chisda admits in the case of the lower courtyard, because it sees a face of ten handbreadths; thus the lower may join separately but not together, while the upper may join neither separately nor together.

sub.desc_en: Rav explains that Rav Chisda concedes regarding the lower courtyard, because it sees a face of ten handbreadths, so the lower courtyard may combine as two but not as one, while the upper courtyard may combine neither as one nor as two.

items.text: Rabbah bar Ulla's explanation: Upper courtyard enclosed up to ten cubits
items.text_en: Rabbah bar Ulla's explanation: Upper courtyard enclosed up to ten cubits
items.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ulla explains that the baraita refers to a case where the upper courtyard is enclosed (with a roof or partition) up to ten cubits, making it a separate domain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah bar Ulla answers that the case is where the upper courtyard is enclosed up to ten cubits, providing a different resolution to the objection.

items.text: Objection: If so, the seifa allows either option
items.text_en: Objection: If so, the seifa allows either option
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the upper is enclosed, then in the case of less than ten handbreadths difference, the lower could choose to join either separately or together, contradicting the baraita's ruling.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if so, the latter clause of the baraita would be problematic, because if the partition is less than that, the residents could choose to combine either as one or as two.

items.text: Rabbah brei d'Rava's answer: Lower courtyard breached fully into upper
items.text_en: Rabbah brei d'Rava's answer: Lower courtyard breached fully into upper
items.desc_en: Rabbah brei d'Rava answers that the case is where the lower courtyard is breached entirely into the upper, making them effectively one domain.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah, son of Rava answers that the case is where the lower courtyard is breached entirely into the upper courtyard.

items.text: Clarification: The baraita's ruling applies only to the lower courtyard
items.text_en: Clarification: The baraita's ruling applies only to the lower courtyard
items.desc_en: The Gemara clarifies that in this case, the lower courtyard may join only separately, while the upper may choose either; and the baraita's statement 'less than this they join separately' refers only to the lower courtyard.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves the difficulty by stating that the baraita's ruling 'less than this they join separately' applies only to the lower courtyard, while the upper courtyard may choose either to join separately or together.

items.text: Marimar's teaching and halakhic conclusion: Gedud and mechitzah combine
items.text_en: Marimar's teaching and halakhic conclusion: Gedud and mechitzah combine
items.desc_en: Marimar teaches that a gedud of five and a mechitzah of five do combine; Ravina asks Rav Acha brei d'Rava if he teaches anything about mechitzah, and he says no; the halakha is that they combine.

sub.desc_en: Mareimar teaches that a gedud of five handbreadths and a mechitzah of five handbreadths do combine.
Ravina finds Rav Acha, son of Rava and asks him whether he teaches anything about a mechitzah.
Rav Acha answers no, but the halacha is that a gedud of five and a mechitzah of five do combine.
The Stam rules that a gedud of five and a mechitzah of five do combine.

items.text: Inquiry about new residents arriving on Shabbat
items.text_en: Inquiry about new residents arriving on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether new residents who arrive on Shabbat are prohibited (from carrying). Rav Chisda cites a baraita about a large courtyard breached into a small one, and Rabbah says it was breached before Shabbat. Abaye insists it was certainly before Shabbat, citing a ruling that once permitted, it remains permitted.

sub.desc_en: Rav Hoshaya asks whether new residents who arrive on Shabbat are prohibited from carrying in the courtyard.
Rav Chisda cites a baraita about a large courtyard breached into a small one, implying that the new opening is treated like a door.
Rabbah objects that the baraita may refer to a breach that occurred before Shabbat, not on Shabbat itself.
Abaye insists the breach certainly occurred before Shabbat, citing a ruling from Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda that once an area is permitted on Shabbat, it remains permitted.

items.text: Dispute about a wall that fell between two courtyards
items.text_en: Dispute about a wall that fell between two courtyards
items.desc_en: The Gemara records a dispute: Rav says one may carry only within four cubits, and Shmuel begins his opinion (the text cuts off).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces a dispute about a wall that fell between two courtyards, stating Rav's position that one may carry only within four cubits.
The text begins to record Shmuel's opinion but cuts off, leaving his position incomplete.

items.text: Opening statement of the dispute
items.text_en: Opening statement of the dispute
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents the principle that each party may carry up to the base of the partition, setting the stage for the story about Rav and Shmuel.

items.text: Story of Rav and Shmuel
items.text_en: Story of Rav and Shmuel
items.desc_en: The Gemara recounts an incident where a partition fell between two courtyards, and Shmuel instructed to use a cloak and belt to create a temporary partition, while Rav turned away. The Gemara explains Shmuel's actions were for modesty.

items.text: Explanation of Rav's behavior
items.text_en: Explanation of Rav's behavior
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why Rav did not object to Shmuel's action and explains that Rav turned away to avoid appearing to agree with Shmuel's lenient ruling.

items.text: Mishnah: Courtyard breached into public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Courtyard breached into public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and the Sages regarding a courtyard breached into a public domain. Rabbi Eliezer holds that one who carries from it to a private domain is liable, while the Sages say it is like a karmelit and one is exempt.

items.text: Gemara's first explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.text_en: Gemara's first explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Rabbi Eliezer's ruling is consistent with his principle that if a path is chosen by the public, it becomes a public domain, as taught in a baraita.

items.text: Objection and resolution regarding the path
items.text_en: Objection and resolution regarding the path
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects based on Rav Giddel's statement that the path must be lost, and Rabbi Chanina's statement about the dispute being over the place of the partition. The Gemara resolves by rephrasing the dispute.

items.text: Alternative explanation: sides of the public domain
items.text_en: Alternative explanation: sides of the public domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers an alternative explanation that the dispute is about the sides of the public domain, with Rabbi Eliezer considering them like the public domain and the Sages disagreeing. The Gemara clarifies why the Mishnah mentions 'from within it' and addresses the Sages' counterargument.

items.text: Mishnah: Courtyard breached on two sides
items.text_en: Mishnah: Courtyard breached on two sides
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei regarding a courtyard breached on two sides, a house breached on two sides, or an alleyway whose beams or side-posts were removed. Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between the current Shabbat and future Shabbatot, while Rabbi Yosei argues they are the same.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the breach size
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the breach size
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the case, considering whether the breach is exactly ten handbreadths or more, and concludes with Rav's statement that it is exactly ten handbreadths.

items.text: Initial case: breach at a corner
items.text_en: Initial case: breach at a corner
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a breach at a corner, noting that people do not make an entrance at a corner.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the case of a breach at a corner, noting that people do not make an entrance at a corner.

items.text: Question: why not apply 'mouth of ceiling' to two sides?
items.text_en: Question: why not apply 'mouth of ceiling' to two sides?
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks: if a house is breached from two sides, why not apply the principle of 'the mouth of the ceiling descends and seals' as with one side?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why a house breached on two sides differs from one breached on one side, where the principle of 'the edge of the roof descends and seals' applies.

items.text: Rav's answer: diagonal ceiling
items.text_en: Rav's answer: diagonal ceiling
items.desc_en: The school of Rav answers in Rav's name that the case is where the breach is at a corner and the ceiling is diagonal, so the principle does not apply.

sub.text: Beit Rav in the name of Rav
sub.text_en: Beit Rav in the name of Rav
sub.desc_en: Beit Rav answers that the case involves a breach at a corner with a diagonal roof, where the principle of 'the edge of the roof descends and seals' cannot apply.

items.text: Shmuel's challenge and response
items.text_en: Shmuel's challenge and response
items.desc_en: Shmuel says the case applies even with more than ten cubits. The Gemara objects that then it should apply to one side as well, and answers: because it is a house.

items.text: Contradiction from Shmuel's view on 'mouth of ceiling'
items.text_en: Contradiction from Shmuel's view on 'mouth of ceiling'
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency, citing a dispute about an exedra in a field where Shmuel rejects the principle. It resolves that Shmuel accepts it for three walls but not four, but then objects again, leading to a resolution similar to Rav's.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects to the previous resolution by asking why the case of a house breached on two sides should differ from one breached on one side, where the principle of 'mouth of ceiling descends and seals' is applied.
The Gemara further objects that Shmuel's own view contradicts the principle of 'mouth of ceiling', citing the dispute about an exedra in a field where Shmuel restricts carrying to four cubits.
The Gemara resolves that Shmuel rejects the principle for a four-walled exedra but accepts it for three walls.
The Gemara objects that the contradiction remains, since the house in question has three walls.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by applying Rav's earlier explanation: the case involves a breach at a corner with the roof at an angle, where the principle cannot apply.

items.text: Reconciling Rav and Shmuel's positions
items.text_en: Reconciling Rav and Shmuel's positions
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel does not accept Rav's diagonal case because the Mishnah does not mention diagonal, and Rav does not accept Shmuel's view because it would make it an exedra, consistent with Rav's ruling that an exedra is permitted. The dispute about the exedra is cited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara explains that Shmuel rejects Rav's diagonal case because the Mishnah does not mention diagonal.
The Gemara explains that Rav rejects Shmuel's view because it would make the courtyard an exedra, consistent with Rav's ruling that an exedra is permitted.
The Gemara cites the dispute between Rav and Shmuel regarding an exedra in a field, where Rav permits carrying throughout and Shmuel restricts to four cubits, to support the explanation.

items.text: Dispute about the measure: ten or more
items.text_en: Dispute about the measure: ten or more
items.desc_en: The Gemara records two versions of the dispute: one where all agree on ten cubits and disagree on more, and another where all agree on more and disagree on ten.

sub.desc_en: The first version states that all agree on a breach of ten cubits, and the dispute is only about a breach larger than ten.
The second version reverses the positions: all agree on a breach larger than ten, and the dispute is only about a breach of exactly ten cubits.

items.text: Transition to Rav Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Transition to Rav Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a statement by Rav Yehuda, continuing the discussion.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara begins to cite a statement of Rav Yehuda, which appears to be a digression or introduction to further discussion.

items.text: Dispute about the beam of four cubits
items.text_en: Dispute about the beam of four cubits
items.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba states that a beam of four cubits permits carrying in water. The Gemara clarifies that according to one version, there is no dispute about a beam of ten cubits, and according to another, the dispute aligns with Rav's view.

sub.desc_en: Rav Nachman bar Abba states that a beam of four cubits permits carrying in water.
The Gemara asks who is the authority behind this statement.
The Gemara clarifies that according to one version there is no dispute about a beam of ten cubits, and according to another the dispute aligns with Rav's view.

items.text: Abaye and Rava's dispute about a sukkah on a porch
items.text_en: Abaye and Rava's dispute about a sukkah on a porch
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that Abaye and Rava's dispute about a sukkah on a porch with or without partitions aligns with the dispute between Rav and Shmuel. Abaye holds that the principle of 'the mouth of the ceiling descends and seals' applies, while Rava disagrees. The Gemara concludes that even according to Rav, Rava would reject the principle here because the partitions are not made for the sukkah.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that Abaye and Rava's dispute about a sukkah on a porch with or without partitions (פצימין) aligns with the dispute between Rav and Shmuel.

The Gemara explains that Abaye holds the principle of 'פי תקרה יורד וסותם' (the mouth of the ceiling descends and seals), while Rava rejects it, and asks whether Abaye follows Rav and Rava follows Shmuel.

The Gemara resolves that everyone agrees regarding Shmuel's position; the dispute is only according to Rav, and even Rav would reject the principle here because the partitions are not made for the sukkah.

items.text: Rabbi Yosei's ruling on eruvin
items.text_en: Rabbi Yosei's ruling on eruvin
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei's statement 'if they are permitted' means to prohibit or permit. Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Yochanan rule that it means to prohibit, and a baraita supports that Rabbi Yosei said they are prohibited for the future and for that Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether Rabbi Yosei's statement 'if they are permitted' means to prohibit or to permit.
Rav Sheshet and Rabbi Yochanan rule that Rabbi Yosei's statement means to prohibit.
A baraita supports that Rabbi Yosei said they are prohibited for the future and for that Shabbat.

items.text: Halakhic ruling and Shmuel's position
items.text_en: Halakhic ruling and Shmuel's position
items.desc_en: Rav Chiya bar Yosef and Shmuel dispute whether the halakha follows Rabbi Yosei or Rabbi Yehuda. The Gemara questions Shmuel's consistency, citing that he ruled like Rabbi Yehuda regarding eruvin. Rav Chana of Baghdad clarifies that Shmuel's ruling applies only to eruvin, not to partitions. Rav Anan explains that the distinction depends on whether the breach opens to a karmelit or a public domain.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara reports a dispute: Rav Chiya bar Yosef rules like Rabbi Yosei, while Shmuel rules like Rabbi Yehuda.

The Gemara objects: Did Shmuel really say that? It cites a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between eruvin of techumin and eruvin of courtyards, and Shmuel ruled like Rabbi Yehuda regarding eruvin.

Rav Chana of Baghdad asks Rav Yehuda whether Shmuel's ruling applies even to an alleyway whose beam or side-post was removed, and Rav Yehuda answers that Shmuel's ruling was specifically about eruvin, not about partitions.
Rav Anan clarifies from Shmuel himself: the distinction depends on whether the breach opens to a karmelit (a semi-public domain) or to a public domain.

items.text: Mishnah: Building an upper story over two houses
items.text_en: Mishnah: Building an upper story over two houses
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that Rabbi Yehuda permits carrying under an upper story built over two houses or under bridges, while the Sages prohibit. Rabbi Yehuda also permits eruvin for an alleyway that is open at both ends, but the Sages prohibit.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the case of building an upper story over two houses, and Rabbi Yehuda permits carrying beneath it on שבת (Sabbath), while the Sages prohibit.
The Mishnah adds that Rabbi Yehuda also permits establishing an עירוב (eruv) for an alleyway open at both ends, while the Sages prohibit.

items.text: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.text_en: Gemara: Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that Rabbi Yehuda's leniency is not because two partitions are biblically sufficient, but because he holds that the principle of 'the mouth of the ceiling descends and seals' applies. Abaye challenges this from a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits carrying across a public domain with two side posts, but the Sages reject it. Rav Ashi supports Rabbah from the Mishnah's use of 'furthermore,' which implies a consistent principle.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah asserts that Rabbi Yehuda's leniency is not because two partitions are biblically sufficient, but because he holds that the principle of 'the mouth of the ceiling descends and seals' applies.

Abaye objects by citing a baraita where Rabbi Yehuda permits carrying across a public domain with two side posts, but the Sages reject it, implying that Rabbi Yehuda holds that two partitions suffice by Torah law.
Rabbah responds that from that baraita one can indeed infer that Rabbi Yehuda holds two partitions suffice, but from the mishna nothing can be learned, as it may have a different rationale.
Rav Ashi supports Rabbah by noting that the mishna's use of 'furthermore' implies a consistent principle, which aligns with the idea that the edge of the roof descends and seals.

The Gemara explains that if Rabbi Yehuda holds that the edge of the roof descends and seals, then the mishna's use of 'furthermore' is appropriate, as it introduces a new case with the same principle.
The Gemara concludes that if Rabbi Yehuda held that two partitions suffice by Torah law, the term 'furthermore' would be superfluous, so the mishna supports Rabbah's interpretation.
The Gemara marks the end of the chapter with the standard formula 'we return to you, all roofs'.

items.text: Mishnah: Finding tefillin on Shabbat
items.text_en: Mishnah: Finding tefillin on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses the laws of finding tefillin on Shabbat: one may bring them in pairs. Rabban Gamliel says two pairs at a time. The distinction is between old tefillin (which may be worn) and new ones (which are exempt). If found in bundles, one may wait until dark to bring them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with the rule that one who finds תפילין (phylacteries) on שבת (Sabbath) brings them in pair by pair.
Rabban Gamliel states that one may bring them in two pairs at a time.
The Mishnah clarifies the distinction: the leniency applies to old תפילין (phylacteries), but for new ones one is פטור (exempt) from bringing them in.
If the תפילין (phylacteries) are found in bundles or wrapped piles, one waits until dark and then brings them in.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on carrying tefillin on Shabbat
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute on carrying tefillin on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: the first Tanna allows only one pair of tefillin to be carried out on Shabbat in a dangerous situation, while Rabbi Shimon permits passing them from one to another until they reach the outer courtyard. Rabbi Yehuda allows passing a barrel even beyond the techum, but the Sages object that it cannot go farther than its owner's feet.

sub.desc_en: The first Tanna rules that in a dangerous situation one covers the tefillin and proceeds, implying only one pair is carried out.
Rabbi Shimon permits passing tefillin from one person to another until they reach the outer courtyard.
Rabbi Yehuda allows passing a barrel even beyond the techum.
The Sages object that a barrel cannot travel farther than its owner's feet.

items.text: Gemara's analysis: Is the Mishnah not in accordance with Rabbi Meir?
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis: Is the Mishnah not in accordance with Rabbi Meir?
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's limitation to one pair of tefillin contradicts Rabbi Meir, who allows wearing all possible garments. Rava resolves that in both cases, the Sages treated the act as ordinary attire, so the limitation follows the weekday practice: one pair on Shabbat, just as on a weekday.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Mishnah permits only one pair of תפילין (phylacteries), not more.
The Gemara asks whether the unattributed Mishnah is not in accordance with Rabbi Meir, who permits wearing all possible garments.
The Gemara objects that if the Mishnah were Rabbi Meir, he would allow wearing all possible garments, as he does in the case of rescue from a fire.
The Gemara cites a baraita that explicitly attributes to Rabbi Meir the ruling that one may don and remove garments all day long to rescue them.
Rava answers that even according to Rabbi Meir, the Sages treated the act of wearing תפילין (phylacteries) like ordinary weekday attire, so the limitation follows weekday practice.
Rava resolves that just as on a weekday one may wear only one pair of תפילין (phylacteries), so too for rescue the Sages permitted only one pair.

items.text: Rabban Gamliel's view: Two pairs, and the Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Rabban Gamliel's view: Two pairs, and the Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: Rabban Gamliel allows two pairs. The Gemara questions his reasoning: if Shabbat is a time for tefillin, why not more than one? If not, why limit to two? Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak answers that there is a place on the head for two tefillin, so two pairs are considered normal attire.

sub.desc_en: The mishnah states Rabban Gamliel's position: one may bring the תפילין (phylacteries) in two pairs at a time.
The Gemara asks what Rabban Gamliel holds: if he holds that שבת (Sabbath) is a time for תפילין (phylacteries), then one pair should be permitted but more than one should not.

The Gemara objects: if he holds that שבת (Sabbath) is not a time for תפילין (phylacteries) and the Sages permitted rescue only in the manner of normal attire, then even more than two pairs should be permitted.

The Gemara answers: actually, he holds that שבת (Sabbath) is not a time for תפילין (phylacteries), but the Sages permitted rescue only in the manner of normal attire, i.e., in the proper place for תפילין (phylacteries).
The Gemara objects: if so, then one pair should be permitted but more than one should not, because a second pair would be out of place.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak resolves the difficulty: there is a place on the head to place two תפילין (phylacteries), so two pairs are considered normal attire.

items.text: Applying the same reasoning to the arm tefillin
items.text_en: Applying the same reasoning to the arm tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the arm tefillin: how can two pairs be worn there? Rav Huna's precedent of tying bundles on the arm is considered, but rejected because it is disrespectful. Instead, the Gemara concludes that there is also a place on the arm suitable for two tefillin, analogous to the head.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: granted the head has a place for two tefillin, but what can be said about the arm?
The Gemara proposes Rav Huna's case where a person ties bundles on his arm as a possible precedent for wearing two tefillin on the arm.
The Gemara objects: Rav Huna only spoke of avoiding disrespect, not that the arm is a suitable place for tefillin.

sub.text: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's analogy
sub.text_en: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's analogy
sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves: just as Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said there is a place on the head for two tefillin, so too there is a place on the arm suitable for two tefillin.

items.text: The Tanna of the school of Menashe on the placement of tefillin
items.text_en: The Tanna of the school of Menashe on the placement of tefillin
items.desc_en: A baraita from the school of Menashe defines 'on your hand' as the biceps and 'between your eyes' as the crown, specifically where a baby's fontanel pulsates, as taught by the school of Rabbi Yannai.

sub.text: Baraita from the school of Menashe
sub.text_en: Baraita from the school of Menashe
sub.desc_en: The baraita defines 'on your hand' as the biceps and 'between your eyes' as the crown, specifically where a baby's fontanel pulsates.

items.text: Resolving the dispute: Two possible underlying principles
items.text_en: Resolving the dispute: Two possible underlying principles
items.desc_en: The Gemara considers whether the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabban Gamliel hinges on Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's principle, but rejects that. Instead, it offers two alternatives: either they disagree on whether Shabbat is a time for tefillin, or on whether mitzvot require intent. The first Tanna holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin (so only one pair) or that intent is required; Rabban Gamliel holds Shabbat is not a time for tefillin (so two pairs are allowed as attire) or that intent is not required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the dispute between the first Tanna and Rabban Gamliel hinges on whether they accept Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's principle that there is a place on the head for two tefillin.
The Gemara rejects the proposal, stating that both sides accept Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak's principle, and instead the dispute is about whether Shabbat is a time for tefillin.
The Gemara offers an alternative resolution: the dispute is about whether מצוות (commandments) require כוונה (intent), with the first Tanna requiring intent and Rabban Gamliel not requiring it.

items.text: Second alternative: dispute over bal tosif
items.text_en: Second alternative: dispute over bal tosif
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a second alternative: everyone agrees that intention is not required for fulfilling the mitzvah of tefillin, but they disagree about whether intention is required to violate bal tosif. Tanna Kamma holds intention is not required, while Rabban Gamliel holds it is required.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks: can we say that everyone agrees that intention is not required for fulfilling the mitzvah of tefillin, but they dispute whether intention is required to violate bal tosif?

items.text: Third alternative: dispute over wearing tefillin out of time
items.text_en: Third alternative: dispute over wearing tefillin out of time
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers a third alternative: if Shabbat is a time for tefillin, then everyone agrees that intention is not required for either fulfilling the mitzvah or violating bal tosif. The dispute is about wearing tefillin out of its proper time (i.e., on Shabbat if it is not a time for tefillin). Tanna Kamma holds intention is not required, while Rabban Gamliel holds it is required.

items.text: Rejection of third alternative and return to original resolution
items.text_en: Rejection of third alternative and return to original resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara rejects the third alternative: if so, even Rabbi Meir's single pair would not be permitted. Additionally, the analogy to sleeping in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret (which is punishable) is problematic. Therefore, the Gemara concludes that the original resolution (the first alternative) is correct.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that if the third alternative were true, even Rabbi Meir's single pair would not be permitted, and further notes the problem of sleeping in the sukkah on Shemini Atzeret being punishable.
The Gemara concludes that the original resolution (the first alternative) is correct, rejecting the third alternative.

items.text: Identifying who holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin: Rabbi Akiva
items.text_en: Identifying who holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin: Rabbi Akiva
items.desc_en: The Gemara identifies Rabbi Akiva as the one who holds that Shabbat is a time for tefillin, citing a baraita where Rabbi Yose HaGelili derives from the verse that the mitzvah of tefillin applies only on weekdays, not on Shabbat or festivals. Rabbi Akiva disagrees and says the verse refers only to the Passover offering.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks who holds that Shabbat is a time for tefillin, and answers that it is Rabbi Akiva.
A baraita is cited where Rabbi Yose HaGelili derives from the verse that the mitzvah of tefillin applies only on weekdays, excluding Shabbat and festivals.
Rabbi Akiva disagrees and states that the verse refers only to the Passover offering, not to tefillin.

items.text: Reconciling a mishnah with Rabbi Akiva's view
items.text_en: Reconciling a mishnah with Rabbi Akiva's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a difficulty: a mishnah states that the Passover and circumcision are positive commandments, implying they are not prohibitions. This seems to contradict Rabbi Akiva's view that the verse refers only to Passover. The Gemara resolves this by citing Rabbi Avin's principle that 'beware', 'lest', and 'do not' indicate a negative commandment, but here 'beware' of a positive commandment is a positive commandment.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether a mishnah that lists Passover and circumcision as positive commandments contradicts Rabbi Akiva's view that the verse refers only to Passover.
The Gemara objects that if the verse is only about Passover, then a negative commandment (לאו) is also present, contradicting the mishnah's classification as only a positive commandment.
Rabbi Avin in the name of Rabbi Ilai states a principle: wherever 'beware' (הִשָּׁמֶר), 'lest' (פֶּן), or 'do not' (אַל) is said, it indicates a negative commandment (לא תעשה).

The Gemara resolves the difficulty: even according to Rabbi Akiva, the principle applies only to 'beware' of a negative commandment (לאו), but 'beware' of a positive commandment (עשה) remains a positive commandment, so the mishnah's classification stands.

items.text: Challenge: Does Rabbi Akiva really hold Shabbat is a time for tefillin?
items.text_en: Challenge: Does Rabbi Akiva really hold Shabbat is a time for tefillin?
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the assumption that Rabbi Akiva holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin, citing a baraita where Rabbi Akiva explicitly says that tefillin are not worn on Shabbat and festivals because they themselves are a sign, as derived from the verse 'and it shall be a sign upon your hand'.

sub.desc_en: Even if you say Rabbi Akiva: 'guard' of a negative is negative, 'guard' of a positive is positive.

items.text: Alternative: The tanna who holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin is Rabbi Natan
items.text_en: Alternative: The tanna who holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin is Rabbi Natan
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the tanna who holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin might be Rabbi Natan, who permits wearing tefillin at night. Since night is a time for tefillin according to the first tanna, Shabbat might also be a time. However, the Gemara rejects this: Rabbi Natan might hold that night is a time for tefillin, but Shabbat is not, as Rabbi Akiva himself distinguishes between night (time) and Shabbat (not time).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the tanna who holds Shabbat is a time for tefillin is Rabbi Natan, based on the baraita where Rabbi Natan permits wearing tefillin at night, implying that Shabbat too is a time for tefillin.
The Gemara rejects this: Rabbi Natan might hold that night is a time for tefillin, but Shabbat is not, as Rabbi Akiva himself distinguishes between night (time) and Shabbat (not time).

items.text: Alternative: The tanna is from the story of Michal bat Kushi
items.text_en: Alternative: The tanna is from the story of Michal bat Kushi
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests another tanna: from the story of Michal bat Kushi, who wore tefillin and the Sages did not object, and the wife of Jonah who went up for the pilgrimage and the Sages did not object. This indicates that the Sages consider these as positive commandments not time-bound. The Gemara then considers whether this tanna might hold that Shabbat is a time for tefillin, but leaves the question open.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes that the tanna is from the baraita about Michal bat Kushi, who wore tefillin without objection, and the wife of Jonah who went up for the pilgrimage without objection.
The Gemara infers from the Sages' lack of objection that they consider these positive commandments not time-bound (מצות עשה שלא הזמן גרמא).
The Gemara objects that perhaps this tanna holds that Shabbat is a time for tefillin, leaving the question unresolved.

items.text: Opening argument: women's exemption from time-bound mitzvot
items.text_en: Opening argument: women's exemption from time-bound mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by citing Rabbi Yosi's view that women may voluntarily perform time-bound mitzvot, then questions whether this applies to tefillin found in the market — if a woman finds tefillin, is she obligated to return them? The initial answer assumes Rabbi Yosi's permissive stance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara introduces Rabbi Yosi's view that women may voluntarily perform time-bound mitzvot (סמיכה) and applies it to the case of a woman finding tefillin, concluding that she may return them voluntarily.

items.text: Tanna's dispute on tefillin found: new vs. old
items.text_en: Tanna's dispute on tefillin found: new vs. old
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a Tanna who distinguishes between new and old tefillin: Rabbi Meir permits returning both, Rabbi Yehuda forbids new ones but permits old ones. This sets up the core question of whether women's obligation depends on the mitzvah's time-bound nature.

sub.desc_en: The baraita presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda regarding found tefillin: Rabbi Meir permits returning both new and old, while Rabbi Yehuda forbids new ones but permits old ones.

items.text: Gemara's inference: women obligated in non-time-bound mitzvot
items.text_en: Gemara's inference: women obligated in non-time-bound mitzvot
items.desc_en: The Gemara notes that the Tanna's dispute only concerns new vs. old tefillin, but both agree women are obligated to return found tefillin. This implies that women are obligated in mitzvot not governed by time, contradicting Rabbi Yehuda's earlier stance.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Tanna's dispute that both agree women are obligated in non-time-bound positive commandments.

items.text: Counterexample: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yosi on women's authority
items.text_en: Counterexample: Rabbi Meir vs. Rabbi Yosi on women's authority
items.desc_en: The Gemara challenges the inference by noting that Rabbi Meir might hold like Rabbi Yosi (permitting women's voluntary action), while Rabbi Yehuda might hold like Rabbi Yosi as well. The cited baraita shows Rabbi Yosi explicitly allows women to lay hands, contradicting the assumption that women are always obligated.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that perhaps the tanna holds like Rabbi Yosi (Rabbi Yosi), who says women's laying of hands is optional, not obligatory.
The Gemara rejects this possibility, asserting that neither Rabbi Meir nor Rabbi Yehuda holds like Rabbi Yosi.

The Gemara proves that Rabbi Meir does not hold like Rabbi Yosi, citing the mishna that one does not prevent children from blowing shofar but does prevent women, and an unattributed mishna follows Rabbi Meir.

The Gemara proves that Rabbi Yehuda does not hold like Rabbi Yosi, citing the Sifra where Rabbi Yehuda (as the anonymous authority) rules that only sons of Israel lay hands, while Rabbi Yosi and Rabbi Shimon permit it optionally.

items.text: Stam's resolution: the Tanna is Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Stam's resolution: the Tanna is Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes that the anonymous Tanna in the tefillin dispute is actually Rabbi Yehuda, who holds women are exempt from time-bound mitzvot. This resolves the apparent contradiction: women are not obligated to return tefillin because the mitzvah is time-bound.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the anonymous Tanna in the Sifra is Rabbi Yehuda, who holds women are exempt from time-bound positive mitzvot.

items.text: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on tefillin found: threads vs. straps
items.text_en: Rabbi Elazar's ruling on tefillin found: threads vs. straps
items.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar distinguishes: found tefillin threads (for the blue dye) are invalid, but the straps are valid. The Gemara questions why threads are invalid — perhaps because they were dyed for the garment? Straps too might be woven for the garment. The answer: only when the items are clearly cut/separate from the garment is there no presumption of labor.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Elazar rules that found techelet (blue wool for tzitzit) in the market: tongues (לשונות) are invalid, but threads (חוטין) are valid.
The Gemara questions why tongues are invalid (presumably dyed for a garment) while threads are valid, and answers that the threads are twisted (שזורין).
The Gemara further questions that even twisted threads might be intended for a garment's fringe, and answers that they are cut (מופסקין), as people do not go to such trouble.
The Gemara objects that even twisted threads might have been made for the garment's edge (שפתא דגלימא).
The Gemara resolves that the ruling applies to מופסקין (clearly cut-off pieces), where people certainly would not go to such trouble for a garment.

items.text: Rava's objection: is making an amulet like making tefillin?
items.text_en: Rava's objection: is making an amulet like making tefillin?
items.desc_en: Rava challenges the logic: if a person would not bother to make an amulet (a cheap item), why would they bother to make tefillin (a sacred item)? The cited Mishnah says old tefillin are exempt from return, implying people do not bother to make old ones. This supports the idea that found items are presumed not to have been intentionally made.

sub.desc_en: Rava questions the logic: does a person exert himself to make an amulet in the form of תפילין (phylacteries)?
Rava cites a mishna that distinguishes old תפילין (phylacteries) from new ones, implying that people do not exert themselves to make old ones.

sub.text: Rabbi Zeira to his son Ahava
sub.text_en: Rabbi Zeira to his son Ahava
sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira instructs his son Ahava to teach a baraita that found תכלת (sky blue) threads are fit because a person does not exert himself to make them.
Rava objects that Ahava's teaching does not resolve the contradiction, citing the mishna that new תפילין (phylacteries) are exempt from return.

items.text: Rava's final resolution: the dispute is between Tannaim
items.text_en: Rava's final resolution: the dispute is between Tannaim
items.desc_en: Rava concludes that the disagreement about returning tefillin is actually between Tannaim, not about women's obligation. The baraita explicitly states: one who finds tefillin returns them pair by pair, one for the man and one for the woman. This shows the obligation applies to both genders equally.

sub.desc_en: Rava resolves the dispute by stating that the question of whether one exerts oneself or not is a matter of disagreement between Tannaim.
The baraita is cited as evidence: one who finds תפילין (phylacteries) brings them in pair by pair, whether the finder is a man or a woman, showing the obligation applies equally.

items.text: Opening Mishnah: New vs. old tefillin
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: New vs. old tefillin
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both new and old tefillin are permitted according to Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yehuda prohibits new ones and permits old ones. The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether a person bothers to tie knots in new tefillin.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that both new and old tefillin are permitted according to Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yehuda prohibits new ones and permits old ones.
The Gemara explains that the dispute hinges on whether a person bothers to tie knots in new tefillin.

items.text: Definition of old and new tefillin
items.text_en: Definition of old and new tefillin
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita from the father of Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak defining old tefillin as those with straps that are both attached and tied, while new ones have straps attached but not tied. This implies that everyone agrees a person does not bother to tie new tefillin.

sub.text: Baraita cited by the father of Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
sub.text_en: Baraita cited by the father of Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak
sub.desc_en: The baraita defines old tefillin as those with straps attached and tied, and new ones as attached but not tied.
The Gemara concludes that everyone agrees a person does not bother to tie new tefillin.

items.text: The knot of tefillin: tying vs. bowing
items.text_en: The knot of tefillin: tying vs. bowing
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why one cannot simply tie a bow (עניבה) instead of a knot. Rav Chisda says this proves that a bow is invalid for tefillin. Abaye counters that Rabbi Yehuda holds a bow is a valid knot. The Gemara resolves that the bow must be made in the manner of their knot, and cites the halakha that the knot of tefillin is a law from Moses at Sinai.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks why one cannot simply tie the tefillin straps with a bow (עניבה) instead of a knot.
Rav Chisda answers that this proves a bow (עניבה) is invalid for tefillin.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Yehuda holds a bow is a valid knot, so the proof is not universal.
The Gemara resolves that the bow must be made in the manner of their knot, citing the halakha that the knot of tefillin is a law from Moses at Sinai.

items.text: Checking tefillin bought from a non-expert
items.text_en: Checking tefillin bought from a non-expert
items.desc_en: Rav Chisda quoting Rav says one who buys tefillin from a non-expert checks two of the hand and one of the head, or two of the head and one of the hand. The Gemara questions this, suggesting that if buying from one person, one should check three of the same type, and if from multiple sellers, each should be checked. It concludes that the buyer wants to ensure the seller is expert in both hand and head tefillin. A baraita from Rabbah bar Shmuel and one from Rav Kahana are reconciled with Rabbi's opinion on chazaka.

sub.desc_en: Rav Chisda in the name of Rav rules that one who buys tefillin from a non-expert checks two hand-tefillin and one head-tefillin, or two head-tefillin and one hand-tefillin.
The Gemara objects: if buying from one seller, why not check three of the same type; if from multiple sellers, each requires separate checking.
The Gemara answers that the buyer always buys from one seller, but wants to verify the seller's expertise in both hand and head tefillin.

sub.text: Gemara's objection from Rabbah bar Shmuel
sub.text_en: Gemara's objection from Rabbah bar Shmuel
sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita of Rabbah bar Shmuel that says one checks three, which could mean three of one type, but the Gemara resolves it means three including both types.
The Gemara objects with a baraita of Rav Kahana that says one checks two of hand and head, and explains that this follows Rabbi's opinion that two instances establish a חזקה (presumption).
The Gemara objects: if it follows Rabbi, why does the baraita mention a third bundle, since Rabbi does not require a third check?
The Gemara answers that Rabbi concedes regarding bundles bought from multiple sellers, so even a fourth or fifth bundle would require checking.
The Gemara confirms that indeed even more bundles require checking, and the baraita mentions 'third' only to exclude the presumption (חזקה) that two suffice.

items.text: Definition of צבתים and כריכות
items.text_en: Definition of צבתים and כריכות
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the terms צבתים and כריכות from the Mishnah. Rav Yehuda quoting Rav says they are the same: צבתים are bundles tied in pairs, and כריכות are bundles tied many times.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks for the definitions of the terms צבתים and כריכות from the Mishnah.
Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav explains that צבתים are bundles tied in pairs and כריכות are bundles tied many times.

items.text: Bringing tefillin on Shabbat eve
items.text_en: Bringing tefillin on Shabbat eve
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says one may darken (wait until night) and bring them. The Gemara asks why not bring them in pairs. Rav Yitzchak brei d'Rav Yehuda explains that if one could bring them in pairs and finish before sunset, one does so; otherwise, one darkens and brings them.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may darken (wait until nightfall) and bring the tefillin.
The Gemara asks why one cannot bring them in pairs before Shabbat.
Rav Yitzchak brei d'Rav Yehuda explains that if one could bring them in pairs and finish before sunset, one does so; otherwise, one darkens and brings them.

items.text: Danger: covering vs. carrying less than four cubits
items.text_en: Danger: covering vs. carrying less than four cubits
items.desc_en: The Mishnah says in danger one covers them and proceeds. A baraita says one carries them less than four cubits at a time. Rav resolves the contradiction: one covers them in danger from gentiles, and carries less than four cubits in danger from bandits.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction: the Mishnah says in danger one covers them and proceeds, but a baraita says one carries them less than four cubits at a time.

Rav resolves the contradiction: the Mishnah refers to danger from gentiles (where covering is safer), while the baraita refers to danger from bandits (where carrying less than four cubits at a time is safer).

items.text: Abaye's challenge to the Mishnah's interpretation
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge to the Mishnah's interpretation
items.desc_en: Abaye questions the Mishnah's ruling, arguing that if it deals with danger from gentiles, the continuation (Rabbi Shimon's opinion) would be even more lenient, which is problematic.

items.text: Resolution: Mishnah is missing a clause, and the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon
items.text_en: Resolution: Mishnah is missing a clause, and the dispute between Tanna Kamma and Rabbi Shimon
items.desc_en: The Gemara resolves that the Mishnah is incomplete: it originally distinguished between danger from gentiles (where the leniency applies) and danger from bandits (where one carries less than four cubits). The dispute between the first Tanna and Rabbi Shimon is explained: one prefers carrying less than four cubits to avoid the appearance of Shabbat violation, while the other prefers passing to a friend to prevent carrying four cubits in public domain.

items.text: Explanation of 'and so his son' and the case of a hundred people
items.text_en: Explanation of 'and so his son' and the case of a hundred people
items.desc_en: The Gemara explains the Mishnah's phrase 'and so his son' refers to a son born in the field. It also clarifies the case of a hundred people: even though it is difficult to pass the book, the method of passing to a friend is still preferable.

items.text: Question on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a barrel
items.text_en: Question on Rabbi Yehuda's ruling about a barrel
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rabbi Yehuda's ruling that one may give a barrel to a friend, asking whether he contradicts the principle that an animal and vessels follow the owner's feet (techum).

items.text: Resh Lakish's answer: water has no substance according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.text_en: Resh Lakish's answer: water has no substance according to Rabbi Yehuda
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish answers that the case involves pouring water from barrel to barrel, and Rabbi Yehuda holds that water has no substance (mammash), so it does not follow the owner's feet. The Mishnah's phrase 'this shall not go further than the feet of the owners' means that the water in one barrel cannot go beyond the owners' techum.

items.text: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda only nullifies water when mixed, not when distinct
items.text_en: Objection: Rabbi Yehuda only nullifies water when mixed, not when distinct
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that Rabbi Yehuda only considers water nullified when mixed in dough, but not when it is in its own state (in a pot or in a barrel). Therefore, the previous answer is insufficient.

items.text: Rava's answer: the barrel acquired a place but the water did not
items.text_en: Rava's answer: the barrel acquired a place but the water did not
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the case involves a barrel that acquired a place (shvita) but the water did not, so the water is nullified relative to the barrel, similar to the principle that a bed is secondary to a person, or a vessel is secondary to food.

items.text: Rav Yosef's objection and resolution: the Mishnah deals with leftovers
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's objection and resolution: the Mishnah deals with leftovers
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef objects that the Mishnah explicitly says 'with leftovers' (bishyara), implying that only in that case is the leniency allowed. He concludes that the Mishnah indeed deals with leftovers.

items.text: Abaye's distinction: leftovers vs. non-leftovers
items.text_en: Abaye's distinction: leftovers vs. non-leftovers
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that 'with leftovers' refers to a case where both the barrel and water acquired a place, while 'without leftovers' refers to a case where the barrel acquired a place but the water did not.

items.text: Rav Ashi's answer: the case of ownerless barrel and water, according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.text_en: Rav Ashi's answer: the case of ownerless barrel and water, according to Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri
items.desc_en: Rav Ashi explains that the Mishnah deals with an ownerless barrel and ownerless water, and follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Nuri, who holds that ownerless objects acquire a place. The phrase 'this shall not go further than the feet of the owners' means that these ownerless items cannot go further than vessels that have owners.

items.text: Mishnah: Reading a scroll on a threshold or roof, and the dispute about rolling it back
items.text_en: Mishnah: Reading a scroll on a threshold or roof, and the dispute about rolling it back
items.desc_en: The Mishnah discusses a case where one is reading a scroll on a threshold or roof and it rolls out of his hand. If it has not reached ten handbreadths, he may roll it back; if it has, he must turn it over on the writing. Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon offer more lenient opinions.

items.text: Gemara's question about the threshold's domain
items.text_en: Gemara's question about the threshold's domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks about the nature of the threshold: if it is a private domain and the courtyard is a public domain, why do we not decree that the scroll might fall and one might come to carry it?

items.text: Identifying the Mishnah's author
items.text_en: Identifying the Mishnah's author
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah can be attributed entirely to Rabbi Shimon, given that the middle clause (Rabbi Yehuda) contradicts him. Rav Yehuda confirms that the first and last clauses are Rabbi Shimon, while the middle is Rabbi Yehuda.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the Mishnah can be attributed to Rabbi Shimon, given his principle that a שבות (rabbinic prohibition) does not override the dignity of sacred scrolls.
The Gemara objects that the last clause of the Mishnah cites Rabbi Yehuda, who contradicts Rabbi Shimon's lenient position.
Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction by explaining that the first and last clauses are Rabbi Shimon, while the middle clause is Rabbi Yehuda.

items.text: Rabbah's explanation: a trampled threshold
items.text_en: Rabbah's explanation: a trampled threshold
items.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the Mishnah deals with a trampled threshold (איסקופה הנדרסת), and the leniency is due to the disgrace of sacred scrolls.

sub.desc_en: Rabbah explains that the Mishnah deals with a trampled threshold (איסקופה הנדרסת), and the leniency is due to the disgrace of sacred scrolls.

items.text: Abaye's objection to Rabbah
items.text_en: Abaye's objection to Rabbah
items.desc_en: Abaye objects: if the case is a trampled threshold, why distinguish between within four cubits and beyond? The same disgrace applies.

sub.desc_en: Abaye objects to Rabbah's explanation: if the case involves a trampled threshold, why should the law distinguish between within four cubits and beyond, since the same disgrace applies?

items.text: Abaye's alternative: a karmelit threshold
items.text_en: Abaye's alternative: a karmelit threshold
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the case involves a karmelit threshold (איסקופה כרמלית) with a public domain passing before it. Within four cubits, where carrying would not incur a sin-offering, the Sages permitted rolling; beyond four cubits, they forbade it.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the difficulty by explaining that the case involves a karmelit threshold (איסקופה כרמלית) with a public domain passing before it.
Abaye explains that within four cubits, where carrying would not incur a sin-offering, the Sages permitted rolling; beyond four cubits, they forbade it.

items.text: Objection and resolution: a long threshold
items.text_en: Objection and resolution: a long threshold
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even within four cubits one might carry from public to private domain. It answers that the threshold is long (איסקופה ארוכה), so the person will remember not to carry further.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects that even within four cubits one might carry from public to private domain, citing Rava's ruling that carrying through a karmelit is still liable.
The Gemara resolves that the case involves a long threshold (איסקופה ארוכה), so the person will remember not to carry further.

items.text: Alternative answer: Ben Azzai's view
items.text_en: Alternative answer: Ben Azzai's view
items.desc_en: The Gemara offers another answer: the scrolls are not carried but studied while walking, and Ben Azzai holds that a walker is like one standing. Rav Acha bar Ahavah concludes that one may not throw sacred scrolls.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara proposes an alternative answer: the case involves a short doorstep, and one studies the scrolls while walking and then sets them down, avoiding carrying.
The Gemara objects: one might worry that he will study the scrolls in the public domain and then inadvertently carry them into a private domain.
The Gemara answers that the mishnah follows Ben Azzai, who holds that a walker is considered like one standing, so no carrying violation occurs.
The Gemara objects: perhaps he might throw the scrolls, and Rabbi Yochanan states that Ben Azzai concedes that throwing is prohibited.
Rav Acha bar Ahavah concludes from this discussion that one may not throw sacred scrolls.

items.text: Contradiction from a baraita about turning scrolls
items.text_en: Contradiction from a baraita about turning scrolls
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance to turn a scroll over on its writing, citing a baraita that forbids turning a sheet face-down. It resolves that the Mishnah's case is unavoidable, and not turning would cause greater disgrace.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's allowance to turn a scroll over on its writing, citing a baraita that forbids turning a sheet face-down and requires covering it with a garment instead.
The Gemara resolves that in the baraita's case it is possible to cover the scroll, but in the Mishnah's case it is unavoidable, and not turning it would cause greater disgrace to the sacred writings.
