items.text: Clarifying the case of a sloping wall
items.text_en: Clarifying the case of a sloping wall
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah's case of turning the scroll over applies to a sloping wall (כותל משופע). Abaye objects that the middle clause (Rabbi Yehuda) would then allow rolling even when the scroll rests. The Gemara resolves by emending the Mishnah: the leniency of turning applies only to a sloping wall.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Mishnah can say to turn the scroll over onto its writing, since the scroll does not rest on the wall.
Rava answers that the Mishnah's case is a sloping wall (כותל משופע), where the scroll rests on the slope.
Abaye objects that if the Mishnah is about a sloping wall, then Rabbi Yehuda's leniency in the middle clause would apply even when the scroll rests, which contradicts the earlier distinction.
The Gemara resolves by emending the Mishnah: the leniency of turning the scroll applies only to a sloping wall, but otherwise the earlier rules stand.

items.text: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah and Rabbi Yehuda's statement
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that on a wall that is not sloping, above three handbreadths one may roll a scroll to himself, below three he turns it on its writing. Rabbi Yehuda adds that even if the scroll is not removed from the ground by a thread's breadth, one may roll it to himself, requiring placement on something.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that on a non-sloping wall, above three handbreadths one may roll a scroll to himself, but below three he must turn it on its writing.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that even if the scroll is not removed from the ground by a thread's breadth, one may roll it to himself, requiring placement on something.

items.text: Gemara's question and resolution about Rava's statement
items.text_en: Gemara's question and resolution about Rava's statement
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's statement that within three handbreadths the Rabbis require placement, suggesting it aligns with a Tanna. It resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, and it is missing text: the Mishnah actually distinguishes between a sloping and non-sloping wall, and Rabbi Yehuda allows rolling even less than three handbreadths from the ground.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions Rava's statement that within three handbreadths the Rabbis require placement, suggesting it aligns with a Tanna.

The Gemara resolves that the entire Mishnah is Rabbi Yehuda, and it is missing text: the Mishnah actually distinguishes between a sloping and non-sloping wall, and Rabbi Yehuda allows rolling even less than three handbreadths from the ground.
The Gemara explains the reason: we require placement on something tangible.

items.text: Mishnah about a ledge before a window
items.text_en: Mishnah about a ledge before a window
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a ledge (ziz) in front of a window may be used on Shabbat for placing and taking objects.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that a ledge (ziz) in front of a window may be used on Shabbat for placing and taking objects.

items.text: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer about the ledge's domain
items.text_en: Gemara's question and Abaye's answer about the ledge's domain
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the ledge projects into a public or private domain. If into a public domain, one might drop objects and come to carry; if into a private domain, it is obvious. Abaye answers that it always projects into a public domain, and the Mishnah refers to breakable vessels.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara asks whether the ledge projects into a public or private domain, noting that if it projects into a private domain the ruling is obvious.
Abaye answers that the ledge always projects into a public domain, and the Mishnah refers to breakable vessels that one would not drop.

items.text: Baraita supporting Abaye's interpretation
items.text_en: Baraita supporting Abaye's interpretation
items.desc_en: A baraita supports Abaye: a ledge before a window projecting into a public domain may be used for placing bowls and cups, and one may use the entire wall up to ten handbreadths below. If there is a lower ledge, one uses it, but the upper ledge is only used opposite the window.

sub.desc_en: A baraita supports Abaye's interpretation: a ledge before a window projecting into a public domain may be used for placing bowls, cups, pitchers, and flasks.
The baraita adds: one may use the entire wall up to ten handbreadths below; if there is a lower ledge, one uses it, but the upper ledge is only used opposite the window.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the ledges' dimensions and Abaye's resolution
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the ledges' dimensions and Abaye's resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions the dimensions: if the ledge lacks four handbreadths it is a exempt place and even opposite the window is forbidden; if it has four, one may use the entire wall. Abaye resolves that the lower ledge has four handbreadths, the upper lacks four but the window completes it to four, so opposite the window it is permitted as part of the window's cavity, but on either side it is forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the dimensions of the ledges: if the ledge lacks four handbreadths it is a exempt place and even opposite the window is forbidden; if it has four, one may use the entire wall.

Abaye resolves that the lower ledge has four handbreadths, the upper lacks four but the window completes it to four, so opposite the window it is permitted as part of the window's cavity, but on either side it is forbidden.

items.text: Mishnah about standing in one domain and moving objects in another
items.text_en: Mishnah about standing in one domain and moving objects in another
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may stand in a private domain and move objects in a public domain, or vice versa, provided he does not carry beyond four cubits. However, one may not stand in one domain and urinate or spit into another. Rabbi Yehuda adds that once saliva is in one's mouth, he may not walk four cubits before spitting.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may stand in a private domain and move objects in a public domain, or vice versa, provided he does not carry beyond four cubits.
The Mishnah adds that one may not stand in one domain and urinate or spit into another.
Rabbi Yehuda adds that once saliva is in one's mouth, he may not walk four cubits before spitting.

items.text: Gemara's challenge about the Mishnah's ruling
items.text_en: Gemara's challenge about the Mishnah's ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Chinana bar Shelemia taught the Mishnah before Rav, stating that one may not stand in a private domain and move objects in a public domain. Rav challenged him, asking why he abandoned the Rabbis and followed Rabbi Meir.

sub.desc_en: Rav challenges Rav Chinana bar Shelemia for teaching the Mishnah's ruling that one may not stand in a private domain and move objects in a public domain, accusing him of abandoning the Rabbis and following Rabbi Meir.

items.text: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's attribution
items.text_en: Gemara's analysis of the Mishnah's attribution
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that both the first and last clauses of the Mishnah follow Rabbi Meir, but then clarifies that only the last clause is Rabbi Meir while the first is the Rabbis.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara initially assumes that since the last clause of the Mishnah follows Rabbi Meir, the first clause also follows Rabbi Meir.
The Gemara corrects itself: the last clause is Rabbi Meir, but the first clause is the Rabbis.

items.text: Debate about Rava's ruling on transferring an object
items.text_en: Debate about Rava's ruling on transferring an object
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses whether the Mishnah's phrase 'provided he does not take it out' implies liability for a sin-offering, supporting Rava's view, or merely prohibition. Two versions of the debate are presented.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the Mishnah's phrase 'provided he does not take it out' that if one does take it out, he is liable for a sin-offering, and proposes this as support for Rava's ruling.
The Gemara objects that the Mishnah may not explicitly state liability for a sin-offering; it might only mean that it is forbidden but exempt from a sin-offering.

An alternative version of the debate is presented: some say the Mishnah implies exemption but prohibition, which would challenge Rava, but the Gemara deflects by suggesting the Mishnah might actually mean liability for a sin-offering.

items.text: Rav Yosef's ruling on urinating and spitting
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's ruling on urinating and spitting
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef rules that one who urinates or spits in a public domain is liable for a sin-offering. The Gemara objects that this lacks the required 'lifting' and 'placing' on a four-handbreadth area, but resolves that intention designates a place, citing Rava's similar ruling about throwing an object into a dog's mouth.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah is cited: one may not stand in a private domain and urinate or spit into the public domain.
Rav Yosef rules that one who urinates or spits in the public domain is liable for a sin-offering.
The Gemara objects that urination and spitting lack the required 'lifting' and 'placing' on a four-handbreadth area for Shabbat liability.
The Gemara argues that intention designates a place, citing Rava's ruling that throwing an object into a dog's mouth is liable despite lacking a four-handbreadth area.
The Gemara resolves that just as intention designates a place for Rava's case, so too intention designates a place for urination and spitting.

items.text: Rava's query about a person in a private domain and his mouth in the public domain
items.text_en: Rava's query about a person in a private domain and his mouth in the public domain
items.desc_en: Rava asks whether, when a person is in a private domain but his mouth (or another part) is in the public domain, we follow the 'lifting' or the 'exit' for liability. The question remains unresolved (teiku).

sub.desc_en: Rava asks whether, when a person is in a private domain but his mouth (or another part) is in the public domain, we follow the 'lifting' or the 'exit' for liability; the question remains unresolved (teiku).

items.text: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on spitting and the dispute with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei
items.text_en: Rabbi Yehuda's opinion on spitting and the dispute with Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one should not spit, and Rabbi Yehuda says that if one did not turn the spit in his mouth, he may walk four cubits. The Gemara compares this to a Tosefta about eating dried figs with unclean hands, where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between turning and not turning. Rabbi Yochanan says the system is reversed, but Resh Lakish resolves it by saying the case is about phlegm, not saliva.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's ruling that Rabbi Yehuda permits walking four cubits even if one did not turn the spit in his mouth.
The Gemara cites a Tosefta about eating dried figs with unclean hands, where Rabbi Yehuda distinguishes between turning the fig and not turning it.
Rabbi Yochanan says the system is reversed — the opinions in the Mishnah and the Tosefta are swapped.
Resh Lakish objects that the system is not reversed; the case in the Mishnah involves phlegm (כיח), not saliva.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by clarifying that the Tosefta refers to phlegm that has detached, not saliva, and the original distinction stands.

items.text: Resh Lakish on spitting before one's teacher
items.text_en: Resh Lakish on spitting before one's teacher
items.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one who expectorates before his teacher is liable for death, interpreting a verse to mean 'those who make Me hateful.' The Gemara clarifies that this refers to spitting, not just coughing.

sub.desc_en: Resh Lakish states that one who expectorates before his teacher is liable for death, interpreting the verse 'כל משנאי אהבו מות' (all who hate Me love death) as referring to those who make God hateful.
The Gemara objects that the spitting might be involuntary (אונס), questioning whether the harsh penalty applies.
The Gemara clarifies that the ruling applies only to deliberate spitting (כיח ורק), not to involuntary expectoration.

items.text: Mishnah on drinking across domains and Gemara's analysis
items.text_en: Mishnah on drinking across domains and Gemara's analysis
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not stand in one domain and drink in another unless he inserts his head and most of his body into the place where he drinks. The Gemara notes that the first clause follows the Rabbis and the last Rabbi Meir. Rav Yosef explains it refers to objects needed for the drink, and all agree. A query about a karmelit is raised, with Abaye and Rava debating whether a decree applies to a decree.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may not stand in one domain and drink in another unless he inserts his head and most of his body into the place where he drinks.
The Gemara notes an apparent contradiction: the first clause follows the Rabbis (who permit drinking without full entry) and the last clause follows Rabbi Meir (who requires full entry).
Rav Yosef explains that the Mishnah refers to objects needed for the drink, and all agree on the ruling.
A query is raised about whether the same rule applies to a karmelit (a semi-public domain).
Abaye asserts that the same rule applies to a karmelit as to the other domains.
Rava objects that the karmelit itself is a rabbinic decree, and one cannot issue a decree upon a decree.
Abaye begins to cite a source to support his position that the rule applies to a karmelit.

items.text: Interpretation of 'וכן בגת' regarding tithes
items.text_en: Interpretation of 'וכן בגת' regarding tithes
items.desc_en: Rava and Rav Sheishet explain that the Mishnah's phrase 'וכן בגת' refers to the laws of tithes, not Shabbat. They cite a baraita where Rabbi Meir exempts drinking from the winepress from tithes, Rabbi Eliezer bar Tzadok obligates, and the Sages distinguish between hot and cold water due to returning leftovers.

items.text: Mishnah: Drawing water from a spout and a pipe
items.text_en: Mishnah: Drawing water from a spout and a pipe
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may catch water from a spout below ten handbreadths, and from a pipe one may drink anywhere, implying a distinction between catching and collecting.

items.text: Gemara: Catching vs. collecting from a spout
items.text_en: Gemara: Catching vs. collecting from a spout
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why catching is permitted but collecting is not. Rav Nachman explains the spout is within three handbreadths of the roof, making it like the roof. Two baraitot confirm that one may catch but not collect water from such a spout.

items.text: Gemara: Pipe with four handbreadths
items.text_en: Gemara: Pipe with four handbreadths
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that if a pipe has an area of four by four handbreadths, it is forbidden to drink from it because it constitutes transferring from one domain to another.

items.text: Mishnah: Well and ash-heap in the public domain
items.text_en: Mishnah: Well and ash-heap in the public domain
items.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that if a well in the public domain has a rim ten handbreadths high, one may fill water from a window above it on Shabbat. Similarly, if an ash-heap is ten handbreadths high, one may pour water into it from a window.

items.text: Gemara: Distance of the well from the wall and concern about the ash-heap
items.text_en: Gemara: Distance of the well from the wall and concern about the ash-heap
items.desc_en: Rav Huna explains the well is four handbreadths away from the wall, so the rim is necessary to avoid transferring through the public domain. Rabbi Yochanan says even if adjacent, the rim and well combine for ten. Regarding the ash-heap, the Gemara questions concern it might be removed, citing a story with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, and resolves that a private ash-heap is concerning but a public one is not.

items.text: Mishnah and Gemara: Tree overhanging the ground
items.text_en: Mishnah and Gemara: Tree overhanging the ground
items.desc_en: The Mishnah permits moving objects under a tree if its trunk is less than three handbreadths from the ground, but forbids sitting on roots that are three handbreadths high. Rav Huna bar Yehoshua limits the area to two se'ah, questioning the reason.

items.text: Opening principle: A dwelling used for air
items.text_en: Opening principle: A dwelling used for air
items.desc_en: The Gemara introduces the principle that a dwelling whose use is for air (i.e., open space) may not be used for carrying more than a beit se'atayim.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states the principle that a dwelling used for air (open space) may not carry more than a beit se'atayim.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Sheishet on tree roots
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbah and Rav Sheishet on tree roots
items.desc_en: The Gemara presents a dispute: Rabbah permits using tree roots that come from above three handbreadths into within three handbreadths of the ground, while Rav Sheishet forbids it. The reasoning is explained, and the rule is applied to different cases.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara cites the Mishnah's case of tree roots and introduces the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Sheishet regarding roots extending from above three handbreadths into within three handbreadths.
Rabbah permits using the roots because anything less than three handbreadths from the ground is considered part of the ground.
Rav Sheishet forbids using the roots because they come from a prohibited source (above three handbreadths) and thus remain prohibited.
The Gemara applies the dispute to different cases: roots rising upward are forbidden, descending are permitted, and sideways are the subject of the dispute between Rabbah and Rav Sheishet.

items.text: Extension to a beam and corner
items.text_en: Extension to a beam and corner
items.desc_en: The same principle applies to a beam (nigra) and a corner (keren zavit).

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that the same principle applies to a beam (nigra) and a corner (keren zavit).

items.text: Story of Abaye's palm tree and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.text_en: Story of Abaye's palm tree and Rav Yosef's ruling
items.desc_en: Abaye had a palm tree that he climbed via an opening, and Rav Yosef permitted it. Rav Acha bar Tachlifa explains that this was according to Rabbah's view. The Gemara clarifies that even Rav Sheishet might permit it in this case because the roof is considered full.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Abaye had a palm tree which he climbed via an opening, and he came before Rav Yosef who permitted it.
Rav Acha bar Tachlifa explains that Rav Yosef's permission was in accordance with Rabbah's view.

The Gemara clarifies that even Rav Sheishet might permit it in this case because the roof is considered full, and the ruling teaches that one may use less than three handbreadths adjacent to the roof.

items.text: Analysis of the Mishnah on roots three handbreadths high
items.text_en: Analysis of the Mishnah on roots three handbreadths high
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the Mishnah's case of roots three handbreadths above the ground, questioning whether it refers to roots that do not bend back to the ground, and concludes it teaches that even if one side is level with the ground, it is still forbidden.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions the Mishnah's case of roots three handbreadths high, asking whether it refers to roots that do not bend back to the ground, and suggests it must be even when they do bend back.
The Gemara answers that the Mishnah always refers to roots that do not bend back, and it teaches that even if one side is level with the ground, it is still forbidden.

items.text: Baraita on tree roots and climbing
items.text_en: Baraita on tree roots and climbing
items.desc_en: A baraita is cited stating that roots three handbreadths high or with a space underneath are forbidden to sit on, and one may not climb a tree from before Shabbat to sit there all day. However, a pit, ditch, cave, or fence may be climbed even if one hundred cubits high.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens by stating that tree roots three handbreadths high or with a three-handbreadth space underneath are forbidden to sit on, even if one side is level with the ground, because one may not climb, hang, or lean on a tree.

The baraita adds that one may not climb a tree from before Shabbat to sit there all day, and extends the prohibition to any animal, but permits climbing a pit, ditch, cave, or fence even if one hundred cubits high.

items.text: Contradiction in baraitot about descending from a tree
items.text_en: Contradiction in baraitot about descending from a tree
items.desc_en: Two baraitot contradict each other: one says if one climbed before Shabbat, it is permitted to descend; the other says it is forbidden. The Gemara resolves this by distinguishing between climbing before Shabbat and after dark, or between an unintentional and intentional act, or by a dispute about penalizing an unintentional act due to an intentional one.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara notes a contradiction between two baraitot: one permits descending from a tree if one climbed before Shabbat, the other forbids it.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between climbing before Shabbat (permitted to descend) and after dark (forbidden).
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves the contradiction by distinguishing between an unintentional act (permitted) and an intentional act (forbidden), both after dark.
Alternatively, the Gemara resolves the contradiction by a dispute between two authorities (Mar) about whether to penalize an unintentional act due to an intentional one.

items.text: Connection to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.text_en: Connection to the dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua
items.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua links the dispute about descending from a tree to a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua regarding the principle of 'arise and act' versus 'sit and do not act' in the context of blood offerings. The Gemara analyzes whether this analogy holds, considering the presence of a mitzvah.

sub.desc_en: Rav Huna bar Yehoshua introduces a Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua about blood offerings to analogize the tree descent debate.
The baraita states the rule for mixing blood offerings: same-type mixes are given in the same manner, but a mix of four and one is disputed.
The Gemara presents the core dispute: Rabbi Eliezer says give four applications, Rabbi Yehoshua says give one.
Rabbi Eliezer argues that giving one application violates 'do not diminish', and Rabbi Yehoshua counters that giving four violates 'do not add'.
Both sages clarify that the prohibitions of adding and diminishing apply only when the offering is in its own form.
Rabbi Yehoshua argues that adding violates 'do not add' with an active deed, while diminishing violates 'do not diminish' without an active deed.
The Gemara applies the dispute: for Rabbi Eliezer, who holds 'arise and act' is preferable, one may descend; for Rabbi Yehoshua, who holds 'sit and do not act' is preferable, one may not descend.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer's principle of 'arise and act' applies only when a mitzvah is being performed, but here there is no mitzvah, so perhaps even he would forbid descending.

The Gemara alternatively objects that Rabbi Yehoshua's principle of 'sit and do not act' applies only when a mitzvah is involved, but here there is no mitzvah, so perhaps even he would permit descending.

items.text: Resolving contradictions about climbing a tree on Shabbat
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions about climbing a tree on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara addresses a contradiction between two baraitot regarding climbing a moist versus dry tree on Shabbat. Rav Yehuda initially distinguishes based on whether the stump regenerates, but is challenged; the resolution shifts to a distinction between summer and winter, and then to whether fruit or branches fall, with a final story about Rav in Afsatya.

items.text: Resolving contradictions about walking on grass on Shabbat
items.text_en: Resolving contradictions about walking on grass on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rami bar Abba cites Rav Asi prohibiting walking on grass on Shabbat. Two contradictory baraitot are reconciled through multiple distinctions: moist vs. dry grass, summer vs. winter, wearing shoes vs. barefoot, shoes with spikes vs. without, and with a strap vs. without. Finally, the Gemara notes that according to Rabbi Shimon, all are permitted.

items.text: Forcing one's wife to a mitzvah and the proper approach to marital relations
items.text_en: Forcing one's wife to a mitzvah and the proper approach to marital relations
items.desc_en: Rami bar Hama citing Rav Asi prohibits forcing one's wife to a mitzvah, citing a verse. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi adds that such coercion leads to unworthy children. A baraita supports this. Rava's statement that repeating intercourse produces male children is reconciled by distinguishing between with and without the wife's consent.

items.text: The virtue of a wife who initiates a mitzvah and the curses of Eve
items.text_en: The virtue of a wife who initiates a mitzvah and the curses of Eve
items.desc_en: Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani citing Rabbi Yochanan praises a wife who initiates a mitzvah, saying her children surpass even Moses' generation, citing Leah's initiative. The Gemara questions this given the ten curses of Eve, which include her desire for her husband. The resolution is that the praise applies when she appeases him, not when she is aggressive.

items.text: Additional curses of Eve and lessons from animals
items.text_en: Additional curses of Eve and lessons from animals
items.desc_en: Rav Dimi adds three more curses: wrapped like a mourner, banned from everyone, and imprisoned. The Gemara clarifies the ban. A baraita lists other curses: growing hair like Lilith, urinating like an animal, and being a cushion for her husband. The Gemara notes these are actually virtues, citing Rabbi Chiya and Rabbi Yochanan who learn modesty and proper conduct from animals, especially the rooster's courtship.

items.text: Opening Mishnah
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a door in a muktzeh, thorns in a breach, and mats may not be used for locking on Shabbat unless they are elevated from the ground.

items.text: Gemara's question and initial answers
items.text_en: Gemara's question and initial answers
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita that permits locking with a dragging door, mat, or jug if they are tied and suspended, without requiring elevation. Abaye and Rava each offer a resolution: Abaye says the Mishnah refers to cases without a hinge, while Rava says it refers to cases that never had a hinge.

items.text: Objection and resolution
items.text_en: Objection and resolution
items.desc_en: The Gemara objects with a baraita that explicitly requires both being tied and elevated from the ground. Abaye and Rava each reconcile the baraita with their own positions: Abaye says the baraita requires either a hinge or elevation, while Rava says it requires either a hinge (past or present) or elevation.

items.text: Baraitot on thorns and widow's door
items.text_en: Baraitot on thorns and widow's door
items.desc_en: A baraita teaches that bundles of thorns prepared for a breach in a courtyard may be used for locking if tied and suspended. Rabbi Chiya teaches that a 'widow's door' (a dragging door) may not be locked; two explanations are given for what a widow's door is.

items.text: Rav Yehuda's ruling on a fire-basket
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda's ruling on a fire-basket
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda rules that one may place a fire-basket (for heating) from above downward on Shabbat, but not from below upward. The same applies to an egg, a pot, a bed, and a barrel.

items.text: Aggadic exchange about thorns
items.text_en: Aggadic exchange about thorns
items.desc_en: A heretic taunts Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya with the verse 'their best is like a brier' (חדק). Rabbi Yehoshua responds by citing the continuation 'the upright is from a thorn-hedge' and explains that the best of Israel protect like thorns protect a breach, or that they will thrust the nations into Gehinnom.

items.text: Second Mishnah: Opening a door from one domain to another
items.text_en: Second Mishnah: Opening a door from one domain to another
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may not stand in a private domain and open a door into the public domain, or vice versa, unless a partition ten handbreadths high is made. The Sages cite a precedent from the market of Jerusalem where keys were placed in a window above the door. Rabbi Yose says it was the wool-dealers' market.

items.text: Gemara's resolution of the Jerusalem market case
items.text_en: Gemara's resolution of the Jerusalem market case
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions how the Sages could cite Jerusalem as a public domain, given that its gates were locked at night, making it a karmelit. Rav Papa resolves that the Mishnah refers to before the walls were breached, while the Sages' case refers to after. Rava says the Mishnah's ruling applies to garden gates, and the Sages' case is about a karmelit.

items.text: משנת הפתיחה: מחלוקת רבי מאיר וחכמים על מפתח בחלון
items.text_en: Opening Mishnah: Dispute about placing a key in a window
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages (with Rabbi Yosei adding a detail) about a case in Jerusalem where people would lock their shops and place the key in a window above the door. Rabbi Meir requires a partition ten handbreadths high, while the Sages cite a precedent without such a partition.
items.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת: רבי מאיר מתיר רק אם עשה מחיצה גבוהה עשרה טפחים, וחכמים מביאים מעשה משוק פטמים בירושלים שהתירו להניח מפתח בחלון שעל גבי הפתח. רבי יוסי חולק על זיהוי השוק.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah presents the dispute: Rabbi Meir requires a partition ten handbreadths high for placing a key in a window, the Sages cite a precedent from the perfume-sellers' market, and Rabbi Yosei specifies it was the wool-sellers' market.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת במחלוקת רבי מאיר וחכמים על מפתח בחלון, ומביאה את דברי רבי יוסי החולק על זיהוי השוק.

items.text: ברייתא: דיני פתחי שערי גינה וחנויות
items.text_en: Baraita: Laws of gates and shops with keys
items.desc_en: A baraita details the laws of gates of a garden and shops opening to the public domain, specifying where one may place a key depending on the height of the lock. Rabbi Meir and the Sages dispute whether a key may be placed in a window above the door when the lock is above ten handbreadths, with a condition about the window's size.
items.desc: הברייתא מפרטת דינים לפתחי שערי גינה וחנויות הפתוחות לרשות הרבים: אם יש בית שער מבפנים או מבחוץ, פותח ונועל בהתאם; לגבי מנעול, אם הוא למטה מעשרה טפחים מניח מפתח באיסקופה, ואם למעלה – רבי מאיר מתיר להניח במנעול, וחכמים מתירים גם באיסקופה או בחלון. אם בחלון יש ארבעה על ארבעה טפחים – אסור משום הוצאה מרשות לרשות.

sub.desc_en: The baraita opens with the general rule for garden gates: one may lock and unlock from whichever side has a gatehouse, but if there is no gatehouse on either side, it is forbidden to handle the key on Shabbat.
sub.desc: הברייתא פותחת בדיני פתחי שערי גינה: מתי מותר לפתוח ולנעול מבפנים או מבחוץ.

sub.desc_en: The baraita extends the rule to shops opening to the public domain: when the lock is below ten handbreadths, one may place the key on the threshold (איסקופה) before Shabbat and retrieve it.
sub.desc: הברייתא מביאה דין דומה בחנויות: אם המנעול למטה מעשרה טפחים, מניח המפתח באיסקופה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Meir states that when the lock is above ten handbreadths, one must place the key directly in the lock before Shabbat.
sub.desc: רבי מאיר אומר: אם המנעול למעלה מעשרה, מניח המפתח במנעול עצמו.

sub.desc_en: The Sages disagree and permit placing the key on the threshold (איסקופה) or in a window above the door even when the lock is above ten handbreadths.
sub.desc: חכמים מתירים להניח המפתח גם באיסקופה או בחלון שעל גבי הפתח.

sub.desc_en: The baraita concludes with a condition: if the window is four by four handbreadths, placing the key there is forbidden because it constitutes transferring from one domain to another.
sub.desc: הברייתא מסיימת: אם בחלון יש ארבעה על ארבעה טפחים, אסור משום הוצאה מרשות לרשות.

items.text: קושיית הגמרא: טלטול מכרמלית לרשות היחיד
items.text_en: Gemara's question: The status of the lock and the contradiction
items.desc_en: The Gemara analyzes the baraita, noting that it implies the threshold is a karmelit. It questions the nature of the lock: if it lacks four handbreadths it is a exempt place, but if it has four handbreadths, how can the Sages allow moving the key from a karmelit to a private domain?
items.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מהברייתא משמע שהאיסקופה היא כרמלית, והמנעול – אם אין בו ארבעה טפחים הוא מקום פטור, ואם יש בו ארבעה – הרי חכמים מתירים להניח מפתח באיסקופה ולטלטל מכרמלית לרשות היחיד, וזה אסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara infers from the baraita's phrase 'וכן חנויות' that the threshold (איסקופה) is a karmelit, and then questions the nature of the lock: if it lacks four handbreadths it is an exempt place, but if it has four handbreadths, how can the Sages permit moving the key from a karmelit to a private domain?
sub.desc: הגמרא מקשה: מהברייתא משמע שהאיסקופה היא כרמלית, והמנעול – אם אין בו ארבעה טפחים הוא מקום פטור, ואם יש בו ארבעה – הרי חכמים מתירים להניח מפתח באיסקופה ולטלטל מכרמלית לרשות היחיד, וזה אסור.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara objects: if the lock has four handbreadths, how can the Sages allow bringing the key from the threshold (a karmelit) to the lock (a private domain), since this would involve carrying from a karmelit to a private domain on Shabbat?
sub.desc: הגמרא ממשיכה ומקשה: אם יש במנעול ארבעה טפחים, הרי חכמים מתירים להניח מפתח באיסקופה ולטלטל מכרמלית לרשות היחיד, וזה אסור.

items.text: תירוץ אביי: חוקקין להשלים
items.text_en: Abaye's resolution: The lock is less than four handbreadths but can be completed by hollowing
items.desc_en: Abaye explains that the lock is less than four handbreadths but has enough material to be hollowed out to complete it to four. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is whether one may hollow out to complete the measure.
items.desc: אביי מתרץ: המנעול אין בו ארבעה טפחים, אך יש בו חלל שניתן לחקקו ולהשלימו לארבעה. רבי מאיר סובר חוקקין להשלים, ולכן המנעול נחשב כרשות היחיד, וחכמים סוברים אין חוקקין להשלים, ולכן הוא מקום פטור.

sub.desc_en: Abaye resolves the difficulty by asserting that the lock is less than four handbreadths but has enough material to be hollowed out to complete it to four.
sub.desc: אביי מתרץ שהמנעול אינו ברוחב ארבעה טפחים, אך יש בו חלל שניתן לחקקו ולהשלימו לארבעה.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains that the dispute between Rabbi Meir and the Sages is whether one may hollow out the lock to complete its measure to four handbreadths.
sub.desc: אביי מבאר שמחלוקת רבי מאיר וחכמים היא בשאלה אם חוקקין להשלים את החלל לארבעה טפחים.

items.text: דרשת רב ביבי: שלוש הלכות מהמשנה
items.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's inference: Three lessons from the Mishnah
items.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye derives three conclusions from the Mishnah: that one may hollow out to complete, that Rabbi Meir retracted his opinion regarding gates of a garden, and that the Sages' position supports Rav Dimi's statement from Rabbi Yochanan about a place lacking four handbreadths being permissible for both domains to rest on.
items.desc: רב ביבי בר אביי דורש מהמשנה שלוש הלכות: חוקקין להשלים, שרבי מאיר חזר בו מדין שערי גינה, ושיטת חכמים תואמת את דברי רב דימי בשם רבי יוחנן שמקום פחות מארבעה טפחים מותר לכתף עליו לבני רשות הרבים ורשות היחיד, ובלבד שלא יחליפו.

sub.desc_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye announces that he derives three conclusions from the Mishnah.
sub.desc: רב ביבי פותח ואומר שניתן ללמוד שלוש הלכות מהמשנה.

sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's first inference
sub.desc_en: He infers that one may hollow out to complete (חוֹקְקִין לְהַשְׁלִים).
sub.desc: רב ביבי פותח ואומר שניתן ללמוד שלוש הלכות מהמשנה.

sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's second inference
sub.desc_en: He infers that Rabbi Meir retracted his opinion regarding gates of a garden (שַׁעֲרֵי גִינָּה).
sub.desc: רב ביבי פותח ואומר שניתן ללמוד שלוש הלכות מהמשנה.

sub.text_en: Rav Bibi bar Abaye's third inference
sub.desc_en: He infers that the Sages' position supports Rav Dimi's statement from Rabbi Yochanan about a place lacking four handbreadths being permissible for both domains to rest on, provided they do not exchange.
sub.desc: רב ביבי לומד ששיטת חכמים תואמת את דברי רב דימי בשם רבי יוחנן שמקום פחות מארבעה טפחים מותר לכתף עליו לבני רשות הרבים ורשות היחיד, ובלבד שלא יחליפו.

items.text: משנה: נגר שיש בראשו גלוסטרא
items.text_en: New Mishnah: Dispute about a bolt with a knob
items.desc_en: A new Mishnah presents a dispute between Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yosei regarding a bolt that has a knob (גלוסטרא) on its head. Rabbi Eliezer prohibits using it on Shabbat, citing a precedent from a synagogue in Tiberias, while Rabbi Yosei permits it, claiming the opposite tradition.
items.desc: המשנה עוסקת בנגר (בריח) שיש בראשו גלוסטרא (כדור או עיבוי). רבי אליעזר אוסר ורבי יוסי מתיר. כל אחד מביא מעשה מבית הכנסת בטבריה: רבי אליעזר אומר שנהגו היתר עד שבא רבן גמליאל ואסר, ורבי יוסי אומר שנהגו איסור עד שבא רבן גמליאל והתיר.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens with a dispute: Rabbi Eliezer prohibits and Rabbi Yosei permits using a bolt with a knob (גלוסטרא) on Shabbat.
sub.desc: המשנה פותחת בדין נגר שיש בראשו גלוסטרא, ומציגה את מחלוקת רבי אליעזר האוסר ורבי יוסי המתיר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Eliezer cites a precedent from a synagogue in Tiberias where the practice was permitted until Rabban Gamliel and the Elders prohibited it.
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר מביא מעשה מבית הכנסת בטבריה שהיו נוהגים היתר עד שבא רבן גמליאל ואסר.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yosei counters with the opposite tradition: the practice was prohibited until Rabban Gamliel and the Elders permitted it.
sub.desc: רבי אליעזר מביא מעשה מבית הכנסת בטבריה שהיו נוהגים היתר עד שבא רבן גמליאל ואסר.

items.text: גמרא: מחלוקת בנגר הניטל באגודו
items.text_en: Gemara's opening: The dispute is only when the knob is not attached
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins its analysis, stating that everyone agrees when the bolt is removed with its knob (i.e., the knob is attached), the dispute only arises when the knob is not attached.
items.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור: בנגר הניטל באגודו (שאינו קבוע) כולי עלמא לא פליגי, והמחלוקת היא במקרה אחר, אך הקטע נקטע.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating that when the bolt is removed with its knob (בניטל באגדו), everyone agrees it is permitted, and the dispute only arises when the knob is not attached.
sub.desc: הגמרא פותחת בבירור המחלוקת: בנגר הנאחז באגודו כולי עלמא לא פליגי, והמחלוקת היא במקרה אחר.

items.text: מחלוקת ראשונים בנגר שאינו ניטל באיגדו
items.text_en: Conclusion of previous discussion on a bolt with a knob
items.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the earlier debate about a bolt that has a knob at its head: one opinion considers it a vessel because of the knob, while the other disagrees because it is not taken by its handle.
items.desc: הגמרא מביאה מחלוקת בין אמוראים לגבי נגר שאינו ניטל באיגדו: האם יש עליו תורת כלי בגלל גלוסטרא שבראשו, או לא.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara concludes the debate about a bolt with a knob: one opinion considers it a vessel because of the knob, the other rejects it because it is not taken by its handle.
sub.desc: הגמרא מציגה מחלוקת בין מר למר לגבי נגר שאינו ניטל באיגדו: האם יש עליו תורת כלי בגלל גלוסטרא שבראשו.

items.text: משנת נגר הנגרר והמונח
items.text_en: Mishnah: Types of bolts and their permissibility
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that a dragging bolt (נגר הנגרר) may be used to lock in the Temple but not in the provinces; a placed bolt is forbidden everywhere. Rabbi Yehuda permits a placed bolt in the Temple and a dragging bolt in the provinces.
items.desc: המשנה קובעת שנגר הנגרר נועלים בו במקדש אבל לא במדינה, והמונח אסור בכל מקום. רבי יהודה מחלק: המונח מותר במקדש, והנגרר במדינה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah opens by stating that a dragging bolt (נגר הנגרר) may be used to lock in the Temple but not in the provinces.
sub.desc: המשנה מבחינה בין נגר הנגרר, הנועלים בו במקדש אבל לא במדינה, לבין נגר המונח, שאסור בשניהם, ורבי יהודה מתיר את המונח במקדש ואת הנגרר במדינה.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah adds that a placed bolt (המונח) is forbidden everywhere.
sub.desc: המשנה ממשיכה בדין המונח, האסור בכל מקום, ומביאה את חלוקת רבי יהודה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda permits a placed bolt in the Temple and a dragging bolt in the provinces.
sub.desc: המשנה ממשיכה בדין המונח, האסור בכל מקום, ומביאה את חלוקת רבי יהודה.

items.text: ברייתא המפרשת את הנגר הנגרר
items.text_en: Gemara: Definition of a dragging bolt
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites a baraita defining a dragging bolt as one that is tied and hanging with one end touching the ground. Rabbi Yehuda says such a bolt is permitted even in the provinces; the prohibited bolt in the Temple is one that is neither tied nor hanging but is removed and placed in a corner.
items.desc: הברייתא מפרטת: נגר הנגרר הוא שקשור ותלוי וראשו מגיע לארץ. רבי יהודה אומר שזה מותר גם במדינה, והנגרר האסור במדינה הוא שאינו קשור ואינו תלוי.

sub.desc_en: The baraita defines a dragging bolt (נגר הנגרר) as one that is tied and hanging with one end touching the ground, permitted in the Temple but not in the provinces.
sub.desc: הברייתא מפרטת את הגדרת נגר הנגרר: כל שקשור ותלוי וראשו מגיע לארץ, ורבי יהודה מוסיף שזה מותר אף במדינה, והנגר האסור הוא שאינו קשור ואינו תלוי.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Yehuda argues that the tied-and-hanging bolt is permitted even in the provinces; the prohibited bolt in the Temple is one that is neither tied nor hanging but is removed and placed in a corner.
sub.desc: הברייתא מפרטת את הגדרת נגר הנגרר: כל שקשור ותלוי וראשו מגיע לארץ, ורבי יהודה מוסיף שזה מותר אף במדינה, והנגר האסור הוא שאינו קשור ואינו תלוי.

items.text: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: Halakha like Rabbi Yehuda regarding a dragging bolt
items.text_en: Rav Yehuda citing Shmuel: Halakha like Rabbi Yehuda regarding a dragging bolt
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding a dragging bolt. Rava adds that this applies only when it is tied to the door. The Gemara questions this from an incident where Rabbi Tavla saw a bolt tied to the doorpost and said nothing, but answers that bolt was taken by its handle.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the binding law (הלכה) follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding a dragging bolt (נגר הנגרר).
Rava adds a condition: the ruling applies only when the bolt is tied to the door itself.
The Gemara objects: did not Rabbi Tavla visit Mehoza and see a bolt tied to the doorpost without objecting, contradicting Rava's condition?
The Gemara resolves: that particular bolt was one that could be taken by its handle (ניטל באגדו), so it was permitted even without being tied to the door.

items.text: Rav Avya's incident in Nehardea
items.text_en: Rav Avya's incident in Nehardea
items.desc_en: Rav Avya saw a man tying a bolt with a reed and said that this one should not be locked, implying it is forbidden because it is not properly attached.

sub.desc_en: Rav Avya arrives in Nehardea, sees a man tying a bolt with a reed, and declares that this one should not be locked, implying it is forbidden because it is not properly attached.

items.text: בעיית נקימת הנגר והלכה
items.text_en: Rabbi Zeira's question about a bolt that is compressed (נקמז)
items.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about a bolt that is compressed (נקמז). Rav Yosef cites a baraita: if it slips out (נשמט) it is forbidden, if compressed it is permitted; Rabbi Yehuda says compressed is forbidden even if it does not slip. Rav Yehuda says in the name of Shmuel that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding compressed, because it appears like building.
items.desc: רבי זירא שואל על נגר שנקמז (ננעץ). רב יוסף מביא ברייתא: נשמט אסור, נקמז מותר, ורבי יהודה אוסר. רב יהודה בשם שמואל פוסק כרבי יהודה בנקמז, ואביי מסביר הטעם משום דמיחזי כבונה.

sub.desc_en: Rabbi Zeira asks about the status of a bolt that is compressed (נקמז) on Shabbat.
sub.desc: רבי זירא שואל מה דינו של נגר שנקמז (ננעץ) בשבת.

sub.text_en: Rav Yosef's response citing a baraita
sub.desc_en: Rav Yosef responds by citing a baraita that distinguishes between a bolt that slips out (אסור) and one that is compressed (מותר), with Rabbi Yehuda forbidding even a compressed bolt.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מביא ברייתא המבחינה בין נשמט (אסור) לנקמז (מותר), ורבי יהודה אוסר אף בנקמז.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports in the name of Shmuel that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda regarding a compressed bolt.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מביא ברייתא המבחינה בין נשמט (אסור) לנקמז (מותר), ורבי יהודה אוסר אף בנקמז.

sub.desc_en: Abaye explains the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's stringency: it appears like building (בונה), which is forbidden on Shabbat.
sub.desc: רב יוסף מביא ברייתא המבחינה בין נשמט (אסור) לנקמז (מותר), ורבי יהודה אוסר אף בנקמז.

items.text: Rav Nechumi's question about a bolt with a handle
items.text_en: Rav Nechumi's question about a bolt with a handle
items.desc_en: Rav Nechumi bar Zecharya asks Abaye about a bolt that has a handle (בית יד). Abaye says he is referring to a 'bukhna' (a type of tool). It is stated that Rav Nechumi bar Adda says such a bolt is permitted.

sub.text: Rav Nechumi bar Zecharya's question to Abaye
sub.text_en: Rav Nechumi bar Zecharya's question to Abaye
sub.desc_en: Rav Nechumi bar Zecharya asks Abaye about the status of a bolt that has a handle (בית יד) attached to it.
Abaye responds that Rav Nechumi is referring to a 'bukhna' (a type of tool), implying the bolt is permitted.
It is stated that Rav Nechumi bar Adda explicitly rules that a bolt with a handle (בית יד) is permitted for use on Shabbat.

items.text: Incidents with a curtain rod and a beam
items.text_en: Incidents with a curtain rod and a beam
items.desc_en: The Gemara relates that a curtain rod (שרית) in Rabbi Pedat's house was lifted by ten people and placed on the door, and he said nothing, considering it a vessel. Similarly, a beam (אסיתא) in Mar Shmuel's house was used to hold a crossbeam, and he permitted placing it on the door, considering it a vessel.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that a curtain rod (שרית) in Rabbi Pedat's house was lifted by ten people and placed on the door, and he said nothing.
Rabbi Pedat explains that the rod has the status of a vessel, so it is permitted.
The Gemara relates that a beam (אסיתא) in Mar Shmuel's house held a crossbeam, and Mar Shmuel permitted placing it on the door.
Mar Shmuel explains that the beam has the status of a vessel, so it is permitted.

items.text: Rav Asi's ruling on arches of a boat
items.text_en: Rav Asi's ruling on arches of a boat
items.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel asks Rav Amram to share fine teachings from Rav Asi about arches of a boat (כיפי דארבא). Rav Asi rules that if they have a handbreadth, or if they lack a handbreadth but are within three handbreadths of each other, one may bring a mat and spread it over them the next day, as it is adding to a temporary tent and is permitted.

sub.text: Rami bar Yechezkel's request to Rav Amram
sub.text_en: Rami bar Yechezkel's request to Rav Amram
sub.desc_en: Rami bar Yechezkel (רמי בר יחזקאל) asks Rav Amram (רב עמרם) to share the fine teachings he had transmitted in the name of Rav Asi (רב אסי) regarding the arches of a boat (כיפי דארבא).

Rav Amram (רב עמרם) sends back Rav Asi's (רב אסי) ruling: regarding the arches of a boat (כיפי דארבא), if they have a handbreadth (טפח) in width, or even if they lack a handbreadth but are within three handbreadths of each other (so that the intervening space is considered filled by the principle of לבוד), then on Shabbat one may bring a mat and spread it over them.
The Gemara explains the reason for the leniency: spreading the mat is merely adding to a temporary tent (מוסיף על אהל עראי), which is permitted on Shabbat.

items.text: Rav Huna's rams and Rav's advice
items.text_en: Rav Huna's rams and Rav's advice
items.desc_en: Rav Huna had rams that needed shade by day and air by night. He came before Rav, who told him to tie a branch (בודיא) leaving a handbreadth, and the next day spread it, as it is adding to a temporary tent and is permitted.

sub.desc_en: The gemara introduces Rav Huna's rams that needed shade by day and air by night, and that he came before Rav for advice.
Rav instructs Rav Huna to tie a branch (בודיא) leaving a handbreadth, and the next day spread it, as it is adding to a temporary tent and is permitted.

items.text: Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya: A curtain (וילון) is permitted to be spread and folded on Shabbat
items.text_en: Rav citing Rabbi Chiyya: A curtain (וילון) is permitted to be spread and folded on Shabbat
items.desc_en: Rav says in the name of Rabbi Chiyya that a curtain (וילון) may be spread and folded on Shabbat.

sub.desc_en: Rav states in the name of Rabbi Chiyya that a curtain (וילון) is permitted to be spread and folded on Shabbat.

items.text: The canopy of grooms (כילת חתנים) and its restrictions
items.text_en: The canopy of grooms (כילת חתנים) and its restrictions
items.desc_en: The canopy of grooms may be folded and spread on Shabbat. Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi qualifies: this is only if its roof lacks a handbreadth, but if it has a handbreadth it is forbidden. Even if the roof lacks a handbreadth, it is only permitted if there is no handbreadth within three handbreadths of the roof; otherwise it is forbidden. The text cuts off mid-sentence.

sub.desc_en: The Stam states the general rule: a bridal canopy (כילת חתנים) may be dismantled and spread on Shabbat.
Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi qualifies the ruling: the leniency applies only if the canopy's roof lacks a handbreadth (טפח); if it has a handbreadth, it is forbidden.
Rav Sheshet further qualifies: even if the roof lacks a handbreadth, it is permitted only if there is no handbreadth within three handbreadths of the roof; otherwise it is forbidden.

sub.text: Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi (continued, cut off)
sub.text_en: Rav Sheshet bar Rav Idi (continued, cut off)
sub.desc_en: Rav Sheshet begins a further qualification: even if there is no handbreadth within three handbreadths of the roof, the leniency applies only if... (the text cuts off mid-sentence).

items.text: Opening discussion on the slope of a tent
items.text_en: Opening discussion on the slope of a tent
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the law of a slope (שיפוע) of a tent: if it is a handbreadth, it is considered like the tent itself, and thus carrying from it to the public domain is prohibited.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara states that a slope of a tent one handbreadth wide is considered like the tent itself for Shabbat (שבת) domain purposes.

items.text: Discussion of a hat (סיינָא) and a cloak (שרביב)
items.text_en: Discussion of a hat (סיינָא) and a cloak (שרביב)
items.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi permits wearing a hat on Shabbat, but a baraita forbids it. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one case has a handbreadth, the other does not. Then it questions whether a cloak worn with a handbreadth is also forbidden, and resolves by distinguishing between tight and loose fitting.

sub.desc_en: Rav Shisha bar Rav Idi permits wearing a hat (סיינָא) on Shabbat.
The Gemara objects that a baraita forbids wearing a hat on Shabbat.
The Gemara resolves the contradiction: one case has a handbreadth (טפח) of brim, the other does not.
The Gemara questions whether a cloak (שרביב) worn with a handbreadth is also forbidden.
The Gemara resolves by distinguishing between a tight-fitting cloak (מיהדק) and a loose one (לא מיהדק).

items.text: Mishnah: Returning a door hinge
items.text_en: Mishnah: Returning a door hinge
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that the lower hinge of a door may be returned in the Temple but not in the provinces; the upper hinge is forbidden everywhere. Rabbi Yehuda says the upper hinge is permitted in the Temple and the lower in the provinces.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for returning a door hinge: the lower hinge may be returned in the Temple but not in the provinces, and the upper hinge is forbidden everywhere.
Rabbi Yehuda disputes the Mishnah, permitting the upper hinge in the Temple and the lower hinge in the provinces.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on hinges of boxes and pits
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on hinges of boxes and pits
items.desc_en: A baraita elaborates: for a chest, box, or cabinet, the hinge may be returned in the Temple but only pressed in the provinces; the upper hinge is never returned lest one drive it in, which would incur a sin-offering. For a pit, cistern, or attic, one may not return the hinge at all, and doing so incurs a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that for a chest, box, or cabinet, the lower hinge may be returned in the Temple but only pressed in the provinces; the upper hinge is never returned lest one drive it in, incurring a sin-offering.
The baraita adds that for a pit, cistern, or attic, one may not return the hinge at all, and doing so incurs a sin-offering.

items.text: Mishnah: Returning a bandage
items.text_en: Mishnah: Returning a bandage
items.desc_en: The Mishnah teaches that a bandage may be returned in the Temple but not in the provinces; if it is the initial application, it is forbidden everywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states the rule for returning a bandage on Shabbat: permitted in the Temple, prohibited in the provinces, and initial application is forbidden everywhere.

items.text: Gemara: Baraita on a bandage that fell off
items.text_en: Gemara: Baraita on a bandage that fell off
items.desc_en: A baraita states: if a bandage fell off a wound, one may replace it on Shabbat. Rabbi Yehuda says if it slipped down, push it up; if up, push it down; one may uncover part of the bandage to wipe the wound, but not wipe the bandage itself, lest he spread the ointment, which would incur a sin-offering.

sub.desc_en: The baraita rules that a bandage that fell off may be replaced on Shabbat, with Rabbi Yehuda's detailed instructions for adjusting it and wiping the wound.
The baraita adds that one may not wipe the bandage itself, lest he spread the ointment, incurring a sin-offering.

items.text: Amoraic dispute on the bandage ruling
items.text_en: Amoraic dispute on the bandage ruling
items.desc_en: Rav Yehuda says Shmuel ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda. Rav Chisda limits the dispute to when the bandage fell onto a vessel, but if it fell onto the ground, all agree it is forbidden. Mar bar Rav Ashi relates that his father (Rav Ashi) replaced a bandage that fell onto a bench, and when questioned about Rav Chisda's ruling, he said he did not accept it.

sub.desc_en: Rav Yehuda reports that Shmuel ruled the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda's lenient position regarding replacing a bandage on Shabbat.
Rav Chisda limits the dispute: the leniency applies only when the bandage fell onto a vessel, but if it fell onto the ground, all agree it is forbidden.
Mar bar Rav Ashi relates that he was standing before his father Rav Ashi when a bandage fell onto a bench, and Rav Ashi replaced it, demonstrating practical disregard for Rav Chisda's limitation.

sub.text: Mar bar Rav Ashi's question to Rav Ashi
sub.text_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi's question to Rav Ashi
sub.desc_en: Mar bar Rav Ashi challenges his father Rav Ashi, citing Rav Chisda's ruling that the dispute is limited to a vessel, and Shmuel's ruling that the הלכה (binding law) follows Rabbi Yehuda.
Rav Ashi responds that he has not heard of Rav Chisda's ruling, implying he does not accept it, thus justifying his own practice of replacing the bandage.

items.text: Mishnah: Tying a string
items.text_en: Mishnah: Tying a string
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may tie a string in the Temple but not in the provinces; if it is the initial tying, it is forbidden everywhere.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah rules that one may tie a string in the Temple but not in the provinces, and if it is the initial tying, it is forbidden everywhere.

items.text: Gemara: Contradiction and resolution regarding tying a string
items.text_en: Gemara: Contradiction and resolution regarding tying a string
items.desc_en: A contradiction is raised: a baraita says a broken lyre string may only be looped, not tied. The Gemara first resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer (who permits preparatory acts for a mitzvah) and the baraita follows the Rabbis. But then it objects that Rabbi Eliezer would permit even initially. So it resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita follows the Rabbis. It then asks: Rabbi Yehuda's view aligns with whom?

sub.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction: a baraita states that a broken lyre string may only be looped, not tied.
The Gemara initially resolves that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer (who permits preparatory acts for a mitzvah) and the baraita follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara objects that Rabbi Eliezer would permit tying even לכתחילה (the ideal standard), not just after the fact.
The Gemara resolves instead that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Yehuda and the baraita follows the Rabbis.
The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yehuda's view aligns with whom?

items.text: Resolving the contradiction about tying a harp string
items.text_en: Resolving the contradiction about tying a harp string
items.desc_en: The Gemara initially suggests that the earlier statement permitting tying a string might be according to Rabbi Eliezer, but then rejects this. It resolves the contradiction by attributing the dispute to Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis, or by distinguishing between the middle and the side of the string, or by a dispute about whether to decree.

items.text: Mishnah: Cutting a wart in the Temple
items.text_en: Mishnah: Cutting a wart in the Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that one may cut a wart in the Temple, but not in the provinces. If done with a utensil, it is forbidden both here and there.

items.text: Gemara's contradiction and resolution regarding the wart
items.text_en: Gemara's contradiction and resolution regarding the wart
items.desc_en: The Gemara raises a contradiction from a baraita where Rabbi Eliezer permits cutting a wart on Shabbat, while the Sages forbid it. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Yosei ben Chanina offer two resolutions: one distinguishes between cutting by hand and with a utensil, the other between a moist and dry wart. The Gemara then explains why each Amora rejects the other's distinction, and further clarifies the baraita's context.

items.text: Rav Yosef's resolution: Shvut Mikdash in the Mikdash
items.text_en: Rav Yosef's resolution: Shvut Mikdash in the Mikdash
items.desc_en: Rav Yosef cites Rabbi Eliezer's kal vachomer argument and then resolves the contradiction by stating that both cases are by hand, but a shvut (rabbinic prohibition) of the Temple is permitted in the Temple, while a shvut of the Temple is not permitted in the provinces.

items.text: Abaye's challenge and Rav Yosef's response
items.text_en: Abaye's challenge and Rav Yosef's response
items.desc_en: Abaye states Rav Yosef's teaching, and Rav Safra challenges it from a case of a scroll on a doorstep, which is a shvut of the Temple in the provinces yet is permitted. Abaye is silent. Rav Yosef suggests he should have answered that members of a group are diligent, but Abaye distinguishes between priests and ordinary people.

items.text: Rava's alternative resolution
items.text_en: Rava's alternative resolution
items.desc_en: Rava explains that the Mishnah follows Rabbi Eliezer, who holds that preparations for a mitzvah override Shabbat, but even he agrees that when possible, one should make a change.

items.text: Opening discussion on the size of a partition and the small bell
items.text_en: Opening discussion on the size of a partition and the small bell
items.desc_en: The Gemara connects the Mishnah's rule about a three-by-three handbreadth partition to Rava's statement in the name of Rav Chisda, and questions whether it conflicts with Rabbi Yehuda's view. It then explains that a small bell is significant, and why Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about a bell is not redundant.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara opens by stating the Mishnah's rule that a three-by-three handbreadth partition is effective, and connects it to Rava's statement in the name of Rav Chisda.
The Gemara questions whether the Mishnah's rule conflicts with Rabbi Yehuda's view.
The Gemara answers that a small bell is significant, so it is not comparable to the general rule.
The Gemara questions why Rabbi Yochanan's teaching about a bell is not redundant given the Mishnah's rule.
The Gemara resolves that Rabbi Yochanan's teaching incidentally informs us that a small bell produces a sound.

items.text: Mishnah: Salting the ramp and filling water
items.text_en: Mishnah: Salting the ramp and filling water
items.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in the Temple, one may salt the ramp to prevent slipping, and may fill water from the Golah well or the Great well using a wheel on Shabbat, and from the cold well on Yom Tov.

sub.desc_en: The Mishnah states that in the Temple one may salt the ramp to prevent slipping, and may fill water from the Golah well or the Great well using a wheel on Shabbat, and from the cold well on Yom Tov.

items.text: Gemara's question on salting the ramp and the contradiction with a courtyard
items.text_en: Gemara's question on salting the ramp and the contradiction with a courtyard
items.desc_en: Rav Ika from Pashrunya raises a contradiction: the Mishnah permits salting the ramp only in the Temple, but a baraita permits spreading straw in a muddy courtyard on Shabbat. The Gemara distinguishes between straw, which is nullified, and salt, which might be nullified or form a partition. It then explains the case involves carrying limbs to the ramp, which is not a service, or carrying wood to the pyre.

sub.desc_en: Rav Ika from Pashrunya raises a contradiction before Rava: the Mishnah permits salting the ramp only in the Temple, but a baraita permits bringing straw and spreading it in a muddy courtyard on Shabbat.
The Gemara answers that straw is different because one does not nullify it (intends to remove it later), unlike salt which is left in place.
Rav Acha, son of Rava, objects to Rav Ashi: regarding the salt, if it is nullified it adds to the Temple structure (forbidden), and if not nullified it forms a partition (disqualifying the service).
The Gemara answers that the salt is scattered when carrying limbs to the ramp, which is not considered a Temple service subject to disqualification.

The Gemara objects: is carrying limbs not a service? The verse 'והקריב הכהן את הכל' (the priest shall offer it whole) and the Master's teaching show that bringing limbs to the ramp is indeed a service.
The Gemara resolves: rather, say the salt is scattered when carrying wood to the arrangement on the altar, which is not a service.

items.text: Rava's teaching on the courtyard and his retraction
items.text_en: Rava's teaching on the courtyard and his retraction
items.desc_en: Rava teaches that one may spread straw in a muddy courtyard. Rav Papa challenges him with a baraita that says one may only use the bottom of a basket. Rava then retracts his earlier statement and cites Rabbi Eliezer's ruling.

sub.desc_en: Rava (רבא) teaches that one may bring straw and spread it in a courtyard damaged by rainwater on שבת (Sabbath).
Rav Papa (רב פפא) objects to Rava (רבא) by citing a ברייתא (baraita) that one may spread straw only with the bottom of a broken basket, not with a regular basket.

Rava (רבא) retracts his earlier statement, appoints an אמורא (amora) to announce that it was a mistake, and cites the ruling of רבי אליעזר (Rabbi Eliezer) that one must use only the bottom of a broken basket.

items.text: Discussion on making noise on Shabbat
items.text_en: Discussion on making noise on Shabbat
items.desc_en: The Gemara discusses the prohibition of producing sound on Shabbat. Ulla rebukes a man for knocking on a door. Rabba limits the prohibition to musical sound. Abaye challenges with cases of making noise for a sick person or scaring birds, and the Gemara resolves these by distinguishing between producing sound and other concerns like making a hole or smoothing dirt.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara relates that Ulla came to the house of Rav Menashe, and when a man knocked on the door, Ulla cursed him for desecrating Shabbat by producing sound.
Rabba tells Ulla that the Sages prohibited only a pleasant musical sound on Shabbat, not the rasping sound of knocking.

Abaye raises an objection from a baraita about drawing wine with a siphon for an ill person, inferring that producing sound for a healthy person is prohibited, which contradicts Rabba's lenient position.

The Gemara rejects Abaye's inference, explaining that the baraita refers to an ill person who is awake and needs to fall asleep, and the sound of dripping water is melodious, not a general prohibition on sound production.

Abaye raises another objection from a baraita about guarding produce, which prohibits clapping and dancing because they produce sound; Rav Acha bar Yaakov answers that the prohibition is a decree lest one come to pick up a pebble, not because of sound itself.
The Gemara asks about Rav Yehuda's statement that women playing with nuts is prohibited, suggesting the reason might be producing sound.
The Gemara answers that the prohibition is not due to sound but because they might come to level holes in the ground, which is a form of building.
The Gemara supports this reasoning by citing Rav Yehuda's parallel ruling about women playing with apples, where no sound is produced, confirming the concern is leveling holes.

items.text: Discussion on filling water with a wheel and the reason for the prohibition
items.text_en: Discussion on filling water with a wheel and the reason for the prohibition
items.desc_en: The Gemara questions why filling water with a wheel is permitted only in the Temple, and suggests it is due to the sound. It rejects this, explaining the decree is lest one fill for his garden or ruin. Amemar permits it in Machoza where there are no gardens or ruins, but the text is cut off.

sub.desc_en: The Gemara questions why drawing water with a wheel is permitted only in the Temple, suggesting it is because of the sound produced.
The Gemara rejects the sound-based explanation, stating the decree is lest one fill for his garden or ruin.
Amemar permits drawing water with a wheel in Meḥoza, reasoning that since there are no gardens or ruins, the concern does not apply, though the text is cut off.

items.text: Opening of the Mishnah's discussion on Be'er HaKar
items.text_en: Opening of the Mishnah's discussion on Be'er HaKar
items.desc_en: The Gemara begins by recounting that they sowed flax and it was prohibited to them, referencing the context of Be'er HaKar.

items.text: Clarifying the identity of Be'er HaKar
items.text_en: Clarifying the identity of Be'er HaKar
items.desc_en: Shmuel defines Be'er HaKar as a well that was 'cooled' by words and permitted. An objection is raised from a baraita that only this specific well was permitted, not all cool wells. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak reinterprets it as a well of living water, based on a verse.

items.text: Baraita on the unique permission of Be'er HaKar
items.text_en: Baraita on the unique permission of Be'er HaKar
items.desc_en: The Gemara cites the baraita that not all cool wells were permitted, only this one, and explains that when the exiles returned, they camped there and prophets permitted it, or it was a custom of their ancestors.

items.text: Mishnah: Removing a sheretz from the Temple
items.text_en: Mishnah: Removing a sheretz from the Temple
items.desc_en: The Mishnah presents a dispute about how to remove a dead creeping animal from the Temple: Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka says the priest removes it with his belt to avoid delaying impurity, Rabbi Yehuda says with wooden tongs to avoid increasing impurity. Rabbi Shimon ben Nannas specifies from where it is removed, Rabbi Akiva adds a criterion based on liability for karet, and Rabbi Shimon comments on the nature of rabbinic permissions.

items.text: Gemara: Liability for bringing a sheretz into the Temple
items.text_en: Gemara: Liability for bringing a sheretz into the Temple
items.desc_en: Rav Tavi bar Kisna says in the name of Shmuel: One who brings a tamei person into the Temple is liable, but bringing a sheretz itself is exempt, based on a verse requiring sending away those who have purification in a mikveh. A support is attempted from Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's teaching about earthenware vessels, but is rejected.

items.text: Debate: Does the Mishnah's dispute reflect liability or exemption?
items.text_en: Debate: Does the Mishnah's dispute reflect liability or exemption?
items.desc_en: The Gemara suggests that the dispute between Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka and Rabbi Yehuda in the Mishnah might be about whether one is liable for bringing a sheretz into the Temple. It first posits that the one concerned with delaying impurity holds one is liable, while the one concerned with increasing impurity holds one is exempt. But it rejects this, saying both agree one is liable, and they dispute only about which concern is greater.

items.text: Alternative tannaitic dispute about where to remove the sheretz
items.text_en: Alternative tannaitic dispute about where to remove the sheretz
items.desc_en: The Gemara turns to another tannaitic dispute (from the Mishnah) about from where the sheretz is removed, suggesting it reflects the same underlying disagreement about liability: one who says not from the azara holds one is exempt, while one who says from the entire azara holds one is liable.

items.text: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.text_en: Dispute between Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish
items.desc_en: Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish derive from the same verse (II Chronicles 29:16) different conclusions about who removes impurity from the Temple. One holds that since Levites were involved in the courtyard, impurity is not present there; the other holds that priests remove impurity only where Levites cannot, but where Levites can, priests no longer become impure.

items.text: Baraita on entering the Temple
items.text_en: Baraita on entering the Temple
items.desc_en: The baraita teaches that everyone may enter the Temple for building, repair, or removing impurity, but the mitzvah is for priests. If no priests are available, Levites enter; if no Levites, Israelites enter. All must be pure, not impure.

items.text: Rav Kahana's support for priests
items.text_en: Rav Kahana's support for priests
items.desc_en: Rav Huna says Rav Kahana supports the priests, citing a teaching: from the verse 'But to the curtain he shall not come' (Leviticus 16:2), one might think blemished priests cannot enter between the Entrance Hall and the Altar to make metal plates. The verse says 'but' to divide: the mitzvah is for unblemished priests, but if none are available, blemished priests enter; the mitzvah is for pure priests, but if none are available, impure priests enter. However, only priests, not Israelites.

items.text: Question: impure vs. blemished priest
items.text_en: Question: impure vs. blemished priest
items.desc_en: A dilemma is raised: if a priest is both impure and blemished, which one enters? Rav Chiyya bar Ashi says in the name of Rav that the impure one enters, because impurity was permitted for communal service. Rabbi Elazar says the blemished one enters, because blemishes were permitted for eating sacred foods.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon's position on entering the city
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon's position on entering the city
items.desc_en: The Gemara asks where Rabbi Shimon stands in a mishnah about one who became dark (i.e., it got dark) outside the techum. The Tanna Kamma says he may not enter even one cubit; Rabbi Shimon says he may enter even fifteen cubits, because the surveyors do not interpose the measurements due to those who err.

items.text: Rabbi Shimon on tying vs. looping
items.text_en: Rabbi Shimon on tying vs. looping
items.desc_en: The Gemara continues: Rabbi Shimon's position is in a different context, where the Tanna Kamma says one ties (the animal), and Rabbi Shimon says one loops it. Looping, which does not lead to a sin-offering, the Sages permitted; tying, which leads to a sin-offering, they did not permit.
